Review as of November 26, 2017:
Early Access Review: The game runs fairly well, there are a couple issues when it comes to bumping into sides and such. Performance needs to be improved for higher end systems, as even when running at a pegged 60fps the game can seem choppy still. Even in the menu shifting around, some things take a while to load along with other issues. Should be early access/server side things that will likely get resolved by the time it releases.
There are a couple things i'd like to see introduced into the game, the main one being Tire tracks. Going along the ground should create tracks in the ground (shape being based on the tire type), especially along mud and snow etc. Whether the tracks stay on the track until the end of the race or are just temporary is up to the devs, but it would be nice to see to give it that bit of extra "next generation" feel to the game.
Content: There is an okay amount of content. There could be more cups to make up for the quick 1/1 races that show up quite often. I'd guess in order to finish "Career" with full gold it'd take about 5~6 hours. Aside from "Career" there is "Time Attack" as well which could take much longer depending on your skill and how quickly you learn the piston modes and how/when to drift in those. That's not really content though, just a different experience. Still worth mentioning to those who would expect no less from a Kart racing game.
Online: I've hosted occasionally and haven't noticed anyone join yet. This could be because of no one being able to actually join Online, or just a lack of players looking to race (sometimes my hours are a bit off compared to what is likely the peak time for All-Star Fruit Racing). I've seen videos of people playing in co-op at the least, so that's a start. Unfortunately as it is, playing with others online (not co-op) is either a rare sight or just not possible.

I can't see a lot of replayability here, but this is an EXCELLENT game and 100% worth 20$.
I think it's really to their credit that any class of vessel seems to be viable because the only difference between ships is hull, speed, and slots; you can put the same shields on a super-slow destroyer as on a speedy frigate, it's all down to personal preference / playstyle.
The maps are very dynamic, with even bases coming and going with or without player involvement. There are many, many different dynamic events that can occur, most of which usually affect pricing of goods. There's a respectably deep and dynamic trading game here if you're interested in that, but I didn't touch on it much during my combat-focused playthrough.
You can even discover asteroid fields, mine them, and sell the yields.
There are several different factions and each track player reputation and otherwise function well.
I kind of feel like the weapon / gear variety ended up being a little flat, but there was enough to keep me interested for my playthrough and tweak my approach to particular situations.
The hailing system (talking to any other ship) is pretty nifty, but I was a little disappointed by unrealized potential. There was a lot of room here for faction reputation, damage state of the hailed vessel, or other factors could have affected the other party's reactions - but it doesn't, so every interaction ended up feeling pretty same-y. It is thankfully optional, but I wish it could have been cooler :-/
Not really a con, but this is very much an RPG. A couple times I hit a brick wall where I was getting facerolled, and I had to give up on those missions for a while and go build revenue on easier stuff to get geared up and then it was fine. Just keep that in mind. The game's really not too grindy...unless you want to get a destroyer early in your playthrough - they are super expensive. I didn't utilize the method of piracy, but apparently that's a quick buck if you want to look at the steam guide.
I really have very few bad things to say about this game. It's an absolute winner for 20$ and this has been a really fun playthrough.

If you're looking for an open world, building, sandbox game to explore over the weekend - don't hesitate.  This should scratch your itch.  In it's current state you should get AT LEAST 20-40 hours enjoyment.  For $1 an hour, the price seems about right.  However, be aware that it is in EARLY ACCESS and what that entails.
The game is not yet complete and it has several bugs (technical and gameplay related).  That being said, it is still enjoyable to play in it's current state and shows tremendous potential to get even better.  If the devs are as responsive as they seem, then my guess is that purchasers will be in for more treats and more hours of fun every month as the game progresses until it becomes fully realized.
PVP still needs significant work.  It is not balanced in it's current state and base raiding is entirely too easy.  Eventually, however, I think PVP will become a key and attractive feature.  I did have fun in several encounters but I switched to a PVE server until they sort out base defenses.
The PVE is also not ready for prime time yet.  There are some unique and interesting weapon choices.  However, the mob AI is very simple, combat is static and animations are clunky.  I just killed mobs for resources and XP not really because combat was "fun".
The building aspect of the game is probably the most polished feature.  There are a decent amount of options and with a little creativity, you can spend hours building some pretty cool structures.  There aren't many interior features currently (like furniture) and the snap-to geometry is sometimes frustrating but overall building is quite pleasant.

Jalopy - Communist Driving Simulator
Ever wanted to know how it is to drive the finest in Soviet-Communist Automobile technology? Then Jalopy is the game for you! You have been given the deluxe Lada 601, the result of years of Aerodynamic and Fueltechnic research and development. Going from Dresden to (in the current update) Hungary in this pinnacle of Automotive technology is going to be a breeze!
Now, In all seriousness, I have played Jalopy for about 8 hours and so far these are the Pro's and Con's I have encountered in this Pre-Alpha stage of this great game.
Pro's:
- The game has an awesome Driving mechanic and has a lot of features that are usable like in a real car
- It is an original challenge to make a 1000+ KM roadtrip in a piece of junk that needs maintenance and refueling.
- The parts are easily repaired with repair kits that are purchaseable from the Gas Stations found along the route.
- For a Pre-Alpha game, I have encountered a relatively low amount of bugs which were not game-breaking. (Mostly graphical bugs)
- It has a lot of immersion and does a great job at giving that grey, communist vibe.
- The graphics are simple yet very nice. This only proves that a greay game does not need the best graphics to still be amazingly fun to play.
- A lot of replayability, everytime you replay, the route changes and new contraband spawns that can be sold to gas stations.
- The Contraband System works very well and is actually pretty competitive. Some countries have a certain ban on certain items making for example Wine more valueable in the CzhechSlovak federation than for example in the DDR. This also changes everytime you replay.
- It does not get boring, everytime you replay you get further instead of stranding on the side of the road making it small victories when you get further and eventually make it to Hungary (as far as you can go in this update).
And yes, like any game there are some Cons.
Con's:
-The first time you have to restart it is definitely a rage quit, but once you get over that you are even happy since now you can restart and have the fun all over again.
- The parts break maybe a little too fast.
- Difficult to get enough money for larger upgrades.
- Certain Items from the truck often glitch through the world when dropping them, I have lost around 4 crowbars this way and they are not common in Gas Stations. Not everyone sells them and seeing as a crowbar is the only thing that can open locked contraband, it can get frustrating.
Tips:
- Always keep gas and a tire jack with you in the trunk.
- Avoid going off the road, it ruins your tires and your car.
- Don't stop on the side of the road, other cars just run into you and YOU get the penalty.
- Always keep the Airfilter, Engine and Carburator in good state. They have the highest priority. If they are broken, your car does not run or it only goes 20 km/h and hour.
Overall this game has a high replayability which at first feels like repetitiveness, however it keeps getting more fun. Also since this is a pre-alpha, a lot more is going to be added while how it is now is already a lot of fun. Enough to be played for 8 hours. That is how long it took me to get to Hungary.
Overall Score: 8.9/10

This War of Mine is a pretty immersive, easy, understandable game. Unfortunately, it doesn't have much of a replay value in its current state. During the game, you try and survive the horrors of war with 3-4 people in a building that can barely be called home. Food, water, gas, weapons, and supplies are all on a shortage which give you one of three options: kill, steal, trade. Between a month-month and a half, the international forces arrive and put an end to the civil war - you just have to decide what it takes to reach a new age of peace.
With all that in mind, playing through the game twice is enough forever (you can theorectically get all achievements within one playthrough aswell). The "create your own story" or whatever its called has severe limitations to creativity (there's limited traits, can't select how much someone can carry, can't determine their addcitions, etc.), which completely undermines the entire idea of your own story. Without mod support or the ability to play around with map creation, the game gets stale rather quickly.
Short review, but this game is better than the most recent game. 11/10 would assassinate again.

Recently they took away several cards that were part of decks and auto-replaced them with same color, but otherwise random, other cards, often with very different casting cost & almost none of the same functionality.  One example was a 2GG sorc that destroyed a target land (great for the awaken lands in AI decks) with one that was almost a 3G rampant growth equivilent.  Another was an artifact creature that when it died it did 2 dmg to target player or creature, a staple in both artifact decks & sacrifice decks, was auto taken out and replaced with a 2/1 artifact creature that does nothing when it dies, making its place in most decks that sacrificed creatures, artifacts, or had pull out of the graveyard cards pointless, the only saving grace was the colorlessness of it.  It also removed the gates and the wall that came into play to search for a gate, which made the replacement that did not search for a "dual" land hurt color fixing in 3-4 color decks, with no in-game warning.  Why not just tag certain cards as non-PVP or give a notice prior so you could spend a week (when you had time) fixing your deck so it will still work.  These were not OP cards, the most powerful game breakers are still in the game, like a 3 drop 2/3 lifelink that blinks into a non-creature, non-artifact, non-land, non-enchantment permanent that can cause any creature that dies for the rest of the game to enter the battlefield under your control.  Half of the cards taken out are some of the least powerful cards in the game with niche uses that mildly combo with uncommon cards.

Despite the depressing premise, this is truly one of the most enjoyable games I've encountered. The atmosphere it paints, truly immerses you into the story, and gives players' a glimpse of civilian life during a siege. The market really needed a game like this, and I applaud 11-Bit studios for coming up with the idea and the execution.
Gameplay is quite simplistic. Select character and click on icons to get them to perform tasks. The main focus is the decision making. What do you craft or do? Do you go scavenge through the rubble for resources, build tools or craft furniture. Do you scavenge for food or crafting materials? Do you make cook food, eat it raw or let your characters starve (if you have no food)? Do you spend resources towards crafting weapons or tools? When you scavenge, what items are high priority versus what do you forgo? Do you go barter with people or just take what you want? Those are all decisions choices you're faced with in 'This War of Mine.'
I initially was annoyed by the save feature, where the game would only save at the end of days, but after thinking about it more, and comparing it with XCOM's Iron Man mode (no saving during combat), I realised that the daily save does enhance the gameplay. As a player, you start to truly get attached your characters, and it saddens you when they get hungry, tired, sick or depressed. And if they die, you will probably get depressed, and want to reload the previous day. :P
One criticism is that I do wish the game does notify you if a character is idle (ie. Standing around doing nothing). When you start to get more characters, it gets a bit more tricky and time consuming to manage. And to deal with the time issue, a pause button, which would allow you to direct the character's action, but not have the execute it until the game is un-paused, would also be ideal.
Other than that, this is probably the one of the games with the best atmosphere I have played, and is just a well crafted work of art.
RATING: 9.5/10
PS: I deducted a 0.5 point because I feel the gameplay still can be tweaked for improvement (HINT: Pause Button and Designate Action during Pausing). Also it occasionally crashes from time to time, but that could just be my rig, and not related to the application :)

I feel that Grid Autosport is an unfinished game and therefore I would not recommend it.
There's 5 disciplines in this game, Touring, Endurance, Tuner, street and Grid. The Tuner and Street disciplines are too similar and I feel it would have been better to have some sort of off-road discipline instead.
Pros.
Vehicle damage. From full on physical damage to progressive gearbox and clutch damage.
Pretty visuals most of the time and everything outside looks clean and crisp.
Good track atmosphere, planes, helicopters, crowds, pits and even tannoy announcements.
Loads of cars on the track, gritty racing, when the A.I doesn't try and kill you.
Neither good or bad.
Driving physics, the mix of simulation and arcade isn't to my taste, it's more towards arcade than simulation and I would have liked it to feel more alive and direct. Often the cars feel like they float and you're not even connected to the tarmac.
Disciplines, some people will think it's great to be able to choose "5" "different" disciplines for each season but if you don't like a discipline you still need to complete it in order to unlock the 5th discipline. There's no distinction in terms of race rules between the disciplines so they all feel so similar and that's my issue with them.
Cons.
The A.I is horrible, they just seem to follow a set path and totally ignore the player and as you might say they're on rails.
Another issue with the A.I is their pace, they're extremely inconsistent, you can catch them quite easily but once you're in front of them suddenly they spring to life and you cannot shake them, unless they're Ravenwest Motorsport and once they're in front they're are extremely difficult to catch.
The tracks. There's 22 full GP circuits, what CodeMasters have done is taken those 22 and then reversed them or used the Indy version of that circuit, basically the same circuit that has had a corner cut out to make it shorter and now CodeMasters claim Grid Autosport has 100 circuits. I guess CodeMasters are correct but the core aspect of the track is the same as all the others from that location and when you have 5 disciplines to create tracks for it means there's hardly any variations in each discipline.
Loading times, I guess this will be improved in time with a patch but as of now there's a ton of loading times, even when you select a car you have to wait for the image of that car to load and it just seems so slow and clunky.
Race seasons. You pick a discipline and take part in an event, it could be 1-10 races but for some horrible reason you have to race around a track, finish and then race the same track all over again just with a different grid order and it becomes boring very quickly.
No pit stops! It's a game with full damage and without a pit stop there's no way to repair your vehicle so you're just stuck with the damage.
Engine, cockpit and mirror visuals are non-existent, they are straight out of a PS1 game. Cockpit and mirrors are just blurred out so you can't see anything other than outlines and engines look like they were modelled for Minecraft.
The disciplines all have the same race rules, full contact in touring cars is to be expected but it's also acceptable in Grid Autosport for full contact in open wheel events. No safety cars, warning flags etc Just T-bone the car in front and drive off without any consequences.
No sense of speed, you could be doing 140mph and if feels like you're doing 30mph, it feels quite lazy and slow paced quite often.
Online multi player is a mess, hordes of cheaters, clans who purposely crash in to you and constant disconnects.
Grid Autosport has the makings of a great game but it's just not there, maybe CodeMasters bit off more than they could chew with this one, their previous game, F1 2013 which is just focused on F1 is much more refined, detailed, complete and if they had that kind of refinement in Grid Autosport it would have been an amazing game.
Grid Autosport currently isn't average game but it's not a great game, I guess Grid Autosport gets a "fair" rating. 6.5/10.

you expect a sandbox-like mode that lets you tinker around and build a dungeon but unfortunately you never get the chance to build with the overzealous waves of ever-hardening enemies that plague your dungeon every 5 minutes. There are two sides to this review: the game review and the completion review.
Game: A platformer starring an elephant with various fun action moves to accompany you on your quest killing the baddies and rescuing civilians. The is  a4.5/10 difficulty, nothing intimidating here, got a few parts that you may end up repeating, but overall I felt it was a fun experience, that can be beaten by anyone in a couple of hours.
Level design focuses either at figuring a path, dashing through obstacles, or facing groups of enemies.
Every final stage of a world has a boss, which once again are nothing too special, but still fun to fight against.
Completion: This was handled a bit poorly, as the game requests of you to kill all the enemie on one hand, while on the other it also asks to rescue all civilians. So far so good right? the problem is that rescuing civilians also counts towards the total kill counter, so you basically end up repeating a full stage completion without skipping anything in case you missed anything. (and you will) It's pretty bad when you overlooked a single enemy, or got sent to an area which you cannot backtrackfrom - forcing you to restart the whole stage again.
The final cherry on top would be farming 99 lives, I used a macro and let the game do its thing as I was busy with rl stuff, would recommend you do the same at stage 2-1 (simply charge all the way to the left).
All in all, a fun and rather quick to beat game, but achievements can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to the completionists among you, so keep those in mind.

Really great MOBA. Getting into a One v One is so exciting that by the end of the combat my hands go numb :(
All in all, if you really like the team fight aspect of other MOBAs like Dota or League ( I will essentially be using these two for a comparison to other MOBAs), you will enjoy this game.  Games are pretty quick to get into and they don't last for excruciatingly long periods of time like other MOBAs sometimes do.  Even a 0 and 3 loses are as bad as other MOBAs as the game ends quickly and you don't have enough time to really get mad until the next game starts.  Despite the game revolving around fast-paced combat, there are different noticeable play styles.  Support is a genuinely useful role where one can stay in the back and help out, or you can be extremely aggressive and run people through as some characters are meant to do.  The game also makes it super easy to find other players to join up with as one can immediatly invite them to group after a match ends.  Also, a really fun part grouping up is being able to name your own little group.  This specific group also has its own MMR rating rather than a blanket "team MMR." Speaking of MMR, the system itself seems fair and if you ever get put against someone on a skill level beyond yours (like gold against platinum), you do not get punished for losing and you gain double the MMR for winning.  I would suggest anyone to at least try the game, especially since it is free to play now.

Tembo The Badass Elephant is a pretty nice 2D sidescroller which reminds me of the games I used to play in my childhood, like Sonic & Knuckles, for example. The gameplay is quite simple: you have to reach the end of the level, killing enemies and rescuing civilians along the way, and you can also collect peanuts to earn extra lives. Tembo also has a few different abilities, like dashing, or using his trunk as a hammer (or as a water hose), which are useful for fighting the different types of enemies that you'll encounter (and there's a good amount of variety).
As for the story, well, like most sidescrollers from the early 90s, it's not something really elaborate. Shell City, the game's location, is being attacked by a mysterious force, and the military call Tembo to help defeat them. The game has 18 levels, divided in four different zones, with each zone having a final boss. I'd say that most of the levels are pretty good, in regards to design and difficulty progression, although there were a few of them which I found to be rather frustrating, as they required some pretty good timing in order to beat them.
Something I really liked was the art style they chose for the game, which looked like a comic book, including the cutscenes, which, despite having no dialogue, make a good job at presenting the story. The soundtrack was pretty good as well, it felt fitting for this game.
Well, that's all I've got to say about this game. I recommend it.

As a Dungeon Keeper Fan, I saw this and thought to myself "Maybe it will be like it?"
My Result.......KINDA???
Is is any good......KINDA???
Here's Why
Pros.....
1. Similar look and feel to a Dungeon Keeper - it has the similarity of a Dungeon Keeper game, where you carve out your dungeon, and build rooms for your minions, satifying their needs ect. Also I must say that the Graphics nicely detailed, and very colourfull, something that will be very welcome to Dungeon Keeper fans.
2. Rooms/Units can be upgraded/improved - When yoou build a room, it doesn't just place everything you need, no.... it lets you crate your own room layout, you can reserch new rooms, traps, magic etc, which is really a nice addition, also certain rooms can be used to upgrade and inprove your units, which again is very good, something new and slightly different from Dungeon Keeper.
3. Animation are very good - The animations on the units and buildings are very good, when you see your imps/servants breaking down the wall's you actuallt see them hit the wall and it looks like they are actually hitting it, the movement animations are also very good, each creature has a distinct animation when it comes to movement, idle, attack etc.
4. Humour is spot on - I can say enough for the Humour in this game, it's spot on, with silly references, and you can't help but either smile, or laugh, just the right amout of comedy without going to far.
5. Invading the Human world - What we were promised when we saw the end of Dungeon Keeper 2, the hope that we can send out minions to the human world and invade comes true here, and it is brilliant, you actually see the upperworld morph from a bright colour area into a dark decrepid place, when you take it over, it's awesome to see.
Cons....
1. WAY TO SLOW!!!! - I can say enough about this, it's is a very slow game, unit movement is very slow, and your basic imps/servants that carve out the tunnels, take a long time to break down the wall, the pacinf just feels a little but too slow if you ask me.
2. Not enough creature variations, when you build your dungeon, you expect loads of different creatures to live in it, and work together.....Nope each dungeon faction gets 5 creaturs each. That's it.... Come on guys, you could only think of that? utterly dissapointed
3. No Dungeon Vs Dungeon - WHAT??? I can go against another dungeon?? Skirmish is basicly endless mode where you build up your dungeon and take over the Human world Map, and that's it. Huge potential missed for some fantastic online VS mode
If i have to give a review score it will be a 7/10
Are there more possitives than negatives....yeah there is but there's something about this game that, just misses out on getting a Higher score, sure the good things are Brilliant, and well recieved. But the Negatives do hit it hard. They're important issues that need to be addressed if they want to continue with this, and make more.
I would say if you are a true Dungeon Keeper fan, then you'll enjoy this, but feel like it's missing what it was to be a Dungeon Keeper. A great attempt, but not there just yet.
If you haven't bought this yet, I would say it's worth it, but only when it is on sale, and not full price. Keep it on your wishlist, and any sales hit this and you're happy to pay for it, go for it, just don't expect Dungeon Keeper 3 just yet. So it looks like a few of the members of Game Freak got tired of making Pokémon 24/7 and wanted to prove that they could make something that wasn’t Pokémon for platforms that aren’t Nintendo. So once they get the time and resources to do so, what do they make? …A quirky platformer starring Elephant Rambo versus thousands of purple alien robots.
Part of me still can’t believe this game even exists.
(caps are [sic]) plays like a cross between Donkey Kong Country and Sonic the Hedgehog. I say Donkey Kong Country, because Tembo controls very much like Rambi the Rhino – kind of stiff and heavy, not very agile, but fast and hard-hitting. The game is about charging through long linear levels, smashing tons of stuff, sidetracking for secrets, and beating up a few rooms of enemies here and there. When it sticks to this formula, it really works, and it’s a thrilling, satisfying romp. Problem is, it doesn’t always stick to the formula.
Level 1-1 is one of the most sublimely-designed levels I’ve played in any video game in recent memory. It’s all about smashing stuff, keeping your combo going, and keeping an eye out for cleverly-hidden secrets. It’s really fun, and I could honestly play this single level dozens of times without getting bored.
Level 1-2 is also decent, keeping the same smashing spirit of the previous level but introducing some perilous situations such as enemies which shoot bullets, so timing your attacks starts to become important. But when the game hits level 1-3, something goes terribly, tragically wrong.
Level 1-3 introduces precision platforming sections, physics puzzles, cramped hallways full of hazards that slow the pacing down to a crawl, annoyingly long spacing between checkpoints, overwhelmingly irritating enemy encounters, and metroidvania-like nonlinearity (don’t you just love finding a fork in the road and not knowing which way is the missable secret and which way is the point-of-no-return way forward?) – in other words, it’s a perfect demonstration of everything that
play to the game’s strengths. I swear, 1-3 had to have been some kind of beta level that somehow stayed in the game until the end. It’s really, really bad.
Does it get any better after that? Well, yes and no. It’s a mixed bag. A lot of later levels return to the formula which makes it feel awesome to be a badass elephant – I especially loved some of the World 3 levels – but it just as often tries to be a “tactical platformer” throwing you into “bullet hell” rooms with tons of enemies, or pitting you against instant death moving walls or stupid jumps. Having to repeatedly redo long sections you’ve already done a dozen times gets really boring and really old.
Speaking of redoing things, 100% completion is a pain in the badass. If you miss killing a single enemy – and you will, repeatedly – you have to
Full completion has to be done all in one sweep, and tons of parts are missable. To top off the repetetiveness of this game, the final achievement requires collecting 99 lives, and you can't exactly farm for lives very quickly. The fastest way seems to be playing one of the game's levels about 30 times in a row.
The game's objectives seem messy. There are separate badges for rescuing ten civilians per level, but in a baffling design choice, breaking the tanks which hold civilians count as kills, so you can’t get the kill badge without also getting the rescuing badge. Why have two separate badges at all? Also, there are no rewards for speedrunning, even though the game keeps track of your best level times and it seems as though it would have been a fun game to speedrun. Also, there is some kind of scoring system for online leaderboards, but it’s completely downplayed and utterly useless because you can’t see what gives you points.
On the surface, this is a very well-crafted game. It has high production values, looks great, controls well, and has a nice sense of humor. I can’t give it anything less than a 6 / 10 for style and integrity. But at the same time, I have to give it a non-recommend. Levels are overly long, 100% completion is meticulous, and you’ll find yourself having to re-do huge segments (or entire levels) all too often. Sometimes it's a blast, but too often it’s frustrating, boring, and hard to keep playing. If you have a high tolerance for frustration and the persistence necessary to see it through until the end, you might be able to enjoy this game’s merits and laugh at its ridiculous scenarios. But if not, you probably won’t even finish the game, so I recommend not bothering.

Your first reaction may be that this game is a ripoff of other games.
I loved Terarria. I loved Starbound. I love this game even more.
WHY?
The combat and levelling system. It brings the game style to a whole new level. Do you like to craft? Your skill improves as you use it. Do you like to fight? As everything else, you get better as you progress. Also, some variety of enemies make the game more interesting.
HOWEVER
The game runs slow for many, much like Starbound, including myself. I suffer through it, as I think its worth it, but you may not be so inclined.
BUT...
The developer (who is quite active) has narrowed the problem down to the UI, and is completely re-doing it, not a small task. It will take time... BUT when its done, I'm sure the game will be so, so, so much better. And then this game will really shine.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?
If you liked the aforementioned games, and are intrigued by the levelling system, then by all means, you should give it a go. Keep in mind the optimization issues... but if the game is too slow for you, you will know right away and can request a refund.
Also, if you're new to the genre, I would recommend this game the most out of the three. The game does have a tutorial that introduces some basics, and the rest isn't that hard to figure out. Still, if you're having problems, the Crea community is friendly and helpful, so don't be afraid to check out the discussion boards.
All in all, I recommend this game over the other three, not only for the content I touched on, but also because this game has the most potential of becoming better.
My final suggestion: if you're adventurous, give it a try now... you can refund immediately if you have issues. But when the update comes (eventually, be patient), this game should be a must have on your list (if it lives up to the hype).
Anyway, I'll try to remember to update this review when the game is updated, and let you know of my performance difference.
Suggest you read the discussion board "What Makes Crea Different?" if you're curious.

I originally gave this game a negative review, but that was a mistake. I found that exploring and terraforming (digging a lot everywhere) was my key aspect. The main developer (Jasson) was very kind and honest about asking me questions about my review. This game, however, is still progressing, but so far it is just amazing. Now, I will move onto the pros and cons that I have thought of.
Pros:
- Developers are very kind and nice, (I have read forums and I have seen Jasson and a few others responding, which I thought was very generous.)
- Has a great RPG style, with its variety of abilities, armors, and weapons of choice.
- Exploring and digging were 2 of my favorite parts about this game, because that's just the type of player I am in games.
- Bosses are actually tough no matter how far you are in the game, which adds for a neat challenge, where you will actually have to strategically find the pattern of the bosses attacks and learn how to avoid them.
- Game has much variety. (Ores, weapons, armors, etc.)
- Weapons/Armor/Tools do not break, which got me about 11.50% more into this game.
- Artwork is very cool.

Cons:
- Still in progress, just needs more bosses and enemies.
- Grinding sometimes takes a while and is lengthy, but the reward you get is great.
- Game is a bit slow, in terms of framerate, but as long as it runs, I'm ok.
- Researching is a bit tedious, due to having to use materials to research items that use those materials.
Overall, this game is still progressing, but what it is with right now is just absolutely great. The developers and community are also amazing. Overall, just an amazing game as it is.

A spectacular atmosphere isn't enough to overcome all the shortcomings.
I've always had a soft spot for Homefront simply because of it's connections to the film Red Dawn (1984). Its a great concept and the atmosphere delivered, especially early in the game, is superb. But as much as I want to gush about the theme, the game really is average at best when it comes to gameplay. This is an extremely short and extremely linear corridor first person shooter. Gunplay is average, level design is average, enemies are average/bad, variety is average. "Future technology" in the unammaned vehicle and gun turrets miss the mark and fail to really take the game out of modern times. And save for a single helicopter level, no gameplay in the short four hour campaign feels fresh in any way.
Then there's the bad. That short length leads to progressively more rapid jumps in the plot and ever shortening levels. It takes away from the fun theme. Even though the graphics are really old and the resolution is really low, it is still playable and fun even today. It isn't obvious for a game to remain fun after 14 years, especially with all of the flashy new games that come out every day, and with the new technology, but this game is one of the rare games that still manage to do it.

To the point, ASFR feels shallow.
Yeah, it controls alright and it looks GREAT, but the characters, abilities, and mechanics that are in great racing games like Mario Kart Double Dash or Blur are not present here. There's a weak drift system that can easily be abused, abilities that lack oomph or even discernable effects, characters who don't have faster or slower traits or even special vehicles, and sound that seems to wash things out so that you don't even FEEL like you're going fast, or FEEL like your ability really ruined someone's day.
On abilities, some are pretty useless, while others can single-handedly guarantee you last place. The theme of the game is fruit, yet many of the generic abilities have NOTHING to do with fruit. Again, they feel really weak, and you have no control of aiming them. You can't shoot behind you unless that ability is MADE to shoot behind you. Very limiting. Plus, to use an ability, you need to essentially pick up pips and charge it. That's not bad, but with the lack of payoff for ability EFFECTIVENESS, it feels pointless..
Overall, there really doesn't feel to be a depth to this game. For as amazing as the characters and world looks, that's a shame. The balancing and uniqueness of the characters and abilities needs more work as well. I'll keep playing for sure, but as of now there really isn't much enjoyment in it :/

This War of Mine
That said, this little game is just perfect.
Management-complexity wise is not easy, but also not impossible. Mosf of the time your survivor will starve, but that's ok as long as their not dead. :p
The day-night gameplay cycle also complement the game's survival theme. Prioritize between lot of space to bring stuff home, or bring some gun and armor to clear the scavenging location from the enemy.
Morale and Killing system here holds the player to not become a murderer spree and cold hearted b@stard/b1tch, unless you risk your survivor having mental breakdown, escaping from your shelter, or worst... suicide.
Your survivor, when enough material/supply have been gathered, can build crude facilities to support their daily struggle, like Water container, Small plantation for food, or Tool Workshop and many other. Other's will see use if you come across some specific scavenging location.. Few facility are for late game, to produce currency item to trade. Knowing which facility is for, will help greatly in your survival.
If you have completed 1 playthrough, now try again with fewer survivor, harsher climate, more dangerous war flow, and choosing hard location.
Let's see if you can survive.

The addictive system of gathering and crafting in Villagers & Heroes was the main draw for me.  Building a character with a wide variety of skills that produce stuff is always fun.  The game does not disappoint; I had a blast harvesting a huge variety of items and it was easy to start making quality gear from what I found.
My problem with the game is with the questing.  Remember back when the first WoW expansion, The Burning Crusade, came out and the quests in the new zones were streamlined and really fun (at the time)?  Remember how awesome Ghostlands was, because the zone rewarded you for completing the quest line and you didn't have to traverse the world to do it?
Well, the questing in Villagers & Heroes is very much like the questing was in WoW, before BC came out.  In short, a pain in the rear.  Its a serious slog to level up via questing here; the interface is not friendly enough to group your quests by zone, and there's some other glitches (missing quest markers) that twerk your day.  You're going to want to purchase some virtual wings (teleport stones) because your feet will be tired from the running.
Despite all of that, getting to level 14 was actually a pleasure.  I may see how far I can get just harvesting and whatnot, but more questing from here on feels like a bad-paying job.

For people still enchanted and high on the atmosphere of the original 2008 masterpiece, will find solace once again. Is it as good as Bioshock? Course not. Because Bioshock 2 is a different beast altogether. The studio was smart enough to understand that this game needed a completely different perspective on the haunting world of Rapture. So, instead of attempting to improve over the original, Bioshock 2 goes in a different direction. But thankfully, without losing our attachment over the beauty of Rapture.
Unlike Bioshock, this game doesn't feel like a horror movie, a factor for which the original game is most remembered for. In Bioshock 2, the action-packed battles, where things actually were at stake (I do not say this lightly) adds enormously to the thrill of the experience. Bioshock scared the living daylights out of me but Bioshock 2 is far from spooky and more on nerve-wrecking battles. Be prepared to sweat profusely as the game challenges and makes you multi-task. And of course I'm not gonna elaborate on the challenges as they should come more as a surprise ;)
To add to the challenge, the game is huge. I mean ENORMOUS ENORMOUS. Unlike the original, the surprisingly labyrinthine Rapture (thankfully devoid of any loading screens!) will overwhelm the player pretty quickly. I seriously felt dazed as I walked through every area, with doors that led to additional areas. I'd dare say it's thrice as big as Bioshock and not even Bioshock Infinite is a match to the ENORMITY. Being the kind of guy who wants every possible upgrade and search every nook and cranny, this aspect got hold of me quite sooner than I thought. Although it might sound as a negative, Rapture in this game is something I'd have loved to see in the first game. It's nightmarish, which is what Rapture really is.
But that also brings to the little complain I have about this game. Bioshock 2 has a progressive story but the structure in the game plays off like if you want to go from A to B then you need to use the train. But to use the train you'll have to go to place C. But wait! You'll first have to get something something first and yep even before that you gotta do this and that. The intricate way all the objectives just keep on piling on, there's a danger that you might forget the what you actually were doing for in the first place. And in comes the overwhelming Rapture to make you go more dizzy. But hey, when's the game so great, you can't complain much though. If a game can be so complex with unforseen and nerve-wracking choices, then I'm willing to forgive to game for it and point fingers to my own little brain who can't handle so much epicness (As every sub-plot and character do make an important difference and aren't "just there"). But yeah, you've been warned.
I know I've not even covered most of the basics much as is expected (the combat, the enemies) but in that department, the game is pretty much inherits it's parent. The story will probably disappoint the ones who probably expect it to have twists like the original. It's really straightforward. The real magic lies, I mention once again, in how there's connections between the sub-plots and what your decisions are. One will appreciate this aspect more if the player willingly experiments with the decisions he takes and the impact it'll eventually have on story. There are six different endings(!!!) and, thankfully, it isn't as lazy as that of Bioshock where they just quickly wrapped up everything. The pace remains masterfully even, right to the very last minute and it does not betray the player by playing a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥3 minute video. I'm glad the developers learned through the mistakes and gave a deserving pay-off, no matter what ending you get. I'm even glad that it reintroduces some of the old characters either via an absolutely amazing use of audio logs (left behind by the residents of Rapture, detailing the past events) or by actually coming in the picture. There's only one character that physically reappeared but her presence still made a whole lot of difference, both on the story and emotionally.
All in all, even with the dis-involment of Ken Levine (the mastermind behind Bioshock) and even after not tying this story to the original Bioshock universe as the Burial at Sea DLCs suggest, it is still a masterwork deserving of applause. If Bioshock gave you cold feet and frozen spine, this beast will make you sweat. Nevertheless, it felt so good coming back to Rapture and knowing more of it's mysteries.

You play a group of persons with different background stories and abilities trying to survive the war.
That's it ... basically.
You will try to stay alive and look for food, medicine, cigarettes and so on.
It will feel like a grind without end in sight. And that's what the developers try to show you.
You will have to decide, whether you will take the honest path and share with the other survivors or if you choose to kill for your basic human instincts.
Your characters will react to their actions. A murdering scavenger killing innocent people for food will get depressed and may commit suicide.
Another problem is that the game tries to be very unspecific, it doesn't name a specific location for the war, takes ordinary people as characters, has no voice-over and gives no backgroundstory on anything.
It's basically "You are a normal person. There is war. Survive."
And don't get me wrong, I know that this is used to show that war can hit anyone, but it makes the characters and dialogues/monologues seem very flat and unauthentic.
Maybe the developers can give the characters and monologues/dialogues a bit more depth while still keeping the aspect of showing that war can hit anyone.
All in all, I like this game for being unique and carrying an awesome message: ♥♥♥♥ THE WAR

I played all the previous Hitman series – they topped the list of my favorite games. This game is a HUGE disappointment. I honestly do not understand why this game was even released. What happened to the logic of awesome and immersive game play from the previous editions? I don't even know where to start...
1) No weapons selection! In previous games you could select your weapons for the job depending on your style. After all, you are a hitman! But not in Absolution that follows a storyline. Even if you collect some really cool weapons during a level, you start "fresh" with sometimes NO WEAPONS at all into the next level. This makes no sense! Just about the only time you have a nice weapon selection in the trunk of your car is when you need to kill one cripple guy in a desert. Then right into the next level with the same car that you drove straight from the desert, all you have in the trunk is a METAL PIPE, why?!!!
2) One of the biggest points of the previous games, being a hitman, was an ability to change clothes and impersonate other characters to stay undetected. That was the whole point of changing uniform is that you could walk around and plan your ideal assassination. There was a meditative and rewarding aspect to it as you truly felt like you were a pro. This game introduced a very stupid and annoying detection system. Why?!!! What's the point of impersonating a character if you can be detected anyway by just about any other character with the same uniform?! Gone is the calm and meditative approach where you could plan and sneak up on people. You get harassed by the detection system at every turn and still have to hide away or use "intuition" with every step you make which defeats the purpose of impersonation.
3) Seeing through walls - common! That was the whole point of impersonation and calm exploration with suspense that made the game so enjoyable. This very aspect that made hitman and hitman was tossed out the window with the primitive and unrealistic detection system combined with an ability to see through walls – no suspense, no meditative exploration feeling like a pro. The game has somewhat better graphics but it feels like a primitive, start-up games from the 90’s or something. There is no sense of realism.
I heard of such flaws in this version of Hitman, but I ended up getting it cheap on sale; now, I'm having to force myself to finish it with a settled sense of disappointment. I can only wonder as to what occurred to the development team to result into such a major shift for the worse on this series.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is a space strategy game and a real-time strategy (RTS) game which incorporates 4X strategy game elements. This game was developed by Ironclad Games and published by Stardock Entertainment and is only available on PC.
While you may notice another game with Sins of a Solar Empire in its title (Sins of a Solar Empire: Trinity), that is an older version of the game. Rebellion is the definitive and superior version as it not only offers numerous additions to the game, like Titans and new Factions to play as, but also contains everything from the previous versions of the game.
Sins of a Solar Empire does not have a campaign (although it does contain lore and backstory hidden in the game that you can discover through ways such as research and ship descriptions), but instead chooses to focus almost exclusively on gameplay. This is where Sins really shines. Gameplay in Sins takes place in real-time, allowing you to build ships and send them out all the while earning credits through taxing planets and earn metal and crystal through the ownership of asteroids. Sins also implements elements of 4X strategy games into its gameplay. You are able to build structures such as Trade Ports to generate more Credit Income and Research Labs to allow you to research and develop new ships to produce, unlock planets for you to colonize, and upgrade you ships, planets, and structures. All this and more brings more depth and customizability to the strategy of this game that you won’t find in other RTS games. It has been described by its developers as a “RT4X” and that’s a pretty accurate description, in my opinion.
In Sins of a Solar Empire you can build ships which are specialized for different roles such as: Scouting, Colonizing, Deploy Star-Bases (massive upgradable defensive structures), Build and Dock Strike-Craft, Lay Mines, and much, much more. There are Capital Ships which are strong commanding vessels that have various abilities that can be used in battle. There are also a variety of offensive ships that can range from the light frigates and long-range frigates to heavy cruisers and, with Rebellion, small and fast corvettes.
Sins of a Solar Empire was made in 2008 with the original “Iron Engine”. This engine allows the game to render and support in real-time a large number of planets, structures, and hundreds of ships.
The Iron Engine has not held up as well over time, however. Due to the age of the engine SoaSE was made in, this game will struggle to run after about 2 hours of continuous gameplay with a large number of ships. Late-game lag is unavoidable once you reach about a 2 hour playtime.
Any more than an extended 2 hours of play and the game can be susceptible to crashes, mini-dumps, and occasionally desyncs. This does not always happen; some games can run 3+ hours without experiencing any of these. But for larger games with 6-10 players, there remains a higher chance of a player dropping before you reach 3 hours. It goes without saying that the longer your game lasts, the scale of the map, and the number of ships, the higher the chance for a crash or mini-dump. While this can be a probable occurrence in game that takes many hours and are of a large scale, this is not something that should often happen to you, as games usually take around 1-2 hours. But it bears mentioning if you plan on playing 10 player maps with 80+ planets for more than 2 hours. Note: Those with high ping may lag the game more or have a higher chance of disconnecting from the server.
While this game does not have a campaign, it can be played in Single Player, as well as Multiplayer, via the option to include computer controlled bots or ai (artificial intelligence). The maps range from pre-set to randomly generated and games can range from 2 players to up to 10 players at once in maps that can contain as few as 20 planets in one single-star system, to over 100 planets in a 10 star system.
The quality of the Ironclad Online (ICO) Server is generally good, although it will occasionally be pulled down for maintenance. This usually only last about an hour or so. The online community for this game is of an average size; about 30-100 players depending on the day; there are regulars who play almost every day and can usually be found in games throughout the week. You will rarely find yourself alone with no one else online, though, depending on your time zone, you may only see one or two players online and only a few games in progress. It can take anywhere from 10 minutes to 1 or 2 hours to fill a room depending on the size and goal of the room. You can find rooms ranging from Free For Alls (FFAs), 2v2s, 3v3s (Called 3s), 4v4s (4s), and 5v5s (5s). You can also find “Comp Stomps” which are rooms where players will fight against the ai. Game length varies, but is usually between 30 minutes to 2 and a half hours.
The 5s, 4s, and 3s, communities are often populated by regulars and skilled players and are sometimes unfriendly to newcomers. If you are new to the game, it is recommended to played in smaller game such as 2v2s, FFAs, Comp Stomps, and occasionally 3v3s until you have some games under your belt. You can also play with your friends and enjoy private matches with them, either versus each other or against bots.
While this game won’t be for everyone, as different gamers like different things in their strategy games, I would recommend this game to almost anyone. If the lack of a campaign and the chance of occasional trouble with Multiplayer aren’t deal-breakers for you, I would highly, highly recommend this game to everyone who likes strategy games. There is truly no other game like it that bridges the gap between RTS and 4X like this game does. You are bound for hundreds of hours of addictive gameplay with Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion!
Whether you choose to try out this game or not, I hope this review has been helpful. And if you do choose to buy this game, I hope you enjoy it as much as I do!

Writing a negative review for a Civilization game is something I never thought I'd do.  I was even someone who defended Civilization V at release due to the benefits of hex tiles and no unit stacking far outweighing the drawback of somewhat simplified game systems.  In this case however, they have taken the simplification to absurd levels and made a game so 2-dimensional, I simply can't believe that Firaxis produced it.
I suppose I should start with the positives, though there's only one.  The social policy system from Civilization V has been rearranged so there are 4 policy trees each with 3 tiers and upgraded with tier and tree bonuses.  Putting a certain number of points in a tier across all trees, or a certain number of points into a particular tree will net you an additional bonus.  It's still a very static system though, and makes me miss the customizable government system from Alpha Centauri.
Moving onto the negatives we have just about everything else.  The classic tech tree has been discarded in favor of a tech web which is meant to provide the player with more freedom in how to progress in the game.  What it actually does is scatter related technologies all over the place making it very difficult to locate what you're looking for.  The sense of freedom also feels rather false after playing for a while as you are forced into researching specific technologies to keep up with your opponents, deal with aliens, and persue your chosen victory condition.
Barbarians in regular Civilization games have of course been replaced with aliens.  You might expect an interesting alien threat with a lot of depth like the mindworms from Alpha Centauri, but instead we simply have a constant annoyance that requires significant military technology to deal with (one of the things removing freedom from the tech web.)  All alien types appear at the very beginning of the game including the very strong siege worms and they will just move around killing terraforming units and settlers.  They rarely attack military units but are very strong in the early game and will always win if they do until you have invested in military technology.  If you kill a lot of them or attack a nest without destroying it, they will become much more aggressive but that is the most depth you can expect from them.
The AI has been significantly downgraded as well.  In order to promote a wide range of playstyles, Firaxis removed all personality from the leaders, basically turning them into cardboard cutouts.  For some reason they still created a number of factions and are planning 4 more for the first expansion even though the choice of leader has no impact on gameplay.  Diplomacy has taken a similar hit, somehow managing to have even fewer diplomatic options than Civilization V.  The leaders are so passive you can play through an entire game without a single one declaring war on you, even after rubbing elbows with aggressive territory expansion.  No more late game warmongers like previous Civilization games, and no more interesting leaders.  It does however seem to fit with the lack of style in the rest of the game.  There is no  sci-fi UI and sound effects like Alpha Centauri and no interesting technology flavor text (the game uses uninteresting quotes from the new cardboard cutout leaders.)
A "quest" system was added which initially sounded like a promising new way to mix up gameplay by giving players different goals.  Unfortunately 95% of the quests are the same thing: You built a building for the first time, pick one of two miniscule bonuses to permanently apply to all copies of that building for this game.  Half the time I didn't feel like there was even any choice since even after taking every single health bonus possible, including all offered in quests, I could barely keep the value positive even with a small empire.  The system has a lot of potential, and maybe it will be realized in expansions, but at this point it is pretty useless.
I'm undecided on the new affinity system.  In essence each of the 3 paths embodies a specific philosophy which can affect diplomatic relations with other players and provides different units.  You earn affinity points mostly by researching specific aligned technologies in order to unlock more units and persue the affinity-specific victory condition.  While it does result in unit differences between players, the unit variety provided to each player is quite small and I'm not convinced that it actually results in any meaningful differences from a gameplay perspective.
In summary, this game is one huge disaster.  I don't think even 3 expansions can save it, especially if they contain the miniscule amount of content announced for the first expansion. It has been over an year since I posted my negative review on Crea, my main issue about the game having been its performance issues. I am now glad to say that the developers have finally fixed it and, from what I've read, have been working towards improving performance further! I can't say how much more content they've added but I want to shift my negative review into a positive one.
It seems they have not only improved the game a lot but they have added a lot of things, too. The title screen is far better, the gameplay more fluid, and hopefully the dungeons and bosses have something more rewarding. Even if they don't I still have to recommend Crea at this point!

The crafting system is really in depth, and isn't the usual 'you automatically know how to do this' stuff. And, lastly, the developers are very involved. The day after my negative posts they were asking for information, even left a tool in game, to try and fix the performance issue.
So, again, I feel like Crea is worth it. If you want a good game, with good developers, this is your game.

Everything you do grinds towards experience, you have a combo system on weapons and you have some neat magic. But, at the same time, it's still only worth being called an "Early Access" game. 1.2? It should still be in beta!

The developers do have a good idea of what they're doing but, as a lot of people said, the 'bosses' aren't worth doing. Dungeons are bland. Once they improve on the content and performance of the game? It's worth getting. But as it stands you'd be better off buying Planet Centauri, and it's still in beta. But Terraria is even better.
If you can get it for cheap, and I mean less than $5, then I'd say Crea MIGHT be worth it. Otherwise? You're be better off looking elsewhere.

I'm not really a writer, especially not a review writer, so this might be a little rough.
This game obviously takes heavy inspiration from Terraria, which is probably why you're checking this game out, and that isn't necessarily a bad thing. This game does have many elements to prove it isn't a straight up 'clone' as many people have put it.
Positives:
+ Adds RPG elements such as various talents (skills) and leveling.
+ Various skills you unlock as you level up different skill trees as well as new armor and weapons you can unlock help alleviate the grind to a point where (personally) it is practically unnoticeable (I have only played up to about level 30, which is a little over the halfway point).
+ Melee and ranged skills aren't necessarily OP compared to the magic skills, and vice versa.
+ On that note, there's a good variety of combat skills.
+ Every action you take, including running around the world, gives experience towards its respective talent, with each branch (melee, magic, crafting, gathering, explore) giving unique skills to use.
+ Researching various crafting recipes is interesting and rewarding.
+ Dungeons are interesting and there are many different modifiers that can affect how you play through the different floors.
+ The main dev (Jasson) is very involved in the community and very passionate about his game, he's personally helped me and a friend with a few pretty big bugs, some of them game-breaking, and we have since solved them and they are no longer an issue.
Now, regrettably, on to some of the bad:
- Researching is cool, but it can be unclear as to how to progress through some of it, such as when a boss needs to be defeated before you can research higher level stuff.
- Boss fights are kind of boring and too easy, and it isn't made entirely clear how to access the fights (though the wiki is quite helpful). The first boss in particular has this problem, and it is not made clear that you need to fight them at all to continue.
- This might be a personal thing, but I would like to know what weapons and armor upgrade to whichever next tier without needing to do in-depth research on the wiki to figure out which sets I want/need to craft specifically (such as what armor leads to a dead-end and which armor goes up to the max tier).
- Starting out can be quite difficult, confusing (with so much stuff to do), and therefore a big pain unless you push through and get a few skills unlocked and leveled up, but hey, it is an RPG.
And two neutral things:
+/- First is there's definitely less content here than in Terraria, the game's inspiration, but I will defend it by saying that this game appears to have
more content than Terraria did when it released over 5 years ago, so to give it a comparison in that regard, this game is coming along quite nicely. Also I want to mention... that game has been updated for a good 5 years. It
be more fleshed out than a game that released just over six months ago. This is a neutral point for me because I still wholeheartedly think that it's fully worth its price.
+/- Second thing is the chaos crafting. This is where you can craft either a better version of a weapon or piece of armor, or more of an item you need than you can make by just pushing the craft button. Personally I'm a huge fan of this system and it's quite enjoyable and rewarding, however, some people may not appreciate it as much. It can be pretty confusing to someone just starting the game, as it is kind of complicated and strategic as you unlock higher quality levels.
+/- I moved melee combat to a neutral point because in the beginning it's very difficult to get accustomed to it, but at the later point in the game you can actually begin to facetank
enemies, but there is still blocking and strategy involved inside of that.
All in all, I've enjoyed this game as much as I did Terraria when I first played it, if not more than I enjoyed Terraria. There's tons to do, and I'm a sucker for the leveling, crafting, and research systems that have been implemented here. The devs are very vocal and friendly, and not only open to suggestion, but they will also help you as best as they can with any problems that you may run into when you play. They really do care about this game and their players. This game is an easy recommendation from me. I'd be happy to answer any questions people may have if I am able.

Despite the depressing premise, this is truly one of the most enjoyable games I've encountered. The atmosphere it paints, truly immerses you into the story, and gives players' a glimpse of civilian life during a siege. The market really needed a game like this, and I applaud 11-Bit studios for coming up with the idea and the execution.
Gameplay is quite simplistic. Select character and click on icons to get them to perform tasks. The main focus is the decision making. What do you craft or do? Do you go scavenge through the rubble for resources, build tools or craft furniture. Do you scavenge for food or crafting materials? Do you make cook food, eat it raw or let your characters starve (if you have no food)? Do you spend resources towards crafting weapons or tools? When you scavenge, what items are high priority versus what do you forgo? Do you go barter with people or just take what you want? Those are all decisions choices you're faced with in 'This War of Mine.'
I initially was annoyed by the save feature, where the game would only save at the end of days, but after thinking about it more, and comparing it with XCOM's Iron Man mode (no saving during combat), I realised that the daily save does enhance the gameplay. As a player, you start to truly get attached your characters, and it saddens you when they get hungry, tired, sick or depressed. And if they die, you will probably get depressed, and want to reload the previous day. :P
One criticism is that I do wish the game does notify you if a character is idle (ie. Standing around doing nothing). When you start to get more characters, it gets a bit more tricky and time consuming to manage. And to deal with the time issue, a pause button, which would allow you to direct the character's action, but not have the execute it until the game is un-paused, would also be ideal.
Other than that, this is probably the one of the games with the best atmosphere I have played, and is just a well crafted work of art.
RATING: 9.5/10
PS: I deducted a 0.5 point because I feel the gameplay still can be tweaked for improvement (HINT: Pause Button and Designate Action during Pausing). Also it occasionally crashes from time to time, but that could just be my rig, and not related to the application :)

Back in 2007, Sega produced a game called Sega Rally Revo, developed by a studio they named Sega Racing Studio. It was a nice racing game very much in the Sega tradition, but it didn't do all that well. Codemasters does have a history of collaborating with Sega, Sega made a very nice arcade cabinet out of the original Grid, in fact. Anyway, sometime in the early 2010s, Codemasters acquired Sega Racing Studios, rebranding them Codemasters Racing and set them on this game.
Grid 1 is part of the reason normal people stopped playing racing games.
Grid 2 is the type of racing game those people would play, if they only knew what it was.
It looks realistic but doesn't feel it. It's Prototype, not Grand Theft Auto, it's Quake, not Counterstrike, it's Ace Combat, not IL-2 and it's a much better game for it. That's also part of why it doesn't sell.
Codemasters has a problem with branding. They make serious-ish games like Colin McRae Dirt, but they also make relatively silly games like Dirt: Showdown. The problem is they don't make enough effort to differentiate between these two dynamics to the consumer. Grid 2 has no winking smiley face on the cover, Grid 1 has no frowning guy on it. Grid 1 has fully modeled cockpits, Grid 2 doesn't need cockpits. Grid 1 is made so the guy who seriously bought a force feedback racing wheel for Project CARS can feel social by playing it online, Grid 2 is made for beers and game night. But nothing about Grid 2's presentation highlights any of these differences.
Early cars in Grid 2 drift easily through any corner, mid-game cars introduce you to understeer and later cars can drift a lot, but take a lot of care to do so without crashing. It's a nice difficulty curve that keeps players adapting to the cars they recieve. The tracks meanwhile get more and more bumpy, narrow and winding, with more advanced racing modes - from outrun-style checkpoint racing on a circuit to touge - getting introduced along the way. Everything is conveyed in a manner that's easy to understand, it really feels like a game, not a simulator.
And that's the thing, if you make a game with real-world cars it has to either have the words "need for speed" in the title or be another Forza Motorsport. The fanbase expects these real-world cars to feel close enough to their real-world counterparts (but not too close, that'd be scary), including not being able to do fun things like drifting, saving your turn from going sour at the last second, or even go faster than they "should". I want to make it absolutely clear, there's a reason people who don't identify as "racing game enthusiasts" don't play racing games anymore, and it started with Gran Turismo. They've become an untapped market, but just making the game isn't enough, the stigma for "the most stagnant genre" can't just be killed with one game like Grid 2, especially when the people making actually crazy racing games have been either subverted or forced off into mobile land.
The end result is that Codemasters is forced to pander to their fanbase. Because telling people outside it when they aren't is impossible to them.

You play a group of persons with different background stories and abilities trying to survive the war.
That's it ... basically.
You will try to stay alive and look for food, medicine, cigarettes and so on.
It will feel like a grind without end in sight. And that's what the developers try to show you.
You will have to decide, whether you will take the honest path and share with the other survivors or if you choose to kill for your basic human instincts.
Your characters will react to their actions. A murdering scavenger killing innocent people for food will get depressed and may commit suicide.
Another problem is that the game tries to be very unspecific, it doesn't name a specific location for the war, takes ordinary people as characters, has no voice-over and gives no backgroundstory on anything.
It's basically "You are a normal person. There is war. Survive."
And don't get me wrong, I know that this is used to show that war can hit anyone, but it makes the characters and dialogues/monologues seem very flat and unauthentic.
Maybe the developers can give the characters and monologues/dialogues a bit more depth while still keeping the aspect of showing that war can hit anyone.
All in all, I like this game for being unique and carrying an awesome message: ♥♥♥♥ THE WAR

There are a lot of starbound, minecraft, terraria clones out and about these days.  They involve hours of endless grinding for materials and "exploring".  Some of them have interesting quirks like an advanced crafting systems for gizmos and gadgets or a semi-sophisticated battle system.  Both of those things exist in this game which create depth and playability, but the game lacks soul.  What I mean by that is the world is rather repetative, enemies are boring and forgettable, gathering materials drags out for hours and there's limited to no explanation for how to accomplish certain things.  I mean I get that the idea is to explore and discover how to construct and craft different things, but it feels more like a drawn out scavenger hunt without clues to the locations of the things you need.  The game is in early access, and we all remember how terraria and starbound were at this stage, so we'll see how the devs do with creating more interesting content.  For now, I'd recommend holding off on purchasing.

I have been a HL fan since the beginning -- I got HL1 as a xmas present in '97. HL1 DM was the♥♥♥♥♥♥for many many years, so I was totally onboard for HL2 and its DM mode. However, HL2 DM is a different beast altogether. It was good at first, but it had problems, then Valve seemed like they would never update it, but eventually they did. However, the update didn't address any of the big issues, only things like removing wall strafing, and some tweeks to the netcode (which didn't seem to help at all) because the game is plagued with latency issues. Sure, the score screen will say you have good ping, but getting killed around corners, or visually getting the drop on somone results in barely any damage and your death. HL1 had similar issues as it and pc tech matured, which I was able to overcome by simply installing a new, faster video card, but with HL2, proximity to the server overruled any new graphics tech you wanted to throw at it. I ran a HL1 DM server back in the day and it sat in my bedroom, mere inches away from my "play" computer, which showed me firsthand the advantage of proximity, so I was able to recognize the effect in HL2 DM. I haven't even mentioned the physics issues because they are mere annoyances.. with a map full of movable objects (by way of the gravity gun) it introduces more lag for the average player, and those objects also offer the agrivating possibility of getting stuck, or otherwise hampering movement. So, overall, I don't recommend this game mode unless you are highly competitive and don't mind the impediments. I love the game for deeper reasons, but I had to quit this mode as it just never got the love it deserved and I got older and less patient. :)
