There are racing games for car lovers and there are racing games made for people that obsess with details of sending a car around a track as quickly as possible. Autosport caters to the latter. Those who enjoy buying, tuning and personalizing their dream cars should leave this game on the shelf. Grid Autosport offers very little theater, ditching the fictitious racing series and fake Sportscenter news clips in favor of no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t rubber on tarmac racing. Players will find that they are free to move between different touring car races, endurance races, open wheel racing, tuner events and street races. Players level up in each race type independently and in doing so they unlock new events and sponsors as well as Grid race series events. The freedom ends there however. Once an event is selected players are given the choice between two race teams who have pre selected cars and unappealing liveries. While certainly a realistic touch, it takes the joy out of earning your favorite rides and making them your own. Additionally, each sponsor has different objectives and tuning affinities. The higher their affinity for tuning the more settings players will have to tweak their machines so choosing a sponsor is more like choosing the difficulty of a series and additional experience can be earned by succeeding with an underdog team.

The realism continues once players are secured via five point harness behind the wheel. If you are expecting to be at the front of the pack then participating in qualifying is necessary. Forgoing qualifying laps mean fighting to the front of a dense 12 to 16 player field and contending with some seriously aggressive AI. An extensive damage model and strict penalties for cutting corners means that moving up a position or two is a bitter fight. It feels like an accomplishment to move through the pack but since most races consist of two or three laps aggressive racing is essential and often times you will find yourself crossing the finish line with a car that has wrecked steering and is not pushing as much horsepower as when the race started. Race ending collisions can occur and like Grid 2 the damage models set a genre standard. Unfortunately, qualifying means completing every race twice and qualifying isn't a possibility for certain race series. For those who don't have an obsession with cleaving a tenth of a second off of a lap time it's tedious.

Also complicating matters is the fact that most race events have you teamed up with an AI driver who helps determine your placement in the team standings at the end of a season. Perhaps I made a habit of selecting the wrong sponsor, but my teammates all seemed to be tailpipe fetishists who were content to follow the entire field. While it is possible to order commands for your teammate to drive more aggressively or hold their position it seems to have little effect other than hearing your partner spin out if you forget to back them off of the most aggressive behavior setting. Fortunately, the opponent AI also makes mistakes but all too often the work you put into capturing a podium finish is undermined by your teammate, ultimately costing you valuable experience at the end of the season. Gaining experience is essential to progressing through the career so it doesn't take long before the game feels like a grind.

Variety is a hallmark of the Grid series and Autosport offers touring car racing, endurance racing, open wheel racing, street racing and tuner racing. Endurance races take place over a fixed time and the driver that travels the furthest in the allotted time wins. It's is possibly the most challenging race type since careful and consistent driving is required to stay at the front of the pack and protect the soft rubber that keeps your machine on the road. Open wheel racers are incredibly fragile and the threshold between cornering at max speed and being murdered in a nasty crash is thinner than a human hair. Open wheel racing in Autosport is not as complex as Codemasters' own F1 series since adaptive aerodynamics and the KERS system have been omitted but never the less offers a commendable and accessible experience. Tuner races are largely comprised of time attacks and drift events. Street races tend to be the most enjoyable events simply because the excise the game's long list of real world grand prix tracks in favor of the more detailed city based tracks. Finally, touring car events adhere to the addage of rubbing is racing by placing you behind the wheel of road cars tuned to unrecognizable specifications while you bump and bash your way through corners defending your position against a tightly knit field of racers. Sadly, togue events are absent from Autosport and the live route system—possibly one of the most intriguing features in a racing game in years is also absent. Additionally, players varying tastes means that some events will become a tremendous test of patience for some and leveling across all event types is essential to unlock Grid events. Once again the vehicle selection is slim but covers a tremendous variety of machines, including the platypus of the automotive world: the Aussie Ute.

Online is much the same in Autosport as it was in Grid 2 with both weekly challenge events and direct competition with 11 other drivers. Cars have to be earned one by one and leveling up each of the racing disciplines contributes to your overall level and unlocks more slots in your garage. Each car must be leveled up through use, unlocking tuning options and upgrades. This proves to be highly problematic however since it takes an absurd amount of time to unlock enough tuning options for the feature to be usable. Tuning is a delicate art—the kind of thing you would do with a scalpel and Autosport's initial instinct is to provide you with a jackhammer. Tuning options are controlled via sliders and the greater your affinity for tuning, the more settings available along the slider. Also the way vehicle availability is divided between race types and classes within each race type means that it's hard to dedicate yourself to using a single vehicle in order to upgrade it. All this comes together to make online play a grind of it's own.

Autosport does provide an excellent assortment of tracks across it's single player and online suits, many of the tracks in Grid 2 can be found here as well as a large selection of new Grand Prix tracks—many of which are not found in any other mainstream racing games. The most exciting inclusion is the brand new Circut of the Americas with it's tight hairpins, long straits and winding sections. While Codemasters has included a number of details that liven up the real life Gran Prix tracks, races through the game's cityscapes is far more captivating and lively. Presentation wise, Autosport maintains the same high quality as Grid 2 but by popular demand a cockpit view has been added. Corners have been cut however with a depth of field filter that blurs the detals in the cockpit.
utosport makes some strides toward addressing the issues that many TOCA and Grid fans had with Grid 2 but features enough quirks and questionable design choices to remain frustrating. It's a game that caters to serious race fans and shrugs off features that lend themselves toward giving players a sense of progression. You are simply a driver tied to a team that you are in no way invested in, who is, in turn, leashed to a corporate sponsor. It's a bit of realism that most gamers could do without. Autosport is a challenging racing game with perfect handling and tenacious AI but the dense racing fields and low lap counts combined with a rigorous damage model can irritate. Extensive plans for DLC also raise eyebrows and will likely cause would be wheel-men to steer around this entry.

A great RTS title. If you like Sci-Fi / RTS, you should give it a try.
Pros:
* Pretty balanced game.
* Three races with 2 subfactions each. Thus you can choose between six different factions. I like to play as Advent Loyalists.
* Vast Tech Tree for researching, clearly arranged.
* Capital Ships, which fit the role of 'hero'-units, each with their own fun abilities.
* Advent. Who does not love to command an all-female fleet? Purge the heathens!
* It is a game with a lot of different mechanics but they are all easy to learn. Combined, they are a lot of fun and you won't run out of things to do.
* Pirates, Black Market, Diplomacy...
* The developers. They brought out a new dlc last year (in my opinion, the last dlc vastly improved the game play) for this "old" game, showing they still care about the game and the community.

In my honest opinion (and in the opinion of AngryJoe), Homefront is kind of a mixed bag here.
First we have the singleplayer campaign. The AI of your allies are incompetant and take too long to make it to the other area. The characters are less engaging and by the end of the story (which takes 4 F*CKING HOURS!!!) you will not care either way. Another thing is the story itself. It is so unrealistic. The thought of North Korea steamrolling through South Korea, conquering Japan, Vietnam, and other Southeast Asian countries without intervention from countries like China, Russia, and of cource the United States is laughable. Nevermind the fact that in the game, the KPA (Korean People's Army) managed to occupy western U.S. We have U.S forces at the border between North and South Korea, if Kim wants this reality, he would only be dooming his army and people. the campaign makes up with this I guess by throwing in UAVs, humvee turrets, a G.O.L.I.A.T.H tank and even a helo at one point. Early on in the story though you get some pretty dark♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game. Examples include mass graves, labor camps, the effects of white phosphorus on unprotected soldiers, KPA soldiers executing a child's parents RIGHT IN FRONT OF THE POOR ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!!!
Now multiplayer. Ooooohh multiplayer. Multiplayer is pretty much the only good thing that came out of that game! In fact, I say it heavily outweighs the terrible story we were given in the singleplayer. How good is the multiplayer? Picture Bad Company 2 exceppt you can't destroy buildings (FIX THIS SH*T HOMEFRONT DEVELOPERS!!!). Multiplayer server can even hold up to 32 players so you feel you are actually part of a full-scale battle! You can even use both mounted and airborne drones.
I would be very happy if the developers add in a map where the U.S Military and the KPA can beat all seven shades of sh*t out of eachother where they would fight IRL: The DMZ line in Korea! (Better be taking notes Homefront developers!)
In the end I give Homefront a 6/10. It is better than Medal of Honor I guess but unless your into large 32 player battles online, I just can't recommend this game at full price. But since the multiplayer is very strong in this game, I say people should look into it when the price drops.

Brutal game, that gets surprisingly emotional. Some of the choices really make you think, and you get pretty attached to some of your characters. And the game is appropriately unforgiving - there are no save states, so if someone dies (which they will, becuase combat is quick and lethal) they're gone for good. And not only will you feel the loss of a valuable member of your team, but your other survivors will feel it too (and get depressed as a result). It's all a very high-stakes game that's precariously balanced on a wire above a pit of disaster. I haven't played such a high-tension game in a long time, and there's a LOT to be said for this underrepresented point of view in a culture that glorifies soldiers and their conflicts.
Side note - I played a game on an easier difficulty (lots of supplies, short/mild winter, little danger), and it totally sucked the soul out of the title. The struggle is an essential part of what makes this a rewarding and emotionally engaging experience that very few other games are capable of capturing.

It did not convince as much as the first game of the franchise, it still very impressive considering it's made by a different development company.
The story takes you back to Raptor once again. This time you are playing as one of the Big Daddy's themselves. The story takes places 8 years after the first game. The bioshock stories is quite complex and the story in this one was quite enjoyable.
The gameplay is not much of an improvement over the first one. It's basically the same. You have a lot of the same powers as the first game in the series. Unlike the previous game where you should literally save or harm the little sister, it's reversed in this game. You still encounter the same enemies such as splicers. Since you are a Big Daddy it is possible to shoot and use the drill once, which is a welcome touch.
It's not much of a graphics overhaul from the previous game, but that is not a problem. It is also well optimized. The settings and feeling of the game is very dark. It has a horror theme without actually being a horror game. The game has an amazing style and art to it, which makes Rapture standout as one of the most recognizable places in video game history.
Music from the 1930's is played throughout the game, which sets the overall feel of the world. The game depends on voices actors, who does an amazing job to tell the story of Rapture. The ambient sounds also inhance the mood of the game.
It expands the universe of Raptor and pulls you down for one more experience. It is a brilliant shooter, and the setting, story and overall nature of the game is the reason why Bioshock is my favorite series off all time. If you liked the first one, you will enjoy this one too.

In short, BioShock 2 is better than most games you'll find but it is still miles behind the first BioShock. The gameplay is only slightly improved (notably hacking and dual-wielding), but the story is so outrageously bad that it should be ashamed to call itself a BioShock game. The moral dilemas are ill-informed and backwards. Not killing the Little Sisters still has a chance of spawning Big Sisters, and granting Gil Alexander his final request somehow warrants a bad ending. The Dionysus Park level alone is such a textbook example of terrible gameplay and narrative design that playing it. The core of BioShock's gameplay is there and improved, but the story and atmosphere feels fake and hollow. The music and graphics are close enough to the original that you only notice every way they fall flat.
TL;DR
The only thing I can recomend BioShock 2 for is its gameplay, which is slightly improved from the original. Every other part of the game falls dreadfully short. The story is hollow and void of that charming spark the first game had and contains many plot holes that affect the gameplay. It is better than most, but only a maudlin shawdow of the original BioShock.
However, the gameplay is so strong that I give BioShock 2 a recomendation, but only just barely.

Alrighty, so with recent updates, the game works to a much farther extent. It's quite enjoyable, now that I can actually make it work. The aspect of getting better at various tasks as you do them more often is definitely a plus that brings it away from Terraria, as it is commonly compared to. Another thing about it is that it's a sandbox game that has a lore. And it's fairly interesting, though somewhat tedious to collect. Despite this, it becomes much more inspiring to keep playing.

I highly recommend this game as the plotline is just incredible, and the environment is rich and exciting. It is really nice having the achievements put in, and was even nicer that it was given to me because I had bought the original bioshock PC port on steam to replay before this remaster was released. It's incredible to see a game I've known for so long get re-released to be experienced again with better quality. I was a teenager when this first came out on Xbox and I missed a lot of plot nuances, so replaying it was important to deepen my understanding of Rapture.
The third big update 2K released in early December seems to have fixed the major issues that concerned me with the Remaster. I did have one instance of major unexplained lag that led to crashing during a scripted event, which I expand on later for those interested - but ultimately, what matters to me is that I was able to continue normally and had no issues afterward. The other 20 hours of gameplay have been buttery smooth.
I'm on a pieced together frakenstein's-creature rig and if mine can do it, I bet yours can too - a very old Mac Pro running Windows 10, Xeon quad 2.93GHz, only 8GB RAM, GTX 970 4GB vram. I'm able to run it with everything maxed with a respectable framerate (I'm not a 100fps or bust person so your mileage may vary depending on your preferences). Because I was curious and also wanted to provide some numbers to substantiate this review, I launched the game with Steam's FPS counter just to get a clue to give you a ballpark of what I'm getting. In combat it oscillates between 80 and 200 depending on the number of explosions from grenades. With no combat whatsoever just walking around taking it in, it is between 260-300+ with no other characters present, drops to 200 with a Big Daddy hanging out in the viscinity. Didn't have any water to walk through nearby so can't comment on the ripples' impact but I never noticed any major drops.
Regarding the only major crash I had - it did not seem to be graphics related (?), which was unfortunate because those tend to be easier to fix for a basic-level gamer like myself; lower everything, and slug through until fps improves/issue resolves is my first go-to when experiencing problems. The game asked upon re-launch if I'd like to set everything back to default, which I accepted because I assumed the lagging was my doing, being overzealous with my settings. Not even the lowest settings fixed the lag in this one section, and putting on v-sync did nothing. Strangely I discovered I could simply fight through it as long as I was fast enough upon reload (the longer I was there the worse it became until it would ultimately crash around 2-3 minutes in the area), and immediately upon killing an insignificant random NPC the lag disappeared completely. To be more specific (spoilers for those who haven't played it at all yet despite it being like 10 years old!)
As soon as he was dead it went away immediately and even returning to the area with my own max graphics settings back up, it never occurred again. Not sure what that was about but I'm really glad it didn't make the entire area inaccessible. If you happen to experience this issue I highly recommend reloading and just trying to kill him as fast as possible upon opening the door.
I hope this helps if you're on the fence and find yourself reading through my drivel. The game's story is really worth the time, it's quite serious the video game that pulled me into the real story telling genres, and launched me on the path through the Fallout series, Dishonored, Skyrim etc. If not the Remaster, I hope you play it once somewhere, somehow.

THE GOOD:
This is a game that is visually beautiful, with great graphics and sound.  For instance, the details on damage your hull takes is, for lack of a better word, gorgeous.  High production values all around.
THE BAD:
Wow, I just can't get into the gameplay at ALL.  Take all the parts that aren't fun about World of Warcraft, and combine them with all the parts that aren't fun about X3: Reunion.
-Shallow RPG elements.  Shallow dialogue choices.  Shallow, linear plotline buried in a sandbox game.
-An "open world sandbox" that is mostly empty, and is in TWO dimensions.  (This is a space game.)
-Grinding the same bounty quests over and over for money for upgrades.
-Combat is similar to space battles in Star Trek Online, but shallower, with less strategy and fewer options.  I kept wishing for the officer abilities of STO to give it some variance.
-3/4th of the enemy you face are starfighters, which you have to bat away with your turrets. Fighters move in three dimensions; you do not.  To help you hit them, your reticule locks onto them and follows them around.  So you're pretty much just flying in a circle and holding down the fire button.  Against 3/4 of the enemies you face.
-Oh, and by the way, you know that cool "Evil Ways" song in the preview movie on the store page?  Well, you'll think it's alot less cool when you start playing because that song (in rotation with perhaps two others) is your constant companion as you amble around the universe looking for mobs to grind.
THE VERDICT:
Dull.  There isn't much more to this game than the combat, and I can tell the combat is supposed to feel a lot more exciting than it does. First of all let me say that I am playing this game and probably will for a few more months. It has interesting early game play, but the interest gets lost as the game progresses and the obvious outcome becomes more and more evident.
It would be nice to do things like customize the military units. The game choices are pretty shallow.
I dont recommend the game to others mostly because the interface is so poorly designed. Lots of needless mouse clicks and repetive use of the menus. Many tasks that you have to do over and over should be done with out moving the mouse from the top of the screen, then back to the bottom. Then to the middle. You are injuring people when you make them do this.
A well thought out game should not have menus that are inconsistant, for example, you cannot end your turn with out completing all the tasks except the spy menu. You can end your turn over and over and still forget to do the tasks in this menu. Also the same buttons should do the same commands in all of the menus, but these are not so.
I understand that the creators put a lot of thought into how the game looks. But think of the tech tree. I can see the techs in one level of focus. What do I do in the other levels? Any real reason to have them there? Think about it.
I would also caution you that if you suffer from any repetitve motion issues that this game is not for you. The poor design will make you suffer if you play the game for long.
Things like putting very small but important information at the top of the screen show lack of insite by the creators of how we use our computers. Anyone out there wear bifocals? Can you imagine looking thru the top of your glasses for the small print? Makes no sense.
Lastly, do I really need to wait 45 seconds for steam to search the world over to see if I have played the game on another computer? You mean I can never click the menu box and say dont bother wasting my 45 seconds every other time I load the game?
Do I really have to say every time that I load the game I understand that online play is not suited for all players? Really, can not you make a disclaimer that says I understand this and have it done with?
I think that the writers of this game are very inexperienced in what we have learned over the years about ergenomics and the ability to do tasks with out needless movements. Like leaving the keyboard to move the mouse over and over and over again.
So even though at the moment I am going on playing for a while longer, I dont recommend this game.

Homefront is a modern military shooter set in the late 2020s, in North Korean occupied America. Unfortunately the game squanders its setting through unrelatable characters who flip-flop between morals at the drop of a hat, and a very generic Ameri-centric storyline.
Gameplay
The game features Call of Duty-esque gunplay, with little recoil or skill required. Unfortunately, missions consist of "Follow [Character] for a bit so you don't get lost" style handholding and a few unexplained vehicle sections. The difficulty options just reduce the player's health, which on 'hard' mean any explosion in the same postcode is an instant death, and the 100% accurate enemies have no problems dishing out almost instant death
Story
The game ultimately fails to deliver an interesting and compelling storyline in its short campaign (3 hours according to steam, including 30 odd minutes of setting up the game). The attempts the game makes at being morally and emotionally challenging fall flat as your squad feature Connor, the psychopathic murderer and Rianna, initially the voice of reason to contrast Connor flips a 180 after a plot point.
Verdict
Don't bother if you aren't very interested by the setting and COD-esque gunplay. Buy it on sale if you absolutely must, otherwise leave it alone.

Before I start my review i just wanted to say that this game, has the potential to become what Civ5 had become - a great game, but at this moment the later is a lot better in terms of price and content.
The game seems really rushed and uncompleted and you get the idea that 'Fixaris games' thought that its enought to repaint the previous game with more 'alien' colors and....profit... No guys thats just being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and dissapointing the players who basically grew up with the series. I acually wouldnt have been that mad if you offered the same content as in previous game, because before buying it you shouldnt needed to be Einstein to figure it out.
So lets start with pros:
- Web tech three ( in civ 5 we had linear one)
It somehow lets you try out different strategies and finally build some world wonders before AI's ( on Immortal and Diety levels).
- Exploring
Its a lot more revarding to explore , because you get a lot more then anient ruins like in previous games. Dig up crashed sattelites, alliens bones or explore derelict settements.
- You can lauch satellites into space to give your colony different bonuses. Everything from agricultural satellities to mining lasers repurposed for war. What your  little heart desires (i would go with orbital cannon)
Cons:
- Low limit  of  units
You have enought land units if you menage to acquire the strategic resources (which is not so easy), but you only have 2 naval units  nad one air unit. So no submarines or dedicated bombers. Also the lack of mass destruction weapons is quite troubling. Yes you  can built giant robots or even a zerg qeen (for a ton of those rare strategic resources), but i still thing that thermonuclear weapons would be a lot more effective, not to mention fun.
- Strategic resources (yes in this game they are a lot more important than in previous game (not counting uranium ^^ ) )
In this game you have 3 types of stategic resources ( Biomass, Floastones and Firaxite). Basically every affinity ( similar to ideology in Civ5 has a prefered resource for there units, so you basically tied up to that affinity which prefered resourches are near your cities.
-Aliens ( they are more then barbarians from previous game they said, they will be friendly they said...)
Basically there is no serious need to try to befriend aliens and after they kill your 3 explorer that tryed to dig out fallen settalite near there nest you really start to question your peacifull aproach and ask your enginner if he can make some flametrowers...
-Quests
After you build a building or some other logical step you will get a quest with most of the time 2 options, they will lead either to affinity points or what you want extra bonus from that building. It was fun at first, but when you play the game for n time they becomes a nunsense, not to mention that some of the bonus are quite OP.
So in general  play civ 5 if you want content and more interesting gameplay, play this want if you want to kill aliens and mess up new planets accosystems.

Jalopy is a very interesting game, while it does largely deal with driving, there is more to it than just that. Even thoguh the game is in Pre-alpha, it is still very much playable in its current state, though the ocassaional bugs will come out, but that is expected in the current state it is in. We may also end up getting additional polishings of the game as it advances through development.
As of the general release avalible July 12th, 2016, this is what I can say:
Pros:
-Well thought out system of upgrading and repairing the car.
-Interesting approach to the economy.
-Unique time and setting. Few games rarely have such a scenario.
-Very stable for an alpha.
Cons:
-Still in pre-alpha, with all sorts of bugs that can come up. Also, as it is still being developed, you at the current state, you can only go up to CSFR/Hungary Border before having to "Return Home" to try again, so there isn't much.
-Very little instruction on gameplay, you're told the essentials of driving your car, and what each part does, which is great, but when it comes to other things, like the windshield washer or how to open boxes with padlocks on them, you're left searching the Steam and Reddit groups on what is what. Thankfully, these are easy instructions to follow, but I feel these could be put in a tutorial somewhere in the beginning.
-I feel that each country can use things that feel more respective to their countries. I'm sure the developers will add that in later on, but as of now, most everything is in German, even in the CSFR. Having things change in terms of language and general stylistics can help in the form of gameplay.
Overall, I encourage people to get the game. It isn't super difficult to play, but it also presents challenges to players at time too, and the game has a lot of promise. Even at full price, I would say the game is definetly worth it.

I’m going to begin with the negative and finish w/ the positive:
This Hitman game let me down it two very distinct areas.  Firstly is the saving system.  There is no quick save option and the only mid-level saving is done via checkpoints which are placed very far apart and at times/in context that doesn't make sense.  Each time you load from a checkpoint on a new level you'll pull the Jackie Chan "Whaaaa???" meme.  The other thing that lets Hitman down is how meh a lot of the story and killing options are.  Compared to other games in the series there is a noticeable lack of options.  Oh there is a ton of ways to play each mission but relative to earlier titles it's rather constrained. The story too is very meh, not that the Hitman series is known for it's gripping storylines but this one is so forgettable and predictable.  It' doesn't take you out of the game or spoil things, it's just WEAK af.
HOWEVER, the options that are available are tons fun.  Truly Hitman Absolution is a really fun, engaging game, I spent a good amount of time laughing and different things.  From funny situational kills to humorous dialogue.  Absolution is genuinely funny.  Hitman looks absolutely fantastic even compared to games coming out now.  Only rarely do you see(notice) an ugly texture or something out of place. The environments are incredibly rich, they begin to feel like actual tangible places.  It’s incredibly immersive.  The background voicework is also fantastic and commendable.  There are seemingly endless unique conversations in each level, often many of them are quite humorous.  I’ve definitely spent time following NPC’s to hear the conclusion to whatever they were talking about.  The options that exist (which are many, my complaint was compared to other hitman games) to dispatch your enemies are often really quite cool.  All of these things combine into a game where each level is a unique and very engaging.  The details are beautiful, the sound work is fantastic, and you’re given a lot of freedom to do your own thing.  If you’re tired of games leading you by the hand, the Hitman series will set you free.  Hitman Absolution rightly deserves to be included with the other good Hitman games.  Tons of FUN, a MUST BUY!
Also a bonus this game goes on sale ALL the time for $4.99USD or less which is a really great deal.  Plop this thing in your wishlist and wait for a sale. YOU DO NOT AND SHOULD NOT HAVE TO  PAY FULL PRICE FOR THIS GAME!! BUY IT ON SALE!! LOVE YOU!

I have enjoyed every Hitman game made...until this one.  I waited a long time to write this review because I didn't feel I should waste my time.  I have played through twice mining acheivements and looking for other ways to do certain things.  The entire second time through the game I was hoping to find unique and interesting ways through the game.  The problem is for Hitman this game is on rails.  The best Hitman levels (and games) turn the player loose in a level and say do something.  The levels will be generally square and open with various ways to approach and exit.  Absolution was designed around a corridor with cover.  In order to hide the linearity of things the developers do things like lower the light or add fog...but it's still a single corridor with a designed hiding place to sneak past a patrolling enemy.  Sure there are various ways to kill a target...as long as you wait for the target to walk to the proper spot and push the proper button.  It seems that the developers got lost in the "sneak" aspect and forgot about the open world part.
It's not all bad.  The graphics are very good.  The charcter and ragdoll animations are very smooth.  The story is good, probably better than most Hitman games.  It feels like playing a movie.
All in all it's a good game.  But when I think Hitman I think exploration of a level, failing many times to find a good way to get the takedown silently.  This feels like a little too much Call of Duty made it into the game.
If you liked Grid, you will love Grid 2.  Very cool, great graphics.  Love it.

BioShock 2, the very definition of a misunderstood sequel!
And so here I was, about 4 years after I played the original BioShock for the first time (the one on steam was the second) and was left amazed by the marvellously haunting underwater world and history of Rapture, the time had come to see how the story moved on.
Truth be told, I am by nature negatively biased towards sequels of great games, since the result rarely is on par with the originals.
At the same time, from online reviews and friends opinions I was expecting a generally mediοcre sequel, not really bad, but a lot inferior.
What I got instead was a great game that was a lot reminiscent of its predecessor and that at the same time managed to put it's own touch and distinguish itself from it!
The game is vastly big, since, except from its main single player story, which is already long enough to be comparable to the first one's, it also includes a multiplayer campaign, plus two more DLCs, so let me analyze them one by one!
- The single player campaign, for starters: you start out as a Big Daddy (an older model of it actually), with it's two trademark weapons (the drill and the rivet gun) and the ability to escort Little Sisters at their ADAM gatherings, which I found to be a really nice idea to stand out from the first game, since it gave you the opportunity to see the world from a different perspective.
The story is a bit confusing at first, you don't know who you are and what you are doing and I'll admit that, while I initially liked that, as the game progressed on this "amnesia" of sorts got a bit tiresome, since it prevented you from enjoying the story and its (small) twists.
The first game was ahead in that aspect, since it made you start out pretty much confident about who you were and what you were doing, only to destroy that all at its half, with an amazing twist, one of the best of its kind. However the remaining half of the original BioShock wasn't as thrilling as the first one, though it definitely wasn't bad, just decent.
Now, BioShock 2 took another route, to the end of the game you get to know very few things about the protagonist, as, little by little, you learn something more, all until the final levels, where the big twist kicks in and you find all the truth about yourself! The twist was, maybe, just a little inferior from the one of the first game, but it was still very good.
Continuing on, aside from the story, the game made some great additions in the gameplay, that improved a lot the old one. For starters, the weapons/plasmids system was positively changed a bit, making them easier to handle, while at the same time new weapons and plasmids were added, greatly differentiating themselves from the older ones.
Speaking of gameplay, when I first played Dishonored (another great game) I remember describing it as a "stealth based BioShock", well... upon playing BioShock 2 I found even more similarities to Dishonored than the first game and not just in gameplay, but storywise too (ie, in Dishonored you have to save a little girl named Emily and in BioShock 2 one named Eleanor). After all, Arkane Studios was involved in the making of both games, so that probably played its part. However, there too, Dishonored took it's own distinctive path, so I wouldn't call it a ripoff, in fact it even improved on many of these similarities that I noticed between said games (like a fast teleporting plasmid present in BioShock 2's multiplayer, named Aerodash, which was a lot similar to the vastly superior Blink ability in Dishonored... and how much I missed that ability in BioShock 2... ).
Moving on, aside from the improved weapon and plasmid mechanics and some new splicers, BioShock 2 introduced an amazing foe: the Big Sister, who essentially was an evolution of the Big Daddy! I found them great for a change in the game's world, since they were really tough to beat and getting ready to "greet" them was scary enough, sometimes (I even remember getting ready to fight one and getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked, only to be saved by, not one, but two cluelessly walking Big Daddies, that, upon being caught in the Big Sister's attacks, started attacking her as well, saving my lucky self!).
Another big change in the gameplay was the ability to "wirelessly" hack machines, a change which I ended up really appreciating, despite the hack being done in real time, with enemies potentially attacking you.
The graphics and soundtrack were, more or less, similar to the first's, with the former being slighly improved, but nothing too great. In itself that was a good thing, since it made the game stay closer to its predecessor.
The game's levels dimensions were also changed, since the first game had many levels split in two parts (maybe because of limitations PCs had at that time), while BioShock 2 had 9 huge levels, which I mistakenly thought to be few at first, though being slightly smaller in total.
Lastly, the game's main antagonist wasn't as thrilling as the two ones of the original BioShock, but she was good enough.
Thankfully the final levels, upon learning your true identity and onwards, were quite good and action packed, so much that they even provided you with a great ally, which I won't spoil and I'll let you discover for yourself (for a single level you also got to play as a Little Sister, which was cool)!
The ending was, once again, faithful to the original, where some of your choices in the game affected its outcome (much like in Dishonored, too).
- Changing subject, I'll now go to the multiplayer campaign: overall, I didn't feel satisfied by it and that being because the game had some, difficult enough, multiplayer achievements, while at the same time it was not optimized well enough, resulting in a lot of lag (myself aside, I found others having the same problem too) and in almost empty lobbies, making the achievement hunt quite frustrating.
However, that said, the multiplayer part was not all bad, it's gameplay was in fact quite good and balanced (though not entertaining enough) and it took part in a period before the events of the first BioShock, during Rapture's civil war, making it a bit more interesting.
- And to the final part, we get to the game's two DLCs: the Protector Trials and Minerva's Den.
The first one was not much related to the main story, but not totally unrelated too.
Once again reminding me of Dishonored's first DLC (Dunwall City Trials), it comprised of many challenges were you once again assumed the role of a Big Daddy and had to protect a Little Sister during her ADAM gatherings, but with a specific set of weapons and plasmids each time, making the whole thing fun enough, while mixing just a bit of story in it and awarding you with some extra art and trailers of BioShock 2, for every succesful gathering you made.
The second DLC was, instead, a continuation of the story and ended up being really good and long just enough to keep your interest on. You once again took the role of a Big Daddy with a mysterious story on its back, immersing yourself in the game's levels to find it out, all of this happening in another, unexplored, part of Rapture, with new weapons and enemies mixed in (the Ion Laser gun being its coolest addition).
The DLC's ending was good enough, with the final twist being slightly more predictable than the main game's, but not too much, while at the same time providing a good closure to the world of Rapture.
All in all, I found BioShock 2 to be a fantastic game and only slightly inferior to the original, most of it being due to the fact that you were already introduced and familiar to the world of Rapture from the latter. Hopefully the third game, BioShock Infinite, will manage to reignite the marvel of discovering a hidden city, this time in the sky (can't wait to play it as well)!
But don't let that frighten you, since you are once again in for a Shock, so... would you kindly play BioShock 2?

Here it is.....bottom line.
This is a good game, it has its flaws, absolutely, in fact, I will list them:
- AI is not great
- AI is very aggressive in a non-realistic manner (i.e. ramming, bumping, etc.)
- Racenet online challenges need to be sorted because many are leaderboards based on timed laps, yet the AI is there preventing time to really be the challenge due to the above issue.
- Codemasters loves DLC, so much so that key components that should be present in the game, are pay for (i.e. garage space, additional "special" vehicles, and the one I am most irritated by is XP boost.
- No Touge for drift, though we are told it is coming as a DLC (and see my point above)
Now the good, then some explanation on the reason I reccomend the game.
The good:
- Fantastic sim-like racing
- Each vehicle handles a little different, and you need to learn the vehicle, the track, and improve your skills based on that.
- The multiplayer, although lacking spectate (ahem, this is needed yesterday) is really tons of fun with friends.
- Racing teams online, thats right you and your besties, can enter as a team, in custom cups or whatever, ultimately competing against other teams and their standings.
- Relatively good visual graphics and audio
Now, after reading all of that, the game is a brand new release, and here is why I reccomend it, regardless of the negatives.  This is the best there actually is right now in PC racing.  In fact, I would venture to say that for a while this will be the standard, although we will have to see how Assetto Corsa and Project CARS turns out, but as for now, this is the crowning king.
However, the DLC, about that, yeah, I don't like it, but I think that if the company themselves would market this as an MMO with a monthly, then release the features as they have been, then everyones jimmys wouldnt be rustled.  The bottom line, right or wrong, DLC is the new gaming concept over subscription.
Think about it ESO $50 then $15 a month, WoW pretty much the same, SWTOR on its release was the same, you get what I am saying.  In fact many MMO's especially FTP, and games like The Secret World, offer issues on a quarterly basis, that expand the game, this is really no different.
Am I defending the DLC tactic, not really, but on the same token the company has to have some motivation to support the game after launch, unlike MXGP, and other lesser games.
The true test will be what this game is like in a couple of months, and then see if the bugs and AI issues have been sorted out, at that time I will eat my review, but as of now I reccomend the game, and hope these issues are sorted.

Space operas are in short supply, and if there's one thing that Rebel galaxy does well, it's nailing the feel of a space opera. Western-themes may be a staple of the genre (FireFly, StarCraft), but the soundtrack and environmental colour grading really help to sell the setting. Voice acting and facial animation are unexpected but welcome in a game at this price point.
Sadly, the gameplay does hold up in the long run. The grind escaltes throughout the game, and there isn't much increase in combat variety or tactical depth beyond the first couple of systems.
If you see this game on sale, pick it up for a few hours of unadulterated space opera. And if the developers decide to update the game (or release a sequel), I'm more than ready to come back to experience whatever they come up with.
Pros:
- Fantastic soundtrack reminiscent of Firefly (the TV show).
- Gorgeous 3D planets, nebulae, and asteroid fields.
- Broadsidebased combat in a 2D movement model feels like ship combat in Assasin's Creed, removes a lot of the issues these games usually face.
- Overall feels a lot like old 2D spacesim favourites like the Escape Velocity series.
- Warp/cruise system pretty good at reducing time spent staring at space (though not perfect).
- Choice of ship addons materially affects combat feel.
Cons:
- Enemy dificulty ramps very quickly, especially after the first solar system.
- Grinding for cash to buy bigger/better ships is tedious.
- Trade and mining are innefective ways to make cash.
- Story missions are very linear.

Having now played 60 hours into my first Rebel Galaxy playthrough, I feel i can give this game a solid review.
- Awesome graphics (on max settings) that somehow find the right balance between cartoon-ish and realistic.
- The ships are very customizable and they all look amazing, with pros and cons to each of them.
- Custom music for any area of the game. (if you want to have shopping mall music in your space stations more power to you)
- Simple yet effective combat system that relies heavily on shield management and ship positioning. (unless you want to repair at every station you dock at)
- Accessible trading system. (buy when red, sell when green)
- Good replayability due to the procedurally generated star systems.
- WARP INHIBITED BY STELLAR MASS (this will be burned into your psyche) Literally everything kicks your ship out of warp once you are within 3.0 sm (solar mile??) of it. At least give me the option to smash my ship into an asteroid at warp if i'm that dumb.. this would be equivalent to getting demounted in an MMO every time you were within a few meters of a large rock or a tree... or another player.
- While vast, the galaxy, and the solar systems feel lifeless. You will realize very quickly that you are playing a single player game in the cold loneliness of space.
- Mining, is borderline pointless once you're at the point in the game where a single upgrade is well over $1,000,000. This is because the average mining drop is either obtanium or meteoric diamonds which sell for $1,000~, and $20,000~ respectively.
- I found the default music to be irritating after listening to it for over 5 hours, though some people like it, at least there is the option to play without music or use your own.
- The combat is mostly automated and based on whether your ship is stronger than the other one or not... not much outmaneuvering is possible in Rebel Galaxy, so you don't get rewarded for being a better pilot than your opponent.. that and the enemy AI is pretty terrible.
- The economy and commerce of the game is completely random, so it makes trading at times very frustrating. Also, some comodoties becomes obsolete due to the limited storage space you have because of how little they sell for. There is also no way to sort or filter the viewing of the comodoties at stations, which you'd think would just be common sense. Any game in this day and age that has an auction house type system has the ability to sort and filter it. What i found to be the best way of making money was to just amass a ton of expensive comodoties and fly around the galaxy and rescue merchants. After resucing them, they will buy your stuff for the max market value, and you also get the cargo of whatever ship they were under fire from.
- The story is very simplistic with some unique enemies generated from the missions, but overall it lacks any sort of emotional attachment to the characters or development of said characters. I will say however that
Overall, the game was fun to play, and advance with the new ships that i upgraded to, but i'm skeptical that i'll be coming back for round 2 anytime soon. Maybe if the weapons were more varied or the trading and economy was more flushed out the game would feel warmer and more dynamic, but i guess this is what you get for a budget title.

Homefront is a FPS game with resembles from the Modern Warfare series from Call of Duty. The only difference is that even if both are very linear stories this game is doing such a poor job because you can't take any actions yourself.
For example; everytime I want to take out an enemy because I know he will spot me I shot him and for some reason I fail the mission since everyone notices but the next time I waited I still had to kill the same bad guy but only 1 second later and this only because the NPC you follow trough the whole game tells you to do certain stuff...
Pros
- Firearms
Here it isn't very good but I liked it and specially the sniper mechanics.
- Graphics?
That's about it and it's not very good today anyway. The only thing that makes me place this on the pro side is that the game is 6 years old when I write this weview and it looks good for those standards.
Cons
- Bugs and Glitches
This because the NPC you follow can get stuck on eachother and you have to restart. The enemy NPC can run trough your friendly NPC:s and start shooting you in the back even though there were 10 frendlies covering it.
- Story
Terrible story that the screenwriters shouldn't be proud of to include in their CV. The problem is that 95% of the story is so obvious on what's happening next, the 1-liners are so bad that some shouldn't even exist...
The ending is also really bad, it just screams sequal and now I know it got one but that one isn't much better what i can see from the reviews.
- Voice actors
Same as the story above, this was made horrible by all the characters but specially the main female lead named "Rianna". She drops the worst things and it sounds so fake it's almost funny to hear her.
- Firearms (Here as well)
One thing that isn't great about this is that every enemy have different weapons and I never ran out of ammo... Only time it happened was when I intentionlly stayed far away to sniped the enemies down.
- Graphics (Also on cons?)
Yea the problem here was that the game saved itself all the time which made it freeze and when it didn't save the game went down to 5 FPS anyway every 30 seconds for some reason. I know it shouldn't since I'm running on a 1070 GTX overclocked card that can play everything on high or ultra settings but this didn't like my PC which made me die way too many times because of the frame rate drops.
- Multiplayer

Villagers and Heroes is a classic MMORPG that has been compared to the likes of Runescape and WoW. While I feel that a direct comparison to these games is less than accurate, I would go so far as to say that players from these other titles will find it an easy transition in terms of game play and mechanics. If you have not played these other titles, you will find that the base mechanics of game play are not that difficult to pick up on, thanks in large part to the games opening quest which serves double duty as a well crafted tutorial. While the game offers many of the traditional aspects found in other games of this genre, it has an acceptable learning curve. The main thing that differentiates this game from those previously mentioned is that it is more casual than hardcore, which results in a friendlier community than the average game of this nature.
Like many other games in the fantasy genre, V&H has a medieval setting in which characters engage in three related aspects of game play. Combat and exploration, gathering, and crafting. There is an additional element of game play with the inclusion of villages. Characters can join join a stand alone or guild village where they maintain a house which grants additional storage, raise crops in their own gardens, and maintain a small ranch which yields components useful for crafting.
Despite being squarely in the middle of a somewhat crowded genre, V&H offers a few aspects that make it somewhat unique. The most unique aspect in my mind is an add on to crafting referred to as the Gnog station. Through gnoging, a character can take existing gear and modify its looks and aspects. They can add and remove the various feats and abilities inherent to gear to create custom gear tailored to the individual needs of the character. Another feature that was added just this past year is the ability for a character to be "Reborn" which allows them to reset their combat stats and advance their character with bonuses, without the loss of non-combat achievements. My most favorite aspect of the game however does not have so much to do with the game itself as it does the games community. The owners and staff at Mad Otter Games have a reputation for being receptive to their customers, which results in player driven development. In actual game play, a player will find the game itself to be well moderated, which results in a play environment remarkably free of Trolls and Drama-llamas. Of all the on-line games I have played, Villagers and Heroes has perhaps the most friendly and welcoming community that I have ever encountered.

This is a great new take on survival games. The charcoal background and visible gray and depressing ambiance and pallet of the game greatly compliment the theme of the game. I also even enjoy the receptiveness of it. Having an aspect where every day is the same and you have to power through each and every day of the game. No civilian is going to see the different events every day in a warzone, a lot of the days are going to be identical, and the repetitive nature can cause complacency, and in this game, if you get complacent, somebody raids you and injuries are all around. Then someone throws a wrench in the gears and screws you over. I do feel that the game would be better if there was a bit more randomness to the personalities of the people you meet in the game. In terms of collecting, I like that there aren't a lot of weapons like guns, which seems as though it would be extremely realistic, most military forces in the city would have seized them anyway. I would also like if the buildings or areas to search where a little larger. But overall, a great game that really makes you think about surviving in a war torn city as an everyday normal person turned refugee. Graphics are well polished and the gameplay is very smooth. In addition, anytime you go into an area where there is possible danger, I find myself with a quickened pulse and adrenaline rush. You never know whether the sound that you just heard was someone dangerous, or a simple rat. Sometimes those people don’t even make a sound until you startle them. On at least one occasion, I have run to the exit when a single door opened, the man turned out to be a trader inside the building, but I wasn’t thinking he was very friendly. Also, in some areas, other people can show up halfway through your scavenging and really complicate matters for you. And if you finish a game, good on you. It isn’t easy and I’ve found that it really makes me want to try another round, to see if I can do better. Great game 9/10

I have to say that I recommend this game, especially for people that are looknig for a relaxed and low pressure game  supported by a great community.

A cautious thumbs up. I can't get out of the EA habit despite being burned frequently, but Citadel's core matches up to what I want: A High Fantasy ARK-like with less annoying survival mechanics and more magic.
As of now I've mostly spent time levelling, building and exploring on a solo game. The game is already enjoyable to look at, although the asset pool is currently a bit restricted and the map seems too small for long term enjoyment. On the bright side this significantly reduces download and install size (about 7GB installed as of this review), which makes it ideal for trying the game out on lower bandwidth connections.
A performance perspective:
Unoptimised UE4 engine game, expect heavy performance dips and strain on both CPU and GPU. Not recommended for minimum spec PCs until there are some proper optimisation passes done.
It can just about manage a consistent 35FPS on a GTX1070/ i5-4670 with high settings; although significant additional strain can be accounted for as I've only played on a self-hosted server/custom game. More RAM will also help, 16G is borderline if you want to host, but should be okay for solo and when joining a server. Installation on SSD is recommended as loading times are quite bad.
The game's primary focus is magic, with gathering, crafting, taming and combat tied into spell based mechanics. The spells themselves are lovely to look at but sometimes feel rather useless. Combat feels bland, as the AI is so bad that half the time whatever you're attacking will ignore you completely, or become incapable of pathing to you.
The skill system is basically the same as ARK, with everything from spells to recipes to building options sitting behind a level requirement and skillpoint cost. I feel it's overused, at least the basic equipment and buildings should be available from the get go (wooden walls and floors, chests, level 1 gear). A man's shack is his castle and nothing give a player a sense of investment like a home, however shabby.
The death system is quite forgiving, which I like - you don't lose equipment, although you do lose loot in the inventory (which encourages people to take an occasional break to dump it back at the shack). The equipment does lose durability with each death so if you can't repair or replace it, you still need to be a little careful. Mobility is in the forms of mounts (tip: Direwolves make excellent riding beasts) and flight, provided either by a broom that fills your only accessory slot or a potion. Flight drains mana quickly so you either need a large pool, lots of potions, or high natural regen to use it for more than a couple hundred meters.
The game is very clearly still under development; with glitches aplenty, atrocious AI and animations, and essentially no element of risk just yet. However the devs are responsive and appear keen on supporting the game as long as people are keen on playing and feeding back. Given a little TLC from both sides, I feel Citadel is one of the EA games that may actually see (successful) release before everyone is bored of it. I'm recommending it as I think it's a title worth supporting, but I wouldn't recommend it as a polished experience AT ALL just yet.

This game launched in a horribly broken borderline unplayable rate. Servers quickly become unbearably laggy after 10+ people are online at once. This makes every aspect of the game at best tedious and at worst completely unworkable. It is also plagued by many, many different bugs and crashes. The game also suffers severely from some really boneheaded decisions in the gameplay mechanics.
The bugs, crashes, lag, etc can all be fixed. So I'll not focus on them. Instead I'll talk about the gameplay design and where it falls flat. Though it is worth noting that amidst this trainwreck of incompotent programming the devs first patch added in a new glove and hat. Really focusing on the important things...
First of all, you have four weapons to chose from, each with an associated attack skill tree. If you don't use staff you are gimping yourself. They are not remotely balanced. Axe does the same damage as staff at a range of 5ft vs staffs infinite range. Staff also casts faster. You'll be using the starting attack for at least the first 20 levels so this is kind of an important thing to get right.
The gameplay revolves entirely around chugging potions. Everything you do eats your mana pool ravenously, but you can completely mitigate this by spamming potions, none of which have cool down. PVP fights are a contest of mashing mana potions, spamming the same attack skill over and over, and mashing heal potions the second you take damage. At the moment PVP is decided by who lags less. Nothing else.
You can tame and ride dragons, but they are completely useless in combat (enemies have 5000hp, for example and its fire breath tics off 1-5 hp at a time at a very slow rate. I never managed to get it's melee to connect. It can spit fireballs that do fair damage at you when it's hostile but once it's tamed it forgets it's only usefull attack.
Enemies are so easy to kill due to braindead AI and horrible pathfinding (in a game where you fly around shooting fireballs). The devs adressed this problem by making you get less xp from killing higher level enemies.
Also the game really suffers from the devs complete unwillingness to take any chances whatsoever. In a game about mighty wizards contesting resources and forming grand alliances your magic is limited to what would amount to first level D&D spells. You can shoot fireballs, lightning, etc. But you can't cast divination spells to locate people or mobs, you can't cast illusions to hide your base, you can't enchant things, etc.
Exploration is severely lacklustre owing to a really small amount of enemy types and re-used repeated assets. I found a dungeon named "the inverted tower" which was a stairwell down about 4 floors to a cave system I'd seen a 100 times before loaded with about 6 different enemies which were copies of ones I'd killed a thousand times before.
The building system is quite detailed and you can make a lot of cool things with it. But you wont want too because it's trivially easy for someone to come and smash your walls down and destroy your building. I'm talking like 3-5 minutes for 4 layers of honeycombing with stone walls to be completely breached. You're better off building a little 2x2 shack in the woods and hoping no one spots it.
The broomstick, used for flying, is very fun. But eats mana like no ones buisness. Meaning while flying you will be tapping that potion button once every 30 seconds minimum. I put nearly all my xp points into my mana pool and at level 26 i couldnt fly for a straight minute without my mana bottoming out. The broomstick is rendered further useless because it eats up a trinket slot (of which you only get one!) meaning that you can either fly or wear jewlery, not both. You definatly cannot wear a ring and a necklace, that's right out.
Overall it seems like the devs looked at games like Ark and Rust and said "lets copy those games! But we need to differentiate ourselves somehow? I know... Wizards!" and that was about as far they went with the concept.  This is a broken game full of bad design choices and missed opportunities. Maybe they'll fix it in the future, but the patches and design decisions so far do not fill me with hope.

Being a fan of arena fighters since my early days of gaming I came into this already knowing how these types of games are to play out. As a result I probably have some personal bias on the game but will try to avoid any major criticisms that because of my personal opinion.
So to get things started, Archeblade, a product of Codebrush Games is a fast paced arena fighter/brawler. This means that you’ll be fighting other players in a competitive skill based arena.  This can turn off a lot of people as when you just start the game you will be playing against people that have more experience that you and can combo you properly.  This being said the tutorial doesn’t do well to teach you anything advanced but it does teach you the fundamentals of combat. These fundamentals are something that I personally have a quarrel with. The combat is fun but the lack of creative fighting techniques spoil the longevity of the game.
Whereas most arena fighters have a move and counter move system in place, Archeblade focuses on the character in play more than the overall skill needed to play that character. It’s not that the player isn’t necessarily good at the game but the character they pick in certain matchups lack significant counter play. This MOBA style approach to characterisation works well as a team based mechanic but falls off when it comes to unofficial community made “gamemodes” where one would play to compare the skill level of the players.
Another issue is the community itself. If you are living in or near the US, then finding games should be a breeze. Finding games from outside the US, like Australia, is very difficult. The large amount of unpopulated servers means that there is plenty of room for a growth in the player base but at the time of this review there aren’t enough players playing this game. This is a shame because the game is by no means broken. A game like this needs a healthy fan base to push the game forwards. A small community isn’t always a bad thing, but when you only have enough people to fill out three or four games conflict ensues. The really good players will reside in these populated game rooms and constantly beat on the newer players which ruins the experience for the new players and forces them to quit the game. Of course the competitive nature of the game makes it so there is a discrepancy in players skills but there isn’t enough offered to fill the void between them.
These issues are major roadblocks for the game but can be changed in the future. The game itself is actually very enjoyable.  The fast paced game play is nothing new but is done well mechanically. A lot of the bugs have been cleared up since early access and the addition of new characters make for constant shifts in the Meta game. This makes the tedious nature of fighting in the same arena a refreshing experience as something new is always on the horizon and new additions brings new game play mechanics to the table. The new additions can also be rather daunting however for newer layers as the amount of game knowledge required to master the game keeps expanding. This isn’t a bad thing necessarily as the drive to learn and to master the game can in itself be a reason to stick around. Visually the game is quite appealing considering the amount of work has been put into ensuring the game runs at a playable level. Not everyone has a fancy gaming pc and the developers know that and catered for performance rather than over the top graphics. The art style very heavily influenced by Eastern Asia with the body model exaggerations and flashy visuals you’d see out of your typical shounen manga. The environments are pretty but do not distract you from the game play and in some cases are interactive.
Overall the game is a very fun arena fighter. It’s free with the option of cosmetic monetary transactions. Those wanting to get into the arena fighter scene might not find what they seek due to the limited player base and lack in creative game modes but the overall impression is that the game is enjoyable for the moment with lots of room to grow. The issue is that there are other more polished arena fighters games of which may take some of the potential Archeblade player base away from them, pushing Archeblade community from its dire need of growth and expansion.
To summarize the game is satisfying, pulling off a perfect combo whilst dodging that of your opponents is still as thrilling as in any other arena fighter and the amount of skill that some of the top tier players have is still there. Those interested in the game should give it a try but with the abundance of unfilled servers it might be a good idea to grab a few friends.

I'm not too far in, only 7 hours, but I have to say I'm enjoying it so far. Everyone goes into this game comparing it to Terarria, so I will make my points comparing the two for those of you, whom like me, want something worth playing in the same genre. The crafting system does take some getting used to, but i like the combat and RPG element.  The more the use particular skills, the more points you get to level up the tree those skills are in.  It's a neat system that encourages you to use whatever playstyle you like without having to rely heavily on gear for modifiers.  I've seen people complain that it can be grindy, but I don't see it anymore in this game than in Terarria (which i put EXTENSIVE time into, about 800 hours).  Sure, you have to grind out some baddies to get materials, but i remember building grind traps in Terarria and sitting there for hours on end collecting mats.  I like that you can customize your toon into a class build without having to rely specificly on armor sets, something I did not enjoy about Terarria.  The collecting/gathering is done well.  You can upgrade your gathering skill and collect large amounds of tiles at once, instead of having to chip away 1 at a time, another thing I am enjoying over Terraria. I do prefer Terarria's highlight mode, which will allow you to auto dig tunnels in a diagonal fashion to form easy stairs up or down.  This is something I haven't quite been able to perfect in Crea yet. They have mini-instances which you have to go into and complete objectives in order to escape.  They also have spawn rooms where you have to vanquish all the mobs and spawners, then you receive a huge loot stash.  So far, I feel both of those elemnts are rather rewarding.  There are random chests and ore to stumble across, and even spells that will light up  said chests/ore for a brief period of time so you can better see them.  I did hate having to rely on Spelunker potions in Terarria, and those spells have made me incredibly happy so far.  The higher you level them up, the higher grade ore/chest will be highlights. They also employ a waypoint system which makes traveling around a lot easier than having to build minecart tracks all over the entire map.  Overall I think its pretty good.  I enjoyed Terraria. I am now enjoying Crea.  When i get toward end-game content, ill re-review and let you know if anything changes.  As of right now, I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes this genre of gaming.  Just remember; It's not Terarria. It's Crea. Terraria was fun, and so far, Crea is fun ;)

5/10 fun to start, but flops in the end.
Alright. So after putting in about 20 hours, I have some new opinions.  One thing that Terarria does well which Crea does not is events and bosses.  When the goblins spawn for the first time, or that first night when the Eye of Cthulu attacks, it's crazy exciting, and gives you an objective to complete.  Kill those baddies.  It may mean you need to get some better gear, change the layout of your house, enlist the help of a buddy, w/e.  Crea is dissapointlingly lacking in this department.  Around the 15 hour mark, I found myself just looking for the next set of gear... then realized... why?  There is no main objective.  I don't have a supreme being to kill, or waves of monsters to defend my home from.  It just becomes the same 20 monsters that you need to kill over and over w/o any pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.  In short, it gets boring.  I have not even needed to dig in the last 10 levels.  Everything you need can be obtained from monsters, spawners, and dungeons.  So I have this massive world, but have only explored 1/4 of it ( ran through the entire map to see the different biomes/monsters) and feel no reason to even bother checking out the rest.  I read up on the bosses to see if/when they would spawn, and it seems all of them are non essential to progress in the game and can be avoided entirely.  What started out as a really interesting game has, after a few days of play, fallen flat.  If you enjoy mindless repetition and have no desire to accomplish and "end" to a game, then Crea is for you!  As for me, not so much.

I don't write much reviews, but I feel that this game needs one from me.
I have followed the development of this game closely, and everything I read made me believe this was going to be a good game. So naturally I pre-ordered the game. I never have been someone who buys a DLC, though a pre-order bonus is something I usually take.
First impression is that they did listen. This is a game with good graphics, and cars handle as they should. Not unlike in Grid 2, that if you learn how to slide in every corner, you are guaranteed going to be faster than everyone. I started doing multiplayer directly. I learned that like in every multiplayer game, the sooner you start with multiplayer, the easier it is, because you get access to the faster cars earlier. I started out doing streets discipline because that is what I loved from Grid2 most too.
This worked for me. I like the cars and the tracks I drove were nice. It did seem the same tracks were in the rotational though, but on the forums they mentioned to do something about that. It immediately came to me that this game has a steep learning curve. Nothing you do will guarantee you to win and many things just don't seem to work and you have to figure out why. For that reason I wrote a beginners guide to Multiplayer with all the do's and don'ts. A lot of people are thankful to me because it answered many questions they had.
If a game has this, that is not a good sign, but lets try and keep things positive. I mean, you learn how it works, and then it works.
I started doing Open Wheels with a friend in custom lobbies with AI to fill up the spots. This is where I found out that CodeMasters made a big mistake with this game. The AI is badly programmed. They say they are very fond of how the AI is, and that it is very realistic. This is a lie. The AI really is AI (artificial) It follows the racingline, and if you happen to be there, they are happy to crash into you pushing you away. They'll get you to spin off the tarmac easily, and if you try that with them, they seem not to be harmed at all. They break early so you easily crash into them unless you take the inside corner and use them as a moving wall.
Grid multiplayer has a damage system. Basically, when you damage your car, at the end of the race you have to repair your car which costs money. The real problem with this is that the AI does not seem to care and happily crashes into you, causing you to have a high bill to pay. There is also the impact rating that tells other drivers how clean you drive. Even if you attempt to avoid all contact, the AI easily can cause such accident that your rating becomes yellow, causing other players to think you are a bad driver.
Then there are the racenet challenges. They suffer the same problem: They included the AI in most of the races, and you start at position 12. This means that it is no longer a race to get the fastest time, but to find out how you can effectively take over 11 cars in the first 2 corners. The faster you do that, the faster your time is. Thats all there is to it really. CodeMasters has mentioned that they'll look into this, but CodeMasters also mentioned they really love the AI and are not planning to make any changes to it. Lets hope they decide to remove the AI completely.
I did some single player too. I started doing Streets as that is what I did in Multiplayer too. I had to learn how to adjust to the AI. I basically learned that: crashing is good, do everything you have to do to get in front of the AI as quickly as possible trying to minimize the damage as much as possible, and you will guaranteed win. Of course, everyone else learns this too, and they take these experiences to multiplayer. Yes, this game has a lot of crashes and rammers in multiplayer too. You'll have to find custom lobbies if you want to avoid this.
There are other issues too that are small problems and thus not worth having a section per item. I'll list them as good and bad points.
Good points:
- Good graphics
- Physics of the cars are very good.
- When you start a race, you get to see the map so you always know what the track is going to be like
- You can enable raceline which helps greatly in learning the cars and tracks, both in SP and MP.
- Most settings are shared between SP and MP.
Bad points:
- AI behavior vs you
- AI in multiplayer vs repair costs
- AI in Racenet Challenges, doesn't make sense, see above.
- Keyboard players have a big disadvantage over controller players in Endurance (basically, forget this mode all together)
- Big learning curve
- Time spent waiting too long
- MP, time before first race can easily go up to 10 minutes if you're out of luck, but on average it is 5 minutes or more)
- Game says cockpit view, but it isn't really a cockpit view. No working dials, everything blurred.
- Assists aren't really assists. Except for ABS, the rest makes you go slower and loose bonus points, giving a false sense of help.
- Menu system is hard to navigate and reponds slow.
- Quitting MP takes a lot of time, you cannot quit when you want to and have to wait for a certain moment before you can quit. ALT-F4 works, but you'll loose your progress.
- Cheating happens in MP, even though CodeMasters are banning cheaters.
Long story short... Grid Autosports on paper is this: the best things from Grid1 and Grid2 together. The actual outcome however isn't this. With a short development time for this game, yet a full price, it is clear the game is a quick job trying to generate money because of the negativity around Grid2.
If you are very good at racing games and you want a bit of realism, yet you want to have a challenge, you'll love this game. If you are not very good at racing games, this game just isn't going to make you happy. Any other racing game will do it, just not this one. If you don't want too much realism in how your car drives, this game is not for you either. Grid1 might be, Grid2 definitely is going to be. If you have raced a lot in Assetto Corsa, this game is not gonna do it for you.
