Rapture (also known as the North Atlantic Project and the Rapture Colony) is a massive underwater city forged by the personal dreams of Andrew Ryan to escape from the political, social and religious anxieties of a post-World War II world. It was established on November 5, 1946 and finished in late 1951. It is located at 63° 2' N, 29° 55' W, which places it at about 433 kilometers west of Iceland's capital, Reykjavik.
The hours spent playing this masterpiece were the perfect encapsulation of why videogaming is such a favourite waste of time for so many of us. Thrilling, terrifying, moving, confusing, amusing, compelling, and very very dark. BioShock isn't simply the sign of gaming realising its true cinematic potential, but one where a game straddles so many entertainment art forms so expertly that it's the best demonstration yet how flexible this medium can be. It's no longer just another shooter wrapped up in a pretty game engine, but a story that exists and unfolds inside the most convincing and elaborate and artistic game world ever conceived.
If anything, it’s BioShock’s combat set pieces that don’t impress much nowadays. BioShock is well-known for being the ‘scariest’ of the three games – there are a couple of jump scares that will catch you out even today – but it’s a surprise to revisit and see how much shooting there is here. This is where the game falls down, and its boss fights are a particular low point; neither particularly fun nor overtly challenging, they end up being altogether pointless. It’s cool to meet the characters themselves, but fighting them is just a nuisance.
BioShock opens with a bang, but the overall plot focuses more on making an emotional impact than an explosive one. The year is 1960, and you're flying over the Atlantic Ocean. One mysterious plane crash later, you're floating in the water, apparently the lone survivor, surrounded by the flaming wreckage of the aircraft. But there's a lighthouse on a tiny island just at the edge of your view. Who in their right mind would put a lighthouse this far out? You swim closer and discover a small submersible called a bathysphere waiting to take you underwater. After catching a breathtaking view of what's below, you're sent into the secret underwater city of Rapture. Masterminded by a somewhat megalomaniacal businessman named Andrew Ryan, this city is driven by its own idea of total freedom, with capitalism completely unhindered by governmental meddling and science unhinged from the pesky morals of organized religion. Sounds like the perfect society, right? Well, even before you step out of your bathysphere and into the city, it becomes obvious that everything has gone horribly wrong down here. The city is trashed, and genetic freaks called splicers roam around, attacking anything that gets in front of them. At the heart of the matter is a powerful, corrupting substance called ADAM, which makes all this genetic tinkering possible and allows you to get your first plasmid power, the ability to shoot lightning out of your fingertips.
Strong as this work may be, it's the licensed music from the '40s that really sticks with you.The varioussongs pulled from historyboth sound great and helpfurther Rapture's pervasive atmosphere, making the now-ravaged city feel like a dystopia frozen in time. And while we loved just about every song that played in the broken down jukeboxes and record players, the Andrew Sisters' Bei Mir Bist Du Schon ("With me, you are beautiful")stands out.
We don’t really need a conclusion, do we? It should be obvious by now that I'm going to give BioShock the maximum possible score. There really is no doubt about it.
The game is superbly crafted, a masterpiece of game design which will tug on your heartstrings and stain your pants in equal measure. It’ll leave you gripping your desk in excitement when the plot takes a new direction and it will leave you shaking with anticipation whenever the screen gets a burst of static.
Important, gorgeous, dramatic? BioShock redefines what these words mean in the games industry, leaving past peaks like Half-Life 2 by the wayside. BioShock is quite simply a triumph that we cannot gush enough praise for.

Large to the point of it feeling completely pointless each time you use an ability as it is possilbe to completely fill out your chaos on an ability that is necessary to use in a single click. Pretty much everytime you click something you run the risk of trashing the item and wasting all the resources. This same process is used to smelt ores. Sure you could just smelt it normally, but you will recieve 1/2 - 1/3 as much ore as you would by torturing yourself with the chaos crafting system. You will be motivated to go through this because you need as much smelted as possible to try the "minigame" (random dice roll) when crafting the actual items as many times as possible in hopes of getting an item with something besides pickup distance. I'm honestly not sure whether or not I recommend this sh!tshow of a game. Hitman Absolution was the game that started me off with the Hitman series in general. Then I found Blood Money, which basically revealed to me just how bad Absolution is.
The staple of the Hitman series is strategic freedom. The ability to take on every assassination on your own terms and do whatever you want. Another staple was actually assassinating people. They never focused too much on the story, and focused more on delivering excellent gameplay. Sadly, Absolution flies in the face of all that. Levels are packed full of linear, scripted action sequences, with Agent 47 sprinting across burning buildings, dropping some nothing personnels and some high noons with his overpowered abilities.
The game focuses on story so much that there are levels where you don't even assassinate people. Sequences where you literally just sneak past enemies using obviously laid out stealth routes until you reach the small part of the level where you need to kill someone. There is a level where you literally just fight your way through a bar brawl to interrogate the owner. There's a ♥♥♥♥ing level where you simply get your Silverballer pistols back from some old gun dealer. There is literally no "hit" in these levels. Literally. Not even figuratively.
The game's alright as a stealth game. It's got a ♥♥♥♥ing abysmal detection system, though. It works on a little meter. So when someone's looking at you, you'll see a little spike around the edge of your vision, and once it spikes to its fullest, you're spotted. But if you spike it all the way up to near maximum and then take cover, why, the guy who was just staring right at you for three seconds straight, literally doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ He's been staring right at you, but because you rounded a piece of cover just in time, you're absolved of your sins, lad. He doesn't know a thing.
The story is an uninteresting pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Completely uncharacteristic of Agent 47 and way too emotional and dramatized. It was dangerously close to 47 having some drawn out kiss scene. Not to mention how Nixxes thought process of designing a character was just "Lets have a load of nuns that are also assassins and♥♥♥♥♥♥lel so much random xD". All the characters try to seem unique, but in the end, they're trying so ♥♥♥♥ing hard. All the villians are the kind of guys who eat puppies and burn orphanages down for fun, and everyone else is just given odd character gimmicks to make them seem interesting.
Beyond all that, what does this game have? A damn fine combat system. Although it's really ♥♥♥♥in' strange for a hitman game to have that, it has that. The combat system is really fluid, and fighting people is pretty satisfying. The game doesn't fight with you when you want to aim and shoot. You can do it in practically any situation. The excellent cover system also complements the combat system perfectly. Agent 47 moves around cover pretty consistently and it's highly reliable. Combat in this game is pretty fun.
All that's really left is the Contracts system. People can basically designate a specfic target for you to kill on a certain level, the disguise you'll have to be wearing for the kill, and how you'll have to kill them. It can lead to some pretty creative and puzzling assassinations, and is actually fun to mess around with for a short while.
All in all, the game is a good shooter, a hand-holding stealth game and a terrible addition to the Hitman series.

Graphically and soundwise this game is on par of it's two predecessors. Sadly the story is a bit behind the first part, and even a bit more lacking than the second part.
I have so many games seen with the "Damsel in Distress" leitmotiv that it's getting boring. The series as a whole is a jewel of the Hidden Object Genre, it's well engineered, but the story is a bit lacking - if you have to hunt over a series of three games almost the same story (sorry), then something is terribly, terribly wrong.
Don't misunderstand me, the game is as it is good and wonderful, but if you play all three you might catch up with the repetitive storyline, on the other hand the solution of the story redeems the antagonist a lot, by making him victim of the circumstances.
This said, I am fighting with myself to recommend this game. On the Pro side is the wonderfully done graphics and soundtrack, that can draw you into the game. And the ease with which you can play this game as casual as you wish. On the Con side is the repetitive storyline throughout all three parts of the game - and for me a good story has more weight than fancy graphics or soundtrack, however the story isn't messed up, it's just three chapters telling the same only deepening the thread by adding some more lore, and the first episode did that best...
So there is a kind of anticlimatic thing here, with the end of the first story you wanted to know more, the second story catered to this, but finally fell short and the third part caught up with the shortcomings of the second part, but lacked a bit by rinsing and repeating the first story.

I recommend this game with a dire warning, if you played the first and second part it's at least the finality that will make you play this game - if you didn't play the other two parts, you might play it stand-alone and have fun, because you aren't filled with spoilers already. On the technical side of the game I can't complain.
Addendum per 13:20 2017.10.04: I have to add, this isn't the weakest storyline of Artifex Mundi but neither it's their best. The "Demon Hunter" and the "Time Mysteries" series are in my opinion worse, I don't dare touching the 2nd and 3rd part of Demon Hunter, and I don't dare touching the 3rd part of Time Mysteries by now.

The game suffers from a enormous lack of polish.
This is made obvious by on one hand the glaring problems with servers, the UI, the management of crafting etc, and on the other hand a complete lack of a consistent world. Different mobs wander around seemingly at random and they have no reason to be there except for the player to find them and kill them. Camps are uninspired and the "caves" aren't more than little holes in the mountain that can often be explored in under 5 seconds.
While the UI, servers and such problems might be solved later down the line I doubt that the shallow "world" will ever be much more than it is today. If the game even tried a bit of world building it would make everything much more interesting.
Why not give the player a reason to be were they are? Maybe the world is a new discovery and loads of different wizard guilds are sending apprentices to explore and further their guilds magic knowledge?
Why not make orc settlements that worship and protect ancient monoliths instead of having single orcs wandering without purpose in the woods? That would make for a much interesting raid than the current camps.
All that aside the game is a grindfest, and probably isn't worth your attention if you play alone. There are plenty of games that do building better and the combat plays like a poormans Skyrim. In my opinion this is a cheap cashgrab and a very lazy attempt to "renew" the oversaturated survival genre.

After becoming completely addicted to the original Bioshock, I wanted to buy and play Bioshock 2 here as soon as possible. There are two things I must critique it for before I can move on which is to say that even though it's the second game in the series, the controls are actually very noticeably wonkier which I had to get used to in order to keep playing and the game occasionally crashes so you have to save often in order to try to prevent losing progress (I literally lost about 2 hours and 35 minutes of gameplay due to this issue). Other than those things however, I honestly don't understand why Bioshock 2 is consistently deemed not as good as other Bioshock games by most of the Bioshock fans. I honestly enjoyed it equally as well as I did the original Bioshock, not particularally favoring one over the other (though in a few ways I do actually prefer the second one versus the first). The game stays true to the psycholical horror film and continues to try to freak you out, and while the original Bioshock is still creepier by far, Bioshock 2 does succeed in being creepy in its own ways. I'm looking at you Big Sisters! While the animation for the original Bioshock is really good especially for an older game, the animation for Bioshock 2 is breathakingly beautiful. I also liked being able to use both a plasmid and a weapon at the same time. It also gives you even more moral choices versus just the either rescue or harvest the Little Sisters bit that the original Bioshock had giving you a lot more to think about. I literally felt like the game was trying to test me to see how far I'm willing to go in order to accomplish my goal. Overall, well done. Definitely a game worth buying and enslaving your life away on. And so fellow Bioshock fans I must ask you this: would you kindly begin thinking better of Bioshock 2?

I have played every GRID game there was, and I have to tell that every one features quite a unique gameplay. In case of this one - I have to admit - by looking at the screenshots I expected a redone GRID 2. I was both disappointed and surprised, but compared to GRID 2 this game is a completely different animal. It looks different, it feels different, and most importantly it drives different.
Autosport is not a simulation yet, but it is definitely a hard game. In the beginning it's difficult to keep your car from sliding, and even Formula 1 GP racetracks seem somewhat narrow.  While the first two GRIDs focused on reckless arcade action with drifting involved even in ordinary touring races, here it's not recommended. You have to fight for grip, but after three seasons I easily got my driving style right with nearly no driver aids (I only left the ABS on) and no tweaking of my gamepad options (Logitech F710) was needed at all.
Probably the only two things I dislike about the game are the cockpit cam and drifting sessions. In case of cockpit most people complain about its looks. I actually liked the looks, but after three races I switched to hood cam and discovered that the game runs smoother. Is it a shame? Maybe, but TOCA RD 3 didn't have a proper cockpit cam and I didn't mind. In case of drifting sessions I don't like that it feels like a completely different physical model, and the car isn't that different from the ordinary racing car, which you use on different tracks - of course then they handle quite differently. Additionally I hate that drifting was embedded into series full of racing. In most series you use the same car for almost all races. In the first TUNER event I used three completely different cars. So this gave the feel that TUNER series is just o compilation of things which didn't quite fit other series.
Otherwise I recommend it. It definitely is a proper racing game, but no longer one for casual racers.

The concept and art style of the game are great, but the actual gameplay is pretty bad. I'm not just saying that because it's 2017 and I'm unfairly judging a 10 year old game; I had these same complaints when Bioshock came out. The combat is horribly unbalanced and poorly thought out. The wrench and the tommy gun are probably the only weapons that work well and have appropriate levels of ammunition. It feels like the designers originally wanted the game to be survival horror, but they also wanted the game to be fun, so they went half way and created a game that is neither scary nor fun. It always feels like there is a shortage of resources that forces the player to switch back and forth between weapons and plasmids, but the shortage leads to a feeling of anger and frustration.
Pistol:
Maximum pistol ammo is 48  bullets, but it can easily take 15 bullets to kill enemies later in the game, and that's with all of the pistol upgrades and playing on normal difficulty. If the enemies are going to be bullet sponges, I should be carrying 200 bullets. Is the game supposed to be survival horror where I'm sneaking around due to a lack of bullets, or is it supposed to be a fun game where I shoot things? The game has no sneaking and it has no bullets, so I get the worst of both worlds.
Shotgun:
Bioshock has the worst shotgun in any shooter I have ever played. Its effective range is a couple yards even though it fires 00 buckshot. In real life, buckshot's effective range is about 50-100 yards. It should be possible to shoot things across the room and have them die in a few shots. The original Doom shotgun and the Duke Nukem 3D shotgun are a lot closer to how a shotgun should work. Bioshock is a bit more like Doom 3 - the shotgun is useless. In addition to doing no damage and having no range, it has a 4 round magazine. It might be more effective to swing the shotgun like a baseball bat.
Camera:
The inclusion of a camera for research is just mind boggling. Here's how this plays out: You'll buy 100 camera ammo then take about 5 pictures per encounter for every enemy you encounter. Just run up to them and keep clicking the mouse button until it says it didn't take a picture because the score was too low. After seeing maybe 5 of each monster type, you'll have every monster type maxed out. Then you'll never use the camera again. What was the point of including this in the game? It's just mindless busy work.
Grenades:
The grenade launcher is awesome, but the ammo limits are stupid. You get a max of 6 of each type, and it takes about 6 grenades to kill a big daddy on normal difficulty. Since every other weapon in the game is basically useless against a big daddy, this means you'll carry grenades just for the sake of killing big daddies. It's like the game is mocking the player. We get this amazing weapon to carry around, but we can't use it on anything because that ammo is reserved for killing one specific enemy type.
Chemical Thrower:
This is another one of those really bizarre design choices. The chemical thrower can do all 3 types of elemental damage - fire, cold, electricity. The cold and electricity essentially do no damage, so those act very similar to the plasmid powers. This means you would be expected to freeze an enemy with the thrower and then switch to a different weapon to inflict damage. This is a horrendous idea. Switching back and forth between guns and plasmids is easy because it just involves right clicking. Switching back and forth between guns is a lot more involved because it involves hitting different numbers on a keyboard, and people playing on console would probably switch weapons using the D pad. It's a lot clumsier than clicking a single button to toggle back and forth. The chemical thrower seems like an idea that would work if it were possible to assign it as a plasmid power instead of a gun. Since that isn't possible, you'll probably just resort to using the plasmid versions of elemental damage and not using the chem thrower at any point in the game.
Seeing Enemies:
Bioshock is one of those games where enemies blend into the background very easily. I find myself using the fire plasmid just because it marks targets effectively. I can always see an enemy that is on fire.
The damage in the game is so incredibly broken that I'm certain this is the reason the game gives free respawns when you die. On normal difficulty, 2 shots from a big daddy rivet gun will kill you, and there's no way to dodge them other than line of sight.This means you will die all the time. If one of your hacked devices fires a stray bullet that hits a big daddy, you will die in a few seconds unless you are already behind cover. Rather than fix the stupid amount of damage done by enemies, the game just gives the player a free respawn with no loss of equipment or ammo. They know players would be punching their monitors if the game did a game over screen every time that happened.
The awful combat means the story and the environment are the only reasons to play the game. It's an interesting story with an interesting environment, but the game has no replay value at all.
I will say that I like how this remastered version has video interviews with the creators of the game, and they explain some of the back story. It really does convey a sense of putting emphasis on story and setting rather than putting an emphasis on gameplay and balance.

Rebel Galaxy is a new twist on the old formula "Elite" (which is itself based on the Traveller RPG). You start in a wimpy ship you roam local cluster, dock with various stations, and when you can, buy a jump drive and jump to a different system in the cluster, and perhaps follow the main story missions and see what happened to your aunt...
The different part here instead of of 3D space, the fighting is on a 2D plane (you can only turn left/right), and instead of weapons that aims ahead, your weapons are a mix of auto-aimming turrets and broadside weapons. And there are a WIDE variety of weapons, projectile, beam, missile, with different effects on shields and armor/hull. The ships also vary from little frigates to huge dreadnoughts (all of which can be bought). In fact, different factions have different availability of weapons and ships!
Add this to events within the system that affects the economy, and dozens of commodities to trade, and you're never short of things to do. You can stay peaceful and just do commodity trading and speedy delivery, or even just go mine an asteroid field (with mining lasers), or you can go all crossbones and threaten traders to give you their cargo (or just shoot them and pick up what's left from their wreckage. Or perhaps, be mercenary and go after bounties and undertake missions from Mercenary Guild or Merchant Guild (if you pay the fee). With 6 levels of weapons, over a dozen "components" to enhance your ship (armor, shields, and deflectors, plus scanner enhancements and more) there are many ways to outfit the ship the way you want.
There are also plenty of models of ships, from fast frigates all the way up to dreadnoughts, as well as haulers (freighters).
There are even mods that added more weapons plus make the previously unavailable ships available.
The problem with this ship is once you finish the story missions, the game feels just like grinding, as you had to do missions to afford the bigger ships and better weapons (and those cost a LOT, with a single Mk6 weapon worth one of the smaller ships, and a larger ship can mount up to 16 of them...)
And depending on who you shoot, your relations with that faction and that faction's enemies increases or decreases.
But basically, you're making your way in this open world, and leave your mark on it. Add it to the music and it's a good "twist" on the genre that hadn't seen too much innovation.

Pros:
- Space dogfighting. The broadside cannon system is interesting, and keeping the fighting mostly in 2D solves a lot of the problems associated with this idea. It's enjoyable for a while.
- Good story. Interesting enough for the length of the game.
- Great soundtrack - look for the playlist on Spotify. I love how when combat happens the music gets more aggressive.
Cons:
- So damn grindy. In between story missions you'll need to buy improvements on your ship. Have fun doing tons of redundant quests or flying everywhere trying to trade for money.
- Speaking of trade, it's largely a waste of time. While you can certainly make money flying around and taking advantage of market conditions, there's never enough stock of anything to make large amounts of money without making the rounds of every solar system. Towards  the end of the game trade is outright worthless as any cargo drop from a ship is worth more than an entire shipload of cargo that you purchased.
- Mining is worthless unless you get lucky, don't bother.

Homefront is, perhaps, one of the most egregious offenders in the world of short campaign FPS. I completed the single player portion  in around 4 hours on the Hard difficulty (at least an hour was spent on the final, 7th, level). That is a disgustingly paltry amount of content. There is a harder difficulty but, while it might have doubled the playtime of the story mode, it would have invariably made the game even less fun.
It's a shame, the idea of fighting a guerilla war IN the US could be done in a truly engaging manner if only we were made to care about any of the characters or their motivations. The North Korean soldiers are inhuman, they are monsters, which is supposed to make you feel like you're a hero but, becuase the hostile factions are essentially caricatures and your allies are poorly fleshed out, it falls flat.
When I downloaded this game I knew it wasn't going to be anything special but the level of mediacrotity truly astounded me. Only two weapons in the entire game felt good, the pistol and the shotgun, everything else felt like a paintball gun. To the game's benefit, barring effective range (shotgun), all the weapons are pretty well viable in any situation but to accomplish that it feels like they just change the fire rate and appearence for most of the guns.
The game's difficulty curve is another problem. It feels like the developers designed the game with as many cheap ways to kill the player as possible. In many situations I would go up a ramp or turn a corner or hide behind cover and instantly be killed in a way that feels, as a player, completely unfair.
If you want to play a guerilla warfare in America game, I recommend Freedom Fighters.

This game give you alot of feeling. In other games, if you kill a member of the innocent, you just kill him. There's no major consequence. But in This War of Mine, you need to deal with the survivor's pain and the stuff they say are really sad and hard to ignore, unless you're a cold blooded killer yourself.
Overall, a great game. Gotta have to play a bit to really master it though.

This game is not new but even so the fun factor that is missing from so many games, is very high with Bioshock 2.  Achieves the rare combination of good graphics and non stop fun game play.  The tasks, abilities and powers you find for your character in the game, along with the story, are perfectly paced in such a way that it takes an awful lot of gameplay to even make you feel like stopping for a while. I am easily bored by a lot of games, and tired of wasting money on games I get bored of after 5 minutes.  As carefully as i try to choose games (by watching the YT  videos and the demo if they have one that works)...I often buy a game and just play it for a few minutes, then never play it again, because they lack fun factor and bore me to death.  Not this one.  The story is easy paced, introduced very gradually while you get used to the game elements, and the story progression is extremely well crafted.  Story pacing is genius, allowing you to simply take it  in gradually,  rather then beating you over the head with it as in "infinite".
It's easy to suspend your disbelief at the story, which is important,  because what a story you are living.  You are Subject Delta, an old time diving suit wearing, plasma wielding ubermensch with super human powers achieved by dosing yourself with "plasmids".  You are in an underwater city called "Rapture" (the story gets explained to you along the way as much or as little as you  choose, by dozens of tape recorders simply lying around  that you can play and listen to if you choose to).
"Rapture " is an underwater city built in the late 1950's as some kind of social and corporate experiment.  Rapture has apparently lost its novelty and most inhabitants have left.  It is underpopulated and is fast becoming decrepit.  It is leaking seawater, breaking down, and slowly failing but is still filled with (hostile and drug addicted) human inhabitants, led by your nemesis Dr Sophia Lamb, the overlord of Rapture.  She is a perfect  villain who is a sort of female Heinrich Himmler, and she hates you with a passion for some reason.  It's clear she has no compunction to using and manipulating people,  including her own daughter, like a Dr Mengele in some kind of Nazi experiment while getting them to obey her at the same time. Dr Lamb  will regularly taunt you over the PA, and send legions of her subjects the "citizens of rapture" (the drug addicts) to come and attack you.  But you are more then capable of taking them on by yourself, since not only are you armed to the teeth with a metric ton of 1950's era weapons (shotgun, gatling gun, rivet gun, mini turrets, spear gun, rocket launcher et. al.) but you also earn, find and choose even more "biological powers"  (the "Bioshock" elements) that you emit from your own body like a lethal bad breath - these are powers (achieved by "Plasmids") that you find or earn as you go along.   The array of powers you can get to fight back against the hostile citizens of Rapture is impressive:  the ability to throw flame on people attacking you, stun them with electricity, throw small cyclones on the ground that will toss them in the air and injure them, freeze them into ice.  You can send out a scout to invisibly see what's up ahead and spot traps and enemies before they see you.  You can put out a decoy and watch as your enemies attack it while you hit 'em with a nasty plasmid or weapon.  And a lot more too.
Every time you earn another plasmid, it is accompanied by an amusing 10 second long 1950's style black and white intro film that explains what you can do with it.  And the more powerful plasmids ("flame", "freeze" and cyclone trap plasmids) also have 2 or even 3 levels you can choose to make them even more powerful.  Along the way you  pick up, or buy ammo, cash, med packs, "eve" (the substance that powers your plasmids), booze, smokes, and free weapon upgrades.  You also get to hack or destroy all sorts of door locks, machine gun turrets, safes full of cash and ammo, and security cameras.
The game is  well designed and the all-important fun-factor as i said, is very high. Replay value is also high.  The DLC "Minerva's Den" is more of the same, but just as fun as the base game.  It is worth playing too.  IMO this is the best of the Bioshock games, the first one is just about as fun but the story elements are not quite as refined.  "Infinite"  is a good sequal and worth playing also, but maybe a little too refined is the only way i can describe it.  Sliding along steel cables in the air is not particularly fun and loses its novelty pretty fast, for me, nor does "Infinite" have much of an engaging story despite the hyper-realism and abstract philosophy elements that do little but muck up the gameplay. Not to mention, that dragging Elizabeth along slows down the story despite her eye candy appeal, which is all she is pretty much good for re. fun factor.  But it is this game that I find myself playing over and over.

(For the record I've played the original Bioshock and completed the game so ignore my hours on this remastered version)
An absolute classic. The graphics have been greatly improved and makes the game look incredible for a 2007 game. As of the newest updates the game runs both smoothly and seamlessy - as of my 10 hours with the game I've experienced no corrupted save files, no crashes, no FPS drops, no freezes etc. It runs very well.
Now onto the game itself -
The gameplay itself is extraordinary - the seamless way that both guns/shooting and genetic superpowers are woven into the game make for an incredible experience. As a shooter is holds up really well - there's a large variety of guns/shooters including machine guns, shotguns, pistols, crossbows, rocket launchers. Then on the flip side the plasmid variety ranges from shooting fire, freezing enemies, electrifying enemies. Even innovative ideas like causing enemies to attack each other or hypnotizing Big Daddies to protect you. The gameplay is fun, innovative and original.
The game also has an incredibly rich story. The story has interesting villains, a heap ton of twists and overall a rich and immersive experience that really drags you into the game. Although the game itself is linear, the immersive story actually makes this a positive trait of the game with the way the story unravels and the many secrets you find along the way. Definitely one of the best stories of a game I've played in recent years.
The atmosphere and immersion is a 10/10 and arguably one of the best traits of the game. The city of Rapture and the way it's created, the mystery and awe of it creates a cryptic and incredibly immersive experience. I can't put it into words, you just really feel like you're in Rapture. The many cassette tapes and radio messages also add to the immersion providing backstory and world building for the underwater city.
Cons - The final boss is somewhat underwhelming although it doesn't take that much away from the game. The linear style of the game and lack of side quests can be argued to be a negative trait of the game but in my opinon the linear style just adds to the immersion and builds up the incredible story even more whilst taking away very little from the gameplay. In fact the lack of side quests just makes the game a much more fulfilling experience, rather than adding pointless side quests that run the risk of taking away from the immersive experience and story.
Conclusion - BUY BUY BUY. In fact buy every game in the trilogy. All 3 are fantastic games that are definitely among the top games of the FPS genre.

When juxtaposed against all of the titles Battlerite can be most easily compared to, it seems like a game that would evaporate into obscurity.  Yet when I started the game up, fully expecting an arena fighting riff on the typical MOBA formula to not hold my attention; I was pleasantly surprised with how well-balanced and straight up fun the whole experience turned out to be.
Typically when I play a game like League of Legends it feels as if I’m waiting for AI controlled creeps to catch up and am tethered by both the pace they run and defending their fragile health bars.  It reeks of escort mission banalities that I despise in other games.
Battlerite from Stunlock Studios shuns the towers and AI-controlled creeps of similar games and instead focuses on 2v2 and 3v3 Arena battles that play similar to a MOBA but incorporates elements such as skillshot abilities and no respawns during rounds.  Think Wildstar meets Arena of Heroes or Hunger Dungeon.
You are asked to pick a loadout before readying up, this involves picking one passive ability for your hero that will persist throughout the match.  These passives are tied to a specific ability; granting effects such as longer debuff duration, healing on hit, and many others.  There is a 2-minute time limit to each round, first to win 3 rounds wins the match.  The match structure alone facilitates much faster gameplay and dynamic strategies compared to Battlerite’s peers. Most MOBAs have universally accepted strategies for who is perfect for what lane and what the perfect composition of support, ranged, and melee.  Battlerite trims the fat of these games and focuses solely on team-fighting.
Thankfully, Battlerite’s smaller maps and hero count allow a player to become pretty familiar with most heroes’ capabilities after a few matches.  Plus there aren’t lanes and tower locations to memorize!  Maps are instead dotted with health and energy pickups.  Energy confers the use of some more powerful abilities such as genre staple Ultimate moves.  There are also EX movies that use this meter, requiring a bit of resource management and deciding when it might be best to go for higher-risk moves.
The game really shines in the most heated moments when you try to outwit your opponents with quick reflexive mouse clicks and guessing their next moves.  Baiting a ranged opponent into using a spell with long casting time while you close the gap with a melee type or using your hero’s mobility skill to dodge an ultimate attack are immensely satisfying.  Deaths never feel unearned and you’ll always think to yourself about what you could’ve done to avoid your opponent’s onslaught, no cheap kills from creeps!  It’s this feeling primarily that I think will keep players on the hook, being a purely skill-based game makes it a standout in the crowded Free to Play battle arena genre.
Currently, there are 21 heroes available for purchase with a weekly rotation of 6 champions available for free.  It costs $30 to buy all champions or $5 to buy a single one.  Frustratingly, the premium currency cannot be bought in $5 denominations so you’ll have to buy a $7.50 currency pack if you want to take the piecemeal route.  You can buy them from in-game currency accrued during matches, but it will take a LONG time if you want to take that route.  This gets doubly frustrating since familiarizing yourself with each hero’s abilities also allows you to counter them better, but the price isn’t too steep and I would highly recommend buying this pack if you also want all the future characters Stunlock trots out next.
Verdict
Battlerite is easily recommended to anyone who enjoys MOBAs but even more easily recommended to folks who dislike the AI and objective-based trappings of these kinds of games.  Working out strategies with friends and executing a perfect gameplan or analyzing what you did wrong and making adjustments is more compelling than any other game I’ve played in this genre.  If Stunlock can maintain this momentum and really throw some weight into marketing the game well, we may have sleeper hit on our hands.

I'm old enough to have fond memories of playing Privateer and Freelancer.  I picked up Rebel Galaxy hoping to renew my love for those games.  While I didn't quite find what I was looking for, I found a solid game worth playing.
For people who loved the aforementioned games for the open-ended exploration, the ability to build your bankroll by buying low on some planets and selling high on others, upgrading ships and weapons as you progressed, and the intriguing storyline, this game is definitely worth playing because it does all of those things well.  For those who loved those games because of the thrill of small craft in-cockpit open space dogfighting, you should probably look elsewhere. Rebel Galaxy managed to take the inherent 3D nature of space and reduce it to 2D, implementing a colonial era ship "broadside" style combat as if on the surface of invisible water.  It isn't necessarily bad, but not my cup of tea.  Essentially, you can really only do one thing, turn and fire over and over.  It gets repetitive after a while and eventually I found myself wishing I could auto-resolve battles to move on through the story.  That being said, the combat was not so off-putting as to keep me from playing until the end of the main story.  Bottom line, this game is worth what you pay for it but don't expect a masterpiece.

Crea offers compelling exploration, gathering, crafting, building, and character customization experiences. Unfortunately, it also offers a poorly explained "chaos" system that may or may not pertain only to crafting and terrible controls. Be prepared to unexpectedly fall and to be overrun by enemies while switching item and spell sets or trying to use your grappler.
Combat is rarely fun regardless of weapon choice or enemy type and it is often very difficult, like when ghost-like enemies called Harvesters move and shoot through terrain in a tight cave system, killing you without much of a chance. Some monsters seem to trigger a jarring player-character teleport like what happens in some network games when players have network latency issues. I did find a boss or something rather boss-like that seems to be invulnerable until one figures out how to drop its shield or does so by accident, but I haven't yet defeated it because it and its minions are better at attacking me than I am at fumbling with Crea's controls.
The user interface could use some work too. For example, the set-switching feels clunky (especially while in combat), it looks and feels strange to have placeable items hovering at the mouse pointer when I just want to gather or harvest, and after picking up a spell or item icon there does not seem to be a way to cancel dragging the icon (e.g., the escape key, which closes overlays). On top of all of that, overlays just kind of end up all over the place, blocking the view of the game environment. It would be nice if they could be more neatly arranged and controlled (e.g., auto-arranged, snapped, and toggled in sets) and perhaps translucent.
Hopefully Crea will improve in time. I am sure many people will enjoy the game as it is, but it stopped being fun for me long before I could discover all it has to offer.

Rebel Galaxy: Ah what a fine Adventure made by 2x Developers :) Imagine a Firefly Space Adventure with Mass Effect's space flight bits and the naval combat from AC: Black Flag. You can trade, mine or fight & each one has it's affect from Rp point of view. For example, let's say you are bringing food to a station in famine: you can increase your profit by blowing up relief ships heading to the station (or not). You can negotiate your way out of fights by dropping cargo, bribe officials to smuggle illegal goodies out of a station :P Definitely Worth a buy at full price for ppl who enjoy this Genre & why not for newcomers heh. Pirates & Aliens fighting with the player in the mid. Add a bit of mining & different upgrades for ship & there's decent Low Budget Space Flight Boom Boom :) Liked the sideways navy-like battles. Your actions affect your reputation with the citizenry, the militia & various Pirate Factions.
Series of story missions take you from one side of the sector to another & each mission, main or side is marked with its "risk level". That Allows you to judge whether to take it & do right away or take some time to upgrade your equipment first. Soundtrack in Rebel Galaxy is Atmospheric, Real gritty & includes world country rock tunes. Soundtrack had big impact on my decision whether to buy RG when watched the Trailer :) Paid full price at Steam & happy for supporting Devs :) Only 2x Negative things to say are: Can't Look Map inside Station & Can't use "Engage Warp" Keybind separated from Interact Key. For ex: Using Tractor Beam to take items. Frustrating as need to wait to pass some item(s) floating in space or take them before can activate Warp.
Also sometimes "Engage Warp" Pops to screen with delay. Not good when in rush to catch Pirate Lord or in a hurry to save some Ally. Minor things ofc so didn't ruin Goodiness lvl :) Ppl who look for a well engaging story aren't going to find one, but the characters have tons of personality & story is ok :) This is good work as 1st adventure from Double Damage games. Whenever I finish a Hidden Object Game, I wonder whether I should review it. I mean, it's a HOG, right? We know how these things work, don't we? You typically expect a cliched story, some dodgy voice acting, and yet that strangely chilled out mix of adventure, puzzle and hidden object shenanigans. But hey, I really enjoyed this one, so you get a hear about it.
I'd say this is probably the best HOG game I've played. I wouldn't put this (or in fact any HOG) into any kind of classic game category, steady on! But still, as these things go, this was a good one. The story isn't quite as one-dimensional as it first appears, the voice acting is probably the best I've heard in a HOG (this isn't saying much, admittedly, but it's far less cringe-worthy than most), and the rest of the game is well put together. There's the usual ridiculousness of having to find a dozen misplaced doodads in order to open a simple door, but that's part of the appeal! In fact, it's modestly challenging in places, but never enough to stump you. Some of the hidden object scenes are quite difficult (cleverly hidden, rather than pixel hunting), some of the other puzzles are moderately inventive, and the game isn't over in three hours like some of them. Amazingly, the bonus chapter doesn't feel like it was put together by the intern, and is actually a) quite long and b) the same quality as the rest of the game.
If you've never experienced the strange appeal of these games, I'd say this was a pretty good jumping off (or in) point. They are very frequently on sale or in bundles, so keep your eyes peeled.

When I purchased this game, I wasn't expecting much due to it being early access, what I received instead was a large world with interesting creatures and apells. Some of the servers I've played, mostly PvP, have actually had really friendly and helpful people who won't necessarily attack you on the get go, I hope that mentality stays. Within this review I will list the positives, negatives and what I think the developers could do to change the game to benefit everyone.
*************************************************************************************************************************************
Positives;
*************************************************************************************************************************************
- The building system and buildables all look like they belong in the world, they don't look too abstract or too hyper unrealistic, they follow the medieval/fantasy patterns that you'd expect to see. (Wood looking a bit worn, stone looking a bit weathered and the last looking like your local arch-mage has summoned it).
- The dungeons and other areas to fight all prove a challenge at the right level, whilst this will also be in the negatives, the dungeons are easily a challenge  when you play solo, the mobs hit as much and give as much back, yesterday I was pushing through a whole cave of demonic imps and at the end, it felt like a boss fight when a huge black dragon was waiting for me - also felt satisfaction and a sense of "Yeah I dunnit" when I slew it.
- The spells are diverse and interesting, some kill at long range and some kill at short range, surely good as everyone has different play styles. I currently roll with fireball and lightning storm on my staff, and enrage and pacify on my melee. Whilst not ideal, it works for me which is what the games spell system is about. "If it works for you, use it.
- Broomsticks are a really good way of travelling and the developers really nailed the system of broomsticks, they're a nuisance in PvP, but it's expected. The speed and grace of your zoomstick compare to nought. (Except for a black dragon).
In general, the game play is exceptional, sometimes challenging yet rewarding and always gives you something to do.
*************************************************************************************************************************************
Negatives:
*************************************************************************************************************************************
- The mana system is pretty annoying, given that every action you do other than crafting and walking costs mana. It has no passive regeneration so if you're stuck up a mountain without mana potions you're good as dead, which is unfortunate.
- Health pools/Mana pools, not the ones you can build, but the ones located in safe zones and throughout the world are completely useless. They restore your pool extremely slowly which is annoying, no doubt frustrating.
- Some dungeons have too little mobs for too much of a reward, what I mean by this is that it feels sort of cheaty receiving upgrades when you slew two zombies. If possible, dungeons should be instanced and fleshed out so it actually feels like its not just a cave - the downwards tower is a fine example.
- Some of the bugs in the game are pretty bad - game interrupting & convoluted. My companion in my party logged off & relogged into a wall and couldn't play the game any longer.
Whilst there are more negatives, I can't really think of what to write compared to what other people have written.
*************************************************************************************************************************************
TL;DR
*************************************************************************************************************************************
In short, a good game for what it costs. Good exceptional gameplay that you can spend whole hours immersing yourself within,
with amazing beasts, dungeons and spells. However, some bugs ruin the gameplay and it gets repetitive at times.
*************************************************************************************************************************************
Suggestions:
*************************************************************************************************************************************
- Instead of using the trinket slot for broomsticks, perhaps a slot for broomsticks would be better than replacing amulets.

I’ve reviewed HOGs which had pure excuse plots they obviously cared nothing about. I’ve reviewed HOGs with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plots they took way too seriously. I’ve even stumbled into an HOG or two which had a fairly decent plot. But this is the first time I’ve seen an HOG that is fairly accepting of how campily nonsensical its plot is.
Our protagonists (Err... Mrs. Mom and Miss McGuffin?) have been dealing with cursed pirate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for three games now, and they can no more be bothered to pretend to be surprised and horrified than Princess Daisy can be bothered to gasp in shock when Bowser busts in on her harborside museum exhibition  in order to kidnap her to his undead pirate island. The fact that the pirate crew consists of a bunch of comedy skeletons who can't brandish their cutlasses without provoking peals of laughter doesn't help.
The game is weirdly inconsistent, actually. Most of the plot that has to do with Davy Jones himself is played fairly straight, and there are some really daft "scare jump" scenes that are presumably not intended to be humorous. For instance: there’s “someone” sitting in a charge, wearing 18th century clothes and a powdered wig, facing away from you. When you click, there’s a freaking scare chord, because the revelation of a spooky skeleton is such a goddamned surprise.
Incredibly incongruous because the heroines clearly don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Within seconds, they've torn off that skeleton’s arm and used it to retrieve a key on a table right outside the door, so I guess it wasn’t THAT much of a shock. All while maintaining the same “well gee-shucks, I guess we better deal with this skeleton pirate and get home in time for dinner” tone.
I know most of my "Quality voice acting in Hidden Object Games" videos are skipped, but
. It's kinda amazing just how mellow everyone are about this PotC ripoff... I mean, spooky skeleton situation. (Also, check out the end of the video, as I leave my daughter hostage while Davy Jones threatens to murder her, and go back to her regular location - she's still there, whining at me to hurry up)
Puzzles are fairly generic, though also intuitive and mostly-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t free - exactly the sort of thing you'll see a dozen times over if (for some daft reason) you decide to play thirty HOG's in a row. A few bloody stupid spots – a lot of “keep on clicking at random until you’ve cleared all the leaves / brushed away all the dust”. One particularly dumb moment is when you need water for a plant – you can’t get it from waterfall, you have to use the sea water on the same screen instead. No comedy puzzles that would really keep in tone with the campy skeletons. You can skip Hidden Object Scenes with Mahjong games, something I've never once tried.
One negative - the game is often fairly vague about what you need to do in order to progress. You click on an obstacle and get a statement essentially saying "this is an obstacle" rather than "I need to use Item X on this". Your inventory generally isn't so full of inventory items that trying them all out is a chore, but still.
No guide, good map with fast travel enabled, fairly little backtracking (and what there is mitigated by the fast travel option).
Generic but decent gameplay, unintentionally (?) hilarious cutscenes and interactions.

8/15 update - 16 days later. An update has rolled out every Weds (at least) for the last few weeks. Server stability has improved and more content is being added on a regular basis.
This game has some early access bugs but is otherwise an excellent time.
Point of reference. I play on a small private PvE server most of the time.
As of 7-30-17... These aspects are based on the game itself, not your particular server where player characters in a pvp setting (yes there is a pve only option too) may affect your individual experience or your particular pc and its different hardware/software configurations which may cause their own issues. This review assumes the game worked for you in its current state at the time this review was written.
The Best:
-You feel like a budding Sorcerer King with every step of the journey and progression. The spells all have great impact and when you cast them you really feel like you're wielding elemental wrath (at least with the staff, that was my weapon of choice).
- The building system is beautiful. Whether you're making a nice wooden house or a sky scraping wizard's tower your place can be absolutely gorgeous and striking.
-The beasts you can tame are likewise well modeled and excellent to utilize.
-The Company has realeased several patches and some new content over the first few days after the early access launch. these folks care about their game and want to make it worth your while.
The Worst:
It's early access so there are many emergent problems.
-Server stability (which has gotten much better over the last few days) is good but expect you may have the odd crash as you are out in the world going about your business.
-Voice communication is currently choppy and hinders RP
-Frame rates and server latency can cause some combats to be jumpy and enemy AI is very basic
The Future:
There are a few fates in store for this game
1- Early access reviews will slap the 'Mostly negative'/'mixed' stigmata on the game's rating and there will not be enough players to maintain the company's revenue and the game will slowly collapse.
2- Continued development, steamlining, content increases, and bug fixing will make this game into a stable magical experience to quicken the blood and make your dreams of being a Socerer King among mere mortals come true.
Should I buy it? :
- Do you love the fantasy sandbox genre and have a few bucks to spare and some time?
--- Then yes you should. For the price of a movie and a meal you'll get more hours of entertainment out of this than those same respective purchases
- Are you just really excited after seeing an intro video or a streamer?
--- Add this game to your wish list and keep your eye on it carefully. Read its news page for the next few weeks and watch the patch notes. Keep watching the videos and the streamers
- Are you hung up about this game and its competition (which was released a few days before this game) and don't know which one to get?
--- If you want to support the underdog indie studio try to make something special then get this one. If you want to get something which was a bit more polished at launch but whose company is a bit laggard in development then go with the competitor.

Bioshock 2 places the player back in the undersea world of Rapture.  The game takes place several years after the events of the first game.  In this game you play as Subject Delta, a Big Daddy that is trying to find his Little Sister.  There is more to it, but I'd rather avoid any major spoilers.
Rapture looks better than ever in the second entry of the series.  The graphics have been improved in every way.  There isn't any undersea combat, but walking around at the bottom of the sea was a beautiful experience.  The combat and controls have been vastly improved in every way.  Although it was sad to see that the old hacking system was removed, the new one keeps you in battle and has a far more fluid feeling.  The story isn't as interesting as it was in the previous game, but it is far from bad.  They probably should have fleshed out the story from the Minvera's Den DLC and used it for the base game instead.
Despite all of the positive aspects of this game, I cannot recommend it.  I don't know if this game is a sloppy console port, but it sure feels like one.  I played this with a GTX 960 (a much better video card than the suggested 8800 GT) and I thought my computer was going to have a meltdown.  The game runs so poorly that the developers should be ashamed.  I spent some time reading other reviews and it doesn't seem like I'm the only person that has had this issue.  I rushed through the game because I was concerned about the strain it was placing on my computer even after drastically reducing the settings. Sad, it might have been fun to play through a second time.
If it weren't for the performance issues I would recommend this one. Alas, here we are.  Purchase and play this game at your own risk.

This game has a lot of nice things going for it, the aestetics are well designed and while the humor is not brilliant it does have its share of chuckle worthy moments.
But, it is abysmally slow. Like in dungeon keeper you rely on mining gold in order to drive the expansion of your dungeon, but where dungeonkeepers imps are efficient little speedfreaks the worker units in Dungeons 2 move more like arthritic old men and very large ammounts of time are spent waiting for them to collect and move gold to your vault so it can be spent. This is further aggravated by a very restrictive population cap that prevents you from keeping more than a handful of workers around without comprimising your army size. It is possible to upgrade your workers to move at a more acceptable pace, but by the time these upgrades become available you have progressed so far that they no longer usefull.
The game does not, in fact, have very much content to it, but it is artificially padded by this resource throttling. The campaign is fairly short and skirmish play pretty lackluster. Most of the skirmish maps are taken directly from the campaign and simply stripped off their narative and objectives.
I had some fun with this game, but only after i started cheating to give myself gold and speed up progression to something a little faster than continental drift. I cannot recommend getting this game unless these pacing issues are adressed, which seems unlikely.

This is one of my favorite games on steam, even though I have not played very much. It is like a combination of Starbound and Terraria, and has many other things as well. The research system makes things a bit more difficult and helps to balance out the loot you often get when you go into dungeons or high level areas. The idea of things getting harder as you go out into the world is one of my favorite features and really helps to make the game interesting. You have to take risks and go out farther to find rare materials as well as to level up faster when facing tougher enemies. I also really enjoy the chaos crafting mini game (even though I am terrible at it) because the increased chances of modifiers and quality can make a very powerful weapon or tool. The talent leveling system is also pretty good, you have to use the talent a good bit to improve upon your skill in it. There is also a character leveling system which gives stat points as well as improving all stats. The bosses seem to level up as you defeat them over and over, so that is nice, is keeps the game interesting. Well, one boss is always the same level as the player which means that boss fight is pretty even unless the player improves their combat talents. Again, this is one of my favorite games and I can't wait to see what's in store for it.

TlDR; It's nothing like Dungeon Keeper and falls off in far too many areas. Not worth over 5$.
Alright to start off I have played Dungeons 1 and the special steam eddition one.
I should have known after the special edition that it would not be a good game but I tried to believe
in Kalypso. Yeah that didn't work too well.
So let's talk graphics. They are pretty decent. The landscape changes as you take certain areas in the overworld and that can seem cool for most people. However, if you do not have a good computer it will be terribly laggy when things like this happen.
Minions. The minions are.. alright? I can't find the exact words to use to describe them. They need more diversity. In the original Dungeon they had quite a few interesting minions that actually had decent consepts that simply needed to be refined and expanded. There is an enchantment system where you can give a buff to your minions but the buff tends to rarely be worth anything. Even if it is worth a little something there is no heavy effect on gameplay that would make you want to search for them.
Concept. The concept of sending your minons to the surface is an interesting idea but VERY poorly executed. The positioning of the characters is terrible. There is very little you can do to organize your minions and organize them for battle. You are more or less throwing them at the enemies hoping for the best.
Comparison. We can compare this to a lot of Dungeon Keeper similar games but let's compare it to the ones that stand out the most. The Original Dungeon. This was what got me so into the game series. Retaking your throne from your crazy girlfriend and having tons of challenges and boss fights up to that point? It was quite a few hours of fun and while the replay value wasn't much it had a lot that could be polished. It got me looking forward to the sequals. Dungeons 2 is nothing like Dungeons. It feels more aimed at children with its very cartoonish feel. It is less dark than Dungeons 1. The Overlord or main character from Dungeons 1 is.. well gone. It may have something to do with the steam special which admitibly I didn't finish because it made me cringe with all its Lord of the Rings references and terrible gameplay. However, it is just not the sequal you'd expect at all. It feels like a new choppy game.
Dungeon Keeper. The god of dungeon games. A lot of people think most games can't hold a damned candle to it and they would be right in my opinion but you have to give other games a chance. The style for most of these games was obviously taken from this then pardon my language but it is as though someone took a big steaming♥♥♥♥♥♥on it. I have yet to see a decent revamped version of it and Dungeons 2 is no acception.
But I'm rambling! Overall, the point of this is that the gameplay is not even close to worth 10$ on sale MUCH LESS 40$. You'd have to have very poor taste to enjoy this game.

I'm not a motorsports fan, but every few years I get a hankering for a good racing game--probably because I played so much
on the SNES as a kid.
There's a certain appeal to chasing after mathematical perfection while thumbing one's nose at the limits of space-time.  In a pure race, you have only your wits--and, well, the mechanical works of art representing the pinnacle of human locomotion help too.  (This is why Mario Kart, with its muddied waters, is just a "driving" game--not "Real Racing.")  This is the thread that runs though my enjoyment of the handful of racing games I've played over the years:
(SNES)
(Xbox)
(Xbox)
(Shamecube)
(Xbox)
(PC)
Before playing
(
), rallying was my favorite real-world racing theme for a video game.  I guess in some ways it still is; there's nothing quite like barreling through the wilderness, scraping by on barely-managed chaos.  In a hillclimb event (known as "Trailblazer" in
), a spoonful of dirt or snow can mean the difference between a record time and a wrecked car.
But as exciting as rallying can be, point-to-point racing can get pretty lonely.
included events like Rallycross to tide me over, but at some point I missed the nudging and dancing that goes on in a closed-circuit race.  Enter
.  Dividing its content into five different driving disciplines (
,
,
,
, and
), it plays like a lovingly-crafted tribute to motorsports of all kinds--even ones I didn't know I could appreciate.
The Touring and Street events really hit the spot for bumper-to-bumper racing, but in order to unlock special GRID events, you need to reach a minimum level in every discipline.  I've also dabbled in Online a bit; finding a race is difficult if you don't have a group of friends to race with, but the weekly Racenet Challenges can be played alone.
The game subtracts vehicle repair costs from your winnings, which encourages clean driving.  When I first started out, I was sidling up against the AI drivers at every corner in attempts to wrestle away a position or two (pretty much how I've always played racing games aside from
)--it still happens, but now I'm more conscientiously braking to avoid collisions and earn places with grace rather than grit.
Codemasters' love for the chase really shines through in
; and if the other events can manage to get their hooks in me the way Touring and Street racing have, this may be the last racing game I play for a few years.

For example, version 1.0.10 was an unstable opt-in beta attempt to fix some multiplayer issues.  It did fix some of the issues but created others.  We just clicked on the live stream button in the game which took us right to Jasson live, then he reproduced the problem, tracked down three issues and fixed them, and had a new version 1.0,12 out the same day.  Now we are up and playing again,  The problems that are left are minor annoyances which Jason is aware of and is working daily to fix, and will have fixed them all soon.  This game is worth the money, and the developers back their product and give the highest level of service and help imaginable, in my humble opinion.  I am totally happy with the game and with my experience with the developer. I originally played and beat this game on my Xbox 360 a couple years back. And after getting it free on Steam through a graphics card I got on my PC, I've decided to play through the campaign again.
Warning! There may be spoilers ahead!
In Absolution, you play as a bald man named David Bateson, who has a UPC code on the back of his head. You eternally look like you're up to no good, yet by slightly putting your hand in front of your face, you can temporarily avert suspicion, then run behind a wall until the person chasing you decides to give up their search, putting you back in the clear...sort of.
Not long into the game, you shoot a naked woman who is taking a shower, and then help a young girl escape a life of treachery. These are some very emotional scenes, as you, a clone who is normally incapable of emotion, suddenly develops a conscience and becomes a really cool, fuzzy hearted contract killer.
Powers Boothe (one of your bosses) is now angry at you for helping the little orphan gal, so he decides to make you dead. But you don't want any of that, so you decide to make him dead.
In order to stop Powers Boothe from tracking and finding you, you cut the UPC symbol out of your bald head with a toothpick or something else that is sharp. And then, instead of buying a wig, you hide the gaping wound with a ginormous band-aid. It looks like it hurts, but David Bateson doesn't care.
Making things worse for you, a really scuzzballish cowboy and his half-wit son start trying to have you knocked off (because they're evil). Violence ensues, more thugs and lowlifes come after you, and you're still bald.
Eventually (and this is way later in the game), some nuns try to convert you to their religion, but you don't want to be preached at, so you politely decline. They take offense to it and try to kill you while you're at a peaceful motel, relaxing. You are forced to defend yourself...and that's that. They die. You also go into a cornfield.
Not long after this, David Bateson, who is tired of being the target of these villainous fiends, overcomes all the evils of life and defeats the scuzzballish cowboy, Powers Boothe, and countless NPC's.
In the end, the little orphan girl is safe. The nice lady you shot in the shower is no longer dead, and everyone lives happily ever after.
I hope that review helps everyone. All in all, I enjoyed the game. I would like to make a quick list of things that would have been fun to have in Absolution, though:
-The old mini map from Blood Money and Contracts
-Upgrading and selecting weapons before each mission
-A wider variety of colorful missions like in Blood Money (The neighborhood with the clown, and the cajun wedding with alligators immediately come to mind for me)
- The ability for David Bateson to grow hair
- I'd like to be able to shoot goblins
- I want David Bateson to be able to ride a pony and wield a sword
- More clowns
- Cool weapons, like a bazooka with a silencer, or a really pointy pencil
- The ability to use magic
- I wish David Bateson could fly, go invisible, and cut guns in half with his mind
That's it! I would definitely recommend this game to a friend, or to someone who is not a friend.

I don't FULLY understand the pile-on distaste for this game. It's not without bits of warrant, to be sure, but I've enjoyed playing it overall. I only played the game's single player campaign, so I've nothing to offer on the multiplayer game.
It plays just fine. I've had no issues with the controls, no issues with hit connect or anything like that. I adjusted absolutely nothing before knocking through the campaign. I haven't had a buggy experience at all, and it runs appropriately well.
The presentation, aside from the sort of hammy story that absolutely plagues the entire Call of Duty genus of games, is altogether just fine. Nothing looks or sounds unacceptable in any way (perhaps somewhat dated even at its release date), although I'm sure sticklers for specs and performance maximization would find plenty wrong that I'm just not tuned to find.
The report and impact of weapons is satisfying and varies fairly well, even if it seems like the great bulk of weapons are automatics effective at medium-long range. For what it's worth, the weapons you have are usually what you'd prefer in most situations.
The game is never particularly difficult. You may give a few sections a try again or two, but don't shop here for any masochist hardcore challenges.
In all, it's just a perfectly serviceable Call of Duty-esque corridor/situation shooter to plow through if you don't want something to think or care about any deeper than knocking down the next target in front of you. It's certainly nothing rev... oh, goddammit, after that near-pun, I have to just end the review.

Also the game seems a lot darker and more brutal than previous titles. For me this was ok, since I like the brutal kills and takedowns. It's a matter of personal taste, some will like it some will not.
Can't complain about difficulty options because there is a lot to choose from: easy, medium, hard, expert, purist.
If you are a veteran fps player I recommend choosing hard or expert and if you're a new player then easy or medium is for you. Keep in mind these difficulty options really affect gameplay when you decide to go for a sneaky run. If you decide to go on a rampage and shoot everybody, its really no challenge at all, since 47 has a decent amount of HP. Even on hard difficulty I've felt being OP. Don't get me wrong you still have to use cover and you can die pretty much fast if you don't.
So if you like nice graphics, darker setting, brutal takedowns etc., this Hitman is for you. Cheers!

After 6 long years since Hitman: Blood Money, Hitman Absolution was finally released with lots of good expectations (I even pre-ordered), and while it has great improvements over past games, it is ultimately a big disappointment.
The plot starts with 47 assigned to kill his former longtime handler Diana Burnwood after her betrayal on the ICA, 47's employer. When the finds her, he shoots her, but she explains her reasons to him and he decides to honor her wished, betraying the Agency, killing the people involved in the conspiracy while eluding it. While it's a more personal story, as promised, it's really poor. Much is unexplained or poorly so, it takes itself too seriously but with many poor attempts of humor.
Apart from 47, Diana and Victoria, pratically all characters are awful, have horrible lines and quotes and seem stoned all the time; it made me laugh watching the "Making of" video when the lead writer stated he rewrote several times the dialogues to make them good(!). By the way, while 47's iconic voice was initially replaced but eventually restored to David Bateson, Diana's voice wasn't so lucky; the new actress (Marsha Thompson) made her sound misfit and much older, which is ironic because the original actress is not only old enough to be her mother but sounded much younger and natural.
The gameplay improved A LOT, with plenty of options for 47: cover, shoulder swap, aiming, crouching, sprinting, hand-to-hand combat (with a little QTE); it favors shooting and stealth, being much more flexible than previous Hitman games in gameplay, which is excellent.
There's a new feature called Instinct mode. With the excuse of 47 being a superhuman, he can see through walls, highlight characetrs, routes, objects. It was clearly made to appeal the casual public, and unfortunately it's often needed to be used, especially for disguises (more of this below).
The graphics are mostly excellent, which beautiful enviroments, good effects and detailed main characters, especially 47; many other NPCs and secondary characters aren't as well made, looking a little cartoonish; and the bloom effect is overloaded (47's bald head shines more than the Sun).
The music is unfortunately just ok, since the Amazing Jesper Kyd is not present here; it's dynamic but with little remarkable scores and many annoying pieces of coutry music.
The missions' replay is compelling, providing plenty of options to eliminate the targets, giving more rewards for that.
Unfortunately there are 3 flaws which compromise the game a lot:
1. Level progression - Most levels are linear, from A to B, divided into segments where you only have to avoid or engage the enemies to progress, in few opportunities you can actually explore the areas to kill the targets.
2. Save/checkpoint system - Not only you can only save between missions and at each level's segment start, you also have to find the checkpoints to reload the level if you fail, but all enemies respawn (excepy for the targets), which can lead to lots of frustrations and waste of time if you have trouble to eliminate the targets. Plenty of unnecessary trial and error because of that.
3. Disguise system - By far the VERY WORST FLAW of the game; Hitman's stealth always has been designed to hide in plain sight, which means using cleverly disguises not to be detected and making your progress as efficient a possible. In Hitman Absolution the disguises only work if you use Instinct (which is limited) to fool the guards/enemies/cops,etc., which is... to hide your face with your cap/hat/...! Not only is unrealistic (in real life it makes you MORE suspicious, not less), but ridiculous to see and counterproductive, which means you can't really rely on disguises, but using hide and seek to progress though the missions, which make them more complicated than supposed to be. Again, plenty of unnecessary trial and error because of that, especially in the linear levels and the poor checkpoint system.
An interesting mode is Contracts, where you can play and create user-made Contracts. While the idea is very good, is limitating because of the previous issus described and is restrictive of the melhods used to kill the targets.
This game was a chore to finish, I only made it because I wanted to be done with it and I was curious to see how the story ended, and I say when I finally did I was much more relieved than satisfied.
Overall, the game it's not awful, but only worth buying in sales deals (although the normal price is pretty lowered nowadays). Grade: 60/100.

It's an ok game, nothing to coo to critics or completely avid gamers who absolutely adore shooters, but, this game is certainly... Different. Many compare it to postal but, gotta remember folks. There's a difference between people who go out shooting for the hell of it and people who just can't get others to leave em alone!
Anyways. On with the review.
======================
Gameplay
======================
Hatred isn't really too hot on gameplay, it's pretty much, go around, kill folks, execute them in gruesome ways to get your health back, complete the objectives, so on. So forth. What does make the game interesting is it's physics, the fact that it's an isometric shooter, but has detail when it comes to destructable buildings and explosives, which. Airs on the side of being tactical. Mostly, spree killers are far from it. They're. Spontaneous. However in this game, it starts spontaneous, but later on gets more tactical as you go along, attempting to survive waves of swat teams and armed civillians who get rougher and rougher, you gotta think ahead before you do what you're gonna do.
Calculate your best routes of escape, where the reinforcements might show up and so forth. In that aspect. It was interesting, Apart from that though? It's a little repetative with it's "quests" Torch this building, kill said population here, it gets a little samey in that aspect.
=================
Art / Graphics
=================
Surprisingly where this game shines, it's outstanding the level of detail this game has art wise, which. In some respects makes it sad that it's a isometric shooter, commonly zoomed out from said detail, but that's possibly what gives it, it's charm with it's art direction. As for the effects? The fire is crisp and ambient, the explosions are fantastically done and as for building demolition, screen effects, rain, lighting and atmosphere? It's surprisingly art....-y... For the type of game that it is. Honestly, artists of this game. Give yourselves a well earned pat on the back. As the Art / Graphics. Displayed the mayhem quite well i'd say.
==================
Sound
