I don't think there's much I can add to the numerous reviews already here, but I'm going to go ahead and add my opinion anyhow.
I've played the game some.  And then some.  I've never played Terraria (beyond the first few minutes of trying it), and never playing Starbound (though it's on my wishlist).  So playing this presented a new type of challenge for me.  I like platformers, I like building houses, I like exploring, I like crafting.  Perfect!  Backtracking a little, I like recipe based crafting.  I don't like Minecraft style crafting where you put certain things in certain places and hope for the best.  Wood + metal = Barrel!  I shouldn't have to worry about the design necessary to create it.  (Some people like to...  that's fine with me.  I don't.)
Early game I found myself getting my butt kicked...  mercilessly.  Again, new style of game...  plus playing a platformer on a keyboard has never been particularly easy for me (I'll rock MegaMan on a controller all day long though).  As I learned the enemies, their attacks, and my own skills I became a much more profecient killer.  Now, at level 50 with 50 Arms level...  there isn't a damn thing that frightens me.  (Aside from the dark.  That's still scary.)
There are beginners guides out there if you need them, or just want them.  I'll just give a little tip...  gather.  Stone, wood, and especially ore early game...  that's what it's all about.  Investing in good armor will save your♥♥♥♥♥too.  Also, when you find boxes and loot them, feel free to gather the box too.  Bows are tricky but allow you to stay mobile.  Also, pressing down while holding either direction will cause you to tumble.  You will avoid all damage while doing this...  including falling damage (there's an achievement associated with this).
Learning new recipes can be challenging.  You learn stuff based on material drops you've gotten, or things you've crafted.  Keeping a researcher near your boxes keeps you from having to grab items from your boxes in order to see if you can learn something new.  Additionally, most materials have different rarity tiers.  (White, green, blue, purple, gold...  just like rarity for weapons and armor.)
The developer is great, he's always working on the game and generally streams as he's doing it.  He's constantly reading the comments/questions on his channel and answering them while he works too.  So far he's the first (and only) Twitch subscription I have.  Updates are released frequently, which is great.
Lastly, dungeons are instanced temporary maps that have different goals.  The end goal is always to make it to the crystal, but some times you have to avoid damaging monsters, sometimes you have to kill them all, sometimes you just have to flip switches.  There are also different affects applied to your character or the mobs making the instances constantly different (to an extent).
The ultra rare stuff is hard to find.  I have yet to find some things and I have most all of the bosses on farm mode and have traveled to the four corners of the map.
All in all, I recommend the game.  It isn't perfect but Jasson strives at getting it there, and then revamping what already exists.

I quite enjoyed Crea, the game is very similar to Terraria, with some variations.  Crea has your character leveling up, spending skill points, wielding magic, etc. You level skills such as tool speed, attack boost, defense boost, tool reach, and more. The crafting system takes its own direction as well, using research to learn new recipes.  This system allows the game to feel like more than just a clone.  Is the addition of RPG elements enough to set Crea apart from the other games like this..  I'd certainly say yes, it's unique enough to offer the hardcore 2d sandbox gameplayer, while keeping all the core mechanics that make the genre fun.  Building, crafting, looking, exploring and killing,  can all be found in one neat package..  While Minecraft is the king of 3d sandbox games, the market for 2d sandbox games exploded, and has brought about many games of various quality, Crea isn't the first but it's one of the best.
Much like other games in the genre, Crea has no real purpose outside of the users own imagination, build yourself a mammoth base, stock up on the rarest of materials and gear, or explore the depths of the earth and see if you can find out what makes the world tick.  Outside of the mechanics that are present in other games, the newer elements such as leveling, and gaining skill points really sets the game apart.  The RPG elements are a breath of fresh air.
RPG elements (leveling, skills, etc etc etc)
The Modding Community is fairly impressive and getting better
Full controller support
Great big worlds
quite a few bugs and glitches
Tutorial could be a bit more involved,
Combat could be tweaked a bit to be more inline with other games of this genre
If you enjoy sand box games, using your imagination and exploring an amazingly fun world, Crea will be right up your alley.  So many positives about Crea, that the few negatives are greatly overshadowed.  I think if you enjoy other games in the 2d sandbox genre, you'll love this one as well.  It has loads of content, loads of mods, and will leave the gamer feeling engaged.  I highly recommend the game to any and all sandbox gameplayers..

This game is an unmistakable descendant of Terraria, and it stays true to the look and feel of the original with many similar game play elements. However, there is enough innovation and variation here to make it well worth playing. It's a relaxed, explore-at-your-own-pace game -- ideal as an enjoyable, long-running endeavor to play whenever you have some free time. Drop in to explore, collect resources, expand your home base, kill some ugly creatures, and then call it a day. Your world is saved and will be waiting for you to explore and build when you return.
If you need high-octane battles and constant action, youll not find a happy home here. On the other hand if you enjoy exploring and learning, there is more than enough depth to keep you entertained for many hours. Progression is limited by how much you have leveled up your talents and how much research you've managed to complete. Both of which gently guide you toward the next thing you need to learn in order to advance. The environment is forgiving, and the consequences of dying are almost none; you can feel free to give any idea a whirl.
Having played 50+ hours so far, there have been many aha! moments, but there is still a lot to learn. Its quite addicting if youre prone to getting lost in the details with games like this. When you divide the price by the number of hours worth of quiet enjoyment you can get out of this, it looks like a real deal. Even better if you have friends who play and you can arrange some multiplayer fun along the way.

As a fan of
, I like this game for both the whole living-on-the-edge vibe, and for the slide-guitar soundtrack. It's cool.
But as an astronomer and lover of
fiction, I'm disappointed.
First, in space a real spaceship does NOT slow down just because you kill the engines. There is this thing in physics called "momentum". You know, the whole thing about an object in motion tending to stay in motion unless acted upon by an outside force? In space there are very few outside forces that would cause a spaceship to slow to a stop just because the engines are off. At the bottom of a gravity well, like, say, on the surface of the Earth, a vehicle like a car will slow when you take your foot off the gas because of friction. Silly programmers... If you're gonna make a game set in space, at least pay attention to how things BEHAVE in space.
Second, even though the POV can be moved around in 3 dimensions the actual game play is 2-dimensional. You can go right & left (port & starboard), but not up or down. Remember
? How did Kirk beat Kahn? Because Khan was operating in only 2 dimensions, whereas space is 3-dimensional.
I mean, c'mon, guys! If you're gonna go to all the trouble of programming a game that is smart enough to have you colliding with ice chunks, asteroids and planetary objects, can't you figure out how to deal with 3 dimensions?
The last item is that, like so many other games, once you’ve got the basics down it’s “lather, rinse, repeat.” It would be nice to have more different kinds of missions - medical rescues, something that involves landing on some of the worlds instead of just flying by, I dunno. Something other than just blasting things to smithereens.
Ah, well. Given the limitations, I'm gonna have to give this game 3.5 stars on a 1-5 scale.

DO NOT BE LURED IN BY THE TRAILER - THE GAME HAS CHANGED AND THE TRAILER NO LONGER ACCURATELY REPRESENTS THE GAME YOU PURCHASE.
When you look at the trailer, please take note:
- Hurling large structures around with 'Telekinesis' is no longer a 'thing'.
- Flying is significantly slower than what you see.
- You will never come across that many people in one area, doing anything together. If you're lucky, you might stumble across a duo farming.
Recommended for a short-term experience. Concerning actions and behaviour by the development team, and an elitist god-complex community of moderators on the official Discord make it very hard for this game to progress, or maintain a reasonable playerbase.
Positive:
+ Recommended because I managed to squeeze 350 hours from this game which means I well and truly got my money's worth out of the title. Most people will probably get 10-20 hours from the game then move on - but the time spent in game will be enjoyable.
+ The game is a great experience for those who like playing solo, or with one other player. Building WAS fantastic at launch and the landscape allows players to get very creative.
+ The absence of survival mechanics (eating/drinking/body temp) enables players to concentrate more on building and creativity without hassle.
Negative:
- Absurd AI. Aggro ranges for mobs vary depending on lag and spontaneous bugs. You can 'trap' mobs on walls and in doorways and attack them from an area they cannot reach you. This enables low level players to grind on high level trash and level very quickly. It took me one week to level from 30 - 60 playing a couple of hours a day.
- Material requirements for building and crafting, introduced in a patch at the start of October. Building USED to be very accessible - a magnificent sandbox for lovers of building. The material requirements have been increased beyond reason, to a massive negative response by the remaining playerbase of 130ish people (source: steam charts).
- Elitist moderators. Moderators of the official Discord are not members of Blue Isle Studios, but rather, BIS 'Groupies' who refuse to call out the development team when they make significant mistakes. Any players who voice their concern at the state of the game are generally shunned by the moderators, ultimately turning players away. This has had a large effect on the struggling playerbase.
- Development team doesn't TRULY listen to the community. The community manager publicly admitted that the reason for increasing building material requirements was to slow expansion of large bases, as their servers are struggling. Servers average 2-3 players when busy. Rather than listen to the community and address major concerns, the developers are employing 'selective hearing' and implementing changes that a very small percentage of the community desire, and not addressing the issues that cause troves of players to leave.
Summary:
The development team, and the community manager, need to engage with the masses, rather than the handful of moderators in Discord. Why did 4,000 players leave immediately after release? Why did 3,600 players leave after the first major patch? If you ask the Discord moderators, this is 'normal' for indie development. I beg to differ.
The difference between a good development team and a poor one, is their capacity to listen to the advice of the majority in their gaming community. At present, they do not, but claim that they do in patch notes. Again, look at the numbers - the evidence is there.
While this game is in Early Access, it will be impossible for the community to increase. The ONLY hope this game has will be at 'Launch'. If they cannot fix the issues that made so many leave during EA, when the game finally launches, it will suffer and die off very quickly.
Approach this game with caution before committing time to it!

A "meh" recommendation. Ever play a game that just drips with high production values and class, but you still don't like it? That's how I feel about Hitman: Absolution. I realize that it's something plenty of people will enjoy. I just didn't. Do I think it's worth picking up? Sure, if it's on sale. And you're bored.
If that sounds like I'm getting ready to drop some grade-A hate, I'm not. At least, I don't want to. There is so much about Hitman: Absolution that just reeks of care and attention. The graphics are amazing. Not necessarily a reason to buy a game, but they are. The voice acting is superb (Keith Carradine and Powers Boothe? Hell yes!). The soundtrack works incredibly well, giving an almost Bond-esque ambiance without ever getting too loud. While some levels are occasionally re-used, there are a lot of different locations and settings. And as far as the story goes, I felt incredibly close to Agent 47 (he's quite sympathetic, despite his stoicism). Sneaking from cover to cover feels fluid and natural. Weapons are deadly (headshots are a breeze with the Silverballers).
So what's my problem?
Most of the levels are claustrophobic (the opening Chinatown level and the cornfield level are exceptions). The paths through the levels are restrictive. And some levels don't even bother to hide their linearity (final rooftop level, among many others). There's no way to level-up Agent 47. Upgrades are unlocked based upon how high of a score you received upon completing a mission. But the points system clearly favors a specific path – even penalizing for non-target knockouts. I was never a fan of the Assassin's Creed games' “full synchonization” mechanic either, but this just ticked me off. There is no loadout customization; you start every mission with choke-wire and (after you unlock them) the Silverballers. Other weapons are acquired by finding them or picking them up from dead enemies – but it doesn't matter, because you'll be back to the piano wire and Silverballers once the next mission starts.

Disguises are actually not a problem; there are plenty of them around. Using them is sometimes strange, though. If planning to ghost through a police station, DON'T try to use a police uniform as a disguise. Why? Because if a cop gets too close to you, he'll detect that you're not a real policeman. Makes sense, I suppose. But in a level crawling with police, disguising as a police officer becomes a questionable strategy – which seems counter-intuitive to me. Much better to knock out a homeless person and take his disguise, since the officers won't detect you. But then, dressed as a homeless person, you won't be able to enter restricted areas without attracting attention anyway. Several times I just lost patience and started taking innocent people out to facilitate progress – and several times got embroiled in a full-on gun battle. Which actually wasn't that bad. If you're careful, 47 has a ton of health, and headshots are 1-hit kills. Add in the deadly Instinct combat mode, which has elements of the VATS system from Fallout, and 47 becomes an absolute wrecking ball of death.
There were some great moments, though. Ghosting through the flaming warehouse while troopers searched the premises was a thrill. Heading deeper underground through a mining facility with guards everywhere was a delicate game of cat-and-mouse. And trying to take out three henchmen in Chinatown with throngs of people everywhere was easily the most enjoyment I had. Somehow I thought every level would feature that amount of variety and detail, and I'm disappointed that (to me) it didn't. Recommended because Hitman: Absolution is polished and does what it sets out to do, but ultimately it's only a mediocre game that is sprinkled with some great levels.

If you’ve been following my reviews for any amount of time, you know I love Hidden Object games, and that some of my favorite have been done by none other than Artifex Mundi. Even the previous games in the Nightmares From The Deep series I really enjoyed. However, for some reason I can’t quite pinpoint (and perhaps it was a mixture of several things that ended up having me dislike it), Nightmares from the Deep 3 didn’t quite make the cut for me.
In Nightmares From The Deep 3 you take on the role of Sara, who along with her daughter is kidnapped by none other than Davy Jones. Sara is then tasked with saving her daughter from Jones and a dark pact, and helping lost souls along the way. This is the last installment on the series, and the most disappointing to me.
The audio and video were of the expected quality: the character’s looks keep slowly improving as time goes by, the backgrounds are as beautiful and detailed as ever, and sounds and music keep improving as well.
Like in other games of theirs, they added collectables in the way of seahorses and pirate cards. The difficulty of finding them was reasonable- they were sufficiently hidden not to be obvious, but not all extremely hard to find, making for a nice extra challenge if you are into collecting stuff, or are a completionist.
They also made use of pets again. The dog, which is the choice pet this time, is truly adorable, and I loved that you could pet him, but compared to the reviewed Clockwork Tales, the functionality of it as other than a fetch tool and a companion was lacking.
Some of the cutscenes were also lacking a little – the most memorable one was a boat rowing scene were the rows moved but there were no hands on them. Hey! Magic! For a company that likes to pay so much attention to details in most their games, this was… surprising. It’s such a little thing, but it takes so much away.
My other big complain is that, unlike in some of their previous titles, their find-by-picture Hidden Object scenes were very forced. The items you were to find were force-blended with the background, such as by just changing the hue from what it was supposed to be, instead of having it just be lost among a bunch of similar items; this was a rather cheap move, made it difficult in all the wrong ways, and I didn’t like it at all. Besides, I generally find the find-by-icture scenes a lot more tedious than the ones were you’re given a list.
As far as the rest of the hidden object scenes and puzzles, they were fairly average for the company, which is a good enough thing. Puzzles, logic, and extras were of a decent difficulty and pleasant to play. I particularly liked having to play a board mini-game with one of the characters as way of moving forward, as it was different and inventive.
Onto more technical aspects, I was having a lot of troubles this time around keeping it from crashing while alt-tabbing on windowed mode, which I never had a problem with before.
As for the story, it was not too bad, but the whole Davey jones thing didn’t entirely “click” with me. The whoe thing felt longer than previous games, and not in a good way. I think it was more boredom that made it seem longer, than actual length in play time.
That said, if you love Artifex Mundi and hidden object games, and if you’ve played the previous two games of the series, Nightmares From The Deep 3: Davy Jones is a nice final installment to it and definitely a mus-have from a fan/collector’s point of view. For everyone else, there’s nothing overly special about this one, even if it’s not a bad game per se.
Would I recommend it? I do think I would still recommend this to other HOG players.

I appreciate what this game is trying to do. My main complaint, though, is the lack of variety causes the game to feel repetitive and mechanical shortly after you've figured out how the game works. It can be challenging in the beginning when you're learning which supplies you should prioritize and when, the most efficient way to acquire those supplies, the most efficient way to feed your party, etc. But once all that is figured out (which I would say takes a couple hours at most), everything becomes routine and monotonous. As a result, you lose a lot of the empathy previously established for the characters in your party as you send them out to do the same thing over and over again with negligible risk of harm.
It's the type of game where the first couple weeks require a bit of experimentation and trial and error, but once that's all sorted out, the remaining weeks are nothing but going through the motions and waiting to win the game.
Still, I would recommend the game. It is interesting when everything is new, and the aesthetic and gaemplay are refreshingly different. Just don't expect to get too many hours out of this game, unless you are a completionist and can't help but beat the game with every possible combination of party members.

Although I love playing Magic in paper format, I have to downvote this game. There are some very good aspects to this game, but the bad stuff overwhelms the good.
The good:
Card pool-  Includes cards from Magic Origins, Battle for Zendikar, Oath of the Gatewatch and Shadows over Innstrad) Big variety in game mechanics, card flavours and deck archetypes.
Solid start- After completing the Campaign, you will be rewarded with basic cards needed to start building some archetypical decks.
Not too grindy- First win of the day, Campaign and daily quests help you aquire gold faster.
Deck building for magic veterans- Useful card filters, deck stats and deck appearence customisation. Could be better (grid of cards would be better than scrolling through all cards).
The bad:
Noob unfriendly- Biggest offense this game makes is that it confuses and discourages new players. This game is not for someone who wants to learn to play MTG. Magic 2014 is vastly superior at teaching new players. This game introduces new mechanics way too fast, and Deckbuilder Wizard doesnt really explain deck archetypes. No explanation for card sets,flavour, mechanics nor card types in booster shop.
Matchmaking- I don't know how many people play this game, but queue times are horrible (3-4 minute wait before youre kicked to start screen). There is rarely an option to cancel your queue, which means you'll need to restart your game if you're stuck.
User Interface- Ugly and impractical compared to Magic 2014. Pray to god that you don't missclick something or you will be prompted with a window explaining you can't do something rendering the buttons you tried to click unresponsive. Many times I couldn't stop time to react to opponent's spell because something was blocking the screen asking for my confirmation. This could be easily fixed with a pop up message in corner of the screen that doesn't need button press to fade.
Miscellaneous bugs- Game is not polished. Some of the huge bugs are: losing priority, cards mix up when there are large numbers of cards on the table, activated ability miscast, timers are sometimes too fast...
Conclusion
If you're new to magic this game will not help you learn the basics.
If you like to play magic in your spare time, few hours a day, this game is not for you. You will waste most of your time waiting for a match.
If you like to play magic for hours and hours a day, the bad things in this game probably won't stop you from playing it.

This game needs help, it started as a facebook game and it is not much better then that. The graphics are cartoonish but that is an art choice, yet it requires a powerful computer to run smoothly on high "detail". Now this game is not for combat, it is about the crafting as it is fairly well fleshed out and wasy to understand. Yet the developers found out about this and placed a stopper on crafting, assuming to stop botting but all it has done is harm the actual player. This is due to the ease of creating other accounts who have no restriction on creating potions to remove this blockade put down by the devs.
Next the lag in this game is atrocious there is alot of skipping, getting stuck in objects and being hit by enemies that are no where near you (this is also tied into the "combat" of the game). I did some research and this lag has something to do with the old code from this games facebook days, but this brings up the games combat system, or lack there off. It appears as a turn based combat system at first however it is real time, its just missing all forms of depth and complexity. All you do is spam combat arts and spells with the occasional auto attack and things die, but each attack has an animation and once the animation is begun it is a guaranteed hit unless a dodge is performed. Except no enemy dodges attacks only players.
This leads to my playthrough being a hammer fest of the number keys and then spamming the z key when it got too much, but that is also down to RNG it appears as i died many times during a roll. Next up is stats of the character, health and spirit restore way to slow. 40 points a minute out of combat is atrocious, this leads to players waiting for a half hour at higher levels waiting doing nothing, there are potions however yet I can only find them in the pay money to the dev section. Death is meaningless, except for the part where you do less damage and take more for 10 minutes meaning you have to wait (or pay the dev).
Now leveling, i was going to beat the game until I spent about 10 hours grinding exp in an area my level only to find my total exp went up 5%. I had to check my numbers but it is about that, the requirements go up exponentially without the gained exp going up a decent amount. So now i have to wait to partake in laggy boring combat that is worth nothing... so glad i can craft oh wait my bot accounts haven't finished. I gave up and went back to EvE online as it is more exciting
So we have a crafting game that makes you pay to keep crafting or exploit a bottable set of commands, horrid lag, bare bones combat, long waiting between battles and death unless your a healer with a level up system designed by morons. This game needs to be pulled down, decompiled and remade by competent game developers who have some idea how to make interesting combat, better netcode, proper leveling system and better anti bot measures then just breaking the part of the game that is worth a damn.

>>UPDATE REVIEW IN 2018<<
>>THE STATE OF THIS GAME<<
Wow after a couple years when Archeblade was abandoned by it's original developers due to it's poor gaming economy and resulting in a bankruptcy act. Plus it's semi-failed attempt in making a new game called "DICETINY: The Lord of the Dice" under their new gaming cooperation "Fakedice". Archeblade had made a small revival by a few new community developers. As of right now, Archeblade is somewhat playable but with a very small active community so there really isn't much players to be match against with. All this game needs is a good advertisement as well as a promotion in the gaming industries and a proper development team to revamp the game. I am willing to tune in this game's community to update any further future events.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>STATUS REVIEW OF ARCHEBLADE FROM 2014 TO 2018<<
Archeblade is a fast-paced thirdperson arena fighter where players are matched up against others in teams. There are characters with different distinctive playstyles as well as stats that allow players to choose from that fits their interest. For instance, there are ranged, support, quick, tanky, and heavy hitting themed characters that contribute to the game's mechanic. Game modes consist of point tracking where kills or capture points are kept record until the timer expires, any team with the higher accumulated points determines victory.
The controls in this game can be a bit gimmicky because the combo system can be both simple and complex at the same time. The movement and attack functions are simple and easy to pick up; however, Archeblade's combat mechanics are very complex since there are combos that be mixed as well as unique strategies. For example, infinite combos can be performed, counter block attacks (a power attack to break guard/block), and aiming and timing are required to hit enemies. Though this game has a few complex mechanics but it is what makes the game unique.
Other than that, here are my points of critique:
The Good:
+ Not Pay-to-Win
+ Nice character and map designs
+ Interesting concept
+ Simple but complex controls and mechanics
+ Wearables are easy to obtain
+ Developer support still exist on the community forums (I think)
The Neutral:
~ Cannot create servers
~ Cannot connect or play with friends properly
The Bad:
- The game is slowly reviving so don't be expecting anything too big or a miracle to happen
- Hacks are still around (why?)
- No anti-cheat system
- Lots of connection problems
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
All in all, Archeblade (before it was abandoned) was a very well performed game but unfortunately it died short after it's official release. But in the end, I hope the new community developers can revive this game back it's former glory, but I am afraid it might take a while due to very low funding/budget.

This game is very clearly heavily influenced by Terraria, but it takes that influence and runs with it in its own direction.
As someone who has dumped quite a lot of time into the sandbox craft/fight/dig games (mostly Minecraft, but also a bit of Terraria), the addition of a skill system in this game is a very welcome improvement. There's an actual sense of progression rather than just weakly gated tiers of items that you can rush through. Of course, there are item tiers as well, but at least at the early levels the skill progression seems to have just as much if not more impact.
Coming from Terraria, the control scheme threw me off for a bit, as there are a total of four (4) hotbars, split between two modes (combat and exploration) and two tab groups each. After I got used to it, I came to appreciate the ergonomics, but there was a bit of a learning curve.
Overall, quite impressed with this game thus far, but there are competing games at a lower price point that are probably better entry points into the genre.

Tembo the Badass Elephant is a 2D action platformer where a city has been invaded by a bunch of dudes that really love the color purple that call themselves Phantom and to respond to this threat the National Guard send in one badass elephant as their first and last line of defense. As you can no doubt tell from that sentence this game is very tongue in cheek and has very little story to the point that I had to look at the store page to describe what is going on. Your job as a badass elephant is to go across the level rescuing civilians and killing every enemy in sight and doing both is must as killing an enemy or rescuing a civilian grants you some Phantom Points which are required to progress through the missions. You can miss a few but the point threshold needed to get past is pretty high and leaves little room for error. Each level has a set amount of points they give you so if you scored 240 the first time around and replay it later on and score 250, you will receive 10 points. It just feels like a really unneeded mechanic designed to artificially lengthen the game in the least fun possible way. Imagine having to collect around 90% of the rings in each Sonic the Hedgehog level and you'll get the gist of why it hampers the fun.
If you are wondering why I mentioned Sonic of all things, well Tembo the Badass Elephant is very similar. From the spin dash attack to the angry looking animal protagonist it would not surprise me if the development for this started off as another Sonic title. The key differences here are that the elephant in this game moves far slower and is able to shoot water from its trunk. Water shot from your trunk can be used for a variety of things such as growing some platforms, short circuiting electronics and using it to spin objects such as valves. Your water supply is limited however and you can restock by drinking from a water supply or finding some scattered water bottles. Water supplies are always placed near the object you need to spray so it is never necessary to backtrack due to needing more water. I wouldn't call them puzzles but they are nice additions that break up the usual platforming and fighting. Fighting is more dangerous than you may think considering that you weigh several tons and move with the graze of a ballerina. You can only take five hits and it doesn't matter if the damage comes from being blasted in the face by a tank or punched by a tiny human as everything causes you the same amount of damage. In order to recover some health you need to find food crates though they are few and far between so you'll be wanting to take things more cautiously instead of going in trunks blazing like a badass elephant.
Your means of disposing of your foes are by uppercutting with your trunk, slide kicks and dashing towards them. Whatever you chose it is always great fun seeing human enemies ragdoll and land many feet away. My favorite mean of dealing with them is to simply jump on top of them leaving nothing but a satisfying splat. There is no blood in this game and it is all done in a cartoonish fashion in case that sounded a tad too violent and you were considering buying it for a child. Humans can also come at you with mechs, helicopters or tanks and pose a far greater danger to you than those on foot. Seeing an elephant fight a giant mech is a pretty awesome sight and most non boss enemies go down in three or less well placed blows. They all have different ways of being dealt with such as tanks shooting a horizontal round at you which can very easily be dodged by ducking and mechs only being susceptible to damage from behind. Once you defeat a vehicle the soldier will fly out from the explosion and you must kill him to get more of the previously mentioned Phantom Points. Scattered around levels are giant purple crates or purple floating TV sets, basically anything that is purple you will want to go out of your way to destroy. Luckily it is a ton of fun to destroy things you don't even have to such as trees, houses or platforms just to see the way everything scatters around the screen by the force of a charging elephant.
Bowling balls are found in some levels and are very useful for flinging at enemies and destroying things you can't reach. Also found in levels are secrets which contain hidden captive humans. While the humans themselves hold no value to you, rescuing one gets you 10 points and you will be needing every point you can get. Once rescued the humans climb on your back and try to hold on as you run and jump around which is pretty amusing. Jumping is nothing special, the only thing different from other platformers is that the elephant can perform a flutterjump to keep himself floating in the air for a few seconds. Jumping and attacking can be a pain at times as timing your attack a second to soon before reaching the ground will cause you to use your spin dash which leaves you wide open to attack for a few seconds. This game is not easy and the checkpoints are far and few between making death feel really substantial. They are not far enough to become unfair but boy will it sting when the checkpoint is in sight and you mess up at the last second. This game really nailed the difficulty in my opinion since it is not easy enough to be boring and not hard enough to be infuriating.
Tembo the Badass Elephant uses a lives system and you will receive lives after collecting enough peanuts to make a jar of peanut butter. Little details like these just make the game feel really charming and there is a lot of creativity in the backgrounds of the levels themselves as well. There are 18 levels in total but 4 of them feature nothing but a boss fight. That's not to say bosses aren't enjoyable but it is a pretty short game that took me 4 hours to complete according to Steam and I did spend some time away from keyboard so I'd wager it was more around 3 and a half hours. There is no real reason to replay the game other than to have fun so I can see that being a turn off for some. Continuing on the subject of the bosses they are always much larger than you and they will not go down easily. Funnily enough the first boss fight is actually the hardest in the whole game and caused me far more grief than any other. After beating a boss you will be shown a few comic book pages in a cutscene detailing what happens next and how you escaped. They look nice and are very goofy though they don't really explain anything, being there mostly for comedic effect such as escaping by flying out of the base using a parachute made of birds. The music is pretty well done and features your typical action sounding array of tracks as well as a few party tracks for when the enemy decides to get their groove on.
The game does not support resolutions higher than 1080p unfortunately, making the image look slightly blurry for anyone running a higher resolution monitor or TV. I have no real other complaints other than the spin dash and at times being unable to tell which path to take causing you to be unable to return if you picked the wrong one making you lose out on a ton of points which you will really need. Each of the 18 levels felt quite different from one another and this seems to be a cause of quality over quantity. This game is wildly bipolar.
On the one hand, it's charming as hell. The 2D art is incredibly reminiscent of Sergio Aragonés (and I swear to god one character is a stand-in for the man), the basic concept is solid and some of the level setpieces work really well. On the other, though, this game basically wants you to serve two masters at all times, and it's incredibly frustrating due to this.
Every stage has 3 counters on it: time, civilians saved, and enemies destroyed. The problem is that you're forced to do X% of the last one because the game gates itself behind enemies cleared every few stages, so suddenly, time is out the window as you find yourself cursing when you need to replay a level since you're 2 short to continue onwards. Aiding this problem is that the checkpoint system is really inconsistent. Every enemy in a stage respawns when you die, ahead and behind you, but the checkpoints don't always keep perfect count of who you wrecked prior, so here's a huge tip: head back a screen or two and ruin everyone's day when you respawn, JUST IN CASE it decided not to count someone*.
Okay, so the time score is just for replay value, burn through the stages when you beat the game. Well, here's the issue with that: I didn't mention the other mechanic aside from "smashing things as an elephant", you can fire water from your trunk to put out fires. Managing this and spraying precisely off-screen or ahead of you becomes the other mechanic you need to deal with, and suddenly levels aren't reaction-based so much as tedious memorization of angles, and don't forget it's limited, so if you screw up, have fun backtracking to get more (especially once the flaming walls you can't just take the hit on and have to douse appear). Oh, but you can't always backtrack! So get ready to die if you're replaying a stage and accidentally head into the "forward" path and lock yourself out of a civilian/enemy count.
This game wants to be a lot of things and it excels at none of them, and the very point I gave up on it was when I reached the first boss, who was actually easier than a lot of minibosses, because unlike them, he had no invincibility frames/ability to guard with flames or armor. I just slammed him over and over and he fell into a pit in 16.2 seconds. It was nice of the game to time that for me. Those 16 seconds (and the next 30, where it revealed how many men I had to grind out for the next gate) were where I decided it wasn't going to improve.
* It did this for me more than once. I started keeping count, I wish that was a joke.

Tembo the Badass Elephant is a difficult platformer made by Japanese studio Game Freak (you may know them because of Pokémon RPG series) and published by SEGA. That shows a big promise, considering also the price of 13 euros, right?
Well, on the first look, the game have gorgeous visual style with comic features (typical comic interjections) that is pointed towards comedy - I mean even the game name suggests you can't take it much seriously, as your character is an army elephant who... is absolutely badass. (He could be the next Expendable!)
Difficulty of the game is high, you can't pick anything like casual difficulty there, so prepare to die (as Dark Souls taught me). But don't worry, it's not that hardcore, expect having few checkpoints and 5 lives per level (if you lose them, you just lose progress in specific stage).
Difficulty is also set high because of the unique movement of the elephant. As the elephant is heavier than average platformer character, your movement will be mostly horizontally wide but vertically short. Also, for attacks you can use only melee attacks (thanks to jumping and charging) but there's one more utility thing - you can splash water with your trunk. That's useful against fire attacks, which you will see against you pretty often.
Length of the game could be definitely higher, I've beaten all levels in 5 hours, considering I've been stuck for about 45 minutes at the final boss. The game offers 14 levels (and 4 bossfights) split into 4 locations. Worth mentioning is the third location, the amusement park. It just brings back the horror from Sonic 3's circus stage - but don't worry, only visually!
As you check negative reviews and discussion, you can see many posts about bugs and bad performance. I've played the game on four years old low-end laptop and had no problem getting 60 FPS. For the bugs, I've found the one that made many people uninstall the game - I couldn't move and when I jumped, I just got shot to the stars (into the place where even textures don't exist). But this was solved only with restarting the game, then it was okay. It surprises me what can happen with "another platformer made in Unity engine", totally didn't expect that. One more thing, which I found half-baked, is the restart level function - it takes you a life! So... instead of restarting, you can just die, it's the same.
In the end, Tembo the Badass Elephant is a disappointment for a platformer coming with relatively higher price (for the genre) and made (and published) by popular studios. Still, it offers some entertainment and I quite enjoyed my time playing this, so I can recommend to buy it on sale - but only to those who don't mind higher difficulty.

TLDR; I've played a ton of this game, and I remember it. Games like Oblivion, Fallout 4, Skyrim... I play them and forget, they come and go like wind.
Crea sticks in your mind, the game is diverse, fun and very much a good thing. Play the game!
As you can probably, see, I've sunk over 100 hours into this game, over a wide variety of patches, changes and ideas. I've talked with the devs, found fun errors, created amazing things, and killed pretty much everything by blade, spear and bow.
tldr; Crea is Dark Souls lore and exploration in an open world setting. Ambitious, awesome, and has many strands of progress.
Crea is a good, different take on the Terraria style game the genre descends from. Instead of handholding, guides and mysterious landmarks, Crea has tasked you with exploring, investigating and noticing things. I stumbled into the first boss by crafting a Chaos Bed, and then using it. Maybe I should've expected a magical, cloning, nightmare boss, but holy hell was that a pulse pounding victory.
Later, I check the other teleporter tabs and found a new boss I had not seen before, and proceeded to get my stuff kicked in until I found a strategy that worked and actually pulled it off. Was it easy? No. Was it fun? Mostly. Was it exciting? Yes. Like many things, the boss fights are taking a known value [Enemies, lava, water, fallling] and adapting a strategy. Instead of the Terraria style "Build your own" arena, Crea bosses come with an arena, or spawn in a fixed area where you determined they should be.
The crafting game is both light and heavy, and is constantly getting refined. You can make a weapon out of the barest, meagerest supplies possible, or you can forge it from start to finish to be a high quality, polished work, and the quality of the item will reflect this. This is done through a satisfying mini-game, where you race the chaos level you're injecting your works with, it starts out hilariously easy, 25 quality to 100 chaos, but will happily jump up to 200 quality to 100 chaos, and ramp up the challenge to perfect as well.
The game mechanics are crisp, polished and are really based on comitting to an action [without the imput delay of the PC Dark Sous games], and through planning, posititioning, properly levelled skills and the use of the dodge roll, I found myself going from a struggling meatbag to an acrobatic jerk who would dance through the enemies and loot their remains.
Above all, Crea rewards determination. As you do a thing, you get skill points for it, which can make you better at that. Crafting begets cooler crafting techniques, weapon combat helps you combat harder, etc. Not innovate, but well paced and most skills either bring a brand of utility [healing spells, ranged attacks] or help you get better at storming the world [ extra jumps/jump height, grappling ledges, extra inventory slots.] And yes, determination means I wish the game could be faster, but I also feel a sense of attachment for the characters I create.
Overall, Crea is a very good, lightly flawed game. The dev himself is a kind, generous person, who may have dropped the game a bit early, but he had high hopes and a great heart behind it, and I know he's going to keep slamming out updates, content and great gameplay.

Tembo the Badass Elephant is a side scrolling platform game developed by Game Freak and published by Sega. The game was released on PC, PS4 and Xbox One in July 2015.  Whilst the game has got a tag of being Indie, I don’t really agree, given the catalogue of games both the developer and publisher has to their names.
You control Tembo, the bad♥♥♥♥♥elephant (no kidding huh?). Your aim is to stop an invasion on Shell City, to stop the bad guys called The Phantom. As it is a platforming game, you have all of the regular platforming style game play mechanics with a few little twists to them. For instance you can jump and hover for a few seconds rather than having a double jump. You are also able to squirt water out of your trunk to put out fires and to interact with a few objects in the game world to help you solve puzzles.  As you progress through each of the levels, you can also take out enemies, by using various different attacks, such as charge, uppercuts and stomps. The killing of enemies is really important as they act as your currency in the game’s built in gating system. You have to kill a certain quota of enemies before you can move onto the next stage of levels. You can also rescue citizens of the city that have been captured as well, but these add no bonus or server no purposes to the game play it.
The art style in Tembo looks awesome. It’s not mind boggling graphics, but the comic book style just captures the game’s aim perfectly. Whilst it is in the cartoon style, it doesn’t come across as cheesy or childish though. There isn’t any voice acting sadly, but even if there were voice acting, there wouldn’t be much as there isn’t really any dialogue either. The entire story is played out via a comic book strip in between levels and it does it really well.
This game is balls to the wall hard; each stage has three to four levels in it, and they will gradually get harder and harder as you would expect. A few of the levels will have challenging bosses and enemies to overcome, whilst others can also have puzzles and gauntlets that you have to complete. This game had me raging at times when I died, but I was still hooked and wanted to keep going. The welcome addition of a number of checkpoints throughout the levels really helps, and keeps you going when times get tough. I never actually ran out of lives though, so the game is beatable with a bit of skill.
All of Tembo’s levels are really well designed. None of them are your standard platforming style stages. Each one has a different theme, soundtrack and puzzles in. I never felt like I was replaying previous content that was just copy and pasted.  Like I said above, you can collect trapped citizens, and you can also aim to get 100% kills of enemies on each stage if you want to go for the achievement hunting. The game itself playing to completion took me just over 3 hours.  I may go back and try to get 100% rating on some of the earlier levels, but even if I don’t I am very happy with the time I got out of this title.
The only technical issue I had was that I could not get the game to run in 4k. The resolution settings seem to be capped at 1080p but I was able to get 60fps 100% of the time though. Whilst it isn’t a major issue on this type of art style game, the options would always be nice. Game pad is highly recommended due to the platforming elements. I tried with keyboard and it was just disastrous.
Tembo the Badass Elephant was a little bit of a surprise in the rough for me.  I am not surprised at how well the game turned out given the teams behind it, but it is really nice to see a simple idea put into such a clearly carefully made game. The retail price of £9, 99 is absolutely worth it, the game has been known to go on sale for as low as £2, 49 elsewhere but I would not hesitate to pick this up again at the full price.

Autosport had a lot of potential. It's a deliberate step towards a more serious racing game, and brought a lot of features that fans wanted. The game looks brilliant on paper, with a superb selection of cars, better physics, a new AI and glittering graphics. Sadly the reality is, it's a very technologically impressive game but not very enjoyable to play.
Autosport, at several different levels, feels like a game trying to be something it isn't. It advertises itself as a hardcore driver's game, and yet plays like an Arcade Racer. It feels outdated as well; the graphics are outstanding, but the AI and physics feel years behind the competition. If it was priced accordingly, it would be a big hit. Unfortunately, it's priced as a AAA title, which it very much isn't.
The driving Physics just don't match the game Codemasters were trying to create. Autosport feels like an Arcade racer; not even a Simcade, but a full Arcade game. Cars drift effortlessly almost by themselves, pull insane G-forces and reach ludicrous speed on the straights. I don't mind stylisation, but selling Autosport as a "hardcore simcade" is like pretending Mariokart 8 is a Formula 1 team's simulator.
The AI feels much the same as the physics. This isn't a proper circuit-racing AI; it doesn't behave at all like a racing driver, with no thought to rules or self-preservation. It's extremely aggressive, and will frequently ram you for no apparent reason. It also shows some significant perception-related bugs: it will occasionally drive into solid objects at full-throttle apparently unaware that they're even there.

It has a firefly theme to it (the music especially). Which is awesome.
Game plays on a 2D plane. You basically fly around doing missions (basically kill missions, or fly into a bunch of guys and take something and leave while they try to kill you missions). As you fly around you get blockaded by enemies who you have to fly through/around to get back to warp. As you fly around you also run into distress beacons you can go to and either fall into a trap or come to someone's aid while they are getting killed.
Basically killing is the only real solution to anything in this game. I think that's it's major weakness.
The commodities market is pretty lame. You can only put a few things in your holds and most stores never sell enough of anything to fill your holds to do proper buy/sell trading. And even if they did, it's almost never going to be all of the good stuff with a good price. Otherwise this system could be pretty fun if it was balanced and actually changed with supply/demand.
All in all it's fun for a while. Then it gets grindy. Then it gets really grindy. Then you use cheats and give yourself all the money you want. Then you go out and realize there's nothing else to the game and you quit.
If you can get this for $5, I'd buy it for some over simplified naval combat in space with the firefly theme to it. But while this game engine is good enough for some pretty awesome gameplay....sadly, it is pretty void of good content.

Grid Autosport succeeds where Grid 2 failed and is nearly an even match for the original Grid. AI is excellent though often ruthless, car control is accurate but exaggerated, tracks have all been seen before but boast many new layouts, pavement has nuance, and damage has consequences. I’m struck by how consistently the AI races. Once the difficulty is dialed in, every mistake you make pushes your rivals ahead and every perfect line reels them in. Passing a racer is always the slowest line around a corner and I can see the affect it has on me in relation to the cars ahead and behind. It’s brilliant. The race menus are all new for Grid Autosport. Events are organized into seasons that encompass one discipline at a time and must be completed before switching to another. You freelance yourself out to racing teams like in the old contracts system in Grid 1. Each season could be as few as 2 races or as many as 8-10, and can include a wide variety of vehicles. Season offerings are numerous and allow you to lean on disciplines you enjoy and do the minimum in disciplines you don’t. Different race teams set different goals and award more or less points accordingly but, more importantly, different teams offer different cars to align with your preferences in the same races. The points increase your level in each separate discipline and progress you into faster and faster cars. Seasons are competitive enough that you can afford to have numerous non-first finishes and still win so long as you’re near the top. Individual races typically have a 10 minute practice session, a 3 lap qualifying, neither of which can be restarted, and a race which can be restarted. Practice and qualifying can get a bit tedious but are optional. Short comings are few. I wish I could command my own race team and create my own liveries but you could argue that that’s what multiplayer allows you to do. And though there are many new track layouts, you’ve seen all of these locales before in Grid and Grid 2. New facades would have been welcome. I’d say the game is most enjoyable with an xbox360 controller but delicacy on the triggers tires my knuckles which makes the G27 a more comfortable, if not leisurely, choice. Highly recommend. Best fender on fender racing I’ve seen since Grid 1.

I have tons of money (energy) coming in but i really don't have the same satisfaction looking at it as i do in civ 5. Again that's a pretty big nit pick but it just really bugs me.
Also like I said the game is civ 5 but things need to be switched around one most noticeably is instead of social policies you instead have a "virtue tree." It's almost exactly like an RPG leveling up tree, in fact it reminds me a lot of borderlands level up system. Where you have a couple columns (4 in BE) and the more top virtues you choose the better virtues get unlocked lower down on the tree. This is such a downgrade to the social policies where fully choosing a branch is pretty easy and there are lots of them that you can freely mix and mash.They also have huge impacts all on their own. It's an important decision and is a vital choice to make to the development of your nation the way you want it. these virtues are boring and they feel very unimportant to the development to my colony. For example they usually do things like add sience per citizen or speed up border growth things that are not immediate. In comparison to civ 5 where you adopt a policy that makes citizens happy when troops are in cities and boom immediately you see happiness go up it’s very satisfying and it feel like you're doing something.
Democracy is very strange as well because nations are immediately discovered as they land on the planet there's also this whole idea of trading favors for resources and also you can trade science points. For the most part it’s identical to civ 5 even the exact phrasing is the same in some places. the models look really nice and all but i don’t care about any of the nations and there's not much to tell them apart except their nationality. Which can be argued is the same for civ 5 but theres more charm because they were real historical people.Not only that but in civ 5 they have those cool backgrounds and music. don’t remember about the music it wasn't noticeable if there was a change but there definitely is a lack of background.
One last thing i deffinity want to mention is something that sounds good on paper but after a while it really gets old. That’s the quests yes like endless legend but much less fitting and fun. i’m going to compare this mechanic to endless legend because it’s the only other game i’ve seen it in if you think thats unfair well don’t worry it’s not fun even without that comparison. In endless legend you get quests which is one way to complete the game. the questes are simple but challenging and take a bit of time. Also what makes them fun and unique is that they cycle through so you're not doing the same quests over and over every time you play the game. I say that because that’s what happens in BE the first quest you get is simply step by step how to make a second city. It’s uninventive and pretty pointless, but that’s not my real gripe with the quest system. My real issue is that sometimes the game has you make one of a couple choices to complete a quest or as the quest as a whole. you choose between to improvements with a scenario given like if you should make low grade recycled goods or high grade choosing low increases workers improvment speed but high grade improves health of your colonies. The issue is the game asks you these “quest decisions” waaaay to often and the fun of it wears of i found myself just going to the results and choosing one because i was sick of reading all the scenarios.
Thoughts were about all the issues i personally had with the game, but it’s not bad per say just very boring, and i can see someone liking this game. If the things you found me saying you agreed with or if you were expecting this whole awesome new game after playing civ 5 i’d stear clear.

This review was a tough one for me in particular. As much as I like this game I gotta be honest with you guys. Homefront is as entertaining as it is glitchy. To further clear up that last statement simply put, Homefront is a great game riddled with some seriously annoying bugs.
#1) For starters almost every area has some sort of progress bug. Meaning your A.I partners will get stuck in certain locations preventing them from opening certain doors and hatches needed to further progrees through a level. When this happens you may need to reload a checkpoint.....several times.
#2) One design flaw I did not notice years ago when I first played this game was the shoddy A.I design of both the enemies and your A.I partners. I beat this game on it's highest difficulty and on this particular setting the A.I flaws shine brightly. Your A.I partners for the most part are just bullet sponges that have the accuracy of Stevie Wonder letting enemies run past them to charge your position while blocking essential cover points you need to counter enemy attacks.
#3) Enemies on the highest difficulty have the accuracy of John Wick in which they consistently land 98% of their shots the moment they notice your presence (Dear Lord it's unbalanced!!!).
Now it may seem like I'm giving the game a bad wrap but, I just wanted to get those two discrepancies out in the open if you:
A) Decide to play on the highest difficulty you'll know exactly what you're in store for
B) If you ever get stuck in an area you may need to restart your game save several times for the game to correct itself
With that out of the way I'd like to point out the things I really enjoyed in the game.
-If you're a fan of the Red Dawn movies (old and new) and think the concept is pretty cool, then this game is right up your alley.
-I enjoyed the lore and the way it was presented. You can read newspapers to understand the gradual downfall of the country.
-The storyline is good and the dialogue is fairly decent.
-The 3 factions they focus on in this story could use a bit more fleshing out because they're quite interesting. There's the resistance (your faction), The North Koreans and the Outlaws (survivors who are not apart of the resistance but live on the fringes of society shooting and killing anything that's not one of them).
-Pushing through enemy lines actually takes some effort because the enemy will flank you on occassion so that kinda keeps you on your toes at all times.
-Weapon designs are pretty cool and their sound effects are excellent.
-Guns in this game actually feel like they have weight and impact on whatever target they hit.
The greatest praise I can give this game is that the game sets up the perfect atmosphere and mood for the environments that you move through. All and all I have to say by the time I got to the end of the game, the story had me wanting to know more about this world and its lore. I didn't want it to end and it will end abruptly I might add because it's a rather short game for its genre anyway. If you ever find this one on sale definitely give this one a try. It's more fun than you'd expect.

I'll opt for an 85% rating for Grid Autosport primarily because;
* Pack racing is back with softened handling models!  Think more PS1 ToCA and a bit less Grid2.
* Awesome selection of circuits/tracks and vehicles.
* Multiple racing disciplines catered for (like Grid2) with Touring, Endurance, Street, Drift/Tuner, Open-wheelers.
* Wear and damage mechanics fits the gameplay very well.
* Vastly improved UI for tuning tweaks between races.
* The garage system and XP levelling works very well, with a fairer upgrade system.  Aids longevity.
* Streamlined menus and navigation (compared to Grid2 especially.)
* Solo career mode is actually engaging this time.  A definate nostalgia nod to the Alain Menu rivalry of PS1 ToCA days.
* The visuals and audio are highly optimised throughout for low-ultra PC system specs.
* Above all - it's a fun, varied racer with that "i'll just have one more go" factor!
Deductions and downsides are;
* No text chat (or even spectator mode) that makes waiting around in lobbies for the next race rather dull, and democratic custom cups changes almost impossible.
* Region-locked lobby creation is promoting tumbleweed already sadly... - i've only met 4 Americans and 1 Canadian all week [tsk, I fully realise some friends see this as a positive! rotflmao :)) ]
* No gamepad/joystick calibration options contrary to supported wheels.
* Disfunctional team radio feature (and absent from MP.)
* No mirrors (or acceptable interiors for PC due to PS3/Xbox limitations) and fixed 90' headlook views.
Upshot;
* Touring with twelve car Mr Bean-esque pack racing in Minis around Brands Hatch is an arcade game exclusive and hilarious!  Truely it's a sight to behold, so come and join in folks.
* Why sit there reading this Grid Autosport review when you could be on track having fun?

Bitesize Review - Homefront
The Good:
- Environments are varied and mostly interesting
- Guns that you use look nice, seems like they put extra detail there
The Bad:
- Characters are boilerplate and/or forgetable
- Aiming/Gunplay feels off
- Story is predictable, "America, ♥♥♥♥ yeah!"
- Enemies are not really set up in the story, aka there is no main bad guy or voice of the enemy, all generic soldiers
- In game advertising (TigerDirect, Nos Energy Drink, and oh-my-god Hooters, yep, no really, I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not)
- Single Player game is really short (I beat it in 3 hours)
- Multiplayer is completely dead (July 2017)
- This feels like they were trying really hard to make a Call of Duty clone here, but ultimately come up short
The Verdict:
I am a bit torn on this game - on one hand it was not inherently bad, its ok, but for the price they are asking there are better games out there.
For the most part it very much feels like a game that is trying it's best to copy call of duty, but every where I turn in the game it seems to come up short: The gunplay feels less snappy, the characters are less interesting, there is no real build up of story or characters and it all feels like a Direct-to-Video Call of Duty game. Add onto that that the single player game is very short (I beat it in 3 hours roughly) and that the multiplayer is dead and you get a less than good experience.
The only saving grace that I have for the game is that I bought this for less than $1 through a bundle - and at that price I would say this game was worth it - it entertained me for a few hours etc. But here on steam it's listed for $22, which I would never recommend anyone buy this game at the price. For that money you can buy two Call of Duty games on sale, and I know you'll have a better time playing those. I do apologise for comparing it to CoD so much but really when you play this you can tell they were trying really hard to cash in on that formula.

The saying has it that lightning never strikes twice in the same place.  But phantom pirate ships smashing their way through the walls of the same museum?  If you're series heroine Sara Black, it's all in a day's work.  Boasting the usual themes of supernatural evil, love, and redemption,
puts the capstone on a series that has held consistently high standards all the way through.
The cutscenes here feature passable 3D animation, much nicer than the flat-image manipulation found in many HO games.  The voice acting is solid, if somewhat hammy, but the overwrought delivery fits well with the melodramatic tale.  The HO scenes and puzzles are well-done, if somewhat unchallenging, in Artifex Mundi's usual style, plus the overworld screens feature their own set of hidden collectibles and optional achievements.  In my experience this is about as good as a hidden-object game can be.

The next couple updates came around claiming to fix this lag and everyone thought it would be perfect, but thats when we found the fatal error. My friends and I would try and play the game but when we would load into the server or even start up the game, an error proclaiming fatal error would appear. We could still load into the game after 3-5 attempts but it didn't end there...... Then came the triangle of fate, where this game went to fun to playable to unplayable. This War Of Mine opens with an Ernest Hemingway quote: “In modern war... you will die like a dog for no good reason.” This is very much indicative of the way the game consciously rejects the action-packed setpieces of countless blockbuster shooters that glorify and romanticize war in favor of portraying war realistically through the eyes of civilians trapped in a conflict they have no say in or part of, fighting for survival and experiencing life at its most cruel.
Like a good arthouse film or album of experimental music, This War Of Mine is very much a mood game. It strongly evokes feelings of intense unease, dread, and despair, so while I wouldn't say that playing it is necessarily a fun experience, it is an immensely absorbing and compelling one. In a starkly pencil-sketched nation ravaged by civil war (no specific war in human history, just a nameless armed conflict with some Soviet-esque flourishes), you control a party of survivors and are tasked with item management, regulating their eating & sleeping regiment, nursing their wounds, making decisions about the fates of other survivors they encounter, and essentially keeping them alive. They are just as likely to die from crossfire during a scavenging excursion for vital medication as they are from taking their own lives out of desperation over the bleakness of their situation.
While the game ultimately does what it sets out to do, maintaining strong gravitas throughout, it falls short in some areas, primarily characterization. The cast of playable characters all feel cut from the same cloth – we're presented with a photo of each (12 in all) accompanied by a paragraph-long bio. Apart from that and some minor differences in their behavior and habits, they are quite one-dimensional, moving & acting much like each other and repeating most of the dialogue. For instance, when the 'depressed' condition pops up under 'hungry' or 'slightly sick' in one character's stats and you have another console him or her, their very brief conversation always plays out in two or three specific ways and you're left to your own devices to fill in the narrative. Also, much is touted about decision-making being part of the simulated war experience, that you'll find yourself torn about choosing to steal from others or deny them help in order to ensure your own survival, but I personally didn't flinch in these scenarios because the strangers in them are even less well-drawn than the main characters in your own party. Whether this is a price of the game being a small, independent production or an overlooked element that could've been more developed, it stands out all the more because the rest of the game is so strong.
You won't always be in the mood to play This War Of Mine, but when you are, it hits the spot like no other game I've experienced. I applaud 11 Bit Studio's choice to take a bold, unexplored approach to this subject matter in this medium, further demonstrating that videogames are a valid art form capable of evoking feelings, setting atmosphere, and telling stories just as vividly and stylishly as any other.

Greetings as always!  Let us get to my next review, Sins of Solar Empire:  Rebellion.  If you have been following my reviews at all you know that I have a weakness for RTS, especially those with depth and expansions.  How does this game compare?  Well to start I have almost 120 hours played and 100% unlock achievement wise…so what do you think?  Anyway Review time!
Lane Jumping:  This game is one of my top RTS to play (alongside the StarCraft Series and the Dawn of War Series), with that said it has some very well done differences.  To begin with the game is designed to be played at a more macro level:  everything from ship-management to research can be done while zoomed out; creating a massive suite of quality of life features, especially shift commands which I find essential in an RTS.  The base line of the game is a space faring real time strategy where you colonize planets that are separated by phase lanes, which are warp points that separate the planets gravity wells.  The idea being that only gravity wells inhibit phase jumps and are really the only things worth fighting over (for the sake of this asteroids, space stations, even stars are planets).  You do a light amount of management of the planets but they act more like a new resource point and less like a planet to govern.  Finally, you can build capital ships that level up and have special abilities.  All this done fully zoomed out or so close you can see your individual fighters flying around.
Benny Hill Time:  The game does have some minor flaws however; one of the biggest is the AI’s overwhelming need to run away from any fight if they have less than a 99% chance of winning.  In most RTS the enemy will send probing attack at you from time to time and depending on the RTS in question they may eventually retreat.  But, they will always come in and at least try to attack.  The AI in Sins will run away immediately when it does some background calculation stating that it would lose the battle.  It doesn’t matter if it has reinforcements coming and only needs to hold you up or this is their capital planet.  Amusingly (and annoyingly) they sometimes get caught in a weird loop where they warp out then come right back and continue doing this until they have the forces to overwhelm you or you slowly kill their entire fleet by staying near the phase lane.  This by far is biggest annoyance of this entire game that and…
Narratives in Space:  This game, like many well thought out RTS have an amazing narrative with an interesting back-story, unfortunately that is where it ends.  I love this game so much and would pay for an entirely new game for just a single player campaign.  But alas, nope… However, where the game fails in a story the narrative is really good.  The ships have voice over’s and even the research you can do allude to a bit of story between the factions.  In addition to that the games art style is amazing including realistic ship designs with a diverse amount of weapon types and sound effects.  The game does tend to do a bit of cookie-cutter in the ways of the roles of the ships where the placement of the ship in the build menus tends to serve the same role as the other factions but they still feel unique in their methods and even abilities.  Oh, and the fact that ships behave like they should (kind of hard to dodge in a big capital ship) is really great, seeing these big fleets line up to shoot while hundreds of little fighters and bombers flying about is amazing.
As I’m sure you have seen I spent a fair bit more time telling you what I don’t like instead of what I do.  I want to be clear, if you love RTS this game should be in your library.  This is why I seem to have a bit of a negative look at it; tis another game so close to perfection it hurts.  So, do I recommend?  You bet I do!  Just do a Google search to change how to make AI stop being such cowards and / or play with human friends.  Up to you, enjoy!

It's pretty hard not to do a joke review about this game with all of the top-tier memes it gives you.
However, this is a game I hold dearly. It has a place in my heart no other game can fill, and it will always be the first computer game I ever had that gave me something to show off to friends with.
You see, if you got this game from a cereal box (like most of us did), you are part of the best generation to experience PC gaming.
Or, who knows. Maybe you played the crap out of text-based adventures back in the day and just happened to love sugary cereal at the tender age of adulthood.
It truly was a good time to get into the idea of gaming on your computer. Not because legendary, classic titles came in cereal boxes, but because everyone of the "common genres" of game weren't set in stone yet and plenty of new companies were making PC games that were always probing an aspect of the video game that hasn't been looked into before. Nowadays the market of new games can be separated into "niche indie titles", "AAA games with PC ports" and the rare "well-rounded good game". Back then... you had the Tycoon series.
Ladies and gentlemen, the Tycoon series of games was probably what saved me from adolescent boredom and actually gave me something fun to do on Windows 98.
Bored after school? Boot up "Extreme Heights" and build another coaster that manages to do 10 loops in a row.
You could basically build whatever park you wanted and force dumb, oblivious NPCs to eat up whatever crap you make. The system was intricate. It was always giving you feedback for how reasonable your setup is, as well as fine-tuning over even the most menial tasks.
The slow nature of the game gave the players a lot of choice and challenge. Do you spend all of your money at once for something that can either make or break the park, or build a bunch of safe, small rides that will only gradually build me money?
It feels a little weird writing this review because of the fact that I never really stopped with RollerCoaster Tycoon games. It's a game I will always respect and my one hope is that it is never lost and forgotten.
The nostalgia value in this game is equivalent to Sock 'Em Boppers and Lincoln Logs.

It is alright. Not great but not offensively bad either. You will get your money's worth but I would recommend waiting for a sale before purchasing this game.
One complaint I do have is that there is a clash of sorts between mechanics and feel/aesthetic of the game. You are essentially playing as Rambo and as such, you get the feeling that you should go guns blazing. The games allows this with its charge mechanic and outright encourages you to use it often. However, there is a mechanic where you can rescue civilians (there are 10 on every level hidden throughout) that, if optional would not be an issue. However, the game prevents you from progressing unless you have killed X amount of villains beforehand. Rescuing the civilians counts as 10 villains and there is a set amount on every level therefore making something that felt optional a requirement.
This added to the fact that the game adds precision platforming at certain points in the game (which would be fine, but it  does not keep with the theme of game), causes the pacing to have this stop/go/stop feeling to it that dampened my experience.  I don't regret buying/playing this game but it is nothing special and you wouldn't be missing out if this game ended up deep in your backlog.

As a free to play game Magic Duels is worth the price* of admission for the tutorials alone: they teach you how to play Magic while managing to be interesting mental puzzles in their own right - mostly in the form of "here's a new mechanic for you, now use it to survive this turn or win this scenario in one turn". It reminds me of the "Magic: the Puzzling" articles from the early days of the card game.
On top of that you get eight single-player campaigns, each consisting of five (or more) Magic duels linked by a story. I've so far played through three of these and they are also remarkably good considering the "price" of the game.
The ability to collect cards and make your own decks is a pale shadow of the real thing (I say this as a former Magic card player out of the game for a good few years now) but has the not-inconsiderable advantage that you don't have to spend any of your own money on it if you don't want to. I've only had the game installed for a week but I look forward to playing with this more in the future, and trust it won't feel too "grindy" - which is a criticism I have heard of the game but have yet to experience myself, but then I'm still working my way through the single-player campaigns as I mentioned.
There has just been a new expansion added, "Shadows over Innistrad", that brought me to this game as a way to try it out when I heard about it online and was interested. It looks very atmospheric, with strong horror/Lovecraftian themes to many of the cards - in mechanics as well as art and flavour text.
This could therefore be the perfect time to join in as a new player, when a set is new, mysterious, and has "buzz" about it.
