As we approach the last act of the
series, we are yet to learn the origin of notorious Davy Jones. So far, so good. But with this final act of the trilogy, I'm happy to declare that we are in for a little more than a
rip-off; an appropriate interpretation that will shed some light to a more fairytale version of the old tall tale.
After challenging the verdict of the infamous sea devil more than once, Sarah Black is in for a little visit from the man himself! During a seminar that she organized to tell the world of the secrets of Davy Jones, the party gets crashed and Sarah gets abducted alongside with her daughter. Davy agrees to spare Sarah by making her daughter sign a contract for her to work as a servant in Davy Jones' island forever. As resourceful and persistent as she is, Sarah takes the quest of rescuing her daughter by breaking all deals that the sea devil holds: once and for all.
As I declared beforehand, the concept of Davy Jones is interpreted as a fairytale, with nuances fitting for a European folktale rather than an eerie Caribbean mystery - which was a welcoming surprise coming from the developer team. Side characters as accursed pirate lords of the old, the eerie sea witch with her own agenda and the ghost of the young, innocent girl trapped in the island vivified the rather dark tone and established the baseline for all Artifex Mundi games: stories of magic and mystery; harbored with imagination rather than grotesque fear, fitting for a HOG adventure.
Here in this tale, we are in for a visual feast: the best and most glamorous artwork the series had to offer so far with shining lights, growing shadows, brilliant colors and otherworldly designs. Both dialogues and the voice acting a pretty well developed, evolving with each new game also. Artifex Mundi seems to topple down its own limits with the application and elaboration put into this one.
As always, a ton of HOG scenes - with fairly different variations - , a collection of imaginative puzzles and a hunt for a handful of collectible items await us in this adventure. The alternating Mahjong gameplay, the interactive map and a bonus chapter at the end comes gift wrapped. You are in for a rather long game; I'd give at least 5-6 hours for the first playthrough, and maybe 2 hours for the second if you are an achievement hunter. One little minus - for me, at least - was that the chest guarding creepy dwarves that we encountered in former games were nowhere to be seen, aside an old one who'd give us a quest item and exhaust his use quite fast! Hey, I was getting akin to those guys! But no worries, here we have - maybe creepier stone guardians who hold the fragments of memories belonged to Davy Jones to present us insight about the background of all affairs.
Without the need to belabor further, here is the last part of a pretty great series and a well above average HOG by its own self. Pick it on sale and enjoy with its previous installations.

The original Bioshock was incredible, and this is an improvement overall.
GAMEPLAY:
I loved hacking in the original BioShock, and in this iteration, it was even more fun and dynamic. The player can now use plasmids and weapons simultaneously, allowing for bigger and badder encounters. The developers are not afraid to throw way more enemies at you compared to the original. The new enemy types are challenging and fun to fight! Most of the new weapons have an equivalent in the first game, so you still have access to a fantastic arsenal by the end of the game.
STORY:
The storyline exposition starts off super weak. You don't really have a great sense of purpose until you meet Sinclair really. At least he has a clear objective you can follow. The voice actors for Sinclair, Eleanor and Lamb rendered an effective and convincing performance. The biggest criticism I have of the game is that Lamb as chief antagonist does not become interesting until the end of the game, redeemed by a few good lines in the last level. The storyline failed to get me interested until the last couple levels. I only got to that point because I love Bioshock's gameplay.
CONCLUSION:
If you enjoyed the gameplay of the original, you'll probably love this. It's definitely an improvement from that perspective. The last quarter of the game the characters start to get interesting. That section of the game when it all comes together, this is pure shooter/RPG bliss.

Magic Duels is a great way to enjoy the classic trading card game in a digital format. And without even spending a cent.
However if you do choose to go the route of not spending you'll be facing an uphill climb, as booster packs contain only 6 cards (including 1 rare or mythic rare), and with the economy in the game set up the way it is, you'll be lucky to unlock more than a single pack a day.
The enemy AI provides a real challenge without being overwhelming in most cases.
The story mode is a nice touch that allows you to engage with the backstory for each set, while also allowing you to use strategies unique to iconic myg planeswalkers which you may not yourself otherwise try out.
The deck wizard feature, which is meant to assist new players in creating certain themed decks is a little lackluster. I felt that halfway through unlocking all the cards of the origins set that my decks were stronger than after finishing unlocking the entire set. Perhaps this is an in-built function meant to encourage players to create their own decks after they've accrued enough experience. But nonetheless, it does feel somewhat clunky.
The regular deck builder could also do with more filtering options, such as searching for certain keywords on cards, but it gets the job done. It just would have been nice to search out synergistic cards with greater ease.
Overall its a pretty fun experience for any MtG fan. But I do think Wizards of the Coast could do with increasing the value of their daily quests. With 4 sets worth of cards to unlock, its a prety daunting task for a new player to unlock all of them, and try to catch up with the meta.

I'm a big post-apocalyptic fan, and I like card games and strategy, so when I saw this listed in new releases I was intrigued. There were no steam reviews, nothing in the entire discussion forum (which is very unusual) so I ummed and ahhed over making the purchase. Ultimately it was the price that made me take the plunge, that and steams robust refund system.
The premise is simple. It's the zombie apocalypse, you have to get a car and resources and then escape the city. You've seen it a million times before. You have a game board which includes the city, inside your base, outside your base, trade, sacrifice and your stockpile. The game presents you with two options to start you off; single player (solitaire) and multiplayer. Since I do not know anyone with the game, and the playerbase is currently tiny, this is mostly a review of the single player game. In single player you are versus no one, but simply trying to get the highest score and escape, with a selection of 8 difficulties from tutorial all the way up to impossible. You can choose how many sets you need to win, how many bases you control, and can toggle an extra dead card.
Your cards are made of up the dead, character cards, action/location/special cards and resources. The aim is to get as many resources into your stockpile, whilst using your character cards to remove the dead cards before you are over-run.Although the premise is simple, the game cards are pretty complicated. I had to do a lot of reading and thinking even in the tutorial whilst trying to get to grips with the cards. They have a lot more depth than many card games, with cards having multiple actions depending on where they're placed.
I have a scavenger card. If I play it on an outside tile, I take a random card from the city, or I can take a card from the graveyard if it's a resource. But if I play her inside, I kill a dead card from my base. If that dead card turns out to be food, I put it in my stockpile. Or I can sacrifice her, and put her in the graveyard to look through the graveyard and take another character card from it. Or I can put her in my stockpile, and add up my score to escape the city. And that's one of the simpler cards. Many cards interact with each other in a multitude of ways, and you can play combos and loops to make a turn last a long time.
In multiplayer you have more depth, because some cards interact with other bases - you can choose to send zombies to another player for example. In solitaire mode, some cards don't do what they should since they can't, and sometimes the only option is your base rather than throwing hordes at your opponent. This game would be a great party game or something fun for a group of friends. It plays up to 8 both locally and online, which is really nice to see, as a lot of games are limited to four. I don't actually have 8 friends, but maybe one day I will!
The graphics are very very busy. The text can be hard to read and the icons don't have mouseovers for more detailed explanations although there is a visual guide to the symbols you can pop up at the bottom. I found it very hard to see at a glance what a card did or how it affected my board because of this and just felt that it looked jumbled and messy - not a clean space. I know art is subjective, but I think it looks kinda ugly - not to an extent that would stop me playing it though.
[Edit 23rd June]As a side note, I brought up a bug regarding achievements and the developer immediately responded and fixed them. Not only that, but the updated the card graphics to be cleaner and easier to read too! 10/10 on listening to feedback.

Crea is a cute sandbox RPG with procedurally generated worlds that is heavily inspired by Terarria; therefore, if you enjoyed playing Terarria, you'll probably have a lot of fun with this one too. Even more so, since Crea extends what Terarria offers with a few new features that are very entertaining and nice.
One of the most important features is the leveling system: everything you do in Crea gives you experience points, categorized by what you do to gain them. The XP are not added only to your character level, but they're also split according to the action you perform: exploring will give you XP in the Exploration category, mining or cutting wood will give you XP in the Gathering area etc. In addition to that, there's a talent system - according to the level you have in an area, you can unlock passive or active abilities that make your character stronger or increases your gathering or crafting skills.
The two main aspects of these kind of games are split in two separate interfaces - there is a setup for survival mode (combat) and another setup for the gathering mode (building); each of these setups comes with two separate toolbars that you can customize according to your needs. Switching between the setups or the toolbars is very easy (one key press). However, having this kind of design makes it a bit difficult during early levels to perform both combat and gathering during the night, since switching to combat mode makes you lose the only source of light you have, leaving you in complete darkness to fight with your enemies, unless you put down a torch every few steps. This problem falls away at later levels by the time you acquire luminescent weapons or a spell that conjures a light orb that follows you.
The enemies are of various types and come with different fight mechanics: some of them should be meleed from behind, others can be killed easier using ranged weapons. This makes good use of the double toolbar setup for the combat mode, since you'll need to have both a melee set of weapons and a ranged one. I found the difficulty of the enemies at lower levels a bit too high, even on easy mode - they do a lot of damage; you need to parry or dodge a lot since the majority of them can kill you in 2 hits.
Crea has Dungeons, how cool is that!!! Independent areas on the map, that despawn after completion, dungeons provide a lot of fun and... very cool loot(since you can snatch all the goodies and fill your house with shinies) :)
The crafting aspect of the game is extensive; you can craft the plain old way, by one-clicking (oh and by the way, crafting with this method is instant, there's no progress bar or waiting time until you get your desired item). As an alternative to that, the game features Chaos-mode, which is a mini game that makes use of crafting talents gained through leveling in order to produce better or more items. The crafting recipes are discovered by researching but you are only able to research recipes you have mats for. On one hand, this limits your crafting possibilities to items that you have mats for. On the other hand, you can't see a full list of everything that can be researched; if you want to craft a fancy item, you won't know in advance what you need to gather in order to research it, unless of course you spoil it for yourself by consulting the Wiki.
The clean interface features moveable windows, which is very useful while crafting, either for organizing your inventory and the needed mats or for comparing the stats between the crafted gear and the equipped one. However, even with these moveable windows, I found it quite annoying that I don't have any indication when a mob attacks me while having my screen full of these windows. I believe that a blinking screen or a red border would be very useful in this case.
The basics of the game are summarized into a short and concise tutorial; the information that it provides is in my opinion enough not only to get you started, but also to make you understand the mechanics of the game; the rest is left to the player's own exploration.
Apart from some small bugs that didn't disturb my gameplay enjoyment too much, I had only one problem with the game: it consumes quite a lot of PC resources despite the fact that it shouldn't; the lighting or having multiple things happening in the background is very CPU hungry, often causing spikes; after 3-4h in game my PC already starts to struggle with the high CPU usage and tabbing out doesn't help it at all. Since the developer is quite active in the forums, I have faith that this optimization issue will soon be addressed and fixed.
I had a lot of fun playing Crea so far. I feel that it's a wonderful and well designed game that is worth the asking price. For the nice graphics, hours of entertainment, Steam integration with achievements and workshop, I highly recommend this game.

Known for being the company that houses the slaves that will forever make Pokemon games for the next century, once in a while Gamefreak comes out with a game under the tentative title, 'Notpokemon'.
Tembo stars the eponymous elephant out to save the city from an invading army out to conquer the once peaceful city. Called back into action by an old war buddy, Tembo leaves his peaceful island for the chaos of the metropolis. I like the character, I like the premise, but I don't like the lack of funding. Then again, this was meant to be a download-only title for consoles, which tend to be short, bite-sized games that don't risk much of the publisher's finances.
And despite being a short experience that ends rather fast, it packs a lot into that small space. Tembo is a platformer that's more horizontal than vertical. Rather than jump high and far, Tembo moves with urgency and agility. It's the difference between Sonic and Mario platformers; Mario specializes in vertical motion whilst Sonic moves horizontally. Likewise, Tembo is about moving with a never-ending dash that hits enemies in his way, an aerial spin dash that goes in at an angle to crash onto enemies below, and a forward slide that ducks below fire. For an elephant, Tembo moves a lot like a Hedghehog.
But don't confuse it for a Sonic title. The constant dashing with ocassional jumping is often interrupted by a fight with a helicopter or tank. Or a large room requiring you to dodge fire carefully, move a giant ball to a location, or to carefully launch yourself from one area to another using spinning gears. Tembo is about balance; balancing speed and maneuverability with timed platforming segments requiring thought out movement.
This is compounded by the enemy and civilian scoring system. Each level has 10 civilians to rescue, with some requiring a bit of level exploration rather than just dashing through the entire thing. Instead of just going forward, you're more likely to take the vertical path to see if any civvies need rescuing, and you're more than likely to encounter enemies that add to your enemy score. Each level has a set score, and defeating all enemies in the level and rescuing all civilians gets you a perfect. You can't ignore this neither, since you need a set score to unlock the 4th level in each world and move onto the boss. Unlike what a lot of bit*h reviewers said though, it's pretty easy and there's absolutely no need for alarm. If you're trying to 100% a level though, you end up feeling like a real queer for missing one or two enemies and might disdain playing the level again just for that.
I don't like it as much as I loved Drill Dozer (another one of their titles), but it's still alright. I wish there was more variety in the levels and soundtrack, maybe more endless running segments like the one on the train (where you have to escape an incoming wall of electricity). Otherwise, I've got no complaints. I love the concept though, and wished they really fleshed the hell out of it and had a Rambo three desert level parody, with a ton more cutscenes. But for what's here I liked it enough to recommend it.

I love Autosport, it really does feel and play like the old TOCAs and Grid 1. Combined with tracks that are very fun to race on, like Mount Tremblant, Autosport Raceway and Okutama (which I love trying to take flat out), Autosport is just fun.
I have only raced the AI in Street and Open Wheel so far, haven't gone online yet.
I love racing the AI, they are tough to pass at the higher difficulties and are quick. They tend to be brick-like and absolutely stable on the track when you collide with them (which you will because they tend to be a bit blind and don't acknoledge your car at times). You will spin and they will not. It's a great thing that you can't just shove them out of the way, however it does feel one-sided because of how easy your car gets shoved out of the way.
The career mode is nice but does not hold a candle to the career mode in GRID. In Autosport you only sign contracts to drive with other teams, with minimal ability to change the car's handling/sponsors/liveries. You don't have that team building you had in GRID, so you can't hire a teammate, upgrade your car, change sponsors for more XP, etc. In the different disciplines you do tend to race on the same tracks over and over, just with different configurations, which also makes career feel a bit thin. I read that sometimes you get stuck with different events in career that do not align with the path you chosen, meaning that if you choose to do street you get stuck with a drift event. I'm not sure if I will like that, however I haven't come across it yet.
While racing, depending on your settings, you gain XP which is used to unlock higher disciplines. Going without assists, locking your view to cockpit (why would you do that, the cockpits are terrible), and higher difficulties = higher XP gained and faster career progression. You can eventually unlock a GRID league, which is all 5 disciplines combined.
Graphically, the game seems really optimised, I have 50+ fps on a rig with a GTX 580 on ultra settings. It is pretty nice looking, with nice details on the cars (not project cars good). CM did a great job making the racing environment seem alive, with announcers announcing incidents, the crowd cheering, helicopters and other outside events making the tracks seem 'alive'. The cockpits are terrible however, they were just put there to appease those who complained about them missing in GRID 2. They are blurry, the mirrors are useless, and it is a bit distracting for me to drive using that view.
Need to try out online before I give my final verdict, but I do really love the game because of the racing. The racing is pure fun, the packaging can use a little more work.
Pros:
The racing AI is tough at the higher difficulties
Can choose what path in career to take (in a way)
Lots of tracks and cars to use
Cons:
Career mode is a bit thin
The AI are tanks and blind
Cockpits are terrible

Pros:
- Great music
- Grout sound
- Outstanding graphics, especially considering the low system requirements
- Dialogue is almost completely voiced and the voice acting is solid - if you liked the campy voice acting from Star Fox 64  you'll get a lot of that from the australian space pirates as you blow them to smitherines.
Cons.
- I'm only 6 hours in as of the time that this review is being written, and gameplay is already starting to feel repetitive - that's usually a bad sign.
- Combat is kinda meh - you can only move in two dimensions, making it less like a true 3D space sim and more like a watered-down version of Assassin's creed's ship battles, except without boarding actions. (On the other hand, some players might appreciate the simplicity of not having to navigate 3 dimensions)
- Trading / mining / playing the economy is much less intuitive than other swashbuckler open world space games, and your cargo hold starts out way too small to trade items in bulk.
- Mining lasers are REALLY overpowered early on, to the point that they almost ruin the experience - they have perfect accuracy, do bonus damage to shields, burn right through armor, and when used on asteroids they tend to obliterate them without leaving any minerals behind.
- Enemy ships have infinite ammunition for their missile launchers - you, on the other hand, have VERY limitied ammunition for YOUR missile launchers. If you run into an enemy destroyer equipped with shield-buster missiles, you're pretty much hosed.
I'm giving this a thumbs up because I got it 66% off for $6.79, and the soundtrack alone is probably worth that much - but honestly I think $20 is asking a bit much when you can play Endless Sky for free (sure ES's graphics and music suck by comparison, but honestly I think the gameplay and story are better)

Gotta Go Fast! - Wait a second, that's not a Hedgehog.. that's an elephant! A damn cute and cunning one on top of that!
This elephant ain't lackin' in speed though and additionally he has the moves to back it up! Mario would be proud!
Tembo the Badass Elephant is inspired by Games from the Sonic and Super Mario franchises. Little details like a similar death animation as Sonic's or enemies hiding under vegetables just like in Super Mario 2 are direct tributes, but he's not just a clone. He packs his own punch.
Being able to constantly dash gives this game a definite sense of momentum and Tembo's skillset containing Upper Cuts, Dash Rolls and Ground Stomps (Makes more sense for an elephant than for a plumber once you think about it) makes him a versatile fighter and not just a nimble runner.
In order to master his entire skillset you'll absolutely require time and practice. The beginning can be a little bit harsh and although you didn't intend to dash into that enemy or speed roll into that pit those instances will occur, even in the later stages when I thought myself to be more experienced, pressing the wrong buttons can get you killed faster than you want to. I definitely want to see someone speed run this game with the utmost precision.
The level design is interesting and the game doesn't overstay its welcome. The difficutly ramps up at a good pace and never hits a brick wall ceiling (It's not one of those super insanely difficult platforming games).
The story is being told in a comic strip fashion - fitting for the art style, which in itself is well suited and appealing,
I can recommend Tembo The Badass Elephant to any 2D platforming fan out there in a heart beat!

This is the kind of game you shouldn't play to have fun.
Don't get this game if you want to blow off steam by shooting people. The controls are poor and the difficulty curve is stacked against you. The AI are both stupid and clairvoyent, and only when you don't want them to be.
Don't play this game for a conventional story. There is none, outside of something you could find in a Dethklok or Cannibal Corpse song.
This is the kind of game you should play if you want to know how to integrate game mechanics into story telling.
Play this game for a very interesting example of story told through in-game mechanics. The aesthetic of the game makes things harder to see. The executions break up the pace of the game, and can't be avoided as health comes from them. The combat is unfairly difficult, buggy, and prone to AI which at times are beyond stupid and above clairvoyence. The lives system is as brutal and unforgiving as a coin-eating arcade game from the nineties. The end of the game is anti-climactic and truly resolves nothing, if there ever even was anything to resolve.
But all of this brings forth a message. You are not rewarded for playing. The game progressively punishes you more and more until it either breaks you or makes you look like something you're not. It is never supposed to be a fun time, the same way as a killing spree isn't.
My overall verdict: Don't play the game. Try to pull it apart and see how it really works, without all of the noise and controversy. Maybe you'll find something you didn't expect to find.

Homefront review
================
Note before I start: I only played the single player campaign. I have no interest in the multiplayer.
I'm sad to report that this game falls victim to nearly all the problems with modern FPS shooters.
✓ seemingly infinite waves of cannon fodder thrown at you until you do some particular, often suicidal job
✓ storyline that insults my intelligence. Not even talking about the setting and backstory. I'm talking about the actual, in-game story.
✓ "tactics" that insult my intelligence. No, "flanking through the back yard" does not mean "keep going through this street full of enemies until the corridor takes the shape of a back yard".
✓ "we only tell you the part of the mission that pertains to this next corridor section."
✓ Hollywood grenades
✓ generally terrible AI (not following you when necessary, but waiting for your lead; not noticing the enemies right in front of them)
✓ invincible AI teammates
✓ regenerating health
✓ no legs or body. You don't even have a shadow
✓ sniper mission
✓ vehicle missions
✓ "We do everything as a team, so you take that church all on your own" mission
what's worse:
✓ The campaign is incredibly short. Got through it in one sitting. Keep in mind that I'm not the best at shooter games and had to redo quite a few bits. Instead of going for full-time action adrenaline explosions everywhere, some more pacing, realistic fights and good setup and tension arcs could have made for a much better campaign.
✓ often get stuck on terrain while prone
✓ no way to lean around corners. No leaning means enemies can simply fire at you and you'll take full damage just to have a peak.
✓ inconsistent AI. Sometimes, the AI empties an entire clip on you from 10m away and you survive. Other times, they manage to easily shoot and kill you from 40m away while you're lying behind a truck and shooting through a narrow opening.
The good things:
✓ skippable cutscenes
✓ I had a couple of hours of my life that I didn't have to wonder what else to do to keep myself busy.

Relative to the other Civ games out there this is more than a step backwards. There are a lot of little things done wrong and I’ll try to hit on a couple as concisely as I can, addressing people familiar with Civ5.
One of the problems is your opponents don’t start the game on the map, they drop in randomly at later turns. The same is true with this games version of city-states called outposts. So when you’ve explored at little like other Civ games you start to think about where your second city will go, but it’s extremely unlikely you’ll get to put one there without a fight because of outposts popping up. Instead of just worrying about other nations building a colony unit and grabbing the land you wanted, you have to deal with that plus cities and outposts popping up literally anywhere. All Civ games are random, but this adds a dynamic randomness that is just annoying.
Another thing is the map is filled with “miasma,” which is green fog that damages units. It makes the game more tedious exploring and colonizing especially with the large amount of aliens (barbarians) floating around. You can also gain the ability to make this miasma not harmful to your units. But, even when your units are immune to it your automated workers will still clear it from tiles when it can only benefit you if your opponents aren’t immune to it. This just shows a lack of polish they were starting to gain in the series.
Even little things like the quotes when you gain technology or build wonders aren’t as good. In the games where the quotes were tied to historical figures they were a lot more interesting. The made up quotes try to be funny or show personality but are mostly just stupid and don’t add to the flavor of the game.
Another issue is all the buildings have secret abilities that you don’t know until you build one. Like you get to pick between two resources that all of the buildings of this type will produce. If you knew that ahead of time you might have chosen what buildings to build in a different order. As it is there is just more things to remember for the next game if you want to get good and play the game smart.
The fluid technology paths just add to the sense that you’d really have to play the game a ton of times to make good choices on which order to do your research.
It’s not complete crap, but it compares poorly to other Civ games in pretty much every way it is different.

Though I think the game itself to be very original and quite enjoyable, I cannot recommend it to any Linux users because of their abysimal (or lack of) support for the platform.
When I bought the game about three months ago, believing their promise that it would run on Linux, I was surprised to see that it just refused to run on my Ubuntu box.
After searching the forum for an answer, I found that the problem was an obsolete version of a library the game was using, and the problem has been reported by multiple users long before I bought the game.
Due to this issue, any recent installation of almost all major Linux distros will fail to run this game. And if I understood correctly, all it takes to fix this problem is to recompile (or repackage) their game using the latest library.
Now, 3 months have been passed since I bought the game, and almost half a year since the issue has been initially brought up, but there's no official patch or even acknowledgement of the problem except for a forum post by another user who says he or she heard that the company said it will be fixed in the next version.
So, I lost all my respect for this game company, at least as one which claims to develop Linux games, and I would discourage any Linux users to buy games from them.

As a bonus, here's some tips for both the standalone game and OpenRCT2 (based on the "Build Your Own Six Flags Park" Scenario):
- Start slow. Don't go right into building coasters. Build food stands and simple rides (Ghost House, for example) until you have enough people in your park. Otherwise, you will have blown all of your money and spent at least $20,000 of your $100,000 loan.
- Go easy on the inversions for most rides. You can have a big coaster with a lot of inversions, but don't do it for every ride. Not only does it become confusing after a while, but your guests won't like it.
- (OPENRCT2 ONLY) You can go fast, but don't go TOO fast. 200 mph should be fine, but don't do a 50 lap coaster going at 500 mph. This will probably crash the game.

I think this game falls under a "wait and see" category, even though I did mark this as a recommended review. I decided on this because while there are notable flaws, my overall experience wasn't negative and the developer seems to be constantly working on the game. I picked Crea up during its -10% release sale. The developer has said the next sale will be in December 2016, at ~25% off.
I suppose the first game people jump to in comparison is Terraria. I loved Terraria. I rarely think about Terraria when playing this game. I would draw more similarities to Starbound. I didn’t like Starbound, but Crea doesn’t draw out the same dullness I felt from there.
Crea has two leveling systems. The first is the general character/combat level that increases as you kill monsters. Your stats go up, you get a point to allocate, simple enough. The second is the Talent system. Whenever you take an action, you have a chance to gain experience in a corresponding Talent, Arms (Weapons), Syle (Magic), Gather, Craft, and Explore. It’s a very nice system that feels rewarding… aside from Craft. I’ll talk about that later.
Graphics are nice, I like the more subtle colors compared to Terraria, while still remaining crisper than Starbound. Music is nice and accompanies the slower gameplay very well. Even though the gameplay is slower, I never really felt like my character itself was too slow. I know in Terraria the initial startup movement is extremely painful, but it feels good in Crea. Even with a Sprinting talent unlocked, I often forget about it simply because the normal walking speed is a great pace. The time before a grappler can be obtained is smoothed out with a Ledge Grab talent, and you can unlock a Double Jump talent farther in. Way Crystals are sprinkled throughout the world, and you can harvest them and create your own. You can choose any Way Crystal as your spawn point and teleport back using warp crystals that grow around Way Crystals. These grow back in pretty large numbers, so you’re never really low on them.
Now, Craft… it just feels bad after a certain point. At first, you’re blowing through it like every other talent. And then it stops. Why? Because you’ve already crafted what you needed. So you’ll find yourself running around, have all your other Talents continue going up in level… while the game is waiting for you to grind Craft. And it’s not supposed to be just random junk either. Nope. You have to craft things close to your level to actually gain exp. And only sometimes, because gaining Talent exp is through chance. Now, I will say I can’t tell if there’s a level indicator on non-level-restricted items, and I’ve seen some mentions about candle crafting working (which is somewhat cheap), but the whole idea just feels very contrasting with the other talents. It’s usually huge spikes in research followed by large droughts, you have to actively work on it with some vague concepts, while all the other Talents just happen, and it feels tightly linked to progression.
Overall, though, if you happen to look up Craft help and get through it’s not horrible. Crea has potential. Multiplayer needs to be ironed out but singleplayer seems fun.

Archeblade is a Free-To-Play 3rd person multiplayer action game that tries to pull off the idea of a multiplayer Devil May Cry, does it succeed? Not exactly. The concept of the game is to play in team vs team multiplayer matches and buy new characters with your in-game currency (like League of Legends for example) And the modes consist of your standard Deathmatch modes and Point Domination modes. The characters vary from strong brutes to fast assassin types and each character has several moves to choose from. The problem with the game though isnt so much the concept as it is the execution, since it suffers from performance issues, confusing interfaces and flat out boring combat. While it does have some good things going for it, it has an overall and overwhelming blandness to it that prevents it from reaching a wider audience.
THE GOOD:
> Character designs are interesting
> Moves look cool
> Can sometimes be fun
> Scantily clad female characters are R34 waiting to happen
THE BAD:
> Latency & Performance issues
> Lack of players

I often forget that Game Freak is capable of actually producing interesting thoughts in between rounds of rereleasing Pokemon every few years and seeing how many household appliances they can put eyes and a mouth on, but sometimes they decide to show that they can. Tembo the Badass Elephant sounds like the name of some sort of bad wacky Adult Swim game at first glance, but the game itself is actually pretty fun. It feels kind of like Donkey Kong Country with a little bit of Casino Night Zone thrown in for good measure, and while it's not all that difficult it's not dull enough to bore you either. It is a bit short, being only 18 stages long (it took me around 4 hours to complete it), so it may not be worth the full $15 price, but I personally thought it was a good length, since platformers tend to start to bore me after the first several hours unless they have a particularly good idea going on. My one regret is that Steam didn't release the refund policy earlier.

"Featuring 18 cleverly designed 2D side-scrolling levels, a whole host of deadly enemies and a unique comic book style art..."
That's all fine and dandy. Even the price point is ok. Definitely ok. The graphics are neat, the art style is colourful and pleasing to look at, the gameplay is so so. I hate it when games use the stick for potentially suicidal actions such as a groun d pound attack...the press-x-while-in-mid-air-to-commit-suicide-button is also a no go. The game also suffers from frame rate problems. There is no graphics options menu, you can only choose between 3 presets. That would be ok IF the game ran well, but as it stands my i7, GTX 970 and 16 gigs of Ram are apparently not enough to run the game without constant frame drops, even on medium, which is laughable and takes away the fun. I COULD let all of that slide and still "recommend" the game simply because it's cheap and it's not bad per se, BUT here is why I won't:
Back to that first quote...18 levels. Usually in a jump n run you beat a level to progress. That also means the average Joe will eventually beat a level, even if it means just getting through. Tembo does not allow for that. In Tembo each level has a certain amount of points you can achieve. For example, level 1 could have 322 points. You beat the first level, you go on to the second, then the third, but THEN you need 600 points to unlock the 4th level. After that you get a boss, which nets you a good amount of points. Ok, I thought, so far so ♥♥♥♥♥♥, I barely got the points together (700 or so), only to realize that in the next world I needed 2,400 points, which equates to about 90% of the total points available I'd say (I usually complete a level with 80-90%). You gain these points by killing enemies and rescuing civilians. There are 10 civis in every level, finding them takes a bit of effort at times. If you don't find all the civis you won't get the best score, if you don't kill all enemies you won't get the best score. So, you need to kill all enemies AND find all civis. Still doesn't sound horrible? The levels are usually set up in a way that makes backtracking impossible, so in order to get the required points you have to replay a level from the beginning...and you don't know what you miss (apart from the civis), so you kill everything again and get every civ again, only to realize that you just collected 2 points at the end of the level...yes, 2. ♥♥♥♥ you. Apart from that you will gather peanuts to fill Peanut Butter jars. When you die a jar is emptied. I have no idea what happens when all the jars are empty...according to the web, you just get 5 new lives, but you have to restart the whole level instead of reviving at a check point. Very, very annoying and superflous.
The game can be fun for about an hour, until you realize you have to grind your way through the rest of the game. I can only imagine the amount of points required for stage 3 will be even stricter, so I won't even bother. I don't buy games to play levels over and over again to find all the hidden stuff in order to progress with the story. So, no, Tembo is a bad elephant, not badass.
Edit: Extra minus point for unskippable credits -.-

Bloody good game. I was skeptical at first, but the more I play it, the more well designed I think it is.
I read an article that Codemasters designed the game to be a mix between sim and arcade, trying to hit a sweet spot. I think they did a bang up job. The racing is solid. Cars take damage and you can check the condition. When car parts like bumpers and side view mirrors come off, they hit the road and bounce just like they would in real life. The single player is a lot of fun.
Now here's some important info. You do level up in the game, and how many points you get is determined by what options you have on that make driving easier. The game takes away bonus point percentage if you are driving automatic instead of stick, if you have the camera view outside of the car instead of in the interior, the difficulty of the bots, if you're using a trail marker, stuff like that. I think that's smart and will cater very well to the hardcore crowd.
The AI in this game, is the only thing on my list of complaints. They will slow down to not slam into you, but they will run you off the road and slam you from the side. It's like playing with 12 year old trolls.
You can race many types of cars in this game, and they are categorized by 5 disciplines. F1 cars are also included. The amount of cars in this game will have you hooked. Very key in a racing game.
How's the online? For one, I don't notice any lag, really. I think the game might have a server system because I've been racing with mostly Americans/Canadians. I am located in Miami, FL, FYI. Also, you can play with your euro buddies as well. I just haven't ended up in matchmaking with any, but I'm sure others probably have.
Let me make this clear: YOU CAN ONLY UNLOCK CARS ONLINE. The single player is fun but its just for achievements. You unlock everything in multiplayer. You can play with other people or do the RaceNet challenges to make money and XP. Very important. You can also start car clubs and earn XP for it. You have to go to
to do it. As far as registering an account, you can do that in-game and there's no e-mail verification.
To conclude, I will tell you something you don't hear often in this day and age. This game has little to no bugs. I haven't experienced any. It is very fluid and well-designed. After playing this game, I am extremely satisfied with my purchase. I've been recommending it to friends. I say get it. It's not a complete sim and it's not a complete arcade.

It's a great game!  Basically, it plays like a hybrid of Rise of Nations and Star Wars Rebellion (an excellent but largely unknown 4x game from 1998).  It's a slow moving RTS that's constantly forcing you to make a thousand important decisions, but doesn't force you to make them within a fraction of a second.  Though it's an RTS through and through, it feels a bit more like a turn based strategy at macro level, and a bit more like a conventional RTS at the micro-level; at the planet level, you can micro-manage things in standard RTS fashion (though your units' AI is good enought that micro-management isn't really required for casual play), but at the macro level, you have to commit to moving fleets between planets (i.e. you can't turn them around half-way).  It's a really cool mix!

The last 20 days were more than boring as an effect. Once you got a functioning supply chain running, there's nothing compelling you to risk anything.
I got the house boarded up completely, 1 rifle, 2 guns, 2 rainwater collectors, 1 veggie garden, 2 rat traps, a distillery, herbal workshop and so on.
Basically I could produce all the food I need, bandages, alcohol... I was self-sufficient. The rest was a lot of skipping days.
Summary:
Get it on a sale, it's worth your money and time. You'll probably get 20-40 hours of fun and enlightenment out of it. It's beatiful while it lasts. Just don't expect too much depth and longevity.

When Sarah Black isn't saving pirates's soul or freeing mermaids and a village, she is a curator for a museum. However, after having managed to undo pacts with Davy Jones, the mighty pirate wants his revenge. And when her daugher, to save her, signs a pact with the devil, Sarah is again embarked in an adventure to save her child but this time, in Davy Jones's own lair. What she will discover will make her understand that maybe, Davy isn't so evil that she thinks...
The plot is again well constructed and is better than the prequels, though again, Sarah's daughter is in distress for the second time. And as in the first game, your enemy is only someone suffering from a broken heart, making him likeable.
Anyway, I found this game a little longer than the others but without any real changes from the previous ones. The gameplay is still find items, solve puzzles and hidden objects games. And the difficulty is also well balanced
As usual, the graphics are still beautiful, though now, it's a mix of the first game (ship) and the second game (village). The surreal ambiance is still present: talking skeletons for example. Now, the items you have to find for achievements are easier to spot than in the second game. The soundtrack is still agreable to hear.
The game concludes well the trilogy as you're finally uncursing Davy Jones. As usual, Artifex Mundi delivered a great game, that must be in the library of every HO lover but also any player interested by trying this genre! Don't hesitate!

Citadel in my eyes can only be enjoyed with friends on a custom server - I couldn't stand playing on some random server all of which are PVP and most of the world is already destroyed etc. Don't get me wrong, having 30-40 wizards in one session can be cool, but it really withdraws the fun very quickly. At the moment, we're playing in a group of 6 and are probably expanding on payday to around 8-10 which is more than enough for us. It's a fun game but here are some Pros and Cons:
Pros
- You can tame so much! (Dragons!)
- Great looking for an early access game
- Custom server is a bit of a hassle, but can be stable after set up
- The leveling system works well if you are in a group, because if someone doesn't have a skillset and you do, that's where team work can be fun
- Large open world with different things to do, not so much survival as far as Ark having to feed animals (which I hated micro management of pets)
- Quick turn around support; playing this on the first night I only got 20 minutes on a server due to fatal errors, which were hot fixed the next day
- I feel taht it has value for money
Cons:
- Major sync issues between personal client and server (unable to interact with or have your tamed beasts follow on your client due to sync issue, this needs looking at ASAP as you can loose your pets for no reason what so ever)
- The games EPIC settings really struggle with high end PC's and not sure why, possible optomization issue?
- Invisible wall at the top of the map, hope this is expanded on in the future
- Buggy AI that will blank you / one shot you on sync server lag
- XP becomes a grind once you've done a new task a few times over
How it can improve:
- The client sync issues need to be picked up ASAP as this is causing a ton of issues
- Maybe some more objectives in game e.g. a raid boss style area like some other parts of the map with mini bosses would be really interesting
- Pets should be accessible to those in your house/party
- Fix bug relating to not seeing people on your map or being identified on your HUD even if they are in the same party
Otherwise I would strongly recommend this game, as far as very early, and I mean very early access games go, this is amazing. This is better than most that have been in development for 1-2 years.

It's fun arcade racing game. Cars are very slidey and you need to drift most of the corners if you want to play optimally. Some people don't like it but I find it very satisfying to pull off series of turns while drifting perfectly.
Singleplayer is racing on different tracks with few special events dropped here and there. It's nothing special.
Multiplayer is where this game shines. You have experience level and you get money from races. You buy new cars with in-game money. If you're just starting out you're in bit of a disadvantange because you can't use all cars. Once you're about level 30 you'll have access to all the cars you will ever need. Multiplayer works fine and there aren't any lag issues. It's fun with many people but can get crazy if you have collisions enabled. Most of the matches don't have rammers and even if you get rammed in the beginning you can usually recover if you're a good driver. There are still many players during evenings. If you can't find any matches you need to change you steam download region to London. I think it's the best multiplayer arcade racing game on PC at the moment.
That being said I can't wait for GRID Autosport. I expect this game to die once it's released.

I must start out by stating that this is the first Magic the Gathering video game I have ever played. I am also very new to the card game itself, and I think it would be wise to state that so everyone knows the way I am thinking. Anyway, onto the review. The game is great, again not being able to compare it to other Magic games on Steam. It's whole job, or for what I found out, was to introduce the game of Magic to people who know not a whole lot about it, or to help new players get started with a solid tutorial. A very good game for anyone who wants to get into any sort of Magic game, cards or PC/Mac. The step by step instructions help a lot, and the mini tutorials (sorry, but I forgot the name) found in matches where you use new types of cards, help a lot. The screen doesn't get crowded and everything is very visible. One great feature is where you can use the mouse wheel and look at any card that is played. Not only does this help by being able to read the card, you get an explanation of what certain key-words mean.The game also features nice music to go along with the whole "magic" mood. The graphics look nice, and the animations are fun to watch. The two things I almost forgot to mention are first, the ability (in single player atleast) to stop the timer from running out. For those who do not know what I am talking about, you have a timer to play certain cards (instants) during the attacking/defending stages. This helps a lot so you can figure out a stragegy for who to attack and what your next plan of action will be. The other thing I almost forgot is the deck builder. This is one of the main parts of this game, and is done pretty well. There are two options for building decks, building one on your own, made for people who know what they are doing (no offense) and for people who don't realy know what they are doing (again not to offend anyone) like me, there is a handy "Deck Building Wizard" . Now this thing is amazing in my opinion. You start by picking a theme for your deck, be it more spells or brute force, and the deck wizard will pick out cards you have based on what theme you picked. It then gives you a few options to choose certin types of cards, then auto gives you land cards. After that you just pick a character you would like for the deck, and background, and your all set.
Thanks for reading my review. Like I stated at the beggining, this game is made for anyone who wants to fid out about magic, get to know the rules better, or even if you just don't have anyone to play with at the moment and feel like casting some spells. I know this review was based on good parts of the game only, but for the time I have put into this, I have not found anything wrong. I must state that the reason for this game being such a low rating, is that most players want to play competitavely and dislike it for that reason....Just thought I would make that clear.
Again thank you for reading my review and I am sorry for any grammar errors. Keep on gaming!

Crea is a game I really want to like.  I helped kickstart it years ago, and have been following along with the development.  It has a lot of good things about it, but plenty of bad, and right now, I cannot in good concience recommend this game.
Of course, there are bugs.  Many of them, though I have only been stuck by graphical glitches, unlike some.  I expect the major game-breakers will be resolved in the next few weeks, so I won't "mark off" for that.  The major gameplay areas of concern for me are combat, research and the "fun" factor.
Quite simply, combat is too hard and unforgiving.  This is related to both the monster-leveling, which makes the same mobs get strong and stronger as you move away from your base (and it does not take long before they one-shot you), and the odd combat upgrade system in general.  As there are no visual variations, an oil slime that you can easily kill in one area is instant death elsewhere.  This makes for frustrating play.  The intent is for you to level yourself and your gear, and grind to become better.  Unfortunately this is not obvious, and makes the game exceptionally gear dependant.  I could never add enough health, attack and defense via leveling to make up for the wrong tier gear.  The combat system itself seems to be more geared towards missile weapons and hopping and dodging, as even fighting correct level mobs is a 1 vs 1 affair.  The monster-leveling system ensures that facing a few mobs at a time is likely death.
Research is the second major flaw in the game.  At its core, the idea is that you research items you find and unlock recipes to make things.  Sounds good so far.  The problem is that there is essentially no guidance or progression.  You're left to your own devices to randomly research items you find, craft random items on the off chance it is something that will be researchable and unlock something else, and stack up piles of items for potential future use, because even if you have already researched an item, you may need to use it again for something else when you level up your "research trait".  Overall it is a confusing mess, that doesn't add much to the game except situations where you have copper ore and a forge but cannot smelt it because... you need vines?  Multiple that by hundreds of item combinations and you begin to see the issue.
It may be the above items, or something more subtle, but the game does not really feel "fun".  It is interesting for a litlle while (5 or 10 hours) while you figure out the mechanics of the system, but it's not deep enough or polished enough yet to hold my attention.
All of this said, I do want to like the game, and it is a far improvement over what it was like a year or more ago, so I have hope that the developer will take this sort of feedback to heart and the game will improve.  I'll keep my eye on it and update this review as patches change the gameplay.

Crea is a very fun addictive 2D sandbox game. Although it may at first glance seem similar to other competitors such as Terraria, the game strives to provide a unique experience through its unique talent and research systems.
+ Great Art Style and overall feel.
+ The research system is really cool. It works by consuming items in your inventory that are in a specific recipe to in turn unlock partial knowledge of that recipe as a whole. I was truly surprised as to how well this system fits into a game like this, not to mention how well the crafting system works alongside this.
+ The talent system works great and feels well implemented into a game of this nature. It is extremely fun both level up and improving your player's stats, as well as improving various perks in different skills that all rank up independently from each other.
+Great amount of exploration and lots to do.
+Trading Cards, Achievements, Workshop Support, etc.
+ Mac and Linux Ports much appreciated. It only took Terraria like 2 years and millions of sales to make some of those.
- REALLY BAD STUTTERING ISSUES. Although my frames per second was generally good (30-40 fps) considering my lower end hardware, the game would often freeze for multiple seconds at a time. This was mostly apparent during combat and crafting and was also reported by other users.
- Decent amount of bugs (Although the game did just release from early access)
-No Dedicated Servers
- LACK OF EXPLANATION: While there is some tutorial, the game could do alot better at explaining some of these elements.  It almost seems as though the developer assumed everyone playing also owned similar games such as Terraria or Starbound, and the game as a result is very unfriendly to beginners. There are various community guides to help supplement this thankfully, and although the game may be hard for some to initially get through with enough time this can be overcome.

Crea is certainly an extremely well thought out and well made game, and its unique research and talent systems alone make it worth buying.  Although, if you haven't played other similar games such as Terraria and Starbound, you may want to take a look at them first to get a grasp of the genre and how to play these kinds of games. However, if you've already played Terarria, enjoy RPG elements, and don't care about dedicated servers, Crea is definitely worth a purchase.  Just beware of some stuttering issues if your computer is lower end.

When I played Grid 2 I thought "great cars and tracks, too bad the engine is garbage, and where are the Grid 1 cars and tracks?"  Grid Autosport put a simle on my face.  The "Street" discipline has a mix of the Grid 1 & 2 cars and tracks (not sure if everything's there yet) and a great physics engine. Boss's nephew write that or something?)

And if you love memorizing brake points, or just need a cure for insomnia, there's some solid content in here for you.
Some reviewers seemed to be expecting a simulator.  From a Grid title?  Get real.  It's simcade all the way, and more power to it!  If you want to set toen-in angles or somesuch, Dirt 1 is still around, but this game focuses on getting the feel of driving at the edge of traction right, and the rest can hang for all I care. (And, yes, the heavy cars wallow around like pigs - if you don't find that fun there's that whole open wheel brake-point-memorizing thing just for you.)
There are 3 or 4 driving games in here, and one or more is likely to appeal to everyone.

Codemasters quickly recycles the widely panned and commercially unsuccessful GRID 2 into GRID AutoSport, the third title in the franchise.
While the physics and handling have been mercifully changed from drifty to grippy, almost everything remains the same; limited number of maps, never-ending menu pages and options, insufferable lobby wait times and regional locking in multiplayer matches that prevents players from finding each other without Steam 'download region' manipulation.
Multiplayer matches are often lag-ridden disasters and are almost always marred by collisions (both accidental and deliberate) despite long standing complaints and suggestions for improvement from the Codemaster customer base.
A painful grind through neverending levels of cars, disciplines and options was soon to be revealed as nothing more than a sinister DLC scheme with the release of the "XP Boost Pack" that promises to alleviate the pain of progressing through this game.
With yet more DLC coming soon from this unapologetic publisher, other aggravating elements of this game will likely be revealed as little more than deliberate problems designed to attract the player to purchasable solutions.
Luckily enough for racing genre fans, Codemasters will finally face serious competition later this year with the full release of Assetto Corsa, Project Cars and 'Next Car Game,' all titles that will hopefully realize that racing fans would like to spend more time on the track than in menus and lobbies and once they have purchased the game, they'd appreciate not having to pay more to dodge its worst elements.

If you're looking for a racing sim: this is the wrong game for you. If you're looking for a fun arcade racing game: you could try this game, but Need for Speed or Grid 2 would be recommended if you're an arcade racer. This game is in the middle of being a racing sim and being an arcade game.
You have to be able to control a fast racing car on track to play this game, but you don't need to driver super realistic. Sliding a bit trough corners are OK, but you have to fight cars in this game more than in Grid 2. I, my self, am a fan of the racing sim games, those were you have to hit braking points and apexes about perfect to have a chance, where sliding trough corners isn't the fastest way to finish. For me this game is fun to play, but not a game that satifies my racing sim needs. This game is just for fun in my opinion, not a game where you try your hardest.
AI may not be perfect, they love to drive into you hard or gentle, enough to make you annoyed at some times. ALWAYS be careful when overtaking or defending. The game still is fun though, but again: just for fun, not a game for the hardcore sim racers.
The game runs very nicely on my computer, with high graphic setting. Average FPS on a decent gaming PC with high graphics can be between 45 and 50 FPS, so its fine.
I would recommend this game, but remember: not a sim racing game for those of you who want that. Don't expect that. Handling is much better than arcade games though, so its not too unrealistic.

If you are a Firefly nut, you will love this game. There are basically three things you do.
1. Follow a really transparently obvious storyline that might have been a two-parter episode. I mean, honestly, you'll open the sector map... and ask yourself a really obvious question... and chances are pretty good that the first boring old answer you come up with - because you've seen it a thousand times in movies, television, books, comics, other games, more or less everywhere - is the big reveal. But God forbid I would put a spoiler in the review, right? Right. So just open the sector map and you'll go "oh, THAT story" but it won't be my fault. And then yeah, sure enough, it's that story. No real twists or surprises or anything.
2. Get in a bunch of space battles because people jumped in your way for no good reason. That's what passes for content in this game, since it's the major thing that makes the primary storyline take more than an hour or two to play through. Edit out the journeys from system to system, and you could hammer through the storyline in twenty minutes. Random encounters are the brakes that slow you down, because you're on your way from point A to point B and you get interrupted by someone who wants to fight. At first, this extends the game by making you run from battles you can't win, and later it will extend the game by making you fight battles you can't lose.
3. Do a boatload of procedural missions to earn money so you can upgrade your ship and turn a battle you can't win into a battle you can't lose. I'm counting radio and distress signals in this, because while they are handed out at random just like the battles mentioned above, you don't actually have to respond to them. This is the other way the game puts the brakes on you: by making things expensive and forcing you to either do missions or trade cargo to earn money. But you only get minimal tools for trading, and you can't get very much cargo space, and by the time you can make more than about 50,000 credits trading you can easily make 50,000 credits from a much faster and easier procedural mission.
So you're basically FedEx with guns. But then there's this Western-sounding cowboy style soundtrack, so clearly you're supposed to be more like, the pony express in space.
If you are anything like me, you are already thinking "THAT SOUNDS AWESOME" and clicking the buy button. But if you're... I don't know, more critical of the genre? More demanding?
There's honestly not much else TO this game.
And once you claw your way through the millions of credits you need to upgrade every single thing on your ship to the top level, the battles become really trivial. Which I really like, because I get to play around and swap stuff into my loadout until I figure out what matches my fighting style, but honestly it doesn't matter much what I use - because it's mostly a question of whether I kill the ship in five seconds at close range or eight seconds at long range.
If that would make you ANGRY, you will probably not like this game. If you are the kind of person who jumps into the forum and whinges about how you blasted through the campaign in six hours and now nothing is a challenge, you should definitely give this a pass.
But if that is your idea of a good time, just buy it already.

When it comes to Artifex Mundi, this isn't my first rodeo. I was blown away by
. That spectacular game has lush visuals, great music, and a strong balance between puzzle-solving and hidden object searching. So now that I've played through Nightmares of the Deep 3: Davy Jones, all I can say is that it's more of the same.
For once that's a very good thing.
While I haven't played the previous entries in the Nightmare from the Deep series, I believe the story works just fine on its own. You take on the role of Sara Black, who has enough evidence to prove that Davy Jones is more than just some locker sitting at the bottom of the ocean. Unfortunately, Davy isn't too fond of his secrets being exposed, so he storms your little convention, captures you and your daughter, and things go from bad to worse very quickly. Still, as tradition dictates, your puzzle-solving skills will help save the day. After completing the main-story, an epilogue chapter is unlocked. If I were to apply hard numbers to everything, I'd say you have about six hours of Pirate adventures to look forward to.
When it comes to hidden-object games, I consider presentation to be among the most important qualities. Nightmares from the Deep 3 is vivid, and relies on some great cinematics to further the story. To me, cinematics can be more than just bleeding-edge tech. The cut-scenes in this game evoke a certain charm. Since most are handled from a first-person view, they give off the impression that I'm on a theme park ride like Pirates of the Caribbean (obviously). They do a fine job of bringing the player in the story. Sometimes it can be a little kitchsy, but to me that's just part of its appeal. The artwork is very good, and offers a surprising amount of personality. My only complaint is that at times the voice-acting could use a bit of work. One incident in particular involves someone talking to you like you're a silent protagonist. It's one of those conversations that can go something like this:
"Hi, how are you? Really? You found the thing? That's good. Oh no, Johnny did what? He's such a kidder!"
Sara Black is perfectly capable of speaking, which makes the scene a little weird. Other than that and a few moments where the subtitles don't match up with what someone is saying, it's fine work.
The adventure portions of this game are polished. For the most part you're going to be collecting items, and finding the proper use for them. Surprisingly, not once did this ever feel monotonous. Everything moves at an efficient pace, and the puzzles themselves require just enough effort. You'll never find yourself blindly clicking through them nor stumped for an hour or so. Finding the hidden objects is also a well-designed experience. Aside from the lovely images, each scene can be completed quickly, but when I got stuck, it was because the object was actually well-hidden. It's important to note that you'll be spending more of the adventure experiencing the story and artwork, not hunting for pixels or bumbling through an obtuse brain-teaser.
This may be only the second Artifex Mundi game I've played through, but I'm getting an idea of the formula they work with. I noticed that a number of puzzles in this game are similar to those found in Grim Legends 2. With that being the case, I could make the fair assumption that the other games will have some repeat puzzles. However, this is something that I only took notice of after completing my play-through. Nightmares from the Deep 3: Davy Jones is stunning, and has so many lovingly-crafted scenes that I never paid any attention to whether or not I'm solving the same problems.
All in all, this is another superb title for fans of the hidden-object genre.

This game provides almost everything that I would want from an MMO. However, there are a few downsides. I'll start with the bad first.
First off is the Vim System. It is kind of a negative thing for the game, but I can understand why it was put in. Vim is sort of like your crafting stamina, and it unlocks when one of your skills reaches 16. After you hit that point, everything you do when it comes to that specific skill will take up Vim points. Now, they do regenerate over time, but it's like every other game that has energy regeneration: few minutes at a time, and you only get one point back at a time. That wouldn't be so bad if you didn't need mass amounts for quests. The more you craft at a time, the more you use (e.g. one at a time for one Vim, or 50 for 150 Vim.) Gathering only takes one for each click, and sometimes you get three items instead of one, so that's not too bad. The biggest issue with this is that it greatly limits what you can do in the game each day. Sure, there are refills that you can buy (with in game tokens that you can earn, no real money required) and perks that cut down on how much is cut out, but if you don't have enough tokens or those perks yet, things can slow down pretty quickly. There are small "free" refills that you can get to drop, like 15 Vim cornucopians, but those aren't very common; there are also big refills, but that requires you to level the skill. If you're running low, and you're only around 10%, you're better off coming back later. The good side of the Vim system, though, is that it DOES slow you down. Without it, you would see level 1s taking up all of the high ranking gathering spots, and people who could actually craft with what's gathered there wouldn't be able to proceed because of the farmers.
Second off is the way your skills work. (I'm going to be giving you my point of view, since that's all I really have to work with here.) The good thing about the skill system here is that you have 6 set usable combat skills. The bad thing about the skill system is that you have 6 set usable combat skills. Now, on my priest, that's not too bad; I get a personal heal, a shield I can give to anyone, and the rest are damage spells. However, if I want to be able to heal SOMEONE ELSE, I need to find a piece of gear with that specific skill on it. If I want to keep that skill, I have to keep moving it from gear piece to gear piece, and believe me, that can get expensive pretty quickly, especially if you want to keep A LOT of skills that benefit you. If you have more skills that the free slots cover, you have to either abandon all hope for them, or use special stones to be able to tack as many on as that gear piece or weapon has space for. (You can also earn these in game, but if you're like me, and acquire a lot of pieces with great perks, youre going to run out of them VERY QUICKLY. They aren't exactly common for daily bonuses.) However, this does force you to think about which ones benefit you the most, so no one person can hoarde all of the skills and be insanely overpowered.
The third thing that I found to be a little irritating is crafting costs. Now, to craft things, you need to go to a station with all of the materials required (that you gather yourself) and craft whatever your skill allows. Now, a few friends of mine and I have sort of agreed that it's a "station rent and craft time" cost, but the higher up you get, the more expensive things get. That's a little annoying counting that I have to gather up all of these insane things to craft it in the first place. The sellback value isn't too great for them, either. The most recent thing I crafted cost me around 15 and a half silver, and it sold for a measly 24 copper. Pretty crappy, right? It feels pretty imbalanced. However, with how much hunting and questing most people do to kill time getting back Vim, I suppose most don't notice.
The fourth thing is the party/friend system. This one isn't necessarily a bad thing; it's just more of an annoyance. When adding someone to your friend list, you have to be standing right there with them. There's no "Add Buddy" button on the friend menu. You have to track them down and do it yourself. And, while we're talking about the friend list, let me tell you what you can do with your plethora of friends. You can see their name (good, that's needed), their level (also good, I suppose), and if they're online or not(very good; I mean, you can't whisper them if they're not online, right?). Aaaand..that's about it. You can't do anything with them. Can't unbuddy them, can't invite them to a party, nothing really helpful for people who are doing their own thing and then decide to be in a party. You have to do all of that stuff in person. (Well, in character, I guess. You don't have to walk all the way to your buddy's house to do things in game.) Oh, and the party invites work the same as a friend invite. Have to be able to click on them.
The last bad thing that I've noticed about this game is how you discover new areas. In most MMOs that provide a means of fast travel (which, by the way, isn't free in this game. It requires travel stones to go from one area to another.), you only have to enter the area to register that it's been discovered. The two exceptions that I've run into are WoW and this game. Like WoW, you have to activate a specific something to be able to travel there. In this case, there are travel pads that you have to run over. You get a free travel stone for discovering it for the first time, and bam. Area is now open for travel. However, that is also the drawback. If you're entering a new area that is just below, at, or just above your level, you had better be methodical about killing everything along the way. Most areas have the travel pad around the middle of the map if there isn't a town there. If you die before you run arcoss it? Better hope you have a resurrection stone. Don't have any left? You get to try again from the start. It's still labaled as "undiscovered". Better hope that things haven't started respawning yet.
Even through all of the bad, there are a lot of fantastic things that I love about this game.
First off, it's free. No pay-to-win here. The only thing that I might recommend paying for is extra storage if you like to hoarde everything. But, even that's not necessary. You get a total of three bags to start off with, a vault (with, I don't remember, 25 or 30 spaces?), and, if you decide to get the free house license, ANOTHER storage vault. So, unless you REALLY like to hoarde EVERYTHING you pick up, you don't need to buy anything with real money.
The second thing I love about this game is that there is no limit to what skills you can learn because everyone can learn everything. Want to focus soley on mining and smithing? That's cool. Want to max out just your plant lore? Go ahead. Want to be a master in all things ore, wood, clothing, food, and potions? No one's stopping you! The sky is the limit, as long as you have patience for all of the Vim you're going to be blowing through.
Other than that, it's really just your basic, run-of-the-mill MMORPG. There's things to fight, places to discover, quests to complete, and lots of fun to be had. If you're looking for a casual game to play alone or with your friends, this one is one that I recommend wholeheartedly. 9/10

Citadel: Forged with Fire is obviously not a finished product. It's rough around the edges and there are numerous points to be adressed before even getting to new content.
But first and formost, after reading plenty of the reviews on here, I feel compelled to state that this is NOT A SURVIVAL GAME in the way people expect it to be (In fact I don't personally qualify it as one).
A large quantity of people have expected this to be rust, with magic. It's not. it's more akin to Reign of Kings with magic, and actually a large room for expansion on the concept. The game is freshly released, a little buggy, there are some latency issues, and its slow on basic exp rates.
The game feels very slow as a solo player. and some of the crafting paths feel like they're trying to encourage group play. (like needing to unlock the forge, to unlock the crafting bench, to craft the brromstick you also unlocked, when if you take 1 point wrong you'll have to wait till lvl 11 to craft the daft thing) and gathering, even with the spell seems slow unless theres atleast 2 of you. You also can't place things like the forge or the chests etc, against diagonal walls. encouraging you to build purely square buildings. but due to my next point the speed seems somewhat justified:
this isn't the kind of game where you're encouraged to hop servers every time you die. this isn't rust.
This has massive potential, and while I do find the graphical set backs for some to be an issue (After seeing Ser Winter play the game in its full graphical beauty; I run Specs that should allow me to benchmark all settings on high, but have to play with everything on low, except texures which are on high, otherwise the game leaks video memory like a mother ♥♥♥♥er and crashes), I think in the coming weeks alot of the issues that jump to mind will have been patched and resolved (Its been 3 days and we've gotten 3-4 patches already for issues put forward)
TL:DR// the game is definitely more fun with friends or in a group, if a bit slow to start. combats buggy, some connection issues for some, but wait a week or two and its more than worth buying.

It isn’t easy to explain “THE AWKWARD STEVE DUOLOGY”.  But I will bravely state that it manages to pull off a deceptively-unique experience that shines a spotlight on the thought-process of an awkward person with anxiety.
This game captures the humor and turmoil of a seemingly mundane task as an anxious person might see it.
The humorous distractions peppered throughout the experience mirrors the real-world mental exercises overthinkers go through to avoid that which brings them fear, no matter how ridiculous. It blurs the lines between creativity, humor, and fear, which is something every awkward person can relate to.
The artistic license used in “Steve’s” interactions with everyday items helps to reinforce how silly the overarching fear may actually be. At the end of the day, I don’t believe this truth is lost on Steve.
The final product is an experience that may hit too close to home for some.
