The problem with this game is that It doesn't feel like Hitman. It feels like Modern Stealth Game #479283345
I've played every Hitman Game since Condename 47 and heard a lot about this game being casualized so I waited until a sale.  I can't say I didn't expect it, but there was a part of me that was hoping that they kept the spirit of Hitman alive, and I was dissapointed.  If you are new to the series just get Hitman 2 or Blood Money. Those are the two best games.  If you are REALLY in need of more Hitman, well....I guess it's not terrible.
The main issue with this game is the element of surprise is gone.  Instead of having a map you can now see through walls by pressing control. Clues, will also jump out at you, kind of like Batman Arkham Asylum. The problem with this is you never have any doubt of whether something will work. It will tell you outright if a disgusie will work. It will tell you outright when you have been spotted.  This kind of ruins the expiramentation aspect of it.  You command your super-powered stealth assasin, trudge through levels, pick pre-packaged routes and methods of carrying out your missions, many of which are not even assassination oriented but just straight up sneaking, then watch cutscenes to advance the story.  The story is not that good either.  While in the other games it was kind of a backdrop, this game moves the story front and center.  It tries to have you believe that the guy that wiped out an entire funeral procession at the end of the last game is actually a good guy this time, and he has to protect a little girl.  It has pretty much every cliche and emotional ploy in the book. Even the soundtrack has fallen to the "BWOOOOOOOOOM" Inception cliche, which is a shame because I really like Jesper Kyd.
The locales are no fun either: you have a dingy marketplace, a dingy hotel, a dingy stripclub, a.....orphanage full of bloody dead nuns (wtf), a dingy factory, a dingy lab, a dingy cemetary. Maybe it's because of the lack of good gameplay but I felt the violence this time around is kind of distasteful, like it's just trying to be edgy for the sake of being edgy, and the oversexualized nature of the women in the game just felt....unecessary. I guess Blood Money was the same way, but Blood Money had a very different tone to it.  It was over the top and kind of cartoonish. This game demands to be taken seriously, yet does not have the writing or the gameplay to earn it.
The game isn't all bad.  The graphics are great and it runs very smoothly even on older systems.  Contracts mode brings back some of the old Hitman style and adds some randomization to it.  There is definitley fun to be had in Absolution, but it just feels like another stealth shooter.

Crea is a 2D RPG-ish sandbox game featuring digging, exploring, crafting, building, and fighting - all the usual sandbox shenanigans - with the addition of skill points to add a whole new layer of character progression beyond the usual gearing-grind.
The game starts you off on a random stretch of a vast, procedurally generated world filled with multiple biomes, both on the surface and underground.  Each biome has its own set of dangers and rewards, containing scary monsters, hazardous dungeons, and all the shiny rocks you could ever want in order to build the castle of your dreams.
Crea's main enhancement to this basic sandbox structure is a skill-progression system to improve your character (in addition to the usual process of finding/crafting better gear).  As you perform any activity in Crea, you gain skill points which you can spend to become even better in related talents - digging gives you points for gathering skills, fighting allows you to invest in combat skills, etc.  This allows you to improve your character over time, and also focus on whatever niche you prefer, be it a warrior, a magic user, or someone who just reeeeally likes digging holes.
Crea also features a few other uniquely nifty ideas to build upon 2D sandbox-crafters of yore, such as dungeon portals which can buff the monsters - or nerf you - in random ways to create a truly challenging experience.  There is also a clever research system to gain access to better tools, deadlier weapons, and snazzier furniture - which is a nice way to limit starting players to necessary items early on, while providing plenty of extra choices as you progress through the game.
While Crea has quite a bit going for it, there are still some issues to be aware of before you commit to that 'buy' button.  The natural downside to the extensive amount of progression that Crea offers is that the game is not exactly newbie-friendly.... at all. There is very little tutorial to go on, so you will likely need to make quite a few side-trips to the forum before you become comfortable with the game - or even to get familiar with the controls, which are not always intuitive. The game's visuals will also probably displease some users - the 2D sprites scream 'indie title', although in the end they get the job done just fine.
All-in-all, Crea is a neat addition to the 2D sandbox-crafting genre, with plenty of extra features to make it stand out from similar titles.  If you're new to the genre, Crea is a fine way to spend potentially endless hours exploring, digging, fighting and building, though you should read up a bit on the game first to make the start a little more pleasant.  Meanwhile, for those simply looking for a game to fill that Terraria-shaped void in your life after playing it to death for the last few years, Crea will certainly do that and then some.

Beyond Earth is good. Perhaps not the best Civ game (at the time of writing this, it's only had a few updates and no post-launch DLC, so there's still time) but certainly far from terrible. The shift to alien planets and post-space cultures is really interesting, and adds some new dimensions to the gameplay. The tech tree has changed considerably as have other core mechanics, whilst still retaining the same structure as previous Civ games.
It's not problem free, though. The UI is intensely confusing to start with and feels more like it was designed for its style rather than its functionality. Units and buildings feel less interesting than Civ V, and overall your progression over a period of time is less than in other Civ games. You don't have eras, instead the only real sense of progression comes through increasing your affinities. Leaders have a much smaller set of vocal responses too, and you can hear the same phrase only a few times before getting fed up.
But on the whole it is a good game. It's perhaps looking a little weak compared to its siblings, but it is important to remember that Beyond Earth is still in its infancy, with at least one expansion to come. I do, however, think it's worth getting for its aesthetic and its world-building. Firaxis are really trying to make it come alive.

I'll start with the obvious. Crea is a sandbox RPG, which has a lot of similarities to Terraria. Crea is more about the characters personal development through levelling up and talents, along with weapon and armour upgrades. Crea also has a really cool research system behind the crafting. You need to find the pieces of what you want to make and research them to discover the recipes they can be used in. You can also use scraps (that can be easily obtained from research) to discover parts of the recipe without using the components you have. The crafting system goes even deeper than that, by using "Chaos" to imbue your items.
Crea feels good to play, the mechanics all work well together and nothing feels too clunky. There are a few inconveniences, like being unable to use skills unless you're in combat mode. However the trade-off for that one is that there is a toggle for combat and building/exploration, which is a huge quality of life advantage. The world looks good, and there is some good variety in the biomes, items and enemy types.
Crea shouldn't be written off purely as a Terraria clone, it's a game that takes the fundamental idea behind it and produces a fantastic experience. Having said that, if you liked Terraria and want something similar, this is definitely your best choice.

---I received this game from the developer in order to review it. You will get my honest feelings about the game (both good and bad).---
For review purposes, most of my playing time took place just before and just after the game came out of early access (around Version 1.0.0) Also I used a keyboard and mouse to play.
Crea is a Sandbox game with RPG and Crafting elements. When you first start the game you get a sword, shield and a mining tool and that is pretty much it. From there you need to fight, explore and scavenge your way through the game, mining elements and creating items with recipes you unlock during play. The game really is quite in depth and takes quite a bit of time to get used to. I feel like after 18 hours of play, I have barely scratched the surface of what is offered in this game. There are 3 equipment slots and 3 accessory slots on top of weapon and shield slots. As your character levels up you can level up 8 different stats and on top of that there are 5 subsections (Arms, Syle, Gather, Craft and Explore). Each of these subsections have their own level and points awarded for reaching certain criteria and there are between 10 and 20 different spells and abilities to unlock using these points for each subsection. The game really is quite in depth and again I feel like I have only scratched the surface.
Crea really is a great Sandbox game with a huge amount to discover. Hopefully if things continue in a positive direction, it will easily leave its competition in the dust. In the following section, I will go into a bit about what makes this game great and a few things it needs to improve on.

The final chapter of the Nightmares from the Deep trilogy.
Game: Museum Director Sarah Black and her daughter Cory are kidnapped by the infamous Davy Jones during a public and seeming well attended museum presentation about Davy Jones (compiled from all the information Sarah had gathered during her first two adventures).  (All I can say about that is getting donations and funding for the museum repairs and more exhibits should be easy after such a supernatural, flashy, and public kidnapping.)  I digress.  The ever resourceful mother-daughter team manage to break out of their jail cell and attempt to leave Davy Jones ship but are recaptured.  Davy Jones is going to kill Sarah but Cory makes a contract with Davy Jones to save her mother's life.  Davy Jones instead of outright killing Sarah forces her to walk the plank.  (Typical pirate)  The adventure begins here.  Find Cory and break her contract (and every other contract Davy Jones has ever made along the way, including Davy Jones' own contract.) Sub-storyline: Find out even more about Davy Jones and just how he became the infamous "devil" of the sea, and why.  And who that mysterious girl ghost is and her relationship with Davy Jones.
First I would like to say this game is nearly perfect in my opinion.  Good storyline: pathos, adventure, mystery, tradegy, redemption.  A slew of side characters that are both helpful, and depending on their nature intimidating, scary, amusing, or sincere.  Nothing seems forced or padded, the story moves along by "area" with little back tracking, and the various and variety of puzzles are intrigated well within the story.  It is NEARLY PERFECT because IN A SINGLE PLAYTHROUGH on expert level/mode the player CAN GET ALL BUT ONE ACHIEVEMENT (play three games of Mahjong).  Had the Bonus chapter picked up the Mahjong achievement (and counted toward any other unfilled achievements) this game would have been perfect.  Not that I mind a second playthrough, but a second playthrough just to get achievements is tedious.
Puzzles:  The usual fare for this series, nothing too hard, challenging or head scratching, just enjoyable little romps of finding objects or the pieces of something.  Mahjong, the signature of this series, can be played as well.
The Hidden/Secret Finds are seahorses, puzzle pieces, and amusing pirate cards all but one relating to the other pirates the player meets on the island.
In this game I really like how the achievements are done.  They are divided up into three areas on Davy Jones' ship, and as each achievement is fulfilled the blank picture is filled in giving that area of the ship a complete look by the end.  The achievement I liked the best which amused me and made me very happy was the animal interaction achievement.  I do not know how many times I have clicked on birds, fish, bats, insects, and rats/mice in other HO games just to see what happens, and now I get an achievement for it.  Tres chic.
The artwork, music, and cutscenes are all well done and appropriate for the time and place heard or seen.
All in all, I highly recommend this game.

It says recommended, but it's more of a "meh". The point is to simulate being in a war with limited resources, but I (personally) find having barely enough to get by very stressful. You go out and get your resources, but you come back and find yourself raided. You get a large supply of food, but then you run out of building materials. It's a never ending cycle of debt.
I REALLY like the concept of the game, but I simply find it too dreary to play. I'll play more and update this if it changes, but the pacing is so slow. It doesn't help that while the music is reminicent of moments in The Walking Dead (a good thing), the time before the music loops is so short. It increases the feeling of dull repetiveness.
Despite all of this, I'd still say it's a recommend. It's a "survial" simulator and you have to make hard decisions. The dialog is short but to the point, and while not particularly emersive, the minimum details leaves it to the player to slowly piece together the puzzle of what's happening in the world. I'd say give it a shot if the constant feeling of "Two steps forward, one step back" won't bother you.

I don't remember a game which made me care so much about my characters. For example, Marko, my dear Marko. I took him out as a scavenger most of the nights. We had had our bumps on the road but so far so good. I sent him to the supermarket to get some supplies. When I got there, a woman was being assaulted and I told Marko to step in. Marko fired his first shot but I didn't notice that the soldier also had armour, so it didn't get the job done and he responded. The soldier started shooting Marko with his AK47 while he reloaded. The damned woman got in the way and I was afraid of killing her (Marko had had his fair share of depression caused by killing innocents), so I watched helplessly Marko being shot down like a dog and I literally just stood there, looking at my screen. I could not believe that after all the things we had gone through (I mean, I had already listened on the radio that the war was about to end), Marko was dead, specially over something totally unnecessary and foolishly. I will not be analyzing the actual game in this review because most of the negative reviews on this product are not about that, they are about the "Remaster" and frankly if you haven't played Bioshock yet, you are depriving yourself of one of the most beautiful and enjoyable video game expirences of all time.
I see a Helluva lot of hate for the remastered version of this game and let me start by saying: yes, it was pointless.
Was it a total abomination?  Was it as bad as Skyrim Special Edition?  Did it♥♥♥♥♥♥on the legacy of the original, far superior counterpart with no remorse, scraping it's♥♥♥♥♥♥covered boot in the face of its father?
Eh... no.
It is the exact same game with slightly better graphics.  Mostly just added foliage outside in the ocean and better textures.  Ya know, the standard remastered reworks.  As far as I can tell there is nothing new added in game besides these graphical adjustments.  There are however the added inclusion of "Director's Commentary" tapes that you can find and then access these neat little videos and interviews with Ken Leviene, the creator of Bioshock, and one of the game developers.  There is also a virtual museum added in there with a bunch of cool concept art and scrapped ideas and models.  It's really cool to walk around and see all of it and you really get a grasp on how... indecisive the development of Bioshock really was.
Now I don't have anything negative to say about this game.  It's just Bioshock with a couple little add ins and some new graphics.  I do see a lot of people ragging on it for crashing constantly which yeah ok my copy crashed once.  I purchased this through the Bioshock Collection, and I recieved both the Remasted and original copies of both Bioshock and Bioshock 2 and I originally intended to play through the classic Bioshock.  i was sorely disappointed when the original copy kept crashing after I got out of the bathosphere in the first friggin level.  I tried 3 or 4 times before I gave up and moved to remastered which crashed once and after that I played through the game smoothly.
I feel like most of the negative reviews of this game are just butt-hurt hipster purists who refuse to play anything but the original version of a game and despise any "remasted" or "special" editions of classic games.  I think remasted editions are awesome and can bring amazing, classic, and revolutionary games to a newer and younger generation.
However Bioshock was in no need of remastering.  I would have wated for the game to be older and the graphics to be more outdated and then remastered all of the 3 games for next gen 4k ulta processing high resolution graphics throttling super ram visuals.
Just imagine Bioshock with the graphics of the new EA Battlefront.... passing over the reef crest, laying eyes of the beautiful, expansive 50's era neon metropolis sprawling out before you on the ocean floor.  Walking through a stream of water and watching the liquid run down your field of view.  Stalking a Big Daddy and Little Sister with the crossbow, determining the proper time to strike and BAM!  You hop out with a flurry of intense lighting bolts and sparks and oop... need to change my pants.
Over all I have no complaints other than I feel like the remastering was premature.

Pros:
Cons:
This is game is worth the price. However, keep in mind this is not a AAA title and has an indie feel to it. It feels like Dungeon Keeper 2 with respect to building a lot of traps and the "heroes" invading your dungeon. But, on the same hand it feels like WarCraft III with respect to adventuring to the overworld.
Dungeons II has a lot going for it. The Narrator keeps things interesting poking fun at the player and the heroes alike.  The story is a rather generic because the heroes did x to you, you are going to wipe them out. Game mechanics are quite servicable and generally work as expected. Upgrade trees and processes provide enough tool tips to know what you are supposed to be doing the first play through. The creatures are entertaining to watch in battle and roaming around the dungeon as we. Traps work as indicated. Enemies are designed for a casual experience (excellent if you like to enjoy a bit of a challenge with a story).
As for some of the cons, the game was far too short (in terms of number of missions. There could have been many more missions. I felt that the game was artificially longer due to the way that you get higher level rooms/creatures (upgrading your throne room, then researching rooms, and then having to upgrade your population limit which caps if your throne room is not a high enough level).
All in all, Dungeons II is an entertaining narrative to play through regardless of its short comings. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoyed the dungeon keeper games (bearing in mind that this is a more casual experience in terms of difficulty).

Perspective from someone who is not a die-hard fan of Bioshock
Unlike the first Bioshock game which had a pretty good story and atmosphere, Bioshock II's story by comparison, while not necessarily bad, is rather straightforward and provides for less of an emotional impact than that of the first game.
Despite that, however, the gameplay is phenomenal. Compared with the first game where you play as a human who started out simply armed with a wrench, Bioshock II imediately throws you into the game from the perspective of a Big Daddy, equipped with body armor and a giant drill.
Only Con - The game is pretty short, even if you do explore each map. I finished the game in only 6 hours. There is "some" replay value, but that's only to get the multiple endings, which I probably won't do.
Tl;Dr -
Story is not as good as the first game, however still decent by itself.
Gameplay & Combat are definitely an improvement in Bioshock II.
Finishing the game doesn't require much effort. I finished in 6 hours.
-Buy during a sale.

That's why being a fan of lookalike titles you are always looking for something new and innovative to be in the forthcoming product. And truly, Crea possess some interesting elements and features which make it distinctive compared to its predecessors.
Without further go, I really enjoyed Crea. It might look similar for the newcomers at the beginning as you are thrown into the world, given some instructions and set to go. However, the further you progress the deeper game immersion becomes. As usual, you gather materials, kill monsters, craft gear and build a home for yourself. Then you dive deeper or travel farther to explore new horizons repeating all that on a greater scale. Sounds familiar, indeed, but there is more to it than what is seen plainly on surface.
The most developed and well designed part of game is crafting system. It's interesting, it's catchy and what's even more important it's complex. You can't just "I got the deer muscus now I can make an *Uber 2156 Annihilator Optimus
". Here you have to actually research each material figuring its specifications and how and where it can be used - and you will need to do that several times learning more and more of a particular item as your researching (crafting) level increases and so do your skills. Therefore great or just regular items can be created when you collect enough materials to both analyze and use them in the crafting process. Though sometimes you can find prepared recipes as well. There are only few stations each usable for certain categories of items. You can "improve" them by finding (mostly in random chests) different techpieces. What's absolutely worth mentioning is 'Chaos system' which allows you to craft better items giving them additional stats or special characteristics depending on how well you manage to keep the "Chaos" from ruining your work using different features and talents to do so (that's sort of hard to explain in the review but I hope main point is still comprehensible).
Next, there is also an extended talents "tree" with different branches. You gain points by running around, killing monsters, shooting
fireballs, breaking blocks and crafting and then allocate them to affiliated sections thus learning new fighting techniques and new spells as well as improving yourself and your more pacific skills generally. There are quite enough of such abilities so you won't be bored and can always try playing a new style, like battlemage or rogue-archer.
Finally, lets talk about the world you are in and its content. As usual, you can create several sizes where each will have ground, sky and underground levels with different biomes. You can travel only by foot or by crystal waypoints, unfortunately, but who knows if wings or transport will be added in the future updates - that would surely be nice. Monster are unique and each has its own style and combat pattern so as abilities while some may be challenging to face in the early stage. There aren't many monsters though, to be honest. Bosses prove to be even more tough and provide a necessary degree of "buttpain" if you don't master evasion or figure what is the right way to fight them. Exploration aspect is solid enough with many caves and hidden goodies underground like chests or rooms with pages about the preset or world's past.
Rather doable element is fighting/gathering: you have to switch between 2 modes which also have two tabs each which might be confusing a bit to those who were previously playing games like Terraria, for instance. You will constantly need to switch to fighting if you are mining underground, but It's still somewhat versatile system in the end. In-game animations are well done and lovely (except for the jumping). Graphics is pretty common to the genre but still has some charm to it mostly due to beautiful and full-blooded arts, though backgrounds are rather simple. Effects are stylish and there is physics in place - shooting ball of earth may destroy a block or drop icicles from the ceiling which will damage enemies when fall, for example. Main game menu is simple too but that's not to be concerned of. Interface is fine but small improvements could still be added (for example, bigger fonts). Soundtrack is nice and plausible to hear.
Technically, there is nothing to be concerned of. Game is out of Early Access and was granted almost bugless state. The only issues I had so far are two crashes which appeared during boss fights when game was acting a big laggish and light sphere (the one serving as light source) dissapearing after you travel via crystal or die and a couple of sound effects missing (harvesting plants and logs underground, for instance), but that's not critical mostly. Performance & optimization is great overally and game runs smoothly on both powerful, mid-end and "cozy" specs like Mac Air (well, nothing surprising as it's not really resourceful).

Hatred is a controversial isometric shooter in the vain of Running With Scissors' first Postal, running on Unreal Engine 4 and developed by the newly formed Destructive Creations, an offshoot of The Farm 51. The game's first trailer in late 2014 caused one of the most notorious outcries out of anything else at that time and then released in 2015 to mostly negative critical reception while having more favorable opinion on Steam, especially by the game's own fanbase, who'd largely been following the development up until release. Prior to that the game's greenlight on Steam was almost denied when DC submitted to the ESRB which gave Hatred the infamous AO rating causing it to be pulled which resulted in further outcry from the rapidly developing support. It was overturned by none other than Gabe Newell himself, all in which generated further news coverage than was honestly deserved. If people didn't actually like Hatred they supported it solely to♥♥♥♥♥♥off SJWs and/or represent freedom in gaming. The initial release in June was an un-optimized buggy mess before gradually being patched up to have much better performance without sacrificing visual fidelity a month later. Hatred was updated again with new content in September along with an engine update that subsequently broke everything DC did. While most of the severe issues were addressed there was compromises regarding the game's visuals in exchange for the new content. Workshop support was implemented sometime after and as of now Hatred has since been left as-is with no further updates, likely from the clusterfluck that is its current state.
The story is as bare-bones as they come. You play the Antagonist (yes, that is his official 'name') who decides one day he's had enough of this world and his cold bitter hatred as the game's title suggests overcomes his own good sense (or lack thereof) and he becomes determined to put an end to the human worms who feast on the earth's carcass (yeah, the writing isn't that great, maybe a result of Polish to English translation with it sounding much more badass over there than it does over here). Our anti-hero had been stocking up just for this occasion and readies an AK-47 with 300 rounds of ammunition, a big♥♥♥♥♥knife and a handful of frag grenades before going out his front door and shooting up a bus stop outside his home, much to the confusion and horror of nearby residents. He then goes on a full-blown rampage in his neighborhood while dressed up like Eric Harris, with hair that Nathan Explosion would admit is quite brutal, quickly attracting the attention of the cops. Not content with letting his gun do the talking, Antagaman also drops occasional one-liners in a voice best described as trying too hard to sound cool, like an evil Jon St. John (if Duke had a son that went on a killing spree this would be it). He succeeds in massacring the suburbs and the local police station before being chased through the sewers by SWAT teams, only to escape and cause yet another scene at a marina (that fish smell does get to you after a while) before boarding a train which somehow everybody has access to firearms on and only now does he come to realize his penultimate objective: reach the nuclear power plant, and maybe get the new Linkin Park album. Only then will he know true cleansing and die spectacularly and go to hell after unleashing armageddon with a cold blood as the marketing blurbs say. It's suppose to be FKN METAL so what do you expect?
Gameplay is most similar to Postal, with the majority of the action taking place from an isometric perspective where the goal is to kill [x] amount of hostiles in the form of police, SWAT and military in order to proceed. Even the levels are inspired from P1, with the first one being called Home, an obvious reference to P1's first level, and featuring locations like a truckstop, train station, city and even an army base near the end of the game. Most levels are fairly large in size and permit largely unrestricted movement, with Home, Marina and Downtown being the highlights of the game. In addition to the primary goal there are sub-objectives in the form of side-quests sprinkled throughout that net additional respawn points when completed in order to keep playing after dying in real-time, as once all of these are used up you will have to restart the level from scratch. The most controversial aspect of the game is the encouraged murdering of civilians, who are often defenseless (but can fight back) and can be subjected to various executions when downed but not killed outright. These temporarily take control away from the player to show off a Manhunt style cinematic kill up close as a visual reward, with the mechanical reward of regaining back health. Executions are the only form of healing in Hatred so you will want to do them often, be it on civilians or hostiles, with the former often being seen as a stash of medikits in the tougher levels who you'll want to spare until you really need them. Regardless of what you're doing, every single thing you do in Hatred involves killing people and this goes on for seven levels which may not sound like a lot but you'll be spending on average anywhere from 30 minutes to an hour on most so you're looking at around 6-8 hours playtime. Of killing people over and over. More interesting than this though is the 'destruction system', an in-house development by DC that makes for some incredible scenes of, well, destruction. Buildings can be gutted out with explosives and fire, and bullets will often remove pieces of a building when colliding and this can make for some very visceral fights, easily the best part about Hatred and I'd love to see this kind of thing implemented in more interesting and better realized games.
Visually the game is adequate, it's UE4 so lighting and particle effects look really nice, the models and texture work aren't anything phenomenal but get the job done for being mostly outsourced. Destruction looks amazing as stated prior and the visual feedback from shooting people is pretty decent with some cool small details and particularly nasty, realistic looking blood (at least in pre-September builds of the game). The game has an interesting aesthetic with almost everything but red and certain choice colors being monochrome, likely to create a dark and disturbing atmosphere and it works for the most part. Sound design is good, with satisfying feedback from weapons and explosions and the voice acting is OK when people aren't repeating the same lines over and over, their screams are quite effective, especially women when they're on fire. The music, composed by Adam Skorupa is quite nice and fitting to the bleak tone of Hatred, at least when the game isn't ripping you out of immersion, which it does every 30 seconds.
Criticisms include almost everything. The game's always been buggy, glitchy and lacking a lot of polish, both in the gameplay and the performance, of which the latter is much better now but sadly the game took a hit in the visual department for this in the current build including altered lighting, less dense FX, downgraded destruction, and flatter looking blood which seems to be more a result of forgetting to put back in the specular highlights when a lot of the decals were replaced in the September update. The new content in the form of a survival mode, absurd difficulty modes and a few more side-quests is shallow at best and workshop mods are few and largely WIP. The community is practically dead since the hype train has left. As a result I can't really recommend Hatred, at least in its current state, as I still enjoy playing it every other blue moon when reverting back to an older build, but that doesn't necessarily mean that the game was a lot better, no, it was never that great to begin with, it just looked nicer. Overall, if the devs no longer care about the game, why should I? If you're seriously itching for this kind of game, buy POSTAL Redux instead.

This game was Codemasters' last chance to make things right. They blew it completely. Here is why:
1. Cockpit views - a bloody shame when compared to the lovely one that the original GRID came with.

6. Blur - once you deactivate that, your eyes suddenly feel like they don't need glasses (yes, it's that bad), but you will instantly see how shoddy the textures were made; the rest of the game is similarly crafted
...
Given this trainwreck, Codemasters claim that they listened to the community was a blatant lie. Unless acting upon the feedback was optional (in their opinion). You get the picture, I hope. In my not so humble opinion, this game and its developer by extension have managed to insult the first (legendary) GRID again, which to this day remains the undisputed champion. Those many awards back then were well deserved, but Codemasters as it is today does not deserve your money for this game right now. Do yourself and your wallet a favor, enjoy the first GRID (the game that does it right) and ignore the 'pretenders' that followed afterwards. Cheers.

Crea is a 2D sidescrolling game with building and slow deliberate combat. It is similar in many respects to Terraria and Starbound. It's a decent game for what it is, but it should still be in early access as it is buggy and lacks polish. As it is now, I cannot recommend this game. If you'd like to play a game like this, you're probably better off playing Terraria as the devs there have had a great deal of time to refine the game.
+Talent points are constantly being gained, so your character is always improving as you play.
+Procedurally generated worlds.
+Built in mod support. If the game is able to maintain dedicated players, then it should have a good deal of extra free content.
+Skills that enhance mobility, such as sprinting, ledge grabs, and double jumps can be obtained quite quickly.
+Fast travel system. Saves you from retreading the same ground over and over again.
+When compared to Terraria, digging is more satisfying earlier on due to upgrades allowing the mining of multiple tiles, making it less tedious to dig through areas.
+Spells that you are able to access early on make it easy to find ore and chests.
+No contact damage on most, if not all enemies, so you can't just take damage by bumping into them.
-Visual feedback is a bit lacking on spells.
-Enemies are neither knocked backed or staggered by your attacks, making combo attacks less than usefull and making ranged combat seem like an objectively better option.
-Enemies are sparse in the underground and tend to ignore you. There isn't much down there aside from the occasional crystal that teleports you to a dungeon, small rooms with chests in them, and of course, ores.
-Only THREE options in the settings menu: volume, fullscreen options, and resolution. Sound effects and music aren't even separated, so if you want to listen to your own music or a video in the background, you're going to have to mute the sound entirely, or let the sounds overlap.
-I've encountered a bug that has destroyed all my furniture, chests, NPCs, and many of my waystones (used for fast travel). The bug happened after teleporting back from the first(?) boss. I was able to pick up all of the furniture and items in the chests, but the Renma cores (a fairly valuable and rare resource) used to create the NPCs and my waystones were lost. I'd imagine there is a way to create new waystones, but I'm not sure how far along it is in the game.
-Very small weapon variety at least in the early game. There are a few different spells, but not many.
-Most chests (aside from ones in realm crystals and dungeons) locked and you have to rely on random drops to get keys for them or use lockpicks.
-A lot of the gear you get from chests have high level requirements for the time you're able to get them, so you'll be waiting a while before you can even use them.

This is not my first dance at the rodeo. Nor is it my first sandbox experience. Having platinumed the PS Vita version of Terraria, and having tried virtually all of the other sandbox experiences out there (many of them merely watered down derivatives of the genre-leaders) I can't say I was massively enamoured with the thought of sinking more time into another. I was a little jaded, tbh.
However, I'm glad I did. Because Crea has certainly been worth my time so far. The graphics are simple but functional, the music isn't to my taste but I can turn it off without having to mute it in the volume mixer, and the game runs stable even if it could do with better optimisation.
If you, like me, you have run the gamut of sandboxes, then you'll basically know what you'll be getting into, with the pleasant exception that the devs have clearly put some thought (and work) into Crea. The lore, the levelling, the intuitive controls (using a Xbox 360 controller at least), the crafting and the overall experience.
And an actual working (and coherent) tutorial - hallelujah!
The combat is fast-paced and frantic.
The crafting is logical and varied.
The levelling is Skyrim-esque.
Would I recommend it?
Definitely, the game as it is is worthy of your time and money, and the post-release roadmap, if it can be realised, looks particularly intriguing.

Crea is a sandbox rpg game with a lot of farming, digging, gathering and exploring. The graphic is simple 2D graphic, however its not bad.
Heard from friends, that Crea is a Terraria 2.0 game. I do own Terraria, but my library pretty huge so not had time to play that game yet, i cant confirm that information.
Crea allows you to level your character in many different ways. Your gathering, crafting, arms skills, spell skills and alone your hero get different experience and all these have different leveling system. Reaching next level on those experience trees unlock purchaseable abilites/boosts for your character. So you can see, character development is pretty deep in Crea.
You cant craft any item you want right away. you need collect materials/ingerdients and then you need study those items, research them and then develop what could you craft from those. Sounds painful? its not, its fun, even if the research process destroys the item. New armors, weapons, building materials will be available as you progress through the game and as you research how to create those items, Crea offers a long and enjoyable gameplay while you build up your character, its house and clear hostile fauna.
Sadly i not had much time to play Crea yet because of Euro 2016 and Copa America, but i allready love it and would recommend to anyone, its a pretty decent game for its genre, developer definetly spent a lot of time on it and one of the few games on steam what actually left early access and now officially released! Homefront is probably one of the most marketed games of last-generation. The advertising had simulated a declaration of war on mainstream websites which caused some confusion outside of the gaming world. This all of course began right in time with the ROKS Cheonan sinking, and the North Korean artillery strike on Yeonpyeong Island, with then-developer THQ denying that the game was leeching off of the national coverage. Coming in from publisher Deep Silver, only after they acquired the rights from the now dysfunct THQ, is an FPS title that's centered around revolution.
The entire plot is your typical, universal tale of revolution. It's the year 2027, and two years ago the Korean-American War began. Robert Jacobs, the character that you will be playing as, is awakened in his apartment in Colorado and ordered by Korean troops to get on a bus, where he will enter a re-education camp of sorts in Alaska. He is eventually rescued by resistance fighters Connor, Rianna, and Boone, and taken to their hidden resistance camp. The remainder of the game is spent fighting the Korean troops and their overall police state, with very little in the way of plot. When it comes down to it, none of the missions really line up with each other, and there's no true sense of what the ultimate goal of the game is.
Man oh man, where to start with Homefront. It's another one of those first-person shooters that's difficult to write about, purely due to the fact that it's so generic. If you've ever played any other shooter, you'll know what to expect going in to this one. It functions in similarity to the later Call of Duty games, where you have regenerating health and must constantly follow and appease your AI friendlies. In fact, you are in complete servitude to your AI crew, primarily bull-headed Connor, who demands that you follow him and stick close by almost constantly. He orders you around like you're a piece of trash, and even tells you how you should be firing some guns. To make matters worse, the AI in this game is horrendous, especially when it comes to your team and the people you're required by in-game law to follow; often they will get stuck on walls, or fail to progress at certain points, leaving you sitting to wait it out for minutes that seem like hours.
Speaking of characters, the entire cast seem to be cardboard cutouts of generalized emotions; Connor is nothing but an angry, yet otherwise emotionless, controlling jerk, Rianna is your typical "I'm over-emotional but I'm trying to hide it since I'm a hardened bad girl but it comes out every once in a while" chick, and then you have Hopper who is the stereotypical quiet nerd. The guy that you play as, Jacobs, is a mute pilot with no personality whatsoever, as is typical for many FPS titles. There's no supreme bad guy, no arch-villain, no total monarch that needs to be taken down, just an onslaught of bad guys that need to be shot over, and over, and over for 7 levels that equal about 4 hours.
One redeeming quality about Homefront is its graphics. They aren't jaw dropping by any means, but the game looks good even some six years later. The character models are a little less impressive than the environments, especially given that most of the enemies look exactly the same, but at least you'll have something nice to look at while you're being bored to death. The soundtrack isn't half bad either, though it's also nothing to jump up and down and write home about. These two things are minor compensations for an entire game that's filled with terrible AI, a yawn-summoning plot, dull dialogue, and some of the most generic characters to ever exist in a video game. The true question here is, why would you play Homefront when there are so many better titles out there?

There is no contest that despite the reused plot, Davy Jones is the best one of the series with its excellent hidden object scenes and puzzles, interesting story progression, and quality voice acting.
After the shallow beauty of the Siren’s Call, the Nightmares from the Deep series returned to its roots in this final chapter. So much so that the story is almost the same as in the ‘Cursed Heart’: the protagonist’s daughter gets kidnapped by a pirate’s ghost, and she has to follow them to a mystical island to learn the secret behind the pirate’s tragic past.
Despite this… reuse, the story does a much better job with great characters and good dialogues, making it one of the best titles in the Artifex Mundi stable.
The game offers good variety by using all three common hidden object scene types: item list, fragmented object, and sequential. The balance isn’t perfect though, as most of the difficulty is shifted towards these scenes and left the usual Artifex Mundi type puzzles quite easy.
Not that it makes any difference, as Davy Jones is an excellent closure to the trilogy and a great hidden object game overall.

Davy Jones is the third installment of Nightmares from the Deep series by Artifex Mundi. Previous installments as follows: The Cursed Heart and The Siren’s Call.
Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Custom Cursor, Voice Overs and Full Screen. Wide Screen is automatically supported in the game.
Game Difficulty Modes: Three game difficulty modes – Casual, Advanced and Expert.
Cinematic/Dialogues: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. They can be watch over again under the video section the extras. There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scene without having sit through it.
Game Music/Sounds/Voiceovers: The music definitely sets the mood for the game. The sounds aren’t intrusive as the game progresses. The voice overs in the game are nicely done.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is an option to lock the inventory panel in place.
Notebook: Two section – Notes and Objectives. Notes section is for the story and clues from the game. Objectives section is for all the objective from the game and the completed ones are checked off.
Map: The map is interactive. The ability to fast travel to different locations in the game. Useful map indicator icons, the legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Fragment Items, Shadow Items, Traditional word list with some and/or no interaction required. For the traditional word only, the sonar feature show you the shape of the item. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the extra section.
Mahjong Gameplay: This game feature is optional for those who don’t want to go looking for items in hidden object scenes.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve.
Game Ending: There is somewhat an ending in the main portion of the game but the bonus chapter extends it a bit more.
Game Bonus Chapter: Can be access after the main portion of the game is completed.
Game Achievements: Both in-game and Steam achievements. There 32 different achievements to earn in the game but they also comes with certain requirement into order to unlock them.
Game Collectables: Three different sets of collectables in the game. 10 Pirate Cards, 12 Seahorses, 1 Puzzle (24 Pieces.) They are scattered throughout the entire game.
Game Concept Art/Wallpapers: 12 concept art and 3 wallpapers.
Game Soundtracks: 6 soundtracks from the game.
Game Trading Card/Badge: This a special feature only available in the Steam’s version of the game. The game drops three different trading cards only once and the rest of the cards: Community Market, Booster Packs and Trading. The game badge can be crafted after having all the card in the inventory then it can be upgraded four more times.

+ Sound effects are nearly flawless in quality and implementation; ambient noises add to a paplable atmosphere
+ Pencil effect is mesmerizing, and lends the game a style of its own
+ Line of sight is extremely well-represented, and adds to the suspense of not knowing what's in the next room until you're close enough to be at risk
+ Scavenging creates at atmosphere pregnant with tension
+ The soundtrack pulls the player into the game and engulfs them in emotions appropriate to the theme
+ The player-controlled characters are presented and developed so well through one's actions, that one will find a deep emotional investment forming; the player will really care about what happens to these people
+ Different surivors have various skill sets, making each one somehow valuable to the others
+ Scavenging locations remain static, but their contents and risks are all randomly generated
+ Graphics are crisp and meticulously detailed; animations, too, are seamlessly rendered with little clipping issues
+ Crafting is slightly basic, but the costs and desperation for materials makes prioretization the crucial factor; crafting is less about hoarding items and advancing, and more about making difficult selections
+ Frankly put, the game makes the player choose between devastatingly hard choices; this is further expanded, in that the characters are designed to react emotionally to the consequences of such decisions
+ Myriad factors exist to affect one's characters, including sickness, depression, hunger, and temperature; such needs must all be balanced via crafting, trading, and scavenging for materials
+ Custom play options increase replay value
+ Taking life in the game is intimate and often emotionally involving; this is exacerbated by the reactions of both the victims and the player characters, who often slide into debilitating depression as a result
+ Random events can affect the safehouse if one isn't prepared, such as raiding and murders
- Bartering feels slightly unbalanced; the player always leaves a trade feeling screwed over, and many common items seem inordinately expensive

Pretty well made game, game mechanics work well for the most part. Art work is strong and noticeable, using a pencil sketching style, but the reason for not recommending this game is because I simply didn't enjoy it. I don't care for survival games too much, but tried this out at the recommendation of a friend. Despite not caring much for the genre I trucked through and did complete a single "story" and survived until day 23 :)
This War of Mine is played as a small group of survivors living in a large house. Each night 1 survivor may leave to search for goods while the others stay and sleep or guard the house. Your house has many utilities you can build- a small garden, a heater, rat trap for food, a stove, etc. You use these utilities and workstations to craft goods you'll need to survive. While you can eat raw food, cooked food does much better for filling you up. You'll need to board up your house where, I would assume, collateral damage from the war has created large gaps in the walls and windows. Both your day cycle to build items, harvest goods, and interact with other survivors, traders, etc, and your night cycle to find new goods, are timed with a clock in the top left corner.
Your survivors each have a different skill set. I got Bruno, Pavle, and Katia as my starting three. Bruno is a good cook who can create food using fewer resources. Pavle runs fast so he can avoid danger or run from it while scavenging. Katia is a good bargainer so she can squeeze more out of your trade deals. Later on I got Cveta and Arika with "Good with children" and "Sneaks quietly" skills, respectively. I saw in the build your own game section there are quite a few survivors, all with their different skill sets.
The scavenging is done only during the night and if you don't manage to exit voluntarily before the night ends, then your character gets "caught out" and will have a delay before he and his scavenged goods return. To scavenge you first pick who will go, then where. The where is very important as each area has certain resources- building materials, weapons parts, food, traders, and even danger! (Gasp!) Revisiting some areas will show development of the region with new people taking over or previously present people disappearing. Scavenging is as simple as clicking on highlighted rubble, desks, drawers, cabinets, etc, and after a moment to inspect the spot, you get an inventory screen showing what you have and what you can take.
War is hell. I knew this well before playing this game and I'm strongly against coercive force and am a supporter of the non-aggression principle. I like to role play and empathize with the characters I'm playing as, whether it's Mass Effect, Deponia, or Civilization 5. I made the decision early on I would help anyone I could and wouldn't harm another person. I knew somewhere in the "teens" days I wouldn't make it far and I was ok with it. Trading couldn't get me enough food or bandages, bandits hit the home every single night, and I couldn't scavenge everything needed. I stole from armed bandits a few times, very carefully, and thanked the Lord for Pavle's large inventory space and his fast running. In the end, we just didn't make it.
If you're into survival games, and the life and death aspects of it, then pick this up. It has an amazing human element to it and I think was extremely realistic in how it handled the precious few resources available and the decisions on how to use them. All in all, bottom line is I would not freely recommend this game to a friend. It has a niche audience and isn't fun. It's challenging and engaging, but this means it's not for everyone.

TL;DR - Overall, this is not a bad game. I was just hoping for so much more.
For the most part, this is a Civ 5 reskin on another planet. The research tree has been converted to a research web, starting in the middle and spreading out in a direction you are interested in. While this has been done before in other games, it's still a pretty neat mechanic that I personally enjoy over the traditional tree. There exists a Health System to limit the expansion of your Civilizations which provides you with buffs or debuffs if you haven't expanded in a while or if you have committed to the appropriate research topics. I found this seemed to hinder me more often than it helped me when I focused on a conquest campaign but on a research intensive run it seemed to aid me. Re-tasking trade convoys becomes a tedious chore in the mid to late game that leaves you quite thankful that there isn't a 'corner the market' economic victory
A questing system has been added to this version of Civilization. While they do add flavor to this bland drink of a game, their only true purpose is to add affinity points to one direction or another. Please make no mistake, the tales the quests themselves weave and the rewards you receive for them are interesting, but in the long run they do little to affect your game.
I found that the various endgames leave your victories quite hollow and vague. Each endgame I experienced felt like they were the prologue of some other work of science fiction rather than an end to the one I was playing. Perhaps the developers wanted the end to feel open, or were leaving room for sequels/expansions/dlc/etc. I managed to get to three of these endings before I lost the desire to replay to game to see others. Truthfully it feels like someone walked into the developers studio one day and said 'Times up. Ship it as is."
I cannot recommend this game. But the reason I can't recommend this game is a terrible one: nostalgia. At some point, this was tagged as a 'spiritual successor to Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.' Alpha Centauri was one of my all time favorite turn based, civilization style games. This game is *sort of* like Alpha Centauri in that it is also a civilization style game that takes place on an other planet. But this is where those similarities end.
I'm sure there are other who will enjoy this game. I just don't.

This game sure has a lot of mixed reviews on here and it does suffer from some annoyances. Even at times it seems like a bit of a step back from grid1, but don’t let that stop you from checking it out.  The game is fun, its arcade racing it’s what you would expect from it and I am having a great time with it.
I love simulators, racing with a wheel and everything, but it’s a different animal.  It’s putting down laps, tuning, putting down laps, and tuning some more it can get to be a little bit of grind. There is no real carrot on a stick in the sim world to keep you going and wanting to unlock things its all about the driving(which is prefectly fine).   However this game is just grabbing the controller, throwing the car all over the place, drive tons of different cars, go into corners way to fast and just have some fun.
I’ve always been a fan of codemaster racing games; I got into them back on the ps1 with the Collin McRae games, and then onto TOCA, all good times.  Coming to this from the first Grid it does seems a little dumbed down I suppose.  It was nice to have to save up money to buy cars instead of just getting them handed to you, and doing the Le Mans race between season ect.  However the career board got a bit overwhelming with having so many events to do all at once.
That is one nice thing of how the career progress’s, and not overloading you with races. Instead you are going through each region one at a time.  The race types are pretty much what you would expect, nothing to terribly annoying or un-fun.  I am a big fan of drifting and the way the cars handle for the drift events is really horrible, they have too much grip and will just catch some grip and send you into the wall a lot.  It’s weird to get used to because you basically have to drift wrong to get anywhere with it, so I was a little let down by this. A lot of people just complain that drifting is in the game, and its “drift to win” but while actually racing there is plenty of cars that you don’t have to drift, you can still do perfectly fine with them and are they are quite a bit of fun.
There’s no cockpit view… yeah you hear it as the biggest complaint.  For me I got used to driving in bumper view way back from gran turismo finding it not only more of a sense of speed, but also better for nailing apex’s and having a good idea if you’re about to lose your back end, and save it before it’s too late.  I do however prefer to use cockpit view having played a lot of sims using a wheel, but this is not a big deal for me personally I do fine driving in bumper view and have fun with it.
One thing that bugs the hell out of me is when you do a flashback it’s not replay mode like it used to be unless you completely total the car.  It was interesting in the last games to watch you’re crashes in slow-mo and enjoy the amazing damage model before resetting it back.  Also the AI are complete Asshats and smash the crap out of you all the time seemly for no reason other than for the hell of it.  It wouldn’t be so bad if you could actually get back at them, but if you hit them they don’t move at all.  It’s pretty damn lame and one thing I am yelling about all the time.  If they don’t want to race clean that’s fine, but when you can’t take them out for being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥than its pretty frustrating.
Also in terms of the AI the difficulty seems to be all over the place.  I started out at Medium and was having no challenge and bumped it up to hard.  Then the WRC races start and for no good reason other than to make it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥the AI in front gets a massive lead and its damn near impossible to chase them down even if they are in a much slower car, it doesn’t seem to matter.  So the regular races are stupidly easy and the championship races are stupidly hard and you always start in the back.  If you can’t get up to 3rd in the first turn you can’t win in a championship race, and good luck getting past the AI that can’t hold a race line to save their life and if you are holding your inside line get ready for a pit maneuver or someone quickly moving in front of you so you smash the hell out them.
Overall, the game is fun, it might not be as good as the first grid, but it scratches the itch with not many racing games on pc that lean toward arcade when you want to just have some fun.  I see no point in going back to play grid 1 so this is perfect.  I would like to see some more customizing, buying parts, a little bit of tuning, I know this isn’t the style for these games, but I refuse to pay M$ for an xbox1 and I really miss Forza.  Also this DLC is getting out of hand and it has been for a long time.  It’s pretty much the price of a second game if you would have bought them all as they came out. Buying them in the bundle is a good deal, but it feels like it’s all stuff that should just frickin be in the game anyways.

GRID Autosport feels like what GRID 2 was supposed to be. It's sort of a split between 1 and 2.
For starters, you're back to the fairly open method of choosing races that was in GRID 1. You get a little board of different types of disciplines (Touring, Endurance, Open Wheel, Tuner, Street) and you can choose any of them right off the bat to dig into. They each come with different events you can sign up for, and each race has a few different sponsors you can race for, for differing amounts of XP based on how well you follow their requests. Generally, what you see is what you get in regards to what types of races you do. Touring is usually just touring car races, fast paced pack racing with you and 15 other racers. Endurance is powerful supercars that you race for 8 minutes or so. You have to watch your tire wear in this discipline, so lighter braking and safer turning. I haven't had any issue with my tires exploding on me yet (I play on the Medium difficulty) but they do tend to get close. Open Wheel is small cars that are, as you'd expect, open wheeled. So far it's been mostly Formula 3, but I haven't progressed too far in that discipline to say for sure if it'll become more. This discipline is also incredibly fun, which is a nice change from the stressful races that Open Wheel brought along in GRID 1. Tuner is light weight and small race cars and American muscle cars, which seem to be usually time attack (post the best time) races. Street is more along the lines of what you got in GRID 2 in the early tiers. There's a lot of hatchbacks and muscle cars in pack races. In addition to the above, there's a "GRID Championship" that unlocks after you get level 3, 6 and 9 in each of the disciplines. The GRID Championship is just all the other disciplines crammed in one event series, and gives you more experience to level the disciplines. There are also small "cup" events in some of the disciplines that'll pop up and break up the rest of your racing. They're small events of a few races, and the best is definitely Drift.
The AI is fairly typical of a racing game. They'll still follow their line regardless of how much you're in the way. It becomes especially upsetting when they hit you, and you go spinning off the road, while their car seems to be made of dark matter. Thankfully, they don't seem to be broken when they work for Ravenwest anymore. Gone are the days of watching those black and grey cars that you know you outpower speed off and leave you in the dust.
Speaking of, you don't seem to be able to have your own team anymore. You work exclusively for the highest bidder, and your codriver is whoever the team wants to stick with you. Most of the time, they're useless. You do have the ability to tell your codriver what to do, to an extent. You can tell them to defend/hold/drive normally/push/attack. Attack seems to be the only way to see them gain any positions, though, and I so rarely have them in a good place that I ask them to hold or defend, though the few times I have they lost their good position and I had to tell them to attack anyway.
The handling feels a whole lot better than it did in 2. The cars have some weight to them, and the tires don't want to squeel across the road with every turn (with basic assists left on). Not being able to drift around every turn and win by massive amounts of time anymore took some getting used to, but it's wonderful. I plan on turning off all the rest of the driver assists soon to see how it feels without them.
The feeling of speed seems a bit inconsistent, at least to me. Cars in Tuner and Muscle classes feel like they move really slow, despite the HUD telling me I'm going at 100mph. Then I jump in a Touring car and feel like I'm blasting along, but only doing 80. It might just be the way they handle, but it feels fairly odd.
It looks good, for the most part. The tracks and the cars are well rendered. The cars have a good shine to them, the liveries look good. The damage model on them is pretty weak, though it is a step above a lot of other racers. Cars still split apart by the seams like in GRID 2, so you'll get that weird piece of body flapping like a bit of loose skin. If you tap a car in front of you going into a turn, you will get scrapes all up and down the hood, regardless of how hard you hit. Does the same on the sides of your car, and presumably on your rear. It's not really a big issue, and I understand why it was done, but it bothers me a little. The backgrounds are, as is typical of racing games, weak. Low res, 2D trees that sparcely populate ugly, jagged hills. People in the stands are straight out of an RPG on the PS2. Perhaps the biggest issue as far as visuals, is the car interiors. Maybe I looked at it wrong, but it seemed like the reintroduction of cockpit view was a big deal for this game, and they are absolutely ugly. You don't get any movement on anything but the wheel, which becomes especially noticable when you're driving stuff like the open wheel vehicles and see the speedo screen make no effort to do anything. And considering this was stuff that was in DiRT 3, it's fairly shocking.
I like the game. It's got a good simcade feel that leans a bit more on the sim than the arcade, it looks good, and it plays fun. But it still feels like a step back from GRID 1. It's a step forward from 2, for sure, but there's still that gap.

Crea is a crafting sandbox RPG that places you in an alien world and tells you to survive. YES, this is a 2D crafting adventure sandbox RPG, much like Terraria. That does not mean that it is the same game, though. A large part of the time spent playing Crea is used to gather materials from above ground, underground, and enemies. While this may sound very familiar and common, it's the rest of the game that truly makes it shine.
Crea focuses on small, randomly-generated dungeons that appear throughout the world, each with unique rules that the player must follow to complete them. Instead of a few large dungeons or giant bosses, the dungeons in Crea can spawn any time you destroy and enemy spawn or just randomly on the map. These dungeons range in size from 1-3(+?) floors and contain treasure and a variety of enemies who all want nothing more than to stop you from reaching the exit crystal. Unfortunately for you, you can't just hack away or start exploring, since each dungeon has a unique set of rules that the player must follow to avoid failing the dungeon. Some of these rules include: a time limit, not attacking enemies, invisible enemies, defeating an extra-strong enemy in the dungeon, etc. This makes every dungeon run a unique experience that requires the player to quickly adapt and decide on a course of action immediately upon entering a dungeon. There are also different colored crystals that will take the player to a simpler dungeon that only requires the player to destroy 1-4+ monsters spawners to receive a chest full of goodies.
One of the most unique features of this game is that you have to discover crafting recipes by gathering and researching the components that are used in them. Instead of just gathering materials all day and dumping them into chests, you go to you research bench (once you make one) and use the materials you collected to start learning different recipes to help you survive and, eventually, thrive.
Another great feature of Crea is the talents system. During gameplay the player receives experience for completing different tasks, such as mining, fighting, and exploring. These different types of experience level up different categories, such as gathering, combat, and exploration and allow the player to purchase different skills or abilities using those experience points. This allows the player to learn everything from new attacks to better weapon proficiency to passive and active skills to double jump and ledge grabbing. These different options allow the player to customize their character in whatever way they see fit to enhance their Crea survival experience.

Tembo the Badass Elephant is a game with plenty of style and for that, I can't help but praise it. I adore Tembo's art design, rich with cartoony animations and Regular Show-esque character designs. From Tembo's giant "badada" stampedes to the hurrays upon completing a level, this game just screams charm.
But playing Tembo is another story. This game doesn't know if it wants to be a fast, momentum-based platformer like Sonic or a more methodical, precise platformer like Mario. The speeds between jumping and dashing are so, so different from each other, which makes the level design have to compensate for both (and it really doesn't). Some stages prefer speed over precision, or vice versa, so you're constantly fighting between game speeds solely to dodge a bottomless pit or outrun an incoming hazard.
Considering these speed issues and the levels that exacerbate them, Tembo is FAR too short for its asking price. There are three worlds to see (four if you count the extremely short final world) Aside from finding hostages and defeating enemies, there's nothing to do here aside from leaderboards. There just isn't enough meat on this game's bones to justify a $14.99 US price point.
This is such a shame to me, because this should be the birth of a series. Tembo is a platformer hero in the making, one that I'd love to see return. But this is a game that's stuck between two very different kinds of platformer designs, so it has to juggle both and stumble around so much. If the game could decide what kind of platformer it wants to be, the level design would follow suit and things would feel more cohesive and complete. Right now, though, this already fumbling platformer is hurt even more by a terribly low post-game content count.
Pros
+ Great animation, art style
+ Clever level aesthetics
+ Smashing through stuff is fun
Cons
- Constantly shifting between two different speeds is cumbersome
- Very very short with low post-game content
- Schizophrenic level design

This is one of those games that makes me wish that there was a neutral rating. The game is a straight-forward shooter with a very short campaign and lackluster combat. There are plenty of weapons, but the ammunition is short for many of them. You'll be using various iterations of the M4 rifle for most of the time. One chapter allows you to use a sniper rifle, but pulls you into medium range combat. There is also a pretty awesome light vehicle at your disposal for the first half of the game, but its usage seems really clunky. Oddly, this makes me actually want squad tactics in this game, since your squadmates are pretty variable in their effectiveness. Not that it matters, since there is little character development, let alone any plot or setting development.
There is a lot stuff going on, but none of it resolves or really goes anywhere. Take the evil NK officer who appears at the start of the game and just before the midpoint of the game. He just disappears, even though he has far more development and characterization than most of the characters you meet. Such development would have been useful and more poignant,
.
There are a handful of technical issues. One of the most glaring is the fact that enemies sometimes shoot through walls. I'm not talking about through flimsy plywood. Rifle rounds penetrate several layers of concrete and metal. I guess I shouldn't be shocked, since those rounds can hit the chassis of a destroyed vehicle with such force that they bounce.
I feel like there were a number of ideas mixed together, with the shooter idea taking over, but not dominating. The game starts off feeling like a grim view of an enemy-occupied USA for a few minutes before being smashed into by the modern-warfare shooter truck.Apart from being fairly straightforward and underdeveloped, the game is OK.
The multiplayer is pretty much gone, but a handful of players still exists. This is a shame, since the multiplayer is actually well designed and really fun. It is sort of a mix of Call of Duty and Squad-combat Bad Company 2 gamplay with vehicles.

I have about 38 hours in this game, and my experience has been mixed but generally favorable.
The game is plagued by bugs and instability, and the art and lore can feel awkward and rushed.  Balance and progression are a bit wonky, and controller support is functional but problematic in some situations.  Often, it is not clear what you need to do to progress, and the game gives you no hints.  In fact, there are points at which you may not realize there is anything left to do at all, and it is easy to find oneself wondering, "Is this really all there is?"  For example, the mannequins in the game have an item description that says they are for displaying armor and outfits.  In truth, placing an outfit on a placed mannequin causes it to come to life, and it is the only way to encounter an NPC.  Some of the mechanics also feel forced and tiresome, such as the novel crafting system.
Do I sound like I hate the game?  Great.  Nothing could be further from the truth.
For all its flaws, this game has the crucial, undefinable ingredient that Terraria clones to date have lacked: a soul.  Your home feels meaningful, as does the world around you.  Just when you think you have seen everything the game has to offer, you see more--and not just new items with better stats.  The lore, awkward as it can be, does inspire genuine curiosity, and when I head off to explore, I never really know what I am going to find or where it will be found.  The monsters are more than just red-hot floating blobs of damage with slight variations on the same AI, and so different approaches to different enemies really does pay off so long as you are not over leveled.  I have 38 hours in this game because it is a very good game with a lot of potential, and it can only get better from here.  The developer's unique process, while unconventional, has created something I have thoroughly enjoyed.
For what they are asking, this is game is a steal, and if you at all enjoyed Terraria, you should buy Crea.  It is not quite on par, but it is the closest to Terraria's heart and soul that any game has come in the years since.  Beyond the clear value to you as a consumer, these dedicated developers--so thoroughly involved with their community--genuinely deserve your money for what they have accomplished.  I want to see more heart in games, so I reward it when I see it.  I see it here.

Short version: Slippery, counter-intuitive controls. Ridiculous gating to progress. Uninsightful level/foe design that punishes going fast. A speed game that punishes speed. Bad framerates on some levels. Agonizingly short.  Sadly, shockingly not fun.
This hurts. I saw Tembo on Youtube and decided it'd be an amazing game to pick up for speedrunning and going for leaderboard times. I was thrilled with the fast, slick feeling in the first few levels, but little problems began to chip away at the fun until, by the 2nd boss, I was grinding to progress. Let me break down the points above.
Controls: They're very simple. You have a run button, a jump button, and a spray button. Unfortunately, you're forced to constantly release and re-press the run button to maintain momentum. Hitting a wall cancels your run, hitting a jump pad cancels your run, taking damage cancels your run. In most "fast" games, you'll automatically resume running once the block is cleared, but not with Tembo. That alone is a small but frustrating complaint when the game encourages running at all times with a painfully slow normal walk. Furthermore, while running Tembo handles like, well, and elephant. You shouldn't expect on-a-dime movement control from an elephant I know, but this also takes away from the feel of the game. Also, in many situations, Tembo will roll into a ball and begin bouncing when he lands from a jump or smash; unfortunately in many cases you're forced to watch him bounce several times before you regain control. It's just tedious to control him.
Gating: To progress past certain points in the game, you have to gain a certain number of points. You get these by trashing property, killing foes, and rescuing civilians. This would be okay except passing these requirements on the first go requires almost perfect play.  I found myself having to go back and replay EVERY level multiple times to reach the boss of each act. This felt like a grind, as I was forced to take multiple paths and aim for perfects just to see more of the game. You should reward 100% (or in this case closer to 95%) completion, not require it just to progress in the game.
Design: Again, Tembo presents itself as a game about going fast and smashing tons of stuff. Unfortunately practicaly every corner of every level, and every enemy, is out to punish this. You're frequently assailed by foes who will completely stop your momentum and deal you damage unless you come around from behind and attack them from the back, or wait for their attack cycle to open up. You'll see jumps that are just a bit too short to make while running at full speed, forcing you to slow to make them. You'll be sniped by perfectly timed bomb throws from enemies out of reach above. You'll see situations that look like you could pull off awesome looking tricks, only to look like a fool because the floaty controls won't let you do what you want. It's an exercise in frustration knowing what could have been if only the game cooperated with you a bit more. You can have challenge but still allow speed; the early Sonic games are great examples, and almost none of the lessons taught by those games are applied here.
Performance: Simpy put, a 2D game like this has no business having framerate drops in 2015. Tembo manages to do this. Even with settings on low, my FPS was dipping down to the 30s on some stages. Most notably the ones with a lot of fire.
Short: There's 18 levels. Each level takes about 5 minutes on average to clear the first time. The game is $15 right now. If that math checks out for you, that's cool. I don't feel this game is worth the $15 price point at those figures. Playtime is inflated by forced re-dos of prior levels to pass gate points. I don't consider this part of the value.
A lot of these problems feel baked into the level and very game design, and can't be solved with a simple patch. It makes me sad; smashing things fast as a badass elephant sounded like a lot of fun, but Tembo is not. Give it a pass, or at least wait for a sale.
