This game is an open-world sandbox game, similar to Terreria, Starbound, and the like. You can get randomly generated small, medium or large worlds in single-player or multiplayer modes. Homefront has an interesting premise that briefly satisfies, but the single-player campaign is extremely short (barely 4 hours) and the multi-player (what little there is) is over-run with hackers. It might have been worthwhile once, but now it is little more than a curiosity piece.
Total size on my hard-drive: 12 GB
+ Nice graphics (Unreal 3).
+ Cool premise. The idea of North Korea conquering all of the United States is nonsense, but still an intriguing “what if” scenario.
+ Decent voice acting.
+/- Single-player story has the capacity to shock. Everything else about it – from the level design to enemy design – is painfully average. No real bosses, just shoot your way through. A handful of weapons, but only a few that are useful. The characters have little, well, character.
+/- Multiplayer is surprisingly still alive, but the few matches I was able to join were wrecked by wall-hackers and aim-botters. The maps are large, and feel very open while providing plenty of cover. Get a group of friends together, and you can have fun. When compared to other modern fps games like Battlefield 3 though, Homefront is competent, but nothing special.
- Running feels like the player character is mired in mud.
- Early levels look impressive, but distance objects in later levels are extremely low-res. Did the devs run out of money? There are other hints of a larger game – like the hub-like areas where you’re allowed to click on NPCs for some scripted dialogue.
- Linear corridor levels.
- The "stealth" sections are completely scripted. Just do what your AI team-mates tell you to do, and you'll be fine.
- Checkpoint-based saving. (Manually saving hard-saves the last checkpoint.)
- Little enemy variety. You have your basic solider, sniper soldier, and rocket-launcher soldier, with the occasional tank that takes three rockets to destroy. And there's also the automated gun-towers that somehow run on propane? (Throw a grenade to blow them up.)
- The story mode feels like bits and pieces from a much larger game. The threat to America is done well, and there is some loss and sacrifice; but we never spend enough time with any of the characters to ever care.
- There are several situations that unravel like this: an enemy soldier is scripted to advance to a certain point. If you have already advanced to that point, he’ll advance anyway, making his way blindly to his destination. Other times he’ll spawn instead marching to his destination – which means he’ll immediately begin firing at you, point-blank. It comes off feeling like the enemy AI is aggressive, when really it’s nothing of the sort.
- This “programmed destination” thing plagues your AI team-mates as well. Several times I had a nice spot in cover, only to see myself moving slowly to the left or right. The AI controlled team-mate was literally pushing me out of cover and into enemy fire, because I was in his spot.
- Iron sights is bound to right-click, as I would expect. What I did not expect is that right-clicking is a
. Right-click once, and iron sights are engaged until you right-click once again. This might work in a dedicated sniping game, but it’s a bad choice in a game that tries to have fluid and engaging combat. Ammo isn’t common, either, so precision is preferred over spraying bullets.
Homefront also requires the PhysX Legacy driver (if you’re on Radeon). Not really an issue – I have several games that require it. What is an issue is that, after installing another game that uses PhysX (Starpoint Gemini 2), Homefront claimed PhysX was corrupted, and wouldn’t launch. Repairing PhysX in the list of programs didn’t work. I was intending to try some more multiplayer, but had been so underwhelmed by everything to this point that I just uninstalled. An interesting premise isn’t enough to recommend Homefront. Worth a purchase? Only if you’re curious, and probably not even then.

This is a pretty fun platforming game by, surprisingly, Game Freak. Yes, the Pokémon developers. While I have seen many people comparing this game to Sonic the Hedgehog, personally I felt it was more similar to Donkey Kong Country. Especially the two more recent entries in the series (Returns and Tropical Freeze). It is a very momentum-based game with lots of destruction, cannons to shoot yourself out of, things to interact with, and enemies to wallop. It lends itself very well to speed-running. At the same time, there are numerous secret alcoves and collectibles to track down, encouraging a slower-paced and more thorough playthrough of each level too.
Tembo himself is very entertaining and pops with personality. I can't think of another game with an elephant as your main playable character. Your arsenal of moves isn't huge, but there are a fair few abilities and they all have their uses (even the slide-kick which I initially underrated). The animations are cute and fun, and that's not just for Tembo either. The enemies have amusing animations as well. In that regard I am reminded of the Metal Slug series.
The game isn't perfect though. In addition to the already infamous launch problem, at the time of writing this review there is still another bug in the game that sometimes makes you pinball uncontrollably around. The only way to correct this is to log out of the game and load it back up. I 100% completed the game (except for the "collect 99 lives" achievement) in about 5 hours and experienced this pinballing glitch three seperate times. Sadly, the game is also pretty short. Hopefully it will get some Steam Workshop support or something to help with the longevity. One final note on the negatives as well, the music is extremely bland. It's not to say that it is irritating, it just is entirely unnoticable and forgettable.

Hitman: Absolution (HA) looks pretty, but the gameplay is a bit different then previous Hitman games. If you played all the previous titles in the series as I have, you will begin to miss the open-sandbox effect of levels, as well as being able to choose your weapons before a mission. HA only has a few big levels, while others are quite small and seem more to me like filler rather than an actual level. HA tries to make it seem as if there are more levels to make up for this, but even bigger levels are cut up into different smaller areas. I also feel the need to mention that the levels are very linear. They are open-world to a point and the game pretty much holds your hand if you choose to use Instinct Mode (Think Eagle Vision from Assassin's Creed). A way around that is that you can either turn a lot of the features of Instinct Mode off. or just opt for the extremely hard Purist difficulty where all HUD elements are removed and all your are left with is a crosshair.
This game does have it's memorable moments as with the other games including a few funny accidents, but it just doesn't strike me as a proper Hitman game due to the more story driven approach. All in all, I still would recommend this to someone for what it is if they're looking for a stealth game to play. Overall, I would recommend just getting the newer 2016 Hitman game as it's more in line with previous games.

Artifex Mundi continues to impress with Nightmares from the Deep 3: Davy Jones, one of their best hidden-object adventure games to date. More so than their previous efforts, Davy Jones has an intriguing sense of personality and strong cinematic style that make it feel more like a big-budget title than an indie game. Artifex Mundi's detailed artwork has also gone from modestly attractive to drop-dead gorgeous; I think Davy Jones is one of the best looking games I've seen from the past couple of years.
On the negative side, I still find the relatively linear, inflexible puzzle design to be irksome. There could be a lot more replay value if the game were designed with multiple puzzle solutions and different paths to take. More length would have also been nice, to make the game feel more epic and give the writers the opportunity to tell a more complex story. Still, the 5-6 hour, $10 game standard has its own appeal, and could be part of the reason why Artifex Mundi has been so successful.
It may be the third game in its series, but Davy Jones stands alone, and is one of the best places to start if you're curious to experience a hidden-object adventure game for the first time. I'm already looking forward to the next time I dive in and rediscover all of Davy Jones' secrets.

While Beyond Earth is most certainly a Civ game it has its own unique feel, seperating it from prior entries in the series. The general atmosphere and feel of the game certainly are different due to the setting being the future instead of the past there are gameplay elements that are unique and make this game feel different from previous Civ games. The largest gameplay difference is easily the technology web, instead of steady progression forward one must carefully study the web, decide what is important to them and their gameplay style and strateegically navigate the web in order to achieve the advanced techs desired. The second most standout gameplay element is affinities. No affinity is clear cut better for one type of victory over the other but instead each affinity represents a philosophy of how to achieve such a victory. I find affinities do little to influence strategy (beyond the decisions nessecary to advance your affinity level) but instead add replayability and a degree of customability to your civilization. Questing and victories are different from prior games, questing being new and victories having been changed. The enw victories require various steps yet still do not feel overly unique and different, at least as far as planning the victory goes. Quests are interesting but are largely irrelevent, a simple decision on occasion based on your overall strategy. Quests do hold potential for modders though and I would recommend looking at mods that take advantage of this system to see its full potential. All in all Civ Beyond Earth is a fun game, but one I would consider an alternative to Civ V as opposed to its succesor.

I had a coupon for this so figured I'd give it a go even though I'm not too keen on hidden object games... and I never played any of the other games in the series (turns out that doesnt matter, they are unrelated series). I was pleasently surprised by the game, and played the entire main game and then the bonus one in a little over 7 hours...straight. It is quite addictive, and this game gives the hidden objects genre a breath of fresh air. It's rich in plot, mystery, and intrigue.
Okay, honestly at first... the narration... I was pretty convinced I had just bought a game for 7 year olds. I turned my volume down and continued onward. It tells you in the beginning to turn the sound up for a better gameplay experience and maybe it's just me, but I felt better just reading the captions.
I played it through the entire time on the middle (advanced/intermediate?) setting, but there is the option for expert which offers it's own acheivement and does make the game harder with click penalities and turning off visual clues, etc. There is also a easy mode if you have kids or you are really really lazy.
There's  the obligatory stereotypical find the hidden objects, but multiple types: the empty silhouette (figure out what object you must find from the shape), the list of words and then there is the interactive which is quite neat ( Here's a non-spoiler fake example:  say you need a hot cup of water, you would need to find a cup, a heat source, and water and combine them to acheive the result.) These puzzles also help you by giving you a useful item you may need on your quest. Also, strange but nice, is the option to play a round of mahjong instead of the hidden object search. (I think there's also an achievement for playing 3 rounds of mahjong.) It may sound weird, but it comes in handy when your raging for the last thing on your list and don't want to use a hint or skip the puzzle (which are also achievements).
There are also tons of puzzles that involve logic skills and can take some time. Also, I found it quite interesting that you can travel between parts of the map freely once youve discovered them, and often need to go back and forth to complete objectives. That aspect really sets it apart and truly makes more of a point and click adventure first, hidden puzzle game second.
Bottom line: worth 10 bucks? Probably not. Grab it with a coupon or when it's on sale, it's a great time killer and was unexpectedly fun. I'll buy more from the series when they're cheaper. It's 7 hours of my life I won't get back, but sometimes that's better than just watching TV, and it's totally worth a thumbs up.

I wasn't gonna leave a review yet, but I have some things to say that I believe are relevant if you are considering buying this game right now:
First of all, the biggest issue this game has is that people are leaving negative reviews on an EARLY ACCESS game solely because the game has some server issues or bugs, which are being fixed DAILY by the devs. Every day this game has been out so far it has received a patch aimed at fixing it's issues and stability. The devs obviously care about this game and plan to make it work.
Buying an early access game and giving it a negative review for the reasons mentioned above is like getting what you asked for on Christmas but throwing it away because you didn't feel like unwrapping it. This game has been fun and interesting in the little bit of time I have played it and I can tell it has a lot of potential, not just because of the concepts and features in it but again, because the devs care about it.
I personally am glad I bought into the TESTING EXPERIENCE so that I have the chance to help this game become as good as possible by giving feedback and helping the devs out as much as possible. If this isn't your intentions when buying into an early access game, you probably shouldn't buy early access games. I could see negative reviews being appropriate if the game just had bad ideas or things in the game weren't making sense or fun (assuming you could play it without server issues or bugs), but almost all of the negative reviews are just people complaining about the server issues and bugs, which if I had to guess will be fixed soon and I highly doubt those people will change their reviews after that happens.
In the end, if your PC meets the spec requirements and you want a game as described on Citadel: Forged with Fire's store page, and to be a part of it's development process, then this early access game is probably for you.
I personally highly recommend this game, as I see nothing bad about it. Just an early access game having a rough start but also has a lot of potential and will be a lot more fun once the bugs and server issues are resolved.
I will say if you want to jump in an enjoy it right away, as I originally did, that might not happen due to the issues I've experienced. However you may have a different experience than me and right now I am waiting for some more fixes and patches, but I am still very optimistic about this game.
EDIT: I'd also like to mention, since a lot of people are comparing Citadel: Forged with Fire to survival games, that this is NOT a survival game. You won't die no matter how long you stand around, unless something attacks you. There is no "food" or anything like that. There is however health and mana potions you can craft, but that still doesn't make it a "survival game".
What you actually end up doing is farming experience and crafting materials while also unlocking spells, building shelter, crafting gear and exploring/fighting enemies/looting.
I have played this game a bit more since I originally posted my review, and the more I play the more it seems I am enjoying this game.
EDIT: this review is still relevant. People still haven't a clue what "early access" is meant for.

You'll see I have 11.1 hours played. What it should say is "11.1 hours spent trying to get the game to play."
Every 15 or so minutes, the server crashes. After the server crashes, you have to wait sometimes up to 10 minutes for it to come back. When you get back, various bugs may occur that could potentially cause you to have to make a new character on another server, only for this process to repeat.
The game crashes over, and over, it takes a long time to even get into a game. Sometimes the game just boots you back to the main menu the moment it loads into the server.
I wanted so badly to like this game. This game looked like everything I wanted, it had polish, magic, monsters, exploration and sandbox gameplay without annoying survival elements and the stress of having to check in on stuff every day and spending hours and HOURS AND HOURS taming monsters. The overall gameplay, what very little I was able to squeeze out of it, was actually very enjoyable. Eh, except...
Enemy AI is beyond terrible. Sometimes they don't even attack. A level 1 character can get lucky and take down a level 35 enemy if they have enough patience. I'm guessing this would extend to your mind-controlled creatures (or Tames), making them borderline useless for base defense.
Animations are awful. Some enemies barely have animations, so it's difficult to tell when you need to dodge or when you have an opening. The game can be played in third person, but it's wonky and your character moves like they have... Problems.
The only input you get when you take damage is your screen fills with Red. My gamer-instincts tell me that this indicates I am very near death, because the intensity of the red is the same when I take 100 damage versus 5 damage. This creates bad game feel.
This next one isn't much of a complaint, just something I noticed. Some of the starting spells operate mechanically 1 for 1 with old Quake weapons. Rocket Launcher is Fireball, Lightning Gun is the gauntlet spell, etc. Not bad, just weird.
This game has a metric buttload of potential. It really does. In the state it's in right now, though, I feel like I've been ripped off. I know it's Early Access and you're supposed to "Expect bugs", but I expect something that's worth 20 dollars. They should not have released the game at all for MONEY in the state it's in. I don't feel as though the devs had the players' best interests in mind, rather, they worked long enough and wanted to start cashing in on their game. This doesn't bode well, in my mind, and I hope they can prove otherwise.
I'll be asking for a refund, regardless of how many hours Steam thinks I """"played""""" the game.

I'd say give it a shot if the constant feeling of "Two steps forward, one step back" won't bother you.

Unpopular opinion time: This is my favourite Bioshock game.
If you could hold back on the torches and lynches for a few moments  I will explain my position. The original bioshock was a masterpiece. What this game does is build upon that. It's a hard task to make a sequal everyone wants to a game that everybody loves, and so this game gets a lot of hate. But if Bioshock 2 had come out without the original ever being released, it would no doubt get the same praise the original did.
The story, and more importantly the story-telling is perfectly crafted. There's a couple silly design choices like the image of the girl appearing when she's talking to you, which just come across as a poor attempt at being creepy. But beyond that there's a wealth of great story-telling. Audio dairies play a huge part again in immersing the player into the world, and the Lamb is a fantastic "villian" in that at times I was questioning whether she was indeed correct. I always find villians who's actions I can justify, to be far more impactful.
The moment in the game that clinched it's place as the best in the series for me comes towards the end. I won't spoil it in this review but you'll know which moment it is when you get to it. It feels extremely calming and terrifying all at once and had me wishing it would never end for the duration.
Like with the other bioshock games, I recommend picking up the triple pack since all 3 games are superb in their own regards.
Also, make sure to get the Minera's Den DLC for another great piece of self-contained story with a great twist.

You also cannot possess your creatures, not a big deal, but it always had a charm to see your dungeon from first person perspective.
Also the game is very very short, and once you finish it, you probably won't want to do a second playthrough for quite some time.
Lastly, many, many people who buy this are unable to finish the game at all. There is a game breaking bug where levels will not load and the game simply hangs. 32 hours and counting... that is how long i have played this game. it now ranks in my top .5%(yes, I do mean one half of one percent) of games on steam ranked by hours played. Suffice to say, I have enjoyed it very much, and this is considering I had my doubts that I would get into this game at all going in. Anyway, lets get into it.
You all know the buzzwords by now: sandbox, rpg, survival, crafting etc, and that is all well and good, but I would like to talk about exactly what compels me to come back to this game time and time again. I think it comes down to the fact that there is always something different that I am excited to do next.
There is usually at least one skill that I am excited to level up. The leveling system is packed with options. Your character as a whole will level up, in addition to acquiring skill points in different categories including syle(magic), crafting, exploring and more. Each category is loaded with different skills to learn. Each set of skills has its own method for accumulating points to buy the skills.
Combat consists of both physical and magic attacks, along with a set of skills for each. The fighting itself feels right. You have hand to hand and ranged weapons, as well as a variety of spells at your disposal. Monsters are scattered throughout the land, and you will also be able to enter dungeons that exist outside of the world. I particularly enjoy that each dungeon comes with a specific set of rules. A dungeon may have invisible creatures and no healing allowed, for example. The dungeons can be found in the wild, but you can also craft a NPC who will allow you to jump right into a dungeon that you can create to your specifications. The dungeons keep things fresh with their changes from one to the next.
Exploration is also a great way to spend time. I spent much of my time wandering around taking in all the sights and collecting new items. There are various biomes above ground, and an immense world of caverns and secrets when you venture underground. Hours upon hours can be spent exploring any given world. I must say that the one downside of the randomly generated worlds would be that you may have a tough time finding certain items. In my case, There were a few items the game expected me to acquire around the time when my character reached level 10, but due to the random nature of the world, the biome that contains them ended up being far, far away from me. I made it to level 20 or so before I found I had no choice but to venture out to retrieve the items. Unfortunately, the creatures there were all level 40 and could crush me in a single hit. I am willing to accept this task as a chance occurance, but it did slow my progress in the game.
The crafting system is based on recipes. I would go out exploring, and each time I returned, I would run over and see what new item recipes i could uncover with the items I had gathered on my journey. New uses for items will become available as you level up, so there was always a chance that some old random item would suddenly become very useful again. There is also a system that involves chaos. It adds a unique twist where you try to improve the quality of your items before the chaos gets too high. It certainly helps to differentiate the crafting system from other games, but may be a bit confusing for beginners.
In the end, everything is done well. That is what makes crea so great. I can set off to mine for some ore, only to have it turn into a great adventure into a dungeon that gives me some key items to open up a new pile of goods to craft. I love that the possibilities seem endless everytime I leave my home base and set out into the world. Nothing seems like a chore, and the next epic discovery may be waiting right around the corner.

Let's make this abundantly clear. This game does have it's bugs, and there's a number of them; but that shouldn't be the absolute decided factor between picking up this game in my opinion. Jasson (Siege Games main developer) does a weekly live stream where he let's players chat and discuss various issues with the game. He is, without a doubt, 100% on top of all issues that are being addressed.
Now, in my experience thus far, I actually haven't came across a single bug that's been mentioned by other players. More specifically, Audio/Graphic issues. I have 14.4 hours (as of this review) and I've yet to experience one hiccup. The game itself has enough content for a CASUAL gamer. You have boss fights, you have character progression, you have researching/crafting. There's plenty of pros to this game in it's current state, and that will only continue to grow.
One thing I see that's mentioned quite a bit is the learning curve. Here's what you need to understand. The game is new, and the fanbase is relatively small currently (Approx. ~1000 players). The Wiki doesn't have much information, so you're really reliant on exploring the game yourself and actually taking the time to LEARN it. If that's something you don't want to do, and you just want a mindless tutorial you're going to skip over anyways, then this isn't the game for you. The best way to learn the game currently IS TO PLAY IT.
At first, I was extremely intimidated by the game. I spawned next to a crystal with what seemed to be a teleporting option; I quickly ignored it and moved on. A few hours in I really started to understand it's purpose. For nearly 10 hours of gameplay, I had NO idea you could use spells such as proficiencies, in passive mode. I kept switching to attack mode to cast my spells. Again, I figured this out because I PLAYED the game.
TL;DR:
The game isn't in bad shape at all. There's major and minor bugs, but every game will have those. Stick with the developer, report the bugs, and I PROMISE this will make Terraria seem like a childs game. Also, on a side note. Jasson is the only developer, and on his stream June 13th, he mentioned wanting to hire a C++ coder to help fix bugs and improve content. One thing I truly admired about him was his excitement seeing people on Twitch playing his game. He's clearly working his very hardest to listen to players and fix big issues. He took questions/issues DIRECTLY from viewers on Twitch and fixed them right in front of your eyes. The guy shows a lot of promise, and so does this game. I highly recommend picking it up while it's $15. One thing I do recommend (this is for Siege Games), ask some big players of your game to help expand the content of your Wiki. Provide starter guides, more explanations, and clarifications on items/crafting/chaos. Let your players help other players.

First of all, this review is going to be based on the few hours of gameplay time I have, most of which was spent experimenting with the very basic mechanics. I'm sure there are many, many more features than those I have come across, but I assume it would require a considerable amount of time spent playing the game for me to experience those. So, let's get right into the review.
Crea was fully released a few weeks ago. It has a concept extremely similar to that of Terraria, Starbound and other 2D exploration games, but is unique in some aspects. As soon as I started up the game, I noticed it has a very appealing menu, although simple. Upon creating my character, I began in the centre of a large, randomly-generated world. The graphics are cute and an in-game tutorial is available. I must admit, it took me a while to work out how to harvest trees because of the two modes - building and combat - which are merged into one in other games. One of the downsides to Crea is that despite the integration of a tutorial, some things are quite hard to discover how to do - well, for me anyway. I must admit, I still haven't worked out how to place wood.
Some things that makes Crea unique is its research, talent system and spells. By crafting a research desk, you can use collected items to research new weapons, armour, furniture and tools for crafting. I also found the talent system quite interesting. Over time, you build up talent points which you can then spend on making harvesting or combat more efficient, allowing new abilities or unlocking spells. By using equipped spells, you can make your attacks more damaging, heal yourself and give yourself other benefits in combat.
Overall, Crea is a fun little game to play in your spare time. Hopefully I won't get addicted to it like I did with Terraria. Aside from the frustration when I can't figure out how to do something, I think I will find myself coming back to it time and time again. There seems to be a lot more to do when you get into it a little bit more.
7/10
-Cute graphics and menu design.
-Good, fitting music.
-Crafting system tells you what you need to craft the desired item.
-Interesting research system. -A talent system that lets you improve your character's skills.
-In-game tutorial (although brief).
-Difficult to learn how to do certain things.
-You have to play it quite a bit to truly enjoy it.
-Having to switch between building and crafting modes is a pain when you get ambushed by an enemy.
-There aren't a huch amount of character customisation options.

This is a preliminary review as I only have played for ashort time. But given that it is now on sale I might as well get my first thoughts out as I disagree with some of the negative ratings received by the game.
This is a *little* and *charming* game. From what I have seen so far, worth the $20 I payed for it. I never played Dungeon Keeper so I don't have that point of reference but I played the Majesty 2 game so I felt right at home with setting tasks to the units rather than directly teling them what to do (as you would in a game like Starcraft). Here you point to a location and indicate you want to mine its gold and the game engine will assign workers to mine the gold. If you want units to fight a monster you pick them up and drop them near the monster. Once they recover from the fall they will attack nearby enemies. So the units are sort of autonomous and you have indirect control. You concentrate on improving your economy, hire units, discover locations (by sending workers to mine rocks), place traps, drop units near enemies.
The game holds your hand by having a narrator telling what to do. It is not particularly funny but I don't think it is intended to be funny. It is intended to hammer the message set when you see the intro movie: the game doesn't take itself too seriously. You will not be pulling your hair trying to figure out what to do next here. The narrator tells you. I like that sort of game.
Would the game be worth $40? I do not know. When I finish the campaing and when/if I get around to update the review, I will tell you. For now I can say that  for $20 it is totally worth it.

I ran through this game in about 5 hours, but I was really playing into it, and have played lots of platformers before. I'd recommend this game for anyone who loves a good platformer, there's a lot here for them. A steady 4/5.
What I would say, however, is that there's a lot here, but it's not used much. What that means is, that there's a lot of assets and mechanics that are in this game and they all work extremely well. There's a lot of ideas here. But there's not enough content that would let me give this game a 5/5. What I would recommend to the developers would be to offer some type of map editor or something like that. That way there's a lot more replayability, and there can be a community. I was grinning ear to ear when I got up to the third world and all of those switch and pinball mechanics came into play. However, the game abruptly ends after that without much use of the mechanics. Those interesting cactus plants in the second world only got used twice.
If I had an editor for this, I would make tons of levels. Tembo is a joy to control and has a ton of interesting moves and ways to move. The ideas for levels would definitely flow. The levels that are offered are all well constructed but they feel like examples to something more rather than a full game by themselves. After completing the game, I was only left wanting more.
Once more, I give this game a 4/5. Amazingly put together and constructed, but lacking any real replayability, and leaving the player wanting more, much more!

that make bugfixes their number one priority; something very rare with EA games these days, albeit unfortunately.

You know how you have something you enjoy doing that you feel maybe isn't the thing you should really be doing?  Like maybe you like eating at McDonalds, or jacking it to videos of Swedish weightlifters.  That's the way I feel about Artifex Mundi games.  I have them all, I've finished them all, but as much as I like them, I feel like I should be playing somehting more substantial.  Somehow I just like the calmness of it all.  The bland, monotone female protagonist, the puzzles that pretty much repeat from game to game, it's a simple, familiar formula, and it's comfortable.
I can't really complain, I've gotten many hours of gameplay out of these point and click games featureing the same woman who for whatever reason cannot stop losing her daughter to various demons and ghosts that seem intent on kidnapping her.  Personally, if I was this ladies daughter, every time she wanted to go on a trip, I'd be like "Um, no thanks, but I've been kidnapped by demon ghosts the last five trips, I think I'll sit this one out."
Overall, I really have a good time, or at least a relaxing time, playing these games, as the puzzles are not really challenging, and the scenes are well done.  If you are looking for a game that won't stress you out, or are someone who values bland voice acting, I would suggest that you try pretty much any Artifex Mundi game.

Rebel Galaxy is a space swashbuckling game, like the old privateer and freelancer. The player is free to play as a merchant, bounty hunter, smuggler, pirate or mercenary for hire, or even a little bit of each... although a bit of imagination is required since all of the missions (apart from the main story line) are only made of a few lines of text: go there, do that, and claim the reward.
Nevertheless the game is as entertaining as its ancestors. The music also is an integral part of the experience.

Ah, the great cash-grab that was
. An extremely ambitious (and at times genuinely enjoyable) experience which in the end manages not to live up to its potential.
The Good:
Voice acting is solid. While it's not the quality people who play COD routinely will be expecting, it's not bad either.
Level design is also pretty decent. Yes, the campaign missions become repetitive very quickly, but once you get past the fact the devs are literally recycling the same house roughly 30 times per level, it's easy to ignore.
The Bad:
Writing. Your character is a silent protagonist, a trope which was proven dead back in 2001 when the original
came out, although some developers tried to keep selling the dead horse for some years later and it probably won't ever completely leave the FPS genre. Still it makes it very difficult to immerse yourself in all the WTF things this game throws at you, or care about any of the one-dimensional squad mates you have.
Your team consists of Boone, whose dimension is the fact he's your leader, Rianna, who is female, Hooper, who has a very enthusiastic pet robot, and Conner, who is angry. I got four missions into the campaign and this was all I knew of these people, which may not seem surprising until you remember this game only has about 10 missions in it total.
The world itself isn't much better. There's a lot of work going into the game's set up itself, very reminscent of the
remake released a year later, although that manages to be a far better experience overall. Still, since we don't know anything about any of the characters, it makes it hard to figure out how they fit into the world, and it's therefore very difficult to see what sets this game apart from, say,
or
.
Still, I can handle a shallow shooter if at least it's good, but sadly this game fails there as well. A lot of the shooting is just plain
: my favorite examples of this are the Remingon 870 whose pickup icon indicates a red dot sight, though the sight itself never rendered any time I used it, or the hit boxes for several objects, which are signficantly larger than they should be (i.e., the game treats destroyed cars like completely solid objects, and you can't through the windows or windshields). The firing sounds for a lot of weapons (specifically the Diablo and M16) sound like airsoft rifles, which doesn't help, and most weapons in general feel very bland (particular note goes to the Chinese AK, SCAR-L, M4, and ACR, which I have yet to notice any significant differences between).The game tries to keep a COD-level of weapons and attachment combinations available to you, but they're mostly the same weapons with the same attachments, which most often don't matter anyway (there's no significant difference between the holographic "scope" and "ACOG" attachments, for example).
The game also isn't quite sure where it wants its difficulty level to sit. The first mission is surprisingly easy, especially for someone who's sat through other similar shooters, but by mission four (the point I gave up) you're fighting enemies who will gleefully kill you through walls using RPGs with blast-radiuses measured in miles. Fortunately, for the most part your character has a lot of health, but this is good because in place of an actual sprint option you're instead given a "pleasant jog" which isn't significantly faster than your regular running speed. Worse, you're not able to do fairly logical things, like transition from sprinting to being prone; instead the game assumes you want to completely stop and stand up as straight as you can, apparently in an effort to kill yourself quickly.
is probably worth maybe 20%-50% (if I'm feeling charitable) of its current asking price; for as old as it is and as shallow as it is, there's no reason to spend anything more than $10 for it. Honestly, I can't recommend this. There are simply too many other better shooters out there.

Taming animals does exist, but from what I can tell it’s time and level limited, so hopefully there won’t be any 10+ tames later in the game. But I have yet to tame anything so I am not exactly sure how it works yet. (Will update when i get a chance to know more. As I don’t have the tame skill yet.)
Keep in mind that this game is still early release.
So far, I have had 2 crashes in 4 hours while playing with a friend. ( Note: I was hosting. ) The graphics demand is a little on the high side. But I am playing with a Radeon HD 7850 and I can handle most settings on or around mid. Most people will have a better card and should be able to handle more. Even with that the game does look beautiful.
The available spells Currently seem a bit limiting, as each weapon only has one spell/skill associated with it. I shoes staff and am noticing that even though it is an AOE weapon I often need to hit the enemy directly in the face to guarantee it will hit, and have yet to hit 2 enemies at once even when they are on top of each other. Hope that will be fixed in an update soon.
Suggestion: expect to rely on health and mana potions. This game does not seem to support health innate health regen, so you will either need to keep a constant supply of health and mana potions or find some similar alternative. Especially, since level 1 enemies are rare and level 5’s and up are found out of the gate. (The game does not go easy on you, but it is still far more leisurely than ARC.) That being said me and a friend were able to kill a level 35 dragon with both of us at level 8. (using a lot of potions and cover) And while mana regen isn’t really that bad, in battle you will definitely notice how slow it really is. This is only compounded with the occasional respawn right on top of you. So make extra sure you are safe before opening your inventory. (Died a few times in the middle of the road while crafting a health potion, because of that.)
Don’t get me wrong, there are lag issues. Both client side and server side. But with an early release I kind of expected a few hiccups. Time will tell how well they are handled.

Bioshock 2 has a rather unfavourable reputation. It's seen as so non-canon, so unambitious that rarely is it discussed by fans and critics in the same breath as other 'Shock games.
But Bioshock 2 isn't for those people. Bioshock 2 is a game for people who want to creep around more of the Bioshock 1 universe, were rather fond of the gameplay of the original and fancy properly stepping into the shoes of a Big Daddy as opposed to the shallow facsimile at the end of the first game.
Even though it might be hitting on the same beats, Bioshock 2 isn't aiming to be the revolutionary, disorienting, dramatic tour-de-force the first game was, or the one Infinite was trying so hard to be, and that's just fine. Instead, it just wears the first game's clothes and tries really hard, like an endearing little brother. It's almost like a ridiculously well-produced fan game or total conversion mod.
Accept the game for what it is, and Bioshock 2 actually becomes a rather lighthearted experience. It's easy to have fun with it when you know not to take it so seriously, especially when its got the presentation and solidness of a Bioshock game.

To the senses, this game is amazing. Beautiful graphics and with accurate and detailed sounds easily draw you in. After that, however, things can become a bit muddy. Is it a sim? Is it an arcade racer? It's difficult to tell exactly what this game was intended to be. And while it may seem a bit pedantic to complain, there's a point to be made. When going through the first few minutes of any game, it is essential to get a good feel for how things handle. Physics and controls are VERY important, and once you get a handle on what to expect, the better you become. That goes doubly so for racers. In a simulation game, physics and car characteristics vary from vehicle to vehicle, but all within reason; opponents follow the rules of their car. Conversely, arcade racers are allowed some wiggle room with drift or grip handling and wacky doodle physics to make the ride fun; opponents follow their own rules of performance. This game just kind of screws you around with everything. Car handling is weird and unpredictable, and the moment you get a hang of how goofy your car is, they make you switch to something else that is equally ridiculous and goofy. The "marked" opponents that you're supposed to "watch out for" have god-like attributes to their vehicles in most cases, as they always shoot to the front and away from the pack. So while you're busy flopping around trying to deal with your car on a new track you cannot practice on (another huge gripe), the marked opponent, in the very same car you have, is inexplicably way ahead of you.
I don't exactly hate it, I'm still trying to get the hang of it, but everything is just so imbalanced that when I try to treat it like one type of racer, I'm immediately punished for it. Where's the fun in that?

This game is great; they have improved on almost every aspect of Grid 2 and gone back to the games roots. I played Race driver Grid for about 200 hours when it first came out, I loved every moment of it! I found that Grid 2, while I still really liked the game it still fell short of my expectations.
Well, Grid Autosport is everything I could have expected and more from a racing game! The cars feel realistic, the sound is amazing and the graphics are stunning! As for the gameplay; I would not go as far as to say this game is a racing simulator but I am not sure that is the point of Grid. Grid 2 had a very arcady feel to it; sliding around corners, bashing into people, etc; Autosport however will punish you severely for doing those kinds of things, the damage system is relentless and if you do not take the racing line or brake properly you will lose valuable seconds off your laptime through spin outs or driving off the track!
The multiplayer is really entertaining; in fact I prefer it to the single player mode. You have access to every car from the get go, however they are "Loan" cars, so you cannot upgrade them and they typically do not perform quite as well as Brand new cars (due to their condition rating). This adds a realistic feel to the game and also inspires you to buy your own cars and tune them properly!
Tuning is another important feature of this game, once you have purchased your first car and begin to race with it you will begin to unlock upgrades and tuning options to make the car perform exactly how you want it to! I found this really helps me set my cars up based on my driving style.
Earning money can be tough in Grid Autosport multiplayer, however that is the point! If you crash your car or the loan car you will need to pay for repairs, this encourages you to drive sensibly, take the racing line and brake properly ( No more e-brake!) the cleaner you race, the more money you get and the closer you will get to owning your own beautiful motor car!
If you liked Race driver Grid then you will love Autosport!
Pros
-Beautiful Graphics
-Fun and Realistic gameplay
-Amazing sound
-Endless car tuning possibilities
Cons
- Voice chat and some connection issues online
- Long loading times
Overall 4.5/5

I played a lot of Dirt 3 on xbox. I've played even more on PC after buying a wheel set. This game very much reminds me of the road equivalent to the Dirt series. It's not *so* realistic on it's easier settings that I struggle to play it, so dialing down the settings toward a harder difficulty makes it feel like I'm working and actually accomplishing something.
The game has a "team" dynamic to it, where every season (collection of races) you choose a sponsor and race with team mates. The objectives are great because there are a bunch of them each race, and some for the season.
In most racing games I'm left restarting a race to beat it every single time I barely come in second or crash in the first corner. Grid makes me feel like I'm "accomplishing" something even if I place 6th in a race or 4th overall, like it's part of my career.
It's not a replacement for Forza or GT in the sense that you don't acquire a garage full of cars that you individually tune and buy parts for. Each race you have a practice period on the track if you choose to use it, as well as a qualifying portion if you choose. Or you can just jump straight into the race.
So far I am really enjoying the game, probably because the physics remind me so much of Dirt. One con for sure is that the driving lines are absolutely terrible. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this to anyone for full price - maybe because I've purchased WAY worse games for $60, let alone $50. Overall I'm satisfied.

As a 2D sandbox RPG, it's hard not to compare Crea to Terraria. Despite a somewhat similar pixel-art visuals and side scrolling adventuring, Crea has a lot to offer to be it's own game. While not a huge fan of the genre, I have still found the time spent so far to be enjoyable.
Crafting is done by learning recipes through researching the different elements  you gather from exploring, or that you craft from the base materials. It's also nice that you're using the same blocks to build the side and back walls of your buildings. Combat is dynamic and doesn't feel too one-dimensional with various creatures fighting you in different ways. Some of them are also peaceful and won't attack you unless they're getting attacked first. The leveling and skills are interesting and the points you gain to spend in there areas are amassed through experience. If you're mostly avoiding fights, don't expect to have much points to spend to improve your fighting skills.
This can be a bit problematic sometimes because, in the case of fighting, it takes a bit before you can craft decent equipment so you might struggle with the wildlife when trying to explore the world in search of crafting material for research and building. It's hard to fight until you get the hang of it and some decent equipment ans skills, and it's hard to improve your skills and equipment if you're having trouble exploring and dying from attacks. Some type of monsters can only be found in certain areas so you sometimes need to grind for items that you need to explore a different area. (Like gathering wood and oil to make torches before doing some underground exploration.)
While the game adds elements of lore that you can find through your explorations, the content feels a bit thin. There's also little to no explanation about some elements of the game (like teleport crystals) and you're left to find out for yourself what they're for.
Overall, the game has enough to offer for fans of the genre. With the limited content, it's probably better to have people to play with to make the experience more enjoyable, but even as a single player game it's easy to sink quite some time into this.

A solid and good looking platformer.
Pros:
+Excellent level design - Levels feature hidden areas to collect people and peanuts; there are often novel and fun ways to   dispatch enemies.

Cons:
-As of now in game resolution only goes to 1080p, not a problem for me but should be known and hopefully something they can patch in to either scale or add bars.  This is a hand drawn game so the art assets exist at the level they were created at.

Overall:
Heartily recommend, here is a game that is a relative rarity on steam, a classic platformer done with higher res and detailed graphics, the stages are diverse and controlling Tembo is blast. This will fly under the radar as there is not a lot of word of mouth, except for the negative type from the day 1 issues. The story is decent, but fairly forgettable; the skeletons are actually the most interesting characters in it.
This game has 8 different voice actors to bring across its storyline; I especially enjoyed the skeletons. There's an enormous amount of animation, mostly for cutscenes. The game is made for 4:3 screens and does run on older computers, but all of the pictures have painted margins so that the scenes fill a 16:9 screen as well.
Give the scope of the game (casual puzzle adventure), you will get about 6 hours of gameplay that are well crafted; I got a free copy via the "Davy Jones Welcome Giveaway", but it is certainly adequately priced, even if you missed the -40% release promotion (still ongoing as I write this).

Rebel Galaxy is a space swashbuckling game, like the old privateer and freelancer. Instead of piloting the ship from the cockpit, it is from a sort of 3rd person view and the capital ships move and fight in a 2D plane, while fighters buzz around in a 3D environment with asteroids and debris. The game is rather simple, yet beautiful, with a thin storyline stringing together the different planetary system the player visits. The player is free to play as a merchant, bounty hunter, smuggler, pirate or mercenary for hire, or even a little bit of each... although a bit of imagination is required since all of the missions (apart from the main story line) are only made of a few lines of text: go there, do that, and claim the reward.
Nevertheless the game is as entertaining as its ancestors. The music also is an integral part of the experience.

Wearing his headband, Tembo the badass elephant snorts derisively as a giant mechanical dragon roars loudly, while the Phantom forces standing on it cheer. Behind the keyboard, I blink. What am I supposed to do? Ok, my strategy for this game so far has been charge wildly, so let’s do that.
Hopping across the gap that separates me and the dragon, I send Tembo charging into the mechanical beast. The dragon launches bouncing balls of fire that barely miss me because I’m repeatedly ramming its massive 16-wheel treads. Trumpeting loudly, Tembo hammers into the dragon over and over again pushing it back, back, back – and then over the edge of the platform, into a boiling lake of lava.
The dragon howls and dies. Tembo trumpets triumphantly. And I blink at the screen, going ‘is that it?’ First boss fight, 30 seconds. Huh. Wasn’t expecting that. But then the next level starts, Tembo’s tossed into a forest, trumpeting loudly, and I start chuckling again.

"Its overrrrrrrrr,Mr's Black" and so begin's the third part of one of the best selling series ARTIFEX MUNDI have published to date,but is it a satisfying end to the trilogy and have they met the fan's expectation's with this release???????
So after going to Skull Island and saving the day,then answering the siren's call what can we expect to be doing in this brand new (and completely thrilling) chapter in the trilogy??????????
Well as the name would suggest (DUH BIT OF A GIVE AWAY THAT TITLE) we will be facing of against none other than a certain Davy Jones (wonder if we will finally find out what he keep's in his locker,more than likely old classic edition's of Playboy if you ask me...............but who know's??)
Nightmares from the Deep 3: Davy Jones Official Trailer ...
So let's get onto the meat and bone's of the game and first up gameplay,now to anyone familiar with HOG's (hidden object game's to anyone not in the know) the gameplay will come as no huge surprise as it follow's the staple diet of other's of its ilk and doesnt mess with the formula too much.There were parts that felt fresh but on thinking on it as i write this review i have seen them done before but never better.Now the gameplay will consist of you doing the usual for this type of game,but for those who dont know this mean's you will play through the story and at certain point's you will have to search static screen's for hidden object's ranging from broom's to feather's for an arrow ECT,but you will also have to solve puzzle's with some of the object's you find say a pair of garden clipper's that will prune those peskey thorny vine's.
You do get a map and this help's as it show's you all the location's you have visited upto that point and exactally where you are,but it also show's you which location's have things to do in them,therefore you will rarely get lost and that's one of the game's best draw's.With all that being said the gameplay is solid and measure's up to anything the genre has to offer.
Ok next up graphic's,these range from the static kind whilst solving puzzle's or searching through the hidden object scene's to animated scene's that help the story to flow along (which it does with ease).The game look's crisp and is the best looking one out of the trilogy and its a joy (at least for me) to actually get to see the one and only Davy Jones at last,as he has been mentioned on a few occasion's in the previous two game's and he look's great now we finally get to meet him in the flesh (well actually with his mask on he look's like he belong's in TRON riding a light-cycle).I will say this there were a few time's i did struggle to see some item's and that was either because i had been staring at the screen to much "AARRGGHHHHHHHHHHHHHH,my eye's" or sadly that some items are a little to difficult to spot,but to be honest this didnt happen to much and didnt in any way take away from my enjoyment and my time with the game.
Ok next up music and dialogue,the music in game does its job and for this sort of a game never does get on your nerve's which is actually a problem in a lot of hidden object game's.The cast all do a great job with the character's they portray and mention must be given to the voice actor playing Davy Jones as with all his pirate twang he really does sound like he just stepped out from a Pirates Of The Caribbean movie,anyway speaking of Davy Jones this was the first time i came across him in game in all his glory (doesnt he look like some sort of pirate who wanted a part in TRON but failed his audition ) -

After playing the first two parts i am glad to see the story coming full circle and it is both a satisfying game to play through and one that will (as ever with this series) leave you wanting more.Now without spoiling it for anyone this is the collector's edition and there is more to it once the curtain role's on the main game but as Nerissa would say from The Wolf Among Us "My lips are sealed".
But trust me once you have finished the main game and the extra part which is called "The Stolen Treasure" you will want more so lets hope that ARTIFEX MUNDI make one as if they dont i'm moving in with the developer's until they do,and A- i like to eat lot's of thing's with garlic in and B- i snore a HELL of a lot.

Now this is what I like. Riding into combat guns blazing with music blasting out of the speakers. So far so good. The game is very good, it looks good it plays reasonably well. You can be a priate, a stickler for the law, or something inbetween. I will raise a couple of points on the negative side though. The game is based around fixed values in equipment. In other words if you have hull plating absorbing 10K damage, it will be 10K damage no matter what size ship you have. Same with weapons, and shields. This means that having a natural progression up the available ships gradually increasing in size, is in fact a terrible idea. This sice all your are doing in buying a bigger ship is making yourself a bigger target. If things scaled with the ships this would be a good idea, but as it is it's not, just find yourself a fast ship with good amounts of ports, and upgrade the equipment to max, and you're set. Second negative point is that once you've done the story, there really isn't much to do, the sandbox in which it is set isn't very varied, same type missins with the same type people. However don't let these things discourage you from getting the game, since it is still awsome for those 30-40 hours it will take you to complete the story, which isn't bad for a game these days.

Playstyle.
Graphics.
Awsome Soundtrack.
Good storyline.
Freedom.
Pasting aliens with your guns.
Minuses:
Static values for equipment.
Limited play after completion.

Rebel Galaxy is an indie space game with a variety of star systems to explore and endless number of procedurally generated missions to complete. It shares some similarities with Freelancer, but the core gameplay is rather different.
While the game does feature trading and mining, the main draw is clearly the space battles. Unfortunately the combat itself is a rather shallow experience. All ships apart from enemy/allied fighters are restricted to a 2D plane and all your main weapons are fired as a single broadside, so in practice the game often feels more like a naval game than a proper space game. It's fun in small sessions, but gets repetitive really quickly.
This isn't helped by an extremely poor item system and ridiculous economy. Both seem to be lifted straight from a bad MMO, which doesn't make any sense in a single player game. Overall you spend way too much time traveling through empty space and grinding pointless side missions to earn enough cash for the next tier of upgrades so you can actually continue with the main game.
The setting is quite generic but has enough of a Firefly vibe to keep things somewhat interesting. Unfortunately the main story is not that memorable either and there's not enough variety with the side missions. There's also a faction system, but this didn't seem to add much to the overall game.
While I found Rebel Galaxy enjoyable in short sessions, overall I'd consider it too flawed to recommend. Between the shallow combat and the repetitive missions the game got boring well before I finished it.
The good:
- Combat can be fun in small dozes
- Bigger space battles can be impressive and quite hectic
- Nice soundtrack
The bad:
- Shallow combat mainly restricted to a 2D plane
- Repetitive missions and random encounters
- Grindy with extremely lazy item design
- Story is forgottable and the ending is extremely lackluster
- Trading and mining felt somewhat pointless
The ugly:
- Some graphics issues in DX9 mode, switching to DX11 fixed these
- Overuse of shader effects and some of the weapons look downright terrible
- Even the small space rocks inhibiting your warp drives
- Warp pairing with friendly targets is a broken mess

This is a high quality first person shooter.
I played mostly single player, although there is a multiplayer mode in which two teams try to capture and hold control points.
The single player campaign had some really awesome gunfights. In addition, there were several fun mini-games, like in one mini-game you're piloting a helicopter gunship; in another you're the gunner on a humvee. There's a large variety of mission objectives so you're always doing something new which keeps gameplay from getting stale. Enemy forces range from infantry to helicopters to sentry towers just to name a few. There's a good selection of weapons some of which have secondary fire modes and many of which have different kinds of scopes.
The graphics were good for a game that came out in 2011. I played on the highest graphics settings with no problems and my gaming rig is hardly state of the art. The music was forgettable but appropriate. I encountered zero bugs.
Voice acting and sound effects were good.
The single player campaign was short; I was able to beat it in about 5 hours on Normal difficulty. Some people may be put off by the length but personally I'd much rather have a short high-quality game than a long low-quality one, and the fun factor of Homeland remains high throughout the campaign. Also, considering how cheap you can get this game nowadays (in 2017) it's a good value for your money.
The storyline was a mixed bag. One of the greatest things about Homeland is the setting; you're a guerilla fighter in a run-down enemy-occupied United States. Seeing everyday "American" things like a Hooter's restaurant juxtaposed next to, say, an enemy tank is really surreal and emotionally powerful.
Unfortunately the enemy occupying power is North Korea, which to me seems like a totally improbable adversary in this context. There's a whole elaborate backstory told through newspaper clippings about how the technologically backwards North Koreans managed to become a military superpower and take over the USA; alas it's not the least bit credible and it had me wishing for another more realistic enemy. This is just a minor gripe however about an otherwise great game.
Overall I quite enjoyed Homefront and if you like first person shooters I'm sure you will too!

CCP should have dumped the time and money they wasted on Dust, into a glossy version of this! While RG is nowhere near as complex or graphically equal (Ships & Stations) to EVE it works! It is truly fun and addicting.
RG is simple to jump into while being moderately challenging down/up stream. You’ll hear people complaining about cargo size, trade issues, routes, quantities, ETC. These folks just haven’t figured out how to navigate the many hurdles and differences RG brings to the table. The one thing you won’t hear much of (if any) are bugs and faulty programming. The depth of RG was also surprising. I was expecting a couple dozen hours of game play tops; and a much smaller universe.
The day you warp into a hot LZ, slide in sideways and unload with a dozen (or two!) turrets, broadsides and missile launchers… you’ll grin ear to ear and know what I am talking about.
My RL is in deep trouble if games like this start getting top of the line graphics, 6DOF, flight stick support, more storyline, juicy-lore and a much larger sandbox. Then there is VR, holy-pod batman! I’ll be checking out Elite Dangerous and Everspace once Santa hooks me up with my VR gear.

Truth be told, it isn't the best when it comes to the amount of content featured: 50 ish cars and less than 20 tracks, not including the layouts, as well as stupidly overpriced DLC just for (mostly) modified versions of existing cars.
It also handles almost nothing like the original Race Driver: GRID. Any car can drift, even Grippy-type ones, with some handbrake persuasion. About the only thing that's improved instead of replaced is the damage modelling. Frankly, Codemasters should've renamed the game if the only thing keeping it in touch with the original GRID is the premise of tackling multiple motorsport disciplines, from straight up races to touges.
Visually, there's no denying it; GRID 2 looks beautiful, and for once I accept the large amounts of lens flare and lens grime, only because there is no true Dashboard Camera. This game really doesn't need it anyway.
Sound design is also amazingly well done. It's quite rare to see a racing game do the Skyline R34 engine and exhaust sounds as close to the real thing as it gets, and then there's the tunnels and terrain echoing.
Career mode offers varied racing disciplines, and the multiplayer is very solid, but it all depends on your ability to look past the changed features, little content and LACK OF COCKPIT VIEW *grrrr* for an otherwise pure racing experience.

This game is really something. I don't generally write reviews but this time I felt compelled.
While its important to note this game is in alfa it doesn't feel that alfa. For sure there are graphical glitches, a bunch more content is needed and there are a few anoyances (you can't rotate the camera being my biggest complaint to this point). What you can say for this game is it has a ton of potential. It doesn't pretend to be something its not. Its a game about factory design with tycoon elements.
One thing I would say is that the game is not for everyone. If your looking for fast paced action with complex problems flying at you left right and centre then this just ins't that. There are periods in that game where you just need to sit back and let things happen such as revenue pouring in or research on new tech being done. That being said this game is really good about multi montior mouse changeover so its not a problem to just turn on a movie or a youtube video while you wait.
I would like to see this game go in a similar direction to Kerbal Space Program. Not in the ridiculous phisics sense but in the sense that its a creative space where you can use your creative skills to push that game to its limits.
The game also has a excellent model that i really feel could be applied to producing other things. For example, in your factory you have these ambiguous resource imports. Now, you can make a production line to create the individual parts in house but you still need the raw resources. Thats where this game could expand: mining, and if they were really ambitious, transport. Thats when this would become a real tycoon game.
My apologies to those reading this because a lot of it is ideas for the devs but I think if they want to make this the definitive production tycoon game, that would be the path to take.
I would also seriously recommend that they open this game up to the modding community.

Pretty well made game, game mechanics work well for the most part. Art work is strong and noticeable, using a pencil sketching style, but the reason for not recommending this game is because I simply didn't enjoy it. I don't care for survival games too much, but tried this out at the recommendation of a friend. Despite not caring much for the genre I trucked through and did complete a single "story" and survived until day 23 :)
This War of Mine is played as a small group of survivors living in a large house. Each night 1 survivor may leave to search for goods while the others stay and sleep or guard the house. Your house has many utilities you can build- a small garden, a heater, rat trap for food, a stove, etc. You use these utilities and workstations to craft goods you'll need to survive. While you can eat raw food, cooked food does much better for filling you up. You'll need to board up your house where, I would assume, collateral damage from the war has created large gaps in the walls and windows. Both your day cycle to build items, harvest goods, and interact with other survivors, traders, etc, and your night cycle to find new goods, are timed with a clock in the top left corner.
Your survivors each have a different skill set. I got Bruno, Pavle, and Katia as my starting three. Bruno is a good cook who can create food using fewer resources. Pavle runs fast so he can avoid danger or run from it while scavenging. Katia is a good bargainer so she can squeeze more out of your trade deals. Later on I got Cveta and Arika with "Good with children" and "Sneaks quietly" skills, respectively. I saw in the build your own game section there are quite a few survivors, all with their different skill sets.
The scavenging is done only during the night and if you don't manage to exit voluntarily before the night ends, then your character gets "caught out" and will have a delay before he and his scavenged goods return. To scavenge you first pick who will go, then where. The where is very important as each area has certain resources- building materials, weapons parts, food, traders, and even danger! (Gasp!) Revisiting some areas will show development of the region with new people taking over or previously present people disappearing. Scavenging is as simple as clicking on highlighted rubble, desks, drawers, cabinets, etc, and after a moment to inspect the spot, you get an inventory screen showing what you have and what you can take.
War is hell. I knew this well before playing this game and I'm strongly against coercive force and am a supporter of the non-aggression principle. I like to role play and empathize with the characters I'm playing as, whether it's Mass Effect, Deponia, or Civilization 5. I made the decision early on I would help anyone I could and wouldn't harm another person. I knew somewhere in the "teens" days I wouldn't make it far and I was ok with it. Trading couldn't get me enough food or bandages, bandits hit the home every single night, and I couldn't scavenge everything needed. I stole from armed bandits a few times, very carefully, and thanked the Lord for Pavle's large inventory space and his fast running. In the end, we just didn't make it.
If you're into survival games, and the life and death aspects of it, then pick this up. It has an amazing human element to it and I think was extremely realistic in how it handled the precious few resources available and the decisions on how to use them. All in all, bottom line is I would not freely recommend this game to a friend. It has a niche audience and isn't fun. It's challenging and engaging, but this means it's not for everyone.

I'm new to the GRID franchise, however I have heard excellent things about it and decided to jump in here with Autosport. When I first launched the game, wow. I've been a Forza diehard for the past 4 years and this is certainly a change. If you just want to read why I don't recommend, skip to the bottom. Before I go too in depth, here's a list of the pros and cons:
Pros
- Engaging career mode
- Beautiful graphics
- Decent physics
Cons
- 1 BUG
I'll begin with the pros. The career is broken into different classes, Tuner, Touring, Endurance, and others. In each class, there are seasons that help you progress along your career as a racer. You'll sign on with different teams, such as Oakley Racing, for the season, you'll get a teammate, rivals, etc. Normal race car driver stuff. Each event (usually, unless it's a special event) has practice (for tuning, if available), qualifying, and one to two races. I found this to be much more fun than the career of Forza, where the races were short, limited, and very boring.
I have yet to try online but we'll get to why in a minute.
The graphics are gorgeous. At full tilt, it looks pretty real. Just be careful about your computer's proccessing power. It'll give it a run for its money.
Physics are ok. I have yet to get into the higher classes to see if grip really becomes a factor. Something does feel slightly off...
BUG REPORT BELOW [FIXED - SEE UPDATE]
"OK, so why didn't you try online?"
Great question! There's a bug... And if it wasn't for this bug, I would highly recommend this game. There is a bug that causes a screen "freeze" where the car and audio freeze for about half a second at random on all graphics levels. "Why's that such a huge deal?" Glad you asked. Every second counts in a race. So, if you're going through a technical, winding, difficult turn and suddenly everything just glitches out, you're focus is broken. This bug will work itself out, but it starts the race again before the screen can catch up. So you'll hear the car move (and incidently go off the track or hit other cars) before you can see it. "So what does that have to do with online racing?" This glitch freezes your car. In a tight race, where it's bumper to bumper, turn for turn, close quarter racing, a sudden stop ruins it for everyone. I may not feel the effects besides the glitch, but I'll inadvertently make everyone else despise me.
To sum it all up, great game that needs MAJOR bug fixing. The core of the game is great, however that one bug disastorously effects the gameplay, making it almost unplayable. If I was a potential buyer, I would wait until there has been a patch and one that has been reviewed as a proper fix.

[UPDATE] I tried uninstalling and then reinstalling the game and now it works fine. It must've been a glitch that occured during "pre-loading" when I preordered the game. Now I fully recommend the game!

The UI for this game is probably one of the clunkiest I've ever seen. Not only is it a hassle to just access items and actually build, but it is painfully slow when everything else in the game runs smoothly. For example, if I wanted to place down a torch while exploring, I would need to stop whatever I'm doing, open my inventory, grab the torches, place one down, and put them back in my inventory. In games like Terraria and Starbound, you could have items in a sort of hotbar where you easily access them while on the go, making exploring easier and faster. With Crea it just feels like a chore. Building is no better, with you having slowly place down each block one at a time. And as I mentioned before the UI is horribly slow. When I first entered the game the UI wasn't even there, it took almost a solid minute to appear. I couldn't build, couldn't research, I couldn't even see my inventory. Research is also kind of confusing. The game will tell me that I've unlocked an item, but when I actually try to craft it, its nowhere to be seen. I'm not sure if this is a bug, or maybe I'm just doing something wrong but I have no way of knowing.
Besides the UI issues and bugs, the game is okay I guess. I mean I can tell that alot of effort went into making this but in the end it just ends up feeling like a second-rate terraria. It does have alot of original things going for it like the fighting and leveling system. The music and art style are nice too, but as for the game as a whole, I just can't reccomend it. Overall I'd give it maybe a 4-5/10. At least the developer is active and is currently addressing many of the bugs within the game, but in my opinion the game should have stayed in early access.

The nice thing is lives (or peanut butter jars) are easy to stock up. So when you do hit a difficult part, the game gives you a fair shake at things.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is an engaging 4x RTS sci-fi strategy game that is great for both newcomers to the genre as well as more experienced players. If you prefer strategy games that focus heavily on micromanaging however, you may want to look elsewhere. SoaSE:R is more oriented towards streamlined, large-scale gameplay. As a result, it's relatively easy to get into, even if you're not too familiar with strategy games. Don't let this scare you off if you're a veteran to the genre though. Automation of certain features can be turned on and off, allowing for a bit more of a complex experience. There are also a variety of difficulty options and plenty of challenging maps. At higher difficulties the AI are quite competent, and should you find yourself wanting a smarter opponent, there is a good multiplayer community. Replayability is very high, with six different factions to choose from and over a hundred maps. Mods increase the replay value even more.
All in all, SoaSE:R is a great strategy game, broad in scale and wide in audience. Hours fly by as you're playing it, and you'll feel like a true space conqueror.
