Sins of A Solar Empire" Rebellion starts strong and ends with a whimper. Had I known that the Sins series is essentially an unofficial remake of the 2001 PC game Conquest: Frontier Wars, another cult favorite whose ambitions far outstrip its abilities, I could have saved myself a few bucks.
For reference, I purchased this standalone expansion on a 75% off sale for $10. I definitely don't think it is worth the full retail price of $40, especially when you can purchase the classic Master of Orion 2 for $6 on
, or the Homeworld Remastered collection on Steam for $35, both of which do nearly everything that Rebellion attempts much more competently, despite being substantially older games. I also left the game running overnight on a minimized window a couple of times, so while I went through about 6 sessions I haven't actually played for full amount listed. Still, I can't see how the experience would be improved by playing more than I did.
The initial mix of RTS and empire management is good, as you start with a single planet and expand, slowly building up your fleets and economy. I liked switching back and forth between a system view and galaxy view as I built structures, directing my fleet and keeping an eye on my scouts. The problem is that nothing in the mid to late game is particularly satisfying and generally boils down to a monotonous slog.
Partly this is due to the economy and game speed. Everything in Rebellion, from the ships to research to defensive structures, is just incredibly expensive and research takes an inordinate amount of time to complete. Only one faction can improve research speed at all (by a meaningless amount, given how many techs there are to invest in), and the bonuses you can research to improve your economy offer very minimal benefits. Ships also travel very slowly, even when the game speed is set to 4x or 8x normal, so I found that my late game was spent just zoomed out looking at the galaxy screen waiting for my fleets to arrive at an enemy planet.
This is compounded by the technology that allows you to improve your fleet size, which both takes a sizable initial investment and creates a permanent future penalty to your income. This penalty is applied regardless of how big your fleet actually is, and with the final fleet tech is a staggering 75%. This is not only completely backwards from every other RTS I've ever played, where your military costs scale with the units being actually supported, it creates a situation where your massive and expensive fleet can be wiped out and is now irreplacable because the very tech that allowed the creation of that fleet slows your income to almost nothing.
Speaking of fleets, the tactical element of Rebellion is sorely lacking. Initially, you need to carefully consider which ships you build, because you will be limited to about 10. By the mid game there's no real tactics anymore because you have to have so many of each type of unit to beat the computer that the only option is to group everything into a giant blob, send it against an enemy and sit back while your ship AI fights the AI's ship AI.
The AI deserves a dishonerable mention as well. On normal difficulty the AI is passive to the point of absurdity. I only finished 2 of my 4 normal games, because my fleets had annihilated everything so far and were clearly going to curbstomp anything it came across, so my inevitable victory was obvious but still several hours away. On hard, I was beaten with 30 minutes by a fleet several times the size of anything I could have conceivably built. Browsing the Rebellion forums, it turns out that the hard AI gets a 1.5 or 2x bonus to income, with the hardest difficulty gaining a mindblowingly stupid 8x bonus. You wouldn't play with another person if they had hacked the game to give themselves an unbeatable advantage, so why should you put up with it in an AI? The tips to beat the hard AI boil down to "find a chokepoint, turtle until your fleet is big enough". My idea of fun that ain't.
Finally, and most disappointingly of all, there is no real difference between any of the 3 factions. Each has essentially the same units, which are used and countered in exactly the same way, and almost entirely the same tech trees (with very minor differences in layout and order). So when you get down to it, once you have played one or two games of Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion, you have seen everything the game has to offer.
Sometimes, like with Master of Orion 2 or Homeworld, the mechanics or story are fulfilling enough to make coming back to the game worth it. Other times, like with Rebellion, it is not.

+ The 'one more turn' mentality is still present in full force
+ Indigenous wildlife boasts much more of a challenge, of a variety, and of a better collective design than barbarians of the previous installments
+ Combat against cities and units is as well-implemented and satisfying as ever; the audio design and smooth animations make for a very fulfilling experience
+ Upgrades are free of resources requirements and are universally applied amongst all units of that type; does well to eliminate the need to hunt down and manage obsolete units
+ Research tree is vastly improved; it can be daunting at first, but the superiority of this system comes through on subsequent playthroughs (once the player is more familiar with the 'branches and leaves' and what they unlock)
+ The three possible affinities are a welcome addition and do much to offer great variety and customization in the mid- to late-game
+ 'Favors' are a very welcome concept, and work perfectly to improve productivity of player-AI interactions and general diplomacy
+ Sleek, aesthetically pleasing, and functional UI
+ Effortless and rewarding to experiment with mods through the Steam workshop
+ Satellites are a welcome addition, adding another layer of possible resource buffs to the game without cluttering the map
+ Stunning environment designs; flora and resources really stand out in beautiful and creative ways
+ Espionage and trade work in largely the same ways as in Civ V, with some minor improvements
- Culture is now an empty and lifeless statistic in the absence of art, musicians, etc.
- Confusing loss of custom game modifiers as compared to the previous installment of the series
- Steep learning curve, mostly due to alien and unfamiliar terrain features
- Finishing a game is underwhelming, and does little to reward the player, especially compared to previous installments
- Health, as a resource, seems to be a slightly poorer implementation than the happiness of Civ V, and feels unreasonably difficult to manage effectively
- There are no more natural wonders to be found, taking a bit of fun and reward out of exploration
- Quests are boring and repetitive; they do little to add to the game's dimensions
- The available factions feel somewhat bland and uninteresting
- There are no faction-specific units; the only difference between factions lies in the starting bonuses
- AI have almost no aggression factor whatsoever, even into upper middling levels of difficulty

Production Line does something very unique. You can build cars right from the start, no problem, just put down 6 production buildings and voila. However it's not about you just building cars, its about you building them efficiently. In order to do that you have to split up your production line.
For instance you have a factory thats Producing chassis. You want to replace that with a more complex variant that consists of multiple smaller factories that produce smaller steps of said chassis, the result will be exactly the same but it's much more cost and time efficient than the simpler building. Then you want to split those up as well and so forth, you can even produce some of the components yourself instead of importing them from other manufacturers saving you even more money in the process.
The comparison with factorio was made quite a bit in reviews and i have a differing view. Factorio isn't better than production line, and production line isn't better than factorio, they are completely different. In factorio you're not punished if you produce 10000 copper that's not melted and just sitting around. You simply have enough or not enough of a said ressource. Efficiency in factorio is limited to how quick you can reach the endgame with the rocket.
In Production line it's all about cost efficiency and eliminating steps in your production that cost you money while staying ahead of the competition, you have graphs that tell you how you're doing in average. How many factories are waiting for input, how many factories can't work because they are lacking their ressource input etc. The difficulty is solely dependent on what you want to achieve, a sandbox without outside pressure currently. In factorio you have (optional) creeps that give you a sense of urgency while ressources run out.
It's a really good system but it lacks longevity. If you are absolutely ok in the current state that the game will most likely motivate you for anywhere between 7 and 12 hours, then by all means get it, what is here is complete and so far almost bug free and if you enjoy ressourcemanagement games then you will love the new style of this one. Or you are a maniac that loves to optimize systems into the tiniest details just to get another % off the graph, you might stay engaged longer.
I recommend this for what it is, not what it could be, i feel though i've seen what it has to offer after 10 hours.

I really struggled with giving this game a like, but not for that reason. The short version is I got the interactive directors cut of Wolverines for $5. That is worth a like. I would call this game a good B movie.
Long version (spoilers):
This is not a great game. I kind of picked it apart on my play through, and these are in no particular order.
The graphics are sub par, and I don’t mean that in the "it's not ray-traced at 4K so it's crap" kind of way. The visuals are muddy. Thank god the KPA doesn’t know what camouflage is, because the way everything blends is too much as is. More than this the LOD (level of detail) is very inconsistent. It really looks like every model uses the same texture resolution. While things like loose bricks look great, trucks look pixilated. Also, the game seems to have abandoned ANY post processing adding to the muddy problem. Those things aside though the game does a good job of selling the apocalyptic landscape. Trash and clutter are everywhere, and the graffiti is remarkably well done. The levels are dense, and complex, and chaotic. That is perfect for a semi-casual shooter like this. Best part, real business names. I got to shoot a KPA in a Hooters. It’s more fun than it sounds. I also got in a fire fight in a blazing Tiger Direct store, symbolic really. Every time I tossed a grenade I yelled “NewEgg!”
The animations are acceptable. The facial animations look like Saturday morning cartoons since everyone has about two expressions and lip syncing didn't happen. All doors kick down the same with the same dust animation. Finally the weapon animations look like they were sped up after being animated at a realistic speed. That being said the animation are not buggy, and are actually really smooth and consistent. Taking into account how mal-proportioned the characters are the animations look pretty good.
The story… OK, let’s play pretend. Let’s pretend that N. Korea had a GDP above $10. Let’s pretend that the DPRK’s NADA (National Aerospace Development Administration) has ever launched anything but a propaganda campaign. Let’s pretend that China would tolerate the Kims making a power play before them. Let’s pretend Russia wouldn’t turn N. Korea into glass for fun. This game does get one thing right. In an invasion of the US, the military would be the least of your problems. Despite the huge suspension of disbelief, I actually wanted to finish the story, and was disappointed when it ended at chapter 7. That alone earned the like rating.
Just going to get this out there, this game wants to be Call of Duty: Modern Warefare (series) sooooooo bad. Problem is, they didn’t do anything worse, and actually did some things better, despite the lack in overall polish.
*spoiler*
“Why We Fight” opens with a solid 3 minute presentation on why we need the Geneva Convention, and it is so much better at it than “No Russian” and (and Davis Family Vacation for that matter). I will readily stack “Heartland” Against “Back on the Grid” and “Golden Gate” feels like “Iron Lady” without being tedious. “Firesale”… meh Spec Ops; The Line did it better in “The Gate” Unfortunately Connor is always there spouting 80s action movie one liners (I swear he was plucked from Command and Conquer: Renegade or a Schwarzenegger film). Price was so much cooler. Hell, Sandman is better than Connor. That aside, Rianna is a nice squad mate. Now I choose to ignore that she is dressed like that in a war zone. It’s not overt, but ARs and midriff only mix at a trade show. She does make up for that by giving the Bechtel test two to the head in every chapter. Nice to see we are getting closer to equality. I think of her as an early draft Miranda Lawson.
Game play is alright. The controls are sloppy, but I knew that going in. That is just how THQ does things. Weapon damage tables are really good for a COD clone. The shotgun is actually useable. All the weapons feel different, but there are some glaring issues. The M16 has a 20RD magazine, and does not use M4, or Diablo SMG magazines. The M200 rifle has no kick when fired standing (at least compared to what a .338 should do to your shoulder) and somebody got “clipped” by a 20MM cannon. The Goliath thing is… Juggernaut. For a game that mentions taking cover in every level, there is no cover system. Over all, it’s alright. Buy this, buy Wolverines, either way it's worth a couple bucks.
Do you like Civ V? Keep playing that. Are you bored? Is this on sale? Pick it up

For someone like me, (who loves Codemasters' games as well as the orginal GRID) the standard version of GRID 2 is dissapointing and deviates from what made the original game so good.
I really want to praise the fantastic visuals, incredible sound design, with impressive roster of cars and a decent online multiplayer, but there are some glaring problems. I could go on about the horrible americanised story, which is tedious and dull. I could do a rant on the 'Truefeel' handling system that robs the car's identity when driving and I could rage about the omission of the cockpit view, but these aren't the true reasons why, I just can't in good faith, give this game the recommended verdict.
The actual reasoning is it's DLC, which is FAR too overpriced. At £25 for all the DLC you get the following:
- 5 Tracks (15 routes).
- 24 Cars (2 liveries).
- A 15% discount on every in-game purchase in online multiplayer.
- Instant access to every online car.
(This doesn't include the free demoliton derby game mode)
That may seem much, but as the game is £20, it's far less value, while creating a massive player disconnect in the multiplayer.
Overall if you like GRID stay the hell away from this, and wait for GRID Autosport. This is too much of a cash grab that tarnishes the GRID name.

Bad stuff: I enjoyed this game for 5-10 hours, and then it got boring. It's too easy to stay cash positive. I would appreciate more goal-oriented gameplay. Factorio is a better sandbox factory-flow game, and always will be. This game adds the business side of things, which is very interesting. They should make that side more dynamic. Give the competitors character, have them sabotage your factory, stuff like that. If you're not satisfying demand for a given model, have your customer base tank. As it stands now, I could just keep all of the markets wanting more, and still make millions of dollars without worrying about sales at all. Also, consider adding random defects into workcenters! That would keep things dynamic for sure. Would be difficult to not make it annoying though...
Good stuff: Still, this is a well-made early access game. Despite what other people have said, the game didn't crash at all for me. It runs very smoothly for my medium-sized factory. Some of the interfaces are a bit janky, but it's not too bad. The tutorials are remarkably helpful and widespread for an early access game. I only had to google 1-2 things that I didn't understand just by playing. Figuring out the process flow is easy, because it's all laid out in order in the menu. Research works well. Various improvements seem reasonably balanced. I could go on, but you get the point. All of the pieces that currently exist are pretty well-done.
Verdict: The devs have built an excellent platform with a lot of potential, but it's not there yet. Adding some character and dynamic challenges to the mid/late game could make this an awesome sim.

Its a good game, but for now I dont think there is much to do. You see the major flaws that the game has way past the 2 hour line.
+ graphics are nice
+ controls are intuitive
+ nice UI and item management
+ skill trees have good variety
+ no food or thirst meter
+ level up system is good
+ taming of animals, as well as enemies in general
+ some animals can be mounted
+ taming only lasts for 30min and can be extended with scrolls, a good mechanic in my opinion
+ fly with a broomstick like a witch
+ magic and spells are well implemented
+ gathering resources isnt as tedious as in other games, you can even gather stuff with magic from a distance
+ party up with people or let them join your guild
+ the building is really good and easy, no tedious crafting of building materials
+ caves that sort of resemble dungeons you can go through to get better loot at the end
+ dragons in various forms
+ huge map
+ unique resources and crafting recipes
+ you can play it in singleplayer
+ fast travel towers, where you can teleport between them
- the leveling up and exp rate is super slow on standard, even on 3 times the rate it feels slow to level up
- the best way to level up is to kill animals and enemies, but at some point it gets boring, because there are just a few enemy types in the game so far and you will be killing harmless horses without even collecting their loot.....
- having an animal as a mount is pointless, its not really faster than sprinting by foot (which you can do infinitely) and its useless because flying with the broom gets you up hills and mountains and is a lot faster
- the games performance is awful, GTX 1080 and the game runs from 30 to 60 fps constantly jumping and being more in the 30 than I want it to
- you cant repair your buildings, I guess this is going to be fixed, but even when its supposed to work, you gotta unlock the repair skill which you get way past your building stuff and inbetween that time, you cant repair your damaged walls at all
- it gets boring real fast, the map feels the same no matter where you stand, there arent any cool points of interest other than the dungeon, which can be super difficult to master if you play on your own, some absolutely can only be done with a group
- weapons break down without any meter telling you when its going to break
- its buggy, had several crashes and game breaking bugs, like enemies not fighting back
- you can only equip 2 spells to one weapon (left and right mouse button) which is super annoying as you have to constantly switch out spells, like the taming spell with the gathering spell, back to the damage spell
- PVP can get unbalanced if you dont pick the right weapon, an axe for example has a short range spell and good melee damage, but has no chance against the super fast wand that has a long reach and "machinegun" spells, almost every player I encountered had this weapon
- PVP battles can drag forever, as there are no cooldowns on potions
- right now, you can just log out during a fight to avoid death, there is no timer on logout
- you always have to create a mage/wizard character, there is no real barbarian warrior melee option here
- character creation is very limited, with only 4 faces and hairstyles
- enemy NPCs attack you, while you are in your home, attacking the outside wall, as if they know you are in there.....
- on some points of the map there are literal mana and health pools, where you can swim in and regenerate your health and mana, but its so unbelievably slow, its like every 2 seconds you recover 1 point, its tedious when you go there with 150/400 health points
- enemies have no ragdoll, they die in fixed animations, which is a huge letdown for me
Like I said, the game is actually quite good, but I wouldnt recommend playing it right now, as other games in this genre give you way better gameplay and content. The magic to be honest didnt really do much difference in the long run. Instead of flying on a dinosaur you fly on a broom. Instead of firing a pistol, you fire your magic shots. Keep an eye out on Citadel, maybe it gets better with time, for now, save your money.

This War of Mine is brutal. It does not glamorise war, nor does it show it to be 'cool' or 'fun', like many games do. This War of Mine presents war and the effect is has on everyday people in an honest light. Along the course of your play through, you will bond with your small team of survivors, learn their weaknesses and their strong points and will soon begin to feel comfortable as you establish a routine. As the game progresses though, you will have to make some difficult decisions that will cause you to reconsider your play style. Do you rob a defenceless elderly couple for bandages to help your dying survivor back at the house? Or do you risk sending your survivor to a central conflict zone where bullets fly constantly? This is where This War of Mine succeeds. It doesn't need any flashes and bangs, it just presents war, and the hell for the people within it.

Initially I picked this game up on steam sale, only knowing it had some serious hindering bugs on its release. However at this point I can thankfully say throughout my whole playthrough I encountered no bugs at all and it was one of the funniest things I had seen in a long time.
So to kick things of, the game doesn't focus too much on setting up a dungeon, since defending it is easy but by consistently sending troops above to go on missions. That is against the preference of some but I found it to be a satisfying strategy experience. Aside that the resource and upgrade systems are balanced while the units and factions presented(Demons and Horde) feel different, which is good.
Finally I believe the biggest positive aspect of the game is the campaign. Holding a satisfactory length, it is literally decorated by the game narrator(whose name evades me at the moment but you have probably seen him from Stanley's Parable where he was pretty much the star of the game) who offers scathing comments on everything, from the events that happen to reacting when the player does nothing(please do not do nothing for 5 minutes on the first dungeon mission, you will love the response).
As if that wasn't enough the campaign has tons of popular references concerning the enemies you fight and what they say, most famous ones stemming from Lord of the Rings and Warhammer to other games from the same developers. It even has a specific mission dedicated on referencing the Game of Thrones characters, each one in a unique and hilarious way.
Also worth noting the achievements are nothing hard and can be achieved by one multiplayer game and through the main campaign. After saying that I definitely believe the game is worth the purchase, now that it works properly you can enjoy the fun it offers to the fullest.

This game is beautiful but on a dark scale. It has that feel of the "Last of Us" Where you craft and have a limited amount of space in your backpack but intstead of fighting a infection, you are fighting to survive. Not only do you have to keep your characters from starving but you also have to keep track of their mental state as well. Every little action has a big repercussion in this game. You are constantly asking your self "What should I take with me to scanvenge? What do I need? I'm running out of inventory space, what do I really need more food or materials?" This game is about trade offs and man does it suck when you choose to take the wrong tools to scavenge and the whole place is boarded up. Damn it! I should have taken the crowbar instead of the shovel! That little error can cause a character to die.
This game is extremely challenging, you are given just the bare amounts to survive. You constantly making choices, well yes, I could rob these people of food (of course in real life it doesn't affect you) but in game, your characters take a mental toll. Your choices could drive your characters to depression, they stop eating, and they starve to death.
I find my self chewing on my nails because scavenging gets so stressful, soldiers are just on the other side of that door. What will they do to me if they find me? Kill me? Trade with me? I rather not find out.
The soundtrack to this game fits the mood so perfectly, it's a blend of sadness with a hint of hope.
If you hate games that stress you out, I would not reccomend this game. But if you love a good challenge, I highly reccomend "This War of Mine" for you.

Much closer to the original Dungeon Keeper games than its predecessor!  Once again you play the role of the evil dungeon keeper and build up your dungeon, fight off heros, gather gold, and upgrade your rooms and creatures.

- You get the visit the 'Overworld' above your dungeon and take the battle to the heroes instead of always waiting for them to come into your dungeon.

- The dialogue of the narrator is humerous

- Creatures can roam around the dungeon instead of being stuck in their spawn location and you can pick them up then drop them anywhere in the dungeon.
- You don't have to capture heroes to collect soul energy just kill them like the good old days of Dungeon Keeper
- You have to maintain your creatures by paying them gold and brewing beer for them to drink

Cons:
- Campaign is short

Overall it was fun to play this game and would recommend if you liked the Dungeon Keeper games.

This game is an awesome and is addictive with Starbound and Terraria elements to it, but with its own type of flavor. The game is early access has occasional hiccups, but can be easily fixed with an update or two. It’s a refreshing take on 2D sandbox/rpg type of games which is a good commodity.
Let’s start with the gameplay. It starts out rather easy as you can get a short tutorial on what to do. You can easily manage controls on an Xbox controller or PlayStation controller which can be helpful. The graphics are pixelated like any other retro game. I’m a fan of these retro games as I grew up in the 80's and 90's playing those console games in their prime. The skilling up/leveling up system is very unique and different from Starbound and Terraria which makes this game stand on its own. I enjoyed exploring and creating my homes, teleport points, forges, and loved the crafting aspect inside of it. This game is very time consuming and can be very addictive at the same time.
The game isn’t perfect and still is an early access game which comes with its bugs and glitches. The game has unusually long load times when you first start out which I found awkward knowing this is a pixel 2d sandbox game and isn’t a really big game that should be doing so. I found that it did take much more memory than expected as well which I heard the developer is seeking to fix. In terms of the multiplayer aspect, there should be some dedicated servers steam side to help everyone connect with each other to make this game even more fun. I hope that this is also fixed and implemented in the finalized version so I can even give this a higher grade on my review. Anyways I found this game to be quite fun, addictive, time consuming, and refreshingly new. I hope this game can fix these glitches and whatnot to make this an even better game.

TLDR: Depressing but a dam good game - play for 5 hours and it feels like 5 minutes. Runs fine on my craptop. Play on your own with the curtains closed - allow yourself to get sucked in and let the feels flow.
*
Pretty dam depressing. So much in fact that it sometimes comes round full circle - like when I was chasing a woman around her house with a crowbar trying to put her out of her misery after she saw me beat her boyfriend to death and ran away crying...
"Stay still i'm trying to help! D:"
*Bash Bash*
"THIS WAR CAN'T HARM YOU ANY LONGER!"
*Bash Bash Squelch*
"NO TEARS ONLY DREAMS NOW!"
*
What I liked is that its pretty accurate as to how a group of survivors would react over time as they did what they had to do to survive.
For example it seems to be that if you want to be bandits and go around murdering and robbing people you have to ease your survivors into it - if you start the game and immediatly go stab up some old people your survivors get pretty depressed pretty fast.
But if you start off stealing a few things from some homeless guys, then maybe clean out a church, and THEN murder just one guy or so your people start to get less affected by it.
Around day 35 I was gunning down hospitals full of blind and injured orphans for their socks and bisquits and my guys could hardly give a dam.
*
The big problem with the game, in my opinion, however is that like the Telltale games Walking Dead  games - despite how much I liked the game I can't feel like it has much replayabilty.
The first time is nerve-wracking, shocking and depressing with each action being very much like how you would actually behave in such a situation. But after the first playthrough you know how everything is going to play out - less anxious, cautious decision making and more just doing what makes the playthough the most efficient based on the now fully known game mechanics.
EDIT: The "Make your own story" mode freshens things up enough for a second playthrough but still feels like i'm cheating myself out of the experience that the game is ultimately trying to provide.
***
Oh and one of my survivors froze to death at 21 degrees celsius. Glicth or not, idk about you ****ers worldwide but here in Britain that's "♥♥♥♥ this♥♥♥♥♥♥i'm going living in the fridge" weather.

If you’re interested in a deep review of this game going over pretty much all the features it offers and what it does right and wrong then I uploaded the review ->
<- just for you.
What you should enjoy:
+ The art style, it's very well realized and is nice to look at, everything is well modelled and polished, the lighting and effects look great and once you get a huge dungeon built and fully working it just looks and feels wonderful.
+ Content. This game would suck without all this content so thank god there is a good hunk of it here to dig into! It's defiantly the highlight of the whole game. There are two factions to enjoy here and both are unique and have their own speed of progression, play style, unit and room appearances, upgrades and god powers. Each faction has three tiers to go up from starting at tier one with the basics going up to tier three with the most powerful upgrades and units you can get, requiring to do some kind of super evil act to tier up like killing lots of unicorns so it's not just something you can do and toss away you have to earn it, making the tiers feels special and important. Alot of work went into making all this content and it's easy to appreciate since it makes the game last ages if your and upgrade hog like me and simply have to get everything before steam rolling the enemy, it feels great.
+ Fun gameplay. The game doesn’t expect too much from you most of time, giving you plenty of time to get started and dig in each mission before heroes start attacking your lovely dungeon and distracting you. The over world is a great new feature to this genre, the added RTS is a great distraction and makes the game last way longer then it would without it and makes it truly feel like you’re fighting back and eliminating those nuisance heroes once and for all.
+ Polished experience. You want a bug free dungeon game that runs fine, hardly crashes, goes pretty smoothly and doesn’t really ever let you down or block its own progress? Then look no further, I could never find a single bug in this game that ever effected gameplay, progression or caused frustration. The only thing it does is start up slowly, that's about it.
What's not that enjoyable at all:
- The RTS combat has to be the first thing, as original as it is added to a dungeon builder game it's clear these devs just don't know how to make satisfying RTS gameplay, which is a shame but you can't expect them to when they make dungeon games. The combat is way too simple to be fun or engaging for long, after your first few fights your already over it, then it just becomes a necessity not something you really want to do more of. Unit abilities and the 'god powers' you have to select from generally make a fight quicker by only afew seconds and it's easier to just not use them all, making them kinda irrelevant but it's nice they are there anyway. It's like they are there almost to distract you from the fact the combat is so super bland.
- Annoying narrator, yea I did put him in the plus section for being quirky but hes also really overdone. Anyone that plays this game will either ignore how naggy he is, not like him for it or just flat out hate him, there is no true in between here he is just that naggy and hand holding your just like, ugh, please just stop nagging me and let me do my thang. I guess if the devs paid for him they are going to use the crap out of him aren't they? And that they did.
- Ugly graphics choices. Although the graphics style looks great it could have done so much better with another graphics engine that really let all their hard work shine like it should do. The unity engine they are running it on must be freaken old cas the AA options are abysmal, only FXAA as an option should never be a thing, it's not even well done FXAA as it blurs the game to the point all detail and fidelity is lost, it's better without it on but then you have to put up with insane jagged edges everywhere on everything. It will drive you insane if graphics matter to you at all, seriously, it's a real shame.
- Awful performance. Yep I’m gonna say it, this game runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥ totally and complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ It runs fine at the start where your dungeon is simply a throne room and nothing else but as you inevitably expand, more effects show up on screen, more units, more models, more stuff in general it runs worse and worse to the point where you can barely get over 20-30fps. Anyone that says under 60fps doesn’t effect gameplay doesn’t know what they are talking about or are blind cas under the 50fps mark and a game becomes less responsive and fluid, directly effecting how much you can interact with the game and thus effecting experience, it's that easy. You think turning all the graphics down to low will help too? Pff good luck, it will probably give you another 20 frames max but that’s it, if it runs like crap to begin with it will still run like crap. I have an average computer that most people will have if you’re wondering.
- Way too easy. The game is abit tricky at first when your units are low levelled, not upgraded and you have few of them, but then when you build a big army and beef them up the game is a total breeze. At mid game there is no longer any intensity or worry your throne room is gonna get destroyed because you can easily call back all your units with one simple spell and stop the enemies anyway. After the start there is no challenge or depth to this game, the enemy waves stay the same as they started and never get hard or frequent enough to give you any concern, even then some well placed traps will kill most of them. A simple difficulty setting for the campaign would have easily fixed this but oh well I guess.
- Hard to manage your dungeon. It's silly but sometimes you forget where your rooms are and have to keep looking for them... the god powers are binded to really weird keys like k-7, and k-1, what the hell does that even mean? You never know what your workers are actually doing, if they are mining gold for you or not, how much income they are actually making, how to make them bring it in faster, no way to make them prioritize tasks, no way to set different minions to different tasks so they are more effective, nothing. If you want management there is none in this game, you just build a pretty dungeon, build units to run it and watch, yep that’s what you do. Occasionally you'll send combat units out to fight then boom you win. The game is so simple sometimes you swear it was made for kids...
- Very linear gameplay and  storyline. Your evil, you got killed by heroes, you want revenge... yep that's it. If your looking for storyline then wow you are so in the wrong place, lol. Each missions is pretty straight forward, do the usual, build up your dungeon, steam roll enemies along a super linear path all the way to enemy base and destroy it, boom done, go to next mission, rinse repeat. It's about as interesting to read as it is to play.
- The game doesn’t take itself, or the fact you are supposed to be evil, seriously at all. This... makes it feel like a kids game most of the time and I’m not a kid so yea. It's pretty clear dungeon games where you being an evil sadistic a-hole ruining what’s supposed to be a happy, perfect world should never a kids game, it should take the evil thing more seriously and make you feel truly evil not like you’re kind of just acting like you are. I think the devs probably got this now... maybe.
- Multiplayer. What multiplayer?! If you got this game for playing with friends you made a bad buy my friend, the multiplayer is simple and sucky, just play the single player.
Overall this is a 6.7 out of 10 for me. I can't recommend it because of all the badly executed mechanics, graphics options and the sheer amount of negatives this game has that are so bad they are easy to point out and explain. Get it on sale, give it a try.

This game is an interesting mix of: 70% Euro Truck Simulator, 20% papers please and 10% FTL (or Rougelites in general). You play as an unamed person who travels across the crumbling Soviet Union with your uncle, in a car that is less reliable than the drill in PAYDAY2. Whether you should buy the game in this VERY early state is going to come down to whether you think the game's future potential out weighs its current lack of content. My play time has been extended a bit by being AFK (about 45 mins) but the rest is from doing a fair few runs of the game. At time of writing there are only two towns you can reach before the game tells you to restart; on average one complete run from the start to the second town takes approximately half an hour, assuming you don't run out of gas, the engine block doesn't commit sepaku or run out of money. I would say it's worth taking a chance on this game if you like driving games and cars in general as there is a fair amount of vehicle maintaince (though very simplifed) and Eastern Eurpoean history. With my current playtime I have fully upgraded the car and no reason to play anymore until the next major update. So make of that what you will.

Between RCT and RCT2, definitely go for RCT2, as it's really easy to simply add all the old scenarios back in, in addition to hundreds of custom scenarios the fans have made over the years.
Unfortunately many of the RCT2 scenarios feel a bit off. Something I liked about the original and many of the custom scenarios is that they mostly felt like places you actually might build a theme park, like around a giant lake. With a couple exceptions the RCT2 scenarios mostly go for weirdness, like building a park on mars, or for stuff that doesn't feel quite realistic, like building a park around the great wall of china. I know that's quite a dumb complaint, and it obviously doesn't mean you shouldn't get the game, but I never could get into building a park that really felt quite right around the grand canyon. Since there are so many great ones available it doesn't really matter.
However RCT2 is an excellently designed sequel in that in almost all ways it is a direct upgrade over the previous game (and it's much better than its successor RCT3 in a lot of ways too.) There are more rides, better decorations, among lots of other improvements. This game is a classic through and through and at the heart of things its just really fun to make an amusement park, and you really owe it to yourself to try it if you haven't already.

I picked this game up during the summer sale for $20 and I feel like I got my money's worth.  I enjoyed playing it overall, enough that I'll pick up the planned DLC when it comes out.  I have no interest in multi-player, so my review is based solely on my single-player experience.  Here are just a few bulleted items that came to mind while I was playing:
Liked
- Art style: cartoonish like DK, detailed, colorful, and original
- Voice work and writing: great work on the narrator; he's pithy and verbose, but doesn't become annoying.  Story is simple and about on par w/ the DK games
- Gameplay: I enjoyed the dual dungeon-digging and overland-conquest idea, I think it worked.  Even though neither was as deep as a game that just focused on one or the other, there was enough there to make a fun game
- Research and upgrades: there's quite a bit to dig into here as far as upgrading your units; if you're a completionist like me, it can be time-consuming to max everything out.  Even though it's fairly linear progression, there are obvious results in your units' competence from your research
- Multiple factions: although the second villainous faction doesn't come heavily into play in the campaign, there's great fun to be had playing as both villainous factions in skirmish mode.  I felt like this adds a bit of longevity to the game
- UI: everything in the game is fairly straight-forward and easy to navigate.  Aside from issues I had assigning spells to hot-keys, I think you'd have to try pretty hard not to grasp how to manipulate the game world here
- Developer presence on the Community page: this might seem stupid, but it's immensely gratifying to have people involved w/ the development present to field questions.  Many games I've purchased have no dev presence here and it's often incredibly frustrating working w/ other players to figure out game issues.  I had several questions that I posted  here and they always got dev attention eventually
Could Use Improvement
- Adjustable difficulty: much of the game was too easy for my tastes, the campaign needs difficulty options
- More reward for exploring: this was a big thing in the DK games, digging out out every nook and cranny yielded interesting rewards. Similarly for the overworld. I felt this was lacking a bit here
- Campaign could be longer and more free-form: there's a tad too much hand-holding as you go through
- Mission variety: I'm on the fence w/ this one b/c I see where the devs made the attempt.  There are several missions where you make forays into opposing dungeons and a mission where you have to ambush overworlders while they're en route to a meeting; however, I would like to have seen this variety pan out more. I like the fighting between dungeon concept, I wish it had gotten more screen-time and more robust gameplay instead of the simple set-piece scenarios we got.
As I said, I enjoyed this game enough to keep an eye out for the DLC.  I didn't play the first Dungeons game; I was scared off by the negative press it got.  However, I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed DK, despite its flaws.

This game literally lifts UI and gameplay mechanics directly from Homeworld. This is not the same as trying to expand on Homeworld's ideas, which other games have done; I mean this game literally uses the exact same UI elements and mechanics, except everything is implemented way worse. It even tries to imitate Homeworld's hand-drawn/sketched cutscenes by using renders of gameplay with a digital filter put over it to make it LOOK hand-drawn.
The only original part of this game is the ability to choose what part of space to go to next. Unoriginality is not a problem in itself as long as you iterate on the old ideas with new ones, but this game doesn't do that. I had no big expectations from Crea and thought it would be yet another one of these new uninspired games trying to jump on the bandwagon of the sandbox genre. After playing it for five minutes, I knew how wrong I was. Those 5 minutes suddenly turned into 3 hours and I had to make myself stop as it was already 2 A.M.
It could be argued that Crea looks exactly like other similar games, and although that might be true, Crea knows how to combine ideas that we have all already seen in other games with a lot of new ones, creating a perfect mix with hours and hours of entertainment and freedom. It contains not only the tools to set free your creativity, but also a concealed complex game with its own lore. You can choose to ignore it completely, or you can try to delve deeper. This certainly translates to many hours and many different possible approaches to the same game.
It’s, simply put, a 2D Minecraft. Although as complex as Notch’s game, Crea helps its players and guides them through the game, making external online searches unnecessary, something I must really thank the developers for. I have not found too many negative things, but I believe more sounds are needed (for example for enemies), more game modes (creative or permadeath), weather effects and a bit of enemy balancing (if you explore too much, you suddenly encounter very high-leveled enemies) Otherwise, I honestly could not ask for more, as the game is awesome as it is.
In my opinion, this game receives a score of 9 out of 10. Once more mods are created and those game modes are implemented, this game will become the ultimate 2D alternative to Minecraft.
Pros:
- Fun and easy to put a ton of hours in
- Awesome tools for creation
- RPG elements perfectly implemented
- Bits of lore and lore related features
- Interesting achievements and cards
- Mod implementation
- Fair price
Cons:
- More sound effects would be nice
- Weather effects missing (rain, snow, desert storms…)
- More game modes would be a great addition
I personally can’t wait until a hunger/thirst mod is created. I’d also like to address some of the problems other people have mentioned: It is true that the game takes long to load, but it isn’t longer than a minute and I’m used to waiting more than 5 minutes for Crusader Kings II to load. Once the game loads, you no longer have any kind of waiting time and everything is seamless.
I’ve also noticed that the game opens like 5 different processes if you check using task manager. I’m not sure that’s the most efficient way for the game to run, but I have personally not experienced any kind of lag or bug in my 6 hours of gameplay so far and once you close the game, all those processes close along the game. I have a 6 year old crappy laptop, if that helps. If you are worried about the game, I encourage you to watch a few gameplays on youtube, which surely helps more than just reading reviews and then decide for yourself. Have fun!
Disclaimer: I received this product for free from the Developer in exchange for my honest and unbiased review.

Please note; this review was written for Pre - Alpha 0.4, the game under review is therefore not necessarily reflective of the final version.
I would like to begin by assuring you, if not made evident by the positive declaration heading this review, that I have enjoyed what I have seen so far from this game. While it is in pre-alpha state, however, it is still a paid for product and must be reviewed as one.
TL;DR for those who don't want to go through the whole review: Game's good, go buy.
Browsing 'YouTube' one day, I came across a video featuring 'Jalopy' posted by the famous internet based videogame journalist 'Jim Sterling'. In this video, Mr Sterling gives his thoughts on his first few moments of gameplay and, from what I saw, I became immediately enammoured with it.
I quickly leaped onto the 'Steam' store and searched 'Jalopy' in the search box. Considering what I'd seen of the game through the aforementioned video, I put the game on my wishlist and purchased it shortly after.
I'd describe this game, if pushed, as a rogue-like with elements of a driving simulator; in which the player is tasked with travelling from location to location along partially randomly generated routes trading for supplies and performing maintenance in order to journey for as long as possible.
The game is undoubtedly buggy, very buggy. A comprehensive selection of screenshots featuring some of said bugs can be found on my screenshot library. Despite this, however, the game is a ton of fun, even in it's pre-alpha state.
There may not be much to do and explore at present but what is here is incredibly enjoyable.
STORY:
There really isn't one yet.
The premise is simple in that you and the old man are travelling from Berlin to (seemingly) Turkey, crossing across multitudinous borders, sleeping at motels, and trading at gas stations along the way. It is your job to keep your vehicle well maintained and manage your wallet well, selling goods to traders and smuggling goods across the borders.
GAMEPLAY:
Gameplay namely consists of driving along motorways and country roads as a means to travel inbetween cities, occasionaly stopping in order to pop the hood and maintain the engine or change the tires. Keeping fuel, oil, and water levels topped up as appropriate is also essential (the water less so as it's used for the wipers).
Supplies for vehicle maintenance, and for trading, can be purchased at the occasional gas stations sometimes present along the various routes, or at marts (refered to as markets) that can be found in cities. It is also at these places that items found in boxes (found lying to the road side along the routes) can also be sold.
The above is of great importance as sleeping at motels, and upgrading the vehicle at auto shops, requires money, but once you get used to how trading works in the game, you'll be making hundreds of dollars before you know it.
MUSIC:
There's little music in the game save for what can be found on the radio, for which I have no comment, save for that it does indeed sound like a radio. What music and other sounds are present, I do feel add to the overall atmosphere of the game and authenticism of the setting.
GRAPHICS:
Polygonal, but I find it endearing. Yes the graphics are basic, but everything looks like it belongs and it gives the game some visual identity to seperate it from other games made in the Unity engine.
---
I enjoyed this game very much, and even in this early state, it comes highly recommended. If you're into games that feature resource management, vehicle maintenance, or trading; then this is very much a great choice of game.
Well worth playing and replaying.

Spent around 50+ hours in this game, finished it after obtaining MK6 equipment and being able to get the more expensive ships and guild ships.
Having played through this with a good friend watching it live on Stream for the majority of the playthough i can say i enjoyed this title a lot.
But i have gripes, gripes that comes from that it's meant to be played with a controller.
There is a distinct snapping with aim assist in this game, this paired with no pitch control (Y axis for your spacecraft doesnt exist, but exists for other smaller crafts and various world objects/projectiles)
The game felt huge at the beginning but the main storyline skips through sectors mid story, which leaves you just going through sectors without a reason to stay (unless you are doing trading, mining or hunting).
It feels like this game was ported over from a Console, but that could also be good.. hear me out.
In 50+ hours i have not had a single crash or bug, nor any weird software issues at all.
This could very well be thanks to that the game is polished in that sense, framerate feels solid aswell.
Game is beautiful (even if nebulas are tiny dust clouds compared to real life), the game allows custom music for: Idle, Combat, Space stations, ambient & main title.
This is a very nice addition and lets you (once you get bored of the ingame music) put your own tracks for various interactions in game.
Game plays well, no stutter or dips in general performance.
I highly recommend playing this with a controller, as with a mouse the snapping / aim assist gets very frustrating once you wanna have more of a freelook aiming.
Story should be made longer, or added with DLC as it felt short and kinda rushed, especially compared to the amount of sectors you dont even do any type of missions in at all. (you mainly just go find npc for mission->go and talk to npc->gate->gate->mission->gate back->gate back->find npc who gave mission->talk to npc.
It does have some issues in those areas i mentioned earlier, but because it performs so well, and compensates with positives i can only give this a thumbs up.
Improvements for a sequel in my mind would be:
Expansive story, more side quests (not just mission board money makers), get rid of aim assist/snapping and give us Y axis / Pitch.

Rebel Galaxy is a bit of a strange bird. It is a spaceship game with a serviceable story told within a pseudo-sandbox game world. The game itself seems polished on initial inspection, but after hours of play certain odd design choices and rough edges start to show themselves.
But is it fun?
After accumulating 24 hours in the game and just now finishing up the main quest line, I have to say that it IS definitely fun. While the game has a tendency to force you to grind procedurally generated missions, a common issue in open world sandbox games, I have to say that this is one of the few games where the grind did not bother me! Rather fun combat, decent mission variety, and a plethora of (somewhat) profitable side activities keep the game fresh and the amazing looks that the ships have make you want to keep going until you've got that one last shiny battleship. Another thing to note is that this game absolutely BLEEDS Firefly (a fairly popular short TV series) and really captures the feeling of flying around the galaxy in a trusty ship while smuggling goods and blasting other pilots to space bits in a way I, personally, haven't experienced before.
Before I get into the nitty gritty details of the game, here's a TL;DR score: 7/10 (I'd say drop it down to a 6/10 if you don't really love spaceships or Firefly).
Sound:
If you overlook the fact that there really shouldn't be any sound in space, the sound is, in general, pretty good! Lasers sound like lasers, cannons go boom, and explosions seems appropriate! They can get a bit repetitive after a while, but that's to be expected in a longer game like this.
Music:
The music is awesome! If you've seen Firefly the music will really give you some flashbacks to the show. However, the selection in the game seems rather similar and you start to hear the same thing over and over again. Got to the point where I had to mute the music at times.
Voice:
The voice work in this is passable, but nothing special. While there weren't really any cringe-worthy moments, I never felt like the actors' performance or the script really pulled me in. The aliens and robots sound pretty neat though!
Graphics:
The game is pretty freaking gorgeous in my opinion. While not the most graphically impressive game out there, the galaxy looks pretty vibrant and the graphical effects that surround your ship when you are warping around the map is pretty great. The ships themselves look awesome and there are a couple of different ship lines in the game that offer varied ship aesthetics! The UI looks decent but is nothing special.
Gameplay:
The gameplay in this title is a bit of a mixed bag. The combat is a blast, however little things about it can start to bother you. For instance, the game is played on a flat plane, however at times when ships get close to you they tend to leave that plane to fly around you and at times this makes hitting them with your broadsides feel like a total crapshoot. Unfortunately, if you don't like the combat in this game, you might want to look elsewhere as the other activities in the game such as mining and trading are somewhat underdeveloped and are in general nowhere near as profitable as combat missions which will result in the currency grind becoming much more difficult than I believe it should be. One other huge issue I had with the game was that the UI is very unfriendly for mouse and keyboard users. Everything else in the game works fine with a mouse and keyboard, but the UI is clunky and is not mouse friendly at all, in many cases requiring you to use WASD to navigate. Lastly, certain weapon types in the game seem rather underpowered, in some cases to the point of being completely useless, and there is very little meaningful change-ups in terms of the gameplay as the game progresses.
Final Verdict:
I think this game is a lot of fun. While it is definitely rough around the edges and features a noticeable grind, it kept me playing for a full 24 hours and I am not the kind of person who typically enjoys grinds in games. Would I buy it at full price? Probably not. However, I think the game is worth a play despite all of its flaws and I would certainly recommend it to anyone looking to pick it up during a sale or in a bundle. Rebel Galaxy gets a thumbs up from me!

If you're looking for a "straight to action" business/industry simulation game and/or have a car interest, I recommend this game for you. You start the game by loading up an empty factory with a set amount of starting capital, with only one objective: make more money by producing cars.
The game is all about setting up self contained production stations for each part required in a complete car along a conveyour belt system, trying to figure out an optimal setup.
Pros:
- Charts and production data are very well made for the perfectionists out there.
- Nice looking graphics and animations. There's hundreds of simultaneous animations on screen at all times without making your head hurt.
- Sound and music is very good, even though there's only one song on repeat.
- UI is minimalistic and fairly easy to understand.
- Core gameplay is very solid (as in creating actual production lines).
- Alot of car types and upgrades to use.
Cons:
- This is a trial and error game. If you get below 0 capital, you lose immediately without warning. This means you have to start over alot until you figure out how to build proper production lines from the start, since it's too expensive to rearrange a factory with a non-optimal setup.
- No option to move or rearrange production lines. You can only delete them and get back 50% of your money.
- Once you've figured out a working production line, there's not much else to do except adding more upgrades to your cars and change pricing every now and then to stay competitive.
- Only current age (aka modern) cars and features. I would've like to see my factory evolve from let's say the 70's to 00's which would've made the research feature more realistic and interesting.
- No employee management. Everyone have fixed salaries and work 24/7 at their stations.
- No maintenance depertment (every factory needs this), would add more dynamics to the game.
- Crashes ALOT. I don't think I've been able to play this game for more than an hour without a crash. If you do pick it up, save OFTEN.
All in all I would recommend this game to business simulator veterans, but it is very obvious this game is still under heavy development and to the cautious buyer I would say wait until there's more features or the game's on a sale.

This is a racing game made for racers.  People who genuinely love motorsports.  People who have actually DONE motorsports before.  People who know what racing really is like in real life.
This review is written having only played the game with a G27 racing wheel and only manual sear shifting with all HUD's disabled for the most racing like experience.
I've done my fair share of track days and i can tell you, think is the most realistic car racing game i have played.  There's plenty of people complaining the game feels too slow, the cars don't grip in corners blah blah.  Well guess what, those people have never driven on a track in their life.  When on a racing track, unless you're in a ultra fast ferarri or koensigg or something, guess what, you feel SLOW.  That's how it is.  Your car is slow.  People are so used to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ car sims that put so much emphasis on feeling like you're flying along or arcade racing games that let you go around corners at 400kph that they have no idea what it's actually like to race a car.
So more on the good parts.
The handling of the cars:
Fantastic.  Cars handle how they should. FWD understeers coming too hot into a corner, or if you put power down coming into a corner and you can even get the♥♥♥♥♥out with lift off oversteer when driving really agressive.  All of that is true in a FWD cars handling characteristics and they are all spot on in the game.  RWD cars oversteer if you power on too much mid corner, or over a crest.  You can really feel the suspension working.  Coming super hot down a hill into a banked corner?  Your suspension will start to wallow like a real car trying to deal with sideways g-forces, and if not careful in a RWD car, will cause oversteer.
Graphics:
AMAZING.  Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥  The attention to detail is amazing.  From the different exhaust outputs of the cars (some will be obviously running rich, some not, etc) to the in car view of the dash being out of focus (because you're looking at the track, not the car) but obviously having some type of MOTEC carbon fiber HUD in place of the standard cars one, to the general cars decals and body panels.  The world around looks so gorgeous, beautiful lighting, amazing scenery, and really perfect track textures.
Racing modes:
The only thing the game is missing in terms of racing modes is drag racing and rally.  Which is not a downside to me.  Drag is always a short lived interest in racing games and rally is much a massive part of racing it really does require its own game.
One massive thing to note is the different racing game modes all have different racing styles.  Touring cars are mega aggressive, open wheelers really require you to be careful with damage on and time attack is like how time attack is with sporadic cars you have to deal with.
Sounds:
I love the fact you can hear the tyres gripping, the straight cut gears int he gear box and the pop from fuel injectors still being on when your changing gears, because screw fuel efficiency.
Its the little things:
To me what really makes this game great is the little things.  Like picking a perfect line through a series of corners then coming out and realising you just shaved a second or 2 off your lap time.  The spectators not being 2d, the clouds and lighting are so gorgeous and the cars look amazing. Even the simple and elegant UI still keeping perfect functionality.  The fact you log in, and the game says with voice "Welcome back (name here), there's some new events in the touring car championship, go check them out!".  You can really tell Codemasters have really put their heart and soul into this game.
Summary:
If you're a grown adult that loves racing, and has done it before, this is the game for you.  If your some pimply teenager that thinks GTA and Need for Speed are racing simulators, this isn't for you.

What a compelling story this game has. It tells a story that is often untold, being a civilian in a war. The atmosphere created within this game is surreal and the pencil artwork of the environment lends itself beautifully to the game. The story line alone is enough to warrant buying this game but there's so much more to it. This game makes you think. It makes you weigh out morality and righteousness against desperation and survival. It always keeps you on your toes and once you're done playing it, it really makes you dwell upon the fact that the events in this game actually happened in the siege of Sarajevo.
The gameplay itself is simple and easy to pick up. It is a point and click game with minor elements of strategy, stealth and combat involved. The crafting system is fairly wide and easy to pick up and learn on the fly. And the characters are unique and you can even have the option to create your own. The moderate cast of characters gives this game some replayability as well. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good story and simple gameplay elements.

The "best"/least mediocre Bioshock game. I actually kinda liked this one.
The story and themes try to copy Bioshock 1 but it kind of ends up being a blander copy in that regard. But screw that! It actually manages to be fun throughout the whole game (unlike Bioshock) and the story isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ multi-dimension quantum magic pretentious hipster drivel (unlike Infinite). Basically, you're one of the first Big Daddies, and part of Rapture's Splicers have turned, in the 8 years since the first game, into a "Family" led by Female Andrew Ryan with a different philosophy, aka, Sofia Lamb. Your daughter is being controlled by her to be the Ultimate Citizen, and you want to get her back, as a Big Daddy would. There are twice as much endings this time (I didn't check the differences between them because I can't be arsed to), and the difference between these, besides harvesting or rescuing Little SIsters, is that they also depend on certain characters that you save. Or not. Bascially, instead of having 1 choice, you have 4.
Gunplay is sort of between Bioshock (mediocre) and Infinite (less mediocre), and though it is slightly more linear than Bioshock at times, it doesn't waste hours of your time with backtracking (hence the shorter gameplay time even though I explored through most nooks and crannies) and the guns are slightly more original than Infinite's: Instead of the WW1 weaponry, you have the Big Daddy's Rivet Gun, a sort of minigun instead of that♥♥♥♥♥♥Tommy Gun from BS1, a harpoon launcher, a one-handed shotgun and Bioshock1's grenade launcher. You can also dual-wield plasmids, and the upgrades for both plasmids and weaponry are also more original than the 2 other Bioshcok games. Compared to both Ken Levine's Bioshocks, the game also has a lot less full of HP-bloated bullet sponges (though it gets more offensive in this regard towards the last 2 or 3 levels).
Bioshock's Little SIster gameplay of harvesting or rescuing Little Sisters after fighting disgustingly HP-bloated enemies turns into adopting or harvesting. If you adopt them (You're a Big Daddy in this game, forgot to mention that) You can reenact the worst level of the first game where you go around letting them harvest ADAM (the magical space-slug chemical that allows you to upgrade your magic powers aka Plasmids) while playing tower defense.You only have to do this once though (for tutorial purposes *sigh*) and in later times you can just send them to the nearest vent and rescue or harvest them. The Big Daddies are not bullet sponges anymore because you have more powerful weaponry (now, there are Brute Splicers for whatever reason, which take up the seat of annoying bullet sponge that charges at you.) To keep a certain amount of dificulty in harvesting/rescuing Little Sisters (even though all difficulty in the Bioshock games is fake because you can just respawn with almost zero cost near where you "died"), at the end of the level, come Big Sisters to get the ADAM you got back. They are sort of a combination of Big Daddies (the charge at you) and Houdini and Spider Splicers (they jump around, and throw fireballs and whatever objects are in the vicinity, at you.) They are not complete bullet sponges, and are fairly fun to fight against.
Overall, it's not really a great game, but it sure as hell is better than ♥♥♥♥ing Infinite. And the first game as well.

This game is quite well made considering that a one-man dev did it, and it is pretty fun despite being much of the same thing. Admittedly, the second half of the game isn't as enjoyable, but it's still fun and the end of the story is worth waiting for.
The tutorial only teaches you how to move the camera, which is useful but not enough. The codex (manual) is just extra trivia that is rather devoid of content. So, in the good old-fashioned way, you'll learn how to play this game as you go. However, it's actually very simple (if a little buggy), so the learning curve isn't that bad.
Other things: there is decent if slightly repetitive music; combat is pretty much the same the whole game and late-game all the enemies are a pushover. There are a few bugs, chiefly one where when you select the tactical map and move units from there the green line that appears continues into the normal map and gets in the way for the rest of the battle (I uploaded a screenshot). The other main one is if
. Finally, if you are purchasing a unit or upgrade while you jump, it will be lost with no refund (although that is not so serious). Stuff also randomly shimmers, ostensibly to make you notice it, but it just gets annoying after a while and you can't turn it off.
The game would be even better if units weren't so generic - e.g. right now combat experience doesn't matter at all, so if one of my units is at low health and I am at the build limit I might as well make it suicide to build a new ship with full health, which makes no sense. The battles are also essentially the same regardless of who your enemy is and so extra differentiation would have been helpful. Finally, the game's difficulty (and fps for that matter) drops drastically towards late game after you amass enough units and cash - you can afk for 5 minutes and win without any stress at all. I played the second half of the campaign at 4x speed because my fleet was about 10 times stronger than the opponent's
.
However, all of the above comments don't take into account that this game was developed by one person, and ultimately that means that the absence of these things is more than understandable. If the developer had more resources, this game would be fun to play for hours and hours on end. As it stands, it is still worth purchasing, but not necessarily (although still acceptable) at full price. As of the time of writing there is still a while before the Summer Sale ends, so grab it now! This game should bring at least 8-10 hours of fun that is very fun, even accounting for the bugs. Oh, and there are multiple maps too!

Hitman Absolution is relatively difficult to evaluate on its own merits, like most games that belong to beloved franchises.  Ultimately, my verdict on Absolution was that it's a very good stealth game, but not the best Hitman game.
I did a Silent Assassin playthrough, and most of the levels felt more like Splinter Cell levels than Hitman levels.  It was a lot of distracting enemies and timing movement between cover.  That's not a bad thing by any means, but I understand why someone expecting a game like Blood Money would object.  There are far fewer assassination missions in Absolution than in any previous game.
The few full assassination missions are enjoyable and very open - if the devs had gone more in that direction I think that the reaction from the hardcore fans would have been more positive.
I'd give this game a recommendation for stealth game fans - I thought it was better than any Splinter Cell since Chaos Theory.  As a Hitman game, however, it falls short due to relative dearth of assassination missions.

Welcome to a simulation of socialism, comrade.
Ever wanted to know what it was like to drive a Trabant across the eastern Soviet bloc without paying thousands of dollars to travel, to buy the car, in the inevitable back breaking repairs, etc? Jalopy is the deal of the century in comparison. You and your batshit crazy Uncle drive your Trab... I mean, err, Laika, across a procedurally generated Soviet landscape circa 1990 (which is pretty accurate, honestly, grey colours, hotels in which you can hear monsoons in the hallway, and snarky 24 hour store clerks), trying to keep the rolling deathtrap on the road and get to your destination.
The devs clearly have a deep love for the car, which can be repaired and modified at the side of the road or at a Laika dealer, who of course will sell you better parts than the ones that you scrounged from Uncle's garage/barn. You can measure this car's acceleration by holding a stone up in your hand and watching the wind erode it, which is pretty much exactly how Trabants are. You add gas AND two-stroke oil to the two-stroke engine through a gas tank mounted over top of the engine. Makes you feel privileged to drive that 1989 Tercel, doesn't it, comrade?
There's lots of bugs, as befits an early Alpha access title, some of the more amusing of which are Laika dealers ripping you off for car upgrades that never show up (wait, is this a bug?), Uncle's brain falling out and having him stuck in the car/motel/floors/stairs/traffic. The extremely amusing multi-car pileups that occured even with your hazard blinkers on as you tried to fix your beleagued people's car don't seem to occur anymore, which makes it easier to fix your car I suppose.
But honestly, there's enough humour and heart here for anyone who doesn't mind a first-person strategy simulation with a decidedly Griswold Vladivostok vibe. I'm sure it'll come together. Well worth the money to watch the devs take this road trip somewhere.
Just don't fix the car. It's fine, comrade. Smoke is healthy. You are lucky.

This game is a worthy successor to the Dungeon Keeper franchise, incorporating many great elements of creature training and management.  It delivers exactly as advertised in this regard, and if you enjoyed DK, you will enjoy this as well.
For myself, the game shines in the same place as its inspiration- skirmish mode, where you are free to sandbox until your heart is content, complete with the old gem nodes for a modest but endless stream of gold.
Dungeons 2 expands on the old Dungeon Keeper model, by allowing you to venture on to the surface, and take a much more direct hand in controlling your creatures, more akin to a traditional RTS framework.  While not as elegant as a mainstream, big name RTS, it is more than serviceable and provides a nice addition to the game, as well as additional tactical situations.
There are two factions you can select from- a familiar, wacky feeling pile of goblins, orcs and the like, or a darker pack of demons.  While playing somewhat similar in a broad sense, they differ in enough ways to impact dungeon planning and creature selection.
This is a very solid, enjoyable game, and worth every penny.

My wife and I were looking for a free to play online multiplayer game to try out together. There were a few criteria for our search: 1) Both of our machines had to be able to run it (she has an older laptop with a low-end graphics card; 2) It had to be free (not interested in subscription-based MMORPGs); 3) It had to have a 'casual' feel to it so that we could focus enjoying the game rather than trying to figure it out. We sifted through the Steam searches, and came across this one.
I've seen Villagers and Heroes decribed as the "not too smart, but cute love-child of World of Warcraft and Runescape." After sinking 26 hrs into it, I'd say that description is pretty accurate. It's not a very complex game, but it's a fun game. My wife enjoyed a lot more of the gathering/crafting -type quests, and I was much more interested in the dungeon crawling and boss matches, but we were both able to play through the game together and have a lot of great nights with it.
The only CON that I need to add in here is the housing system. We were both really excited to purchase houses in one of the villages of the game, but they just act as inventory space (you can't enter them, customize them, or anything). Furthermore, you need to sign into the game every week to pay your 'rent' to keep the place... and I'm away for work quite often so when I came back after a project, both of our houses (and all of our stuff) was gone. I submitted an in-game ticket for support, but one month later I still haven't received a response. Damn.
Oh well, it was still a lot of fun while it lasted. If I get a response back and our stuff is recovered, we may take it back up again.
