This is an old review based on the base game, so I'll keep it relevant to that but I warn you:  if you enjoy playing 4x strategy games, stay away from this one.  It's not headed in a reletively good direction.  Take this review with a gigantic grain of salt.
Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth is a game seemingly intended for veterans of the 4x strategy genre and not Civ fans
.  I believe this ultimately hurt the game, but it does not detract from the gameplay if you are prepared for it.  The game does differ in a lot ways to Civ 5 in many ways and has many different mechanics in terms of how to allocate your time and resources, but it is also similar in some aspects.
When I first began playing this game as a sort of newbie to the series starting from Civ 5, I did not find this game very engaging and I felt like the game was lacking in a lot of ways that made Civ 5 such an outstanding title (if you include dlc).  It was not until I had played and understood a more complicated 4x strategy that I began to play more about this game (specifically Endless Space).  Now that I do understand more about this game, I'll attempt to explain some of the more basic elements.
Affinities:
Affinities are basically the freedom/order/autocracy of this game, just much, much more important.  Affinities are what define your civilization.  There are three kinds: Harmony, Supremacy, and Purity.  Affinities affect how other civilzations react to you and what sort of victories you can achieve.  Delving deep into an affinity is necessary to win certain victories and is beneficial towards your military, as units grow in power as your affinity strengthens.  The more you develop into an affinity, the more your civ becomes like that affinity.  Your actions quickly become louder than your words as you and the other civilizations advance into their affinities and you will find friends and foes alike based on nothing but your ideology.
Science:
Probably the most important thing in the entire game next to affinities.  The science web (yes that's web, not tree) comes in two parts: branches and leaves.  Branches are the basic parts to a technology that allow you move further into the web by researching them.  Leaves allow you to speciallize in a tree. Unlike branches, you can't progress further into the web by reasearching leaves. Leaves, however, often offer better benefits than the more generalized branches do.  Unlike Civ 5 where the science tree is linear and you must keep up research in order to progress as a civilization, you can pick and chose exactly what technology will help you the best for what you are trying to do.  As a new player to this game and games like this, that's a lot of choices to pick from and it can get confusing at times.  It's important to understand what victories there are, what victory you want to pursue, and decide on researching technologies based on what victory you want.
Virtues:
Like previous Civ games, culture is also an important aspect of the game.  Culture allows you to obtain virtues which provide boosts to your civilization.  There are 4 virtue trees: might, prosperity, knowledge and industry.  Delving deep into a tree will boost combat, food, production, energy (money), science, culture or health based on which trees you chose.  Once again, this game provides with the choice of what virtues you want to pick, and how you want to allocate them.  If you chose to speciallize in a tree, you will get unique benefits the more you put into that tree.  If you chose to go into multiple trees, you get unique benefits generalizing into the same level in each tree.
Spying:
Spies provide nice, one-time bonuses you your civilization ever so-often.  Spies can establish spy networks, siphon money, steal science or even call giant siege worms to wreak havoc on another civilization's city.  Spies, although not vital, are very helpful to your civlization's goals.
Aliens:
You can make aliens friend or foe - it's entirely your choice.  The harmony affinity allows you to be at peace with the alien life on the planet and even use them against your foes.  Supremacy and Purity, however, could care less about the aliens.  If you don't wish to make the aliens friends, they quickly become nuissances that must be dealt with from time to time.  Keep in mind, though, that attacking the local wildlife can put you at odds with other civilizations bent on protecting and preserving the alien life.
Miasma:
Some of the most annoying stuff in the game.  Miasma covers certain land tiles on the map and it slowly deals damage to units that end their turn on it.  You can get rid of the miasma by researching the right technologies and using workers or satellites, or use the miasma to your advantage by delving into the harmony affinity allowing them to instead heal your units for the same amount every time a unit ends their turn on it.

Homefront is a first person action game developed by KAOS Studios and published by the now defunct studio, THQ. Homefront tells the story of a resistance movement fighting back against a near future Korean occupation of the USA
The game play is a very generic FPS. Graphics wise, it looks nice, but you can tell the game was released in 2011, it looks better than most games released, however it shows it's age when comparing it to more recent titles. The graphical options are wide varying
All the maps in the single player are very well designed, sadly you can't really explore because you are constantly reminded to keep following your squad leader. You fight through various different environments such as the streets of suburbs, department stores, and baseball fields, all of which show a disturbing outcome of the quite scary "what if?" scenario from a Korean invasion
The single player of Homefront will take about five hours to complete; this is pretty short and the game ends on a massive cliff hanger, I would of liked to have seen another two or three more missions to tire up the loose ends in the story. Multiplayer is still very much alive in Homefront, I have only played in a couple of games but I had no problem finding a map full of people to jump into
I would like to recommend Homefront; however I would wait till it is on sale, which would be an absolute bargain if you could get it for that again in an upcoming sale

If you wanted to get into MTG, then this game is a good introduction. The tutorials do a good job in explaining the basic rules of the game and by playing on a computer, you can't cheat or misplay cards. So the game is great for teaching MTG. You also get a few cards to start building your own decks and get hooked on the principle of a traiding card game.
But  there are many problems with this game:
- Card and deck managment is horrible (it is clearly made for consoles and not PC), there are no real sorting options for your card collection or in deck building, so building a deck can be horribly tedious, especially in combination with the bad controls
- Game controls overall aren't that great on PC
- I often experienced, that after completing a daily quest i didn't receive the reward for the quest or only a smaller reward than indicated
- The different difficulty levels all feel the same, often games on Hard difficulty are quite easy while you get crushed on Easy
- Sometimes the AI makes stupid decisions
I personally never played against other players or coop, so I can't talk about that part of the game.
So in the end this game does a good job of getting new players into MTG, but after a while the players might get frustrated with all the problems of this game. (Maybe that's the plan behind the game, so the players start buying real MTG cards after they get hooked, but who knows ;) )

Rapture after a long, long, time:
To begin with, this games deals with some seriously heavy stuff in a very quick and dirty method. I do believe, because the subject matter of secularism and atheism are core to this game, then many people quickly dismissed it as a bad game.
Summary:
This game is a 7.5 out of 10. I like the combat, the mechanics with the little sisters and gameplay. The downsides are the subject matter little to no explaination and how limited the choices are for the player as far as combat is concern.
Gameplay:
You are a big daddy with the ability to dual wield plasmids and guns. Ideally, you could kick down any door and win any fight except against another big daddy or big sister. Not so much in this game. You are incredibly weak to any multi prong attack, which the game throws at you continuously. The big sisters are not as big of a hassle as are a group of three basic enemies attacking you from different directions. For most of the game, you will have to retreat and slowly kill off the enemies one by one or charge through one to cover.
Next, after about half way through you get two gene tonics that make the game silly, water of youth and camo. Combined, you can regenerate and hide from most situations. Camo makes the last battle silly. Then you can combine these two with scout 2. The game becomes a cake walk from that point. Shady corner? hide under a waterfall and scout ahead. Enemy ambush? Hack their machines or plant your decoy 2 or decoy 3 and watch it backfire. Even in the last battle, you can sit camo and let your scout handle the enemies with plenty of traps.
Finally, the last mechanic is the traps. Three of your weapons have a trap amo and a fourth has a turret. You can secure any area, until you hit the cap for a particular trap: something like six  proxi mines, etc. Plus you have a plasmid trap that can be armed with the level 2 with any other plasmid. This makes setting up environmental traps easy. Oil spill? fire trap it. Open water? eletro trap it.
In conclusion with gameplay:
You are not going to be kicking down doors and taking names. You are going to be sitting back in a secure area, and slowly whittling enemies down with any number of traps and turrets you have set up.
Story:
The original bioshock was a nose thump at Atlas Shrugged. (To explained the title: Atlas is a titan from Greek Methology , who is punished by Zeus, to hold up the world. What was he punished for? fighting to defend the titan's from the god's rebellion. In other words, he was an enemy soldier taken prisoner and forced into a humilating pushiment.) This one is a nose thump at secularism and atheism. Basically, Andrew Ryan, who is an atheist, wants the people to be happy. A problem with atheist is that you are meaningless, which is kind of heavy. So he hires another atheist, Mrs. Lamb, to come  and make the people happy. Well she does, by making them believe in a Christ-like figure, "The Lamb," who will make everyone happy. "The Lamb" will do this by taking away freedom of choice and of thought and forcing everyone into becoming a happy communistic society. Still people are unhappy, but are zealots towards this new goal to obtain fufillment. So when they are forsaken by their messiah, they turn sucidal.
You can say that many people cannot handle the end result of their beliefs thrown at them. It isn't pretty in most circumstances and rarely is the kind of ending they would want. Since many people of my generation are of these beliefs and they are being held in such high regard, then getting the end result thrown in their face would turn them away from the game. Still, the game doesn't exactly convince nor inform the player what philosophical climate they are stepping into. You get anti-religious cult versus unknown player. Your moral choices really don't play much into the story other then making the messiah evil or relativily good.

is a game that is
meant to garner a new fanbase like GRID 2 was(might've succeded, although at the cost of disappointing many, including me), but is meant for people who enjoyed the first game: Race Driver: GRID(aka GRID).
________________________________________________________________
Gone are the 'Oh you're turning into a corner? Drift mode activated for "fun"!' handling physics of GRID 2, the nonsense storyline, the annoying and useless engineer guy, and a linear career mode.
On the other hand, making a welcome return is an emphasis on real-life circuits such as Spa, Jarama, Circuit of the Americas, Mont Tremblant; cockpit view; a career mode that is reminiscent of Race Driver: GRID with 5 separate disciplines(Touring, Endurance, Open Wheel, Tuned, and Street).
________________________________________________________________
Besides that, the gameplay has been tweaked to put a little more realism into the game. The physics, they're arcade that mimics a sim, but they're more believable than what GRID 2 and even Race Driver: GRID offered. As a result, races are no longer a drift fest or is drifting the best way to get around corners(quite the opposite), and something called understeer finally exists.
Also, free practice sessions have been added to race weekends, giving players time to get used to the track and tweak their car's setups(yes, you've heard that correct, you can now setup your cars, although it's simplified compared to sims). Qualifying sessions are now available as well, finally making any grid position that isn't P10-12 possible. These two sessions are not compulsory and can be bypassed, but that's only recommended for casual racers with AI difficulty set to easy.
Adding to that, race lengths are now extendable with the choice of 2, 3, and 5 times the original length. Don't like 3 lap touring car races? Why not have 6, 9, or 15 laps! It's possible now and I have to say it makes the career mode much more enjoyable.
Speaking of race weekends, the race engineer is also a lot less intrusive and gives helpful advice instead of saying 'good job' every minute. Players now can also ask their engineers to get an update on the car's status, teammate or rival's track position, or the gap to the driver ahead. Another thing, the engineer is now British.
________________________________________________________________
Then, what are the downsides? Plusses outweigh the minuses(of course, my opinion), but there are some to note.
First off, it's not a revolution, but an evolution. You won't find anything that'll catch your eyes for being so brand new. In fact, there are quite a few recycled contents. The track selection has some new additions like the beautiful Mont Tremblant or Sepang and CoTA, but other tracks are ones that were featured in either Race Driver: GRID or GRID 2(no new city circuits).
It's a similar case with the car lists too. Although we see some new cars(all of them are great) like the Ford GT40, A1GP open-wheeler, Caparo T1, Classic Mini, Lancia Delta, and McLaren P1, many others are ones that previous games had as well. In-game soundtracks are also the case where you see recycled contents, with the soundtracks being remixed versions of GRID 2 soundtracks. They're better than GRID 2's, but still, remixed musics are remixed musics.
Adding to the list, there's the cockpit view. Oh people are going absolutely mad over this. Yes, the game doesn't have a 3D interior modeling and uses the exterior mesh for cockpit views, making them low-res and undetailed. I personally have no issues with this and I like that Codemasters have added an alternative cockpit view that zooms in to the front windshield alongside the standard one(many games go for this, but I find them distracting because of car's interior taking up too much space on screen), but yeah, having a detailed interior with working dashboards like in other Codemasters titles would've been better.
________________________________________________________________
I haven't had the opportunity to drive around every track or drive all the cars in the game. However, after 2 days of playing, I'm already liking the game more than the previous two games. Had GRID 2 been like this game, I would've fallen in love with it. It took a huge disappointment and more waiting, but I'm glad that Codemasters have listened to fans' outcry and worked to fix it. GRID Autosport is not a groundbraking game, but a delightful fan service for those who waited for a sequel to Race Driver: GRID. If you were one of those people, I'd recommend that you give this game a chance.

What a compelling story this game has. It tells a story that is often untold, being a civilian in a war. The atmosphere created within this game is surreal and the pencil artwork of the environment lends itself beautifully to the game. The story line alone is enough to warrant buying this game but there's so much more to it. This game makes you think. It makes you weigh out morality and righteousness against desperation and survival. It always keeps you on your toes and once you're done playing it, it really makes you dwell upon the fact that the events in this game actually happened in the siege of Sarajevo.
The gameplay itself is simple and easy to pick up. It is a point and click game with minor elements of strategy, stealth and combat involved. The crafting system is fairly wide and easy to pick up and learn on the fly. And the characters are unique and you can even have the option to create your own. The moderate cast of characters gives this game some replayability as well. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good story and simple gameplay elements.

I would give this game a solid 4/5, which is amazing considering it was just released. Between the levelling system, crafting, skills, and world exploration, this is a must-buy.
As far as critiques go, I would say that the skill levelling needs to be tweaked a bit. It is very rare that your crafting level and your player level coincide, resulting in you not being able to use the armor/weapons that you can make or not being able to make the armor/weapons that you need. This takes away a lot of the game's momentum, as it results in you needing to grind crafting recipes or monsters before you can continue to progress. Also, with the crafting system, it's nice that you can pay scrap to learn a recipe if you just can't figure out a couple of the ingredients, but this system would work a lot better if you could just pay 50 scrap to uncover each individual part of a recipe. Also there needs to be a more reliable way to get scrap; the scrapper machine (or whatever it's called) gives like 1 scrap for every 5 or so good items you destroy (totally not worth it).
Also, I may be missing something, but it's really hard to use combat skills in combat. If you wanted to use more than 4 combat skills (plus heal), you're basically SOL since your toolbar is full. a toolbar with more slots would help alleviate this problem.
Aside from these trivial critiques, the fact remains that this a superb game. More immersive than Terraria and more fun than Edge of Space or even Dig or Die. Buy it while it's on sale!

It's difficult to review a game like this without making reference to the Dungeon Keeper series, since this game is effectively a Dungeon Keeper clone with a twist. It breaks with the classic Dungeon Keeper formula in a few key areas, which is sometimes for the better, and sometimes for the worse.
One aspect of the game I enjoyed the idea of was being able to send your creatures to fight on the overworld, something I always felt was lacking in Dungeon Keeper. In the overworld, the game switches to a more traditional RTS control scheme heavily inspired by Warcraft 3 (a game it makes reference to multiple times; more on this later), but lacking the polish of a proper RTS. This is where I felt the game was lacking - controlling units is clunky, and selecting individual units is difficult (you have to be VERY precise with your mouse clicks and it's hard to tell where your cursor is actually pointed because it's a big fat hand), which is a pain, since most units have active abilities (like Warcraft) which help them and their allies in combat. Overworld combat therefore often degenerated into two blobs of units ramming into each other, with the strongest unit blob emerging victorious.
Another aspect of the game which I like in principle, but which was flawed in execution, is the ability to choose from two different factions - the Horde (another Warcraft reference) consisting of various green-skinned races, and the Demons (also referred to as 'The Flaming Legion'... yes, they did it again). In terms of mechanics, both factions play quite differently, however, the Demons require more micromanagement, are more difficult to use, and are just not very fun to play with in my opinion, which leaves me coming back to the Horde every time. There have been hints floating around that the devs are planning to bring in the Undead as a third faction. Watch this space.
The underground aspect of the game plays like a simplified version of Dungeon Keeper. I like that you can now fill in areas of the dungeon you've mined out (so now my obsessive-compulsive tendencies are satisfied by perfectly shaped dungeon rooms and corridors. Researching upgrades is clunky, as you have to go to the appropriate room to do it; research takes places in three different rooms, two of which have multiple sub-menus for research, so it's difficult to tell what's yet to be discovered. Spells are, for the most part, not that interesting or useful.
For me though, the worst part of the underground game is how easy it is to defeat waves of invaders after around the 15-20 minute mark. The difficulty of the waves doesn't really scale into the late game, and the top tier traps (like the Horde's Red Alert-esque Tesla Coil, and the Demons' giant tentacle) feel a bit redundant. The other thing I dislike about the game is the lack of replay value. Once you've played through the campaign, you've experienced everything the game has to offer. There isn't much strategic choice or flexibility in the game, so once you've figured out a winning formula for building up an epic dungeon from scratch, the game simply consists of following that same formula every time until you have an army big enough to stomp the overworld do-gooders.
In terms of style, it's clear that the game is made by a German developer, since all rooms have an 'efficiency' rating, and beer is now an important resource that you must ensure a constant supply of, and your breweries are decorated with little Bavarian flags. In contrast to the grim, grainy visuals and dry, dark humour of Dungeon Keeper (hallmarks of its British devs), Dungeons 2 is bright and cartoonish, and its sense of humour is silly in a very Monty Pyhton-eqsue way. Most of the jokes come from the game's narrator, whose voice will be immediately recognisable to anyone who has played The Stanley Parable, which the narrator himself references in one of his many, many, fourth-wall-breaking moments.
There are also multiple references to many other aspects of nerd popular culture. It's clear the devs are gigantic geeks from the things they make reference to. 80% of the references are related to Game of Thrones or Lord of the Rings, I also picked up references to general pop culture (Two of my Nagas were called Kardass'shian and Kanyay'Wst), the Warcraft Universe, Warhammer, Gamergate and The Quinnspiracy, a couple of youtube videos I haven't seen in years (including Trololo and They're Taking the Hobbits to Isengard). I chuckled at a lot of the references, although the relentless Game of Thrones stuff started to get stale.
All in all, this is a game I would recommend. It certainly brings back feelings of Dungeon Keeper nostalgia and despite being quite formulaic and lacking replay value, you'll get a good couple of dozen hours of fun gameplay out of this game before it starts to get dull. For those who miss the way strategy games used to be, despite all their flaws, Dungeons 2 will fill that gap while it lasts.
Now to move on to War For the Overworld, which I've heard such good things about.

Deathmatch part of Half-Life 2 was released separately around two weeks after release of Single-player portion. So yea, nowadays you will have to buy it separately.
Community is small but living. Sometimes you will have over five or ten players in each of five servers or so. Sometimes it's just fourteen players filling up single server. It still is enough to have fun with basic stuff. Community has preference of playing either Deathmatch on some low-gravity killbox map or team Deathmatch on Runoff map, which is quite horrible.
So yes, you got Deathmatch. And you also got Team Deathmatch, which divides players between Combines and Rebels. The only difference is reskin of useless melee weapon.
You will also can find some people playing cooperative mod (usually invasion style thing) or roleplay ones.
It comes with few official maps, though most likely you will only get to see Runoff. Which is badly made, giving Combine side a rocket launcher right at the start, while making Rebels have to walk back to get more or less good weapons. It also has a looong dead end, which only has shotgun at the end, as if it's some kind of super weapon.
It's quite standard deathmatch game from older times. You got arena, you spawn in random spot or so, you have to collect pickups, there is no leveling. You don't usually survive encounters, so don't expect to be able to run away to get some health, it's kinda chaotic.
Being based on Half-Life 2, it brings physics into gameplay. Mostly it comes to ability to pick any object with gravi-gun and throw it at opponent. Another common tactic is using it to throw grenades that you put onto ground. It's not much of use otherwise, you can't get much of creative uses of gravi-gun in game where amount of kills is what counts. You may try to make ladders somewhere or try to block doorways with objects, but it's weak tactics.
Weapon balance is where HL2: Deathmatch fails. There are two things that win the games: explosions and revolver.
Any explosion has huge radius and would kill anybody immediately. And rocket launcher has rockets that are homing to the spot that you are pointing it, so players rarely escape whoever has rocket launcher. Those who don't have such weapons can just lob grenade onto floor, grab it with gravi-gun and then throw it as opponent, making sure that it will explode near player. Which requires timing. But still.
When you don't get rocket launcher, you should go for revolver. It's a highly accurate hitscan weapon that requires only two shots to kill players, or even one if it's a headshot. Let's say, a skilled player can dominate both long-range and short-range as long as they know how to aim. After all, you can use Zoom, even though you have to release Zoom button before being able to fire. Nothing much that other players can do against that.
Otherwise, you will use either crossbow or shotgun for short range. Yes, crossbow. Revolver is more effective at long range. So you just insta-kill people at very close range with bolts, as long as you can predict. Otherwise just do double-shot with shotgun. Yes, double-shot, alternative fire. Always do it.
Everything else takes too long to kill and thus is quite useless.
So, what we got there, is a Deathmatch that feels tucked on the Half-Life 2, keeping weapon balance that was designed for single-player. It's not terribly balanced and fun. But I guess it should be amusing with bunch of friends, to fool around.

I think the biggest problem of this game is in it's name: if it wouldn't have been called "GRID" it could get away with what it is. But people look at it and expect the experience they had with Racedriver: GRID, which this game doesn't deliver.
First of all, unlike Rd:Grid the game doesn't allow the player to customize his driving experience.
Rd:Grid was like "you wanna play with keyboard? fine, here is a bunch of assists so you can handle the car with those keys. you get better at it, turn some of them off and get extra enjoyment!" or "ofcourse a car would slide, but only if you are not carefull enough with the throttle in the exit of the corner. still cannot tame it? just move the TC slider a little bit backwards". This freedoms resulted in great accessebility and immense fun of driving whatever you input device was.
Instead, GRID 2 says "we got TrueFeel(tm), we have World SIDEWAYS Racing, we are all flashy and hooked up on fans which you gotta impress, so you are going to play the game OUR way!"
Obligatory drifting. Oh gosh, i didn't think i ever see it this series. Thing is, you cannot tell if you are faster without it. It has  become part of the game.
Again, comparing to Rd:Grid, sliding the car was never an option if you were going to set a time. You would go for a clean line, resorting to sliding in rare instances, and yet it was fully up to the player. Sliding a corner made you feel "Hahaha yeah!" or "Oops, steady, steady!". GRID 2 does it like "Right, here we go again...".
Not knowing all that, I jumped into it with my itching fingers ready over arrow keys and was for a surprise. "OK, it won't be easy", i thought, and i got better at it, although still failing to have as much fun as i expected. But i kept my hopes up by thinking, "OK, maybe if i get a controller, i might actualy get to enjoy it...". WRONG. No ingame customization for controller device leaves it almost as clunky as keyboard. (to be fair there might be a way to make it better by editing xml file, but that's yet to find out). As it turned out, reading different forums, the game was desigined primarily for full-on steering wheel controllers, walking straight past keyboards and pads like they are history. Only a handfull of those hardcore devices seem to provide a player with  full control over the car. Yet in a game, that positions itself as leaning towards arcade driving experience...
Another complaint is the track design. There are not a lot of tracks and locations to choose from. Racing tracks are alright. The trouble hides on city circuits and winding road courses. Like if half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥controls isn't enough, these end up being littered with hazards, things to hit or send a car flying off the road. Moreover, there simply isn't enough room for 12 hotheads to have their way through, making every game mode a demolition derby. This was not an issue in Rd:Grid.
Coupled with turtle-paced progression of multiplayer, which doesn't reward you for anything besides placing in top 3, you will soon find that if you can't enjoy the driving in this game, there is nothing else left to look for.

Despite delay of the first expansion for Magic Duels content with assurances that it will be released when ready, release of the pair of expansions (Oath of the Gatewatch and Shadows Over Innistrad) failed to update issues players have reported such as support for team 2HG and introduced many others. Among them is implementation of what was intended to be a quality of life fix where priority is passed automatically when the only actions that could be taken are at instant speed, but instead a crippling feature that makes playing spells before the end of phases with floating mana or activating other phase-sensitive abilities is an impossibility at many points.
The people responsible for this game knew ahead of time how important quality was to the playerbase that supports them, and have yet again failed to deliver in a massive way. It does not matter if balance improvements and new card pools were implemented when those efforts are undermined by horrific quality control and update/hotfix speeds that rival snails in a marathon.

This is a tough one. Homefront generally is a subpar CoD. That's one reason why it's a negative review. The other is that the game offers moderately ok gunplay, shallow characters, stuck on terrain bugs, basically no innovative features and an incoherent plot that only takes you about 3 to 4 hours to complete. Just when you think things start rolling in the US again, the game is suddenly over. Just like that. No conclusion. We don't even know up until the very end what we even did and why we did what we did and how THAT helped win the battle. Which is disappointing.
That isn't to say that Homefront can't be a nice little experience. Especially the setting and the disgusting nature of the occupation are pretty well presented. The graphics aren't ugly, but nothing to look up to either. Crysis 1 looks better for example, but is a lot older as far as I can recall.
Homefront is simply a game of missed opportunities and at still 20 bucks I can't recomment buying it. Got it during a sale for 5 bucks, which is "ok-ish". If you like CoD gameplay, grab it, if not, just leave it. Unfortunately the whole Homefront project got pretty much abandoned and "remade" into something, which is apparently just as mediocre. It's sad, because if you extend the story by about 100 to 200% (so maybe 6 to 8 hours at least), spread in some more interesting missions, for example infiltration or something in the wilds, I dunno. Not just shooty shooty though and garnish everything with some interesting characters (Hell, the Duke has more character than these guys) and a well-thought out plot with maybe a bit better gameplay as well. And you have yourselves a winner. As it stands right now, this serves as a 10 dollar prequel game to an actual game.

Like flash games? Well here's an over-glorified flash game for you. In Survivor Squad you control up to 4 members of a squad on missions to eliminate all zombies in an area, exploring and looting as you go about it. You can then craft new weapons and supplies at your bases, which cost those same resources to establish. You spend gas to travel from area to area, and there's a store. The fact that I can tell you everything about the game four sentences says a lot about what you're getting here.
-The controls are horrendous. your squad has really little to no AI to speak of. you have to tell them where to move, where to turn, and occasionally where to attack. If they're alone and a zombie sneaks up behind them, they're dead because apparently they didn't hear it a flesh-eating monster running up behind them and think to turn around and shoot it. They only ever turn to shoot something nearby them if a teammate spots is spotting it beside them in their cone of vision that extends about four yards in front of their face, because hooray near-sightedness. And they also don't start shooting until the enemy is halfway into their cone of vision. Making guns nearly-useless, due to the fact that they also refuse to reload by themselves. They'd rather stand still and get eaten than reload. No, YOU have to select them and hit R manually, or they're ♥♥♥♥ed. You also cannot tell them to turn and face a new direction without moving first. Which is a hell of a ♥♥♥♥ing hassle.
-The "Story" is pathetic. After going easy on you for the first few levels, prepare for story-based missions where you have to help some guy, or retrieve some item, while pushing against an UNLIMITED tide of zombies until you accomplish your goal, with your UNLIMITED ammo, where enemies charge you from all directions, leaving you finding your squad walking back to back a few feet at a time in what is the most boring mission layout I have ever seen in a game.
-The voice ac- oh wait, there was no voice acting. Or maybe there was and it was so bad I didn't remember it. I'm going to stand by saying there was no voice acting. Leaving you to have to actually READ things others are saying while your squad is being eaten alive because you forgot to check the bottom of the screen to see if they were out of ammo and needing you to hold their and and hit R.
I'd tell you everything else that's wrong with this game but there is literally nothing else to criticize, the game is too small to have anything else to criticize. At least it has two other game modes, survival and sandbox. Sandbox being essentially story mode but without the story-driven ♥♥♥♥ missions, but it also has no ending as well. Just repetitive gameplay until you die or get bored.
4/10. If I had no other games available, maybe I could push myself to finish the story mode at least, but thankfully, I do have other games available, and if you do too, do yourself a favor. Steer clear so far of this game that you forget it exists.

I will start the review with some preface. I am burnt out on MOBA genre. I played DOTA back on WC3 when it was a custom map and played ALOT of Heroes of Newerth, to the point that the genre just is not fun. I hate the type of stress and rage coming from the long drawn games.
So why am I giving this MOBA recommeneded?
The main reason is this is an actual arena fighter. There are no creeps. The cooldowns are short. There is no mana. Just pure brawling. The second reason is the games are short. The rounds last roughly 1 minute to 3 minutes and the game is played as first to three. This brings the stress levels down considerable while still being extremely competitve.
The Main Positives:
+The tutorial does a good job at teaching the games basic such as the EX-Abilities and how some of the more complex mechanics work.
+The heroes feel diverse in style and gameplay.
+You can pick different talents that alter the playstyle of indvidual heroes. That you can pick and customize at the beginning of every match. On top of that you are allowed to see everyone's talents after everyone is locked in which allows the players to come up with counter strategies during the timers between rounds.
+The game has a practice mode (with no CD and Inf Energy options) which allows you to try all the heroes and understand their strengths and weaknesses.
The Main Negatives:
-The game can feel unbalanced at times if you get put into a rock paper and scissors matchup before the match even begins since you pick heroes before matchmaking starts. Talents attempt to balance this but won't help hard counters.
-Chat is DISABLED by default until you enable it yourself.
-If you play solo you cannot pick heroes with randoms as you lock in your hero before the match begins so friends are a perferable way to play. (Game is only 2v2 and 3v3 which makes it easier if you don't have many friends).
-Heroes are priced differently (I imagine this correlated to release date). Some heroes may take several hours to unlock. (Think LoL or Heros of the Storm).
Overall, I like this game. It is the great MOBA and one I have enjoyed winning and losing in. The game is FREE TO PLAY so there is no excuse to not giving it a chance.

Crea is a procedurally generated 2D sandbox RPG. The gameplay focuses on collecting/harvesting material and environmental objects/enemies in order to craft items, learn recipes and level up talents. The large and expansive world (if you choose to create such a world) includes multiple terrain/biomes, dungeons, creatures and objects. The world is fairly dense, and a day/night cycle creates a truly immersive setting. Crea is definitely recommended to those that are fans of the 2D sandbox RPG genre (there really aren’t that many on Steam). For everyone else, I would advise waiting for a deeper sale, or go in with a few buddies on a 4-pack (individually cheaper this way). Online multiplayer is supported.
----06/10/2016----
When you first make a character (after creating a “small/medium/large” world), you will then be left to proceed at your own pace. Equipped with two modes, Combat & Build, your character will often be switching between the two in order to harvest in peace. The Combat system utilizes a customizable two handed approach, along with a jump and roll-dodge mechanic. A health and stamina bar will limit your prowess.
Talents, or skills, are categorized under Arms, Syle (Magic), Gather, Craft, and Explore. Each talent must be unlocked by reaching a certain level, then purchasing with the pre-requisite amount of TP (talent points) – earned by performing actions from that particular category. Some of the skills include: Ledge Grab, Refine, Tool Proficiency, Fireball, Dash etc.
Characters may be equipped with a Helm, Chest and Leg armors, along with 3 accessories (disregarding Combat/Build equipment). The character is progressed through an XP level system, and the stats that can be modified are: Health, Stamina, Attack, Defense, Intelligence, Mind, Agility, and Luck.
There is a plethora of crafting categories and sub-categories that include armor, furniture, outfits, recipes, tools etc. Not all crafting objects/recipes are learned at start. Research must be performed, which generally occurs in the form of retrieving a new item and interacting with the Research Desk.
As of this review, the developers have fixed multitudes of minor bugs and a few major bugs reported by users through Steam reviews and from their website/forums. Originally in Early Access, the official release was launched during this review process. When referring to the Steam News or Discussions board, you can see very active involvement from the developers. I don't want to be that girl who complains this wasn't as good as Blood Money, but... not as good as Blood Money.
For the most part it's a pretty functional game, and the levels can be really fun in places, but tone-wise you can tell this one's from different people. The game still wants to be the kind of game where you drop pianos on women in crow costumes and watch the mob torture a lawyer on a rocking horse (looking at you, nunsploitation nuns) but it also wants to have heartfelt moments between 47 and... whatever the girl's name was?... It very obviously set the tone in the first mission where Diana, our long-time handler, has gone rogue, and we're going to murder her in the bathroom, so dressing like a chipmunk and leaving a dude in the desert to be run down by a homicidal ice cream truck feels kinda out of place.
And it isn't like Blood Money didn't have dark moments--we murdered our canary, for god's sake--but somehow that game worked where this one didn't.
Also, not to send my gaming brethren into throes of hysterics, but Anita Sarkessian was right. The sexism in this game is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥. You don't really have any female characters with any kind of agency. Diana had a lot in Blood Money, where she was very obviously off doing lots of stuff when we weren't there, making deals with unseen forces and walking around with her face conveniently obscured by the environment, but in this game she's dead before the end of the first mission, and the girl who replaces her as the driving force doesn't really do anything besides (a) get sick and (b) get kidnapped. There's nothing there to balance out the fact that you spend an entire level creeping around in the dressing room of a bunch of unaware strippers.
Also, the physics felt kinda wonky sometimes. In particular I spent half an hour trying to shoot a disco ball onto someone's head, but it kept sailing off into the crowd, killing innocent bystanders and drawing the attention of many burly bouncers who then shot me repeatedly.
In summary, it is funny the first time you dress in stars-n-stripes yoga pants and punch a Mexican wrestler to death, but then you stop and think about American imperialism and then you're really sad.

When it comes to Hitman:Absolution, it is really a hit or miss. If you want an "open world assassination game", check out Hitman Blood Money or Hitman 2016. Otherwise, if you want a linear story driven experience, then this game could be just for you.
Agent 47's handler, Diana Burnwood, has betrayed the Agency, an organization of professional assassins. After 47 kills Diana as part of his mission, he feels bad for Diana and decides to carry her final wish. 47 is to protect a girl named "Victoria" from the Agency as she will be turned into a killer just like 47. Agent 47 takes the girl and begins a very dangerous journey.
For me, the story was not that interesting. Sure the voice acting was superb (I thought Dexter was pretty interesting), but overall, I thought it just did not fit with the "Hitman" theme. However, I felt the gameplay, in a way, overshines the story.
---
---
Sure it isn't the same open world game as Blood Money, but the trade off was a much more detailed game with a lot of replayability.
Repetition is a key role in enjoying Hitman:Absolution:
Repetition tends to be a rather negative term when describing a game. However, if you were to play Absolution in a blind playthrough, chances are, you probably won't enjoy yourself and you might end up with a low score. I found the game to be fun around my third playthrough, where I understood the map and found many different ways to assasinate a target. Sure you could just shoot your target when he's in a certain spot, but why limit yourself there? Why not poison his food or make his death look like an accident?
---
---
The disappointment of this game comes from the fact that the majority of the missions aren't really about assassinating anyone. Your objective most of the time is to sneak (or you could just shoot your way through everyone) and get to a door and watch a cutscene unfold the story.
The checkpoint system made angry at times. You could complete a level 90% but if you didn't activate the checkpoint at the 50% mark, you now have to start from the beginning. Also, have fun with all the enemies that have respawned...
Yes, I was rather mad when I found out disguises were rather pointless most of the time. It assumes that everyone knows each other by heart as if they were all childhood friends or brothers. My guess is that IO wanted to make it "realistic" in a way. For example. if there are a ton of cops in a room, you can't really just put on a cop uniform and act natural. However, maybe the cops don't know the janitor that well, so if you got the Janitor's disguise, you could sneak around freely, but make sure you avoid other janitors. It sounds like a good concept, but with the linear level design and the enemy placement, you might just find yourself playing with the default suit and playing like a ninja.
This score brought more of a Noire theme to the table. There are some good orchestra pieces, but nothing really impressed me. However, what impressed me a lot was a lot of the side dialogues you can hear from characters. I even sympathized with some unimportant NPCs in the game.
Instead of a typical 3rd person multiplayer, there is "Hitman:Contracts". This mode is simply taking the missions from the story mode and changing targets, making players follow specific rules, and choosing what they have to use. This mode is for people who enjoy a challenge from others around the world and you can see just how good of a Hitman you really are.
I am on the verge of saying "stay away from this game", but I still think it is enjoyable for what it is. I'd say get it on a sale so if you felt disappointed, you won't think you wasted a lot of money.

Review Score: -4.5/10- As of Nov. 17, 2014. 'Lacks Visuals, Traveling a'Bore, Indecently Expensive'
Comical Liner: 'I once had this game, it was very fun until it uninstalled itself, then I forgot the game existed..'
Quick Summary; Before you slip past the scoreboard, I'd like to say.. If this game was specifically for a kid, I'd give it a 5.5 or possibly a 6. The game seems a bit... Underdeveloped. Sure it has it's "Greats" And "Heights" Such as many other games, but this game doesn't have anything to draw itself onto "Uniqueness" - And have something new to the table of MMOs. However, even despite this it can be pretty decent for someone with a lot of time... Otherwise, prepare to spend a lot of time traveling, and playing very carefully as potions derived/created/or bought ingame, are pretty faulty; Except the Paid by real money kind. Enjoy.
Pros:
- Game seems appropriate for a 'First time RPG'
- The look and theme persisted- It had a WoW-like feel, a bit more cartoony.
- Game is child friendly it seems as well, but that's about where it ends.
- Crafting seems pretty fun. It's great that you can train any skillset.
- Combining multi-items into better or more stylish items is neat.
Cons:
- Traveling across this game is tedious; Time-consuming and tedious.
- Did I mention traveling in the game feels like a grind in itself?
- If you died, while traveling, get ready to pay real money to revive..
- Or pay money to travel to wherever you attempt to go.
- Mana and health dies out pretty quickly, so stock Lots of garbage potions.
- Reliable, usable, and good potions are only purchasable via Real Money.
- Generic Quests. i.e. Collect 10 XYZ, Bring XYZ to XYZ, story driven? No.
- Controls feel like it's still in Alpha, Keyboard and Mouse sometimes conflict.
- Everything feels instanced, get ready to wait at every turn.
- Music.. Is.... That's all I can say without violating terms of agreement.
- Same generic sounds played for everything; NPC, Damage, Damage Taken, etc.
- I don't recall anyway to "Speed up travels" meaning... Real money to Travel.
- I was told by a friend you can have a house and XYZ, but it's just a "Stash"
Ending Conclusion; Don't play it unless you really... Really.. Want too, or it's already there for your niece, nephew, son, daughter.. And just wanted to play it. Otherwise, steer away, your money is worthwhile in other Indies that aren't trying to squeeze your wallet.

I wish I could recommend this game - it has a solid, fun set of core mechanics, and the narrator is quite funny.
Unfortunately, the control scheme and interface are too obnoxious. In the dungeon you have one control scheme, and another on the over world. On the overworld you can select your units in a traditional RTS fashion (drag over them to select everyone). You can't do this in the dungeon however, meaning that if you want to move many units to the overworld, you have to select each on individually, and then drag them each on the dungeon exit. Considering how often you'll want to go back and forth between the dungeon and overworld, all of this micromanagement gets old quite fast.
In addition, the dungeon can get pretty crowded at times, making it difficult to click on the unit/room you're actually trying to access.
Also, there are a number of annoying bugs. At one point I had to quit to the main menu and reload my game because one orc stayed in my hand, preventing me from dropping it or doing anything else. Another time an orc on the overworld suddenly woudn't attack, and no enemies would attack it (but his friends could still attack).
This is a game I really wish was better. If they fixed these irritations it could be quite fun.
Edit: as one commentor pointed out, you can use the group hotkeys you set on the overworld to select units in when they're in the dungeon. This helps a bit, but when you select units in the dungeon, it automatically moves you to the dungeon view, which gets obnoxious if you're trying to send them to the overworld.

Citadel: Forged with Fire is a multiplayer rpg similar to titles such as Ark (Gameplay) and Rust (Building). It is set in a fantasy world similar to the Elder Scrolls setting with a limited amount of things to really do.

Citadel is unique due to how the games integral structure works. Unlike other games of this genre, Citadel has a skill tree. The extensive skill tree spans 4 different sectors including; Building, Spells, Weapons/Armor, and Potion/Scrolls. You're able to learn how to craft items in these categories by points earned from leveling your character. This serves as Citadels major strength.
The gameplay in Citadel is very buggy and distorted. Much of the PvE combat is fought by safespotting non-ranged enemies from tall structures such as rocks and hills (One of the previous reviewers also noted that the game has 100's of characters. This is simply not true, the actual exact amount of enemies is 16). This boring form of combat is the only optimal form of combat due to the melee combat being very repetive and sluggish. As of the current state of the game (July 28) there is no form of blocking or defending against enemies. PvP is quite literally the biggest downfall of the game. From early on, many players you encounter can be killed in one single hit. The low health on players under level 10 causes players to die very quickly (also accounts for PvE). The broomstick/flying mechanic in the game, although done well, is very tedious as players need to carry massive amounts of mana potions to sustain their flight. I'm not sure if the devs are aware of how terrible it really is, but if you give Citadel a shot, the flying has got to be one of the best and worst features mainly due to this mana problem. Last note on gameplay is the combat while in flight. The flying causes spells and melee attacks to not work and what you aim at will not be hit by your spells.
One of the last topics i want to talk about is building. The building in Citadel is great and offers so much variety and different ways to build while not being a grind to get built. The problem though is that sometimes after server restarts, your buildings will despawn. Another problem is that due to such slow xp gain and how long and grindy it is to level up, the only structure you can build until level 25 (When you unlock stone which is hard to raid) is wooden structures. These structures are extremely weak and can easily be raided in mere minutes.
The most prevelant thing in all of Citadel is the absolute terrible lag the servers have. You will experience crashes multiple times, fatal errors on startup, problems joining, extremely high ping, bad network issues, but to be fair, when the game is not lagging, it runs very smooth on many setups. I get around 60fps constantly on the highest settings (when the server isn't lagging ofcourse).
The last thing i wanted to touch on is the XP and Leveling. The system for leveling implemented in Citadel is an extremely long and tedious grind. In tandem with the terrible PvE combat (the main source of xp), you will have to grind your way to higher levels which will take hours upon hours killing monsters in a boring and tedious fashion. Expect to murder 1000's (Yes thousands) of blood orcs and tear your hair out at the bore to follow.
Citadel: Forged with Fire is a beautiful concept that will inevitably work itself out. The devs are motivated to improving the game and release multiple updates every day. That said, the game in its current state ends up being a very repetitive and boring concept once you hit level 25. At its current stage expect a max of 25 hours of gameplay until you can't bear the boredom. I hope to see more added to the game and i wish the developers good luck.

Boy, what I could say about this one. Yes, you would expect that a lot of sequels suffer from the "sophomore slump", but I personally liked this entry even more than the first. One would imagine that playing as a big daddy may give you the ability to feel like a tank, as well as mowing down anybody that steps in your way. While it's true that the protagonist has more power than the previous, it doesn't necessarily mean that you will be indestructible. This is where I think the developers did a great job. Strategy is as important as ever, especially considering that the adam gathering moments requires one to carefully prepare an area before setting a little sister down.
What really struck me in this game is the combat system improvements over its predecessor. In the first game, Jack could either be wielding a weapon or a plasmid, never simultaneous. In Bioshock 2, Delta not only can use both in tandem, but it seems to work to maximum efficiency. Reloading and being bum-rushed at the same time? Fire a plasmid, finish the reload, and blast splicers into a billion pieces. I was very satisfied with the rush of having to take down multiple opponents using a mix of strategy and skill, as the splicers, big daddies, and big sisters seemed to be well polished AI.
All in all, if you loved Bioshock 1, I strongly recommend this as it brings nice closure to the city of Rapture. Even if you never played the first one, the combat system and its very self-contained story will guarantee to keep you entertained for hours.

Let me start by pointing out that I do not own Grid 2 and only ever played it for less than 5 minutes, so I can't make any comparison between these two.
Grid Autosport is a good racing game, and when I say that, I mean that it's a fun game, in which the racing feels fast, fierce, fun, challenging, and rewarding. It does not feel like reality, but it isn't one of those over the top arcade racers either. Overall, the racing is fun and satisfying. The AI is tough, sometimes even a bit over the top, especially in the touring car races. However, I'd much rather have overall tough competition and feel like I've fought and raced hard for every point, than go through a grid full of cars going on rails, not bold enough to challenge the human player. The only problem I have with the AI is that your team mate seems to be pretty much rubbish every single race, which leaves you fighting for the team championship alone. I've only done the first few seasons, so perhaps this will change later on. Nevertheless, I would very much like my team mate to be the biggest challenge in any race, which is not the case at least at the moment.
The graphics are nice enough, I doubt anyone has much complaints about them. The cockpit view, as stated a gazillion times everywhere, is not as good as it should be, but it's there nevertheless. I don't mind the blur or the bad textures inside the car, however I do find it annoying that looking around will flip the view straight to sideview, instead of smoothly "turning your head". You can remove the blur by the way, with some tweaks to the game files (google). The textures won't get any better though, neither will the displays start functioning. Like I said, to me it's just not important. I do understand that some people feel otherwise. For me, it does the job.
The handling is probably not quite perfect, but as soon as you get used to it, it is actually very much fun and satisfactory. I would like it to be slightly less airy, but I've already got used to it and have no complaints. In the worst case, it's going to make you feel a bit strange for the first few races, while getting to grips with it. It's not sim, but it clearly has some elements of more sim-like handling. I've played all assists off, with a gamepad, and it's good fun and extremely challenging at times. I can clearly feel that a steering wheel and pedals would much better suit this game. Even with the gamepad though, I really enjoy the challenge the handling gives me, trying not to break traction, not to lose the rear end while cornering, not over-correcting, etc. The sense of speed is brilliant. At some of the street circuits, or the fast road circuits, you really feel the rush, trying to stay on the throttle as long as you can, braking late, feeling like you're surely going way too fast! Just so you know, I'm playing with very hard AI, no assist, and manual gears, with a ps3 gamepad.
There are a lot of smaller things I like about the game, things like being able to change the duration of a race, being able to command your team mate and so forth. The team mate commanding could be better, but it's a nice addition. As an example, I was in a race fighting my way through the pack since the starting order had been reversed, while my usually very slow team mate was at the front, thanks to the high starting position. I found myself third when the final lap started, with my team mate in front of me at second. I'd told him to be aggressive, and thought to myself that perhaps I should tell him to slow down a bit, seeing that he was a bit all over the place going for the first position, and we needed the points to complete the team objectives. I then thought "nah, let's go for the 1-2", and a few corners later he spun trying to overtake and dropped to the back of the pack. So the team orders definitely added something there, as I felt like an idiot afterwards :D Not a huge thing, but nice small detail.
Multiplayer seems to be great. I was doubtful about the "gaining xp" and "buying cars" business, but I have to admit that it adds more depth to the game mode. There are loads of options, from cups, single races, and time attacks (with everyone on track at once), to something called destruction derby, which I have not yet tried as I have little interest in that sort of racing, but it shows some variety nevertheless. Being able to have your own club with friends or others is a great addition, from creating liveries to trying to finish well to gain reputation. There are quite a few maldonados out there, so sometimes patience is tested.... very much. I guess you could find a group or a league, but most my experiences have been fine, and the racing is surprisingly good, especially as the damage tends to take the crash heads out quite soon after the start. Damage is nice by the way. Nothing spectacular, but done very well still.
So, like said in the beginning of this review, the game is good. To me it felt like a good deal as well, as it was £29 on release, as opposed to the usual £39-£59 most new games seem to be. I'm sure people who bought Grid2 might feel differently, given that the game is less than a year old, but myself not being one of those people, it felt like great value. It's a solid racing game, and I'm going to spend a lot of time with it I'm sure. Hope this review is helpful to someone!

Crea is a cute pixel like game much akin to Terraria. You harvest items like trees and minerals and then research these items so that you can craft them into different objects. There's a lot of exploration to be done which involves walking on the surface of the world or digging below. Beneath the surface you will find creatures, different kinds of minerals and treasure chests. The treasure chests can only be opened with keys that you can find by smashing pots or even by picking the locks using a lock picking skill which can be acquired by leveling up. There are lots of other skills you can acquire in different categories. If you explore a lot then your exploration XP increases and you can spend those XP on different skills to do with exploring like jumping higher or running faster. If you fight a lot you can use the XP on different skills to level up your weapons etc..
I have started to enjoy this game now but I have to say that you need to be VERY patient and do a bit of research into how this game works. The GUI is a bit confusing when it comes to crafting and in my opinion it is just harder to craft things than it should be. Perhaps its because I have never played a game like this before but I found it really difficult to work out what to do to start off with.Some people like the fact that you have to work out what to do whilst others prefer knowing from the off how to do things. I had difficulties with equipping items I had created and found the whole crafting side very frustrating. After 5 hours of playtime I am starting to figure out the procedure. First of all harvest your items whether its by chopping down trees, killing monsters or digging the ground. Eventually you will have enough resources to craft a research bench. Once that is crafted you can research into the resources you have found which will give you recipes for new items i.e. better weapons, furniture,spellls etc... Once you have these recipes you need to craft a work station to build them. If your inventory is full and you craft the item then the item will fall to the ground! You can buy another inventory bag or craft a chest to put your things in though, however I havent found enough resources to craft one yet.I think there is going to be a lot of grinding in this game to get the resources you need to research and craft items to eventually explore further away lands. The further away you venture from your starting point the more difficult it becomes and you will find yourself being killed by one hit of a flying fishes tongue or something. Once you have upgraded your character and have better armor and weapons then you can expand your horizons a bit and even visit other worlds through teleporting through the crystals that are laid out throughout the world. The graphics are nice if you like pixel like sprites and the music is relaxing and calming. The game got released yesterday and Jasson the developer seems very nice and responsive to any suggestions you might have.
Overall I would say that if you like these types of games then it is a very good example of one. It has a charm about it and you find that you can play it for hours and not get bored. Try not to get too frustrated with the crafting side of things. It may seem frustrating and baffling at the time but you soon get used to it and then you will find that you proceed quicker. Even though there is a basic tutorial system it is not enough to answer all of your questions I found and I had to research the internet or ask friends how to do things. This is an area I think can be improved on. The game is quite difficult to start off with and you will find that you wont be able to venture too far away from your starting point without leveling up and getting better weapons. With Steams refund policy theres no excuse not to try it out though just be careful that you don't accidentally play over 2 hours as this game has a habit of devouring your daytime.

In may 2011, terraria was released, pioneering the 2D sandbox genre. At its time it was a pretty minimalistic game with no story and limited content, but over the years it gained more and more content that eventually made terrraria one of the most underpriced games on steam.
With the success of Terraria, other developers began taking an interest in making their own 2D sandbox games. There were a lot of promising ones that went into early access, but they quickly found themselves unable to compete with terraria that already had a good headstart and was continously being updated. Those that did make it out of early access have all been failures.... that is until now. 5 years after the release of terraria, Crea has just become the first good 2D sandbox game to be released since terraria. Crea is better than terraria in some ways but also worse and I will explain in detail all these
Here is how Crea is better than terraria:
- Crea has a backstory that gets revealed as the game progresses.
- Crea has slightly better graphics.
- Crea has a leveling up and research system that creates a sense of progress and pretty much eliminates the need for a guide NPC.
- Crea has a tutorial that helps guide the player in the very beginning. luckily, the game is fairly intuitive once you get used to the new system in comparison to terraria.
- Crea has better native modding support than Terraria.
- Crea does not require a wiki in order to play and discover the world on your own.
Here is how terraria is better:
- Terraria is underpriced, crea is fairly priced.
- Terraria has more content, although this could change since terraria has reached its limits whereas Crea will continue to get updates going forward.
- Terraria performs better, lower PC requirements, more optimised code.
- Terraria's music is slightly better.
- terraria's controls are slightly better.
All in all, if you are looking for a 2D sandbox with a more RPG feel to it, Crea is recommended over Terraria. If you are a fan of terraria who is looking for something new but similar, Crea is recommended for you. If you want more freedom in what you do in the game, dislike a RPG progression system, or want a lot of content then terraria is recommended over Crea.

This little/big title has elements of several games that tried (and continue to try), yet even with big name publishers at times, failed. This one got it right.
Let me explain....
There are several space strategy titles out at present, some of which seem enamoured with "Battlestar Galactica"'s Season One, Episode One "33".
One such title is "The Fleets of SOL", a partner title to "The Battle of SOL". But, unlike "Nomad Fleet" ("NF") it has stuck firmly to the formula of saving transports and 'jumping out' before becoming overwhelmed (which happens - a lot). Unfortuately for "TFoS" this is where the gameplay basically ends, whereas "NF" expands.
You have the misnamed rogue/FTL element of a starchart to plan your jumps across the maps of course, and I say misnamed as it is now so common that it's semblance to "FTL" is barely worth mentioning.
"Ceres" has it, although graphically more elaborate, as does "Battlevoid Harbinger" and "Distant Star: Revenant Fleet", "Infested Planet"....ad nauseum. Let's just call it for what it is now - a 'Jump Map'.
As the previous titles have much in common, in that when you reach a sector you have several options of buying, repairing, interracting with species and of course fighting they might be forgiven for falling into a pool indistinguishable from one another.
"Nomad Fleet" is different in that it is a real space RTS, with the premise of jumping your fleet across a star map to survival, reaearching, building, harvesting and fighting as you go.
This is a game light years better than "Into The Stars", more elaborate than "Battlevoid Harbinger" and more accessible than "Ceres", a game published by Iceberg but indecipherable in it's gameplay. A game, in other words to avoid.
One comment I hear most often is the camera control. It's fine. You want a bad camera, play "Shallow Space" - it's woeful, even after just being upgraded. Really, the worst i've encountered in a long time.
Bottom line, this isn't "Homeworld 2.5" but unless you are looking to sink 30-60 minutes into a single mission then that's a good thing. It is "Homeworld Lite", though in many regards. The mechanics you are familiar with are there; the graphics are detailed enough to be immersive; the soundtrack is very atmospheric; the camera quite satisfactory. The missions enjyable.
Looking to play a "Homeworld" type of game, with BSG elements and don't have the time to sink in a heavy "HW" session then there is pleny to like here, given also the variety of missions. Easy to learn, quite easy to master, it will scratch that itch that many others, some mentioned here, have failed to deliver.
Final Verdict: 8/10

Having played it from the start for a good amount of hours and having lots of experience with 2D Sandbox games as a whole I would like to share my thoughts with you folks!
Crea is a truly refreshing game that goes in a lot of different directions , most notably it's very much an indepth RPG game compared to others in the genre like Terraria/Starbound where most of your character relies on what gear you're wearing. In Crea however you'll be leveling up your character through lots of different means , by crafting , combat , exploring , magic and gathering too. This works nicely as you're always working towards something on your character and you can't just rush it down in no time , the progress you make feels meaningful and thus your character ends up being a lot more valuable and unique , especially as you'll be able to divide up 2 points to stats per character level up. This allows you to tweak some stats your way as much as you want , want to be more tankier? Get more health and so forth.
The research system is also a thing of great fun and really allows you to start from scratch in this game and just work your way up , you don't really have to check wikis or anything like that instead you'll research materials and gain new items/gear to craft that way. It really makes for a good incentive to gather new items , to find new biomes and to kill to new monsters and bring that all back to base to see if there's anything new hiding within the drops!
I love the crafting system aswell as you're able to in a very similar fashion to Final Fantasy XIV take part in a crafting minigame for pieces of armor/weapons to try and make the quality better , to give it a better roll in stats and potentially lots more stats. You can also just craft the old fashioned way and hope RNG smiles in your way , so either way it's a very nice bonus!
The aesthetic to Crea I've loved from day one , especially since I spotted the first boss , to me it has a unique style that differentiates itself from other 2D Sandbox games superbly. Music wise it's such a relaxing damn game , especially the main theme just tinking away in the background as you go mining or just walk around this strange world is a great joy.
All in all I very much enjoy Crea and really wanted to do my part and provide my side of why I dig the game and whaat makes it unique. If you want to see something further indepth on it I'll include the video I made on it originally down below , thank you guys a lot for reading and hopefully it wasn't a terrible read!

This is a pretty short game.  There's definately some replay value there, with the multiple fleets and randomized sectors, but to be honest, most people will probably play through maybe twice.  I'll start by saying it's fun!  It feels like Homeworld, as many people have said, and wasn't too bad all things considered.  I got it 50% off for $5 and don't regret it.  $10?  Maybe with some interface tweaks.  Keep that in mind.  This is a thumbs up, and it was definitely worth the $5.
So, on to the bad.
Fleet controls are...  well, there's no nice way to say it.  They're bad.  The 'list of ships' on the bottom shows a full icon of selected ships, but you have to scroll down !! with the incredibly wide, one-ship tall menu...  Not scroll line by line, but you can get stuck halfway between lines.  Selecting a particular single ship is near impossible, or even a particular class of ship if you have too many fighters.  Which you will, because...
Anything other than fighters and corvettes are p a i n f u l l y s l o w moving, to the point that they're basically useless (short of extra carriers to carry more fighters).  One awesome aspect to games like homeworld were that different ships had different uses.  In this game, it kind-of works, but because of how hard it is to arrange a fleet (or the impossibility of getting ships to move together), any use of frigates or larger becomes pointless except as 'close in defense' of the mothership.
Research.  Okay, that's fine.  Let me upgrade my ships and unlock new ships.  I decided to sit and defend a space station because it had a 'never before seen class of ship' inside and it needed time to repair.  I figured I'd get the research item or something to be able to build it.  Nope.  Sacrifice half my fleet for a single 'destroyer'.  Oh well.  Games like this are like that.  But the issue with research is kind of like that.  You can finish all the research within the first or second sector and never see another bit.  It's a superfluous feature that's kinda useless.  But hey, unless that research involves strengthening your fighters, it's kinda pointless anyways.
Camera controls.  Oh god, the camera controls.  Rotation is around a spot just barely in front of the camera, unless you're 'focused' on a ship or group, then it's around them.  Panning breaks focus, and is incredibly slow.  Dunno what to say about it other than that.  The camera controls are pretty bad.  Not unusable, but...  Feels like half the time I'd be commanding my fleet was spent trying to move the camera in a way that I actually can do so.  This is especially bad after a mid-mission cutscene, since it doesn't revert the camera back to your fleet (and you may not even realize the 'cutscene' is over until you're taking damage).
Resources.  Seems kinda weird to be honest.  If you don't hit the right sectors, you might never see any resources at all.  Which would be bad.  Some levels of 'randomization' need to be a bit less random, sometimes, it seems.
All in all...  I feel this game might have been prematurely released.  All the little balance issues and interface/control issues could easily be ironed out with a bit of testing.  I don't regret buying it, but I think it needed a little bit more polish.

Like flash games? Well here's an over-glorified flash game for you. In Survivor Squad you control up to 4 members of a squad on missions to eliminate all zombies in an area, exploring and looting as you go about it. You can then craft new weapons and supplies at your bases, which cost those same resources to establish. You spend gas to travel from area to area, and there's a store. The fact that I can tell you everything about the game four sentences says a lot about what you're getting here.
-The controls are horrendous. your squad has really little to no AI to speak of. you have to tell them where to move, where to turn, and occasionally where to attack. If they're alone and a zombie sneaks up behind them, they're dead because apparently they didn't hear it a flesh-eating monster running up behind them and think to turn around and shoot it. They only ever turn to shoot something nearby them if a teammate spots is spotting it beside them in their cone of vision that extends about four yards in front of their face, because hooray near-sightedness. And they also don't start shooting until the enemy is halfway into their cone of vision. Making guns nearly-useless, due to the fact that they also refuse to reload by themselves. They'd rather stand still and get eaten than reload. No, YOU have to select them and hit R manually, or they're ♥♥♥♥ed. You also cannot tell them to turn and face a new direction without moving first. Which is a hell of a ♥♥♥♥ing hassle.
-The "Story" is pathetic. After going easy on you for the first few levels, prepare for story-based missions where you have to help some guy, or retrieve some item, while pushing against an UNLIMITED tide of zombies until you accomplish your goal, with your UNLIMITED ammo, where enemies charge you from all directions, leaving you finding your squad walking back to back a few feet at a time in what is the most boring mission layout I have ever seen in a game.
-The voice ac- oh wait, there was no voice acting. Or maybe there was and it was so bad I didn't remember it. I'm going to stand by saying there was no voice acting. Leaving you to have to actually READ things others are saying while your squad is being eaten alive because you forgot to check the bottom of the screen to see if they were out of ammo and needing you to hold their hand and hit R.
I'd tell you everything else that's wrong with this game but there is literally nothing else to criticize, the game is too small to have anything else to criticize. At least it has two other game modes, survival and sandbox. Sandbox being essentially story mode but without the story-driven♥♥♥♥♥♥missions, but it also has no ending as well. Just repetitive gameplay until you die or get bored.
3/10. If I had no other games available, maybe I could push myself to finish the story mode at least, but thankfully, I do have other games available, and if you do too, do yourself a favor. Steer clear so far of this game that you forget it exists.
