I want to clear up that im not going to include Grid 1 to this review.
Gameplay on the tracks are mainly based on acrade style racing. Its all about investment in a new league of sport and becoming the number #1 contender and the number 1# fan.
What I like about Grid 2 are the tracks. They are fun and challenging to race on in career mode and online. The car personaliztion is near enough good, throwing in real life sponsors to put onto your car and personalize.
I was disappointed with the physics in use of the cars as the developers focused on the powersliding instead of clean turn exits to build better momentum through the corners. You may think thats essential for a great game but the handling will lead you to wreckless driving in most modes challenged on. Online as an example is almost unplayable for these reasons because players cant take full stable control around the corners for a clean race.
Another thing I was disapointed in was the input controls on the game. For a controller it wont be much of a problem driving cars but for keyboard users it will be. Most racing inputs ive used was the simple w,s,a,d & (Arrows) and have no issues playing them smootly. For Grid 2 its difficult as its not keyboard friendly in a way of keeping your car stable around the corners and attempting most clean races. Ive tried both controller (F710)  & keyboard and its a major difference how you perform in the game.
Cockpit is not required in the game which is another downside for a latest racing release. DLC packs have been scattered around as typical developers want more money off you.
Pros:
+ Tracks to drive on
+ Personalztion
Cons:
- Controls are unstable
- Not Keyboard friendly compare to most racing games
- No Cockpit
- Codemasters greedy DLC Schemes
- Graphics are not as good for its age

TWoM is, in a word, shallow. It's not terribly hard to predict the sorts of basic dilemmas the player will be presented with, but it is surprising how poorly they are executed.
I raided an elderly couple's home and the old man followed me around trying to guilt trip me. Once he started repeating lines, though, I remembered I was just playing a video game. I accepted a stranger into our home but nobody interacted with her at all. In fact, besides mechanics-related dialogue ("This shovel is doing its job." and "I'm glad I have this shovel" - yes, those are two actual lines from the game), the characters only assert their humanity through short blurbs in their bio.
The game has a needlessly confusing interface. What does this circle icon mean? What effect does this item have on the person using it? What is the difference between "parts" and "components"? Why is overflow text and inventory always handled by dragging instead of scrolling?
This is just a survival game with shallow, repetitive guilt trip elements. Imagine the depth of a horror game that just throws cheap scares at you every 5 minutes. Now imagine that there's actually only two cheap scares - a ghost that shouts "boo" and a skeleton that charges you. That's the depth of TWoM.

Production Line is management/strategy game and has the potential to become so much better, though even in its current state of development it is totally playable and great fun too.
I highly recommend this game!
Version 1.32
Pros:
+ Challanging without being impossible.
+ Good and improving AI for competitors and customers.
+ Stable and runs well even on older systems.
+ Map editor (though basic) is included.
+ Recently added Tutorial is a great help for new players.
Cons:
- Early Access so bugs are to be expected, though i have not had any 'game breaking' ones.
- Still work to be done on game balance for player research (to easy/to quick IMO)
- Currently no 'Sandbox' Mode (check the forums though for ways around this)
- No end game scenario / long term game balance/achievement still needs work
The objective of the game is to build an efficient vehicle Production Line by placings 'slots' that make, fit or manufacture parts for your vehicles. You link the 'slots' with conveyor belts and provide resources to these 'slots' via resource conveyors from fixed points around your factory. The finished vehicle exiting your factory for sale via fixed 'Export Slots'.
With different shaped slots, conveyors that cant cross and limited factory space you start to see where the challange is, fitting it all in as you expand.
All the ususal suspects are there for a game of this genre, a comprehensive research tree, marketing and design considerations for your vehicles, pricing and cost of manufacture vs importing pre-made parts. Also cosmetic choices for car colour and the factory.
...and best of all an active Developer passionate about the game.
Cliffski (Cliff Harris) has been producing regular Dev Blogs over on You Tube and they are are worth your time to watch. If you would like to more more about the coding behind the game Cliff even goes into that in a few of them.
The forums are active with a great player base offering up bugs and suggestions and Cliff is very active there and we have already seen player feedback influence good changes in the game.
Cliff has a strong vision for the game which he is always driving towards and this in turn leads to regular updates for both bug fixing and new content.
If you like this genre of game your money will be well spent supporting Cliff and Prodution Line. I have had many hours of fun out of this already and there are still exciting developments in the pipeline.
I thoroughly enjoy this game.

I've put about 3000 hours in to DotA 2 before starting Battlerite, and I believe this is a much quicker way to get my daily MOBA fix.  If you're tired of needing to find atleast an entire hour of time to play a single match, where most of the time you'd be farming, then Battlerite is for you. Summary at the bottom.
You start with a hero of three categories; Melee, Ranged, and Support, and their roles are fairly self explanatory.
Melee is a dps, which is usually tankier than the other classes
Ranged is a dps, which is a bit quicker and higher damage than the other classes
Support is a healer/protection class, mainly meant to protect your teammates as well as possible.
When you choose you're hero, you'll find that you have a basic attack on your left click, 4 abilities bound to Q, E, R, and right click, and an ultimate ability bound to F.  For balancing, many of the heroes have similiar loadouts, with animations and ability values altered based on role.  You'll usually come across abilities like; Quick Mobility, Ranged Nuke, AOE, Counter, Reflect, Shield, Heal, Root, and others.
After that you'll be given 5 points to upgrade abilities as you think you would need for that match.  For example, one support hero, Sirius, has a heal bound to right click, and you can choose to upgrade that heal so that when it is used on a nearby ally, it also heals Sirius for a small amount, but upgrading that ability means that you have one less point available for your other skills, most likely lowering your dps for that match.
After choosing your upgrades and abilities, you'll be in an arena with your team and play a best of 5 match, with the last team alive winning the round.  A round lasts between 1 and 3 minutes, with an entire match therefore being between 5 and 15 minutes.
Battlerite is absoutely beautiful.  Even with many skills being similiar to each other, every character has a motif, and all of their skills will reflect that.  Heroes are unique and therefore easily recognizable, even without having to spend hundreds of hours memorizing abilities and traits.  Abilities are telegraphed enough that dodging your enemies is possible, but not overly easy, and it makes the game all the better for it.  Maps are simple, and all follow the same basic layout, but still have enough variation that you can easily distinguish between them, without the possibility of getting lost in the fight.
Battlerite, like other games in the MOBA genre, have a rotation of free heroes that changes week to week, that allows people to get used to many characters without having to spend a lot of in game currency, but they also provide a real cash buy out option to own all the current and future characters indefinitely.  Like I've said before, there is a very basic combination of abilities that is the base of all the heroes, that changes slightly between each one, which means that once you get used to the game, you'll be able to play all of them to some degree of mastery even if you've never used them before.
Since there is no items and no leveling, the technical curve of Battlerite as compared to DotA or LoL is much lower, but the mechanical skill is just as higher or even higher.  This game highly relies on your reflexes and quick decision making skill to determine victory, as opposed to the "Macro" of other MOBA's.
The only other issue some players might have is deciding what you would do with your 5 upgrade points, and how to decide how to allocate them.  The way the game fixes this is two-fold.  The first is that they give you a "Default Loadout" which is pre-designed choices that are pretty good given highly varied situations, kind of a catch all that isn't that best in any situation, but can be used in almost any one with some degree of success.  The other way is that they allow you to create your own custom loadouts that you can save to characters and choose at your own discretion.  You might have a character that you have one loadout that is your idea of maxed damage input, one of maxed mobility, one of maxed survivability, or some mix of them.
This game is a fantastic example of a Free to Play game.  All heroes can be purchased with in game currency, or with real money, but either way they will be equal, with payment method not having an effect on gameplay.  You can earn in game currency through weekly and daily quests, as well as achievements for certain tasks you can perform in game, such as playing 3 different support heroes, or leveling your account by playing matches.  The only thing real money can buy you is cosmetic items for those heroes in the forms of lootboxes.  Since there is nothing gained by playing certain heroes often, the weekly rotation means you can try characters at their best and with no disadvantages.

A little bit sad really; I was excited given the game's looks and ideas - Homeworld with roguelike elements, of all things!
Unfortunately the game is desperately in need of some more polishing.  While it seems stable so far, the interface and gameplay are rough around the edges and lack features I'd personally consider important, like the ability to order craft to escort or guard.  Controls and camera could do with reviewing, often feeling sluggish despite fiddling with settings, and doing counterintuitive things.  At one stage for instance, I was instructed to switch from the established right clicking to issue a particular order, to using the left mouse button under particular circumstances - minor I know but the sort of peculiar decision can lead to scuppering a set of commands.  As for the UI. the most immediate example is a lack of ways to organise selected craft or even a default logic - whatever you select is simply in a long list of icons with no grouping or attempt to order them in any way I could divine.
Further the audio feels rather flat across the board, albeit unoffensive.  Except perhaps for response voices, which felt silly and overacted, and became grating rather fast.
Finally the written elements - both narrative and dialogue - could desperately do with going over by an editor.  While I didn't see any outright mistakes, the phrasing was often peculiar and clumsy, explanations obtuse, and all around 'People don't talk like that!'
In the end I would call Nomad Fleet a Homeworld clone right down to the UI design - which is no bad thing in and of itself! - with some really nice ideas but lacking many of the features that Homeworld did brilliantly /despite being the first game of its kind/.  There's no escort functionality, no formations, let alone the ability to designate wings.  Yes, there are control groups, but a game like this - and again, a feature Homeworld had - benefits enormously from the ability to have craft form wings within those control groups rather than operating as a single blob.
So again, a little sad - moreso for feeling I should give a negative to recommending.  The game is obviously trying and I almost want to recommend it simply for that but.. well.

5. It will give you a list of programs. Select "Rollercoaster Tycoon 2 Triple Thrill Pack" it will begin to detect issues with the program
6. Select "Troubleshoot Program"
7. It will give you a list of boxes. Select "The program worked in earlier versions of windows." Then select "Next."
8. It will give you a list of previous versions of windows. Select "Windows XP service pack 2." Then select "Next."
9. Test the program. DO NOT CONTINUE PLAYING. Exit the program if it does work which it should.
10. After you exit select "Next."
11. Select "Yes, save these changes."
12. Select "Close Troubleshooter."
13. Your game should work now. Enjoy!

So, this is a game that, through the rough road that Dungeons followed, has ironically come full circle to become a partial shameless copy of Dungeon Keeper. Now you might be saying to yourself, "why buy a game that's a copy of an older game," and normally I would be saying that to myself too, but try playing the old game on a current pc. The reality is that, when Dungeons came out, everone started comparing it to the old masterpieces, and mostly unfavorably. Kalipso seems to have taken the hint, swallowed some pride, and went all out to bring the fun of Dungeon Keeper back to life with a full slate of new and challenging features into the bargain. They had big shoes to fill; we look back at the old games of the good old days, and they seem to have a golden sheen. I believe they actually had to move to a bigger size for this one. The humor is just as good, factoring in the slight nod they've given to a somewhat younger crowd (16 vs. 18 or 21, depending on how prudish you may be), and the style is familiar without being exactly the same. Fighting across different maps makes it challanging and new. They involve the world in the gameplay in ways that DK never could have, and the cute vs. darkish tension makes me laugh, and maybe you too. I look forward to DLC and see hours of playing this in the future. It's just a good time.

If you like short reviews....then let me just say that 'Homefront' is one of the most disappointing games that I've ever played. If you want to stick around for a bit while I elaborate....then here goes. While the 'Red Dawn' inspired story isn't too bad....the gameplay is super generic. Trust me....everything that this games does....has been done before and done much better. Basically you follow a squad of extremely broken A.I. soldiers and I mean that literally. There will be plenty of times where you can't proceed until your numbskull teammates kick in a door....climb a ladder....or crawl underneath a fence. Sometimes....the person that you are supposed to be following....won't even budge. The guy will just sit there like he is writing his name in his own♥♥♥♥♥♥and you have no choice but to restart from a checkpoint. That's right....I said checkpoint. This game doesn't believe in saving....but that doesn't mean that you shouldn't. You should all save your money and spend it on a game that doesn't feature a rail sequence....where you shoot rockets at trucks....that are actually pretty rocket resistant. Seriously....that sequence is probably one of the worst levels in the history of gaming. Moving on....the graphics are actually quite good....aside from the few occasions where some of your teammates will radiate a glow like they drank the finest water that Chernobyl has to offer. The weapon selection is decent....and you can switch between two firearms at any given time. The controls are fairly responsive....when you are not flying a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥helicopter....that handles worse than a three-legged horse and buggy. Multiplayer is there....but not there at the same time....since nobody actually participates in it anymore. The game has numerous achievements....but I for one am not planning on spending any more time slogging through the kind of game that treats you alright one second....and then turns on you by slapping you in the face....and forcing you to pay for it's own rehab.

Being one of my highest played-games, I am going to have to go in-depth about this.
Here's a quick tl;dr if you're not going to read below - Game's fun, definitely recommend this game despite my lack of friends who wanted to play.
Upon further review of this game, it has extremely high potential. The main problems with it happen to be the neglect it has gained of the past few years, despite anniversary updates. Most of the time the game is in heavy demand of early game rushing, such as bum-rushing for a Titan against your foes or gearing up heavy defenses. Very rarely do you ever see a properly-executed Vasari Loyalist win the game early. Aside from all of that, the Titan progression system is peculiar in design, being almost extremely similar to the capital ship experience system.
The unique amount of the faction splits offer diverse amounts of gameplay, and the amount of danger presented for early-comers amounts to a heavy learning curve should the player fail to adapt. However, should the player adapt and learn the techniques of the AI or players, the environment shifts accordingly, and the same scenario plays for the other AI and players, and should they fail, well, the worlds and asteroids they inhabit will soon fall victim to whomever is nearby and capable.
A quick summary of the entire experience is rather a brief step-back from the normal RTS playstyle, which means instead of taking up dozens of hours or even entire days worth, the Rebellion experience is rather unique in that it can be solved or even executed within a matter of mere hours or even an afternoon. It offers a fresh perspective in which no other can usually compare.

All in all the game provides what is expected with a good interface and a decently paced gold earning/spending system to allow players to acquire more card variety. I would only ask that an option be enabled in versus mode that permits players to match against decks comprised of similar rarit (that would not affect ranking). It would make versus play much more forgiving and enjoyable for players getting started who do not yet have a wealth of rarer  synergetic cards.

Underrated but still underwhelming, Homefront is a game that shows glimpses of promise and has tons of potential, but never fully delivers on what it could be.
Homefront is a first-person shooter set in America during a fictional future in which a coalition of East Asian countries, namely Korea, control vast portions of the country. You play as a former military pilot who is rescued by an underground resistance unit fighting the occupation, with the eventual objective of assisting the scattered remnants of the U.S. military in San Francisco.
While the graphics are undoubtedly dated, the gunplay here is solid, and the game shows you glimpses of this fictional America that could make for an amazing game had they been expanded upon more. Labor camps, fringe societies outside the influence of the Koreans, the resistance fighters or the U.S. government, and so many more areas that could have been expanded upon but never were.
The multiplayer was underrated in its heyday but unfortunately is no longer populated and isn't really worth talking about.
Since you are basically going to get this for the campaign alone, which is VERY short (3 hours on normal), you should only pick this up at a deep discount.

Grid 2 is yet another racing game from arcade racing specialists Codemasters and make no mistake, this is no simulation.  Racing is centred around street circuits, permanent racing venues and a few single stage like events.
There is a wide variety of events available from straight races, time trials, checkpoint races, endurance (7 whole minutes at a time!), drift, eliminator and others.  The best of these is the “liveroutes” events that occur in one of the major cities.  The route is randomly chosen when you start a race and the mini-map is disabled resulting in you having to pay attention to the upcoming corner to judge entry speed.  Though once you have been playing the single player portion of the game for a while it does become easier as the locations while appearing huge are quite limited in how many layouts are available.
The game is absolutely beautiful though, from the various locations like Paris, Hong Kong and Barcelona to all the car models and how damage appears on them.  The game also performs admirably on even modest machines.
My biggest issue with the game is how the cars drive and more importantly how the AI cars drive.  Cars come in two varieties, tail happy and not, that's about it.  Front wheel drive cars drive like front wheel drive cars, four wheel drive cars are glued to the road and for rear wheel drive it's seemingly random whether it's glued to the road or wants to head for the bushes at every corner.  This behaviour tends to drive you to only driving a couple of cars like the Caterham LMP-like track car the Audi R8 LMS.
The opposition AI is also an issue.  Instead of allowing the AI to drive the track and react to conditions and you as they appear, the AI cars seem to be pre-programmed to move around the track in a certain way like robots.  It's frustrating in many ways as you end up making the same passes all the time as you quickly become aware of their weaknesses.  There are also some bizarre changes in difficulty, some races are ridiculously easy on the highest setting while others are quite hard on the lowest.  Both these criticisms could be made of just about every Codemasters racing game, maybe with the next Dirt or Grid they could concentrate on AI?
All in all this is a very decent Arcade racer, it doesn't do anything new or exciting that is deserving of paying full price, but is a good way or wasting a few hours here and there.

Bioshock stormed onto the world stage in 2007, as part of the 'Golden Trio' of Bioshock 1, COD4:MW and Crysis 1, which reignited a vogue in PC gaming. Now, it comes in a Remastered version that allows the more graphically inclined of us to re-indulge in the game.
Overall, I recommend this game without reservation. The concept of Rapture, the ideologies of Ryan, and the ecosystem of characters are highly believable. The art style and music resonate as much as they did a decade ago. The plot is masterful and the gameplay is engaging. I encountered no problems with the Remastered version, everything worked just fine.
There are some aspects which could have been improved. For one, there is far too much hacking: turrets, bots, security cameras, and vending machines all realistically need to be hacked to improve the gaming experience. Especially in the latter parts of the game, it breaks up the action too often.
My other gripe are the plasmids, which I never thought were that powerful after the advent of the Chemical Thrower, which basically can shoot all 3 elements (fire, ice, and electricity). This is an aspect that was improved on in Bioshock Infinite.

I was tempted to go straight from BS1 to Infinite as BS2 isn't really necessary to the plot. I am very glad I didn't skip it. Story is still good. The thing I found the most surprising was how much I loved the drill - So much so that I opted for the Drill Specialist tonic that removed guns.
I highly recommend playing this along with the others.

It's an arcade/sim which does lean much more toward sim than arcade and is the most realistic grid game to date, the only negatives to this game are the racenet website, which you have to use to join, modify or create clubs and the cockpit view while gets the job done and still gives you that immersive feeling, really could have done with a bit more attention.
The online experience is great, smooth gameplay even with players from all around the globe racing together. Great voice chat and mostly grown up drivers. There is a system that punishes players for the amount of impacts they have been in or caused which is proving to help players race more clean.
As for the sim elements of the game, the cars do all have a unique weight and balance feel to them and behave differently under varying circumstances. You have to use your brakes to be competitive in this game and to set the fastest pace. Accelerating at the wrong times or under heavy cornering will produce understeer or oversteer depending on traction, this will throw you off of the racing line or apex which causes you to have to overcorrect the next corner thus, slowing you down and pushing the car to it's physical limitations to stay on the track.
Underrated game in my opinion, it's a shame it's reputation was tarnished from Grid 2 and people aren't giving it a go, or it could have been one of the biggest racers to hit consoles and PC. I hope it eventually gets the credit it deserves. Well done Codemasters, I was skeptical but it has been money well spent.

I played the game for a good five hours now and I can give my first impressions of it. First of all, the thums down has changed to a thumbs up. I'm really enjoying the game so far. Best GRID Game to date
After GRID 2, I was skeptical of the path that Codemasters was taking with the series. GRID Autosport, however, fixed everything wrong and expanded on the series, making it probably my favorite racing game of the year.
Autosport handles more like a sim than the previous two games, but it isn't as advanced as iRacing, RFactor, etc. I'd say it's closer to Gran Turismo and NFS Shift than the first GRID.
- You need decent throttle and braking control, cars will generally understeer
- There is performance tuning (brake bias, suspension stiffness, gear ratios) not as complex as Gran Turismo, but better than other games
- You can practice and qualify before a race to get a better starting position, and you can tell your teammate to speed up, slow down, play aggressive/defensive during a race
The graphics are amazing, but what's better is the level of optimization of this game. On a laptop with a GT 755M, I get 70-90 FPS on high+ultra settings. Most desktops with a graphics card will perform even better, and there's lots of graphics customization in the options. There's even a free official 4K texture pack to download if you choose.
Cockpit view is back, but the dashboard and mirrors are blurred out. For some, this may be a con, but it works well enough when you're driving.
If you're a racing enthusiast looking for a fun game to play on the same level as Gran Turismo and Forza, this is probably the game for you.

So long have I waited for a game like Starbound and Terraria...
Crea fulfilled my wish!
While using already known elements, Crea also throws a great recipe research system into the mix. Innovative, crazy creatures and beautiful surroundings, many treasures to find and randomly generated dungeons.
I have to confess, even after reading the developer's note about buying Crea on official release, I couldn't wait.
Since that's the Early Access version, I will not complain about, but merely mention some negative aspects:
- Before reaching ~lvl 10, the game is incredibly difficult (for a casual player). The monsters are a bit over the top. Especially, if you leave the starting biome too early, you will be confronted with permanent death.
- High level requirements for items: even IF you manage to outrun and kite all the dangers, you might find a chest with very cool weapons...for level 20+. That is, if the chest is not locked in the first place. (In that case, you have to boost your explore skill high enough to enable the lockpicking perk. You will be pleased to find out that you have to craft lockpicks, plus, they have only a certain chance to open chests. Or look for a key within a dungeon)
- the dungeons come with random parameters everytime you enter one (Awesome mechanic). But, you have to figure them out by trial and error. No explanation is given on how they actually affect you or the enemies. This is a minor issue though, because crafting the Dungeoneer buddy will help you sort through the different dungeon modifiers.
- last but not least: at this point, the bowels of the planet ( volcanic fields) are pretty much empty, except for some stray teleporting monsters, who wanted to end their life by blinking into the lava.
As mentioned before, this is absolutely acceptable for an Early Access. And these points don't make Crea a bad game, at all. I fell in love with it. And if you're into exploring, digging, building and crafting, you definetely should give it a try.
Today, the 1.0 build should be released and I am looking forward to it. Get this game, ladies and gents! Support the devs, they created something beautiful, here.

Similar to Terraria you can build new stuff with the resources you find in the world, but in order to build more advanced items you need to do researching using a Research Desk. Luckily it didnt need to be researched before being built.
There are two play modes: build and attack. These can be switched during game play whenever you feel like. But its most likely you need to switch to attack mode when the are monsters attacking you. Each mode have their own hot bars where you can set to the skills/items you want to use at the moment. Skills can be unlocked using experience points that comes from killing monsters, crafting stuff and etc. There are huge amount of skills to unlock and I believe that in the end you will have everything unlocked.
If you really like Terraria, then Crea is the best alternative game. The tutorial could be better, as I played it I had to rely on what I learnt from Terraria in order to progress further, apart from the research and skill leveling part. But the game is really fun to play. It feels like Crea has lots of replayability.

I will start the review with some preface. I am burnt out on MOBA genre. I played DOTA back on WC3 when it was a custom map and played ALOT of Heroes of Newerth, to the point that the genre just is not fun. I hate the type of stress and rage coming from the long drawn games.
So why am I giving this MOBA recommeneded?
The main reason is this is an actual arena fighter. There are no creeps. The cooldowns are short. There is no mana. Just pure brawling. The second reason is the games are short. The rounds last roughly 1 minute to 3 minutes and the game is played as first to three. This brings the stress levels down considerable while still being extremely competitve.
The Main Positives:
+The tutorial does a good job at teaching the games basic such as the EX-Abilities and how some of the more complex mechanics work.
+The heroes feel diverse in style and gameplay.
+You can pick different talents that alter the playstyle of indvidual heroes. That you can pick and customize at the beginning of every match. On top of that you are allowed to see everyone's talents after everyone is locked in which allows the players to come up with counter strategies during the timers between rounds.
+The game has a practice mode (with no CD and Inf Energy options) which allows you to try all the heroes and understand their strengths and weaknesses.
The Main Negatives:
-The game can feel unbalanced at times if you get put into a rock paper and scissors matchup before the match even begins since you pick heroes before matchmaking starts. Talents attempt to balance this but won't help hard counters.
-Chat is DISABLED by default until you enable it yourself.

While not all the planned features made it, most of them I know are challenging features because even Relic (Original Makers of Homeworld) had issues with making them work, they said as much in interviews they gave.
Pros:
Roguelike/RTS hybrid somewhere between Homeworld and Faster Than Light (FTL).
Some decent multi-session replayablility, which for the price is golden in my book.
Difficulty, without having some challenge, your just wasting your brain power.
Consistant Art - (It was not made by the developer, but I don't really care who made the art as long as it is consistant across the board, and it is.)
Cons:
Your overall ability to command ships - It is not huge issues that really knocks this into a con list, it is all the little ones.  The view at times hampers your ability to command, other times it is the ship AI itself, and yet at other times it is the fact its a roguelike and sometimes you just get into impossible to win situations, but makes you feel as if you've done something tactically wrong.
Roguelike issues - One of the problems with "random" is that it is ultimately going to punish you at some point or another, for simply what amounts to a "bad roll". It happened in FTL and it happens here too. Sometimes it can ruin an entire game and it happened to me here too. The difference between FTL and this, is that this takes up considerable more time than FTL, in one play. I could run 10 FTL plays to just 1 Nomad Fleet play - this could be taken as a plus or a minus depending on your personal outcome. For me, having a 4 hour campaign be impossible to win, was flustrating.
Unmet lofty goals - this was made by a single person using Unity.  I realize more than most just what this means to have managed to finish and release a game.  It takes a lot of passion, and a lot of time. That said, the reason why this is listed as a con is that some of those goals just didn't get met.
That takes a lot of courage, and more importantly instills confidence that in future projects he will TALK to his fans and the gaming community about the why of it.
In closing, I would certainly recommend this game as long as you like games of this genre, for those who are on the fence and don't love this genre, I'd say wait for a sale, I doubt any rational person would pile on the hate over a few dollars.

I've had quite a few experiences with open-sandbox games before, but none of them can compare to the experience I had with Crea.
The game visually resembles a Terraria-styled world with a much higher emphasis on character progression and skill-building. If you haven't played Terraria, its a game that is involves lots of exploring, crafting, building and mining to create new gear, items, and decorations for you and your friends. While Crea incorporates all of the core elements of Terraria, it does so in a different way that allows the game to be unique (mining is primarily done at the surface, and combat is more in depth etc.) While the two games share many assets, I will say that Terraria focuses on exploration and that Crea is focused on the RPG elements.
Crea has a very neat experience system that makes everything count. Every item looted, attack used, or ore mined will increase your characters talent in that profession, allowing for upgrades that can be unlocked. This is great because it allows for player to choose how they want to upgrade their character, focusing on ranged or melee combat, or becoming a healing character. It makes the player feel more invested to build their character for online play, and makes mundane tasks feel more rewarding. The combat in the game is made much more advanced by giving the enemies levels to match the player, and when combined with the endless amount of crafting recipes, there's always another reason to improve your characters gear and stats.

This game is pretty impressive considering it is all made by just one guy.
There are just a few rough edges that need to be straightened out.
First off, the camera controls are too slow even on their fastest setting. Commanding units that are spread out over the entire map is a bit of a chore with the camera moving at its current speed. You can hold shift down to make the camera move a bit faster but the difference is only marginal.
Second there is the AI, all carriers will just spew out lighter units that go straight on a suicide run to the mothership. I'm not saying the AI has to be particularily intelligent, however it should have different behaviors that vary based on which faction is controlling the ship. Such as retreating and regrouping when the advantage is lost or just grouping fighters into one force before charging in. In its current state the AI is very predicatable and it makes the game very easy once you know how to prey on its weaknessess. Some variation on behaviors and deployment patterns by faction and location would help immensly in improving replayability of this game.
Overall this game has a lot of potential with just a few things holding it back at the moment. I highly encourage the developer to continue supporting and adding to it.

The hook for buying R.G. is the combat and of course the ships because later on they are HUGE. You start with a fast ship for darting about but lacks fire-power and defence capabilities. A simple sandbox space sim yet entertaining and challenging to keep you engaged despite the short story. Camera view is in 3rd person for traversing the randomly generated galaxies - go to in game options and change camera view to +150 to see a lot more - when visiting outposts the view is oddly first person and this is where you'll: trade/missions/buy tips/hired hand.
First time I played I didn't pay attention to the missions I was taking but you can abandon before starting. The limit of 5 missions was too small for such large maps and the thousands of solar miles needed to traverse. The warp drive is overly cautious so no worries about crashing into anything, be that rocks, planets, enemies or allies - I have however seen the Militia fly into rocks close to stations. The UI does let it down but worth looking beyond this, R.G. looks its best whilst flying.
Starting off it’s best to pick your fights carefully as paying for hull damage is expensive. Thankfully there is no up and down to navigate (KB+mouse or controller works just fine) despite your enemies being able to. It adds moderate difficulty and variety to the play. Enemies don't engage until a certain distance but if you agro too many you can pull them out and take on the faster fighters first.
If you’ve played Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag, well it’s that fighting broadside – R.G. doesn’t hide it’s naval combat style. If you died you reload from the last time you docked, there is no manual saving so ensure you dock before quitting. The music is similar to that of Borderlands series, all tracks are high quality and fits the game to a tea but due to lack of tracks it becomes repetitive too soon sadly.
The game play does get tedious quickly but there’s more to the game such as commodity trading (simplistic stock market style) as this is the key method to upgrading/buying new ships when you get enough cash past the Mark1 upgrades, you could mine for minerals mid game to reap the rewards around asteroid fields as it's less tedious or steal a ships wares. Worth mentioning that the game doesn't tell you whatsoever the price you’ve bought commodities so have a pen and paper to hand or use Google docs in Steam overlay. Events occur in the galaxy that affect prices and there's a good guide on Steam via Reddit that details this.
It’s a game that’s well received for a 2-man studio that runs on just about any PC, here’s hoping Double Damage Games next title is naval-based.
( Sorry if this review seems short but this just about sums up R.G. in the few minutes I had to type this, and as my first space sim. )

So I gave this game a “thumbs up” in whatever Steam’s black and white in a world of gray ranking system calls that. I bought it at a discount, and would suggest that if the high concepts of the game sound interesting that you do the same.
This is a game developed by one guy as his first attempt. Is it a game for the ages? No. Is it a game with an interesting concept? For me, it is. I like the mashup of the concept of Homeworld with FTL style random missions. That's an interesting amalgamation of concepts from my point of view. I'd love it if Mission 8 in HW isn't always going to be the Cathedral of Kadesh. Maybe, like in FTL, it's just some traders, maybe it's an overwhelming fleet of implacable foes that you have to make a fight or flight decision about. Who knows? Not knowing is the cool bit. The Nomad Fleet dev felt the same way and made a game based around that. And I applaud him for it.
Is it as awesome as either Homeworld and FTL in its final presentation? Not for me. In both the technical and aesthetic departments I find it falls short. But should it be? Could it be, given the hoops that one person would have to jump through to make it happen? Well that's up to you. I have to say I can't see how one person could have done it all though. I will say I’m not going to hold one person to the standards of the combined works of the teams he drew from just to mark it… uh, Facebook “thumbs down” or whatever. I’m not buying into that Cluster B binary thing.
Again, this is one guy who wanted to mash together two games, one of which was done by a full-fledged game dev apparatus, with a programming department, an art dev department, with sub departments consisting of 3d, music, Voice, Texturing, Backgrounds and the like, (not to mention Admin, PR, legal and, of course, Management.) FTL was done, albeit by an "Indy" team, but it was just that, a TEAM. And it was a 2D game.
Given that this was made by one guy I thought it was amazing that he had the balls to do a concept of a HW/FTL mash-up and take on ALL the work (or buy the assets on a budget) to make it happen like it did. That's the type of crazy I applaud, and that’s why I give it a thumbs up.
There are *gasp* bugs and such. None of them were "show stoppers" for me. Still, I would watch to see if the developer Is going to patch the game now that it has been fully released.

I decided to buy this game because I love the Dungeon Lords board game made by Zman Games and Czech Games.  I had heard from a friend that Dungeon Lords Board game was based on a  computer game.  After watching trailers for this game I realized it is either based off an early version of this game or based off a predecessor to this game.  In Dungeon Lords board game you build a dungeon as the evil Dungeon Lord and you have imps to mine gold for you, build tunnels, etc.  The Imps are your snotlings or Minions in Dungeons ii.  You also can build traps in your dungeon and hire monsters like Trolls, Goblins , Dragons, Vampires, Ghosts, etc.  The games are basically the same game almost but in computer format as compared to board game format.
As a whole I absolutely love Dungeons ii.  I have completed the campaign and every map including the new ones just added.  I have every achievement except king of the hill and a friend is supposed to help me with that one tomorrow or soon since it's multiplayer.  In dungeons ii which is an RTS (I normally don't like RTS games and prefer turn based strategy so this game is really good for me to like an RTS) you hire snotlings if you are the horde or minions if you are the demons to build tunnels and rooms for you and to mine gold, set traps, admire demons, etc.  You can then do research with goblins or Trolls or nagas or the demon equivalent in their respective rooms.  You can upgrade your dungeon, adventure out into the above world to wreak havoc and mayhem.
After I played the game a lot I decided to read others reviews to see what they thought of the game and I had the same experiences as many of them.  Treasure chests as one person said and I agree are the best trap and they are the lowest level trap.  The reason for this is because the stupid adventurer's in their mad rush for gold will go right after them and not wait for their bard to disable them.  This is not true of any other trap as they will wait for the bard to disable them before adventuring further.  I do like the Rolling stone trap but I think the develops fixed the fact that it could roll over even bards who are immune to other traps.
The demons as I agree with other reviewers are not as good as the hordelings and here is the main reason why.
The fire demons at the low level are not as good as orcs which are the equivalent.  The other problem is that for the demons the admiration chamber is the same as the hospital and that is where they heal.  With the hordelings you only have to throw beds in a hospital and they will lay down and heal.  However with the demons they have to go to the admiration chamber to heal and it requires a minion to sit there and admire them for them to heal.  Also you have to sacrifice a minion to upgrade the demons while you only have to train the hordes.  So clearly the demons are not as good as the minions must dig for gold, dig tunnels, set traps and do everything else the snotlings have to do but they also have to be a sacrifice to upgrade demons which means you have to spend more gold to replace them and they have to admire demons for demons to heal which means they have more duties than snotlings and slows down their other tasks.  They are clearly inferior to the horde which others have also said.
I also feel it would be nice for the campaign to be longer and more maps available as well.  Also I was very disappointed in the fact that you don't get an undead dungeon.  When you go through the campaign and get the nagas to join you, then the trolls it adds them to your army capabilities and when you meet the demons you get to play the demons.  However when you fight the undead in the campaign I figured that you would get to play the undead and then you would be able to build Skeletons, Ghouls, Ghosts, Zombies and Vampires in your next dungeon but you never get the option to build those types of units.  Maybe an expansion in the future will introduce this? It would be fun to get that 3rd faction.
All in all I absolutely love this game.  I have heard references to Dungeon Keeper and maybe that is the predecessor to this game and what Dungeon lords is based on but I don't know as I've never played it and didn't see it on steam.  Because of this game I did buy Dungeons i and The dark lord sequel to it but have not had a chance to play them yet but am looking forward to it.
I would love to see a map creator in this game so that everyone could create their own maps to play.
All in all though I have a few complaints about this game I absolutely adore it and it was totally worth the $39.99 I paid for it.  Or who I am kidding the $39.99 x 3 as I bought it for 2 of my other friends as well.

It had been a good six years without a new Hitman game and finally seeing a new edition to the franchise release felt very satisfying. The game boasted a new, improved engine. Re-done models, high textures and a new crowd system with hundreds of characters appearing on screen at the same time. Furthermore new animations, weapons and overall gameplay mechanics were added in.

Predecessors in the franchise too told a story of their own, but
is the first time we see fully fledged characters with backstories, detailed cinematics and topnotch voice acting from all the supporting cast.

Sadly the gameplay is where
falls flat on its face. Rather than having different assassination levels like in previous games, here you follow closely a plot.


The most iconic mechanic of the Hitman franchise is completely ruined here. Not only are you restricted in your disguise choice, but you're also more easily spotted.


In
we're introduced to the new instinct mechanic. A refillable bar that allows Agent 47 to move past guards undetected, spot usable items around the world and see the move patterns of characters, Not only does this break the gameplay, but if you deactivate it, and it is limited on harder difficulties, the game becomes close to unplayable!

You go through a level of your choice, mark targets and assasinate them in different ways. Later on other players play your contract and try to beat your score.







No. However, it is the worst Hitman game. Playing through the game, you get the feeling that half of it was done by a different team, new to the series. Many of the levels don't fit in with the concept of being a hitman. Some of them are even boring to play! There is some fun to be had, your first playthrough will keep you interested, but not because of the story. And multiple playthroughs are made even easiers with all the new challenges to be unlocked, but be aware!

I started playing this back when it first came to Steam. And I did not like it at all. But it has improved immensely since then, and I can confidently say that anyone that likes a relaxing WoW-like game, will enjoy this.
Pros:
The skills system is creative. Over time you find items that you augment with other items, and if those items contain runes you can choose what's important and add those to your skill bar. It allows you to choose the look of the items too.
The environment, visuals and sound design are actually quite nice if you give them a chance. If you like WoW's cartoony graphics, I suspect you'll like these too.
You can train all crafting and gathering skills. No real need for numerous alts to complete tailoring or blacksmithing recipes.
The quests are no worse (or better, depending on your perspective) than any PvE MMO you'll play. I personally find easy quests enjoyable after a long day at work.
Although there are no dungeons, the game offers good loot progression. Epic loot is pretty epic and that's a good thing for a PvE MMO.
When I first played there were energy mechanics and fast-travel cost real-world money. They have done away with all that BS and the game is much better because of it. The real-money shop seems to be well in control and offers no obvious "pay-to-win" aspects.
Cons:
There is not great depth of strategy against the mobs or bosses you fight. The game is rather simple.
It's definitely low budget. But I think the devs do more with what they have than many MMO developers could.
In summary, I think it's a well done game with a reasonable cash shop, a nice environment, a decent community, and a fun casual experience. Certainly worth a download. And if you don't like it? You've lost nothing but time while trying it out.

After receiving good feedback from the developers, I've been asked to post this as a review.
I just bought this wonderful game today and i've put in a few hours already and i'd like to point out a few minor issues i have, and hopefully something can do be done about them.
Issue #1: During the Campaign i went to pickup a unit such as the Orc, i tried to drop him on the guard room so he would be assigned to guard, the demon-like hand was hovered over the guard room area however, the Orc fell on the outskirts of the room and by that happening he was not assigned to the guardroom. I had to re-pickup the Orc and place the hand over the room in a few different directions because i couldn't tell exactly where he would drop, this was more of an annoyance than an issue i suppose.
Issue #2: I really enjoy the narrator-theme-humor, but some objectives are not as easily completed which causes the narrator to constantly repeat the same line over and over again, becomes a bit annoying - specially when the narrator is semi-insulting me for taking my time, again its more of an annoyance than an issue.
Issue #3: The population cap in the first few missions during the campaign really hindered me when it came to progressing my dungeon - I had to sacrifice workers just to build Orcs to defend my dungeon, and then during the naga mission (which i am currently on) I had to go back several times to either sacrifice workers to build more soldiers, or i had to sacrifice soldiers to build more workers, it was a little hindering on progressing, but nonetheless i got through it.
These so far are my only issues, overall excellent game, I'm a big fan of dungeon management games (I've been playing them since the first dungeonkeeper came out before 2003), I'm very happy about this installment to continue the dungeon-like series, the best part is that it combines RTS with dungeon management.
EDIT: The developers are currently working on all of the issues I've listed here, so props to them and appreciate the hard work they're doing. I sure wish other game developers cared this much about their games.
TL;DR
From an avid RTS and Dungeon/resource management gamers point of view, 9.5/10 highly recommended

Tl;dr - great game and you should pick it up when its on sale. But it has some flaws.
I have dumped multiple dozen hours into the base version before I tried rebellion on steam. I really liked the game, its just so unique and gives you basically everything one could ever want.
For couple euros this costs during sales I would definitifely pick it up again. I never really played mods for this, but they are quite a few you could try.
However I have some complaints, first beeing the poor diplomacy - you basically have conquered the whole galaxy before you make allies or something.
Also I dont really see the big benefit of the DLCs over the base game. Sure titans and especially star bases are fun, but after 1 or 2 games everything just feels so shallow.
In some games I plan every step ahead and rounds take like 30 minutes just because I want everything to work the way I want. But here I find myself switching to times 10 speed after the initial buildup. This is also because fleets are awefully slow. You can send a fleet from on end of the galaxy to another faster then through one planets gravitational field.
Also later on its just spamming units (while leveled up titans are quite a threat still) you have so many diffrent kinds of support ships, but only really few pure fighting ships.
All planets are the same. Yes you have different kinds of planets, but once you research the necessary tech its just like any other (with more or less space)
This are all relatively minor complaints - however for me they still are significant. After every game I finished I have this weird "huh .. thats it" feeling. This game has the problem many strategy games have. interesting starting phase, decisive mid phase and in the end its just hunting down the last ships and bombing down planets. The enemy is done and has no chance to turn the side around. Sometimes games take 10 hours (when u play it slowly and dont use times 10 speed) so wasting the last 2 or 3 without any challenge just by cleaning up the restovers feels a but dull.
The devs should consider making a sins of a solar empire 2 - many things could be handled better and it would probably be the best (space strategy) game ever.
(It could have a lot more features - like stellaris. designing your own nation, ships and things like this. Also some sort of late game challenge. I did not even bother colonizing after the mid phase because I just had no need for more ressources. )

I am going to be blunt: Homefront is awful to the point of irredeemability. It takes all the worst parts of the "Modern Warfare" games and piles on some more crud of its own. The gameplay is terrible; it is incredibly scripted, often for no good reason. The maps have all the appearance of being large and open, but are so surrounded by invisible walls that I constantly felt cramped and claustrophobic. Worse, more often than not the developers didn't even make an attempt to disguise these boundaries with the usual "waist-high fence"; I was just forbidden from progressing in certain directions. And when it wasn't invisible walls that stopped me, then it was invisible mission parameters; stray too far from my AI compatriots and it would be mission over. This meant there was no opportunity for tactical maneuvering; it was down the gullet every time.
Not that staying by the friendly AI did any good; they were some of the most useless allies I have ever had the opportunity to fight alongside. I don't think I ever saw them take down a single enemy. The enemy themselves weren't much brighter - they had lousy aim and bounced rather predictably between two or three pieces of cover - but made up for these deficiencies with numbers. Yes, like all other developers who can't produce worthwhile AI opponents, THQ tried to cover up for their AI's flaws with endless respawning. Like the invisible walls, they rarely made an attempt to disguise the respawns either and I saw more than a few of the bots magically appear right in front of me.
The gunplay was not any more satisfying, and it wasn't helped by the game's use of another tiresome mechanic: the endless scrounge for more ammunition. I really miss the days when I could carry 600 rounds of ammo and not have to go looking for a new gun every two minutes or so. Mandatory stealth missions and♥♥♥♥♥♥poor vehicle sections just added to the disappointment.
Then there was the story and setting, neither of which was convincing in the least. The concept - American resistance fighting a guerrilla war against foreign occupation - is a sound one and can be quite fun (see "Freedom Fighters" for example) but Homefront fails to capture any of the pathos of such a struggle. The constricted maps - which lack any sort of interactivity - do nothing to sell the illusion either, and the characters lack any depth or consistency. Plus, the developer's artistic cowardice - they changed the enemies from Chinese to Korean when the former complained - did nothing to endear me to the struggle.
Perhaps the only good thing I can say about the game - and this is perhaps damning it with faint praise - is that Homefront was an incredibly short game; it's only five or six missions long and can be finished in about as many hours. But I was tired of the game even before I was halfway done through the first mission and was thoroughly sick of the title by the time I reached the end. The best thing I can say about Homefront is that it is the exemplar of everything that is wrong with modern FPS games and should be used by other developers as what NOT to do when creating their own titles.

This is a game which appeals to those who are fans of racing and motorsport. Codemasters seem to have nailed the sweet spot this time - perhaps more so than GRID 2. Let's begin with the driving. When most games try to do "simulation", this usually translates into unnecessarily dull driving with plenty of understeer, no sense of speed, the inability to drift and the inability to turn while braking. In Autosport, you still get the excitement and sharp handling of GRID 2 but with a lot more control. You can really tell a car's limits jsut from the vibration and tyre noise. I'd describe it as a perfect balance - it's deep but still fun and intuitive. For someone that plays a lot of racing games, I usually find that in some games, you are disadvantaged by not using assists, whereas in this game, turning of all assists and using manual gears is actually rewarding rather than punishing. Whilst GRID 2 was more like a Project Gotham Racing clone, Autosport is more like a Racedriver game. Whilst there is a strong emphasis on teams, the core gameplay experience doesn't feel diluted or pushed aside by unnecessary stats, menus and artificial babble. The main selling point of this game is CHOICE. You can do all the cool street racing and drifts in exotic tuners and supercars, or you can go for a more hardcore time attack approach around tracks or do some endurance racing in touring cars and such. There are five distinct disciplines which cater for a wide audience; and is something I've personally wanted to see as a racing game fan. No longer do I have to go to a separate game for each kind of experience - you can get all the racing you want in one complete package. It's just very much pick-up-and-play. Weekly challenges return in online mode, where you have a target to beat in each of the disciplines. Want to just set a fast lap time with Bronze Silver Gold Platinum to aim for? You can. Want to get an awesome drift going? you can. From street racing to track racing to demolition derby, this game has it all. It is a very high quality game in every sense, from optimisation, game engine and lack of glitches to robust mechanics and controls. The game is highly accessible to those who have little experience in racing games with a plethora of assists and difficulty options, but also gives more seasoned veterans the chance to earn more XP by using fewer assists, higher AI difficulty, less flashbacks etc. There's not much clutter here. You can tune your car, but in a similar manner to DiRT 2 and 3. Just a 5-point slider with short explanations. The only complaint I have is that of interior view. Not only is it the worst I've ever seen in terms of the camera angle, but there is ZERO detail (see screenshots), it's just black. This is dssappointing as this was my major issue with GRID 2. If you can overlook this minor flaw, you will find high quality racing game which is more about what happens on the track than the menus.

To be clear, I never really review games, but due to the low amount of reviews for this game in particular, I figured it would help to write one myself. Furthermore, I'll try to be as clear as I can concerning what I've experienced in this game in the short amount of time I've played it. I'm not going to do a pros and cons, so the review might be a little long. I'd rather discuss what the game offers and leave it at that. If you don't want to read a long♥♥♥♥♥review, skip this one entirely.
Lastly, one thing to note, keep in mind that this game is in Early Access. This means there are some bugs, but none of them are gamebreaking from what I've experienced. For example, I entered a dungeon and was suddenly unable to grapple and another time could not jump to the left or right, only up and down. This was fixed by restarting the game.
I think a lot of people will get into this game because of its similarities to other titles, such as Terraria and Starbound. I personally have played only a little of Terraria and quite a bit of Starbound. To put it simply, the things this game does have in common with those is that it's your typical sandbox: you can build, craft, and fight things, all on your own accord. In the meantime, Crea offers a little more variety than I experienced in the other two, with its skill and crafting system, which seem to have more thought put into them, as well as more freedom. I'll cover this later, but in any case, I believe that this is a worthy alternative to the other titles. I had a lot of fun playing and enjoyed all aspects of the game equally, some more so than I did in Starbound/Terraria. The look of this game, including its UI, might not appeal to everyone, but I liked it a lot.

The skill system is one of the big major upsides to this game, imo. This allows more character based progression, putting aside what armor and weapon you have equipped, and allows more of a rewarding experience. Differentiating from the titles mentioned previously, this game allows you to obtain experience and TP. TP is then used to level up skills and obtain new ones, similarly to an RPG.  It includes categories for Arms, Style, Gathering, Crafting, and Exploration. I'll explain each below:
The crafting system is different from both Terraria and Starbound, in that you need to gather materials and research them to discover recipes. This means, for example, you pick up a material, use your Research Table to research it, and discover a new recipe. Under Recipes, you will see the recipe, as well as outlines of the other materials needed. If you can tell what they are, great. You go get them, research them, and learn the recipe. If you don't, then it's a matter of finding them as you progress through the game and discovering the recipe via researching those materials. As well as this, every time you research, you gain scraps, which can be used to skip finding the undiscovered materials of a recipe and discovering it ahead of time. They can also be used to avoid spending your materials researching.
Furthermore, there's also a Chaos system I haven't really explored yet. I might update the review when I understand it more, but from what I gather it allows you to use skills (obtained via the Crafting category) to increase the quality of items you make via a separate crafting process that is optional when making items. I'm guessing that this is mostly used when making Armor/Weapons in order to apply stats or status effects. Again, I'm not sure, but it's worth mentioning in order to emphasize how intricate this system is in particular.
I only want to cover this because I've seen a handful reviews saying that gathering/digging is too slow. I don't know if these people just didn't get far enough in the game to figure out the skill system, or if they're saying it's too slow no matter (which is kind of pushing it). I want to clarify that gathering is slow in the beginning, but as you obtain new tools and gain TP in Gathering, then use it to level skills that increase the power/reach of your tools, it gets
faster. No problem here unless you're just too impatient to level it up.
I got this game for myself and my boyfriend, who doesn't have that great of a computer (to be honest). Neither of us experienced any lag, issues getting the game running, or setting up multiplayer in the beginning. However, as time went on, the game became unplayably laggy for him. We believe this is due to the large amount of processes this game runs in the background for its UI, called "Coherent UI host". I'm not sure if this is a bug or if it's supposed to do this, but by the time it was running 10 or so of these processes, he could not move or use any skills.
I, on the other hand, had no issue playing for long periods of time and have yet to encounter anything other than the occasional stutter when the game autosaves. In other words, if you have a potato for a computer, it might be a little risky to get this game right at this point in time. I say this because the devs said they would update this game early June, which might fix it. Have to keep in mind the game is still in Early Access, so this doesn't affect my opinion of the game overall and I still had fun playing.

This really comes in handy when getting used to the braking in turns. This game is not a game you can simply swing your back end around the corners in. Once you begin to get the hang of it though, the whole thing becomes satisfying and rewarding. I like the way the different racing specialties are set up in the career mode. It allows you to choose from all but the GRID Autosport Series which is apparently reserved for when you've mastered all the others.
As of right now, I've played through a season in both the Touring and Street series'. I have yet to play any multiplayer so I will refrain from commenting on it until I get the chance to join in.

I wasnt interested in playing another Bioshock game, but since It was gifted to me and I didnt want to be rude I accepted it and gave it a try. Bioshock 2 is set in Rapture again but this time instead of playing as a human, you play as a Big Daddy escort for a little sister. I think the idea of being on the other side of combat as a larger and more powerful entity is pretty cool and less scary going up against splicers.  The story started off with the same morbidness of the first game and I was really turned off to it, due to the fact that you are "forced" to commit suicide in front of your little sister which is really screwed up. But thats Bioshock for you! Always putting you in crappy situations where its kill or be killed and you dont have a choice about it. To save time explaining the story because its almost exactly similar to the first one which I already reviewed Ill just list off the things I loved, and the things I didnt. First the things I loved - Once again amazing character design, being able to walk outside in the ocean because you have a diving suit on is really cool, getting to interact with a little sister and carry her around is super cute and fun! Creepy immersive atmosphere, and lastly being on the other side of the story playing as one of the former antagonists from the other game I think was a great creative idea! Now the things I really didnt like - fighting with a drill is not my thing even though its quick its gross, having 40 splicers coming at you from above and behind isnt fun, and also running out of ammo so fast when the game makes you need it so bad! If you are going to make me go on a massacre then at least prepare me for it and let me not have to worry about running out of drill fuel so quickly, especially bullets. Overall I didnt play much because it was the same morbid death run as the last game, but I did like being on the other side of combat much better it gave me a much more diverse perspective on the story. 6/10. I recommend this over the last game because the story was much better aside from the constant massacres taking place which got really boring, the story was very appealing and interesting.

I think that the game should have remained in early access.  It lacks the polish you would expect from a finished game.
Camera controls are god awful.
-
After reading the forums, it looks like holding [shift] will accelerate the camera's movements.  I think it could be a bit faster, but its useable.  Now if only the functionality was flipped since it's a bit awkward on the fingers.
-
Found out on the forums that you can use the C and V keys to adjust the camera height.
- In order to zoom in on a ship, you need to have it focused.  Otherwise your zoom is limited to "really far" and "far" in strategic view or "isn't space pretty" in normal view.
== You're forced to use certain views to perform certain tasks ==
- The normal view tells you absolutely nothing about the positions of ships and their heights.  Which sucks because this is how you're able to actually zoom in closer.  So without this information, you can't finely manuever the resource corvette to the nearest asteroid so that your resource harvesters would only need to travel mere meters to deposit their inventory.
- The strategic view doesn't let you click on the enemy.  So you generally don't know how much health it has, or what it even is until you flip to the normal view.  Then you're able to select it, and then mouse over the icon to view the tooltip.
== What the hell? ==
-
(A recent patch has added this feature.  This point is now moot)
- When you have units selected, they blink in and out.  When you have a ton of units, it's hard to tell what's selected since everything else is blinking to notify you of events like attacking targets and all that.  Couldn't unit selection have a different color?
- It's like there isn't a select all of one unit type command.  I try double-clicking a specific unit.  Nope, it selects that one unit.  To get this to work, you have to select everything.  Then scroll through the list until you find the one type of unit that you want.  Waste of time and forces you to keep your groups up to date.
- The icons are too small and they rely on tooltips to tell you what ship is what.  At one point I just stopped scrolling through the list of selected ships and just looked for the unit with the 8 sided enclosement box.  That was usually the dreadnought and that was all that I needed.   As a sidenote, there is a setting in the options box to scale up the UI, so you can get larger icons.  Useful for a higher resolution I guess.
- I can't select enemy fighters.  It would help if I can tell how much hp they have left so that I can figure out which ships are effective against them.
- The AI is...stupid.  It generally just rushes.   No real strategy whatsoever.  Once I researched the upgrade to perform a localized jump, I just sent a dreadnought behind the enemy capital ships.  One or two just-launched fighters would usually flip back around to intercept, but everything else continued forward.  Easy way to blow up the spawning ship and save myself the hassle of fighting hundreds of snubfighters.
- Why is nearly every jump point a battle?  Some allow me to bribe or trade, but aside from that everything else has me fighting waves of incoming hostiles.  In one game, I had to fight through 10 warp points in a row before deciding that I had had enough and beelined for a known trade point.
- Why doesn't the jump point ever seem to change?  I landed on an asteroid square.  Mined everything.  Jumped out, then jumped back in.  More stuff to mine.  It was a really easy way to rack up the credits.  By jumping in and out and dealing with the interfering ships, I soon had enough money for all of the upgrades after repeating this like 10 times.
- Limited tech tree?  I kind of wish the larger ships had more upgrades besides strategic jump.  Better weapons and the like.  Only the fighters get this upgrade.
- Poor unit info.  It's limited to a question mark and a general description.  For these types of games, you would have a far more detailed entry with speeds / weapon damage / strengths and weaknesses plus a description for immersive purposes.  At one point I had experimental dreadnoughts.  Was there something special about them?  I don't know, there wasn't even a question mark and a general description for it.  Nevermind obtaining detailed info.
That said, the game has potential...maybe...depends on how much support the developer is going to lend to it now that it's been released in an unfinished state.

I'm not really sure when space westerns became a thing. My secret inner weeb wants to point to Cowboy Bebop or Trigun, but it just as easily could have been Firefly or Starcraft or something else entirely. They're the logical conclusion of humanity expanding into space, really, embracing the freedom of an open universe without the unity or enlightenment of something like Star Trek. This is precisely where Rebel Galaxy lives, in a simple wild west approach to space battles and exploration.
You begin the game by inheriting an old junk freighter from your aunt and running errands in it for an old alien acquaintance of hers. Following the main story missions unravels a lengthy, familiar tale of deep space intrigue and ancient artifacts. This is of course only one option of many in the vein of something like Sid Meier's Pirates! because you can just as easily haul cargo, claim bounties, or pirate convoys for as long as the game holds your attention. A fair spread of ships, weapons, and upgrades are available across several factions for you to spend your hard-earned credits on and advance in power.
The moment-to-moment gameplay of Rebel Galaxy is like an arcadey version of naval combat. Capital ships in this sci-fi reality still rely on broadsides for most of their firepower, so you'll be sidling up to just about everything you want to blow away. You also get auto-targeting turrets and a secondary weapon that can fire missiles or flak, as well as shield and speed boosters to expand your tactical options. I wouldn't say there's a lot of depth to the combat but positioning and prioritizing targets can mean the difference between victory and the cold embrace of hard vacuum.
Unless you get really into the mostly generic story you're going to want to spend most of your time amassing wealth for bigger ships and guns. There's a basic commodity system you can play space trader with that requires some attention to trade routes and emergent events, but most of your time will probably be spent on missions. Each station has a mission board offering bounty collections, blockades, pirate hunting, cargo hauling, and more. These missions are assigned a difficulty based on your ship's current loadout, which is terribly helpful because anything above Average carries a very real chance of annihilating you in an instant.
Rebel Galaxy offers a very promising setup and world to prosper in but suffers from a few issues, the difficulty curve being chief among them. At some point you're going to hit a wall where your next story mission or the only profitable missions are High or Very High risk, and if the enemy composition is not favorable to your particular ship you're going to die very, very fast. Upgrading to a larger ship is the easiest way to climb the difficulty curve but can require a LOT of side missions and busywork if the next hull in line isn't very cheap. People who are easily distracted and habitually clear side missions will fare a lot better than most here.
The further you get the more technical issues you'll see crop up as well. Late in the game I started having mission-critical items disappear and enemy ships not properly register as objectives, which led to some aggravating wastes of time. There's also a lot going on in every star system, with pirates and militia lurking everywhere. This sounds cool at first but missions don't account for or clear existing entities in the mission space, so a Low risk battle against some frigates can turn out to be instantly fatal if the game decides to spawn pirate dreadnoughts in that particular sector.
I've had my fair share of frustration with this title, but most of my time in it has been a relaxing and rewarding romp around the galaxy. The systems you explore are expansive, colorful, and full of debris fields and nebulae to explore for secrets and bounties. Warping around has a great feel to it, with rich engine sounds and visual distortions through space. The twangy western feel is out in full force as well, with plenty of rough-spoken captains to deal with, junky ships to pilot and pilfer, and plenty of wailing country rock to fill the silent void.
At times it feels very much like a friendlier, simpler, offline EVE Online, though it never really matches the same sense of scale or vastness. I mean that in the best and worst ways, too, because it never really aspires to be more than a basic space hauling shooting gallery. And yet, there's an undeniable draw to scraping together the credits to land a new class of vessel and taking it out for a spin in the places you feared to tread before. That's where Rebel Galaxy really succeeds, in giving you a universe to explore and plenty of reasons to see it all.
