Bioshock: Remastered has quickly become one of my all time favorite games. Having finished the campaign, I now look back with fond memories of my time spent in the underwater city of Rapture. Rapture is one of the most dark and beautiful locations of any video game I’ve ever played. At times while playing, I simply had to stop and look out the windows of the city at the detail that went into areas of the game you could not even explore! The story had me captivated from the very first mission, and at times I could barely put the controller down. Characters are so fleshed out that by the end of the game, I feel like I had a personal connection with almost everyone of them. The ending (the good ending, because there are in fact, two) was wonderfully satisfying, finishing the story of Jack in preparation for a new protagonist in the sequel. Game mechanics were also wonderful. I play with a controller, so I am not sure how exactly it would work on a keyboard, but I would tense up everytime the controller would shake with the footsteps of a Big Daddy, cyborg creatures tasked with protecting the Adam wielding Little Sisters. However, hacking mechanics did get dull by the end of the game, causing me to use up Autohacks instead of hacking machinary most of the time. One other downside for this remaster was a few game crashes at points, causing me to lose up to around 30 minutes of progress. While playing, I suggest saving after every 20 minutes or difficult battle. Other than these two cons, this game is a masterpiece. One that I would highly suggest buying. But remember, a man chooses, a slave obeys ;)

Bioshock is a game with a lot to like. With excellent gameplay, art design, presentation and story it has all the makings of a 10/10 game. But it falls short of that rating for the following reasons...
That excellent story can be pretty inconsistent in its delivery. Parts of the game feel like a bit of a chore where those beautiful scripted sequences seen in the first levels have been replaced solely by exposition-filled audio logs. People talk about how Far Cry 3 killed off its most interesting antagonist mid-game. Well, Bioshock made that same mistake back in 2007 and didn't really get called on it.
Overall, the ending just sucks. The premise, the execution, everything about the last sequence sucks. Without giving too much of a spoiler on this ten year old game, it ends with your character getting a huge buff so the levels can spam you with low power enemies and one big boss fight that would have seemed cliche in 2000.
Bugs:
I've seen a lot of people complain about bugs in this remaster. Well, I played about two and a half hours in one shot and didn't experience any, so I can't really comment on that. My first run through on the notoriously buggy 1.0 release in 2007 didn't give me any trouble either, so I guess I'm just lucky.
TLDR: A flawed masterpiece in many ways, but still a good game. People say this remaster had bugs, but I haven't encounted them yet. 7.5/10

All the men died either during the scavenger hunts, or later, so heavy were their wounds. Katia fell into the clutches of heavy depression. She wouldn't eat, even though the food's been coocked the day before, she wouldn't see Franko, who brought the provisions. She just sat there, all day long, crying.
She started to get a bit better the next day, at least enough to answer the door. That's when Zlata appeared. Katia let her in, and the positive energy of the new friend helped her snap out of it. More people showed up, things started looking up.
They had some guns to keep the intruders out at night. They stayed in for the most part, only sometimes going to the hospital. They'd ask the nurses for a bandage, and then loot them behind their backs for drugs, to trade them in later for some food. It was low and dirty, the girls couldn't forgive themselves. But that's what hell is all about.
Then the cold season came. They weren't able to make a heater in time, so some of the people fell sick. Some of them spent all their time, waiting to die. The water collector froze, which meant their food was near worthless. That's when I stopped, 4 hours in. I don't think they can make it, and I don't want to see them all die.
Even though it could've been stronger in some aspects, overall this is one of those experiences everybody needs to go through. Player choice is very strong with this one.

There seems to be a lot of negativity around this game, mostly pre-release so let me offer an up-to-date review.
Survivor Squad is a low budget, indie, top-down survival game with elements like a 'flash' version of Breach & Clear. The game tasks you with controller a team of up to four survivors as you try to eliminate a zombie threat in various areas.
The click to move and hold to set a direction is a nice mechanic however the ability to change facing direction while moving or move backwards etc. would be a nice addition.
Personally I like the way you scavenge to craft and the ability to tell your survivors to switch between firearms and melee weapons to control noise and crowds. The game isn't revolutionising any mechanics and it may be a little light on its mechanics and progression but the gameplay works and I was entertained.
Very inspirational. It's touching at times and it gives me the chills. I rate it 10/10 :)

I am someone who liked Terraria. I liked Minecraft a lot, too. I love open world games that are full of exploration, lots of things to do, and lots of loot to drown yourself in. 2d side scrolling games like this tend to be called Metroidvania games.
I first got Crea many months ago and it was rough, unpolished and hard to play. I waited. MANY updates have come out since then so I decided to give it another try a few weeks ago. I am glad I did.
Crea has an in-depth crafting system that actually takes a bit of thought to figure out. You don't just have materials, you have crafting methods. They call it Chaos Crafting. There's a variety of crafting techniques to apply while you are crafting something. It's up to you to find a combination that works well. If you do, you can get some amazing results.
The enemies in Crea are likewise as well thought out. You can't just run up and whack and enemies like you do to Terraria's slimes. Enemies in this game have different attacks, but they all have certain patterns that you can figure out.
What the game needs most is variety in what the player experiences. Once you craft that next tier of armor and weapons you're off to do more of the same, just in a higher level area, battling the same monsters who are simply higher level. The game does have biomes, but as of this review, they're only surface biomes that don't mean a whole lot at the moment.
However, the game is solid enough and enjoyable enough that the $15 price tag is well worth it at this point. Combat is a blast in this game. Since development is still very much underway who knows what we might see for the biomes or maybe even new, different underground zones.
Crea has a ways to go before it could be a contender for king of Metroidvania Mountain. It's not there yet. It's got a ways to go. But it's certainly headed in the right direction.

Playing the original Wing Commander as a kid, I can say that this game is at least less aggravating than that flustercuck of getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in space, thanks to this game's native third person view, nice targeting systems, and limiting player movement to an invisible, flat "surface" in space. In other words, you can't point your ship "up" and fly that way. You drive through space like in a car, only turning left and right. This might be a point of contention to some, but in combat and while exploring, I found this to get on my nerves in Wing Commander, so I honestly prefer Rebel Galaxy's handling of this.
The music in this game is pretty darn cool. Just watch the trailer on Steam if you want a taste. It works really well and keeps comabt and exploration more enjoyable. That said, it's "more" enjoyable thanks to the music; never really enjoyed the gameplay myself. Everything feels like a big fetch quest, even when the missions aren't fetch quests. You go to a space station, spend money to upgrade your ship, talk to an alien, get a mission, and go to another nav point which requires a couple of minutes of flying in one direction with nothing to do, before reaching a fight that involves whittling down enemy shields and hull, one by one, until they're all dead. Then you fly back to the space station again and repeat. I only played for 3 hours, and I got bored during that length of time.
What's worse, if you die, there is no quicksave or checkpoint system while you're away from a space station, so be prepared to repeat lengthy 2-3 minute space travel segments and 5 minute combat segments all over again, just to get to the part you died on before. Everything has a grindy feel to it: earning money, upgrading the ship, the combat itself, etc. I cannot recommend a game that appears to require many more hours to complete, but which left me bored and wanting to play something else within 3 hours' time.

GRID 2 is an arcade racing game made for players using a gamepad or their keyboard. If you want a realistic racing game, you should not buy GRID 2. I was very disappointed... I preordered it for 35,99€ and I have to say it was a waste of money. Because of that preordering I received a free copy of GRID 1, which was a big reason for me buying the game, because I really liked the car physics and graphics of GRID 1 at that time. Do not get me wrong, I still think GRID 1 is an excellent racing game! Actually it is the best I have ever played. I just can't understand what codemasters tried to do with GRID 2, I just don't get it...
I played the first part of GRID and GRID 2 is a totally different game. GRID 1 had a cockpit view, which does NOT exist in GRID 2! For me personally the cockpit view is one of the most important things to make a racing game realistic. The developers said they invested much time in making the cars behave realistic on the asphalt. They failed miserably... Every car feels the same. There is no real difference. Drifting is totally unrealistic. If you want to drift you just have to fastly turn the wheel to one side, then turn it back to the other side and you are drifting. Normally when you're drifting in a realistic racing game or in reality itself you should lose time, but not in GRID 2. It feels like you always have to drift to maintain your speed. So many good game modes (drift-challenge, touge, profi-touge etc.) from GRID 1 are just left out completely in GRID 2. They tried to put a story into the game, which is actually a good idea. You have to show your skills in different racing leagues all over the world to get their appreciation and win them for the WRC (World Series Racing), a league where the best drivers of the world meet each other on the racetrack. The idea is great, but the implementation didn't succeed... It's always the same: Win in leagues, unlock new leagues, win against those leagues, win the WRC, win in new leagues, unlock, WRC...
If you want to play a realistic racing game with great game modes and a cockpit view, buy GRID 1 instead of GRID 2.
If you already played GRID 1 and think about buying GRID 2, because you liked the gameplay, do NOT do that. You will only be very disappointed. It has nothing to do with the previous version of GRID.

I know I missed the boat on reviewing this game when it was new; but just wanted to say that even a few years later I still find this game fun and wish I had more time to put into it. The Hitman series in general is one of my favorites of all time and while this game isn't perfect it was still really good.
I probably spend more time thinking about this game than playing (or rather the series in general), but it will always be one that I return to over the years.
EDIT: I eventually found the time to 100% complete the achievements and really dig deep into the game.
This game has mixed reviews. On the one hand you have people mad that gameplay changes were made and the levels were more linear compared to previous Hitman games. And I have to agree. The gameplay is closer to splinter cell than it is Hitman.
But still, it's not a terrible game. It's crime is being a mediocre hitman game.
As for the storyline, I don't want to spoil the details but I will say that I really didn't like it... until the end. The ending for me redeemed the entire storyline.
So while the gameplay goes in the wrong direction for a hitman game, the storyline still kind of works as an end cap to the old series.
If you have played all the original Hitman games (agent 47, silent assassin, contracts, blood money) you owe it to yourself to see it through to the end. I promise if you give it some time the game isn't quite as bad as it's first impression.
That's assuming you care about the storyline. If you were here just for the "I'm going to do small contracts and kill people" then you will be disappointed.
The entire game (once you know the final story) turns out to be one long mission from beginning to end. There's very few targets to assassinate and most of them are for personal reasons. You don't get hired out to kill people in this game (well you do but.. you don't get made aware of that until the end and then... well... just play the stupid thing...)
There's also a pretty extensive contracts mode which is a first for the series that is designed based on the old forum challenges that hitman fans used to give each other.
Anyway, play this game as a book end to the old series.
Then come play the new Hitman (2016) season 1 and pray for season 2 and beyond. The new one is really good and brings back more of the Hitman flavor you were expecting.
It also goes back in time, where as Absolution is at the end of Agent 47's ICA career. The new hitman begins at the beginning with his training and recruitment into the ICA (which takes place in the timeline years after his escape from his creators ~ the original clone program was not done by the ICA, he was cloned by someone else then recruited into the ICA, most of whom are not clones... and so on...)

A classic if there ever was one. Never played any of the BioShock games? Get this and immerse yourself in one of the most amazing naratives created in the 2000's.
Compared to the original the remastered version doesn't offer a ton of improvements, though. There are higher resolution textures, better looking UI and higher resolution. Everything looks just a little more crisp. This version of the game also adds the challenge rooms that were originally exclusive to the console releases, an hour and a half long interview with Ken Levine and a museum to walk around in that showcases some of the early concept art of BioShock. Also, it has achievements and trading cards!
People have reported the game being nigh unplayable and crashing a lot, but this has very rarely happened to me. In my entire playthrough it crashed twice from what I remember. They also fixed that your game settings would reset after a crash, so that's one less thing to worry about. I'd say the game is pretty stable, but you'd still be wise to save often and save manually. You can use the quick save feature, but it's been known to corrupt itself on occasion. So don't use it exclusively, also make manual saves in new slots.
When it comes to a value assesment, I'd say BioShock is a game everyone needs to have played once in their life first and foremost. That said, 20 dollars is steep for a 10 year old game that got a small graphical polish. On your first playthrough expect to play a good 25 to 30 hours if you include the challenge rooms. There's some replay value in collecting all the audio diaries and maybe doing an evil runthrough using different strategies.
If you've never played the BioShock franchise before, get BioShock: The Collection (which this game is part of) for 20 dollars on a sale instead and you will absolutely not regret it.

Having played through the campaign and zero amount of multiplayer, I can say the following.
The Good:
1) It's a game that doesn't take itself seriously. Filled with pop culture references, narrated by the Stanley Parable guy (which alone makes it worth buying), the game had me laughing several times.
2) It's a good mashup between a Dungeon Keeper/Overlord type game with a healthy splash of RTS. The unit count you end up controlling is low enough to where you don't get overwhelmed, but still great for those that enjoy group unit control.
3) Great game to stream or record for youtube. People are interested in it, but not a whole lot of coverage.
The Bad:
1) Much more RTS than Dungeon Keeping. If you're just looking to build an automated dungeon, this probably isn't for you. A lot of unit micro-management is needed. This is partly because of my biggest gripe in the game -
2) Bard render your traps completely pointless. Traps are pretty effective if they go off, however probably like 90% of waves of enemies coming to your dungeon will have Bards who are immune to traps, and disable them in an aoe. The rest of the troop hangs back and just waits for the Bard, and then they just romp through like the traps don't matter.
I have had people say oh, just use spells to burst him down, except that's multiple clicks and usually takes 4-5 hits to kill a Bard (and that's if they're not healed). Regardless of how you can finagle to kill him off, here's the bottom line: Traps are not nearly as cost effective in the game as just spending your money on units and unit upgrades to murder your dungeon invaders, and that's about as disappointing as it gets. As stated several times, this is a combination of Dungeons meets Dungeon Keeper.  I have played for almost 12 hours, finished 7 missions in the campaign, and still can't get enough.  I do enjoy the game.  That being said, here is what I find that could use some work and/or polish:
1)  Floating hand accuracy is inaccurate - When trying to pick up units in a crowded area, be it tools, beer, or several creatures, it is difficult to grab or highlight the exact creature I want.  The hand "pointer" seems to be around the lower part of the pointer finger close to the palm.  Hard to grab units easily and quickly.
2)  Narrator - While I have found the narrator's humor to be exceptional, there were times I wish he was shut up because he was the one being the &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;.  I like to play out my campaigns over hours, trying to research everything and develop my entire dungeon, and I felt the narrator was trying to keep me on the game's timeline instead of my own.  Also, the advertising for Kalypso games, while funny and original, did get old after the 6th to 7th one.
3)  Unit selection in the dungeon vs. the overworld - I really wish I could select my units in the dungeon as easily as I can in the overworld.  I may be missing a shortcut or other function for selecting in the dungeon, but as of now, having to pick up every unit I want to send to the over world, one by one, is very frustrating.  Especially when I have units set in a guard house that wander over to get beer or pay and I pick them up accidentally and send them to the overworld mission.  It would be nice to be able to shift+double-click on the population count icon to pick up all units of that type into the "hand" and deliver them to the overworld.  Or, let me set the rally banner in the overworld and have the units automatically go to the overworld tunnel from my dungeon.  However Kalypso wants to fix it, I feel it is an issue that should be addressed.
4)  Pay vs. thirst frequency - I found I had no problem keeping up with the thirst demand (experimenting with only 1 dispenser, then 2, and finally 3) and after setting up the 3rd beer producer for a heavily populated dungeon I had excess beer production with no thirst issues, but the pay frequency seems to be, well, too frequent.  I haven't timed it yet but I do know that I was setting up a tinkerer's shop right after a payday hit and it couldn't have been more than 2 or 3 minutes when the next one hit.  With the slow rate of gold acquisition from the "snots", i feel the payday frequency should be lengthened slightly between pay days.
5)  Unit pathing - I noticed when I sent units into combat, more often than not, my orcs at the front of my army would begin moving toward the enemy, come within a few feet of the enemy, then stop for approximately 2 to 3 seconds (while being damaged), then continue foward and engage the enemy.  It has happened on every campaign map I have done and is quite annoying.  I don't know if it's pathing or just a bug, but I feel it could use some attention as it does affect my game play and game enjoyment.  Like I said, it does get frustrating, especially when encountering a large opposing army.
Well, that about sums up what I can remember so far regarding the issues I have found that I feel should be addressed.  Now, on a positive note, I feel the game has been beautifully designed.  I do love the narrator's humor and story telling.  Very unique.  The graphics, though cartoonish, are very visually pleasing and gorgeously done.  The sound is clear and helps me transport myself as if I am really in my dungeon or the overworld area.  Other than the interface issues above, I had no problems adapting to the controls.  I am still working on memorizing the hotkeys for everything (as there are many too remember), but overall the controls are easily learned.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys dungeon builders and RTS type games.  If Kalypso could keep giving this game attention and polish in future patches, I believe this game could be a very reliable and popular sequel to the previous dungeon builders many of us have come to enjoy and value.

It's sad how the trailer contains several of the best parts of this film.

CinemaSins did a video on this movie.  Those who have watched that video might express disdain for this film, sure, and it's not like Warm Bodies is the 'best film ever' or anything close.
But it's one of those feel-good romantic comedies dressed up as a horror film.  There are plenty of funny parts, and sweet parts, and all in all it's the kind of watch that's completely unexpected.  People come to films about Zombies usually for the thrills (or if they're frustrated about Zombies, for the laughs i.e. Zombieland).  This film has laughs, but its main point is in the touching romantic bits and the ending.  As other youtubers have pointed out, the girl's name is Julie, and the boy's name is R....
Shakespeare reference.  I know I know cliche.
A lot of these rom coms get blamed for embracing cliches, and Warm Bodies does nothing to combat that stereotype.  But it does fulfill its role well.  This viewer, at least, left it with one of those warm and fuzzy feelings, kind of like what happens to the Zombies (which was already spoilered in the trailer, geez.)
Honestly the 4+ hour mark is more like I left this film on pause while doing other stuff, and sure this is hardly the most riveting film, but it's a cute movie that features sapient zombies who have emotions and *love* and what not.  The Halloween Sale was a reasonable discount (under $5), and if you can buy the film in the future you should.  The Rental might seem a bit pricey but, hey, it's just $4 at retail, right?

This game is an oddity. I went into it saying 'this game looks like something that was thrown together by a team of primary-school students' and, if you look at pure graphical fidelity, it is a highly amateur-looking game. Seriously, the graphics look like something you'd see on an old 286 computer with a CGA monitor. That bad. But then you start to notice things; elements that are evidence of serious care and talent. Even the title screen looks terrible until you start seeing the subtle art choices, the position of the car relative to the newspaper and book. The trees in the background, the colour palette; they are all so polished and purposeful.
You start the game and are again hit by the horrible graphics. I mean, when I played it, your grandfather's jacket is texture-less so it actually transitions the hold-textures while you're playing. Seriously, its an eye-sore; your granddad with the technicolour monochromatic jacket.
Then you begin building your car - this is a masterful choice of opening. It does not matter that the graphics are terrible, because you begin to bond with this vehicle you are actually having to assemble. There are no shortcuts either (at least, no shortcuts compared to other games of the same ilk) as you have to reach under the steering-wheel to pop the hood and actually put the tires on the car, after jacking it up. You have to pour fuel into the engine, get the oil mix correct, add water to the windscreen cleaner - it is amazing for reason I have difficulty articulating.
After a while you get on the road and everything from bugs, to mud, to rain affect your driving. It is incredible. You pull into a service station, fill up the car, take your wallet, use it to pay the cashier, you can buy tools, stock for smuggling...it is nuts how much to do there is in this game. Boxes on the side of the road can yield unexpected treasures, hotel rooms you stay in have unthought-of functionality. I have not even mentioned how you can stack things seamlessly in your trunk, kind of a mini-game of 3D Tetris.
This game, in pre-alpha, was more fun to play than some AAA games. I like it for what it represents - gameplay over graphics. Trust me, this game is a blast.

I specially don't like the combat, to me it feels grindy instead of tense and fun, there's no going up or down, it is a 2D flight system while some enemies have the freedom to move into the third dimension and even though it may fit the naval combat system, it feels weird.
It has to be said that it is a great game to have been developed by a two man team, but it falls short of what one may expect after a Freelancer comparison, sadly it is kind of misleading and a video about the combat system would help clear things up.
If you like Freelacer type games and think you may like the naval combat system a la ACIII+ ship combats, you should at least try this. I'd say it is a good game, just not for me...

do you want civ 5 a game set in the past with historic races

did i expect this to be a flawless and complete upgrade to civ 5 that improves everything? no.

I'm bittersweet about GRID 2 in particular. I love this game. It's good quality, though I'd still say GRID is much better than GRID 2. Where GRID 2 takes the cake is the lack of limitations for online races. Codemasters didn't take the simulation route like they had done with DiRT 3. There are no driver assists options at all, controls are simple and forgiving. POV cockpit mode was never included and I feel like the developers really messed up with that decision.
One thing that put a terrible taste in my mouth is the ridiculous amount of DLC available. And let me warn you; it's ALL or NOTHING with the DLC. If you own any DLC another player doesn't have, they will not be able to join your game. You'll have to host without using ANY DLC, that means the free car add-ons aren't available either. I have absolutely no appreciation for how Codemasters is trying to conduct business using this tactic, and it'll probably keep me from buying another one of their racing games in the future.

I found this purchase to be a difficult one as a lot of people bad mouth the game for not being a sim or for not having a cockpit view, Then procede to unfairly dismiss the rest of the game due to their inability to do some research before they purchase a game.
I have found the game to be great fun so far, the presentation is a little over the top, but that is something codemasters have been doing since DIRT 3.
The cars handle well, with a good feel of weight vs. power,  powersliding is a lot of fun, the AI is a little plain but it fills it's roll well.
Engine sounds are fantastic, ambient noise is somewhat lacking, but the squeal of steel on steel as you trade paint with competitors is good and tire screech is well done.
The graphics are fantastic and optimised well, with some great smoke effects from tires as you push your car through corners, some of the best reflections on cars I have seen.
After reading all the mixed reviews, I waited for a sale on steam and it was definatly worth the $11 on sale, I would have paid the $30 they ask when it's not on sale, if not for so many negative reviews from disgruntled sim fan boys.
If you like car games at all, I recommend you add this to your game list.

Bioshock2 maintains sort of a middle ground between original Bioshock and Infinite. It's a good game, and the only problem is that the other two are too good.
It has the tactical combat style of the original Bioshock. You can't sprint and your health doesn't regenerate, which makes you much more cautious about using weapons and plasmids correctly. There're creative ways to play, too. Insta-kill big daddy? Sure. Juggle enemies without allowing them to engage you? I've done that. I'd say playmid-only kill is possible for all enemies except for brute splicer.
In terms of storyline, I felt quite motivated to beat this game - much better than Bioshock1 where you're just a random dude with no reason to stay. The connection with little sisters is also strengthened, albeit less impressive than Elizabeth. The plot is not superb, but it adequately portrays the later stages of Rapture universe. The emotional intensity of plot seems to increase as the series progresses.
Aesthetics is good. Nothing much more to say here.
I wish there were some in-water combat. It would have been very cool.
Thumbs up for getting rid of the annoying hacking system.
Plasmids and level design sometimes make it feel similar to Bioshock1, which is what many people criticize. To say the least, this is an enhanced version of Bioshock1 with additional content, and anybody who enjoyed either of the other two Bioshock games will enjoy this, too.

Though it is somewhat enjoyable, I cannot recommend this game. After six hours of playing, I can say that every new race just adds frustration and disappointment.
The AI is a nightmare Sunday afternoon. Whenever a corner comes along, they all slam on their brakes in syncronization and take it at a driving-school safe speed. When not on a corner, they form a massive rolling roadblock between you and the "chosen one;" the AI who started in first. Except in very rare cases, the AI do not trade positions.
If you are tired of the AI, you can try a gate-to-gate race, where every time you pass a truck you get points, every truck you pass increases the points given by the next truck, and losing paint resets the combo. However, you will soon find that the truck drivers are the same AI drivers, except after having been out partying and drinking all night. They have no ability to maintain their lane and seem determined to slam into you as you try to pass.
There are three types of cars. Drift, Grip, and Balanced. To me, drift seems to be like trying to drive a greased whale on ice, grip is the absolute reverse (whatever that may be. A rough shark in sand?), and balanced is so far in the middle that it is incapable of either drifting or gripping. Probably with more practice I could make any of the cars perform, but I simply don't care to.
In summary, I would suggest downloading the demo and just playing that. It's free and has most of the experience of the full game.

Grid Autosport is Codemaster's latest attempt to bring the Grid series back to its roots and right the wrongs done by Grid 2. In my opinion, Grid Autosport has left the past two iterations of the series in the dust and has instead, pointed the series in a bold new direction. The game feels more mature, with a slick menu system, a host of official real world tracks and above all, a heavy focus on the competitive world of motorsports.
Even more enjoyable is the re-tuned driving system and the sim-cade like handing of the many cars in the game. Autosport finally ditches the drift style turning of the first two games. Cars stick to the tarmac and grip is easy to find. This is especially evident in the open-wheeled dicipline, my favorite in the game. The cockpit view returns to Grid, and although it may lack detail, it is a welcome edition to the game.
Content-wise, there is a lot of racing to be done. Most races can be completed in less than five minutes, with the exception of endurance races which test your patience and your ability to maintain a quickly wearing set of tires. All five of the diciplines feel unique and even more impressive is the fact that the AI behaves differently in each. Qualifying is back in the game, along with a practce mode for tracks that you may not be familiar with. Expect to take part in drift events and time attacks as well.
Do not hesitate to pick this one up. It is a great find in a genre that is heavily ignored on Steam. Codemaster's clearly made this game for the fans who felt that Grid 2 didn't stand up to the legacy of quality the developer is known for. Grid Autosport is the Forza or Gran Turismo of the PC, I like it that much.

The spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper . . . or it tries to be.
On the good side, the game is a dungeon manager.  The theme and graphics are what you'd expect.  Unfortunately, that's where my good experience stops.
So many issues . . .
First off, I was able to beat the entire campaign in 25 hours, and that was with a lot of dithering around and trying to figure out some elements of the interface.  I would not be at all surprised if folks finished up in 12 hours.  For a game like this, I certainly expect a lot more than 20 hours of gameplay in the campaign.
The interface.  Don't get me wrong, the interface itself is fairly easy to come to grips with, but mechanically, the interface doesn't do a good job at all of communicating what it is happening.  For instance, your minions can get upset with you and go on strike . . . ok, fine, it's not a new mechanic in this genre.  But . . . why are they on strike?  I can't click on them, they just stand there.  Just one example.  Upgrading units is another real trial.
The challenge level is the worst offender however.  The game is just dead easy.  I remember having to really rush to keep up in Dungeon Keeper.  I always felt like I was just on the verge on falling behind and being run over.  Not an issue here.  Take all the time you like, and when you feel like the entire deck is stacked in your favor, attack.  Attack falls apart?  No problem.  Just revive your troops and try again.
There are so many problems with this game, a game I really, really, really want to like.  The game has the appearance on the surface of being exactly what folks would want in a game like this.  It just doesn't deliver.  Had I spent $5.00 on it, yea, ok, I'd be like, cool.  Wait for the sale, pick it up, and enjoy it at the price it really needs to be.

If you're looking for a fun and stylish dungeon simulator with some simple RTS mechanics on top, this may be the game for you. This game is not an ultra challenging RTS or fast paced micromanagement dungeon simulator. It is however an extremely stylish and fairly polished playground with excellent voice acting and fantastic animation. Everything about the dungeon feels alive, with creatures amusingly waving to your evil hand as it passes over them, doing yoga in the gym, and generally delightfully cavorting about. The world even changes as you conquer things from ultra-flowery heroic scenery to brooding and mysterious dark fantasy.
This is a game I come home to play to enjoy a fun and well crafted experience. The campaign is short and there are only a few skirmish maps, but the entire experience is refined and enjoyable. There is no grind or absurd number of side quests. When I come home from work I don't have 100+ hours to sink into some massively padded RPG or sprawling 4x game. This isn't a game made to strain your strategic skill to the breaking point. And I absolutely love that about it. I can create a beautifully crafted dungeon and simply watch with fascination as it operates.
I was a huge fan of Dungeon Keeper 1 and 2 and I've been looking for a similar game for some time. The big question now is, War for the Overworld or Dungeons 2?
War for the Overworld was ultimately a buggy disappointment which entirely failed to capture the personality and style of the Dungeon Keeper series. It's focus on very faced paced competitive game play resulted in the grim dark creatures lacking any sort of style or flair. They don't struggle in the air when you grab them, they don't interact with your hand amusingly, they just act like robots. Every bit of the clunky UI is geared towards facilitating a competitive experience. The "sandbox mode" is literally just a giant blank map with no enemies. Your creatures are boring. Your dungeon is boring. The game is boring.
Dungeons 2 on the other hand is dripping with style and humor. Your creatures interact in amusing ways, are beautifully animated, and generally give a sense of life to the dungeon you create. The narrator is also genuinely funny. The RTS mechanics are simplistic and I believe that is a plus. They don't distract from the dungeon keeper sim and if anything simply act as an additional neat feature. It feels very much like simplistic Warcraft. You spend time below ground making a big horde then unleash it on the world up top to crush up everything. It' s a jolly good time.
I recommend this game heartily to anyone who enjoys excellent animation, style, and relaxing dungeon simulators.

I had some hopes for this game, which could pan out in time, but not holding my breath.  The concept is to my liking being a cross between driving, mechanic, and rpg sim with minimalist graphics style.   The main issue is that the game mechanics are roughly as clunky as the car you are suposed to be driving.  It feels like playing Car Mechanic Simulator, which also felt a bit awkward to maneuver and place the parts.  Sometimes just putting things in the trunk can be hit or miss.  The buildings are sparse and functional.  I only found a few boxes on the side of the road, though it is possible to by parts at the border.  It is not quite open world as you might think.  There are a few procedurally generated roads on each map.  You choose one road and that's what you drive on.  You pretty much follow a limited path to your next check point and make repairs/sleep at motel.  You don't free roam GTA style by any means.  Parts do degrade fast, and I had a hard time finding a place to stop to make repairs without cars crashing into me.  For some reason the tool kit got used up fast  as if it were a consumable...or just a bug.  I did hit a bug at the border where it wouldn't let me give the papers to the customs agent so I gave up.  It just felt tedious getting to that point.

The core of the game is placing stations and conveyor belts in a factory, in a quest to have a smooth production line (hence the title).  Achieving a smooth flow in this game is much easier than in real life, which is to say that it's pretty tricky.
I picked this game up on the first day of Early Access; in the two weeks since then, there have been two updates!  How Cliffski manages to be responsive on the forums at the same time is beyond me.  Right now, the game is playable and enjoyable; bugs are minor.  Hold off until the full release if you need to have a good-quality tutorial and manual to be able to enjoy.

Soooo...I already played this game, entirely. Just to be sure I wasn't missing something. I did this on PS3.Then a friend of mine decided: "hey you should stream this game. Here's a key for the pc version". And I never streamed it. Why? It sucks on so many levels, but especially in two areas.
-First:
In terms of mechanics, the game is not well designed at all. And I'm not talking about the linearity of the level-design, though that is a big step back compared to the perfect Blood Money (perfect on that point at least). No, the main idea is to resolve an incoherence of the series (the fact that when dressed as a cop, no cop will tell that you look suspicious) by creating this 47 "sense". It is a bad bad bad decision. In theory, well balanced and polished, this would be an ok solution to a "non"-problem. But in execution, this gauge means that you can't be dressed as the type of character that is the most seen in the level, because you'll be unmasked in seconds by these guys, except if you use that sense gauge that emptied itself way too quickly. In lower difficulty settings it can work okay, but when in pro mode, some missions are just stupidly difficult to perform a "silent assassin" rank. Except if you play the game like a Conviction ripoff. That means that, in a HITMAN game, you spend 80% of your time crouching behind counters, taking down people that are not relevant to your objectives...when you should be proudly crossing entire rooms just walking, dressed as a clown, a priest or a bodyguard. The essence of Hitman is to be hidden in plain sight, and that mechanic f-ed it up.
The worst thing is: it is not even a good Conviction ripoff. The game doesn't know how to balance this modern predator stealth kind of gameplay, that we all played from Arkham Asylum to Human Revolution with the Hitman type of infiltration. And that gives us a level-design and NPC placement that satisfes no ends.
-Second:
...and foremost should I say, Absolution is incredibly vulgar and idiotic. And I know, being a fan of this series since the second one, that there is some poor taste jokes in previous episodes. But overall, I think the tone of it all, the focus on the themes rather than the characters, and the fact that the story never really was a focus of the game, merely a way to introduce nice game-design ideas (that be cool to make a hit on a classy boat! let's find some story about drug dealers on the Mississippi river!) gave opportunities to take it as a juvenile way to contextualise the gameplay, and it kept intact the elegant nature of the main character. Absolution can't stop putting "story" in the game. The cutscenes are longer, the game is more focused on that, rather than giving the player a good challenge, and by god why is there so much bad language in this game, and why all the childish sex elements? The Saints are the farther the series as ever been from good taste or even a bit of maturity. That doesn't make the game cool, or mature. It just looks like either an idiot who wants to tell a story with edgy characters, or a kid who wants to look like a bad*ss. Plus, I swear, the story makes no sense, and from beginning to end, you can pinpoint a major incoherence in each cutscene.
TL;DR: The game is poorly game-designed and doesn't know if it wants to be a predator-stealth game, like the Arkham series or Conviction (that were previously released) of if it wants to kinda stick to the Hitman formula. It satisfies non of these two game-designs and tries to resolve an incoherence by creating even more incohenrences. Plus the game talks to you like if you were a complete idiot and use bad language in place of good writting to tell a poorly put together story.
AVOID. Play Contracts, Blood Money or the 2016's Hitman for the real deal. This one is just pretty looking and insults your intelligence.

The first assasin's creed I played was Black Flag. I loved that game and played it for hours and hours.
It convinced me to get the rest of the series, so I bought one and two. I was about to buy AC3, but then I thought "pace yourself, dude"
Then I was muddling through civilians, looking for a yellow dude.
Then I was slowly walking through a city.
Then I was riding a horse.
Then muddling through crowds again.
And then it hit me. It was the ship that was the fun part.
This game takes quite a few pointers from that game, but retains enough of its own to feel relatable, but different.
Missions are a bit repetitive if all you're doing are bounties, but it changes up when you enter a new system.
Now. Two things I really liked about this game were:
1- It's not another freaking roguelike, and no permadeath if you didn't save. You'll lose all progress from when you last docked, tho, so keep that in mind. If you can dock, dock.
2- Your equipment costs as much when you sell it as when you buy it, so you can swap equipment and experiment without having to fear losing money. Which means that finding a weapon in a crate is always great, no matter if it's usable or not.
Anyway. I tend to like more the in-cockpit space shooters, but those have the really annoying tendency to make enemies turn circles with you.
Oh yeah. Did I mention that your turrets fire automatically, but can be aimed manually? that's good stuff.

Many critics of Hitman: Absolution made the mistake to equate the whole series with Blood Money - maybe because this was the only game they have played.
People that know the whole series (including me) are aware of the fact that the very first game Codename 47 was also very mutch about action (think of the end) and even the second part had some hardcore areas that could only be solved by shooting your way through because of the aggressive AI. Contracts was a very dark game and rediscovered some aspects of the story...
Every Hitman game is unique in his own way, so where does this strange idea come from that every part has to be like Blood Money?? Yes, it was with no doubt a great game with a reliable disguise system and fantastic missions - but Absolution also has it's very own strengths: great sound and graphics, smooth and polished gameplay, cool cinematics and a lot of details in most levels. Some areas (like Hope and Chinatown) are bigger than others and this is completely fine. In my second playthrough, I discovered eastereggs, new rooms and new ways of eliminating the target. Yes, story and points system are strange and not every level offers a lot of stealth varieties but the game just didn't deserve all the extreme and frivolous reviews of some "fans".
Absolution is fine the way it is - because it's an individual part of the series that still upholds most of the traditions of Hitman. I rather like to play some new aspects than the same style and content again and again.

Not the Postal-style murder simulator I was hoping for, almost exclusively due to the fact that the game constantly hinders you in that simple goal due to game-destroying design decisions.
The entire game forces you to be cautious and prudent if you want to live; basically, the exact opposite of what you want to do. Enemies can shoot you from far past your area of vision and do way, way too much damage. Executions aren't varied enough, and it's absurd that it's necessary to basically turn them off if you want a chance at surviving (enemies can still shoot you during them). The main character is a stupid parody and has nothing to do with a believable psychopath. Aiming is bizarrely difficult considering you have an unreliable crosshair and will unintentionally spray walls with what limited ammunition you're given, constantly.
It's astonishing that a game ostensibly about a spree killing does seemingly everything in its power to prevent you from doing anything like that. In truth, it's a game about hiding in a room and waiting for the AI to walk in the door while occasionally scurrying out to grab ammunition because it's impossible to fight them out in the open without dying almost instantly.
Stick to Postal. Even with the astronomical downgrade in graphical quality, it at least lets you go on a killing spree like it advertises. And its main character doesn't sound like a 14-year-old Slipknot fan.

Last month, Ironclad released a patch for a game that is nearly ten years old.
Other reviews have talked about how great this game is in terms of fun, graphics (despite the age!), and strategy, but I'd like to focus on how amazing it is that the developers are still supporting the game after all these years. We're not talking simple bug fixes either; the latest patch included a whole slew of optimizations which account for the power of modern gaming pc's and extend the game's memory limit allowing for even more massive battles than before.
This is huge; no developer does this.  In a world where unfinished games get abandoned prematurely by devs, it's crazy when a developer comes back and improves an already successful game to make it even better.
Even if you don't think you'll like real time strategy, give this game a shot. It's a unique take on the formula and mixes in elements of civilization for a combo that is incredibly addictive, even if you only play pure singleplayer.
Absolutely buy this game. You will have hours of some of the finest real time strategy experience on the market and you will be supporting devs who not only make great games, but take the time to make their great games even better.

(Looks at main menu) "Oh no, no campaign? That's a deal-breaker for me."
(150 hours of game time later) "Man, what do people see in this game?"
Seriously though, this game is very long. Don't be surprised if an average map takes 3-6 hours to win, even in a 1 v 1. The reward is totally worth it though. If you like Rts and Empire building games, this is the best.
Edit: Pro/Con list, for those like me who like them.
Pro: Great economics, every credit/second is important, trade ports and refineries add a sense realism, and it isn't necessarily important to focus on direct warfare. It adds a sense of what a real empire's like, with civilian structures and facilities.
Pro: Multiple ways to victory. You can let your enemies battle it out and simply manipulate them from behind the scenes, or you can build a Titan, a dozen capital ships, hundreds of frigates and cruisers, research every piece of technology, get 500,000 credits, colonize 50 worlds and literally crush everyone in your way.
Pro: Huge battles. Play 1v1 on a 6 planet map, or 5v5 on a map with literally dozens of star systems and hundreds of planet's. A system designer lets you create systems the way you want them, though personally, I think it's easier to use the maps Ironclad gives you.
Con: Unfortunately, with huge battles come huge timelines, and Sins of a Solar Empire is no exception. It took me 10+ hours to finish a 5v5 map, and it wasn't even 100 planets. Of course, 100 planets is still on the large side, but there are maps with 200+ planets, so they could probably take longer. This can be viewed as a Pro by some, but for me, it gets kind of boring.
Con: No campaign. This is somewhat evened out by the fact that the games are so long, they can be viewed as campaigns, but even so, if you're like me, you like storylines.

GRID Autosport promised to be a combination of all things great about GRID and GRID 2, which of course sparked a great bit of hype for Codemaster's upcoming racing game, and I myself went as far as to preorder the game with high expectations. I had enjoyed GRID 2 with my friends for countless hours, and a unification of both games sounded to me like what would be the greatest racing experience for the PC. Codemasters truly did do a great job combining the two games and Autosport boasts fantastic graphics and gameplay mechanics. However, to the dismay of it's fanbase, they had actually subtracted one of the better features of the game with the addition of the disciplinary and vehicle class systems for races. One of the best parts about GRID 2 was the ability to use any car of the event's tier you had desired. There's amazing hilarity and joy in racing an X-bow against a GT-R, and going head to head with racers of all disciplines and varieties, but in GRID Autosport, players are restricted to use class specific vehicles in races, for example, from 20 available cars for a drift event in GRID 2 down to a measely 3 in Autosport. There is no challenge against other players. I love the GRID franchise, but Autosport's discipline system really kills the enjoyment of racing with friends. I sincerely hope and pray that Codemasters considers returning the Tier system or implementing a type of Free Class for multiplayer matches in a upcoming patch or downloadable content to return GRID Online to it's most enjoyable state.

With a few more steps in the right direction this will be the successor to Dungeon Keeper 2 we have all been waiting for. The only drawback with the game that I have found in my short play time is the lack of creatures in the game. There are only 5 creatures at your disposal (just different skins for Demons and Horde). This is a real disappointment compared to the 12 or so creatures in DK2 as well as the plethora of rooms it had. I love the artwork and sound effects as well as the new item additions for rooms. These were all steps in the right direction, along with the venturing into Hero territory to earn EVILNESS lol. Still though, the game is sorely lacking right now in characters and scenery. These could be very easy additions though so im not giving up hope. An addon, DLC, mods, etc could solve this issue one their own or together. I thuroughly enjoyed my first few hours but once I saw that the 5 creatures and a similar small handful of rooms were all that were at my disposal I was very let down. I quickly jumped into skirmish mode to check that I wasn't worried for no reason, but my suspisions were correct in that I had already seen all that the game had to offer within a few hours. (There are more rooms than creatures but they don't bring more creatures or do anything that much more exciting). There are also only a handful of traps. For a game made 17 years after the last (well this is the one closest to reaching DK2s greatness) there should have been a ridiculous amount of minions, rooms, and traps. More than its predecessor or even approximately the same (within a couple)! But only 5...I really can't repeat that enough. I was having an absolute blast when I hoped in the game a began the path to ABSOLUTE EVIL! It was a big letdown when I saw that it offers maybe a third of DK2s creation content. It's still a lot of fun at first. I can't recommend the game at its current price and with this severe lack of minions and rooms. (Yes the rooms do more...but come on. By todays standards this feels like a smartphone game's worth of content). It is very well done in the amount of things it does, I will say that. The same narrator is back on board and he is hilarious even now. Even with it tapping into that bit of nostalgia perfectly, it was fleeting due to the aformentioned lack of unlocks. This has all the potential in the world but right now I can't recommend it. This really saddens me...feel like I keep repeating myself but 5 minions!? Come on...5!? Wow you can upgrade their armor and weapons and levels. You could do that in 1998. The furniture in the rooms is amazing...but a handful of rooms that half don't unlock anything new? There is really no room for extensive creativity and the lack of MINIONS lol, means that building little plots for rooms is the most eficient way to go. No more sprawling badass dungeons with Black Knights and Bile Demons, Fireflies, Wizrards, Goblins, Imps, Mistresses, Rogues, Salamanders and more!!!!! (Not to mention being able to turn the heros through the torture chamber which was so much fun to collect a few of each of them). Nope, you get an Orc, a Troll, a ...hmmm they aren't very memorable- wait a....NAGA- thats it. A NAGA... and a goblin. Maybe something else. Who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ The more I type the more I am saddened that they shortened the most enjoyable aspect of the game for me and many others. Look at any rts/city builder and there are ridiculous amounts of units. Not so here. Kalypso, what were you doing!? You had this beautiful game you created with amazing voice acting and artwork. Wonderful sound effects and a logical, exciting campaign (at first). And then you just kind of stopped. Did you run out of money? 5 more units minimum to make it 10 or so total would have been the bare minimum for any game like this. Any RPG in this day and age has more unit types. Hell even Call of Duty has more unit types. It's because this game is so fantastic with what it has that I am so let down by such a gigantic misstep. A huge non-step? I dunno but they had everything going with this game and then just didn't take it further. They laid all this gorgeous, wonderfully executed groundwork, and then they just stopped. I have got to stop..WTF Kalypso!? You broke my heart! ♥♥♥♥ it, I'll recommend it but get your♥♥♥♥♥♥together.

Here are my neatly categorized observations about GRID Autosport (GA).
►Controls:
There are no dead zone options for my Logitec F310 gamepad. There are no options to reduce steering lag (speed of my joystick motion vs steering input). Several users report that a bug from GRID 2 has cropped up in GA concerning steering wheel support. You might have trouble getting your favorite wheel working with GA.
►Physics:
Sudden steering input does not result in under-steer as it should. The cars have a bias towards oversteer in almost every situation. Hitting debris such as broken car parts and cones has little to no effect. Everything feels like GRID 2 with more grip. The physics are not better than GRID 1.
►Graphics:
The graphics look pretty good; especially after installing the high rez pack. Frame rates are fast on my Nvidia 750ti. However, the graphics feel like a step back from GRID 2. The building models of Chicago look WAY better in GRID 2. Blur cannot be disabled in the cockpit. IncGamers review of GA speculates that Codemasters have retrofitted all of the car interiors from a free community mod from GRID 2. Also the RPM and speedometer needles don't move. XD
►Voices:
Teammates say the same thing over and over. If you improve your times on each lap he'll literally say the same thing "thats the fastest lap this race" over and over. This is a clear step back from GRID 1 and a FAR CRY from DiRT 2.
►AI:
On "very hard" difficulty the AI becomes EXTREMELY aggressive. You'll get hit and spun worse than any EA title. At lower difficulty levels the AI does show some signs of personality and can be mildly entertaining.
►Online Gameplay:
In online mode you (supposedly) can race with friends and compete on leader boards. You can also buy, sell and tune cars. Multi-player is dead; the lobby is always empty. I've spent 3 hours waiting. 1 Hour for Friday night, 1 for Saturday afternoon and 1 for Sunday morning. The result? Not a soul showed up. It probably has to do with the fact that there are so many reports of cheating.
As for vehicle tuning I think its sad that a game like Gran Turismo 1 (from 1997) has a much more engrossing and detailed tuning system. The mods don't even feel all that effective. I tuned my engine, lowered the weight and adjusting my gearbox for a bit more acceleration (for a tight course). I'm a pretty good driver, holding several records on a few online racing sims. The result of my mods? Nadda. On average my lap times stayed the same. I call shenanigans!
►Single Player Gameplay:
Single player gameplay does NOT include buying, selling or tuning cars. This is a grave mistake considering the multi-player situation. In single-player you will drive what your team tells you to drive; like it or not. If you don't like open-wheel racers TOO BAD! You will drive open-wheel racers to progress the game; like it or not. All so you can earn XP to go on to more events. LAME. Sadly none of the team building from GRID 1 made it to GA. Too bad.
►Summary:
The game feels rushed and has poor production value. Models and program-code are reused from GRID 2 and possibly even ripped from free community mods. There is no motivation to race in single-player and there are no people to race in multi-player. All I wanted was to earn some dough, buy a car and tune it. And wouldn't it be fun to build a team and climb the charts? All in single player of course!
I don't recommend this title on any level whatsoever. If you already own it I don't recommend buying the season pass. If you're looking for a great simcade grab GRID 1 or Need for Speed Shift (1 and 2 are both great). Heck, I'd even recommend Test Drive Unlimited 2 over this.

The Dungeon Keeper series has been crying out for a sequel ever since gamers were left hanging with the tantalizing view of Horny walking into the sunlight.  This game has the look, but falls frustratingly short in the execution.
The developers decided to compensate for inability to design a discoverable UX or write a decent manual by having the narrator yell at the user.  Repeatedly.  For example:
You're instructed to build an Arena and drop in a creature.  You do so, it happily flails away, gaining experience points.  On to the next bit of dungeon management...except the narrator is still complaining.  You train the creature again, train another, nothing is good enough.  GET OFF YOUR♥♥♥♥♥♥ YOU♥♥♥♥♥♥!!
Repeated.  Every few minutes.
You exit the game in annoyance and search.  The Dungeons2 forums are down, and naming a game this generically doesn't help in search results.  Eventually you find a review complaining about the issue and discover that all the narrator's yelling about dropping the creature somehow neglected to mention that you also must deselect and then right-click on the Arena to choose a previously-hidden icon that levels the minion.  Brilliant!
(For extra fun, you then complete the level and save.  When you return a few days later to give the game a second chance, it has lost your save and has you back in the same level.  With no creature trained yet and the announcer yelling about it again.  Repeatedly.)
There are other interface issues, and the overworld play seems to be basically "Build big army, abandon dungeon, steamroller foes."  Wait for a 50% off sale if you want a little DK nostalgia.

UPDATE:
over a year has passed and i finally checked out the progress. actually a lot has changed, many of the issues i spoke of have significantly changed and improved. UI is more accessible,  the game feels smoother and the different aspects of the game seem to interact with each other a lot better.
im going to edit the review and say yes, now i recommend the game! it's good to see devlopers actually developing the product :)
there are still some questions open, and answers to be given to jesson, the dev that commented my review.
1) story development: yes please! crea is still all about its own game mechanics - they have improved a lot but its all about filling progress bars. character development is very nice, but a little story behind it, maybe even quests and campaigns would motivate a lot more - plus it acts like a feedback when you improve levels and skills.
2) character development: yes please! you have a lot of mechanics already, especially for the huge crafting system. thats perfectly fine, the number of skills is vast. but the main characteristics (like agility, intelligence,...) do not feel like having a real impact on the way i play. more limitations and benefits might help, like minimum values for using certain items and skills. e.g.  a high-intelligence character not better in researching stuff than a dumb brute - a high strength character cant carry more than others - a high agility is not necessary for picking locks.
3) NPCs and character interaction: the idea of building dummies and dressing them up to get a little company for the main character is a little creepy if you think about it, but works surprisingly well as a mechanic to build your environment. but, will there be other npcs? if so, will you be able to interact with them? will there be dialogue and choices even, especially if you implement stories, big and small? it would be a real asset and a unique feature compared to all the tarrarias, starbounds and the likes out there.
former review:
dear crea developers,
unfortunately i cannot recommend this title - yet. As with many early acces titles this one has great potential but it feels a little like things grow over the your heads. i always missed deep rpg elements in similar games but i understand it's difficult to create a whole new terraria or starbound AND add a complete roleplaying system with character development and everything to it. so if it is too much at once, why not mod titles that already exist and really concentrate on your new ideas and things that are really important to you?
anyway, this is just guessing and suggesting.
here a few bullets i recommend to improve:
- the gui is not very smooth. for character display this is not that important but the crafting and inventory menus need simplicity, clarification and coherence to be intuitive.
- the pace feels not right: combat, crafting, moving, mining etc mechanisms need to bebalanced with each other, "speedwise"

While the narrative for the game is fairly bold and intriguing, the gameplay (and the four roads to victory) fail to match up to the endless possibilities posited in the introductory video. Combining this with mechanics that are remarkably similar to its contemporary predecessor results in a game that resembles a fan mod more than a fifty-dollar release by the original developers.
In short? I bought this game. You don't have to make the same mistake.

Now, it's a bit more easier and i'm not complaining, it gives me time to do more in Crea.
Lastly, the modding is something I have great hopes in. There are already some creations on the workshop, but I would like to see a lot more.  This is the game where I definitely want to try to sink my feet into with modding the game. I also would like to see a lot more people play this game, but that's going to come sooner or later. I haven't played a space game I loved in ages. Grew up on Wing Commander, Starlancer and so on back in the day. This might revitalize my interest, perhaps I can find a new one. If I were to summarize this game shortly, it is a large capital ship simulator. You don't do dog fighting like Wing Commander. Instead you are on capital ships of varrying sizes from corvettes (small) to huge dreadnoughts. Battles are mainly about positioning, weapon composition and some tactical flying to ensure you aren't exposed on a flank.
Regarding controls, there is NO NEED for a joystick. I personally played the whole thing with mouse and keyboard, the controls are fine. I'm sure a gamepad would work as well.
A few general notes:
- You can only fly your ships in the X/Y plane, no barrel rolls. I imagine this was a concession as true dogfighting without a stick can be troublesome since it involves 3 or more axes of control. Also, since you are in a big ship such moves would be unecessary as you are a huge target no matter your turning/rolls.
- The ship and weapon variety is fun and provides some different playstyles, I really liked just after I upgraded a ship trying to optimize my weapon loadout.
- Mission variety was ok, but some may be a bit tedious. The escort mission in particular can be quite trying, I'd stick to all the others.
- Trading system is more dynamic than the old games, as you sell more of a commodity to a station the price you get will change. Other stations prices might increase in response.
- There is a random event system that also affects stations in a system. These events may swing prices for certain goods wildly. For instance, if a station goes to war weapons will skyrocket in buy price. Other interesting events include blockades and embargos where a faction will prevent all access to a station. You can of course either run the blockade or eliminate it.
- There is a bounty system rewarding you for eliminating certain designated ships, so destroying things when not on missions is rewarded. The scanner will tell you when this is possible.
- Faction support was good but a bit rudimentary as it really boils down to be a pirate or be with the law. Games like Freelancer or I imagine the new Elite model these relations a bit more realistically.
- Some faction have some VERY nice exclusive upgrades, which reward sticking to them.
- Difficulty varies somewhat, early in the game it easy to get out gunned. Later in the game I found it to be a bit too easy once you aquire the bigger ships. Maybe I'm too experienced at such combat though, some people have said this game is hard...
Overall it is a very nice package from an indie studio. I fully recommend it, even at full price. I'm not sure it is replayable but I got about 50 hours out of it which is really good. After the story you can continue playing the game's missions or start fresh and play as pirates. There isn't any new game+ though, and the story from what I see doesn't change much depending on faction allegience.

This game is what I think is probably the best route 2K could have gone in with makig a sequel to Bioshock. The game puts you in the role of Delta. An Alpha series Big Daddy who is tied to a single little girl. You lose your little girl, daughter of Sofia Lamb (The games main antagonist), and set off on a journey to find her once again.
Along the way you meet a wide and colorful cast ranging from the leader of a makshift town in rapture, to a man turned psychotic due to plasmids. The game provides many choices ranging from the first games usual Rescue or Harvest little sister, to spareing or killing some of the games NPCs. And aside from the first NPC I felt the choices were in the moral grey area in which this man did something terrible to me and others yet is begging for his life and is unarmed. There was no clear cut answer.
The game also provides many new mechanics which I think were good changes. Since you are a big daddy you find yourself being able to "adopt" a little sister to gather a little more adam. Luckily, unlike the first games challenge, your little sister can not die while collecting adam. Yet this does not make things easy as you can die, and when you do your little sister starts all over. You don't even have to do that, you can skip right over it. I also LOVED the new Power to the People station mechanic in which they add a third upgrade you can get when you got the previous two. The big sisters were also a good addition. Although i found them partialy annoying, i realized that thats what they are suposed to be. I found their history to be intriguing and a good addition. I also enjyed the hacking darts which added a new level of choice to the game although i did not like the new hacking system. Oposed to the pipe puzzle this was relativly easier, except for the fact that the needle system didn't pause the game. I would find myself dying in the middle of hacking which in retrospect was a bit of a better challenge. Another challenge was the 5 EVE hypo and health pack limit which really made me greatful for every one i found. It provided a new better challenge.
There were still a few things i disliked about the game. This includes mainly of the Alpha
series ig daddies you have to face. I found them easy yet and annoying barrier in my way. It was like a spider web. When you walk through it it is no big deal yet is a slight annoyence. I found myself running into these a multitude of times which bothered me. I also hated the last decision in the game which made me upset at what was considered the "good" choice. When you play the game you will see what I mean.
The charcter modeling was done so much better. I really felt like every splicer was different and the new spider splicers scared the crap out of me. The game looked overall majorly improved with the graphics like it should.
Another thing was the lore. I found myself playing every single tape and being so interested every time. Even the small stories i found interesting. The world sucked me in yet again with that. It also made me want to explore every area which led me to constantly checking my map.
*SPOILER WARNING*
The endding was HUGELY improved from the previous. There was no clear final boss and I loved that. I also loved seeing through the eyes of a little girl and going around and seeing what they see. Seeing Elanore grown up made me happy sad and seeing how long she waited made me feel happy yet enraged at what Sofia had done. And when sinclair was put into the Alpha Series big daddy suit, I was enraged. It was so sad to see my favourite character of the whole game go out like that. He was in my opinion by far the best character in terms of a helper and a friend in game. I legitamatly felt sad killing him. I got the good endding which endded with delta in the eyes of Eleanor. And seeing the little toy the little sisters made, made me so happy i choose this route. I felt the endding to be one of the most satisfying in all of the gmes i have played.
*NO MORE SPOILERS*
Overall I hgihly recomend the game and rate it a 9/10. Despite what most people think, I feel it is the perfect sequel to the criticly aclaimed Bioshock.

Most of the negative reviews are from F2P newbies that get facerolled by the more simpler champions and get upset because they don't know how to adequately respond. What I mean is that, let say, you're playing a general MOBA game rather than Battlerite: in League, Dota or whatever, it's generally pretty hard to play around a champion you have no ****ing clue what they do right? There are some champions in this game like Raigon or the more recent Thorn that act like pubstompers toward new players, much like how in other games champions like Master Yi tend to roll over low ELO.
The weakest aspect about Battlerite is probably the unlocking the cast, but it's a F2P game. There give you at least 9 champions from the beginning with 3 from each class of Melee, Ranged and Support with Ashka being unlocked through a YT code. Unlocking all the champions through the $29.99 is admittedly pricely but it similar to the SMITE champion bundle you get all the CURRENT + FUTURE champions which is nice if you look at it.
And I must state DO NOT BUY THE $49.99 ULTIMATE FAN PACK *UNLESS* you REALLY like the game and want to support the developer even more beside from buying loot boxes. The Fan Pack only gives you an EXP bonus every game and some minor benefits but it DOES NOT come with the champion pack.
And in contrast, the greatest strength and my biggest love for the game is the fact that it hard to master and entertaining to learn. It reminds me of League back years ago when I enjoyed playing because I wanted to get better. When I lose in Battlerite, beside from the usual defective teammate, it mostly because I *could* have played better or that I didn't play well enough. That's honestly really amazing to be able to blame myself for my own mistakes so consistently.
All in all, the game may not be perfect and there still are a few changes I would like to see but I love the game in it current state and it's far from being unbalanced as most of the review claim.
