I'm writing this review to pass the time while it instals based on what I remember because boy howdy did this game leave an impression. I will update if I encounter any game breaking glitches with the HD version.
Before starting, I will say, if you dislike scary games, me too! This game is a bit spoopy at times, but the jumpscares are minimal. Its really the dimented nature of the setting that leads to a feeling of creepiness and uneasiness. I'd say on a scary level of Finding Nemo to Saw, this game gets a round an Aliens, so lets begin.
I played this game a lot in my teens when it first came out and I'm excited to play it again in HD. Playing with vita chambers turned off is almost a must, because the vita chambers make the game laughable. However, having them turned off, and the difficulty set to max, was one of my absolute favorite game play experiences as a kid, because you had to prepare for each encounter in a way you were going to survive. As such, it forces you to utilize all the tools at your disposal in creative ways to succeed, something few games ever actually accomplish. Usually in a game, you find the gun or the weapon you like best and you just go do your thing. If you do that on hard with vita chambers turned off, you're favorite weapon will be out of ammo, and you are going to die.
If you don't know anything at all about this game, the game play involves ultilizing guns that you upgrade by exploring, and a mechanic called plasmids, which is basically magic fueled by stem cells (Adam) harvest orginally from deep sea slugs! Now, though, its not found in deep sea slugs... and how you wan't to go about getting your Adam is a major part of the story telling.
There's also a hacking mechanic, that lamentably, is the weakest part of the game, as the whole get the juice to the right place with the tubes gets old after a while, but darned it if it isn't really satisfying watching an enemy retreat to a healing station only to die because you hacked it to spew poison in their face.
Without spoiling anything, this is one of the few games I've played that to me, is art. The world is thematic and well crafted, and the story Bioshock 1 has to tell not only makes a statement about gaming, but the nature of choice and morality as a conscious being. This game succeeded years ago in melding visual story telling with propoganda, ads, audio books, people talking to you via walky talkie,and cut scenes to deliver of a theme that many games fail to even come close to delivering in terms of quality today.
I would say a similar game that came out recently in terms of a story worth thinking about was SOMA, humorously also set under water, however that game suffered from rather limited gameplay that this game does not. So assuming this game runes smoothy, and you haven't had it spoiled for you, holy balls is it one of the more meaningful storys you can engage in for a $20 price tag.
Edits from the future!: AIght so I've had it crash once, but that was because I was trying to do too much at once with other applications, and I think it caused it to crash again later, but my biggest issue is I couldn't get it to stream in a way were the game is audible. I was either talking while a played the game in silence, or going deaf for my viewers. I messed with all the audio sliders and ultimately the solution was a combination of turning up my mic volume in Razer Synaps, while turning down the volume my mic was recording at with GeForce. I also changed the game itself from stereo to surround and turned it all the way to 10, which seemed to help too.
Not the best as I will have to change it later for other games... but also not even a problem you don't plan to stream.

Over 4 days, 27 million viewers did other things while 16 teams across the globe gathered to do battle. As the groups stage began these players who do nothing better in their lives would be tested and not every team will prove up to the challenge.
...
At the main event, the remaining twitch viewers watched for their souvenir drops.
...
Tension continued to grow during the half-times.
...
Ever drop was a chance, and every round a devastating profit. Viewers struck it rich, and new items determine its worth. By the grand finals, the tournament had reached a fevered pitch.
But that was August, this November in Cluj - Napoca a new gauntlet will beat Rome and 16 teams will compete in the 7th CSGO major. 8 legends who prove themselves in Cologne and 8 challengers who fought their way to the group stage. Viewers will come back, prices will rise and fall, and history will be made again.
"Sorry Valve, a majority of us only watched these tournaments because of the souvenir drops not to enjoy the actual tournament itself."

Atmospheric game from 17th century that gets you into the boots of explorer who unravels misdeeds and sins of the New World colonists and one special girl whose destiny is tied with yours. This is mostly done by exploration of game maps and by the collection of lost notes while fighting with hostile monsters. There is also an interesting mechanic that lets you switch to the ghost world that acts as parallel and that lets you speak with specters of former inhabitants to find solutions to their cases.
There are multiple stories to be resolved and multiple maps to be explored, some of which are more intersting than others. The gameplay gets bit repetetive after a while (explore the area, kill all the enemies, find better weapons, collect all clues, purify all totems, unlock the access to the next map) but it was still strangely intriguing, mainly because of the visuals (you can set your own level of saturation) and stealth mechanics (cause killing several enemies at once can be quite challenging and you ammunition is limited).
It's clear the budget for the game wasn't big and it shows. For example, there is no voice-acting whatsoever. But with limited money they did probably the best they could, although there is still some room for improvement. Well, and the ending wasn't quite well executed in my book, I was expecting a bit better twist after everything I went through. Overall, I can't say this was a bad game but it has its quirks. I still enjoyed while it lasted but it's definitely not for everyone.

Oh, boy.
Let's get the cliché out of the way: I really wanted to like this game.  I should also mention the fact that I have barely gotten anywhere in this game.
This game triggered Far Cry 1 PTSD in me hard.  If you never played the first Far Cry, I'll try to fill you in: enemies could see you across the map (like, 2 or 3 miles away; no, that is NOT exaggerating), and they could see through ninety percent of the vegetation.  Hide in a bush, they see you.  Hide near a tree, they still might see you.  Oh, and you can't see through the vegetation.  Awesome.
The same damn thing happened here.  I bought this thinking it was going to be some very serious cat and mouse antics, with the enemies with guns and me with a crap bow.  A totally unfair situation that I would have to overcome, and thus feel cool.  An impossible situation that I would make possible.
What I got was a weird bow that doesn't seem to arc its arrows (I mean, it might, but it seems to only come into play if the arrow flies a mile, then it suddenly weirdly drops; I don't know, it might depend on the kind of arrows you use), the stupid Far Cry 1 vegetation issues I mentioned, and sparse game areas that still were kind of small.
Any game with stealth needs some form of tutorial, that way you don't have to spend twenty minutes running, then walking, then crouching at enemies so you can figure out what the hell you are doing, how far they can see and hear, etc.  MGS, Splinter Cell, and Thief all knew this.  This game didn't, and it's probably because most of the budget went to visuals.  I got to say, they are really impressive, and playing with the options was entertaining.  Yeah, that sounds weird, but you have to do it yourself to know.
But past the options and in the game proper was a different story.  What ended up happening was that I turned off almost all of the visual effects and the grass, making the game ugly as hell, but way easier, being that I could then see where the hell I was and where everyone else was.  I could now tell what the hell I was doing.  This also pulled the game's pants down and showed off how little it really had, especially with the AI.  Here's something fun: get the attention of an enemy with a ranged weapon.  Watch him take aim.  And then duck behind something, and stand right back up.  The AI will go from idle or walking animation to aiming super quick, and it looks real goofy.  Enemies that seemed like they were surrounding you and jumping out of bushes are revealed to be morons running right at you getting stuck on things, kind of spreading out as they keep running into things.  You can just keep popping them in the head until they go down in a congo line.  Clockwork.
There is always the possibility of the game getting better later.  But I won't take the trek inland.  It might not be so bad if you don't mind finicky AI and just want a visually stunning game with layers of atmosphere.  I HAVE to give this game that; to not would be a crime.  It's enough that I might just lower my standards one day, drop the difficulty to easy and just breeze through it, if only to see what it has in store in the later parts.  But as a crazy survival/horror game?  I don't know, man.  It was just way too basic for me.

It's a good game that deserves better than the rating it has. Too many people are complaining that its just a mod of Civ 5, or that its not as good as Civ 5. In truth, it is very similar to Civ 5, but in my book, that's a good thing. Civ 5 was a great game.
What's different than Civ 5? The few most interesting things:
1. Game setup is different. You have several choices as to what to bring to the new world, meaning that even two games with the same faction can be played differently.
2. The aliens are significantly different from barbarians. They are always there, but not always hostile, and can often be lived with peacefully. Plus, there are giant alien super-units that are very hard to kill.
3. Spying is enabled in the base game.
4. There's alien gunk called Miasma in a lot of the world that can injure your troops. Similar to what was in Alpha Centauri.
5. Affinities. These are almost like religions in other civ games, except that they are not mutually exclusive. You can level up all three affinities simultaneously if you want. Affinities offer unique units and victory conditions.
6. There are only a few unit types, but they are upgraded by research into affinities. This actually makes the game easier to manage in my opinion. I like it.
7. There are quests, which are kind of like optional mini-objectives that give you a reward if you complete them. It makes the game more interesting by giving you goals to work towards.
So the question remains, is this as good as Civ 5? In all honesty, probably not. But that doesn't mean it isn't great in its own right. I have played through 6 or 7 games now, and I am still enjoying it. If you liked Civ 5, and want a new setting, then I definitely recommend you give this one a shot. I give it two thumbs up.

This game isn't half bad when you get aquainted with the mechanics, though the balance is far from good. The most notable problem is that any character that is listed 'New Player Friendly' has serious balance issues with being at above average damage output, or control output than other characters. That isn't to say that non 'New Player Friendly' characters can't kill those playing the unbalanced ones. But, there is a staggering difference between these two sets of characters.
One in particular that everyone seems to agree on, is Raigon. In which he has a parry that deflects all forms of damage. If melee, it stuns the closet enemy to himself and reflects damage onto the closet enemy. In this case if someone was blindly swinging at the Raigon, they can outright kill their own team mate off Raigon's parry ability. As for projectiles, Raigon's parry deflects all projectiles in the direction the Raigon is facing.
From there, Raigon also comes equipped with a leap, and an ultimate that makes him untargetable for the entire duration. Though those seem a bit alright in terms of balance, it turns back to unbalanced when you note his damage output being significantly high for his kit.
Not impossible to kill, but he is one of many characters that are unbalanced to the point of being considered as an 'OP character'.
Onwards the matchmaking is also a bit strange, though in ranking you can optionally turn on balanced matchmaking, by default you start with very unbalanced and irrational matchmaking for the fastest matches. This goes as far as punishing the player in bronze, and majority of silver ranking.  Gold starts to become more balanced, as well as Platinum and Champion. But early on there is a constant problem of being grouped with people who are 'In Placement' as far as placements go, that's pretty standard placement chances. Where player teams are given 'In Placement' team members to allow the 'In Placement' to get into a place they are suited for.
Where the problem lies, is that the players in the match with an 'In Placement' team member suffer no penalty to losing that match. So this creates matches where one team has an 'In Placement' and the other does not. This completely negates the side with the 'In Placement' of any punishment. If the team with the new player loses, they do not lose anything, while the 'In Placement' member just has a loss on their placement record. Though, on the other team without an 'In Placement' player, if they lose, they lose rank points,  and can drop divions, too.
Overall. The game isn't half bad concept wise, but in reality, it's a poor game with poor quality, and poor balance.
Neat to play in your spare time, but don't give it money or your full attention.

To say "this isn't Alpha Centauri II" is quite spot on, but it doesn't do justice to this game at all. For me, this reminded me of all the things I fell in love with in AC: epic music, completely alien world and the small quotes from the futuristic world, that inspire imagination and paint a picture of the next phase in human evolution. The story is good, and yes, there is one (though it opens up via small quotes from fictional people and books, and civilopedia). Good sci-fi, I say, and quite familiar if you've played Alpha Centauri.
To say "it's just an expansion to Civ V" is kind of right. Most of the mechanics are the same - though a bit rebranded (gold has become energy, happiness is now health, policies are virtues...) - but there are some changes that make it it's own game, like the Tech-web (not a tree anymore, and you can choose your own path) and the Quests, which help you to refine your game. The espionage system was similar to Civ V's, but a bit expanded and seemed to work better.
All in all, if you liked Civilization V, you'll like this, but don't expect too different game. The sounds are damn fine, as usual, and the graphics are quite nice also. Only thing that bugged me with the graphics was the fact that there was too much happening on the screen, and the nature still looked just too much like old timey Earth with glitter and bling-bling, but that's nothing a mod can't fix. Interface was just fine, a bit different from the Civ V, but mainly only layout-wise.

despite all its flaws, survivor squad is an incredible little gem. yes, we have played more zombie games than we probably ever wanted to play. yes, 4 survivors in a squad and left 4 dead copycat "special" infected are as cliche as they get today. as is looting and everything else that goes on in any such game. however, a nice 2-part gameplay with essentially turn-based overview for node/settlement management and real-time top-down shooter for fights is very well implemented.
overview part allows to choose the node to attack, along with showng how much time remains until infected push back. building settlements on large nodes will allow you to generate more resources and use these ase a base closer to where action is, along with defending these nodes when infected do come to attack it.
fight is nicely dark and otherwise low-visibility action where you need to keep the eyes of your team facing every bloody direction all the time to survive. survivors can outrun infected but not for long and not when there are too many of them. choice of melee weapons or firearms also comes into play - melee is quiet and will not attract large amounts of enemies from all over the map while firearms are more powerful but will attract infected from a large area. gameplay elements are actually quite well designed - hearts that will cause more zombies to spawn until destroyed, floodlights and alarms that do the same until switched off. fortunately, last 5 zombies around every building get highlighted so headhunting the last one is not too much of a chore.
both overview and maps for the fights are somewhat random but will start repeating themselves a bit too much at around half or two thirds of the game.
itemization/crafting/upgrades system is solid - find blueprints from nodes, find the necessary ingredients (some are obviously hard to find) and cobble together next useful item. 3 levels of items on each slot is not much but it is enough. survivors themselves will also get levels up to 5, eventually allowing you to select 4 out of the 19 available skills. some are more useful to others for specific playstyle but all around, combined with itemization, the mechanic works well enough.
going through the campaign will normally take 8-10 hours but can take more or less if you rush or try to experience everything. there are also couple minor additional gamemodes like death labs - descending through levels of lab filled with infected starting with 4 survivors and limited budget for items - and survival - nature of which is fairly obvious. multiplayer exists, but it is a regular deathmatch and requires an open port.

Jalopy is good. That's my first statement in this review. The concept for it is really unique, teaches the players about cars, how they work and very generally how to maintain them. In this state it is VERY buggy. VERY VERY VERY buggy. I would totally say hold off on buying it in it's current state unless you want to show support of the idea behind it like I did. In it's current state it is the epitome of an early access game. It's in no way bad, but there are bugs to be had all over the road (so to speak).
For the average consumer: add it to your wishlist and buy it after a few updates or a sale
For the car enthusiests: If you're like me and love the idea of a fun, cartoony car game that also has a lot to teach future generations about our passion, hobby and general method of transportation, pick it up in support of the developers but know that this is VERY early access and you're not really buying it to play early at this point but more backing an idea.
Update: Jalopy and its developers just keep impressing me with every update! They're very active in the community (They even replied to this review). There are some massive content drops that came out expanding the game by double and triple its original size. They've fixed most of the bugs I was talking about in my original review and genuinely care about their playerbase and their game which is more than a lot of devs these days. I really can't reccomend this game highly enough.
If you enjoy rougelikes, cars, European history or supporting a truely amazing Indie Developer, buy this game as soon as possible!
UPDATE:
So as it stands right now, the above review is still correct and I still love Jalopy and their developers. The only reason I can't recommend this product anymore is one specific, gamebreaking bug that's been present since the day the game came out on Early Access (when I bought it). There's a bug that happens for seemingly no reason and everybody has experienced it at some point or another where you're unable to interact with any objects besides the car, including your wallet, making progression impossible until you close the game and relaunch it which resets your progress. This game is fantastic otherwise and has so much potential to be my favorite rougelike but this bug, especially since it's been in the game since Alpha 1, is the sole reason I cannot recommend it anymore. I will happily change my review to positive again once this is fixed and I may even be able to complete a single playthrough of the game, which this bug has prevented me from doing since Alpha 1.

I must have played this game hundreds of hours, not only the steam-version but also an earlier version.
What is very unique about it, is it's great epic battles. You expand your empire. You build your fleet(s). And when the decisive face-off with your opponent finally has come, "Sins of Solar Empire: Rebellion" gives you the most brilliant epic battles you will ever have seen in RTS.
Don't be mislead by my words. There will be lots of matches, where victory or defeat is inevitable and unspectacular. You won't see much of the "magic" then.
Of course that all depends on your game settings, strategy and the quality of your opponents. You can set the game to go faster. Then you will experience 30 minute matches in PvP or PvE, that leave little time for micromanagement and decisions. Or you can really go epic and slow, where you carefully make your choices and feel the electricity in the air ... uhm ... void I mean ... , as your fleets slowly close the distance and hell brakes loose. Then you will see how every choice you make affects the battle and finally turns the tide. Also, "rock paper scissors" still applies. With huge fleets and many different ship types, finding the right line-up is not trivial.
You can choose from a wide variety of settings, to get the game to be more of a minimalistic skirmish or almost turn-based. I once left a slow singleplayer match for a few seconds and it turned out to take me 15 minutes. I had forgotten to pause. When I returned, my fleet had fought off some space pirates but nothing else happened. In other games I might have returned just in time to see the final building of my base collapse.
Whatever floats your capital ship. If you have played the traditional SOASE, the capital ships there were really big and important for your micromanagement. But now you get the Titan, sort of a huge hero unit unique to every faction. Nothing can survive long in the presence of a Titan and as it "learns" it becomes a fleet in being, crushing entire enemy fleets.
Establishing your empire gets a bit of the old "Master of Orion" feeling. You conquer planets, build up stuff on them and in the orbit.
Orbit is a nice key word. The battles don't take place in space but in the orbit around contested planets. The planets are connected through space lanes. That may narrow down your options and spoil the open-world idea of an RTS game fought in space. On the other hand it creates nice tactical elements like bottle necks or flanking maneuvers.
Another great aspect is diplomacy leading to alliances, which even grant advantages in combat.
Unfortunately the game still has some balancing issues in PvP which is not helped by the fact, that the player community has shrunk and you will encounter lots of veteran players. You might get frustrated. But the game also has a great PvE mode and the AI is not bad at all. Sometimes the AI is rushing into a futile battle. But then again they seem to calculate their odds on-the-fly and retreat even before you know you won, only to be back before you expected them to. For SP I would recommend downloading some maps from the community, cause the PvP maps are all about balance and symmetry and PvE should be more about atmosphere and exploration. There are maps out there with huge star systems, where a game will last for days, mind this is still RTS, not "Civilization".
With the option to get AI on your side or more on the enemy side, with - I think up to 8 - teams and difficulty settings, everyone can get a challenging yet enjoyable game experience.
You will need to play hundreds of hours to get all of the tactical depth of this title and still be surprised. And if you really think you have seen it all, you can benefit from the community friendliness of SOASE. The community has been very active and there are not only lots of maps and units and "improved balancing" tweaks but also great mods.
I cannot tell which one you will like best as that depends on your nerdiness. However there are two very impressive mods based on the universes of Star Wars and Star Trek and even a Battlestar Galactica Mod, that i have not tried yet.
Other game developers make you pay for every piece of DLC, cutting off fans from implementing their own ideas. Ironclad Games and Stardock stick with another philosophy here. To try your own ideas, the game comes with two tools, a quick map designer and an editor. Thanks for that, by the way, really appreciated. Ironically that makes the game still attractive today and people are still buying it.
Any negative points? Well, the game is from 2012 and graphics might not be thrilling anymore plus you will play zoomed out most of the time and not see much of it anyway. I have it run smoothly on medium settings even on my old Core2 notebook. Also, if you prefer fast paced RTS with a focus on gut feeling and micro managing small troops, then you might be more comfortable with "Company of Heroes" or something similar. Personally, I like both, but they are very different. I would never start a game of SOASE if i knew, I only have got an hour of time. In Singleplayer you can pause and even accelerate but it will never be a casual play.
Another flaw is that units may take the initiative if not carefully set. Sometimes a ship will come back to the fight although you ordered it away and be destroyed because of some older stance. You can merge ships to different fleets or release them, but every now and then they do what they want. When you command hundreds of ships, that is not what you need. Also sometimes you will have trouble noticing a minor push or incident because the interface is not that well arranged.
So all in all I would highly recommend SOASE:R to anyone looking for a unique RTS experience in a scifi world. The game, at present, is still worth its 75% discount, largely due to the open design and mods. I would not pay more, since it's an older title. If you are not sure, you can wait for a further drop or a bundle.

Ten years later this is still one of the best games I have ever played. I was 12 when I got this for Christmas just after release. I had no idea what it was, I'd seen no adverts, articles or heard any news about it, I started it before eating my Christmas dinner and I'd finished it by New Year, I was hooked. The scares and the atmosphere were so tense I'd go out of my way to explore the whole map, so was not to go in that "scary room" yet. If I could play any game for the first time again, this would be it.
The story is amazing, even as a kid I was blown away by the twists and individual stories behind the power players in Rapture. The graphics back then hold up today and the Remaster is just the icing on the cake! It looks incredible and the settings that you explore are truely stunning, some of the best level design I've ever played through. I played this through on Hard and I felt a struggle at some points, but it never felt too easy or got unbeatbly difficult. It's an 11/10, a true classic to come, it's already proven itself so far!

Really need a sideway thumb at this point, there were definitely good times to be had, but Betrayer mostly suffers from its repetitive structure.
It's a semi-open world game, in that it's divided into several levels, although they are pretty huge.  It wasn't really all that difficult like what I had presumed from the trailer, but there aren't many games like this where you're thrown into the wilderness, relying on ancient weaponry like bows and muskets to survive, and its eerie, silent atmosphere was pretty sick.
Despite my general enthousiasm, my problem stems from the many missions you're given, each levels has Wraiths that need your help to move on to the afterlife; having to do many chores isn't the problem, but the mission structure is literally the hecking same all throughout the game, having to find an item, bring it back to the guy, go see another Wraith, talk to the guy again, it's convoluted fetch quests.  Sure, it's for the sake of the story and you can do multiple things at once, but in gameplay view, it never matters what it is you need to find, one guy has you find a pendant, the other wants a shoe, and both will then task you to find a different Wraith, they all ask you to go to specific points of the map, having you go all over the place, and the story doesn't really pack cleverness.  It became a mindless experience very quick, such a shame.
What made the experience more edible though was, well I've been heavily accustomed to RPG grinding sessions, but also the excellent fluidity of the action, your character is able to wield 3 weapons at once and can use tomahawks and explosives when things get hairy.  You can also use stealth to hit enemies from behind, but what I instead resorted to do is to attract them so to speed up things, none of which are bad strategies, it's just different styles of play.  There's a very good variety of strategies to employ, and when the enemies hoard onto you, it gets pretty tense and it's just great, I really liked when there were ambushes.
Again, there aren't many games like this and it has its moments, but it could've been so much better if they had toned down on the fetch quests, and that's why I'm even giving it a thumbs down, it's because it had seriously bummed me out.

And a large chunk of that 3 hours is you twiddling your thumbs waiting for the next highly scripted segment of gameplay to trigger because you as the player can't do much of anything alone. Despite supposedly being an important key figure in the rebellion (which never gets explained, not that much does), you are led by the hand the entire time and trusted to do nothing on your own. You are treated like an incompetent child. You have zero player agency. You can't even climb a ladder until the game gives you a button prompt. The game literally thinks that you are too stupid to perform even the most basic functions without instruction. I don't mind linear games, but this game is so linear that it makes the Call Of Duty franchise look like a series of expansive open world games with great player freedom. The game also suffers from horrific collision detection problems as well as physX issues, leading to many silly deaths and flat out broken sections of gameplay. The story also makes no sense, has terrible pacing, as you would expect from a 3 hour campaign, and is tonally all over the place. It has it's moments of fun, it isn't all bad, but the good moments are rare and aren’t nearly good enough to compensate for how dull and infuriating the experience is for the other 75% of the time. In all honesty, I wouldn't recommend this game at any price.

Homefront is nothing more than a boring but thankfully short shooting gallery.
The premise of the game is actually quite good and is probably the only saving grace of the game. If you are a fan of Red Dawn than you will be extremely dissapointed as this game has a pretty decent premise but terrible execution. The story is terrible with shallow characters that will leave you with no emotional attatchment at all. Homefront tries to be a serious game but it ultimately fails . Even in its most "emotional" moments you really wont feel sorry for anyone. The graphics are extremely dated. Textures look terrible especially on bigger levels and the same 4 North Korean enemies are recycled throughout the game. Your allies also look extremely bad and are usually blank faced or have some ridiculous stare that was meant to show the intensity of the battle but ends up just making the player laugh. The guns are also pretty bad looking and their sounds are god awful. The voice acting is sub par as well. One of the bigger faults of this game is that it is extremely boring. The game basically boils down to killing a mass of enemies before going and pushing a switch or blowing something up. After the task is complete you run around for a bit more and to it again. Homefront is also extremely easy. The game offers no challenge on medium difficulty. I died about 3-4 times during my run of the whole campaign and that was only because I tried to "rambo" it a couple of times. The only ridiculous mechanic that offers even the slightest challenge is the fact that enemies are ♥♥♥♥ing sharpshooters that can hit you from across the map when they see just a sliver of your shoulder. But even with this just proning behind cover every once in a while will do the trick. This game is also extremely short. I finished the 7 chapters of the campaign in a mere 3.4 hours. That is ridiculous and should not be acceptable by any means even if the game has a good story.  Those 3,4 hours were extremel tedious and painfull. By the end of the game you are just relieved that the nightmare is almost over then Homefront decides to give you one last ♥♥♥♥♥slap across the face by sequel baiting and leaving a cliffhanger. ♥♥♥♥ off at least we deserved a proper ending but nooooo. Dont go near this ♥♥♥♥ing awful game.
TLDR: Everything about homefront is terrible and you would get more enjoyment out of a cup of coffee than this game. Its not worth $19.99 and its not even worth $4.99 when its on sale. Dont touch it. Forget about it. Burn it with fire. Please run before its too late.

I'll be honest, I have a love-hate relationship with Betrayer. Diving in the game for the first time I was absolutely enthralled by the monochrome visuals, the flawless sound design and the incredibly unsettling atmosphere. However, this all changed rather quickly. There aren't many games that I remember that made me feel this torn about what I should feel about them.
Betrayer is a pretty mixed bag in many regards. Starting out you quickly find out that you're an alone guy stranded in 17th century Virginia with crappy weapons and alone against hordes of enemies. The game teaches you to use stealth to sneak past them and pick them off, but it quickly decides to devolve into an endless string of fetch quests with lots of unavoidable combat. Let's be honest, not much sneaking can be done when enemies spawn almost on top of you.
The "endless stream of fetch quests" thing I mentioned is the main thing that killed the game's charm for me. The first time I mounted the bell and was transported to the shadow realm I was scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and had no idea what was going on. When I cleared the area and got to the next one and found out I was to do the exact same thing, I quickly started growing disenchanted. Find all the evidence, dig out all the items, go to the shadow world, talk to the ghosts, rince, repeat many times over, see the ending. It's not a stretch at all when I say that the game plays like a glorified MMORPG.
The story itself would be great if games like F.E.A.R and Silent Hill didn't exist. In the case of F.E.A.R it makes a ton of sense - Betrayer was made by some of the same people. However, you can see the influence Silent Hill had on the game everywhere - from the visuals, to the story, to the inevitable twist at the end that I saw from a mile away. It's a horror game in which I had to put on music after the 1 hour mark and start grinding until I see the ending sequence. And it's not that short of a game at all, it's a 15 hour adventure unless you pretty much sprint through the game.
Overall, the game's vision is commendable, but as an experience it felt like a one trick pony to me, and not a great one at that too.

In rebel galaxy you will find yourself on the edges of civilised space, space stations placed anywhere from the hollowed out husk of a mighty asteroid to in orbit around colossal gas giants will be a sight for sore eyes as you pilot your ship into the awaiting docks, the repair bay will offer you a chance to repair the fractured hull, weapons ranging from ionised bursts of plasma to mighty missle batteries having punched through the shield and torn through the hull damaging systems as well as your own weapons, handing over an adequate sum of currency to the shipwright.
You may choose to offload cargo, either acquired via the mission board (cargo needs to get around somehow), trade with a cargo vessel you pulled out of the fire as pirates attempted to 'appropriate' its cargo or from the ruined husks of the pirate vessels themselves (maybe even the trader too if you're so inclined)
Maybe you're looking for a job? or perhaps to finish one, handing over the agreed upon cargo for a sum of credits, hitting up the mission board to pick out a slew of quests to keep yourself busy as you trek across the system taking on a notorious pirate here, guarding a mining outpost there or perhaps assisting the militia forces take on a pirate convoy, headed by a mighty command ship; there are no shortage of things people want done.
And after all that there's the bar, where you could chat up the tender, asking for news he might be partial to, whether it be as simple as an excalation of pirate activity in the sector, or perhaps that one of the stations in the system are going through some rough times, that being said no one pays more for food than those who need it and where there is demand, there is supply, but whether or not you're the one to supply said goods is up to you.
Or perhaps you're looking for bounties? Slip the barkeep a couple hunded credits and suddenly you've got the locations to a few people someone out there wants dead, and are willing to pay for it.
At the bar you might also meet a merc, spend a couple thousand on a good pilot to watch your back, this section of the galaxy is after all 'mostly' lawless space.
Your visit done, you return to your ship, maybe spend a few thousand credits on an enhanced engine, thicker hull plating or better weapons, maybe even a few new tools to help you along the way, making your weapons deadlier, your aim sharper and those pirate scum a little less threatening.
Whether you want to take to the stars as space trader extraordinare, feared bounty hunter, humble asteroid miner or parhaps cutthroat pirate, (Perhaps a mix of all four?) Rebel Galaxy can certainly accomodate.
{Serious stuff out of the way, I caught a pirate group harassing a salvage crew harvesting the wreck of a giant (at least 12 times the size of my current ship) capital vessel (which you can TOTALLY get later) caught in the midst of a minefield, I noticed a cluster of mines near the enemy vessel on and ended up taking a shot at the explosives, which like a chain reaction of epic preportions exploded (As 'explosives' tend to do) taking out the pirate in a single shot, moments like that is what this game provides, if any of this review sounds like something you'd enjoy than I wholeheartedly recommend Rebel Galaxy.}

Survivor Squad is a top down strategy game, where you can control up to 4 survivors as you clear out level(or nodes, as they're called in-game) by level, looting the buildings and avoiding traps as you go. While in the game, you can pause the game and issue orders to your survivors, which they will carry out when you unpause.
There's a basic resource management in this game. You can loot different materials from the nodes, which are used for crafting various weapons, equipment, and gadgets. Managing the loot you collect in levels can be difficult and meaningful. Since you usually won't have room for ALL the loot you find, do you collect the loot that will let you build better weapons? Or do get the loot that will let you make better armor, backpacks(storage space for more loot), and healing items? Not too long after starting the game, you get the opportunity to "capture" "large" nodes, which will generate basic resources like Wood and scrap, which are the most commonly used crafting material, and Food and Gas, which are used to feed survivors and let them travel to different nodes.
As for the bad:
- There are many instances where enemies will attack through walls, which really screws with the balance.
- Get pushed through walls.
- Get stuck in corners.
- Jam doors shut so you can't pass through them (there are instances where "locked doors" are intentionally, but I'm talking about places they aren't).
- When enemies are ramming against walls because their occasional "walk in a straight line" mentality won't reach you, they'll sort of all stack on top of each other, with very little visual indication they did so. So what appears to be one enemy will turn out to be 18.
- All of the above(minus the 'death stack') happening to your survivors as well.
- Vital interactive environment pieces like buttons that turn off alarms and floodlights wills sometimes be placed in awkward places that your survivors will not be able to reach.
Those are just the bugs I'VE experienced. Others have reported many more. It's been a long time since there's been an update, and I doubt there will be more. Devs have stated that "all promised features are in the game, so it's finished", and other than fixing some game destroying bugs, they've ignored most the rest so far. I'll update this review if that changes.
As for other issues with this game:
- The late game is pretty shallow. Early game your trying to scrounge up all resources you can in order to get better weapons, armor, gadgets, and bigger backpacks. Mid game get's less frantic crafting wise, as not only will you have nodes that gather wood and scrap for you, but there's less to craft. Late game mostly comprises finishing the story and maintaining your territories, the crafting and food supply aspect almost completely forgotten.
- There's some utility features that I wish were in there. Looting the containers in a building loses it's charm fairly quickly, and ordering the containers searched will be tedious. I wish there was a button that tells the survivors to "loot all containers until your full", or something like that.
- Another feature I wish was there was "back to back". Having the survivors back to back, looking in each direction, is the most common and important maneuver. Doing it manually is clunky as hell, and I wish there was a button for it.
Despite all this, it's still a solid game, as most bugs can be ignored, easily worth about $5, though I wouldn't pay full price.

GI racing 2.0 is a racing game which tries to do too many things at once and fails at all of them. The game is in Early Access and it clearly shows it’s not complete yet. The game tries to be an arcade racer yet has features of a realistic racing simulation game. The controls feel floaty and the game runs pretty bad too with stuttering.
The game’s graphics are pretty bad and look so dull and gloomy. I didn’t like the way the game looked at all. The game’s pretty bad in optimization as I had ~35-40FPS throughout the gameplay. I noticed stuttering as well.
Music is nonexistent apart from the main menu, you won’t hear a thing in races other than the obnoxiously loud engine sound (yes, I turned the ‘car’ volume almost all the way down in the options menu already).
Gameplay is your standard races in different maps. There seem to be only 2 different tracks. These tracks come in different variations e.g. a track could be in day time, night time, or day time with wet track etc. There’s a quick play mode where you can select a track and just start playing right away or go for the ‘Tournament’ mode if you have the patience.
The controls feel very floaty and the camera is all over the place. If you play in the cockpit view mode, it’s not that bad but for someone who prefers the third person behind the car camera angle it can be problematic.There's a camera problem, when you press brake fast and try to turn, the camera goes out of focus on the car and you cannot see your car and cannot make adjustments to make the turn properly. There are many other problems such as the car sliding out of control at just even touching the other car at slow speeds, so physics is also not the best in the game. When you turn or move right and left the car feels like it’s strafing left and right and not turning.
I usually don’t give such harsh reviews but in this game’s case I had to. I only played 20 minutes and I couldn’t take it anymore. Just look at the gameplay video posted below as words can’t describe these. Check out my attempt to play a serious game and giving up.

Okay, now for a serious review. I love the idea of a game where you *are* the mass shooter. (This does not make me want to be one.) However, it lends itself to that old "to catch a criminal, you have to think like a criminal" chain of thought. With most of the mass shootings in the US, we have a tendency to just give a death toll, the victims' names, and label it as "a random and senseless act of violence" or something along those lines, and that's a wrap. So what does the general populace learn from these events? Practically nothing.
While playing this game won't instill you with every bit of knowledge on how to combat mass shooters, it does give you that perspective of the shooter; that "I don't care who you are, or that you have a kid; I'm going to kill you or die trying." And it drives home this perspective amazingly. For the experience of shooting masses of unarmed civilians and then that feeling you get (or at least, the feeling I got) afterwards that makes you sit back and go "did I really just get that into killing civilians?", it's a bit of an eye opener.
Through the right observational lens, if you take away the correct information, this game could very well potentially help to save your life. And that is why I strongly recommend it.
Maybe this is just me overanalyzing it, but that's how I perceive it. Still a fun game to play.

This is a hard game to review.  It's a nice game, but EXTREMELY unpolished.  Which is unfortunate, because with a month or two of polish this could be a *fantastic* game, rather than just nice.
The game is a zombie shooter played from a top-down real-time tactical perspective.  You control a squad of up to four survivors, clearing buildings of zombies and scavenging for supplies.  There are special infected a la 'Left 4 Dead', and rudimentary inventory and leveling systems.
Unfortunately, as I said, the game is extremely unpolished:
None of these things are terrible on their own, but together they make the game feel bland and unfinished.  My review is right on the border of positive, because it WAS really fun for an hour or two; but the lack of polish causes it to quickly become boring, then frustrating.  The game feels like it's in early-access, but the devs adamently insist it's a finished product.  Which is a shame, because this game has so much unrealized potential.
If you are a strategy-game aficionado, you will probably enjoy playing this, but maybe wait for a sale.  Everyone else should go play
instead, which is the same game but better in every possible way.

Masha Rescues Grandma feels like some old Flash game coming back from the grave, but there are a few clever adventure game bits hidden under its amateurish exterior.
Masha Rescues Grandma is, from a technological standpoint, extremely limited, as if it was some garage project from 20 years ago. Just like
(the creator’s previous game), it is something we may call a point ‘n’ click adventure, where the game engine is the greatest source of difficulty.
There are no animations, no responsive cursor, no help messages, nothing. You have to guess which items you can pick up, in some cases what they even are, and, finally, where to use them—upon which they immediately vanish as if they never existed.
If you can somehow live with these stone-age mechanics, then the actual game under is, honestly, not half-bad. It follows a certain logic, and—despite the low resolution—the scenery looks pretty. Admittedly, anything over a dollar would be too much for it, but for a cheap price, Masha Rescues Grandma
provide some fun for an adventure gamer.

Feels Endless in replayability and Challenges. Doesn't feel like you can play it enough! Great single player although you'd be pressed to find multiplay in 2017 but there is Lan Ability!. Still one of the better RTS I have experienced, I would go into detail but it's difficult to do it justice or cover everything :D. The factions are diverse and well fleshed out, I don't even have all the DLC at the time of writting this and game feels very fleshed out.
Updating this as it's on Sale, The game only utilizes one CPU core so you may notice a slight preformance hit at the late game. Although it's still rather old game that still holds up it's snuff.  The 3 factions each have a loyalist and a Rebel faction making 6 playable factions. Maying for a lot of depth, It plays like an RTS but the way you build almost makes it look like a turn based game however it's 100% in real time. Maps are generated so no one playthrough will be identical unless you make it so intentionally.
You can start with a couple of scout frigates depending how you tweek the settings, you will immediatly encounter pirates or neutral faction which make rapid expansion more too learn including a rather nice research tree. The Pirate bounty works well with Ai although I can only imagine how it plays out with other players. As I said lan functionality means you can play this game with friends if you so choose, All factions have a star base building which has quite the diversity of upgrades and I believe is limited to a max of seven when you can shell out the crystals.  This makes for interesting mechanics each player can only build one per star system but nothing is stopping two opposing factions to contest a star system or Planet. This makes for quite interesting situations that turn into an arms race. The maps offer somewhat limited movement between planets and stars untill you get more research and access warps and a recon which will detect other players warping in a proximity so you are not caught off guard mid and late game.
There are also warp inhibitors which will slow the opponent from leaving a system you built them in so you can damage their fleet if they do not scout where they are jumping before moving their whole fleet and thier Titan too you. I Enjoy the Flag ship setting where everyone starts with a flag ship, It's a powerful capital ship early but if destroyed that faction is eliminated from the match., Along with a whole plethera of victory conditions. Also I forgot to mention aside from Titans there is also Super weapons ;) All cleaverly balanced with a checks and balances in planet System building limits and fleet logistics.
Game is several years old I'd give it a solid 8.5 /10 maybe a little generous considering the one core limitation depending on your CPU, but I enjoyed almost every minute I have played of this game.

To me Hitman: Absolution is probably the best game of the Hitman-series, it is definately the best looking one of the first 4 Hitman-games, with just beautiful graphics, better than the previous games of the franchise. With the Glacier 2 engine, the game looks so realistic and makes the gameplay a real joy for everyone, who plays it. The characters are looking very nice, especially Mr. 47 himself, who looks better than ever before, especially more realistic, but also the other main characters in the game are looking very good.
But also the gameplay itself is very well done, they kept a lot of things from the previous Hitman: Blood Money and added some new stuff as well, to make this gaming experience just remarkable. Like in Blood Money, you have dozens of ways to eliminate your target and you don't have to fire a single bullet to reach your goals. You can sneak up on him/her or you can make it look like an accident or just go beserk. But the more silent you kill your target(s), the higher is your score and the better your rating, although I find it a bit sad, that you don't have the very bad ratings like
"mass-murderer" or "slaughterer" anymore, the worst you can get is "agent". Of course, when you kill non-targets or civillians, you will receive a massive loss of points in our final score.
Also you can increase your score by hiding dead bodies/knocked out people or remove evidences from the scene and there are muliple challenges to complete, which will later increase your points-multiplier.
The level-design is also very well done, even though it is more linearly designed than in previous games of the Hitman-franchise. But you have pretty large levels in which you have several ways to sneak around to find and kill your targets and achieve your goals. But you have to watch out for the many many guards/cops/handymen you have to evade, without being uncovered. You probably have to try it several times, before you'll find the best way to reach the target, it's sometimes a real challenge, depending on the difficulty level you've chosen.
That's the next point, the 5 different difficulty levels, you can choose between easy, medium, hard, expert and purist. The higher the difficulty is chosen, the more and more observant are the enemies, plus the use of instinct is limited, as well as other help, on purist for example, you have no instinct and help at all and full enemy presence! Real challenging!
Another great addition to Hitman: Absolution is the "Contracts Mode", which allows you to create your own contracts. You can choose one of the levels, mark your target(s) and set contract details on how to kill your target(s), the weapons and/or if the bodies have to be hid and so on. You can almost do anything you like, and you have dozens of possible targets in every level, which is a huge fun! Also you can play contracts, that other people or your friends have created and try to hit the highscore. I personally have spent almost 400 hours with the game and about 350 of them in contracts mode alone!
The conclusion is, that Hitman: Absolution is a great game, until February, 11th 2016 it was the best game in the francise, until it was beaten by the newest installment named "HITMAN". But even after the release of the new game, Hitman: Absolution is still a fantastic game, with beautiful graphics, a very nice story and many assassin-tastic missions. It's still worth playing and as a true Hitman-Gamer you have to have this game!

Masha Rescues Grandma is a minimalistic (both in content and in implementation) tablet adventure game and one of those titles in which you don't really know whether its shortness is a blessing or a curse. It tries to walk on the path of the popular hidden object games (it isn't one however - at least not in the conventional way - so I don't know how that tag got there), but it fails miserably. It's quite obvious that this game is the work of a single person, but there are boundaries within this can be an excuse. The whole game can be completed roughly in about an hour (or even half an hour if you have a slightly developed sixth sense or are just simply lucky).
Masha apparently is an alternative version of Little Red Riding Hood (Rotkäppchen in German and Piroska in Hungarian) whose grandma needs to be rescued (as you have probably figured out already). This rescue means that we have to get out of our house, walk through forests and swamps and reach grandma's little cottage (so we can rescue her). And yes, there's a wolf involved.
The world itself the game takes place in is a strange mixture of the tale we all know and of a semi-fantasy (there's a flashlight in it for example) world with goblins and trolls, where magic is seemingly common. An interesting concept.
The adventure mainly consists of searching around and using objects from our inventory at given locations. One of the first problems comes right here: there aren't any (!) descriptions and occasionaly it's not obvious what some of these items actually are. Some of them are so blurry and poorly drawn, they can hardly be recognized or identified. The second problem is the seemingly intuitional nature of the puzzles, where we have to figure out what to use where without any hints or clues. On one occasion, we find an animal (reptilian?) skull with a gemstone in one of its eyesockets (or nostril) and we have to insert another gem (a different coloured and shaped one of course) into its other eyesocket and thus we get a third gem out of its mouth. There is an active slot in which you have to place the item about to be used, so that can further reduce the chance for success (strangely though, sometimes the game uses certain objects automatically, like keys for instance). The game tries to make up for this difficulty by placing the location of use near (or right on the same spot) the found item (at least sometimes).
There are also some minigames, which do show resemblance to the ones seen in hidden object games, but they are neither original or exciting.
The only texts we encounter are the ones that can be found in the quest descriptions, where usually a monster asks (instead of eating) us to retrieve an item he is looking for.
To say something good about it, well, it's family friendly
, but then again, it's too hard for a child to play. It's also worth mentioning that it's bug free and it
actually be finished (something that's not so obvious regarding many games on Steam as I've learned).
The game is very plain and blurry looking, we only get to see static screens, with some basic animations (fireflies), but I wish this was the biggest problem altogether. The music feels very strange, somehow unfitting. Needles to say there are hardly any sound effects and no voiceover at all.
The main problem with Masha Rescues Grandma is that everything in it is just below average and there's hardly anything worth recommending. The absence of even basic instructions (and logic sometimes) ruins the game and because of it the game also manages to lose its target audience (and everyone else sadly). With some actual item description, a bit more minigames and better graphics it could have been a decent (or at least not so bad) game, ideal for those who prefer non-violent adventures, but in its current state it can only be described as a bleak and bad game.
PROS
+ family friendly
+ basically bug free
CONS
- no item descriptions
- no hints for puzzles, illogical item use on several occasions
- only a few minigames
- very bleak implementation, no voiceover
- quite short (altough this can be a positive feature as well)
RATING
1,5/10

Despite sharing the appearance of most hidden object games these days, this one is more like a very basic first-person point & click with pixel hunting. It's very short (I finished it in a bit over an hour, not enough to collect any cards so I'll have to farm the game on top of that), I've even found a walkthrough (not a speedrun!) that finished it in 14 minutes.
The graphics are okay, there are only two different songs (one basic, one terrible), and there are nearly no animations in the game -- it's all a series of static screens with a few tweened animations here and there. There are a total of 5 characters I believe (Marsha, her grandma, a goblin, some other guy, and the wolf... Does the plant count?), and they only have one thing to say, in broken English. Switch to French if you can, at least it's more readable, although they translated 'my pipe' to 'my (smoking) pipe', rather than the musical kind. Yeah, there are like 10 paragraphs of text in the game and it's still badly botched.
There's no tutorial, so you're left to your own devices when it comes to understanding that the weird 'X' button in the inventory is there to combine objects. The objects are so badly rendered that you'll often wondered what you built exactly. (That things that removes the thorns..? Seriously, what was that?)
Also, if I understood correctly: Marsha is living all alone in the forest, stuck in her house. The way to her grandma's is dangerous, and she has to go through ancient ruins that obviously never visited before. So it's her first time on the road? Maybe she just moved? Why doesn't the story tell us that? Why is the grandma sick? Why do we need crystals to cure her? Is this a drug-related metaphor?
I guess it's all I can say about the game... Starts from a basic idea ("let's redo Red Riding Hood!", like 37 other, better video games), does a basic job at everything it does, and completely forgets to get a soul in the middle. Okay, let's just say if you don't have high expectations, and you find it for a buck or less (I got it from a cheap bundle), it's worth a few cents and an hour of your time. But as a reward for a day's work, I'd rather play something else. 4/10. (So what. I've never given a rating before. I'm trying.)

I'll be honest, I have a love-hate relationship with Betrayer. Diving in the game for the first time I was absolutely enthralled by the monochrome visuals, the flawless sound design and the incredibly unsettling atmosphere. However, this all changed rather quickly. There aren't many games that I remember that made me feel this torn about what I should feel about them.
Betrayer is a pretty mixed bag in many regards. Starting out you quickly find out that you're an alone guy stranded in 17th century Virginia with crappy weapons and alone against hordes of enemies. The game teaches you to use stealth to sneak past them and pick them off, but it quickly decides to devolve into an endless string of fetch quests with lots of unavoidable combat. Let's be honest, not much sneaking can be done when enemies spawn almost on top of you.
The "endless stream of fetch quests" thing I mentioned is the main thing that killed the game's charm for me. The first time I mounted the bell and was transported to the shadow realm I was scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and had no idea what was going on. When I cleared the area and got to the next one and found out I was to do the exact same thing, I quickly started growing disenchanted. Find all the evidence, dig out all the items, go to the shadow world, talk to the ghosts, rince, repeat many times over, see the ending. It's not a stretch at all when I say that the game plays like a glorified MMORPG.
The story itself would be great if games like F.E.A.R and Silent Hill didn't exist. In the case of F.E.A.R it makes a ton of sense - Betrayer was made by some of the same people. However, you can see the influence Silent Hill had on the game everywhere - from the visuals, to the story, to the inevitable twist at the end that I saw from a mile away. It's a horror game in which I had to put on music after the 1 hour mark and start grinding until I see the ending sequence. And it's not that short of a game at all, it's a 15 hour adventure unless you pretty much sprint through the game.
Overall, the game's vision is commendable, but as an experience it felt like a one trick pony to me, and not a great one at that too.

You must investigate the New World and find out what has caused the colonies to go silent.
PROS
+ Interesting idea and world
+ Cool light/dark concept
CONS
- Becomes a tedious collection game
- Combat is painful
- Interest turns to boredom quickly
I went into this game with little knowledge of what it was about and I was surprised at first. Taking place in colonial times gives it a fresh feel and the story quickly gives it a lot of horror flavor... kind of like the Revenant meets Blair Witch. However, things slowly began to slip into boredom from there.
I ran around the maps and collected the items, reading the notes, etc. but It quickly devovled into a "shopping list scenario" where you get thing 1, get thing 2, get thing 3... The things were mostly coin to buy weapon upgrades and ammo making me wonder if all the walking was necessary, but then you need to because you need to find notes and items to give hints to Wraiths and Shadows on how they died which are usually in very interesting (and mostly horrific) fashion.
The combat in between is tiedious and puts you on your heels. The enemy doesn't recoil in pain and comes at you in force. They are faster and can shoot straighter than you. If you are using the bow and arrow, I found it hard to get a headshot (figure out arrow drop) and usually shot over their head. When you run out of arrows you automatically switch to the rifle wasting a shot. The rifle (and pistol) takes so long to reload you'll get in a pattern of running backward while trying to reload for your next shot or trying to put a tree in between you and the enemy but they are relentless (even the large ones are fast) and can lead their target (you) very, very well. You die a lot.
Unfortunately, the game comes off very lifeless and boring. It's like playing a MMORPG but with only NPCs and no human interaction. You do a bunch of collection missions and get some filler text, but there's no life in any of the characters (literally and figuratively). The only "live" character I ran into was the lady in red and she only throws out snippy comments so I avoided her most of the time. It was just boring.
I felt like they had something here but it was unfinished. The spirit world bell was a cool idea. The atomsphere and world crafted was good. The stories of how the colonists died were interesting. It's just that the "game" portion of the game wasn't filled with anything overly interesting so I got bored way too easy.

Another solid racer from Codemasters.
The game is based around startting a new racing code that, this gives the objective some cohegency as you jetset across the globe and build an impressive garage.
A mixed range of car styles and classes, race events and locaions keep the game interesting. Classic American muscle right through to GT3 spec race cars. Standard races, time trial, overtake specials, drift challenges and head to head one on ones through Japanese mountain roads give good range of play.
A tweaked engine that ran the original GRID still has enough power to offer stunning results. The cars sound appropriately meaty too. Music isn't too present, but there's a a cool track that kicks in on the last lap of important races that goes a good way to increasing the drama of the game.
My only criticism would be that the earlier stages are more interesting than the latter, and that there isn't any dynamic weather and time of day options.
If you're a fan of the original GRID, codemaster racing games, or racing games in general I'd feel pretty safe in recommending this to you.

Betrayer's a sort of admirable failure. Playing a game where you are placed into such haunted and foreboding settings such as these abandoned forts and vacant fields, in stark black and white no less, listening to the wind rush through the trees testifying to nature's massive presence and civilization's absence, hunting for clues to discover just what happened to the native and colonial life here creates a unsettling and intriguing ambiance, while offering the player almost no hand or guide at all! Ballsy! Alienated and isolated in this haunted wilderness, the devs want you to crawl around the forest looking for bloody dirt, buried secrets, signs of struggle which lead in some way to a interweaving, tragic story of paranoia and greed in the wild frontier... this isn't a conventional game and it's not telling a story with any likeable figures or hopes for redemption, there isn't anything to find joy in. You'll find ghosts and shadows who have forgotten who they are and won't budge an expositional inch until you dig up their past to reveal their inhuman brutality to them, until they remember all the people they've killed and the anxieties that haunted them in their lives. It's fascinating, but it's a ton of trek-work which is endemic of the problem of Betrayer.
This game asks a lot from the player and doesn't concern itself with attracting you with even a hint towards a promise (like the NPCs who have no facial animation, this game plays with a strict pokerface) for any kind of satisfying reward or resolution; you do a lot of this busy work of solving ghost mysteries and running around the woods only hoping it pays off and, well, I don't think everyone will think what you get is exactly rewarding. In some ways this game is sort of antithetical to a lot of modern, tried-and-true, game design-philosophy that it sort of adopts a, at least in my mind, punk sort of disposition which demands the player engage or walk away. Bt after having gone along and seen their vision through, Blackpowder Games just didn't create a video game that is all that compelling. Betrayer has a strong ambiance, a unique story which is presented in a cool way, and an admirable while somewhat antagonistic philosophy about just how much a player really needs but it's kind of boring, a bit repetitive and schematic, and not always worth the effort.
The addition of map markers in a recent patch speaks as an admission of defeat of vision for this game. If all hidden things are just collectables on a map, what makes this game different than something like Farcry, other than being more obtuse? Try again, Blackpowder Games! I dig the idea, but really do it next time.

Jalopy is an interesting title, I first came across it on Steam Greenlight and promptly gave it my vote, now finally the game is released into Early Access and the main question is, is it good? I would say it is good though it does have a lot of bugs, some small some big, but nothing so far for me that would make me give it a negative review, it's in Early Access so of course it's not finished but the foundation is there and it's pretty solid. Also the game has recieved a couple updates today alone so the developer is clearly working hard on this game.
--Gameplay--
Jalopy is a game where you go on a road trip with your Uncle but before that begins you have to finish fixing your car up by putting in all the essentials under the hood of the vehicl, putting a passenger door on and putting a jack under the car and putting the wheels on. The Tutorial is pretty helpful and gives you an understanding of what you should do even if you aren't too familiar with cars and their parts. After that you choose a route and head off, you have to be careful when driving to not crash or stop (DO NOT, Stop in the middle of the road, the drivers are ruthless and will crash into you at 80mph, and then if they don't push your car out of the way they will reverse and do it again), when driving you may enounter engine or other part faults. You can bring things in the trunk of your car (Which you pretty much must do) which is very helpful as if you break down with no repair kit you are screwed, you can also bring a bucket of water and wash your windows if they get dirty (And a bunch of other things, oil, fuel etc).There are shops and gas stations which you can buy various other things. I haven't gotten too far into the game but that's pretty much all I've experienced so far.
--Bugs--
I feel like this should be it's own catagory since the game is early in development and bugs are heavy. Some big bugs range from getting stuck behind the shop gate and it not opening again, people have said they got stuck in the motel and of course don't forget the insane drivers ramming you at 80mph if you stop.
--Conclusion--
The foundation is there and the game is fun, even if the game bugs out and I have to restart I haven't felt like not playing since it's a pretty fun game and as the game develops it can only get more fun. I give the game an 8.5/10 with an expectation of 10/10 for being an Extremely unique experience with so much already to it.

In Jalopy, you drive an old wreck named "Laika 601 Deluxe", a two stroke, 25 Miles/gallon, 0-100 Km/h within 22,5 seconds etc.
The story starts when your uncle in a trippy coat wakes you up and wants to drive east. So you wake up, get a spare door from a pile of wrecks, slap on some tires, build the engine, plan your path and you are good to go!
While driving, it's good to have a repair kit, a full gas tank, a spare bottle of water&oil and a carjack, because you never know what lies in front of you in this game!
So, now pros and cons:
(I am not putting any not added features in the game to cons because I am writing this review the day it was released)
+ A great gameplay of mixed adventure and car management game
+ Your engine is very fragile, a one essential part goes off and you're done adventuring, so you must be careful
+ Realism in this game is at a quite high level
+ you can pick from different routes
+ not so stunning graphics compensated with a stunning atmosphere
+ SO MANY THINGS IN THE CAR TO PLAY WITH
+ original concept
- Sometimes, the uncle is overreacting a bit
i would definitely reccomend this game and i give it 9,9/10, but if you want a better experience/longer gameplay, then wait few months.

I usually do not write reviews of games, but the many negative reviews suprises me, and I feel that this game deserves better than that: In my opinion, this version of Civilization is the best one ever.
I rarely complete a regular CIV 5 game, as I usually find that it has too many things to manage. Also, I am a sucker for thematically games, and regular CIV 5 just does not hit it for me (Bismarc founding religions BC??).
CIV BE on the other hand, is more streamlines with less to manage without sacrificing having to choose how to build your civilization. The concepts of non-linear techs gives so much more when it comes to customizability. On the thematically side, affinities, the freedom of the techtree, non-historically bound factions and the concept of alien worlds gives me much more than regular CIV ever did.
I keep my fingers crossed for an expansion, as there are so many possibilities within the frame of the theme.

The campaign feels very free and open. Watching your men shoot zombies is very visceral and exciting.

Special zombies are extremely dangerous, and can temporarily disable one of your squad, making it necessary to travel in groups of two or more.
Weapons and armors seem a little expensive, but it doesn't kill the sense of advancement.
Overall, I definitely reccommend this game. A good buy for tactical gameplay fanatics.

I'm going to try and explain this game as best as possible because to me as a gamer, this game can be fit into multiple different genres and categories.  It can be a simple Survival game, an Action/RPG type game, it can be many things to different people but bottom line is it's a great game.  It's not perfect, but it shines in ways most triple A titles just can't, especially from an Independent Studio.  In a nutshell, you control several characters as you scavenge, build, upgrade, repair, replace, craft and and much more, as you try to survive the worn torn city.  The game is broken up into DAY and NIGHT, during the day you upgrade your shelter or sleep off your wounds or sickness, keep an eye on the temp to maintain warmth, ensure your people are well fed, entertained or otherwise satisfied in order to avoid your people getting depression and ultimately, die or commit suicide.  It is a hard juggle between how best to utilize what resources you are able to scavenge at NIGHT when you send one of your people out into the city while avoiding (or fighting) soldiers, other survivors that may or may not be friendly (you can be unfriendly and ambush people yourself) manage your backpack slots and make the decision on what is more important to bring back to your shelter; like the difference between leaving a lot of valuable loot behind like important upgrade or building components or weapons instead of food and medical supplies since you have very limited space to carry stuff and not near enough of anything to make your decision any easier; you always need whatever the hell you can find so the game can get rather frustrating at times but once you get into a good rhythm, learn the best ways to guard your shelter, and manage your supplies and people well, it can be an extremely unique and fun game worth the $20 it is normally but it is a must buy if you see it on a Special or during a Steam Sale event.  It does take a little to get used to playing but once you get it down it is fun and rewarding.  Happy Gaming!!

Well how should i put it...... I've read both the positive and negative reviews and I have to say that both these types of reviews hold true to the facts - its just a matter of inclination from the player's point of view of whether they want to bear the opportunity cost stated in the negatives and (want to) play this game. I personally like this game very much but it does have some issues with plain linear racing - by which I mean this game does have problems with its physics (a certain "overcompensation"), no matter how minor. And yes like another reviewer stated here Grid 2 developers hve gone mad with drifting! They expect a drift for proper corner handling every time a bend comes up! And frankly I'm not a big fan of drifting either. Then there's the damage reporting - which frankly dosen't exist except for a single indicator in the speedometer, and which when compared to Grid 1 (which had 8 - 4 wheels, 1 engine, 1 transmission, 1 suspension and 1 handling) is certainly a big leap downwards. Some will be put off by the abscence of a cockpit view.  Now people reading this review might be thinking why I've recommended this game with all this negativity - well, I'd now would like to tell you why this game pretty much makes its competitors look drab - the graphics is a monumental achievement (compared to Grid 1 - which was pretty darn excellent), the feel and gravity (literally!) is very realistic (albeit slightly problematic physics) - for example you can really differentiate which cars have better torque and which cars have higher rev ranges, and the (car) damage as realistic as ever. So although Grid 2 might struggle to live up to (and even falls short at some points) the name of its predecessor it sure does put one darn good fight with its rivals.
