Jalopy is an adventure simulation game which just launched through Steam’s Early Access program. In Jalopy you get an old car in working order with basic parts. You’re going to use the car to make a journey from Germany to your family’s home and your uncle is along for the ride. It’s not going to be an easy journey though and you’ll need to manage your car along the way by repairing, refuelling and upgrading it. You’ll also have to plan your journey carefully, you choose from three defined routes for each leg of the journey (of which there are currently two) but you’ll have to keep an eye on your fuel so you stop in plenty of time, run out of fuel and there’s not much you can do apart from restart.
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the publisher.
Please note: My game time is due to playing the press version of the game several times, I have also finished the second country currently in the game. The game (in its current state) can be beaten in around thirty-forty minutes.
It can be difficult to find the sweet spot for releasing a game into Early Access. You need to have enough content in there to keep players happy but you also need to leave room for the game to grow based on the feedback from the community. Unfortunately, like many Early Access games do, Jalopy has released with too little content. What’s there is reasonably good but there’s not enough of it to fully show off what the game has to offer (I’ll come back to this later). What’s worse is that the game currently has very little replay value, in my experience anyway. After I played the press version through the first time I had no desire to play through it again, I only did so to see if I had missed anything. Obviously this will improve as the game continues through development but this is a review for its current state and since the amount of content/replayability is an important consideration when buying a game I felt it was something that had to be included.
On to how the game looks, the colour palette is great but the graphics themselves let the game down a little bit. The dull and dreary colours might not be the nicest thing to look at but they do a good job at creating the depressing world your character is hoping to escape by going on this journey. Now, I’m the kind of person who always says that graphics maketh not the game but there are exceptions to every rule. Honestly, I’m not too bothered by Jalopy’s graphics but they’re by no means excellent. It’s not a big enough problem for me to affect my overall opinion of the game but it is a problem for other people which is why I feel it’s worth including.
Right, back to the meat and potatoes of the game. The game currently features Germany and the CSFR, two countries means two legs of the journey with more countries to be added later. The parts of the two countries you drive through are very different to each other which is great. Germany is all about autobahns and the CSFR is dirt-track driving. The main problem with only having two countries at launch is that there’s not enough time in the game for you to really experience any of what the game offers. Two countries means two opportunities to refuel, one opportunity to buy upgrades/repair your car and one border crossing. The border crossing wasn’t overly interesting, I imagine it’s more interesting if you get caught trying to smuggle illegal goods across the border (you find things on the side of the road which can be picked up and later sold for profit) though I was rather fond of how had a similar feel to Papers, Please. Upgrades can be bought from Laika dealerships which are found in the game’s cities and you can also get parts from junk cars left by the side of the road. Repairing your car is pretty simple, you just buy a repair kit and then click on the part you want to repair and it’s magically repaired! Three uses per kit. There’s not much to say about refuelling other than it’s a good idea to refuel whenever possible because unless you want to walk back to a station you’ve passed, you’ll have to restart.
Just a few more things to mention. I’m well above minimum specs and should be at least capable of running it on High settings and yet I was struggling to run it well on Medium settings. The settings are also incredibly basic, you have an overall quality setting for graphics as well as resolution, vsync and a fullscreen toggle; audio is only master volume and gameplay is currently just look sensitivity. My last issue with the game is that it currently has no controller support (and no wheel support, I don’t have a wheel myself but I know a lot of people prefer using wheels for driving games). I found controlling the car with the keyboard controls to be incredibly jerky and imprecise, making the game less enjoyable. Next up, while I’ve only experienced a few bugs, there have been quite a lot of complaints about the game being buggy. I get that it’s an Early Access games and most Early Access games do have bugs but it’s worth knowing that Jalopy is particularly buggy in its current form. Lastly, I had a problem with the tutorial. The tutorial itself is great but unless you Save and Quit after completing the tutorial and then choose Continue when you want to play the game. It’s inconvenient but it’s not exactly bad enough to write home about, the problem I have with this is that the game doesn’t tell you that you have to do this, I only know this because I read about it in the forums which not all players will do. Personally, I’d prefer to just be able to skip it but at the very least there needs to be some information provided to inform the player about this.
An excellent concept for a game let down by its lack of content and a range of other issues. The problem with having such little content is that you can’t fully enjoy what the game is supposed to be all about and that makes an already weak launch even weaker. At the current price and in its current state I simply cannot recommend Jalopy.

First things first, Survivor Squad is a Real-Time Strategy, a genre I have experience with. Trapped in a world swarmed with the undead, you, the player, must help your starting survivor build up a squad in order to scavenge for useful resources, such as blueprints, scrap, wood and weapons, speaking of which, the crafting system works well, and respects your abilities as a player by not being overly demanding. Now, onto the core gameplay. The controls, while simple to use, seem tiresome and outdated, but still provide a solid, strategic experience for the player to immerse themselves into. The AI, while mostly done effectively, can sometimes be troublesome, seeing as the occasional zed can glitch out and just lag back and forth, which brings me to the occasional framerate issues. Alright, I own a Windows 7, but most of my other games, especially the first person shooters, rarely have problems with framerate. Most of the time, in Survivor Squad, the framerate is not bad. However, upon firing a gun, which can alert most nearby enemies, the framerate starts to lag substantially.
However, another redeeming feature of the game is the stealth mechanics. only able to see zombies within your survivors' field of vision, even through windows? Adds a lot of depth of realism to the game, as you never know what kind of horror may be lurking around the next corner. Which brings me to the enemy variety. As well as your basic zombies, you have jumpers, spitters and others I have yet to familiarize myself with. Moreover, when not slaughtering the undead, you have the overworld, which randomly generates the location and name of each place adjacent to cleansed territory. However, this can sometimes lead to inconsistency; why, like in my current game, would Bangkok be right next to Harvard?
Furthermore, you can enter the Death Lab mode, where several floors are randomly generated for your survivors to navigate while the undead are out for your blood served in a cocktail. As I just implied, the mode is insanely difficult and it takes veteran skill to survive even the first floor, seeing as your instant annihilation is preying on you until your inevitable death.
In conclusion, Survivor Squad is a game with the potential to achieve milestones in the RTS genre, and a fresh adventure that keeps you on your toes. I rate this game 8/10.

This is a game that really makes me wish there was an ambivalent recommendation option, rather than just a straight out "yes" or "no".
Pimiko Plus is a simple part market sim part RPG game. It's the kind of game that lends itself to short, 15-ish minute sessions of play. The problems surrounding the game, though, arise from the simplicity of its core gameplay.
The market sim aspect is very barebones. It's what you'd expect- buy low, sell high- but there's not much more to it than that. The game flow is nothing more than just buying whatever's for cheap, and bumbling around any of the 8 locations in total to see where the price has skyrocketed to an absurd level so you can sell your goods. In only a few turns you might already see yourself with the best equipment and hauling around the more expensive goods.
I'm not sure if I'm asking too much, but the game is just so painfully simple. I know that's part of the point of the game, but there's so much potential for something more. You follow the prices from whatever location you're in, it's rigid and there's no room for things like haggling; you just buy and sell. There's no rammification from what goods you decide to deal in, either- it's all basically random when it comes to the prices of items in any particular location no matter how much you buy or sell (though this is to be remedied in a new "realism" mode the developer is planning to put in). All of the locations are pretty much- no, rather- completely the same, with the equipment shops all dealing the same weapons and combat items, and there's no difference in what events or encounters that will occur no matter how far apart they are from another when you choose to travel from one place to another. There is a message at the end of your 30 turn session which discerns the implications of your (probably illicit) trading activities on the quality of life of the people in the game world, but that's about the extent of it, and I have never managed to get anything more than "nothing changed but at least you're richer".
The RPG systems in this game are also very sparse. As I said earlier, you'll find yourself bleeding cash, so in only a few turns you'll already be buying the best equipment. At this point, the random encounters with raiders will be completely inconsequential because you'll be able to deal with a group of three in combat with no problem. It just boils down to clicking the "fire" button because all of the other options in battle, such as throwing items, sweet talking, throwing sand in their eyes, even running away from battle itself are just suboptimal compared to just shooting them. It's nice that different options are there, but they don't hold much of a candle just to mindlessly blasting them until they're dead or flee. The fact that having a weapon weighs you down and that you pretty much want to be overencumbered with trade goods in order to get the most out of the market just exacerbates the idea that you should just be gunning everyone down.
There is also an class system, with the class you pick enhancing a particular style of play, but not by much. You unlock these (as well as skins for Ruho) with tokens you get after a session, depending on how much money you make. The Junker is the best simply because you can save a lot of hassle by letting you see where items are the cheapest, thus netting you more money, which leads to encounters being a complete non-issue. The Raider can punch harder and can negotiate better with enemy raiders and the Doctor can use up a First Aid to get out of a battle for free, but why bother with any of that when you can just shoot everything to death, you know?
All I've been doing so far is harking on the game, so you're probably wondering why I recommend it. It's simple; I'm a sucker for this♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ruho is a super cute "plumpy mama" (game's words, not mine, I SWEAR!) and the doujinsoft style of it just drew me in. The UI is very simple and easy to grasp, and you can move it in the game space however you like, an enhance the overall sim feeling of the game. The pixel art, though not prominent, is really great, which I've come to expect from this developer based on their work on Amihailu. The soundtrack is absolutely killer. The short, coffee break nature of a single session speaks to me because I barely have enough time to sit down and really enjoy a full game of pretty much anything else. Though there's a great lack of variation in encounters and event types, the writing more than makes up for it. I really do like the world that's been put on display, and its a shame that there isn't much in the way of flavour text for the goods you're selling, the locations you're visiting and dialogue/descriptions for the equipment dealers or for Ruho herself, because I'd just eat it all up.
The developer is also actively working to iron out the kinks and plans on making major updates on the game, too. To me, the game was worth the five dollars I spent on it. A lot of it just hits the right strings, at least, for me. If anything sticks out to you about this game, it might be well worth the pick-up for you. I definitely look forward to this game's future.

While not the most amazing or well made game out there, I would say this game is actually fairly well done, all things considered.
Sound wise, there is nothing whatsoever; no sounds, no music. Interface is minimal, and there is no options menu. You get to pick from playing fields of varying complexity, and have to match spheres in 3D space, which is harder than it sounds. One thing this does differently is that a sphere can only move to make a match if there is an ajacent sphere to switch with, leading to cases where in most games you could make a match, but in this game you can't because the ball doesn't have another one to switch with.
There is a hint system, which shrinks all balls down to show a possible match; however it does this regardless of if you can actually MAKE said match, for example often showing a match that cannot be made because if being buried in the playing field, thus requiring other matches to be made first to get to it. When this happens it renders the hint system useless, as it will continue to show that same match until it is made. It also fines you 100 pts per hint, yet on the larger maps the hints are pretty much required. There is a planet in perpetual orbit, which appears to be the earth, and when a match is made the balls shrink and fly to orbit the planet, which I thought was a nice touch.
Another flaw which is not major, but rather off putting, is that the pink ball is semi-transparent, wheras all the other balls are solid. The game goes on until no more matches an be made, in which case a big bang icon on the bottom of the screen will start to flash; this icon can be clicked on at anytime to end the game if you get bored, or when the game is over, causing all remaining balls to fly towards the planet. There seems to be a bug at the end where the earth started shrinking in increments, only to go back to full size moments later. after doing this a few times the resulting resizing caused all of the orbiting balls to be violently flung off into space, after which it didn't change sizes anymore. it only seems to happen on the largest map setting, and it's actually an enjoyable thing to see, so I classify it more as a feature than a bug
All in all a rather simplistic, but enjoyable take on the genre, and definitely worth the price!

So, where to begin with this. It's a nice idea. I've been itching for a market simulator without the city management aspect or what-have-you. But there are many, many flaws with this game that just makes it... meh.
This game is normally priced at $4.99. Four. Ninety. Nine. Even with the 15% off sale going on right now, it is nowhere near worth that price in its current state, if it's state were to even change at this point. If you can manage to get it at a price of $1.29 - $1.99, I would say it's a decent price, with $2.49 even pushing it. It is simply not worth the price.
Think of the market system in this game not like a gamble, but like a boulder at the top of a hill. You don't even have to know what you're doing and you will likely make over 2 million RMD, or whatever the currency is, without even trying. Once the boulder starts rolling, there is no stopping it. With nearly zero risk and near infinite reward, this isn't a market you really want to get involved in.
The encounters are fairly straight forward. You shoot things. Things die. Things flee. You flee. You know, the usual stuff. Expecting to find varying encounters of increasing difficulty? Don't. In my 1.5 hours spent on this game, I have only seen three types of encounters, all of which were the same enemies either solo, pairs, or triplets.
Surprise! This game has replay value (kind of) in the form of a Token Shop. You earn tokens based on your performance in the run, which you can use to unlock three classes along with three unique skins which serve no purpose besides changing how your character looks. Considering how gameplay is mostly the same for all classes, I really see no real reason to play as the other classes. I personally would just stick with the Junker class.
Considering how simple it is to purchase the best weapon in the game, alongside the fact that every town in this game sells the same items in the equipment shop, the shop is only used to gain back health, seducing, or robbing mid-late game. I have seen no need to purchase any of the equipment items from the shop, or Mercenaries and Travellers as well. Once you get the best Rifle from the shop and keep taking the Shopkeeper out to lunch, you are basically invincible.
But don't worry, the game isn't all that bad. There are some prevailing factors that keep this title from entering into the depths of Gaming Hell.
I like the ability to move around the windows and such, but refocusing on the window prior to interracting with them, combined with the fact that the Player Stats screen resets the position you set it to after every encounter is keeping this attribute from being well done.
Simple and clean 2D Pixel Art. Nothing too spectacular about it, but it's at least nice to look at.
It's okay. I never felt as though I wanted to mute the music and play my own through my 1.5 hours.
Overall, it's a semi-decent title with a rediculous price tag. Don't expect much out of it at its current state, but with updates and some changes, it can become a decent title worthy of a price tag like that. If you want a semi-fun/interesting title, this is a must... when more content comes and the price changes.

Absolution feels like it was designed by corporate folks who don't understand what made the previous Hitman games so good, while simultaniously trying to turn it into a 'modern shooter', because "thats what's hot with the kids these days."
On its surface it by all accounts *looks* like a hitman game, but when you get below the surface it clearly seems off. The most obvious problems with this game, again, are that it is trying to be both a stealth game and a modern shooter; Your character in this game is an absolute bullet sponge, able to take dozens of shots without going down, taking away much suspense; why even bother going in stealth you could h shootup the entire place without any difficulty, which again defeats the purpose of this game. Compare that to Blood Money, were you could only take 2 or three shots before dying, forcing you to use your wits and intelligence all the more.
That leads into the second obvious problem: look at the massive weapons arsenal players are given to loadout for missions, with machine guns, smgs, shotguns, etc; A real hitman doesn't need or often even *want* an automatic rifle for a mission, all they need is a silenced pistol and maybe on occasion a sniper rifle; the point of the game is to act with surgical precision, not shoot up the joint like a common thug. Not that there is anything wrong with shootemup gamea, but trying to mix 'shootemup' into such a stealth game just leaves the gameplay feeling a tad confused.
And furthmore something about the stealth gameplay feels 'off', it feels like it has been made too easy. The special kill methods tend to feel forced and contrived, as if the game has a "proper" way to kill the target in mind rather than giving you the range of options to feel free; In Blood Money, the killing methods felt natural and organic.
Absolution isn't what I would call a "bad" game, I guess I would say it feels pretty to look at but mediocre in gameplay. It it is something that interests you it will likely be worth it on sale, but otherwise I wouldn't go rushing out to get Absolution. Blood Money isn't as pretty to look at, but it is worth a look if Absolution interests you.

This War of Mine is a 2D survival game (NOT zombie survival game, you are in an actual war, there are no zombies) when you start with a few people in a damaged building and you are forced to reinforce it, search it through, scavenge for supplies, make weapons, rob or even kill people in order to survive. There are several characters with unique skills each, either it's fast running, strength, skilled scavenging, quiet sneaking (these are the useful skills, perks, whatever you wanna call it) and some pointless like mathematician, good cook (doesn't affect cooking - yes you can cook your food there otherwise you have to eat it raw) etc. Every character has different inventory space (from 8 to 17 I believe). You need to take care of your survivors, you need to keep them fed (''hungry'' status is optimal due to lack of food), you need to keep them rested, because if they are very tired or exhausted they can barely run, which isn't good if you are dodging bullets or leaving the certain area because you have to be back at home till 5 am - during day you can barter with some guy called Franko who sometimes comes to visit you and trades with you, there is no currency, the only currency is what you find, no money, just supplies and you can also craft thing in a work shop, such as beds, fuel metal work shop for tools and weapons and many more and day ends at 8 pm, at this point you pick the one who goes scavenging, who will keep the watch, because you can get raided and you don't wanna get raided, and the one ho will remain in bed and rest for another day. The another thing which you have to keep an eye on is your survivors' mental status, if they kill some bandit or soldier, it's ''ok (killing is not okay but in this game you kinda have to kill), BUT killing another survivors even if the attack you because you tried to stole something from them of didn't obey when they tell you to f*ck off from their house, you will become depressed (at first you'll become sad form robbing people, but this isn't bad, your survivors will be sad almost all the time. So if you become depressed you need to talk about it with another of your survivors, it'll make thing better, the worst status of this ''status tree'' is ''broken'', if your survivor is broken you literally can't do anything with them, they basically sit and cry, again you have to talk to them and if needed, feed them, bandage, anything <-- you can get wounded mostly by getting shot or stabbed, if it's just a scratch (slightly wounded) you can just lay in bed and RECOVER from it as well as sickness, that's the same, if you are slightly sick then lay in bed and recover, no pills needed. Now, if you're at home sometimes may someone knock on your door (barterer included), they mostly want you to help them, either spare some medical supplies, or help with barricading their house etc. I played and finished the whole game in 43 game days (and about 14 real hours) and I haven't encountered anyone knocking on my door proceeding to shoot me, so I can't 100% guarantee it.  If you want to kill someone silently, you can hide and as soon as they walk pass you you can stab them to death but watch out, there may and most likely will be more. And if you are lacking wood you can craft hatchet and chop furniture. Well that's pretty much it, I hope I didn't forget anything. This game is awesome, I haven't encountered any bugs so far, which is great, because this game is still being updated. The only thing I really miss in this game is co-op but that's about it.
I really recommend this game, you need to think through every step, always count on the worst, be patient and you might survive.

In This War of Mine, the focus is shifted away from military operations portrayed in most games. Instead, it is a dark survival game where players control a group of civilians attempting to stay alive in a besieged city. During the day snipers outside stop you from leaving your refuge, offering players time to craft, trade, upgrade their shelter, feed and cure their people. At night they must scavenge nearby areas in search for food, medicines, weapons and other useful items.
This game is very hard, but extremely thought-provoking. One of the best all-around games I’ve played all year. A crisp, consistent atmosphere, intuitive gameplay, and surprising depth create a fantastic experience.

+xcom like coversystem.

Citadel: Forged with Fire Review
=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=
UPDATE 2 (05/08): First week out on EA and the game is steadily being fixed. FPS is much better but there are still issues with PING. Server List Menu has poor functionality but game is now at least playable. Devs have been actively sorting issues out and seem to be off to a good start addressing issues/suggestions.
UPDATE 1: The latest patch has made the game quite unplayable for me atm. I would hold off until the game-destroying bugs are fixed. :)  #fatalerror
I played the beta, so I already have enough hours experience to write this review for the current state of the game (which is what we have to go on, not what could be implemented in the game).
Overall, I love the concept of this game. A sandbox mmo with the feel of a better Rust, a little more optimised Ark (I can actually get on and play, although I did notice there are a number of folks having issues with fps) and all without the survival elements that make those games very tedious - you don't have a stamina bar that requires you to rest, you don't have to drink or eat to satisfy thirst and hunger. Massive plus.
Building:
=-=-=-=
The building in this game allows your creativity to flow, in a similar style to Rust building placement. This with more creativity and with more options, without the really horrible, tedious Ark building system (where you have to craft the items first, then drag those items into hotbar for placement). No, this game allows you to have the regular and traingular foundations BUT ALSO rounded walls for higher tier building. Building is now fun for me.
Bugs and Issues:
=-=-=-=-=-=-=-
That said, there are a number of issues in its current state. It takes a while to find a server that isn\t full and there isn't nearly enough EU servers. There are a ton of US servers so you have more options. Enemies are buggy, they often become static when attacked which doesn't provide any significant challenge. 40 player limit (for now) and not enough servers means, at least on launch day (and as was the case for beta), waiting a while to join a server that is best for your region and even then, there were network issues on a few servers (your ping will be advertised as 100 but jump to 1000 when joined).
The game is buggy, but it is not unplayable when you eventually find the right server for you and the experience is very rewarding, even in its current state.  I don't have the beefiest of pc's compared to current gen, I sport 16GB RAM, GTX970 and i5-6500. And the game averages 40 fps at high settings. Although there are dips at times to the 20s.
Conclusion:
=-=-=-=-=
Although this review is for the current state of the game, I am hopeful that things will continue to improve with a host of bug fixes and I am happy to contribute to this Early Access title because I love watching games, with genre's I like, grow and develop, with a small voice that may or may not get to influence change to form a game that I truly love.
That's as honest as I can be. :)

So, first off, I should say that I bought this game purely for the single-player experience, and can't really comment on the multiplayer.  I gather there isn't much of a multiplayer community to speak of, so I just didn't bother.
My "thumbs down" rating is based largely on the $19.99 standard price, which is NOT what I paid for the game, fortunately.  This game is in no way, shape, or form worth $19.99.  Instead, I paid about $5, which is what I'd say is a fair price for the game in terms of the quality of gameplay and amount of entertainment you get, compared to other games out there.  I went into this game, having paid my $5, looking for basically a diverting shooting gallery, and I got exactly that, so I'm perfectly satisfied with my purchase.  But, again, I wouldn't pay just shy of $20 for it.  As for why, read on.
The graphics are...eh, fine.  I'm not really a graphics snob, so that's not a big deal to me.  They ran fine at max settings on my 6-year-old computer, which makes sense, considering the game came out...5 years ago.  The visuals themseles aren't up to snuff for a AAA title, but then I don't think this game could claim to be a AAA title.
Gameplay attempts to be similar to your basic Call of Duty game, with you as one of 4-5 resistance fighters in a United States under occupation by North Korea.  The game tries to make this ludicrous scenario seem reasonably plausible.  It doesn't really matter who they are, though.  They're the bad guys who've taken over the good ol' US of A, and it's up to you to shoot them in the face and do...pretty much everything else.  Your character, I think, is named Jackson or something, but he might as well be Ramirez from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.  ("Ramirez!  Do [task]!")
Movement is kind of clunky, and the gunplay isn't all that satisfying.  Sound design for the guns is passable, but they tend to have this sort of "clanky" quality to them.  There's probably, like, 10 different common firearms you can pick up, with 2-3 rocket launchers and such, but they all felt mostly the same to me.
There are some missions where you control this or that vehicle or assign this or that target to some mobile bringer-of-death (e.g. calling in a fire mission), but the bulk of the game is what you'd expect it to be: you running around shooting dudes.
Voice acting is nothing special, and you don't end up really caring about the characters.  No surprise there.
There aren't any real cutscenes to speak of, other than the occasional mission interlude where your characters talk a bit before you can equip your gun and shoot stuff.  You get loading screens with the "Voice of America" providing a bit of context for the next mission.
Basically, if you want to play "Red Dawn: The Game" this is about as close as you'll get.  And for that, it's kinda fun, but it's not particularly polished.

My few gripes are firstly -  the mulitplayer. There was such potential for it and so many ways it could be handled and instead it's ended up being a 1 v 1 type thing.
Also, the game has it's fair share of bugs, which I found bearable (the game autosaves before each node) but many people seem to be pretty annoyed by them so if you're looking for a bug-free experiecne this may not be the game for you (but neither will Skyrim or Fallout).

If you enjoy randomly generated games that can get hard but are incredibly addictive then this is for you.

If you expected Sid Meier's: Alpha Centauri (A Brian Reynolds design) then you will be disappointed. I only learned of SM:AC the past year, and even this was enough for Beyond Earth to feel disappointing, when it felt like it was supposed to be a spiritual successor.
The game isn't worth the price, because it plays more or less like Civilization V, with some differences; effectively the game feels like an expansion of Civ V... It plays ok, but doesn't feel special; lacks personality as some have said.
The (promised) modding support is appalling and modded multiplayer is inexistant as such. The game has almost as many if not more synchronization issues than SM:AC, but we're in an era where these synchronization issues don't even make sense anymore in a turn-based game.
My praise for the game will be the graphics and the music. They truly are quite remarkable. But the voice acting gets extremely old in a very fast way and feels generic, as opposed to SM:AC's, where it was philosophical, made sense and was tied deeply with the lore.
My recommendation; stay away from games published by 2K in general. Something smells fishy about them lately. Beyond Earth and Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel were both massive disappointments for me.
I wish Beyond Earth had all the game mechanics exactly the same as SM:AC but looked this pretty anyway. Perhaps less pixels is better in the end... More room for the imagination of the Human mind.

Really interesting concept for a game.
Think of it as a cross between a Truck Simulator game and a Survival game.
You are tasked with making it to the border in your Jalopy (a beat up car)
You start off having to fix up your car.
Adding a passenger door, all engine parts and wheels etc.
What I love about this game is the attention to detail.
eg. you have to pop the bonnet by pulling the handle under the steering wheel.
Any car owner will be aware of this, but this is the first time I've ever had to do this in a game.
There are lots of different attention to detail style mechanics.
These types of mechanics include adding oil to your fuel mix.
The more oil you add the less wear and tear your engine will take.
The less oil you add the better your engine will perform.
Its a nice mechanic and there are many more similar details to explore and tweak with your engine/car setup.
Now the game is in early access and has a way to go before all features are added.
The foundation is here and I am really intrigued to see where this game goes.
Definately one to keep an eye on.

[ For the record, I played the remastered version on the Macbook Pro with 16gigs of RAM ]
Likes:
- Amazing Story
- Smooth Gameplay
- Well designed Levels, weapons, gameplay mechanics
- Well presented choices for the players, that question their conscience.
- Awesome soundtrack and background score + cool recordings
- Rapture and its incredible characters
- Developer commentary (if you're into that sort of thing!)
Dislikes:
- Shooting controls takes a little getting used if you come from a traditional FPS- right click doesn't aim down on sights. It swaps to plasmids. Takes some getting used to.
I played the original game sometime back in 2007 and I remember being amazed by the presentation of the ideas and for the immersive qualities of the game. While this is subjective, I consider the original BioShock to be among the greatest games ever made for how it takes really complex ideas and applies it to its settings, for its incredible environments and steampunk art-deco aesthetic and really well-fleshed out characters. Its just one of those rare games which forces the player to dwell on their choices.
The remastered version did not disappoint me- the gameplay was buttery smooth and I've never witnessed it crashing except for a couple of stutters during gameplay. These stutters occurred twice, towards the final levels of the game and they barely lasted a second before I could resume playing. The soundtrack and background score is incredible and the setting of Rapture has to be among one of the greatest settings ever implemented for a video game. I personally enjoy exploring every corner of a level, looking for recordings that provide exposition about the history of the place and I feel it aids the immersion.
Give this game a shot if you like story-driven games. It will not disappoint you!

This is a working review, as I have only completed about 4-5 levels thus far.
This game is a "meh". It's a mass shooter simulator, obviously. I will not say it's a "bad game" (morality aside) because there are some qualities it has and the work put into it does show. The visuals are pretty good and the game runs well without any hiccups or glitches that I really noticed. The entire aesthetic is black and white with blood and fire being in color. The animations are good, but get repetitive quickly.
As far as gameplay goes, the keyboard controls are atrocious  and clunky. Trying to flee from hordes of cops usually just ends up with you running into a corner or a tree you were trying to avoid and getting stuck there and gunned down (ironic). I do not know how well it works with controllers but it might be better.
The game itself, you run around. You shoot people. You try not to die. So you can shoot more people. That's it. You execute to regain health, although honestly when in firefights I found myself having to execute people to heal, only to be stuck in a long execution cutscene, while cops surround me because the game is still playing out around me. The cutscene does not occur during every execution however which helps. The gore factor is equivalent to any Turok game you've played. Nothing really all that crazy as far as gore itself. Obviously the AO rating comes from the context of the game.
Honestly the gun sound effects are very flat and could have really been improved to give more of an experience to it, but they all sound pretty lame. The physics are pretty cool, you can take out walls, drive through houses, gunfights destroy the environment around you, etc.
Vehicle mechanics are far too sensitive, pressing D or A (steering) the slightest bit to much and you careen into a building or a tree.
The dialogue is nausating. The main characters' voice is overly-brooding, so much so that Christian Bale Batman could take some notes. He says things like "Sometimes I think I kill them too fast" "Let me introduce myself: I'm a man of hate and disgust." " I never thought it would be so easy to slaughter my whole neighborhood. I can feel their pain, their suffering flowing through my veins. It's like the most intense drug and I need more... much more!"..........ugh it's so dark it's just cringey honestly. It doesn't sound badass it sounds like a guy who didn't get hugs from his dad enough.
Conclusion: If you just want to mindlessly walk/run around killing people the same exact ways over and over and over again for an hour or two, then yeah this game might be for you. But don't be surprised when you get bored and play something else in your library and this game collects digital dust. If you're a psychopath and this game gives you a rush and you play this game exclusively for months on end. Get help, seriously. As a professional of killin' people I have to say this game did not impress despite having some impressive qualities.

So, before getting into this review I have to say I am a big space and empire building nerd, so when those two are put together I'm already partial to it, so fair warning.
General Info:
-Sins is a space building empire where you pick one of three factions (with two subfactions each) and conquer the galaxy. Each of the six subclasses feels unique, with gimics from turtling and economy to psionic warfare.  Maps can range from single star systems or maps with up to 3 star systems (could be more, I mostly play on the 3 star systems, apologies if i'm incorrect on this one). You can play diplomatically or militarilly, although really you'll almost find yourself exclusively military, as it's nigh impossible to get everyone alligned together, although it's not hard to get one or two AI allies to join you for tagteaming.
-Gameplay is real time, not turn based. This adds a unique element to the late game, when most factions have hundreds of ships moving in different parts of the galaxy. This can keep you on your toes, constantly watching everywhere for what the others are doing.
-Game is entirely based in space, no land combat (only thing you do on land is upgrade the planet's overall population and other things like bomb shelters for defense).
Pros:
-Fleet combat: Real time combat with hundreds or even thousands of ships duking it out in real time is amazing, and the graphics and spectacle is amazing (especially considering the game's small download size).
-Extensive tech tree and decent pool of ship classes to give you enough to play with different fleet builds.
-Capital Ships and Titans are essentially heroes that level as they are in combat. Every class is unique, and each faction has 6 capital ships, and each subfaction has a unique titan that fits their play style.
-Amazing Mod Support: ModDB has some pretty amazing conversion mods for this game. I've personally tried Halo, Star Wars, Star Trek, and one of the older Mass Effect conersion mods and they are amazing, especially if you find yourself tiring of the base factions.
-Multiplayer support still works at the time of this review (even for most of those mods I just listed).
Cons:
-Extreme learning curve, even if you are used to these kinds of games you'll find yourself feeling slightly overwhelmed or really overwhelmed depending on experience with these types of games. (Pirates are the main issue, as if you very inexperienced and not paying attention to the pirate bribery meter, you might find yourself losing a planet early on to a large pirate fleet, although you can use the pirates to your advantage as well if you have the money for it).
-AI Isnt that bright, and generally doesn't start amassing large fleets until late game, if at all depending on ai difficulty. Mostly the AI like to spam superweapons and harass your planets.
Overall I give this game a 8.75/10. If you like space combat or empire building this game is definitely worth checking out, although the standard price is very steep, I definitely recommend waiting for a sale, as 50% and 75% sales happen fairly regularly.

Please note:  I played the base game on Hard difficulty.  I have prior experience with first-person shooters and I spent a lot of time checking every nook and cranny for more loot.
While its story isn't quite as good as the first Bioshock's, Bioshock 2 more than makes up for it with improved gunplay.  The weapons are only a little different from the original, but they
a lot better.  Maybe it's because I got the tonic that increases your headshot damage and it made everything die really fast, I don't know.
Nothing felt bullet spongey, the only things that had a lot of health were bosses or special enemies that you only see once in a while, and even those can be taken down easily with the right strategy.  The plasmids are all useful and fun, some of the gene tonics are really overpowered a one particular area (not in a way that breaks the game, in a way that's really fun), and the guns all have their own niche in taking down certain enemies.  I used the rivet gun (pistol) the most because it kills most enemies in one headshot (if you have a few upgrades) and the ammunition is plentiful, though I used all of the guns (except for the machine gun) a good deal as well.
I found four types bugs/glitches in 20 hours of playing.  Two of them were game-breaking, and the other two were mildly annoying.
The first is constant crashing , if you could call that a bug.  The second is that once, when I started my game, it kept playing the boss fight music even though I had beaten the boss the day before.  Quicksaving and quickloading didn't fix it and neither did restarting my game.  I had to turn off the game's music until I got to the next area, and that's when it stopped.
The third is that sometimes your left hand will disappear, and you won't be able to use plasmids.  Restarting the game doesn't fix it either.  The fourth is that sometimes when you take items from shelves, the rest of the items fall through the shelf and onto the floor.  Every once in a while they fall through the world and you won't be able to get them.
To fix the crashing, right click Bioshock 2, click properties, click Launch Options, and type -dx9 into the box.  I went from crashing every five minutes to only crashing once in the next ~18 hours, and even then I was alt-tabbing a bunch and had a lot of programs open.
The disappearing left hand bug usually happened when I used the Scout plasmid or changed to the Drill Specialist tonic, though some people have had it happen to them when they zoom in.  To fix it, just spam the Zoom/Aim in key, F1, and F2 a bunch.  If you have the drill specialist tonic and this happens, change that tonic to something else at a gene bank, spam the aforementioned keys a bunch, and then change it back.
All in all, this is a great game and worth a buy if you played the previous game or like first-person shooters.  I advise that if you haven't played the original Bioshock to play that one first, the world and story will make a lot more sense if you do.

This War of Mine is a 2D survival game (NOT zombie survival game, you are in an actual war, there are no zombies) when you start with a few people in a damaged building and you are forced to reinforce it, search it through, scavenge for supplies, make weapons, rob or even kill people in order to survive. There are several characters with unique skills each, either it's fast running, strength, skilled scavenging, quiet sneaking (these are the useful skills, perks, whatever you wanna call it) and some pointless like mathematician, good cook (doesn't affect cooking - yes you can cook your food there otherwise you have to eat it raw) etc. Every character has different inventory space (from 8 to 17 I believe). You need to take care of your survivors, you need to keep them fed (''hungry'' status is optimal due to lack of food), you need to keep them rested, because if they are very tired or exhausted they can barely run, which isn't good if you are dodging bullets or leaving the certain area because you have to be back at home till 5 am - during day you can barter with some guy called Franko who sometimes comes to visit you and trades with you, there is no currency, the only currency is what you find, no money, just supplies and you can also craft thing in a work shop, such as beds, fuel metal work shop for tools and weapons and many more and day ends at 8 pm, at this point you pick the one who goes scavenging, who will keep the watch, because you can get raided and you don't wanna get raided, and the one ho will remain in bed and rest for another day. The another thing which you have to keep an eye on is your survivors' mental status, if they kill some bandit or soldier, it's ''ok (killing is not okay but in this game you kinda have to kill), BUT killing another survivors even if the attack you because you tried to stole something from them of didn't obey when they tell you to f*ck off from their house, you will become depressed (at first you'll become sad form robbing people, but this isn't bad, your survivors will be sad almost all the time. So if you become depressed you need to talk about it with another of your survivors, it'll make thing better, the worst status of this ''status tree'' is ''broken'', if your survivor is broken you literally can't do anything with them, they basically sit and cry, again you have to talk to them and if needed, feed them, bandage, anything <-- you can get wounded mostly by getting shot or stabbed, if it's just a scratch (slightly wounded) you can just lay in bed and RECOVER from it as well as sickness, that's the same, if you are slightly sick then lay in bed and recover, no pills needed. Now, if you're at home sometimes may someone knock on your door (barterer included), they mostly want you to help them, either spare some medical supplies, or help with barricading their house etc. I played and finished the whole game in 43 game days (and about 14 real hours) and I haven't encountered anyone knocking on my door proceeding to shoot me, so I can't 100% guarantee it.  If you want to kill someone silently, you can hide and as soon as they walk pass you you can stab them to death but watch out, there may and most likely will be more. And if you are lacking wood you can craft hatchet and chop furniture. Well that's pretty much it, I hope I didn't forget anything. This game is awesome, I haven't encountered any bugs so far, which is great, because this game is still being updated. The only thing I really miss in this game is co-op but that's about it.
I really recommend this game, you need to think through every step, always count on the worst, be patient and you might survive.

I dabbled a little in the game and all of it against tougher ai opponents, while most of it is a really great game, one or two little things kind of ruins the mood of what i am doing. for example i like to prolong the fighting over a long duration and make the ai come to me while i grind their forces down to the point i can launch attacks on their systems when the chance presents itself. i never leave myself exposed to an attack.
when i finally whittle out a colony belonging to one of the ai enemies and take it over, suddenly every superweapon from every other ai targets that new acquisition and rends it uninhabitable, it not only slows down progress to a crawl, but how can ai's from all the way across the galaxy that has no beef with me or even knows i setup a colony there suddenly have this idea to launch their super weapons at it? i mean all of them?
so while there are some questionable AI actions that ruins the mood a bit, there are also the super weapons themselves;
The novalith warhead attacks a single target causing minimal disruption, now a colony with a planetary shield can take a few novalith hits, which severely limits it's ability to be a superweapon. frankly it's underpowered and absurdly so.
the deliverance signal on the other end is significantly overpowered in comparison and it does far more damage to several colonies with it's overwhelming signal strength and duration. now unless you got a cultural rate over something like 200 over these multiple planets to make it very difficult for the signal to persist for long, otherwise repeated hits is far more devastating than a fleet of ships could evr provide, not only that, but if you kept launching signals against their former worlds after them losing control and you kill off their colonizer ships and colonizer cap ships as well. you won't even need to face the rest of their forces. it should get a bit of a nerf to it.
the last one of the list is a warhead that explodes at a planet, causing all projects to be suspended in planetary orbit until it wears off. if the colony is not under any threat at all, it makes this weapon useless to have and not only that but it don't effect starbases. it's only use is in advance of your main attack force but still is just as uneffective as the novalith.
as it is, there needs to be a balance check there. anyway, these are the one or two little problems i have with the game, the rest of it is very enjoyable to get into and play.

Whether you should play this game largely depends on how well you're acquainted with MtG.
It's a good game for learning the mechanics and practicing some of them against a real opponent. Beginners should not be disappointed, as the title offers a large array of tutorials on pretty much anything.
However, things quickly go downhill for you if you're well past learning Magic. The game is pretty monotonous after playing it for few hours.
Story Mode kind of drifts apart from the actual lore it's supposed to represent. It's also horribly balanced, as the decks we are given on the beginning are too weak, and sometimes too strong by the end of each campaign. Also the movies at the end of each scenario not only are bugged, but the rendering quality is only a little bit inferior to Planescape Torment.
Versus mode is what you'll spend the majority of your time on, but it's seriously flawed. The ranking system is pointless and does not reflect person's skill at game in the slightest. Matches aren't particlarily interesting either due to predictable strategies. That leads us to another point, which is the lack of diversity in cards. Two sets? Like really? After few hours you can tell what kind of deck the enemy plays by seeing their manabase.
The biggest problem with Vs. though is the connectivity. About 60% of the time the match simply won't load. It gets much worse when trying to play 2HG with friends. Matches don't connect for no apparent reason at all. Winning them doesn't feel particularily rewarding either.
Lastly, the ingame shop is the purest work of Satan since creation of DLC for games. Boosters are expensive, coins slow to grind and packs only contain 6 cards instead of 13. AND MY GOD ARE THESE CARDS AN ABYSSMAL HUNK OF SH*T. The odds of you pulling something good are similar to your chances of pulling Black Lotus out of your♥♥♥♥♥ yet people somehow seem to manage it. Literally everyone except you will have 4 copies of every Planeswalker, making you even more frustrated on why you never get any. Also booster bundles make no sense because you get no discount for purchasing in bulk, there's no benefit to waiting.
Overall 5/10 for being a good introduction to MtG and having potential of  being a decent game if Wizards actually took care of it and added content (and fixed everything). Not horrible as a time killer.

Not sure why I can't find this one in our database.  So I'll summarize it with a few bullet points an give a few thoughts:
Genre: Turn-based tactical combat, mild RPG element similar to Silent Storm skill tree. Although there are no classes.
Setting: Post apocalyptic, similar to Fallout.
Graphics/Voice Acting: Although this was released in 2015, it really feels like it was made 15 years ago.  Every dialog seems to have an F-bomb.  Needless really.
Combat: Fairly basic. Each character has 10 action points to use.  Most weapons cost 4-6 APs to fire. Move 1 square = Spend 1 AP.  Reloading generally costs 4 APs.  Swords/axes are very overpowered and you can get a "stun" skill early (costs 3 APs).  Ammo is also scarce to start, so my main character was a shotgun/butcher knife expert.
Skill Progression: No classes, so as you gain a level (max 20) you get a skill point to spend.  Some skills have pre-requisite skills.  Skills also require you to be a certain level before you can get them.
Overall, this game seems very dated an not like a new release.  The screen shots made me think of the new X-Com games but in reality it is nothing like that.  Many of the aspects of this game seem unfinished.  Such as rumors, the nutcracker and even the story-line finishes with a "cliff-hanger".  Some of these elements feel tacked on, but not utilized.  For instance, you can upgrade lots of aspects of your caravan, but in reality, aside from a couple extra sleeping spots, the rest seem just like a way to spend your amassed fortune.  You will get your final equipment half-way through the game, so the second half becomes increasingly simple.  The game is definitely playable, and provides some fun, but I have a hard time actually recommending it when I would have more fun booting up my old copies of Jagged Alliance, Fallout or Silent Storm.

The investigations are poor, they don't at any point include you thinking, the solution to the investigation is only possible when you have the last piece. Well the combat has a few interesting things, i.e. one the stealth includes the wind blowing which is cool and i've never seen that before. The combat has no real punch to it and is therefore more of an obstacle than an enjoyment. This is fine in many games, but this is dragging down an already awful game. On top of that, despite being marketed as a stealth at the start, the combat is so easy you can waltz into every fight and easily win, without using any weapon apart from the bow. As for exploration, there really is nothing to explore, it's a forest with a couple of generic buildings in it. There is nothing here whatsoever to pique your interest as you walk about. This tends to lead to sprinting around to get to your objective, which adds to my next problem.
The enemies will hear you sprinting before you can see or hear them, at least on the difficulty i was playing on, if there are indeed difficulties, i don't remember. So Stealth is entirely out of the window anyway. That whole blowing mechanic? I used it twice in my entire nearly 8 hours.
Colour scheme was cool, and i saw the options to fiddle with it. doesn't make the game good at all.
In conclusion, poor if not non-existant story, no real stakes or intersting characters, entirely generic location, poor combat, poor balancing of said combat, pretending stealth is actually a part of it, also worth noting the notes the games provides you about things you've read are lack luster, often writing a single line about the character, even if you have loads more information.
Overall, feels like a game that the dev's gathered together and thought would be cool to play, but half of them got bored and they were forced to release the game in an incomplete state, or alternatively, the entire game was made by people who hated making it by the end. I absolutely recommend MTGD as an introduction to WOTC MTG. I feel that MTG does an excellent job of teaching the basic mechanics of the game, and the GUI is absolutely fantastic. I recommend turning off simplified targeting once you have a firmer grasp on the game's mechanics.
WOTC MTGO is not a Steam product, the GUI is harsh, at best. MTGO is to Windows 95 as MTGD is to Windows 10. You will also find MTGD a much more friendly environment for the casual magic player. That's the upside; the downside is that if you want to learn to be a more competitive magic player, MTGD is the best starting point, but you'll need to graduate to MTGO for that. I personally have no interest in this, and play magic casually and enjoy the Lore of WOTC MTG as a whole.
I will state, that I think MTGD could stand to improve on the tempo of each of the steps of MTG, as the game could be very easily misunderstood. You could become an advanced MTGD player, and make the move to paper magic and lose to consistently to someone who is but a novice in the game. Learning timing and tempo, and fully understanding the how and the why are nearly impossible in MTGD.
That being said I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone looking to get into Magic, and I absolutely cannot wait until April for the MTG Oath of the Gatewatch and Shadows Over Innistrad content. That is another piece that is most severely lacking in this game. MTGO is a very serious format, and WOTC makes millions of dollars on electronic cards which exist in the cloud. The maximum they could ever hope to extract from a MTGD player is a couple of hundred bucks with each expansion. As such, they do not spend much of any time on developing and delivering the content in a timely manner to MTGD. MTGD has had Oath of the Gatewatch, and is experiencing Shadows Over Innistrad now, while MTGD won't see any of it until late April, if even then, as they've pushed the date back multiple times.
That all being said I continue to play and enjoy the game, and if you have any issues with the game, WOTC customer service is absolutely excellent in their response time and accuracy.

I really want to like this game because I love the whole Firefly thing it has going on. There are definitely things to like about it, but it ultimately is just a very boring space sim with a kinda lousy battle system IMO.
Turn-ons:
+Firefly!
+Soundtrack is great!
+NPCs are marvelous!
Turn-offs:
--The broadside combat. I played the game for 3+ hours and fought a fair number of battles against pirates in that time. I even upgraded to better weapons and different types of weapons. But the combat just never started to feel good. Broadside combat is great with sea vessels because they are both sea vessels. But in this game your ship is confined to a flat plane while enemy ships are flying loops over you and under you as you try to lock onto them. It's more like trying to use a sluggish wooden sailing ship to engage in broadside combat with a bunch of airplanes and submarines. I'm not saying that it's impossible or anything, but I did find it really irritating and it did not start to get better.
--It is very empty and boring. It has all of the things that space sims normally have, such as trading and merc missions and ships parts that can be upgraded and so on. But I put in several hours into this game and I spent most of that time staring at the butt of a ship flying in a straight line toward a mission destination. I seriously just set the controller down on my desk, folded my hands, and watched a picture of a space ship. For minutes. MINUTES ON END. I found out that I could upgrade all of my engines and boosters etc to get some more speed out of the ship, and I was feeling very positive about that at first, but then I realized I was STILL pretty much spending most of my time staring at the butt of a ship flying in a straight line. So much yawn.
--The game seems heavily skewed toward playing as muscle. If you tend to lean a little more pacifist/trader in space sims, then this game does not seem very friendly towards those types. When I first started running missions, I initially was only accepting missions that the game explicitly labeled as VERY LOW RISK, which were usually just trading missions that asked me to go pick something up and bring it back or transport some cargo from A to B. But EVERY SINGLE ONE of these missions resulted in a scripted ambush attack from multiple pirate ships. Literally every time. So there's not really any point accepting the missions that pass themselves off as the pacifist types because this game shoves you into combat literally every time. Every mission is a combat mission. Always. Without fail. Or so this was my experience.
--But did I mention how incredibly boring it is? This was really the thing that made me stop playing the most. Most of my time spent playing this game I did not feel like I was playing a game. I felt like I was staring at the butt of a ship that was doing nothing.
And then it occurred to me that I could be playing a game that felt like doing things. So I'm done with it.
I love the whole Firefly thing, and apparently lots of people think the game is just great, but man... I could not stay awake while playing this thing.

Citadel: Forged with Fire is an interesting beast. It's a softer-core game than ARK to be sure--it feels more like a sandboxed, magically-focused Elder Scrolls game of sorts. The initial grind can be brutal, but that can be remedied (If your computer can handle it) by making your own server for yourself and friends, if you really want. I haven't explored all of the world yet, but what I've seen has been lovingly crafted and carefully tended to. The biggest issue the game faces right now is its optimization (Or lack thereof.) AMD cards seem to render spell effects as more 'boxey' and less fluid than NVIDIA cards, I struggle to get above forty FPS during active moments with spell effects flying, and sometimes it can drop into sub-25.
((A helpful note if you're struggling is to decrease resolution scale from 100 to 90. Gave me 10 FPS, I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not.))
The issues with optimization make themselves very painfully apparent during moments of PVP or interaction with other players. While the building system is functional, players can come and destroy houses and dwellings with relative ease. Ultimately, the game is solid. It's got a fun--though currently somewhat limited--magic system, creative ways to make your homes, and a beautiful world. You just have to get past the jank-ey FPS and performance issues. For many people, that can be a game killer. It isn't for me--the game is Early Access, and it shows. But I think it's worth sticking with it and hoping that the developers address optimization issues, at least so people can solidly keep 50+ FPS. I wholeheartedly recommend playing and supporting this game and showing the devs the encouragement they deserve for what's clearly a  project of passion, despite its current flaws.

1600s America.  A colony has disappeared, and you alone must find out what happened to it.  The consensus on Steam is that the game starts off promising, but after a couple hours you realize the gameplay is repetitive and amounts to nothing.
I agree.  This may be an open world, but you don't explore.  The locations of every treasure chest, every clue, every grave are marked on the map from the moment you arrive.  All you do is run from point to point.  There is no in-world reason for you to know the locations of these things, and it takes away from the experience because you don't follow one clue to the next and uncover the mystery of what happened to this colony.  It's all just there; all you have to do is go and pick it up.  Other than these points marked on your map, there is nothing to see in this game world and no reason to explore.
Furthermore, you do the exact same thing on every map: fight to the fort in the center, ring the bell, find all the points in the "dark world," and then kill all the enemies around "corrupted" totems so you can proceed to the next map.  Repeat this 8 times, and that's the entire game.  Characters (most of whom are ghosts) have nothing to say except to explain the clues you randomly find.  You don't get to know them as people, so you forget them as soon as you meet them.  None of this expands on the "mystery" of what happened to this colony, and nothing you find in the game is tantalizing enough to be mysterious.
The story has no substance, and asthetics aside, the environment is empty.  The game is competently made and everything works, but all of this was done so much better in Fallout 3.  That game gave you a host of reasons to explore: interesting characters to talk to and notes and terminals and pieces of stories to find, side quests that took you to new locations and new people to meet and talk to, all of which created a brand new world to get lost in.  Betrayer wanted to do the same thing, but it didn't fill its game world with anything.
Unlike NMS, this game actually has progression, a purpose and doesn't leave you wondering why you wasted time playing it. All at a much more reasonable price.

Great game, definitely one of the better games of my childhood and still the best around. Has Fps action + the ability to "sprint" with the games physics allows it to be a fast-er point and click shooter if not the fastest and the props/objects effecting it even more make it unique requiring good senses, reflex, smart reactions, coordination with just about everything to play at a decent potential. Where else can you Yoyo a grenade to keep it from 'cooking' it's fuse out before propelling it on it's last fuse reset that you can time for distance and height in coordination with how fast you are moving and your target's speed and the force of the 'gravity gun' you use to propel it with, no where else but hl2dm. Has different kinds of unique weapons like the gravity gun propelling a object to a person to kill them with, or propelling that object against another object to move that away from a distance. And to block a path with many objects or stack objects to reach a platform. Also the crossbow is an example of unique weapons with how it fires in a arch and hard to aim with even with it's scope but can kill a player instantly and with correct positioning can bounce of the floor walls ceiling terrian etc. and with enough practice can be well aimed to kill a player half the map away behind 2 corridors and a room. That is a taste of the Uniqueness of this game, after overlooking it's default multiplayer team vs team worth, there is it's booming in vast unique options to how to play the game with it's community's modded creations, there is co-op themed maps where you can fight with teammates against hordes of aliens, zombies, monsters and cyborgs getting points with the ability to use them to unlock server abilities to costumize your character with a deferent apearence, both in model skin and size, lights that glow on your model, lights that follow your model and more, then there is puzzle maps where you may enter 1 of 12 parts of the map at a time with your team or individualy and complete tasks like finding the exit in a labyrinth or placing and freezing a pile of crates to build a terrian leading to a exit floating high above in the sky or surfing on long slides without falling into abyss to reach a exit or jumping over ditches, climbing and avoiding obstacles in a temple like area to reach another exit to collect all exits and unlock the last portion of the map to complete it. Then there is Roleplay... a blend of multiplayer fps combat with gta style like the need to Purchase weapons or health or armor. Earning money by the minute with the wage given by your level or killing others for their pocket money, then saving that money to invest in a faster method of earning money like growing drugs to sell or printing money both to us on getting more guns or to purchase a home to hide in and to keep your drugs or printer safe, from other players or other players playing as Cops... who may not only steal your illegal possessions but will also place you in jail for some time so that they too may earn the points they need to progress faster and easier in that server. You may also invest in a home to hide from all players and keep your possessions safe, and to meet with your group of friends to prepare for a war against another gang, or to meet with your gang to prepare for a war against the police in alliance with other gangs for fun or for an event to earn more $. Also events are constant and include situations where a monster is spawned in the map similar to the any/many of the ones found in co-op maps that drop money on death. Another situation would be looking all over the map to find an object or player hiden with more $ $ $ that is given to the winner that finds it first. Or when admins just decide the server is full enough for a mass money drop in the middle of the map including weapons and item drops. There are also many more mods but I just thought to name a few of the ones that have me so adicted to this game. This game is worth the very low ticket price for all the fun is has to offer and is very much Alive, if not so is still rich with creativity you never know what's next. I rate it 5 out of 5 stars * * * * *.

This remaster crashed more than five times while playing. First, when I was quicksaving (it deleted the quicksave), so I have been saving manually since then. Once when using the Steam Overlay and then generally when manually saving, especially during playing the DLC. Other than that, I had no serious problems. Now, even if you know the game by heart, you will find it hard to find many differences. The game was already so good-looking, designed to be an example of art in a video game. The unique Art Deco artistic style makes the game's looks almost indestructible by ravages of time. So it was very pleasant to see how much it can be improved without violating its hallmark of quality. Blind Squirrel Games succeeded in remastering most textures, models, decals and even UI while staying true to the original. Sound issues disappeared and the game has no problem in playing more sounds at once, like the original had. What they didn't improve are the annoying and loud metal against metal clinking sounds when hacked turrets or security bots attack enemies. The long-forgotten issues with the original and the raging community forced devs to update the game's options menu, including an FOV slider. The nicest change to Unreal Engine 2.5 is the unlocked framerate of physics making combat much more satisfying. The gameplay and amazing story remain unchanged, with only a new difficulty level being added. I would describe BioShock as a casual shooter (even on the new Survivor difficulty, because you are swimming in resources) with heavy intellectual themes, coming from its incredibly detailed philosophy and narrative. What gives me a rash though, is the last fifth of the game. It is so different from the rest of the game in terms of raw quality that it becomes a mediocre shooter at that point. And when they put an FOV-increasing, tunnel vision helmet on you, it becomes a nightmare that ends soon, thankfully.
8.5/10 (because of the crashes, 9.5 for the legendary original)
+ art, philosophy, science and killing madmen effectively
- crashes, the changes are cosmetic and are indiscernible if you don't know the original well

You know, I really tried with this one.  It hasn't been an easy game to do a Review about. I'm not the biggest Hitman fan, but this game gets A LOT of stuff wrong, and as usual, that's where I will focus first:
First and foremost, remember how in previous games you could save during your assassination contracts? Well, that's gone. And that's the perfect case of "don't fix what's not broken".  I can't believe that the devs changed the "limited amount of saves" feature from previous Hitman games for a f#cking Checkpoint system. IT'S STUPID. WHY. And if that was the only thing they changed for the worst it would be fine, buuuut...
...Sadly, this Hitman game goes quite far from previous games, as it offers a linear story instead of the previous games, where you only cared about your target. Why does it go wrong by adding a story? Because it tries really hard to be Deus Ex. Yes, I just said that. They're from the same publisher, Square-Enix, and yet for some reason Hitman tries really hard to add stuff from Deus Ex Human Revolution into here. Some are great aditions, others feel forced, like having maps be split into little sections. WHY!? That SERIOUSLY removes the freedom of taking your time, and getting to your objective the way you want, now instead there's a few dummied down ways to do it.
The story itself also has a big issue: Remember how in previous games you could choose your loadout before the contract began, and thus choose from the beggining how to handle it? Well, first off, loadouts are out. Gone. And if that wasn't enough, this Hitman game DOES let you go loud, but constantly let's you know that it's bad. Let me explain: Hitman games always had some sort of reward system for when you act silent, however here you can see your score at all times. And what happens when you decide to NOT handle the situation with pure stealth? The game takes points away from you. This is a perfect case of negative reinforcement, something that also happens in Dishonored: the gameplay and shooting/fighting feels PERFECT, but the game penalizes you way to much for it. Now indeed, Dishonored also had boring and easy stealth and it's more complex here, something that I welcome, however I got so sick and tired of how the game CONSTANTLY told me how "killing anyone but the target" was wrong that midway the story I just snapped and started killing EVERYONE. F#CK IT, IF NOONE SURVIVES, THEN NOONE WILL FIND ME. I must also comment on the fact that the game used sexualized women here and there. Seriously. You CAN'T take that sh#t seriously. They want to kill 47 and send a bunch of sexualized nuns with tons of weapons. WHO THE F#CK THOUGH THAT WAS SMART!? WHAT'S WRONG WITH JUST SENDING THOSE SAME WOMEN WITH THE SAME WEAPONS BUT WITH NORMAL OUTFITS!? If you also take to account how the game tried to get attention on Facebook before release, with a sh#tty game that allowed you to "create a contract on your friend's head" for reasons such as "has a tiny♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, you will understand that someone was seriously not right on the head.
The game also sells a bunch of DLC's, but it did NOT bother to say that those DLC's woundn't be ANYWHERE on the story mode. I was seriously expecting to be able to play through the game dressed as Adam Jensen from Deus Ex HR (ironically, the game tries so hard to be Deus Ex it even has DLC's about it), but they were NOWHERE to be found. Instead, they're locked for the secondary mode, Contracts mode...
...And the last thing I'll talk about is the Contracts mode. It's actually a good idea to have two modes, the singleplayer story mode and a competitive singleplayer with online features... But I didn't like it. At all. Like, seriously, letting people make the contracts on the story maps instead of Square-Enix bothering to make more maps for this mode is just lazy as hell. And some of the contracts made by people are just harsh and stupidly difficult. The worst part is that the DLC's are locked for this mode, but if someone doesn't make a Contract that uses them, then why the hell do you even have them to begin with.
Now holy crap I'm being harsh to this game. Does it have good stuff? Yeah. Here and there.
As I've said, the gameplay is perfect. Shooting people, taking cover, using your wire, throwing items and such stuff, most of it takes a ton of inspiration from Deus Ex Human Revolution, but most of it is also done really well.
The music was quite good during the entire duration of the game, and the voices are even better than they ever used to be.
There's a ton of weapons, NPC's and crap on the maps, even though they're split into dumb sections. If you decide to go loud and ultimately f#ck stealth sideways, you're gonna have some fun. Specially because SOMEHOW you're allowed to take tons of big weapons on you, something you couldn't do before.
The story is also good enough. It does have some parts where the writers kinda screwed up and the game didn't make much sense, but for the most part, it's a story that will take you arround 15 or so hours to beat, depending on how loud you go.
Do I recommend this game? It's difficult to awnser, so I'll say it like this: Have you played other Hitman games? If not, do not buy this game. Instead buy Hitman; Bloodmoney, which is by far the best game on the series yet, and does it WAY BETTER than Absolution. Have you played the other games already? Then go ahead and buy Absolution. Do you like games about Stealth? Wait for a sale. You loved Deus Ex Human Revolution? Check this game out.
And don't bother with the DLC's. I got them all for like, 2€ and I still felt dissapointed.
TL:DR Edition: Average stealth game. Buy Hitman; Bloodmoney if you don't have it instead of this one, buy it only if you trully love the franchise, love Stealth based games or love Deus Ex HR. Ignore the DLC's.
