I bought this game shortly after its release, i.e. December 2012, but I only played it for 14 hours. I do not know why, I pretty much liked the game, but still I stopped playing it somewhere in the middle of the story and never touched it for years. At the point when the new Hitman was released, namely in 2016, I thought "maybe I should finish
before buying the new game." And I did so.
Now, as I am writing this review I am absolutely overwhelmed by this game. Let me sketch you why.
I guess, what this game is about is known to anyone reading this review: You're the Hitman, a contract killer. Your job is basically to eliminate targets.
Gameplay:
How you eliminate those target(s) is up to you. There is a great variety of weapons and tools to use in combat. The environment offers different ways on how to approach and/or kill your target(s). You can chose to remain unnoticed and perform a kill that makes it look like an accident, or you just go rogue and shoot at anything that moves. The only thing that may matter to the player, is the score. The score system is quite simple to explain: Remaining unseen and only killing the target will max. the score.
Atmosphere:
The game knows about its strengths. Already the second mission leads you to a crowded
marketplace. The second you enter that place is just amazing. It feels like thousands of NPCs are there, all having their own jobs and goals. In another mission, you start outside of a dirty hotel; in the pouring rain. The atmosphere that is created by that, is just astonishing.
There's a big variety of level designs; you won't get bored. The world is authentic and vivid; something I've not seen in a video game before. (And I've played some parts of Assassin's Creed.)
Challenges:
The challenges exist to hint the player towards the possibilities of solving a mission. Additionally, completing challenges will increase the score multiplier permanently.
Personally, I liked the challenges pretty much due to their guiding ability. However, there are some challenges that are
annoying. But this is, compared to all, a small problem.
Graphics:
Even in 2016, or 2017 respectively, the game (which was published in 2012) still looks decent. The whole scenery is quite cinematic.
Difficulty:
In general, two different difficulty categories exist: "Normal" and "Professional". Both are further subdivided. There are two "normal" difficulties and three "professional" difficulties. In order to complete all achievements, you need to at least pick a difficulty that is seen as "Professional".
You, as the player, can pick the difficulty you like. Even the easiest professional difficulty is quite challenging, but fair, if you come prepared. The selection of the difficulty will only affect your score.
Story:
This game is often depicted as a story-driven Hitman. Well, I would agree, basically. There's a clear storyline that brings you from one level to another. The story kind of makes sense; it's not only about "Kill A at location B", and "Kill C at location D". The missions follow a red line. However, the story itself is quite predictable. Don't expect too much.
Contracts:
Besides the campaign/story mode, there's a new "contracts" mode. In the "contracts" mode, players can create contracts for other players. That means: You pick a level from the story mode, play it, publish it, and then somebody else can replay the level. That person has then to kill the targets that you've killed in the setting that you've selected. For example: Kill the nameless police officer with a brick while wearing a chicken suit. By completing a contract you'll earn money, depending on how difficult it is to complete the mission. With that money, you can further level up weapons.
It may sound like a lot of fun, as this mode offers to challenge other people, but it just isn't. I absolutely do not see the need of doing contracts for earning money and therefore upgrading my weapons, which doesn't even affect the story mode. (I think, in
, you were also able to level up weapons. But there, it was of use in the upcoming missions. Right?)
+ Gameplay
+ Atmosphere
+ Challenges
+ Graphics
+ Difficulty
o Story

Survivor Squad is a fun little game - I understand it's based off a Flash game of the same name, although I must admit I've never played it.
Screenshots and videos might lead you to think it's less tactical than it actually is - careful positioning of team members is essential once you start to get onto the harder difficulties, as it gets pretty unforgiving, but there's enough variety in maps and looting to keep you going for quite a while.
It's not all great - there's a few annoyances, and the 'heart' levels which require you to destroy a 'heart' to stop infinitely spawning zombies quickly get tiresome. It would have been nice to see some 'special' zombie types that weren't literally just ripped from Left 4 Dead too, as much to show that there had at least been some kind of original thought gone into it.
All in all, it's probably about right for its price - it's an enjoyable little time-killer, but most people will probably only get 10 or so hours out of it before they get bored.

Back Story
Let me start by saying that I bought this game a couple of years ago.  Played it for about 10 minutes, closed it, and didn't play it again until recently.  Why you may ask?  Because when I bought it the game required some kind of account with Microsoft to save games in their cloud.  After creating this account, it still wouldn't save.  Think Uplay only worse (if that was possible).  Whoever thinks adding a "feature" like this to a game without any kind of benefit should be fired.  No ifs, ands, or buts... just fired (Still looking at you Uplay).
For whatever reason, I recently decided to see if I could somehow get the game save issue to work only to find that this was completely removed in some patch.  I thank whoever had the good sense to put in local game saves so I could actually play this game.
Review
The game feels almost like more of the same of Bioshock 1.  So if you did not like 1 you will probably not like this.  Personally, I loved the first, so I greatly enjoyed this one.  If this was all you needed to know, then buy it now.  You will love it as I have.
The only negatives (if you can really call it that) that I found are some minor changes to how things work.  For example, hacking is no longer a puzzle.  Instead it is a simple thing of pushing the button at the right time.  Some people liked this new system.  I found it less mentally challenging, and less exciting when pulling off the perfect hack.
The research system was completely changed as well.  Instead of taking snapshots, you have to run a camera on the target then shoot it with guns and plasmids to raise your score.  I liked the snapshots more, but the camera works.  Only real problem I had with it is that once you turn it on, it will switch to the previous weapon you had selected.  This wouldn't be a problem only it would occasionally change the ammo type as well.  Sometimes I would go through special ammo before realizing the ammo type switched.
The other thing is that it this game is a bit harder than the first.  Enemies seem to respawn much faster, which can be a bit difficult in the beginning.  Once your weapons and plasmids are powered up and you have cash to restock on ammo, it becomes closer to the difficulty of the original.
Summary
Overall it was an enjoyable game that you should experience.  Expecially if you were turned off in the past by the Microsoft version of Uplay.

Before playing New York Mysteries: Secrets of the Mafia by Five-Bn Games, I'd never heard of the developer.

The Good.
Strong story telling combined with outstanding graphics, excellent soundtrack and effects, good voice acting, lots of cut scenes that were high quality, original and challenging puzzles (I hang my head in shame that I had to skip two, which I don't often do), original HO scenes where rather than simply finding objects, you needed to find objects that would allow you to interact with the scene in order to find other objects. You get to keep your knife for the whole game! (it doesn't disappear.) Decent length, and a very big bonus content chapter that was as high quality as the main story, expanding on the background to the main storyline while giving you completely new scenes, puzzles, and left me wanting more. Fast travel via the map. I loved it.
The Bad.
Almost nothing. Ok ... I went into the game hoping to find a story set in an interesting gangster era that didn't involve supernatural forces and/or missing loved ones/children ... which this genre really needs to forget about and do something original, it's getting stale. What I got was yet another supernatural mystery involving the hunt for missing children with the mafia mainly background to the main story :( ... but I got over that disappointment relatively quickly as the story dragged me in. A few minor translation problems, but nothing to take away from the enjoyment.That's pretty much it.
I'm hesitant to call this game a HOG, as the HO scenes are more like large puzzles than pixel hunting, it's a puzzle/adventure game ... and a fine one at that. If you like puzzle/adventure games and/or HOGs ... then give this game a go. It's an outstanding example of the genre and has set the bar high for future games. Well done FIVE-BN!

Hitman Absolution is a fantastic game. As a professional killer the game offers you a wide range of possibilities to eliminate your targets. Shoot, strangle, electrocute or poison them, break their necks, slit their throats or let them disappear in different kind of accidents. A great story separates the game in 18 very diversified levels. And while you have the freedom to kill everything that moves the basic idea of the game is to remain stealthy and complete your missions unnoticed like a ghost. This however demands patience. Take your time to investigate your environment before you make your move. Hitman Absolution is no game for nervous trigger fingers.
Every mission is rated. The more people you kill the less points you will collect. This is a great way to reward your play style. Beside the main target every level has challenges. Completing the challenges will grant you additional points. Depending on the selected level of difficulty your multiplier will rise or fall. Besides the personal satisfaction of gaining a high result you can compare it with your friends and other players.
The game also lets you create individual maps based on existing single player levels. These maps can then be played by other players. This however is rather disappointing but it's only a bonus that nobody really needs.

This is a pretty solid HOG imo. I experienced no glitches or crashes while playing it. Most of the achievement will be earned in your first playthrough as long as you don't use skip ever or hints in the HO scenes.
The story follows a journalist hired by a museum director to look into the mysterious disappearences of mafia bosses and children. You travel through many places in New York City through a secret underground train network.
The bonus chapter was imo more interesting story-wise than the main story though it sadly does not get too indepth into the worldbuilding that looks interesting.
A few nuisances about this game; the protaganist almost never speaks. She never has half a dialogue or explain or wonder about things in the game through voice. I was getting used to her being mute (which would be impractical as an investigating journalist) until she randomly speaks when finding an item. I guess they paid some famous voice actress by  the word or something,
Another thing is the few achievements that can only be earned when doing a specific puzzle well, As the game autosaves you have no option to go back and try again if you should fail on your first try; you have to play the game again, and as the game is locked to your ingame profile, you have to create a new one if you want to start over.
Extra bonus for the game for having the areas with the collectable objects open for the entire game. The game also has a Srtategy Guide which if you should so wish can look up and story progress, puzzle solution or location of collectable, without any punishments to your achievements.
The puzzles were decent and the collecable items were decently hidden. The HO scenes uses silouettes instead of words for better and worse.
My playtime is once throught the main story and one and a half times through the bonus chapter; the extra half for picking up an achievement, so the game has a pretty good length and content.

I'm a big fan of turn-based games like A2P, so buying this game was just a natural thing for me to do.  In spite of my greatest efforts to enjoy the game, too much of it is poorly implemented.  For example, while travelling on the world map you may likely come across encounters.  After you beat an encounter, you'll be looking at your spoils from the combat while on the main map.  This would be a non-issue if other enemies weren't speeding to you to attack you, giving you little time to look at your rewards.  The cover system is almost non-functional, as well.  Characters will regularly miss shots that have a 94% hit chance, but always seem to be struck by return fire... the list goes on.
All of this could be overlooked for the sake of enjoying the game, being a fan of the genre.  That is, except for the tragic and uninspired voice acting.  There seems to be one actor who cared about the game - the others sound like they've been sedated and have no interest in their job.  What would be meant as a heated argument with vitriol and resentment instead comes out sounding like a group of school children performing The Iliad while reading from cue cards just barely beyond their sight.  Unless you really have disposable income:  Stay away from "Fallen: A2P Protocol".

At first, I really wasn't sure about this game. It's nothing too complex, but over time it grew on me quite a bit. During a Steam sale, I bought it for only $1.58. It was DEFINITELY worth the money to me. Of course, this game is not for everyone. Here are some of my thoughts:
-The graphics will be very strange at first to most people. Luckily, you can alter the lighting and color to suit your preference. Do not judge it until you walk away from the beach into the forest. It will always look strange at the beach. I can tolerate the game in its original state, but I prefer to set it to "Dark Intensity: 1.8, Light Intensity: 1.5, Saturation: 0.8." If you add color, it will resemble the non-snowy parts of Skyrim.
-There are interesting weapons such as 17th century pistols, muskets, crossbows, longbows, shortbows, tomahawks, and explosives (basically grenades).
-This game consists of two worlds. They take place in the same areas, but one is much darker with undead and friendly ghosts that tell you twisted stories. Occasionally, the undead make me jump when they pop out and scream. lol. The devs did an excellent job at creating a spooky environment.
-There are only forests. Don't expect any sort of weather or climate changes at any point.
-There isn't much variation in enemy type unfortunately, but some of the creatures are fascinating. In the normal world, the enemies you encounter sound like animals. You'll swear you hear a bear, but when you get around the corner, it's just a massive dude in medieval armor. It makes no sense, but my god does it make me laugh.
-If you can't handle walking a lot, you may not like this game. There is a fast travel system, but there is still plenty of time you'll be on foot.
-If you can't stand reading a lot, you probably will not like this game. There is no voice acting, and you shouldn't expect it for this price. It doesn't matter to me though. Reading is good for you.
-Throughout the game, you'll be looking for chests, clues, letters, graves, and digspots. You don't get a shovel until quite a way into the game, so you'll have to do some backtracking eventually. They're marked on the map, but you can remove them. When you enter The Otherworld, you'll have to search for corrupted totems. Sometimes, you just have to walk up to them to purify them. Other times, enemies will spawn, and you must kill them all.
-There are 3 different difficulties. They only affect enemy damage though.
-If you want to it be even more difficult, you can tick the option to make it when you die, you drop your equipment. If you die again before picking it up, it's gone forever. It sounds terrible to me, but I'm glad the option is there for hardcore players.
-You do not get to see your character or customize their appearance in any way.
-Not the best performance in certain areas unless most of the settings are on low. This is with a GTX 970 FTW+, i7 2600k, and 16GB RAM.
-You make a lot of money; it's kinda ridiculous. I had much more than enough by the time I reached the end of the game.
-There's a thin white line on the top and left sides of the screen. I haven't found any fixes online. Perhaps it's not something everyone gets.
-Rarely, I get stuck by a tree or a random place in the terrain. It only happened 2 or 3 times throughout the playthrough. Oh well. I didn't encounter any other bugs.
If it sounds interesting to you even slightly, you should pick it up when you get the chance.

Having only played 4 hours I can safely say that this game is worth the $20. Runs extremely well for early access (980m here; laptop) so I have no idea why people are complaining about optimization. The only issue I have with it is the PVP. There is no reason for lvl 2s to be slaughtered out of the gate immediately by lvl 15s. There seem to be no penalties for this.
So keeping in mind that this is EA here’s my quick rundown:
Pros
•	Responsive controls (even on a controller).
•	Allows for private servers (if you are willing to pay monthly to host it).
•	Fun crafting/building system (genuinely love it).
•	Polished progression system (everything makes sense and works well with the game world).
•	Solid combat system (various spells are interesting to use as well; machine gun wand lol??).
•	Beautiful game world (for an EA game).
•	Inventive mobs and bosses (I assume they are bosses when they are 40 feet tall and on fire).
Cons
•	PVP is terrible as mentioned before (forced to play on PVE server so I can progress).
•	Server stability? (crashed on me; although only once, lost a bunch of items).
•	No story???
•	Some weird animations (even for an EA some mobs glitch out pretty badly; not often).
•	AI is “derpy” at times.
Although I listed few cons those are mostly the result of this being an EA, the most disappointing aspect for me was the imbalanced PVP, so if PVP is something you want now I would avoid this game as PVP hampers actual game progression. Would be better if PVP flags activated at lvl 10+. Overall this is definitely worth a buy if you enjoy sandbox games. Tons of novel ideas here in almost every facet of the game!

Great concept, okay execution. You explore area after area, collecting loot, upgrading your gear, stealthing around supernatural enemies (or going all out on them) and coming across graves and their shadowy occupants, helping them move on with small quests.
Once you finish an area, you unlock the next. There is some back and forth but it mostly keeps you going forward. Along the way, you slowly unlock the mystery of what happened to this small region of the New World to turn it into this twisted place of shadows.
The game was made on a small budget and I think they've done a great job within their limits. It looks fine - and with the default monochrome scheme looks great - it sounds amazing, the music and audio is the game's highlight for sure, the story is just interesting enough, and the gameplay is... well, I think that's the weak point of the game.
The gameplay gets old and samey pretty quickly. I think it's more fun playing this as a stealth game, because once enemies find you they'll just make a beeline for you and you'll realise how underworked the AI and combat is. The thing is, sometimes enemies pop up around you and you're forced into a fight.
But for the asking price, it's definitely worth playing. It's a few hours of light engagement, and I have a thing for games that set a small scope and work hard at being good games within it.

if you bought FE 17 and you hate it, buy this one, it will ease your hard feelings.
Check out some youtube videos and you will see the difference
The gameplay goes like this:
- open interface M and select workers tab which is available only when you are in your farm (home)
- sellect an activity like Plow, Cultivate, Seed and Harvest and then select the field you want it to be done for.
- the activity will be done imediatelly, no tractors or workers on the actual field. So it will take from a few seconds to maybe half a minute depending on the size of the field and your computer speed. If it takes longer then a minute, the game is not crashed but only calculates the things slower. Bare with it, it will be done eventually.
- The only activities workers DON'T DO are Fertilize and Baling the hay. You will need to do them personally on each field. This will take some time and the more fields you have the more time it will take. Fertilizing is pretty fast while Baling the hay is not. So you might want o skip this one even if selling all the bales will get you a LOT of money
- You can skip seasons from Early Spring to Late Spring to Early Summer to Late Summer to Early Autumn to Late Autumn/ This is the only way you can advance in time faster. Of cource, you can wait for each day to pass by but i don't recommend it.
- After Harvest all you need to do is repeat the Plow, Cultvate, Seed and Fertilize steps in the Autumn season so you can have the crops almost ready in Speing season
That's it. have fun and become a great farmer.
Of couce, if you want you can do all the activities - Plow, Cultivate, Seed, Fertilize, Harvest and Bale, and Sell - on your own . It will take you so much time that you will actually feel like you are spending a real time year in the game.

Simulator games have insane controls every time, these controls were okay though.

This game should have been GOTY. I'm not kidding. This game made me feel, and it's one of the best games I've ever played. You play as a collection of civilians trapped in a city torn apart by war. This is the only game I've ever played that has you controlling civilians. Your goal is to lead these people to safety, by staying alive in a city full of bandits and cruelty. Everybody has a unique story to tell, but you can only hear it by keeping them alive. This is no easy task. This city is full of bandits and profiteers, who will not hesitate to kill and rob to save their own skins. But for every two villains, there is a hero. That person across the street might save your life by giving you food, out of the kindness of their hearts. The man who begged you to help save his friend might give you medicine or some valuable trading commodities. But are you willing to risk it? Will you risk your life by attacking a fully armed soldier carrying an assault rifle, just to save a stranger from a fate worse than death? Will you give food to the starving man, knowing full well that you will get nothing in return? Or will you take a different path? Are you desperate enough to rob an elderly couple just for a can of tuna? Will you steal from those kids on the verge of death, in order to get the medicine that you need? You will face these kinds of questions every day. You don't know when this war will end. You don't know if these people are good or bad. You just want to survive another day. But the question remains, how far will you go to survive?
The Good:
+Great art style
+Thought provoking and emotional choices
+Gameplay centered on scavenging and stealth
+Pulse pounding combat
The Bad:
-Can be very difficult for some people
-While combat is intense, it's still basic
Final Score: 9/10

New York Mysteries is a great casual adventure game with a wide variety of puzzles and a surprisingly good plot. Don’t expect any traditional list-based hidden object scenes in it though.
New York Mysteries: Secrets of the Mafia is an ambitious game that tries to push the boundaries of the hidden object genre, but it doesn’t try to change too much.
Like many good HOGs, New York Mysteries knows the importance of a good story: we are following an investigative journalist on the trail of some mysterious child disappearances that always occur at the same time when a prominent member of the Mafia goes missing. While the plot involves a secret society and some supernatural elements, it retains the more realistic thriller-like atmosphere to the end.
Although it is classified as a HOG, the game has no traditional hidden object scenes, only procedural ones, where you have to use uncovered objects to get even more items. The developers focused on the numerous and diverse puzzles instead, including several types that are rarely seen in these kinds of games, elevating New York Mysteries among the best HOG types on Steam.

If Steam allowed a number system, I'd give a 7/10.  I unique and interesting concept nicely executed but bogged down by some conflicting mechanics and somewhat over stylization.
The concept is very interesting and fairly well executed considering there isn't much of a precedent for this kind of thing.  A horror story told in the periphery of a war instead of in it.  But if you are already here you already knew that, and you want to know if that interesting concept turned out any good.
Well, yes and no.  While it did have some really strong moments all done entirely through game play, many times the "game" part of it interfered with the mood it was trying to set.  Keeping everyone feed and happy enough to keep going sometimes got tedious.  And while the game works really hard to characterize each refugee with an individual story, thoughts and opinions,  It just fell short of catching my sympathy and it made it really frustrating when their feelings conflicted with my own.  There was frequently a tremendous difference between my motivations (succeeding at a game) and their's (surviving a war without losing their humanity).  Other games have done this (Spec Ops: The Line specifically),  but the opportunity was missed to make the dissonance between player and character poignant and it ended up just being frustrating.  It certainly drove the point home that the average civilian really is not prepared for a war and the experiences it brings, but it hammers the point home a little too hard.  The game worries so much about the player disconnecting that it grabs the playing by the shirt and says, "AREN'T YOU PAYING ATTENTION!", and I found it making my slightly hostile to the point the game was trying to make.
If you are wondering if this game is worth your time and money it absolutely is.  For all the over-empowering, testosterone driven, one man army and "realistic" war games that have been made since the early days of gaming, it is worth remembering that wars really are quite horrible for everyone except those who do not directly interact with it in any way.  As an Iraqi War veteran, I know what it's like when the public does not fully comprehend what it means to go to war, for the people who fight it or the people unfortunate enough to get caught by it.  War is not hell, it's worse because it's real..  "This War of Mine" is not perfect, but it is very much worth your time and support.

As many of you may be aware, I'm a HOG addict at this point. I won't lie; I love this genre. I love puzzles, I love revealing stories step by step, and I love spending some mindless time on them. Yet, the HOG genre consists of one of the most repetitive gameplays ever. Thus, it is remarkably hard to make anything either new, or even refreshing as a HOG.
is one great HOG, with hours of gameplay, imaginative puzzles that I haven't seen before which comes with comparatively logical item combination. Plus, the story is interesting!
It's New York, 1955. The fearsome Mafioso of their time disappear one by one, leaving only an odd green residue and a butterfly behind them. It is also reported that children all over the city disappear alongside these dangerous criminals, drawing the exact same butterfly as the last thing they do. Our protagonist, investigator and reporter Laura James is contacted by the curator of the New York Museum, where the last disappearance has occurred. Laura is asked to investigate this odd phenomenon and find the missing children if possible. She suddenly finds herself in a picture with a secret organization, old underground passages that trace all over the city and an Indian ghost story. How come all these odd happenings are connected?
Coming up with a strong and interesting story, this is a great game for its genre. Art and environment design are high quality - depicting the hidden beauty of New York City during its shadier years - , with beautiful character design and marvelous cinematics. There is real labor put into this game, I tell you. Voice acting isn't excellent, but it's obviously beyond par. I'm a bit disappointed that we don't hear Laura's voice commenting on something, but it's not a priority.
HOG scenes are not your usual. They are compact; weaved with puzzles and item combinations similar as an adventure game within themselves, designed to reach a singular item at the end. Puzzles are numerous and mostly brain scratching, designed elaborately. I went for not skipping any puzzle for the achievement, so it was a tough and fun experience for me. If you are into puzzle solving, this is a neat addition.
Maybe the greatest bonus of the game is its game time. Added up with the time you'll be spending for many imaginative puzzles and the bonus chapter, there is an approximate game time of 6-7 hours! The gameplay has an usual amount of backtracking, but with the usage of the interactive map, nothing's a chore. You are also given the option of collecting some phantom objects and collection items for achievements, if you are into that sort of thing.
If you are fresh out of HOGs to play, do not think twice.
is an A+ HOG for you to enjoy. The game comes from FIVE-BN games, - nope, it's not Artifex Mundi, but definitely AM quality - a relatively small producer that I suggest keeping an eye on in the future. Enjoy!

I watched the trailers, and the thought that went through my mind was "Awwww Yeaahhhh, post-Apocalyptic X-Com!!".  I waited for a while until it was on sale, because I'm a miser like that, and I got at at 75% off.  Whoooo boy, that was probably the best decision I made.  Quickie run down, Do I reccomend it?  No.  Also Yes, but then more No.
Here is the thing.  The mechanics work simlar to X-Com, maybe even slightly better because instead of 2 actions each round you may be able to run, shoot, and then run, or stab someone three times, or other options.  Its actually a superior action point system in my mind.  The graphics while not stunning are surpisingly good too.
Then come the problems.  The most notable, glaring issues are all related to the characters.  Whoever wrote the dialogue for this game should be imprisoned.  It's seriously that bad.  Most games where people complain about the quality of the story, or the quality of voice acting and writing, I look at them and go "Well, it's really not THAT bad".  The only way I managed to finish this game was to stick my fingers in my ears, cover up the text on the bottom of the screen and go "LA LA LA LA I CANT HEAR YOU".  The dialogue doesn't match the subtext, and both of them are not only gramatically awful, but uninteresting at best and confusing at worst.  The voice actors might as well have been reading the back of a cereal box.  Hell, they were probably hired on Craig's List, because their 'performance' (If i can even be allowed to refer to it as such) was flat and emotionless, not to mention the voices definitely not matching faces. And the overall story was... well 'lacking' doesn't even begin to sum it up.  Possibly the worst excuse for a game in these categories that I have ever seen.
Gameplay you say?  Well there were a bunch of different kinds of maps I guess.... but the game started out being atrociously hard, and ended up being laughably easy, and all because of the same weapon.  Grenades.  The single most important weapon in the game is grenades.  If you do buy this game just remember that grenades are god.   Your low HP characters will be blasted apart by them early game, but then late game when they barely scratch you, don't worry; the enemies will continue throwing them at you even when you are standing right next to them and they set themselves on fire.  Oh, and they take up like no space and are the most valuable things in the game.  Good news, pretty much every enemy carries two of them.  Grab a sniper and just pick off your enemies and grab them for easy cash.

If you're looking for a racer with lots of choice, tweaking, and freedom, this is not the one for you. Grid 2 is a linear experience laden with fluff. It tries to be both an arcade style racer and sim, yet the result is a game lacking all the things that make either of those fun. There's no buying your first car, no upgrading or tweaking, no planning your own path or making meaningful choices. Heck, most of the time you're not even allowed to drive the cars you've "unlocked"; it picks which cars are available to you - often as little as two, sometimes only one - each race.
My biggest gripe has to be the handling. In an effort to make it exciting and "edge of your seat", they've essentially just taken away grip and forced you to drift. You don't even have to brake to initiate drifting with most cars - simply start turning and you'll slide all over (or off) the road. It literally feels like you're hydroplaning at all times with the majority of cars. Some 4WD cars handle reasonably, but you can't stick with one because the game forces you to pick from the cars it wants you to use per event.
The story is groan-worthy. Instead of earning money, you earn "fans", which actually do nothing except open up the next race in the linear career mode. You're beaten over the head with hashtags, fake news, social media, youtube, and narration about how you're going viral. It's painfully bad, like watching your parents try to use some hip lingo they just discovered. It's all just meaningless fluff that makes you want to facepalm and wish they had spent the time on adding some depth or choice to the game.
Lastly, the AI for some reason are absolute homicidal maniacs that give exactly zero craps about you or the laws of physics. 90% of the challenge in any race is managing to find a way around them without getting pummeled to death. They'll occupy the entire width of the road, cruise in front of you and brake, ram you off the track, and bounce you around like a pinball. You can be on the inside going around a corner, and they'll actually turn into you from the outside line, knocking you clear off the road while they continue like a freight train. Inertia? Mass? Pfft. The AI cares not about such silly things.
As for positives, the graphics and damage are lovely, the game runs like a dream even on a GTX460, and I experienced no bugs whatsoever.
TL;DR:
Pros: Pretty and smooth
Cons: Wonky handling, all fluff with no choice, homicidal AI, boring and groan-worthy career mode, no in-car view

This is an EARLY ACCESS game, if it wasn't blatantly obvious it's going to have bugs then you clearly need to do some research on what that term even means. I'm not trying to justify the bugs or poor optimization in anyway. I don't condone that crap but for a game STILL IN DEVELOPMENT, I'll let this one pass considering it has actual content for once.
So far in terms of content, I could say this game has more than the hundreds of dead survival open world EA games that have been in development and never left beta for 3+ years.
Is this the best game in the world? Hell no. Is it a good game? Sure. In the numerous hours I've played I've had tons of fun. Obviously my only complaints would be the optimization but that's an issue currently being worked on and will probably be fixed over time.
So what is it that I actually like about this game? The world is beautiful and vast. There are a variety of things you can do and different playstyles to suit your needs. It's clearly got that ARK: survival evolved formula in terms of the progression grinding but it had it's own spin on it with magic. The spells, weapons and armor you can craft feel more powerful the more you level up/craft better gear. The enemies always feel like they'll give you a challenge once you hit higher tier enemies (30+, 40+ 50+)
It feels awesome to take down a massine mountain giant with a group of friends even though you're overwhelmingly under leveled and one or two hits would prob destroy you. It feels awesome to build up a nice fortress and even go on clan/guild/faction wars with other players.
Hunting down that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ player who killed you and stole your♥♥♥♥♥♥after grinding your♥♥♥♥♥off and getting yourself better skills/weapons/armor? Feels good man.
It feels good when you can tame ANY ENEMY in the game and even strap a saddle onto a ♥♥♥♥ING DRAGON and fly his♥♥♥♥♥where ever you want. The absolute adrenaline you feel trying to escape as you accidentally find yourself in the middle of a lvl 55+ dungeon when you're only lvl 25. Coming back to challange towering demons in an attempt to find awesome loot.
The sense of discovery is strong in this game. I spend plenty of time just wandering around, getting lost and discovering new enemy camps, caves and so on. Time and time again I found myself saying "What the ♥♥♥♥ is that?" when an enemy i have never seen or fought before lunges an over powered attack at me. My fight or flight instincts battling each other while i hesitate only to get one shot and respawn several kilometers away.
I've raged, I've screamed, I've laughed, and fist pumped in glorious accomplishment as I took down my first Pyrant. This is the kind of game that is amazing with friends but isn't that bad alone either. The content is there people. You just have to actually play the damn game to get there. Stop quitting on a game after 30 minutes and crying that it didn't hold your hand.
--------------------------------------------------
In terms of reviews I don't do rating systems since I think they're stupid. However, I do think this game is worth 20$. It's a decent price for the kind of content it currently has. If you're so worried about the optimization then wait a while.
For once I'm confident this game won't turn out as bad as the numerous other trash survival EA games that plague steam.
I don't usually write reviews for games, But it's sad to see people get deterred from something that's actually pretty decent for once.

I have enjoyed the Civilization series for years, beginning with Civ IV. However, Beyond Earth is an installment that made me want to exit and simply continue with Civ V. It is a fairly interesting take on the futuristic world, but it feels more like a Civ V mod than a new game.
Good:
-Non-linear tech tree allows for less "well, I guess I better research ___ so that I can qualify for ___"
-Graphics look great, colorful
-Interesting futuristic take
-Early game is difficult (see below for negative side)
Bad:
-Early game is a nice challenge, but I feel like I spend more time fighting alien "barbarians" than other civilizations. The aliens are VERY numerous and strong, and it seems to be more of a hassle to simply GET TO another city, than to capture the city. Forget about ocean exploration, as there are some almost-impossible-to-beat-or-outrun beasts out there
-I appreciate the futuristic take, but it looses the charm of Civilization. Some of my personal favorite aspects of the game are those that defy history - having musketmen in BC, building the Manhatten Project as Ghandi, etc. - this is absent in Beyond Earth, and the civilization identities are generic
-The victory screens are very bland. I would have expected at least a cinematic to celebrate my victory
-The system of influences seems more of a means to an end than an impactful decision. When I attempted to go for the pacifist route, I still found myself forced to fight against the aliens, and other trees have me simply searching for points to unlock the next unit, rather than having it change my gameplay
Perhaps this will change in a future DLC, but I would not recommend Beyond Earth at this time. I would recommend simply buying Civ V Complete Edition, especially when it is on sale for a fraction of the price.

There are four modes of play. Multiplayer, where you pick a side of the zombie apocalypse, Humans or zombies. Death Lab, where you have to fight through hordes with a timer and make it to the decon chamber of the next lab. Survival, where you generally just try to survive the apocalypse itself. And finally, Campaign mode, which follows a storyline with unique events and a conclusion.
The game itself is incredibly hard and sometimes it isnt fun, but it keeps drawing you back in. The campaign starts out in an empty hospital with the player waking up from an induced coma. You take control of the randomly generated character and wander through the halls until you hear a growling noise, and are pounced upon by one of the dead. A man shoots the undead creature, and you stand up, bewildered and scared. The man explains what happened, in a typical zombie scenario style script, and the two of you go on your merry way.
Wait, havent we seen this before? Oh yeah, like in every single zombie themed  movie or television series-Im looking at you, The Walking Dead.  The whole zombie apocalypse thing is getting rather old to the point where this all seems rather repetitive and all the movies, games, and books just kind of glue together into some ominous pulsing conglomerate of gray mediocrity. Im not sure whether to poke it with a stick like a small child, or to ignore it all together. Since we've obviously decided to do the first option, Let me just state that Survivor Squad isnt that good. It isnt bad, but it isnt GOOD. It's OKAY. A lot of games are okay, but this one just strikes me as mediocre and uncreative. And boring. The game itself is a solid thing, like an idiot, but that doesnt make it good. The game has taken to cheekily calling its special infected "Leapers, Grabbers, Spitters" obviously its referring to Left4Dead. There is also a distinct lack of women in the game, like all the women in the zombie apocalypse got teleported to some island in the pacific, far removed from the events of the world. I mean, what the heck! Thats a bit weird, if not a bit mysogynist.
Okay sure, there are some good features in the game, such as occasional variation in maps, the survivors are randomly created and have random names and appearances, there is some good voice acting, and the modes can be genuinely fun if you have hours of your life to just throw into the wind, but thats about it. The game is more or less suited for an alpha rather than a full release, and thats what caught my attention. "Oh hey, this doesnt look done, why is it being released for nine dollars?"
Over all? Six and a half out of ten. 6.5/10.

In this wave-based action defense game you are the Captain Woody of a little pirate ship. Consequently he has two wooden legs, but that's not really important - it's a joke like most of the game's story content.
Woody stole some gold from the mighty pirate captain Davy Jones. Unfortunately for Woody, Jones sends his armada of sea monsters and ships commanded by various undead to bring the gold back. You have to sail and cannon away at the enemy ships, which there are maybe ten different types, most of them seemingly little more than re-skins of the basic type, though their behaviour does vary a bit.
It is really an armada: there are tens or even hundreds of ships sailing against you each level. This is alright (Woody doesn't really care for realism) but for the fact that the waves of enemies come from four different directions and the waves don't wait for the previous ones to die before emerging. Depending on your mindset, this is either challenging or just frustrating.
Some of the ships concentrate on attacking you, while others race for stealing the gold and you have to stop them fast because you lose if you run out of gold. Initially I thought dying would be final but soon I realized I only lost a tiny bit of gold as a punishment and the ships steal way more than that, making life count little in your quest for keeping hold of the gold.
Destroyed ships drop power-ups that either benefit or punish you depending on their colour. They contain various weapons from mines to kamikaze dolphins. The webs can be frustrating as they stay in place for a really long time and all the ships, including yours, get stuck in them.
This brings us to the controls: they are wonky at best. You can steer left or right, go two different speeds or stop. You can also shoot to both sides. Steering and moving is the wonky part, because the ship takes a brief moment to register your steering maneuver. Don't get me wrong: this is actually realistic. It just makes the steering a chore, making it tedious to hit the power-ups. The worse part is the two-tiered speed scheme: you either go quite slowly or a bit too fast. Gaben help you if you grab a speed power-up, because it doubles your speed but it will stay two-tiered. Speed bonus is often useful trying to reach the next wave of ships before they reach the island, but it makes it difficult to avoid your own mines and webs and to maneuver into a decent shooting position, deteriorating your attacks into crazy sail-by-shootings where most cannon balls miss their targets.
Levels consist of a single island with your treasure and maybe a reef or two, making them very bland and repetitive. Hitting a reef or the island makes you and enemy ships bounce off of them harmlessly. The same goes for hitting an enemy ship, so unfortunately there are no ramming maneuvers either. Only real differences between levels are the reskins of the enemy ships: three different behaviours with different outlook. It appears that later levels also have more enemy ships. Every level also has a different boss, making it the only thing to wait for. They will probably kill you numerous times before you win them, but what gives, you just respawn to attack them again, slowly grinding their health down.
By the way, in the story mode the gold you lost will stay lost between levels, so you might lose the whole story if you lost too much gold in the early levels. The game is challenging but unfortunately rather boring after a while. The story is silly and recited between levels by a person who sounds either bored or over-dramatic.
All in all, I completed the game in some 5 hours in easy, medium and hard settings but didn't bother with the nightmare, because I had obtained all the achievements by then. It could have been much more interesting with ship and reef collisions, less numerous but more dangerous enemies and outsmartable but challenging bosses - now kraken was the only one who qualified.
I can't really recommend this game but if you get it for really cheap (e.g. in a bundle like I did) you may waste a couple of hours on it. The only thing I liked a bit was the only slightly annoying, jolly tune you listen to while blasting the undead ships.

Despite the name, "Secrets of the Mafia" is not really a gangster-themed tale.  The mafia is present merely as a plot device.  The themes of this HOG are more typical of the genre; mysticism, secret societies, and, most importantly, all of it set in a world where everyone uses elaborate puzzle locks to close everything,
and then carelessly scatters essential parts of those locks around the neighbourhood.
A particular innovation in "New York Mysteries: Secrets of the Mafia" that I had never previously encountered is that the HO segments don't simply present you with a purposeless laundry list of items to find (and then, presumably, discard).  Instead, each item in your list (given in silhouette form) has a use within the HO screen, to open a lock, to combine with another item, or to free up some other item.  By the time you've completed the HO segment, each object you found will have been used to a purpose, to ultimately make the very last item available -- that's the one you keep.  In essence, by emphasizing the use of found items for sequential problem-solving, each HO segment is made into its own HO game in microcosm.  This works very well, to my mind, and makes the HO screens feel less pointless.  Of course, the fact the these segments are done in isolation and cut you off from your regular inventory does lead to occasional yelling at the screen "I don't
that!  I already
a knife!" but it's still feels more meaningfully integrated with the game plot than a normal HO segment.

Ok so in my mind, game reviews are supposed to help people decide if its worth spending the asking price for a game or not.
Also reviews are supposed to help people get an idea how the game plays like and what kind of game it is.
Easier said than done for this game.
At its core this game is a mix of Xcom and Wastelands, but without the nonsense.
The tactical aspect was inspired by Xcom but without the blatant trolling, and the rpg aspect was inspired by Wastelands but without the pnp dice fanservice.
To be honest i havent enjoyed a turn based tactical game so much since Warsong /Langrisser (on Genesis) and Vandal Hearts and FF Tactics on PS1.
The story starts out great, you are betrayed and sold into slavery by your own brother, saved by some wandering revolutionary group caravan.
Interesting characters with interesting backgrounds, intriguing lore that leaves you wanting for more.
The tactical aspect is where this game shines, the combat is just fun, not too hard and not too easy, not to deep and not too shallow.
There is a rather simple but nicely done skill tree for each character, the balance between damage, action point consumption, ammo availability and range of each weapon is well balanced allowing each player to enjoy their own personal style.
For the first half of the game (roughly 10-12hrs) i was in gaming heaven, intriguing story, nice characters, good atmosphere, decent weapon and item progression, fair amount of upgrades for your caravan, random encounters, hire new crew members, listen to rumors that give you hints to hidden treasure....pure bliss.
Sadly the dev team did not have enough resources to finish the game, so at some point, the story simply vanishes and is replaced by some generic "go get a list of items at these locations".
All loose ends stay that way til the end which is just a generic improvised stuff made to provide closure.
The item progression ends too, so you are left with the same items you knew from the first half of the game.
So how should i rate this game? The whole experience was 20+ hrs long. First 10 hrs were pure bliss, followed by the disappointment of seeing how the story was abandoned and the game didnt offer anything new...but it still was fun to play.
It is not a finished game, what you get is the first half of a fantastic game, followed by some generic whipped up content to call it a finished product when obviously it is not.
Worth the asking price? Tough question.
Its not a finished product but overall it offers better entertainment than a trollfest like Xcom which costs more.
It offers 20+ hrs of fun, but if you are a story b*tch like me you will be disappointed by how the story was abandoned mid-game.
So is it worth it? On a discount most definitely. Regular price only for the players that dont care much about the story and only want a good turn based tactical combat without the trolling of Xcom.

I play a lot of hidden-object/point-and-click adventure games because sometimes I just want a relaxing gaming experience where I have to
, but I don’t have to
.  Nevertheless, I will be the first to admit that: even when these games are well developed, I can understand why a large percentage of gamers would find them unexciting.
is one of the better hidden-object/point-and-click adventure games I have played, simply because there are so many things done “right.”  But if you don’t really like these types of games, you probably shouldn’t bother with it, because there isn’t anything special about it that will change your mind. However, any gamer who already enjoys this particular genre should definitely check this out.
All of the things you would want a game like this to have, it does have.  Various difficulties, a fast travel map, challenging-yet-intuitive puzzle solutions, collectibles, and achievements.  It also has a decent story and the cut-scenes aren’t horridly cringe-worthy, which many games in this genre can’t truly claim.  Another rare and awesome feature is the fact you can unlock most of the missable achievements from the “extras” menu to replay specific puzzles— rather than having to replay the entire game for one achievement.
One of the best features of the game, though, is the integrated strategy guide.  I think it is a great dynamic and it is certainly easier to use than having to alt-tab to find a guide online.  It is organized so that you can choose to use it: only to help find collectibles, only if you are stuck, the whole way through, or not at all.
certainly won’t be blowing anyone’s socks off, and it probably won’t appeal to gamers who aren’t big fans of the hidden-object/point-and-click adventure games.  But if you
a fan of this type of game, then I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to you, because it is definitely one of the better games in the genre.

In this game you command a squad of up to 6 team members in a tactical missions as well as lead a caravan in this post-apocalyptic world on a story mission.
Tactical combat is organized like Fallout: Tactics, every team member have 10 Action Points, they can move, use items, pick up look and fight using this Action Points. Your fighters have some basic stats to start as well as the same leveling path for all of them, there are no classes of fighters as you might expect. Your troopers get familiar with certain weapons as they keep using them and over time this specialty increases to hit chance of that weapon class, therefor you can craft your troopers as you see fit, you can give one a shotgun, good protection clothes and +HP skills and make him an assault while another one will just keep distance with sniper rifle.
This game is not such well made as XCOM, but all above looks like a solid foundation for a turn base combat game.
Problems start with gameplay.
-I had about one crash every 2-3 hours.
- Enemy AI is blunt stupid and enemies spawn on very small groups like 1-2 of them, so your 6 will kill them before their turn.
Enemies will keep standing in the open and just overwatch with a weapon with very small range and you can pick them off with something with bigger range easly.
The hardest fight is when for the first time you meet a well a armed group with best rifles, after that you take possession of their rifles and game becomes even more easy.
- There are no saves during tactical combat, so you game crashes or otherwise bugs out at the very end its your loss, start again.
- Using cover is kind of hard master when it will actually work and provide cover.
So what is good in this game.
+Post-apocalyptic climat is good, locations look deserted, ruined, repurposed.
+You feel lack of supplies from the beggining to like mid-game.
+Management is nice, you can improve your caravan, sell and buy more stuff for your troops.
+Weapons feel nice, distance is a factor for most guns while sniper rifles use revers distance calculation (the closer to the target the worse is your aim)
Overall game looks unfinished, but developers are still suppoting it and developing. In some time when they erase the problems I might return to it.
I can recommend it for players who like simple tactical combat and don't mind crashes.

Short, unfinished, unbalanced, not well optimized, bugged and last but not least - abandoned (there are no more signs of life from devs at all since 2016-01-27) turn based tactic with very weak AI and a lot of weird stuff. Get it on sale for 5 bucks if you are really interested in such kind of games and don't mind to support a developer/publisher, who basically has thrown a "half baked" product out on market and disappeared after that.
Discovered this title while in early access and went for it in October 2015 after it was officially released and got a couple of patches/updates. Now after 70 hours spent I am pretty sure that I have seen and done everything possible within this game, so for all those of you who ask yourself "should I get it or not?" I got an answer. The answer is - no, unless there is a discount like -80% or better. Now some of you may ask "hmm, but what's wrong with it? Trailer looks promising, screens are looking good... okay-okay there were some bugs, but devs are fixing it, right?" and this question is legitimate for sure.
So let’s go deeper in detail:
1. The game itself is ridiculously short. It consists of ca. 12 main story missions, that’s all. Plus there are so called random encounter events, which are cycled through 4 or 5 predefined maps. Main story maps are predefined as well. The task is always the same - kill them all. In a couple of story missions you need to get to point X and pick up a data, but in order to get there you still need to kill them all. The complete walkthrough will take about 10 hours if you won't waste much time with random encounters.
2. The tactical phase is actually fun to play for a while. It plays pretty the same way like the new XCOM EU/EW. There is also a cover system, but the funny thing is that AI doesn't care about it at all - enemies are just rushing to you (no matter what weapons they have) or going in overwatch. It doesn't depend on difficulty you play - I've tested all possible difficulty settings - always the same behavior, no one takes cover. Furthermore enemies never retreat, never flank, never use medkits, never switch weapons (melee/ranged) and so on. Okay, they manage to use nades at least. But basically they are just dashing to you ignoring everything ready to die in the next turn.
3. The progressing is unbalanced. It is possible to get best available weaponry (gencorp rifles) right in the very beginning via random encounter. Once obtained you will literally r.a.p.e everyone.
4. Weapon setup is unbalanced. There are pretty many weapons and I've tried them all. Some (SMGs, flamethrowers, miniguns) are completely useless. Pistols, rifles and sniper rifles are OK. Shotguns and rocket launchers are too much overpowered.
5. The optimization is not good. The game runs not really smooth on my laptop (i7-4710HQ, 8GB RAM, GeForce GTX860M, Win7-64 Prof.) although it is far beyond the minimal requirements (2GHz Dual Core, 2 GB RAM, Intel HD 4000, Win7)
6. As for today (2015-12-05, v1.1.6) there are still minor bugs, glitches and other annoying things like steam achievements which are impossible to get. Check my reports - some of them are already solved, but latest were not even answered. I guess this game will be abandoned soon or maybe it is already.
7. I can just keep on going this way and mention tons of other stuff like:
a) Mercenaries, which you can hire but not fire - the only dismiss option is to vanish them in combat.
b) If you hire a merc his attributes will be spread in his skilltree randomly. However you can't see his       skilltree before you hire him. If you got him and didn't like his perks selection for any reason - see 7a.
c) Nothing to explore on the game map at all.
d) Really confusing correlation between main and secondary stats.
e) A hit/miss algorithm which is most likely broken. I experienced just too many misses with high-percentage shots like 3-4-5 misses in a row!!! with 80% to hit. On the other hand grenades will never miss, no matter what % is displayed.
f) Caravan upgrades are pointless. There is no use for the most of those upgrades.
g) Sometimes in random encounter missions enemies wont move at all, they will just stand there doing permanent overwatch turn after turn.
Now in the conclusion I have to say that the primary idea/concept of the game isn't that bad at all. The visual art is ok, level design is ok, the story is ok, skill-tree is ok, weapon upgrade system is ok. But the whole rest construct around... it needs at least a massive polishing. It lacks some kind of deepness in this game as well. Something simple like a couple of side quests and explorable map would help a lot. I have a feeling that it was rushed in the very final stage of development. There was so much more potential inside this project, really sad to see what it became in the end.
As I already said in the beginning - I can not recommend this game in its actual shape. The full price of 20$/€ is honestly a joke for this kind of content. Hovewer if you are looking for a short and unbalanced "XCOM-wannabe-clone" with incredibly dumb AI, glitches and a lot of weird things - this game is for you.

It’s really unfortunate that I’ve had my fill after only 3.5 hours of playing
. It’s one of those games that opens up really strong with both a unique visual presentation as well as an intriguing setting. Lamentably, the game just can’t manage to keep what it promises in that first hour or so of playing.
You start out the game washed ashore in Colonial America sometime during the 17th century. With nothing to your person besides a knife, you start exploring the New World, first encountering a maiden clad in red as well as some none too friendly Conquistadors, which at first you get to take out with a bow and arrow and later on even with some era-appropriate firearms which obviously all only have a single shot in them at any given time with lengthy reload times.
All that manages to make
feel unique on a mechanical level and gives it a particular flavor that I personally haven’t seen before. Adding to that is the stark black and white color palette with which the game is rendered, broken up only by an intense red hue whenever you encounter enemies, the aforementioned maiden in red or other objects of interest. There is a setting in the options menu where you can actually introduce color into this world and even control how saturated you want it to be, in addition to controlling the brightness and darkness to set your own preferred contrast, but I wanted to experience it without color since that’s the intended look of the game.
To contrast the harsh brightness of the daytime levels, there’s also a mechanic which lets you switch into an alternate dark version of the game, not unlike
or any number of games. In this dark world, the regular Conquistadors and Native Americans that show up on later maps are replaced by skeletons and the dark world lets you interact with the souls of the people who died in order to solve a mystery.
All of this made the game really interesting to me, but if I don’t want to continue playing the game after barely 4 hours, you can guess what part of the game is the weakest: The gameplay. Now this is not to say that the combat interactions are bad overall, it’s only natural for the weapons you get in a 17th century setting to be of lower quality than modern weaponry. It has more to do with what you actually get to do in this world.
The problem with the combat is that dealing with enemies isn’t all that interesting. The game has a strong focus on listening to your surroundings, since basically everything has a corresponding tone to it. If you’re near a Conquistador, you can hear his grunts. Native Americans cause birds to fly off so you’ll be alerted to their presence. Points of interest also make a unique sound and you can mask your own noises by only moving during gusts of wind, etc. And since I suck at stealth, I never even managed to get close to an enemy in order to attempt a backstab. And that’s when you find out that the regular combat also isn’t all that interesting. Enemy behavior is fairly predictable with most of them just running straight at you. Since they have the same amazing eye-sight as their cousins from the first FarCry game, they can spot you from halfway across the map and make a beeline towards you. So while they’re running towards you, you can pick them off with your bow or firearm and when they get closer, just bunnyhop out of their projectiles and head straight for them in order to kill them with your incredibly powerful melee attack. This also caused me to abandon all precautions with regards to my movement, and instead of taking it slow in order to not alert enemies, I just ran around these maps with reckless abandon and found that in spite of how large they may appear, you can still run from one and to the other in less than a minute and change, only stopping whenever I encountered an enemy, which can be a rare occurrence.
Collecting clues means that you’ll just be running across the length and breadth of any given map you get to explore. While doing that, you can find chests, graves, important objects, notes and letters as well as totem poles. The problem with this is that with every map you explore, you basically head towards the center of it where there’s some sort of village or outpost where you’ll find a merchant and a water barrel that lets you restore your health and after that, you’ll do a perimeter sweep by just picking a direction, and running around in a circle across the entire map in order to uncover everything. Then you enter the dark world by ringing a bell that can be found in every map – again at in the fort/outpost in the center of the map – and then you can do the entire thing again to cleanse objects from corruption by killing all the skeletons and interacting with the wraiths.
I guess my biggest problem with the repetition comes from the fact that you have to explore the same world twice. Almost every game I’ve played with that type of light world / dark world gimmick feels like the developers were too lazy to design a bunch of levels and thought they could stretch out their content by having the player traverse everything at least twice. Which is especially boring in cases where the switch changes basically nothing, as is the case with
, where only the enemies are different.
It’s rather unfortunate that a game that from the outset looked so interesting didn’t live up to what the beginning of the game managed to impress with. In fact, the visual presentation serves as a nice encapsulation of the problems
has: At first, it’s striking and it feels different to everything else, only to then devolve and feel utterly repetitive and monotonous.

I kickstarted this game because I am a fan of Xcom type games and post-Apocalyptic stories. I will say that they tried their best to make the lore interesting. But hackneyed dialogue marred by cliche statements and prolific cursing drags down the plot. Some foul language is endemic to the topic but the writers throw the f-bomb around like it is going out of style. This constant drone of said word dumbs down the plot and alienates some of their customer base.
There is no paced evolution of equipment. I went from basic weapons to A2p weapons with my second encounter. I never felt that sense of accomplishment that you feel when you get that first energy weapon like in Fallout. It was just sort of dropped in my hands.
Character growth is present but the tree seemed to be the same for everyone. This limits customisation and denies the player a chance to really make a character their own.

I wish I had more positive to say about this game but it is quite flawed. Maybe they'll keep working on the problems I've pointed out but I doubt it as their budget probably will not support such efforts.

This positive review is contingent on whether or not the developer ends up making more content (workshop integration would be the best) and reading the updates it sounds like that is planned, so positive review it is.
I love logic games, Zachtronic games being some of the best (Spacechem, Shenzen I/O, Infinifactory, etc), and this game has the potential to sit right up there with some of them...if there were more to it. I played through the whole game in 50 minutes.
But everyone talks about that so let me tell you what I love about this game.
Now, normally I really hate adding pressure to puzzles. It feels like an unnecessary addition to what, in my mind, should be a relaxing experience. But the way timers are used in this game is great, and I feel it really added something I haven't seen in other logic games. Multiple timers, timers that do different things, timers that play against each other, timers that you need to manipulate in different orders and different ways - it's just great. And if you are of a nervous disposition you can always just set off the bomb and study the circuit at your leisure. You can even still interact with the components on the board after the bomb goes off. I'm really glad that feature is in there even though I didn't take advantage of it much. I did reset a few bombs because I knew I was going to run out of time, but overall I actually really enjoyed playing against the clock, and that's about the highest praise I can give for a puzzle game that adds stress as a main element.
So basically, yes, this game is a bit overpriced for the play time, but the developer sounds like they want to continue with it, which I would love to see, so if you want to support the game I'd say go ahead and buy it. It has a lot of potential.

Space.
"ALIENS"
OK, now that I have your attention; get this game. I haven't played another game like it and I would like to. The battles can be epic. Depending on your ship the battles can be tragic losses, but if you can find the weak spot on your enemy vessel you will be victorious even with a puny, weak, little ship.
This game has some pretty cool and unique features that can be extremely beneficial if you choose to use them.
Trading and merchanting being the biggest feature that can be overlooked in the game. If you know the Solar System you are in well and can make trips to and from stations you can make a killing in the market in a few simple hours. Well, with a little luck too, I suppose. Merchanting isn't essential to the game, but it can help you get from 10k to 1M in a few hours if you know what you are doing.
You can become friendly with pirates while maintaining your ties with the other factions. You can try to be enemies with everyone.
The storyline is a bit lacking if you try to drive straight through it.
That's why I jump from story to the open and expansiveness that is this game.
It's ADD with a purpose. If you don't want to go on missions and follow the story you don't have to. Fly around space blowing up anything and everything you can and selling off the garbage that you don't want to keep for yourself.
I think I put in something around 60 hours in this game and I would gladly do it again. Why? Because in 60 hours I didn't visit every Solar System in the game. There are places that I just never went to simply for the fact that I didn't need to visit that area. There are so many side quests that you could play 100+ hours doing nothing but side quests and missions. I personally wouldn't, but you could if you wanted. I prefer chasing down Pirate Lords and killing them for bounties. Bounty hunting can be pretty fun, too. Saving every merchant that gets in hot water can be a bit of a pain, but it's worth it if you're not in a rush.
Seriously, I enjoyed this game and I think you will too.
-pro- Tip: Each enemy ship has some sort of blind spot or weak area you can exploit. If you're just starting the game out and want to take on a bigger oponent try different angles of attack to see if you can deal damage while avoiding the majority of enemy fire.

Fallen: A2P Protocol:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Your name is Herk West. You and your older brother Silas went to Purgatory to meet Maximus (a worshipper of A2P energy) a so-called old acquaintance of Silas. You were supposed to get an A2P Battery Cell (a new type of energy) for your motorcycle when you realised the incredible betrayal from your brother. He sold you to Maximus and you were thrown unconscious into a pit to be sacrificed to the A2P god!   The sound of gun shots quickly helps you to regain consciousness (yep, that would do the trick almost every time) and to your great surprise, you were rescued by Salvador who kindly hands you a Katana….. Now you have to get out of Purgatory and hunt down your loving brother!
Fallen: A2P Protocol is a tactical turn-based strategy game set in a post-apocalyptic world. At the start of the game, you will have to customize Herk by distributing points between the following attributes; strength, vitality, agility and perception. Then, you will be thrown very quickly into the thick of the story and to your first battle.
When you start a mission, you will command 4 characters but sometimes it might be 3 or 2 depending on how you went in your previous mission and assuming you did not have enough scrap metal (which is your currency) to recruit new characters. It works in a  very similar way to Xcom, Jagged Alliance in terms of gameplay where you will have a specific amount of points allocated to each of your characters for movements or actions per turn. As you go through your missions and eradicate your challenging opponent, make sure you search the fallen enemies and take as much ammunition, weaponry (especially the ones with A2P cells attached to it), armour (hats, boots, vests etc..) and medkits as you can. Oh, sometimes you can find items in cars and boxes scattered in the map.
When you finish your mission, you will be given skill points for each of your characters who are still alive and distribute them on a skills tree. Also, you can upgrade your caravan, but make sure you have enough scrap metal to do so.
Use the travel map to go to different locations where you can recruit new characters, listen to rumours which will lead you to hidden stashes but remember this will cost you a fair bit of scrap metal. However, you will be able to trade items there too. So keep on the lookout for awesome weapons and armours!
In terms of graphics, they could have been slightly more polished in my opinion, but they are sound. I enjoy the dialogues but the voice-over could have been better. On the control side of the equation, they are very easy to learn and I really like the camera view; it works perfectly.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Challenging turn-based strategy game
-	Controls are good and easy to learn
-	Levels are well designed
-	Good gameplay
-	Steam achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Graphics could have been better
-	Voice over could have been better executed
If you are like me and enjoy a good turn-based strategy game, Fallen: A2P Protocol is a game you have to have in your game library.
8/10

If this was being marketed as some $50 triple-A title, it would be disappointing, but as they say in the ad, it's 20 friggin' dollars (and that's when it's not on sale). Rebel Galaxy is a very simple game, and that is its strength and its weakness. If you're looking for a game with a deep story, complex controls, or a fully realized universe with a vibrant dynamic economy, then this ain't it.  Rebel Galaxy is just a fun way to pass the time. It's a nice looking space game with simple controls and a good cowboy rock soundtrack. Incidentally, if you don't like the soundtrack, or you just want a little more variety there is a way to replace or add to the playlist in the game's launcher. I like that it lets you add different folders for different parts of the game. You want honky-tonk piano in the stations, smooth jazz while exploring and speed metal during combat? You can do that.
The game is easy to learn and easy to play so long as you understand that running is often a better option than fighting. A fast ship lets you choose your battles and outrun those nasty pirate ambushes that some players seem to have trouble with. It's also a fun way to play. I especially enjoyed the dead drop missions in which I warped into the middle of an enemy formation, grabbed the loot, and hightailed it out of there before they could say, "Prepare to die!"
Are there better games in this genre? Of course. But sometimes I don't feel like firing up an Egosoft title and micro-managing a fleet of traders. Sometimes I just want to have a little fun. Rebel Galaxy was made for those times.

I really like this game. The atmosphere of the 17th century colonial life is very well done. You will probably notice the era-appropriate weapons such as a musket and a pistol with long reload time. Enemies are quite varied too from highly visible conquistadors, hidden natives that use hit-and-run tactics, and ghosts that appear suddenly and attack quickly.
You can play the game with frontal assualt or sneaky kill style. But knows that there are some places that force you to duke it out with the enemies (such as some scripted massive attack). You can choose what happens when you die, e.g. just respawn with everything or dropped inventory that you have to retrieve. You can also choose how deadly the enemies are. So overall I am pleased with the battle in this game.
Many people review the gameplay as clue hunting and talking to ghosts, which is true. But I do like the script about many murders or tragedies faced by these ghosts. I especially love the way any ghost tell you a story, which is a part of the truth that easily mislead you. Until you find more clues and talk to other ghosts that you can put together what really happened. I appreciate the effort, however, I think the delivery of the stories are somewhat lackluster -- just press F to get the shining clues and run back to talk. It lacks involvement of the player. And this form of partial truth is used in almost every story, so it can become repetitive.
8/10 for me.
