This game isn't long, but it has a tight, concise, story that is compelling and beautifully told. This is a game for a person who likes precise, punchy novels.
The visuals in this game are simply amazing. The graphics are not cutting-edge or anything, but the developers did something incredible with what they had. I don't want to spoil anything, but my advice to you would be to play the game for a few hours before messing with..."that" option in the graphics. Trust me, play the game at its default setting for a bit first. Also, the sound design is simply incredible. I don't think I've ever been so impressed with a game's audio work. The ever-present noise of wind in the trees always reminds you just how alone you are while the distinctive noises of the enemies scare the hell out of you when you suddenly hear them out of nowhere. There is also a bell that is important to the story and the designers didn't slack off with making the bell sound great.
The combat is not going to win any awards, but it is sufficient to tell the story and enjoyable. The weapons are fun to use and period-appropriate. Each one has a definite niche and requires a slightly different skill set. The weapons line up well with the enemy types, but not in a paper-rock-scissors sort of arrangement, more like each enemy can be killed with whatever, but it is easier with a certain weapon. Also, I had a blast throwing the tomahawks. If you enjoyed the wing sticks from Rage, the idea is similar: a backup thrown weapon to finish off an enemy you just winged if you don't have time to reload.
Beating this game with all achievements will be less than 15 hours for most people, but it is an enjoyable 15 hours that you won't regret. My only complaint is that there isn't a Betrayer 2, or Betrayer 3, or 4, or 5.

...is a hidden object game. In a plague-ridden renaissance Italy, you are sent by the Duke of Medici to search for his daughter in the town of Apothecarium where something terribly wrong has happened.
You start your adventure at the city gate and progress through the town from there, unlocking branching paths by solving puzzles, finding objects you then assemble or use of different environment pieces of each scene, and slowly uncovering the story.
A variety of puzzles are available, the most common of which are hidden object searches (you have a scene filled with trinkets of all sorts, some shapeshifting, and a list of object you must find in the scene, trying to do so as fast as possible and with as little misclicks as you can. Other common puzzles include jailbreak puzzles (move blocks out of the way to have a specific block reach the exit), filler puzzles (fill a shape using available blocks) and an assortment of unique one-time puzzles.
Each scene contain coins to collect. The speed at which you complete puzzles will also give you up to three coins. These can then be exchanged from the main menu for potions and other permanent effects that will make the game easier. The main menu also allows you to re-do any past puzzles to get a better score.
This game offers plenty of puzzles, so you don't get bored re-doing the same type of puzzles over and over: every hidden object scene are visually distinct, and the unique puzzles offer varying difficulties. You can always skip those you get stuck at or find too tedious to entertain you.
There's a useful note system that tracks any riddles or hints you come across, allowing you to go back at any time for any clue or instruction without having to note them yourself. The task notes are also of great use, as the more scenes you unlock in your progress, the harder it is to remember which puzzles are left to solve.
The story is nearly non-existent, and while it is common for hidden object games to have simple stories merely be an excuse to solve puzzles, there's very little effort made at all over here, only three short exposition journal pages and very few character interactions which are done with terrible voice acting.
This is a much older game whose "Premium Edition" is a badly ported version for newer computers: old resolution, blurry hand-drawn scenes, even the hidden object scenes aren't perticularly nice-looking. Animations are pretty awful, and should probably have been left out entirely of the game as they don't contribute much to the story and even less to the atmosphere.
Most puzzles are extremely easy, very few kept me scratching my head, and hidden object variety is limited to perhaps one bag/box sub-scene and a couple of shapeshifting objects. All achievements (in-game, not Steam-based) are eventually unlocked in a single playthrough so there is little to no replayability, and the extended scenes after the main playthrough are unimaginative and way too easy, an obvious afterthought.
offers nothing that really stands out, nothing to differentiate it from other hidden object games. Genre aficionados will find it too easy, casuals won't find an interesting story to keep their interest. If it's sitting in your library, you might as well complete it, but I'm otherwise not recommending spending any money on this one.

I don't believe anyone actually expected this to be a good game. Even still I was hopeful that I would be able to find some dumb fun hidden underneath the ridiculous title and obvious low development budget, but alas Woody Two-Legs is nothing of the sort. What we have instead is a poorly designed and repetitive game, with impressively low production values and confusing controls that is above all else very, very boring.
As scoundrel pirate Woody Two-Legs, out pillaging ships on Halloween night, you mistakenly taken the treasure of Davy Jones and raised his scourge of undead minions determined to get it back. As is the case with most pirates Woody isn't about to let go of his loot, and so a desperate back and forth begins that you unfortunately must take part of.
Woody plays like something of a twin-stick shooter, with waves of enemies approaching from all sides attempting to make off with the treasure on the island in the middle and sink your ship in the process. The difference here is that you are controlling a ship, and as such have to account for the time it takes to turn as well as only being able to fire from your side cannons. It almost sounds like an interesting concept, until you actually attempt to play it and realize how unnecessarily confusing it makes everything.
Controlling your ship is very awkward and hard to do with any sort of precision, and shooting enemies is even more frustrating do to having to retrain your brain to remember which way your ship is facing and then choose the right side to shoot out of (when you are constantly turning around, remembering which was is left and right is much more challenging than it sounds like). Even if you manage to get the controls down, the gameplay just isn't fun. Enemies come in three barely indistinct varieties, with the only difference being if their end objective is to kill or steal from you, providing no satisfaction to destroy and disappearing in a puff of white smoke. Each of the five level plays and looks exactly the same with no variation save the boss at the end (which also repeat after a point) and how dark it is, and which take an agonizing 10-20 minutes to complete with no change to enemies patterns or any other means to revitalize the experience (which is already tiring after the first few moments).
I was willing to give Woody a chance despite every indication it would be a horrible time, but it surpassed even my low expectations.

tells the tale of a city doomed by a strange plague, spreading disease and chaos throughout Italy. This desperate situation caught the Medici family, imprisoning them, and time is running out.
A mad and powerful alchemist is taking lives by the hundreds, stealing their souls to further pursue his insane dream. Only one brave hero is capable of saving the kingdom, but will he have such strength?
Simple, but with a decent enough plot and serious, but predictable events, this title can still deliver a basic storyline. The player's past is as mysterious as the journey ahead. Stumbling across this infested city, and eventually going deeper to find the root of such evil.
The design is beautiful, using several traditional places, with major influences from a magic city overflowing, together with its deadly effect.
The puzzles are between easy and medium difficulty. The controls are not the best around, but with plenty of puzzles and chests around the game to unlock even more secrets, and fun puzzles, it's hard to remember that troublemaking puzzle. The hidden object scenes could be better, due technical issues...
uses a fantastic in-game store where the player can access extras, not only to help this quest becomes easier, but also a lot more fun. Through out each new area, coins are scattered and collecting them gives the player an opportunity to purchase extra tips, potions to speed up the skipping action, buffs and really cool extras for the hidden object scenes or mini games. A fantastic idea, to incluede a small currency inside the game, to make the hero persue those hidden coins. These can also be earned by completing sequences under a certein amount of time, or completing puzzles. A small but interesting way to motivate the player.
Although steam release states 2015, the original game was released in 2013, according to the Big Fish official website. I believe the development date is much older, or the studio decided to use an outdated/old kit. The resolution used was common 10 years ago, and it's a shame that using 16:9 resolution, the image has to be stretched out. Not only that, as the graphics and animations used aren't that bad at all, with native 1280x720 resolution, this could easily pass by a new game!
The lack of options or configurations is also a problem, the only thing you can possibly change is the sound levels.
This being the Premium Edition, includes an extra chapter that I personally believe it should have been a part of the final and original game. Adding more or less an extra 40 minutes of gameplay, it also includes a more satisfying ending to the story.
There are no Steam achievements, but they are included as in-game extras, the player can unlock the trophies, and admire them in a dedicated room! In Menu, you can access videos, audio logs and even wallpaper. It's nice to have all of these extras.

Overall
has everything to be a major HO release, but lacks the most important thing; more resolutions available, a patch to fix the crash everyone seems to be having at some point in the game, and general tweaks to make the game much more enjoyable! None the less, a stable enough release from
.

Urgh.
Okay so the positives first I guess...
The graphical style is nice - spooky puppets, plague doctor motif, lotsa weirdness.
Contains a built in walkthrough in case you get stuck (on top of the hint system).
You can also skip any puzzles you don't want to play and switch between match 3 and hidden object scenes at will.
Contains a varied amount of tiered achievements (though not steam ones).
A nice bonus system where you can earn power up potions with coins earned from performing well in puzzles/solving optional puzzles.
The negatives.
First up it does not seem happy running full screen on my computer. I'm not sure whether it's the multiple monitors causing the problem or just some hiccup with the game but it immediately lost focus, repeatedly disappeared from my task bar and was a complete pain to get into. Once I finally managed to get focus though it did run fine. Mostly.
Hidden Object scenes contain items that morph between various forms - one of which may be on your list of items to find. Whilst this sounds interesting in theory in practise it is buggy and I had items that refused to be clicked on (for no reason), items that wouldn't register until I clicked on one of their other forms (not in my list), items that glitched so that they continued to flash in and out of existance playing half of their morph animation after being selected.
Game also suffers from classic HOG mistakes - multiple items in a scene that fit a description, items listed in plural that aren't, items mislabelled and of course everyone's favourite, items that there is no way that you could know what they look like because they are some custom thing in the game.
Much of the dialogue/general text is badly thought out - for example at one point I was up at the top of a tower and there was a telescope. I look through the telescope and the text says "this will help me solve that mini game in the library" - a building I had not unlocked at that point. I do a few more things in the tower at which point I realise that the telescope is no longer something I can focus on, so that meaningless clue is now not something I can check back on when I know what it's talking about (luckily the puzzle was easy) - and there is a lot of this kind of stuff around, where the game references things very badly, and sometimes only once before locking you out of that information.
This actually is doubly so for some of the point n click elements. See that lock there with the obvious 4 slots in it? Gonna want to look out for an item with that pattern on it obviously! Oh wait no, it's a circular item where you could never see the back. So much of this...
The puzzles in the game range between good and awful, and there didn't seem to be any guidance on them - get a bit stuck because you're not clear what you're doing? Well you can skip it all together or not... there's no obvious nudge to point you in the right direction.
At one point I tried the hint system, now my actual problem was that I had missed picking up a random key, however the hint system just kept directing me to a completely different location, and hitting the hint button in that location would tell me that there was nothing that I could do there and I should check somewhere else. This was not helpful...
The ending. Whilst I have no wish to spoiler the ending it goes something like this... "hey thanks for that, now here's a key, go do some more stuff" *game immediately ends* Now this is because the story actually continues in the  bonus content but it doesn't change the fact that it really doesn't work as an ending.
Oh and for an added bonus as I exited the last hidden object scene the screen went black... and then stayed that way. Luckily it did have some sort of autosave (as I discovered after having another argument with it refusing to stay in focus) so I was able to complete the last 30 seconds of gameplay without having to replay anything.

I really enjoyed "Bioshock," it really was one of the best games ever made. So naturally, that meant I was looking forward to playing this game. And I was not disappointed. "Bioshock 2" really does manage to keep the fun of it's predecessor, and giving a good story to follow. Though at times, it felt like it was lacking. But I still played through it, and I got a satisfactory enjoyment out of it.
I bought this game with "Bioshock" and "Bioshock Infinite", so after completing the first game, I jumped right in to this one.  The story is very heart wrenching, with an interesting theme, and it expands upon it's setting, while still maintaining the spirit of the first game.
We return to Rapture in this game, eight years after the first game ended. And it looks worse for the wear. Having played the first game, I really felt some of the awe was gone from wanting to explore. But I still found it fun to see other places in Rapture that weren't in the first game, and I really enjoyed the aesthetics, how much of a novelty this city is. The game uses the same graphics from the first game, but it still keeps the setting looking very nice, and I liked how it incorporated underwater areas, which are very gorgeous to go through.
The gameplay is relatively unchanged from the first game. This helps maintain the learning curve the first game had, making it easy for first-time and returning players to get into the game. I still enjoyed using the Plasmids, they're really nice. But I liked how you no longer had to switch from weapons to plasmids, as Subject Delta (the player character) can use both at the same time, which is a definite improvement. I also liked how you no longer needed to divide tonics into categories, giving you one full selection. Like in the first game, you could make Subject Delta your own character with your choice of Plasmids and Tonics to suit your own gameplay style. I tended to focus on hacking more, since I hacked a lot of stuff in this game.
But what I really liked was that you were playing as a Big Daddy, allowing you to get a sense of what it's like being one. Whenever you adopt Little Sisters, you can either harvest them or take them with you to gather more ADAM or take them to an air vent and free them. However, the Little Sister defense got really repetitive for me, and more of an annoyance over time, but I really wanted that extra ADAM for more Plasmids and Tonics.
The plot wasn't as predictable as I expected, and the game really turned up the morality to make it more meaningful in the long run. It still keeps it straightforward and never overcomplicates it with too much plot, like the first game. It no longer revolves around saving or harvesting Little Sisters. You encounter certain characters who have a connection to Subject Delta, and you get the choice to either kill them or let them live. This really affects how the final act of the game takes place. I also liked Eleanor Lamb, and her connection to Subject Delta in contrast to her connection to Sofia Lamb, giving a great theme of parents going to extreme lengths for their child's welfare. I really hated Sofia and her stupid ideas, and this game suceeds in the same place of making an extremely unlikable antagonist, it makes you keep going.
I liked how they changed the hacking minigame, but it's still annoying, as you have to pay very close attention to the needle when it hits the right spot.
The enemy variety is unchanged, but with the addition of the Brutes and Big Sisters. Both of them were extremely annoying, even after I got better weapons, plasmids, and ammo. But the Big Sisters, they add more of a risk to saving/harvesting the Little Sisters, and they make you really duck for cover before you fight them, so they do have a bit of a scare factor. And again, USE THE CAMERA! You'll need the research.
I overall liked this game. It delivered what it promised, the setting still holds up, the gameplay is still easy to learn, and the plot is still kept pretty simple, and the morality is expanded upon to make it more meaningful. I was disappointed that the game didn't really have much else to offer, but it's still a good time. I intend to play this game again soon.

I'm a fan of the noir genre, and I've played many HOGs over the years - so I was very surprised to find this one that combines both features; it was a very fun and charming experience!
The main story features a journalist named Laura, who takes it upon herself to try and solve the mystery behind the kidnapped children and some mafia bosses who have been disappearing from all over New York City.
The main story features elements that are borrowed from the typical noir settings, as well as some paranormal traits, and it also borrows from some Native American folklore, as well.
It's very unique and enjoyable because it has pieces of the HOG and noir comfort zone, but the developers weren't too afraid to step beyond the borders to keep things fresh and unpredictable.
After completing the main storyline, a 'mini-episode' will be unlocked and players can enjoy going just a bit further into New York Mysteries' universe; via an underground city that has been left untouched for years.
But, when one of Laura's previous aquaintances has been poisoned by a mysterious toxin from an unknown plant, it's up to her to explore the abandoned city to try and find the antidote to save them.
As for gameplay, it's a mixture of HOG features as well as some from classic Point & Click adventure games.
It was nice to find and pick objects from a 'clean' scene instead of looking for them in a jumbled mess, like most typical HOGs have players do to progress. And, on the flipside, I enjoyed interacting with the enviroment, turning keys to open doors, mixing chemicals, rejoining torn papers as well as clicking on puzzle pieces.
On top of that, there's some nice cutscenes, along with some voice-acting (Though, sadly, Laura doesn't have much of a speaking part) to really paint a picture for new players.
It's a good balance, there's something for everyone to enjoy.
Now, with all that in mind, I will definitely say that the game was most definitely enjoyable from my end and was worth every penny - six hours for a comfortable playthrough for six bucks sounds fair to me; and with the replay value of revisiting the puzzles and the massive open-world levels with lush artwork, it's almost a steal!
However, that doesn't necessarily mean that it doesn't have some issues, however minor...
-You only have ONE save file, you can't have multiples.
Also, even worse, if you're replaying some of the main game again but want to also replay the bonus chapter, the save data for the bonus chapter WILL overwrite your save data for the main game - and vice versa.
-Spilling text on certain documents.
On some of the books and journal entries, the bottom of the text runs off of the page.
This can prove to be frustrating, I'd like to finish what I'm reading instead of it running off into oblivion or cutting abruptly.
-Bonus chapter's too short.
I can understand that it's a 'mini-episode' and all, but it just felt like the very end was a bit sudden; Laura explores the underground city and rescues her companion, but, there was no real explanation for what happened to the people there.
Maybe it's supposed to be left up for interpretation, but there could've been a little more to it.
Other than that, I loved playing through the game; it was nice to sit down and relax with.

Tiltagon is a game where you must guide a ball through a hexagon path of obstacles as quickly as you can.  Although the smooth graphics, thumping music, and varied levels are all positive, the touchy controls and start-all-over deaths caused me more frustration than fun.  Recommended if you like these kinds of "ball-rolling" games; Not Recommended otherwise.
PROS
+ Lots of different ball types to unlock
+ Exciting, pumping music
+ Tons of levels and an Endless mode
+ Passing a difficult level is satisfying
CONS
- Keyboard controls are useless (4-directional arrows on 6-sided tiles. Really?!)
- Mouse controls, although with customizable sensitivity, are still flawed
- No checkpoints leads to infuriating deaths
- Frequently experienced more frustration than fun

This War Of Mine is not the kind of game i have played before and if it wasn't recommended by a friend or being livestreamed by said friend i would probably not have bought it myself. Therefore i bought it not long after its release in November 2014 and have been putting quite a bit of time into it since then.
Having said that, This War Of Mine is honestly incredibly gripping and addictive! I found myself having played it 12 hours straight right after buying and installing it without realising just how long i had been playing for. At the time of buying this the game basically started completely randomly every time you start over,  meaning you started with different characters at different seasons in the year with different lengths of conflict each time. In one such scenario or story you would start with just one character in your bombed ruin of a shelter, in another you would start with two characters in winter so your characters were more susceptable to illness.
The basic concept of the game is to survive the war with whatever characters you start with. You can craft various worktables in order to make weapons or tools and to brew moonshine or grow herbs and tobbaco to make medicines or cigarrettes. You can also craft beds, chairs, heaters, a cooker etc, but in order to build these you can choose one character to scavenge at night. Of course this means that if you have only one character your shelter is likely to be raided at night and your items stolen. You can also be raided while one of your characters is at your shelter during the night but sometimes they will injure your characters to steal your items.
The random characteristics of this game can keep you gripped for hours without realising it and the look and feel of the game are so fitting with the games setting. Since this game has released however the Devolopers have released quite a bit of content for it changing just how your characters stories will play out. Firstly instead of completly random stories that you could start with they implemented the ability for you to choose which story you play which means you can pick which characters you would then start with. This gives you a little more choice as to how difficult or easy you will find playing through the story but anything could still happen and your characters could still all become deeply depressed, starved or terminally ill, or worse murdered.
The developers have also released a DLC content for this game in which all proceeds go to the War Child Charity and you can choose how much you pay for this content - there are three prices all for the same content and it all goes to charity. This DLC content i believe added 'Graffiti' to the various locations that can be scavenged. This means you can take a picture of yourself and play This War Of Mine as yourself!!
All in all this is a fantastic game with awesome developers who are continuously adding new free content and massively supporting their game and i can very highly recommend this game to pretty much anyone because it will honestly keep you playing for many many hours.

New York Mysteries: Secrets of the Mafia is a really great Hidden Object Game. The story is compelling: you're a detctive  in 1950s NYC trying to solve a string of disappearances of Mafia bosses under mysterious circumstances. In addition, each of these disappearances seem related to another dissapearance, this time of a small child. Somehow butterflies are also related. It's a nice little mystery.
The puzzles are challenging, and there are several difficulty options you can choose from, affecting the amount of help the game gives in the form of visual cues or hints. The music's really cool and fits the theme nicely. I love the retro style and the "period feel" of the 50s and the artwork really showcases that. Overall, New York Mysteries is a high-quality HOG.
There are loads of collectible items (and completing each collection earns you Steam achievements) and there are a lot of different areas to visit in the game. The map is huge, but fortunately, there is also a convenient fast-travel system allowing you to jump around from place to place quickly.
One thing you won't find in this HOG are word-lists and cluttered scenes where you have to cross all the words off the list by finding the items. Hidden object scenes are more organic here, you're given a group of silouettes and you have to work out the objects that fill them. Each of the objects is usually used in the scene to uncover one or more of the additional objects, so the scenes work out more like a puzzle than a straight-up search.
This seems like it is one of the longer HOGs I think I've played, though it's still a game you can complete pretty quickly. I don't really see that as a down side at all though, since the polished and well-presented gameplay and story are really enjoyable.

Grid 2 is a racing game that rewards skill without punishing you for the tiniest mistakes, letting you master a simple system with a forgiving attitude. It may stray too close towards the easy side of the scale at times, and it'll be interesting to see how the game works online (which unfortunately wasn't tested in this review), but its career mode is well worth playing and you won't be satisfied until you've mastered every single corner.
Best Game Moment: Aggressively drifting round a final corner to take first place and win a championship.

One caveat: It's super short, so watch the price. Steam tells me I have 1.5 hours in this game, and 38 minutes of that I was on the phone and didn't bother to shut the game down, and I've played through completely. So it'll take you around an hour if you are somewhat experienced in logic puzzles, probably up to two if you aren't - the levels are very short (there is usually a one- or two-minute timer), and success or failure are often pretty much instant.
What is this game about? It's a logic puzzle game. There's sources of energy and lines on which the energy travels, there's components on those lines, such as switches, logic gates (AND, OR, XOR) and some others, that will change on which lines the energy travels or doesn't. The goal is to either get the energy to certain endpoints (often multiple ones, at the same time) or to cut an already existing energy line, all while avoiding to supply energy to specific other endpoints.
Namely, for most levels, there's a timer with detonator, featuring one endpoint for power which is already supplied by default, one to three "disarm" endpoints that have to be simultaneously supplied with energy to work, and one "detonator" endpoint, supplying which will mean instant defeat. A few levels are introduction levels, which only serve to show off how a part works, and the remainder - slightly more than a handful, really - are the most interesting ones, featuring clocks and detonators as separate parts, with the goal being either to cut power to the clock, to the detonator, or to cut the connection between the power output of the clock (that goes active once the clock hits 00:00) and the detonator input of the detonator.
I don't want to spoil too much, but there's levels with traps, less-than-obvious solutions and some with a simple fix to a very complex problem. It's great fun, if you like logic games, I just wish there were more levels.

That was fast. If I had three words to sum up this game, it would be those three words. Homefront is a game about fighting a guerrilla war against the North Korean Army, which has "liberated" the United States. Now, to this end, the mission was accomplished. North Korean soldiers were killed, and it was in a guerrilla fashion. However, that's not to say I didn't have a few issues with the game. First off, I beat this game in one afternoon. One afternoon. It's more like a DLC, and nowhere near the full-length size most games are nowadays. On that note, if you're bored one afternoon, and want to give a a whirl, hey, go ahead; you'll be done before dinner's on the table. Also, I enjoyed the variety of guns, but combat was not exactly varied. I was more going through the motions, and how I engaged my target depended largely on what weapon I was using at the time. Also, I enjoyed the moments when I got to use the Resistance's robot thingy that launched many rockets (kind of like Black Ops 2's CLAW unit). Overall, like I said, if you have an afternoon to kill, I would say why not? It doesn't bring anything really new to the table, but sometimes, you just need to shoot some bad guys. And Homefront has no shortage of bad guys, let me tell you.
Overall Score: 7.8/10

Although I am recommending this game, I highly suggest new players to Civilization begin their journey with Civ5.
CivBE is in many ways a more basic version of Civ5. I'm going to spend some time in this review simply doing some rough comparisons, and saying what I think would help the overall gameplay. If you stick around and read, I'm sure you'll enjoy. If you agree, lemme know!
I have played a stupid amount of Civ games. I am not claiming to be a Guru of Civ, but I have enough experience I'd consider myself a connoisseur of sorts.
The game does have strengths. The Espianoge system is beautiful, there are more tile improvements, unit upgrades can make a huge impact on the game. It plays great as a military TBS game more than a traditional Civ, and there is a reason for that.
The depth of Culture in CivBE is very flat, for starters. While Civ5 has 10 culture trees, with 6 of them unlocking in later stages of the game, CivBE has 4 of them. Each one more or less serving one generalized line of thinking (Growth, Science, Military, Production). Now this isn't necessarily an issue, but I think the game requires another layer of Culture depth.
I know they already have affinities, but we all know the game is still a little stale. Why can't the Colonies eventually form themselves into another type of government [for example, and completely made up: Oligarchy/Hegemony/Dominion, which would have its own tech tree much like Autocracy/Order/Freedom] that further distinguishes them? It seems strange that after 100 years living on a distant plant, we still refer to ourselves as "colonies". You'd think at some point the foundation of a completely independent state would form as these societies begin to advance beyond the point of their forefathers... (I played a game deep, and literally after over 100 years they were still saying "our colonies", which fails realism to me)
The severe lack of diplomatic manourvering is a bit sad. This game could do with a whole lot of it, and to me there are 2 major weak points in that diplomacy:
No City States, only Stations (I use these words interchangably):
Stations are, in my experience, pretty useless. While they do give you boosts to production, culture, growth and science if you trade with them, they often get blowed up by another Civ. Or they just vanish at a certain point. They play such a non-pivotal role in the game that I don't see much value in them in their current state.
I'd like to see stations form, literally only ever expanding to the first line of hex's immediately adjacent to the station itself, and become self reliant little bases with unique units that can properly defend the station. Why unique units, you ask? So then they can defend themselves from Alien onslaughts and/or Civ assaults more easily. There is also the added bonus they could donate you one of these rare troops once in a while? Or they could gift you surplus energy, science, or even techs.
Diplomatically, you could influence the affinity of these stations. Eventually, if you earned enough favor with them, you could take ownership of the city state (but would not get the badass units it produces, because as a civ you are not a station). And the stations affinities would be flexible through the early and mid games, before become more solidified as the game progresses. Potentially they could even be fixed late game as a mixture, which would require more wrangling from the Civs for influence over the Station.
World Congree/Religion:
I lumped these 2 together because I didn't want to go back and maybe have to change the "2 things" to "3 things". I do not know exactly how a world congress would take shape in this world, but you'd think society would remember that cooperation is  on a global scale has worked (to a degree) in our past. Maybe the world starts with a World Congress once all Civs arrive. It would serve the purpose of providing potential boosts to players early game based on programs that are voted for. Beginning with simple things that would generally help everyone, like Increased Production Yeilds from Farms for 10 Turns, or Science from Grassland Tiles. You can see how this is generally useful, but can be geared towards certain Civ's.
But as Affinities (and maybe them there Goverment types I mentioned before... but I'm a dreaaaamer) progress forward throughout the game, things get tense. As time progresses, certain measures are unlocked based on affinities while earlier ones are locked, never to be seen again. These new, Affinity based Measures could be varied... anything from not allowing Miasma to be dispursed (Harmony), to Adherence to True Earth History (+1 Science +2 Culture for each Purity Affinity), to Digital Memory Recorder (+X Supremacy Affinity points to Civs with majority Supremacy Affinity or No Affinity at all). The Measures available at the World Congress would become less and less lucrative, while also becoming less about net positive things for ones own Civ, but more as a tool to be used to inflict damage on other Civs. This will drive tension as well as a Narrative in the game.
Civs of different Affinities would vote down measures, repeal them, etc. Once a Civ hit a certain Affinity, they could leave the World Congress and take a Pariah State debuff. That debuff would affect them only with World Congress members, not other Pariah states. Pariah states would also lose all of the Bonuses (and potential debuffs) of the world Congress.
Collapse of the World Congress would take place in a few circumstances:
-Half (or 1 less than half) of Civ's leave World Congress.
-A specific number of Measures are repealed or have heavily divided votes.
-War is declared, a Civ petitions the World Congress to intervene and end the war between the 2 primary warring states. If the Vote is a success, peace if inflicted (treaty is forced on any member of the World Congress at war with those states, Pariah states could continue the war but potentially have no more allies to fight with). If a majority of states vote against peace, this will inflict a huge blow to the World Congress and potentially cause its collapse if it has lost enough legitimacy already.
-All Civ's share an Affinity. "We all walk the same path, but in our own way. Freedom to pursue ideas, in line with humanities best interests, will help push mankind to the next stage of human evolution. May you find glory along your path."
Now one could imagine there could be the potential to rejoin WC or start a new WC, but that's... not today.
Religion could be replaced by Cooperatives, which would essentially play the same role as religion... I think I have written enough though.
What I'm trying to say is that CivBE has a stupid amount of potential that simply has not been realized or seized. I lack any technical skill to make things happen, but this is just how I see it.

Short Version: Most dissapointing game I've purchased in the past year.
Wearing my cynical marketer's hat, I can only conclude from the recurrent theme running throughout the intro (follows an Indian refugee), default corporation (Indian, led by aforementioned refugee) and technology flavour text (the historical quotes read by Spock have been replaced with faux Indian/Space colonist mythological quotes, reminiscent of the colonial mythology found in Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars series) that this game is an attempt to dazzle the growing Techno literate Indian middle class. Even if your part of that demographic (I'm not), please be smart, spend your money elsewhere. Sid Meier's games are notorious for demanding a premium, asking a price that encourages you to wait for the sale, but ultimately is proven to be good value. This is the only area where BE has made any progress, upgrading from the usual value-for-money to outright greedy cash-grab. Even after its first big patch/rebalancing , this is still an alpha, full of incomplete and poorly designed features. Hooray, auto-renewing trade routes at last! No, wait, how do you stop them? Still only 8 factions, not enough for even the large map.
Some suggested alternatives:
Play Civ V if you have it
Get Civ V, with all expansions
Play an alpha that calls itself an alpha. More fun for less money, (almost) guaranteed
Read Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars Trilogy

It's a good game, though seems underwhelming when compared to Civ 5... but only if you factor in all of Civ 5's DLC.  If you compare this to base Civ 5 with no DLC then this is the better game.  I think once this game has enough time to grow like it's predecessor then it will end up being an overall better game in the end as well.
I enjoyed the change of scenery, tactics, and playstyle that this game has over the other Civ titles.  For one it feels like you are trying to colonize a new world.  You are on a hostile planet where everything wants you dead, the miasma surrounding you will kill troops, the aliens will eat your settlements, and the other factions will probably turn on you sooner or later as well.  That makes it fun though.  Most of the time it feels like the planet itself is your worst enemy rather than the other factions.
Resources play an even bigger role in this game than in previous Civ games.  Each of the three alignments need a specific resource to build up their unique units.  So rather than planning an alignment at the start it's usually best to adapt to what you have available and go from there.  This aspect makes each playthrough feel even more varied even if you play the same faction.  The unique units really are impressive too at higher levels like the massive aliens you can breed as harmony, the huge siege platforms and robots you get as supremacy, or the armada of hovertanks that can transverse almost all terrain as a purity player can make for some exciting battles.
The AI is a bit... lacking to say the least, even on higher difficulties.  Usually they'll happily sit by and watch as you build an endgame wonder and use it to finish the map.  Sometimes they're vindictive jerks who will ignore others doing the same thing and instead focus all their efforts on crushing you despite you having done nothing to really warrant such actions.  Of course this isn't much different than the nuclear warlord Ghandi from Civ 5 now is it?
If you enjoy these types of games I'd say go ahead and get it.  The sci-fi setting and change in many things does make it feel distinct from Civ 5.  If you're still on the fence just wait for a steam sale on the game or something, as it's still worth checking out.

Apothecarium is beautiful and filled to the brim with content. But it is also incredibly slow and aggravatingly tedious, thanks to the overcrowded scenery and the overabundance of stages.
I wish I could say better things about Apothecarium: The Renaissance of Evil, because it is apparent that the developers put an incredible amount of effort into this hidden object game. And, ironically, this is the problem: they overdid it, especially in the art department.
The game world is pretty large for a HOG, with several dozens of screens. They are full of detail in every nook and cranny, but this also means that finding some of the plot-critical objects is a bigger challenge than it should be: spamming the hint button to find some small item gets boring pretty fast, no matter how good the game looks.
Another issue is with the story. The setup is great and exciting: an alchemist uses the Black Plague that ravaged pre-Renaissance Italy to find the secret of immortality. But, as usual with less professional HOGs, the story quickly regresses into a series of plot dumps, leaving less and less incentive to push forward apart from looking at the next pretty scene.

Overall this is a mixed Hidden Object game that has both good sides and some weaker ones.
The story is a bit illogical and leads the player through the titular town of Apothecarium in search of a lost lady. After few minutes we end up seeing some weird alien creature and a Vidocq like alchemist that tries to hinder main hero quest. Moving on...
Graphics are low res, but that's not the problem here, the locations are beautifull and fantastic. Music is quite ok, nothing special though. What's just lacks in this game is room position - sometimes you don't have a clue about where to go next. Other weak spots - game is a bit illogical. You cannot break glass even though you have a hammer in your inventory. One time you need a key to open a padlock, other time you'll use your crowbar. You attack a working electrical machinery with an hand axe. Good luck with that in rl, that would bring shocking news indeed!
Pros:
- graphics are low res, but nicely drawn
- music is ok
- you can collect coins to buy some minor upgrades
- you can switch to match-3-tiles game at any time during hidden object search minigame. Thus you can find all the items by playing the match-3 game. Fine by me
- some locations are really weird and remind me of Zeno Clash games
- bonus chapter - you can finish it under 1 hour, but still this is nice
Cons:
- come on, the plot is just a filler to the game, it's just bland and pointless
- map is a bit chaotic and it isn't responding sometimes
- game crashed a few times during my gameplay
- the game is set during some plague period but after 10 minutes you won't even remember about this whole theme as you'll be doing random stuff mostly
- the main antagonist is quite bland, there are plot holes, etc.
- sometimes the match-3 tiles game is not working properly as you can match 3 tiles and they won't count untill you match another one or different 3 tiles - that's minor issue but still it should not be there
- game can be illogical sometimes - you have a steel hammer but can't break glass with it? You stand in from of very brightly lit house but the character is telling that there is too dark in there? There are other such situations here.
It's not state of the art Hidden Object game, it's not even close to it (well, maybe when it comes to some graphics design it would be close if those were hi-res) but still that's pretty sturdy Hidden Object game. Sure, the plot is pointless and full of holes, after some time you'd probably end up using walkthrough or hints and just rushing through the game. Still, I don't regret playing this game.

His name is Not Important.
And he is very upset.
So upset...EVERYONE MUST DIE.
What made him upset?
People. They're parasites, scums, and he doesn't care. Life sucks. So life must end.
THAT basically sums up the whole plot of the game.
As far as the gameplay:
Bloody 3D isometric shooter. "Twin gun"? THERE IS NO TWIN GUN combat.
You always use one weapon at a time, no dual-wielding, guns-akimbo. Which is too bad.
Kind of reminds me of games like Alien Shooter or Zombie Shooter, but in full 3D.
You go from level to level, and each level is basically a map with a few locations to wipe out people.
As you complete local objectives, you gain a "Respawn point". So if you die, you can respawn in the level without having to start all over from the beginning. The save system absolutely sucks for this reason. It can be frustrating to run out of respawns given how hectic the combat can be and then have to restart. Objectives might be to massacre a party, wipe out a funeral, etc.
Once you complete certain objectives (sometimes, not all are required) you are told where to go to exit the level.
GAME IS SHORT:
There are only about 7 levels in this game.
From my playtime, I beat this in roughly 6 hours.
I wish there was more to do and that the maps were bigger.
BLOOD:
The game is very violent, with enemies splattering blood everywhere. Bodies and blood stay (use highest settings), so as you go throughout a game map,  you'll revisit areas where you left piles of bloody corpses. The game features "Execution" ability, which IS REQUIRED to regain your HP. lol. You can do this in the middle of combat with armed enemies, or outside of it. When outside of combat, and just slaughtering civilians, you'll get random "mini-cutscenes" showing you performing executions randomly. They are pretty brutal from shanking, throat-slitting, head-stomping, head-exploding, etc. with the victim screaming and Mr. Not Important growling out things like "STF up and die" or "EFFF YOOO", seriously, the guy has no heart. LOL. No witty one-liners like the POSTAL, rather, this dude his HARDCORE.
On the downside, there's no gore or gibs. Seriously. This runs on the UT4 engine and with all the stuff exploding everywhere, no gibs? No guts? WTH?!
DESTRUCTION:
Almost everything in the game world can be destroyed, including the walls, vehicles, props, everything, almost like Red Faction:Guerilla. The effects are great, you'll watch a wall get blown out and turn a mess of chunks that fly everywhere. Explosions/fire effects are absolutely great. You'll find yourself blasting flammable/explosive items just to watch stuff explode spectacularly.
METAL:
You're a big bad death-metal mutha-trucker. You could give a sheet but don't give a fork.
The game Credits were awesome.
PROS:
+I liked the controls, WASD was good. Works best with mouse/keyboard.
+People complain about the camera but I thought it was fine. It was focused "around" the main character, the ability to "aim" let's you see farther away and more of the level.
+Blood and destruction. Lots of it.
+Graphics were great (*game performed well for me)
+Fun gameplay, fast-paced.
+I liked the grey/minimal-color graphic style. It works well here. There is a mod out that adds color, which is pretty interesting.
+You can also drive vehicles too (as long as their doors were left open). A shame the levels were not bigger but you can drive around the area and run people over, you can even drive right into walls and watch them shatter and shatter everything inside as you plow through. A goal to take out people in a grocery market? So many ways to do it. If you get a vehicle, you can just plow through the glass windows and annihilate them. Maybe grenade the vehicle and it blows doing even more damage.
+Lots of ways to take out enemies
CONS:
-Combat is too fast-paced, with enemies hordes turning the whole game into a cluster****.
-(see above) Crack-speed combat makes playing with a controller useless. Use a mouse/keyboard instead.
-Some might consider this game as a stress reliever, but more likely, it will induce more stress lol.
-*Reportedly runs bad on medium to low-end systems. Given that it's UT4 engine, and all one perspective, this shouldn't happen. Probably that almost everything being destroyable is the cause.
-Game is short (beat it in a few hours).
-Game is too difficult, even on easy-settings.
-The main character shooting his weapon should stand out than the enemies around him; because of this, during combat, it's very easy to loose track of who/where/what you are shooting, your ammo, and if you're even hitting anything. At times, you'll swear you barely fired a few shots but need to suddenly reload again. In my opinion, they should have done away with "reloading" all together.
-You run out of ammo too fast, and can only get ammo from killing armed enemies. They don't drop a lot. Some take waaaay too many hits to kill. Given that you must also use ammo to kill mounds of civilians, the developers seriously miscalculated here.
-AI is stupid, the soldiers always try to charge you like it's some QUAKE 1 game. On some levels, you see them taking cover (probably scripted), other times, they're so dumb, they'll bottleneck at a door-way, or manuever around randomly. They should just hang back and take cover. But like I said, they go full QUAKE 1 on you and charge. Sometimes, run right past you.
-Aiming can be frustrating, it's skiddish, when an enemy is up close (see above), you always miss, even if you put the target right on them. Forces you to run back just to shoot them.
-If you run out of ammo, you're screwed. Despite execution scenes showing you with a knife, your only melee attack is "kick" and that just stuns them. lol. fail.
WISHLIST:
-Could use more weapons
-Needs more levels, and bigger levels. The last level was really good---need more like that.
-A 1st Person mode would be interesting.
-Gore/gibs. I think even Diablo III was bloodier/gorier.
Overall:
The game can be frustrating and make you HATE IT for that, but you'll probably keep playing it because it made you so full of HATRED. lol.
4/5.

I don't think I've ever played a game so simultaneously innovative (relatively speaking, within its genre at least) and yet so bewilderingly obtuse and frustrating and cack-handed at the same time. There's a lot to like about this game, but unfortunately far too much of that good work is undone by bizarre design choices and poor execution.
For anyone who's played as many of these hidden object games as I have, you soon start to become all too familiar with the same old tropes and patterns and play. Assume the role of a young woman who's being threatened by some witch or spirit or mysterious murderer and try to undo their spell or curse or stop their evil plot to gain power. Do this by exploring old mansions or semi abandoned towns or temples and find a bunch of objects to gradually work your way closer to the heart of danger and stop it once and for all. Or at least until the sequel. You'll even begin to become very well acquainted with the same objects, too - you'll always, at some point sooner or later, find yourself looking for a watch or a compass or coins or a brush which could be a paintbrush or hairbrush or sweeping brush, or a bow that could be a tied up ribbon or bow tie or a bow you'd play an instrument with or fire arrows from. It's like starting a new Ubisoft game, already you just know you're going to have to deal with lookout points or collectibles or some Uplay bull at some point just as sure as the sun rises and sets every day.
What I initially liked about this one was it didn't seem to fall entirely into the mould of its peers. It had an interesting opening scene that showed some story potential, a new type of hidden object search is introduced in the form of shapeshifting items, and it even has a persistent currency system where you can buy upgrades to enhance play. I'd never seen that in one of these games before. But, sadly, it didn't take long to revert to type. The villain of the piece that at first seemed so powerful and unique, soon becomes just some standard bad guy with nothing special of note. The shapeshifting objects are partially broken and fail to register your clicks far too often. And those upgrades that you're teased with when you first start? Yeah, they turn out to be all but worthless.
Once it's stripped of its initial promise and potential, what you're left with is a somewhat subpar hidden object game that needlessly gets in its own way far too much. Even with the inclusion of an objective screen, the actual next step to progress is rarely ever completely clear (which isn't helped by the overabundance of items you constantly seem to be carrying that don't always have an obvious function in the world). Even something as simple as moving from one screen to another is a task as the usual arrows at the edge of screen are nowhere to be found anywhere in this game. It's way too easy to miss entire areas because there's no indication they even exist.
Then there's the actual application of items that's infuriating. You end up carrying multiple tools that could potentially (in the real world at least) have lots of uses, but you absolutely HAVE to use each one precisely as the game intends you to. At one point I was carrying three hammers and a large stone, but when confronted with a window, had to use the exact item on it to break it then lose the item. Later, presented with another piece of glass, I needed a key for it. You find a small, rusty, old grate at one point and you'd THINK you could at least try smashing it in with one of the aforementioned items, right?... WRONG! You have to find a large saw instead and cut it with that. Although, my favourite was when I had to clear a stairwell full of birds. Firing a large rifle mere feet away from them never made them budge, but setting off some fireworks outside the building? Yeah, that got them going. It's just no fun when it becomes a game of "guess what the developers were thinking" when you're trying to make any progress.
Like I said, there are things to like about it, like the art is all pretty top notch, if not maybe a little overly busy at times, and for the most part the music and audio is pretty decent, even if the voiceovers are a little cringey at times. But hey, it's a hidden object game, would you really expect any less? There's even a handful of pleasant puzzles from time to time... though there are probably just as many that are either pointless or really irritating. But I'm afraid the bottom line for this game in my opinion is, in a genre so saturated with choice, and with many of them being of really high quality, I couldn't recommend this over those. And even in its own right, unless picked up at quite a discount, and unless you think you could stomach the more frustrating aspects of the game, then it's a shame to say that you could do an awful lot better than this and would be best served searching for something better.

BioShock is a fantastic first person shooter that I cannot recommend enough to anyone and everyone as a prime example of weaving a good story into engaging gameplay. You are provided many options to survive the trials and tribulations of Rapture as you, Jack, attempt to find a way out of an underwater utopia-turned-hellscape. Though the maps are on the  small side and were largely built with progressing the story from point A to point B, there is enough content and interesting enemies to warrant exploring every inch of Rapture to get another plasmid, a bit of lore, or an extra achievement or two. Using the tools at your disposal - weapons that seemed hacked together by a madman during the Prohibition era and supernatural powers granted through injections called Plasmids - you will find yourself wanting to keep playing the game, especially on a first playthrough.
That said, BioShock Remastered is littered with multiple crash-to-desktop glitches that also delete save files from the area you were exploring, forcing players to rely on an auto-save - which usually means starting an entire level from the beginning. This by itself would not be a demerit, but with it being a very common occurence especially on the rigs of today and having to rely on community-created guides for *maybe* fixing the problem make an otherwise great game a poor look into the greatness that once was. Despite "remastered" in the title, it is fairly clear that there was not nearly enough quality testing to make this gem from 2007 stand alongside 2 and Infinite as a collection worth picking up outside of nostalgia purposes.
By itself, BioShock Remastered is only worth picking up if you find it heavily discounted and if you are willing to mess around with some game files to fix the common crashing issues.

I bought this game not expecting much at all, just a fun little isometric shooter with some diversity in levels and, this was something I was hoping for more than expecting, some diversity in weapons and enemies. I got none of that. The levels were all the same with the exception of two levels and the weapons all felt the same, not that there were a lot of them. There is one pistol, two SMGs that felt exactly the same, two assault rifles which, again, felt EXACTLY the same, and RPG. Those are all the weapons this game has, nothing else unless you count the guns mouted on certain vehicles. As for the enemies, their AI is useless. I've had so many just walk into my line of fire or walk right over a grenade I threw, so many of them even died because of their own explosives. Beyond that, they're all the same with different armors and weapons, I never felt like I was progressing in any way at all. The vehicles, though a nice touch, felt like an afterthought. They handle poorly and feel weightless. Now, onto the level design, most of the levels felt like a they were copy and pasted, even one that takes place on a military base, felt like the boring suburbs I started in. Worse of all, how short it is. I have 5.8 hours on record only because I restarted when I downloaded the color mod. It was disappointingly brief, even with all the side quests complete I ripped through this game in less than two or three hours. All that being said, I'll likely revisit this game from time to time but I will only ever recommend this game if you find it for 5$ or less, never for the full price.
Tl;dr
Buy it only for 5$ or less, otherwise you're wasting your money on a very short and very repetitive game.

And then there is a randomized endless mode where you have to be careful, but still quick enough not to get left behind on an expired ground tile.
I do have to warn that simple 4-directional input (arrow keys) is definitely not good enough. I used a thumbstick (gamepad). And that's all the controls you need. The physics feel much nicer than in other ball-rolling games.
Another warning is needed: the initial learning curve may seem insurmountable, but it gets easier afterwards.
Graphics are great: shiny untextured triangles are very pleasing to see.

Overall, unexpectedly great game that would be leagues better if it had the budget behind it to support more production.

This game makes me sad.  It should not have been released from Early Access is the state it is in.  While the Dev had made a lot of bug fixes and some UI improvements since launch, there is still a long way to go until it is a game worth spending your time and money on.
As for my 1.6 hours of playtime, it has given me enough experience with the game to know that it is not worth my time to keep playing it as it is.  I am willing to give it another try if more improvements are made, but as it is they may be the second game I have ever used Steam Refund on.
My main problems with the game so far have been-
No customizing your character.  You start with Herk, add some poorly defined stats, and you can choose from 4 different coats and add a face mask or glasses to your Character.  That is it for Character  Customization.  You will always play the man named Herk.
The UI is terrible. This is still true even after the update that did make some improvements, but it is still ugly and requires more clicks than it should to get a simple task done. such as searching a location for items you know are there.  Example. If I am next to an item on the ground, and I press the Hot Key to pick it up, there should be no need to confirm that yes, I really would like to pick up said item.
Combat UI needs a lot of improvement.  When you chose to attack, a circle showing your attack range for the equipped weapon and % to hit for anything you move the cursor over. The main problem is trying to aim past somebody to fire a long range weapon, ignore the to hit % as it is a complete lie, and more than once I am unable to use a melee attack on somebody standing right next to be because of "reasons".
Caravan map needs improvement. The way to travel from location is through the map screen, and there are several problems with it.  First is drilling for items.  You can purchase "Rumors" of treasure buried out in the wasteland.   The problems with this, is you have to find the exact pixel that contains the coordinates of the "rumored" treasure, so get ready to have fun as you click around the map looking for this pixel. Add to this the incredible problem of traffic in the Barren Wastelands, the game feels more like a trip to Walmart on Black Friday rather than a post-apocalyptic world.  There are roving caravans everywhere.
This game has other problems, but I don't feel like listing them all and the Dev has been active in forums and has released 2 patches since release that have fixed many bugs and made some UI improvements.
This game has a lot of potential to be a really good turn-based game, but it just isn't there yet and the rushing of the game through Early Access  is an act of desperation that makes me think that maybe this game will never receive the attention  it needs to be a great game.  I hope I am wrong about this, and the Dev continues to work on the game making the necessary  improvements to make the game enjoyable.

TL;DR Betrayer is far from perfect, but I would wholeheartedly recommend it. Especially on sale.
Essentially, it's an open world first-person adventure game with stealth, shooter and horror elements. Your objective is to unravel the mystery of a cursed settlement in Colonial America; by finding and collecting page fragments scattered across the several medium-sized outdoor levels, talking to the ghosts of the deceased settlers, and shooting possessed Spaniards in the face while you're at it.
The gameplay falls somewhere between mediocre and good. The shooting and stealth systems feel a bit clunky, but work well overall; basically what you’d expect from an obscure action-adventure game. My only major complaint is that towards the end, running around the levels trying to find all of the collectables ends up being a huge chore.
That aside, Betrayer more than redeems itself in other areas. For one, the sound design is outstanding. From the genuinely unsettling ambient noises and shrieks throughout the "shadow world", to the gusts of wind that make the environment feel so very alive, Betrayer succeeds in being fantastically atmospheric, tense and immersive. The heartbeat track which plays when an enemy detects you never failed to put me on edge; not knowing where they were or how many there were.
The writing is also surprisingly first-rate. The page fragments and accounts from the ghosts are very well written, and the storyline is dark, suspenseful and engaging; which is definitely helped by Betrayer’s unique art style. As standard, the game is in black and white with only important objects, enemies and NPCs highlighted in red. However, if you wish, you can bring back the colour by adjusting the settings however you like, which is a very important touch. I’d recommend turning the saturation up slightly, as I found washed out colours provided the best atmosphere, and also contrast between the black and white in the “shadow world”.
Overall, Betrayer is a small, imperfect game which shines through its top-notch sound design, story and art style. Whether it’s for £3.99 or less than £1 on sale, it’s a hidden gem that I think everyone should pick up if they have the chance.

This satisfies my patriotism fetish more than you can possibly understand.
Nonetheless, it's a somewhat dissappointing game. Much of the story felt as if it could have had real, tear-jerking moments, yet the elements are never explored. I think the largest reason for this is how rushed the game feels.
Don't get me wrong, it plays adequately and looks great. Nonetheless, something about the pacing of the campaign just feels...off. Too much happens too quickly. The protagonist goes from a "military grunt nobody who happens to be handy with a gun" to "lord of war who causes the earth to tremble as he breathes in one's general direction" within an in-game week. I had hope for this game. I really did. When I saw a child's parents executed in front of him, and when I hid amidst dozens of murdered corpses within a mass grave to hide from communist invaders, I thought, "Maybe this game won't just be another lifeless virtual duck-hunt." Unfortunately, I was wrong.
I'd much rather the game follow a more humble storyline instead of going for huge "emotional" moments and executing them poorly. Your character is a resitance member. Why not have him act as one? Why not have him smuggle objects, firebomb cars, and raid checkpoints? I was hoping for a game that would convey how Red Dawn (1980s) felt. It very obviously tried to pander to the "MURICA" crowd, which is why I bought it. Even from a totally biased point of view, I think this game fails at what it tried to achieve. A lot of work obviously went into it, yet, the campaign feels like it was rushed out.
I got it on sale for 4.99. That's all I can recommend it for.

Imagine you're playing Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag.  Now, imagine that instead of being stuck with that one, tiny, but somehow infinitely upgradable little ship, you can actually buy new ships as your fortunes improve.  Now, imagine you're in space.  Finally, imagine you don't have to get out of the ship to follow some British ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around the island for 20 minutes in an area that is suddenly, inexplicably teeming with soldiers.
I think I got sidetracked.  Anyway.  This is an excellent quasi-3D ship combat game.  Not a full 3D sim like Freelancer... all player-piloted ships, and those of similar size, seem to occupy the same plane of space.  Rolls, climbs, and dives are not valid maneuvers.  Shields go fore, aft, port, starboard, with no concern for doral or ventral.  Despite this, you don't feel particularly limited in your play.  It's just streamlining something that can overly complicate some other games.
There is some downside.  There isn't a lot of variety to your available weaponry.  The targeting AI that controls your turrets most of the time is kinda stupid, and works in exclusive terms, rather that allowing prioritization.  There are, inevitably, escort missions, some of which you will lose for no good reason.  The in-game economy is a little capricious, which makes moving goods profitably as a trader a bit of a long game.  But I still find it enjoyable to spend a few hours making pretty explosions in space, set to a soundtrack that you might find playing in Jim Raynor's house back on Mar Sara- forgettable, upbeat, twangy rock.

I never write reviews, and I only do so for games that I think are that much fun, that I need to tell everyone!
Rebel Galaxy is a weird thing, it combines "naval" combat with space ships and quite some options to (role) play the game.
The combat, is in one word, different. You fly in 2D space, as the rest of the capital ships do, and only the lighter fighters are able to fly everywhere, but you only fly capital ships.
If you want someone to explain on how you should tackle the combat in this game, then dont read this, I think you should totally find that out yourself. There are some really powerfull combinations but almost everything works together if you set it up logically.
In ways how to play the game, there are different factions.
the Citizens are what the name says, these people just want to live and inhabit most of the stations.
The Militia are a military 'police' faction, taking down pirates but also stopping illegal trading.
The Merchant Guild and Mercenaries Guild are a thing of their own. The Merchants are traders and specialize in getting cargo through the system. You can join them if you want to focus on trading with stations, because the trading and goods system in this game is quite fleshed out!
The Mercenaries supply contracts to you if you join them, also giving you access to better equipment, like most factions do in the game when you join them. They work with and against everyone, its up to you what you choose.
Then there are quite alot of Pirate and Raider factions, you'll meet the Red Devils and Double Jack's first, and you can join them if you play your missions right and work against their enemies, though all of them start out hostile to you.
There is alot more to tell, but you can find it out for yourself. I still havent beat the main story, as i'm to busy working for my chosen faction, which is alot of fun.
If you can get this on sale, defenitely get it, otherwise its still a pretty good deal!

Ok... This is not a very in depth review of battlerite but hopefully you could grasp the concept of the game. I’ve been playing this game for a little bit over 14 hours and I think I could commentate on the gameplay. First of all, this is a MOBA and a hardcore pvp at heart. This game is pretty competitive and the community is not that salty in my days of experience.
There are a little less than 30 champions in the game, each with their unique play style. Each one has a unique ultimate and different abilities such as stun, armor break, shield, reflect, parry and much more. I feel like the developers by not adding that much champions have made the game much more competitive. Since their is only a few of them, ranked gameplay will become more tactical and strategical. It is pretty easy to grasp at the concept of each character and predict their moves, unlike games with tons of legends such as league of legends and Dota 2. My personal favorites so far are Rook and Ashka. They pretty much contradict each other in every possible way. Their is 3 different types of champions. The first type is the melee. As you can pretty much expect, these are the champions that have the most health points, and they just jump straight into battle, tanking for the rest of teammates and can easily take you out in a swipe if your not careful enough. The second type is the range. Oddly enough, the tutorial for the game shows you how to play with Jade- a character who’s main ability is to shoot different types of guns. These range characters can be really resourceful to the team, they act as the backbone of the team and if they are good enough, can snipe other champions into the dust. Last but not least are the support characters, these are mainly the saviors of the round, they can heal other teammates and theirselves, but make sure you know how to use them, they are pretty complicated. A support is most useful if you stay close to them, they are usually the first to die because they are usually targeted by melee champions and they also have the lowest health points of the bunch. So that is my review of Battlerite, it definitely gets more complicated then that with x abilities and different load outs, but hopefully you understand the premise of this game and what it has to offer. So that’s pretty much it... in my personal experience, I would say it’s a solid 8.5/10.

Wow, so many negative reviews! Maybe the game doesn't work for some, but it ran just fine on Windows 7 64bit.
I liked it. In fact, I'd say it's definitely above average for HOGs. It tries to do something different and while it doesn't always work, it keeps things fresh.
The Good.
The graphics are top notch, no definition problems except for a couple of objects in the bonus content.
The sound track is awesome. A mix of classical and modern music that fit the theme. Sound effects are average.
Lots and lots of puzzles, many more than most HOGs, and there are bonus puzzles in most scenes too.
The game tries something different for the first hour, with what felt like crafting and some fps elements mixed in with the usual point and click adventuring ... but then it seems to get bored with it, and the rest of the game plays just like every other HOG you've tried.
The HO scenes have a lot of morphing objects, which at first was annoying, but I quickly got used to it.
The game comes with a bonus chapter that is linked with the ending of the main story.
The game's setting in renaissance Italy is different.
The game is longer than most other HOGs for a similar price.
The Bad.
The voice acting ranges from good to terrible, depending on the actor, but thankfully, those scenes are short and the script wasn't well written for them in the first place.
The story is the usual supernatural fare that HOGs seem to love. No surprises.
The requirement of having a specific object for a specific action is a lot worse in this game than most. There are plenty of times I had a crowbar and/or hammer in my inventory and needed to break some glass, but it wouldn't allow me to because I needed a rock, or had to use the crowbar to break a crate, where I got an axe, and then could use the axe to break the glass! A lot of other HOGs prevent this by removing an object from your inventory after it is used, which is silly in the first place, but in this game, you can see why. It's frustrating to have an knife but be told you need scissors etc.
Click detection for about 4 of the objects was terrible. I saw the vase, clicked on it ... nothing. Found the rest of the objects. Clicked on the vase again, nothing. Started questioning my own sanity. Maybe there's another vase. A couple of minutes of fruitless searching, I click hint .... it WAS the vase. I click on it ... nothing. I click 8 or 9 more times .... nothing. I start clicking on every pixel of the vase .... eventually it registered. This was the most extreme example, a few of the other objects just needed 2 or 3 clicks.
Overall, if you can get the game to run, and if you get past the first 45 minutes and don't get confused with all the added features (that are rarely used in the rest of the game) ... what you have is a very pretty adventure in an interesting time period, with great music, challenging puzzles, and it will keep you entertained for longer than most similar games.
What can I say? It's Galaga. It's functional. And runs fine. Some devs can't even do that and still have the audacity to sell it to you.

As a long standing Hitman fan, this game is disappointing, however I'll try to be unbiased with this.
The basic drift is that this game is too easy and the levels aren't big enough to satisfy the playerbase who were used to big open levels with multiple approaches to how you take out your target/s, however in this game the levels are quite small and claustrophobic to the point it gets frustrating, to be fair some levels are quite open like the late act of the "sexy nun" (I say that with sarcastic quotes) where you run around a giant farm with crops and multiple ways to take out the 3 targets. These are the missions that sastify us ♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Unfourtunately these are too far and few and the rest of the missions revolve around getting to point A to point B and can get quite linear.
The story itself is quite good and well written, it's a more personal story of Agent 47 and has him feeling guilt for (SPOILERS) Assassinating his handler (SPOILERS) and helping her carry out her dying wish. 47 goes rogue and sends you to a variety of levels.
The levels themselves are more like Chapters, they're split up into different sections and this is where my gripes are highlighted, the fact that Square Enix made these levels so linear really annoys me as how you do what you're supposed to do is really highlighted and obvious taking the challenge out of the game.
One other thing that breaks the challenge of the old games is this "instinct" system which basically points out enemies, your target, objects you can interact with and so on. I do play on professional which does limit the instinct system to the point where it is pretty much redundant.
On top of all this, the disguise mechanic is completely ♥♥♥♥ed up. Essentially now any NPC with the same outfit you're wearing can pick you out which is pretty unrealistic, but also ruined a staple mechanic that used to be so handy in the previous installments. The updated system is supposed to go hand-in-hand with the instinct system and this is where the second biggest gripe of the game lies, Hitman really focused on hiding in plain sight and being seen but not heard. You could literally take out the targets right hand man, act like him, take out the target and nobody would suspect a thing. Whereas here you get spotted within seconds, even if you've done nothing wrong.
If you can look over all this, the game still has very shining positives. The cover/shooting system works very well, almost as if you can play this primarily as a shooter, and if on a subsquent playthrough you happen to do this you would think you were playing an actual shooter instead of a stealth game... I also encourage you have a muck around with the contracts mode as this is where I primarily spent most of my time when the campaign was done. And while I have strongly criticized these levels, there are different approachs even if they are completely unrealistic
tl;dr
