Generally, I love hidden object/puzzle games and I hate having to give negative reviews, but this one just didn't have what it took to draw me in and make me really enjoy it.
First, there are severe compatibility issues with no indication that there will be a fix.  The screen flickers terribly on normal settings and in every variety of compatibility modes I could try.  The game does not flicker in windowed mode, but you'll find if you go windowed that the play area is tiny if you have a high-res monitor.  In my case, in order to play the game I had to switch to windows and change my 4k res to half that in order to get the game big enough to see and play.  It's irritating, but it did the trick to let me play without the screen flicker.
The game itself is standard HO game fare with a combination of HO scenes and minigame puzzles along with the usual inventory-based puzzles to complete.  This is a formula that has worked over and over again with this genre of games, but for some reason this game didn't make it work.  I found myself intensely bored after a short time, and only my personal obsession with never leaving a game unfinished made me complete it.
Whether it was just lack of a compelling story, nonintuitive puzzles (I was completely at a loss a lot of the time), less-than-helpful hint system, sloppy map system, or a combination of all of these things, I really did not enjoy anything about this game.  Even the HO scenes were irritating (example: find a jar.  No, not that jar.  Not that jar either.  There were some scenes that had a good five items in the scene that matched the one you were actually supposed to click.)
So in the end, it's not actually the worst HO game out there, and if you can deal with the compatibility issues you might find it more interesting than I did.  However, if you do decide to try it, I would recommend getting it on sale.  But I would recommend going through most of the other HO offerings on Steam first as there are many better.

I was considering giving this game a good review because many aspects of this game are good. Music, graphics and voice acting are all there. It has some of the best scripted sequences that I've rarely seen in a game and features a variety of creative ways to kill your target. But where this game screws up big time is in it's level design and specific aspects of its game mechanics.
For the purposes of this review I'd like to like to look at two other stealth franchises which are Batman Arkham and Metal Gear Solid.
The biggest issue in the game is the level design. The first few missions have pretty decent level design. The AI purposefully has weak points that allow you to slip by undetected. You may find certain guards go into a secluded area allowing you to take them out to progress. Challenging but designed in a way which allows the player to slip by if they use caution. I'd say when you get to about the Dexter Industries section of the game all of that goes out of the window.
When you get to the last 2/3rds of the game the level design becomes ridiculous. I've played through hard and purist modes having done a no kill alerts run and let me tell you, unless you use obscure gimmicks there's no way you're beating this game without any alerts. In certain areas there's that many guards all facing each other all the time with visibility on every area that the player needs to go that it makes it absolutly impossible for the player to go stealthy without cheesing the game.
If you look at mgs 1, 2 and 3, even on the highest difficulty in every level the player is given the possibility and abilities to be stealthy and clean. The guards always have certain patterns designed for the player to take advantage of. While still being extremely challenging if you're good you can always remain undetected. In Hitman Absolution it doesn't matter how good you are, unless you resort to specific gimmicks and borderline exploits in many areas, you aren't getting through without being spotted. In the start of many of the levels such as before the fighting match, there are guards that just stand there having a long conversation, forcing the player to sit there impatiently listening each time you try the level. It just interupts the gameplay and it's extremely boring and frustrating.
What are these gimmicks that I refer to? Well in Hitman Absolution you have two ways to deal with guards cleanly, going behind guards and strangling them (which makes all nearby guards look in your direction) and throwing objects to make a guard check it. In many of the later levels the only way to progress is to keep throwing the same object against the wall, strangling the guard that comes to check it over and over until the way is finally clear. You can either do that or use a disguise to just walk past all the enemies without bothering, but that burns all your instinct meter so don't expect to be able to use it all the time. Certain events like the fight with sanchez become ridiculous because the guy with the disguise you need just stands in a spot with about 12 guards all staring at him and doesn't move. So again you have to resort to throwing wrenches at the wall to lure everyone out which takes absolutely ages. It's tedious and boring, but it's the only option for stealthy players.
Batman Arkham, which while being a considerably easier and less challenging game had what Hitman needed badly. A wide variety of non lethal takedowns to deal with enemies. When you're playing hitman, you have to do the same choking animation every single time while tapping X repeatedly. It's depressing. Every now and then you get an animation of 47 hitting someone against a wall but in the end you're doing the exact same takedown over and over again. Playing non lethally in Hitman is the most depressing aspect of the game, but you're punished for killing guards which means the player is constantly trying to play in a boring way. Think of all the different takedowns in batman, like hanging off a ledge and strangling people with your feet, or dropping ontop of them from a great height, or even jumping people out of a vent. Only having the option of choking people out makes the game extremely tedious but you have to do it throughout the entire game.
I cannot stress this enough that the vast majority of this game is throwing wrenches at the wall and waiting for guards to come and check the sound. This is why I found the majority of the game depressing to play and had to give it a bad review. If they had spent more time working on the AI patrols the player wouldn't be forced to constantly use gimmicks to get through the missions. I got through the later missions using an obscure trick where you use your silenced pistol to alert the enemy then run through them because it's the only time you can get through certain guards without killing them. I'm all for challenge, but when it reaches the point where the player is forced to use exploits to progress, it kills the whole point of the game being a challenge. The levels which aren't like this are actually a lot of fun and if the game didn't have such bad level design I'd be giving it a good review right now.
Another thing which is really annoying is the scoring system. You get scored on things such as how many times you were spotted, how many people you killed, did you hide the body.., etc. Yet on certain missions you're forced to kill people and on others there's actually no areas to hide bodies. The scoring system is always telling you you're playing the game wrong, but you don't have a choice because of how badly designed most of the levels are.
In summary the things which killed the game for me: Gameplay interuptions, poorly designed levels, lack of non lethal options, the scoring system constantly criticising you and gimmicky gameplay. I've beaten the game twice and it was mostly not an enjoyable experience. Sometimes it's fun, but most of the time it's frustrating, but not in a good way. I'd say it's worthwhile if you're a Hitman fan since it has some great moments, but I couldn't recommend it to anyone else. I should start by saying I do plan to continue trying to play this game. I really, really want it to be good, but so far it's been frustrating to no end. The driving physics seem like they could be decent, but all the cars you get in the start are "Drift" class, where drift apparently means "Absolutely no road friction." It's seriously impossible to keep them from sliding. Now, this is bad enoungh on its own, but the A.I. is pretty much completely oblivious to your presence on the track with them, and has no qualms about ramming into you at any speed or position. Not only that, but they don't slide like you do. Ever. So instead of a crash where everyone is screwed up, they drive happily on by while you go careening off into a wall, left at the utter back of the pack. I thought we'd mastered A.I. that tries to avoid collisions in racing games, someone should really let Codemasters know. I should also note that I play with a racing wheel, so I should have the sort of fine control to avoid these things (and can in other games) but apparently that's meaningless here. I don't often ragequit games of any type, but when I do, apparently the game is GRID 2.
TL:DR version:
-Game looks and runs great
-Slick menus and dialog like most other Codemasters racing titles
-Wheel support is great, you can feel the weight of the car and the road easily
-Decent career mode
-Game forces you into crappy cars with no grip
-A.I. isn't subject to the same forces as you (they have seemingly infinite traction)
-A.I. doesn't avoid collisions in the slightest, will run you off the road and laugh
-No cockpit view (Seriously? Why?)
I really, really hope I can at least get some cars with traction later into the game, but for them to force you to drive like a madman and then punish you for driving like a madman at the start of the game is stupid. Then again, Codemasters did decide that making an entire game out of the terrible Gymkhana events from DiRT 3 was a good idea... I guess they're going downhill.

The Vagrant is one of the most beautiful adventure sidescrollers I've played. Background, characters, everything is drawn very beautifully. Yet the story and universe contains a lot of darkness. Certain things need polishment like spirits not looping properly sometimes but I was impressed with how progpressed it looked as an early access. You don't get that a lot nowadays.
Music is quite good, too. It does have a good part in making the atmosphere.
Gameplay is fun. Combat is fluid, you have multiple combo options and some are very situational, but some combos aren't worth getting, as spamming light attack can be more efficient. Bosses are especially hard, and mobs can drive you crazy during boss fights. Generally it adds to the fun, as it presents a challenge, but some bosses, those with lots of mobs, may seem overkill to some (like me). You can spam apples (heal) but that isn't fun. I'd prefer more dodgeable fights instead, like Dark Souls series. This may be a personal experience, and I may need to get better at dodging, but I don't feel motivated to do that when I can spam healing.
Another thing that should be mentioned is the variety of enemies. There are a lot of different types, and they don't just look different. They have completely different move sets.
I can't wait for the remaning chapters to be released, and devs say they are going to fully release the game in Feb/March 2018. I'm really curious about where the story will go for Vivian. Plot thickens with each new development, and I wanna craft those weapons.

Galaga, Japanese shoot'em-up arcade game developed and published by Namco Japan and by Midway in North America in 1981. The objective of Galaga is to score as many points as possible by destroying insect-like enemies. The player controls a starfighter that can move left and right along the bottom of the playfield. Enemies swarm in groups in a formation near the top of the screen, and then begin flying down toward the player, firing bullets at and attempting to crash into them. In later stages, some enemies even break from an entering group in a frantic attempt to crash into the player. The game ends when the player's last fighter is lost by colliding with an enemy, being hit by an enemy shot, or being captured.

You're sent to a town called Apothecarium, where famous scientists are residing, in order to discover what happened to a young noble and her daughter were sent to preserve them of the plague. They disappeared suddenly. But once a bright city, Apothecarium is now in ruins. What happened?
The plot is promising, as it's a scientist that began the curse and behind an evil plan to reach immortality.
The gameplay is the standard one: you search hidden objects scenes, you find items and use them and you solve puzzles. Unfortunately, where the concept is working for me usually, here, in this game, made me watch flies pass by. In other words, I got bored. Bored because I didn't always know what to do, frustrated because some stuff aren't making sense and besides, after a while, resolving the same puzzles in order to have surprises is boring. Even if I must admit that the idea to earn bucks or hints is a nice idea, it wasn't really well executed by having the same type of puzzles.
Also, it is also nice to have in hidden objects scenes items that are changing between two forms. However, having many of them is also disturbing, and two or three aren't even in the list. So you're kinda confused. Also, there is a problem with the translation: you're asking for a "gland" (I play in French) - for me, it's a fruit from the oak. I have one in the scene. However, it was referring to something else, that I know under another name.
There is also a nice shop where you can buy special stuff by collecting coins in the game or solving fast puzzles or hidden scenes.
The soundtrack is correct and the backgrounds are also quite good and creepy.
It's just a shame that I got lost in the way and that I was often left by not knowing what to do.
I'm quite mitigated about the game. I mean, the game is correct. But I didn't even finish the game. Steam is missing a neutral feature or a maybe button, because Apothecarium belongs to that category. Anyway, whoever is a novice in these kind of games should avoid, the rest, well, I let the decision up to you.
Oh well, it's not a complete failure, I will let the benefice of the doubt to this one and recommend it.

This is a nice game. It's sad that it has a mixed rating. The story is a little disjointed in places, where if you don't read the journal you'll miss bits, as it's not all displayed on screen or in the voice acting. The character draws conclusions in the journal about things that were never mentioned on screen. It was weird at the start but I got used to it. You should note that occasionally the answer to a puzzle is pretty much given by reading the journal, so following the story can have it's drawbacks if you weren't looking for clues. Fun, enjoyable combat system for the most part. I liked the inclusion of the broadside weapons tactics. I am a little disappointed I cannot build up my fleet by more than just one mercenary, (I guess I'm a collect them all sort of guy), because I think it would be cool to have a fleet following me around in this game, and it would definitely help with some of the absolutely massive fleets you face in it.
Ship upgrading is very easy to appreciate, and it's actually fun. I haven't found that in many games of late, and it had some apparent parallels to Elite that actually made me want to pick up that game just to see if it was as fun. It's not. The choice of style is actually surprisingly appealing for this game, and I suppose that might be because it plays out mostly in 3rd person, aside from station interaction, which is a menu system.
Well designed overall. The trade system is well defined, but has a few hiccups in that it seems the economy supports very low number of products available. I'm guessing this is a long term game, where you eventually make your way through multiple systems picking up something you know sells much higher elsewhere. Constant disruptions in the economy make the market somewhat unpredictable too.
Slight downside is pirates. More pirates than you can count. They're everywhere, and make up the main 'bad guy' You also start with them hostile to you, but if you wanted, could possibly ignoring the main storyline somewhat, do a number of missions to make them friendly, or maybe just neutral.
The reason it's a downside, is they pull you out of warp everywhere you go, and usually not at a range that make escape feasible unless your ship is capable of dealing with them at that stage. That basically means you run into too powerful gangs, you die. Somewhat disappointing after many hours playing without.
While I mostly like this game, and find it fun, the only other aspect that I find unfortunately lacking is the progress to an end game with the storyline, (which is actually good), that means the systems have to get progressively harder to cross, which is mostly where the pirates come in.
And there's always another faction of pirates, (aliens seem to like this trade), so even being neutral to some, won't help you with others. The mission system also requires you choose between one and another faction too. Either you take a negative hit with another pirate faction, or with the militia, if you choose to try and gain neutral status with the pirates this way, and afaik, there is no other way.
Regardless, it's a fun game. Maybe could use more units in the trade system, (1-2 per station seems standard, of any avail.), and the ability to hire more than one merc, and possibly with bigger ships, or even help outfit there ships, but good in most every other aspect, and you can always upgrade to take on the masses, so that's not really a problem.

Rebel Galaxy ranks among the very few video games I've actually played through to completion.  What contributed to its longevity?
+ An addictive "just one more mission" play cycle.  Occasionally, trade can be lucrative in the early game, but most of your money will come from completing (combat) missions.  Typically, these are pretty short, and, because there are only a few different mission types from which to choose, you'll be able to judge roughly how long you'll spend earning that mission's reward and, ideally, upgrading your ship afterward.  And you don't have to do escort quests (maybe one, I can't remember for sure).  And you
do escort quests.*
+ Fun music which never gets annoying.
+ Satisfying combat.  Sometimes I was overmatched and handily destroyed, but because I usually chose pretty short missions, this was rarely a significant loss of game time.  I only had one white-knuckly combat in which I survived with my ship
damaged, but that combat was
fun.
I could see this game being too repetitive for some, and I do wish the ending was a little more of a big deal (I had to look up a game guide to be sure I actually
finished the game), but this was a satisfying experience and gaming time well spent.
*my escort quest cautionary tale: Every escort quest involves a boring "linked warp," when the computer takes over piloting your ship and you (the player) do
while it make boring little course corrections to move you into just the right spot before initiating warp.  I started one quest this way, then we came out of warp into an asteroid field.  The AI ship had trouble navigating the field, so I disengaged the link, then hooked it up again when I thought we were through the field.  The ships then warped again and arbitrarily stopped... turned out, we were back where we'd started.  The AI got so confused it decided to go back to the beginning in order to start over.  These quests are super time-consuming and not fun, in a game that's otherwise a freakin' blast.  So don't do 'em if you can avoid 'em.

Apothecarium is a passable HOG, though not a great one.  Like many other reviewers, I encountered the flicker issue that made the game unplayable, but was able to make it go away by playing in windowed mode.  Since windowed mode was still sufficiently large for the style of gameplay, I wasn't too upset by this.
Apothecarium has a few odd features for the genre.  Instead of taking you back to replay HO scenes multiple times, you visit each only once in the course of the story, but can then replay them (presumably with a different target list) as much as you like from the main menu.  Minigames can be similarly replayed.  Most strangely, you can opt out of an HO section (and possibly the minigames) by choosing to play a Match-3 game instead.  Also, coins and puzzle boxes are dotted around the screen.  Opening puzzle boxes gives you random boosts (such as accelerating the hint timer) or coinage, while coins, in turn, allow you to purchase powerups at the main menu for use in the Match-3 game.  Since I had no interest in the Match-3 gameplay (honestly, I bought an HO game
to hunt hidden objects, so why would I choose to play Match-3 instead?) I didn't make much use of this feature.
These oddities aside, Apothecarium hits all the usual notes of the HO genre.  It has a pseudo-historical setting, a creepy antagonist, and the standard assortment of progress barriers with bizarre artifacts serving as keys.  In a genre already rife with mediocrity and shovelware, Apothecarium doesn't manage to achieve much more than adequacy, but it
adequate, so I grant it the thumbs-up, if not entirely whole-heartedly.

This game desperately wants to be the 2015 answer to 1997's edgy kill-em-all, Postal.  It plays and looks like a direct homage, and it even directly borrows audio assets from it.  But this game is no Postal.  Thing is, I LOVED Postal when it came out.  I still do, actually.  It's mindless violence, but there's a satire to it.  I feel like maybe the creators were going for satire, and failed miserably?  I'm not sure.  It feels like the crass fantasies of basement dwelling ♥♥♥♥♥ners angry at the world for no reason.   This game was just desperate garbage.
For me, the main thing that separates Hatred from Postal is the objective.  In Postal, your goal is to kill the authority figures.  The Man, trying to keep you down.  Cops, military, etc.  They're trying to kill you, and you try to kill them.  CAN you kill innocents?  Most definitely.  As much as you like, violently.  But that's your own sickness.  The game never tells you to kill innocent people.  In Hatred, killing innocents IS THE GOAL.  The authority figures trying to kill you?  They don't matter.  They're a hindrance, an obstacle between you and murdering innocent people, nothing more.  This game just wants you to murder, and rather than feeling dark and gritty, it feels desperate, like some skinny goth teenager trying so hard to convince people he's scary and dangerous, when we all know his wardrobe came from Hot Topic when his mom dropped him off at the mall.
On a technical level, the game is fine.  Plays pretty smoothly, graphics are decent, art style is kind of cool.  It did crash on me at one point, I don't know why.   You'll want to mess with the keybindings; they're a little awkward.
But honestly, just ignore this one.  It's not worth the controversy, and not worth your time.

HOW TO SAVE YOUR SAVE GAMES AND PREVENT FUTURE LOSS OF SAVE GAMES:
While you're in-game, press the Esc or P button on your keyboard and manually save your game.
This is a little trick that is used for those who play a lot of RPGs (like Skyrim, Mass Effect and such) in order to save the progress manually before proceeding further in dungeons 'n' stuff.
There is also a quicksave button too (F8) which you can use as well.
Therefore, when a crash occurs, you have a backup save in case the auto-save is corrupted which tends to happen.
That is all :)

I remember this game. I remember begging my dad to get me a new graphics card so that I could play this game as it was one of those games which only supported video cards with shader model 3.0 and i had one with a 2.0 feature. I didn't know shader models were a thing till i learned about this game.
So after getting a new video card, an Nvidia 9600 GT at that time, the game ran on its fully glory and I was stunned. I am revieweing the remastered version of the game because I just finished playing it again recently and had my memories restored to me the same way they were 10 years back when I was a teenager :) ok so here goes-
1-Graphics- Simply great, the underwater city of Rapture is rendered beautifully with stunning water and details. They are as good as they were 10 years back. I have to say I visually didn't notice much difference between the original version and the remastered one except for a few texture improvements and better character models. But it was a nice excuse to play the game once again and explore the world. Its lifelike and looks truly like a destroyed utopia.
2-Story- I have to say this game has one of the best stories ever told in video games in 2007 and it still is. The twist is awesome and its unpredictable. The basic plot is you are Jack, a passenger on an aeroplane and your plane crashes in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean near a lighthouse. By taking shelter in the lighthouse you discover a sprawling underwater city oblivious to the rest of the world build by business magnate, Andrew Ryan, for people to be free from government control and ethics and practice their profession as they please without market restrictions. But the time you reach the city it is descented into chaos and madness and with the help of a guy named Atlas, it is your job to discover what happened to this once great city. The backstory is mostly told through audio logs and they flesh out the game characters in a great way.
3- Combat- You fight the deranged people of the city known as Splicers with a large array of weapons at your disposal. But the highlight of the game is there are plasmids which provide you with unique powerups like Electricity, Fire and Telekensis etc to take down enemies using fun and exploitative ways using your left hand. There are mini boss battles in each level in the form of Big Daddies, giant humanoid like creatures with a driller or a gun in their hands through which you can find the currency known as ADAM for purchasing plasmids and their upgrades. You can also purchase ammo,food through ingame dollar currency also. You are also given a plethora of combat, physical and engineering abilties to exploit the security system of the city and turn them against the enemy and hack safes etc to loot precious stuff. Its all done great though hacking can get a little tedious after a while.
4-Sound- Sound is great and in a lot of areas you can hear the old classic songs of the 40-50's which gives a great nostalfia feel. The sound of the guns and enemies are all well done.
5-Remastered version-The remastered version gave us a bonus feature which is a director's commentary through which you can see the behind the scenes footage of how the developers took inspiration,envisioned and finally made the game. You can unlock it by gathering golden reels on each level, though I really wish they were unlocked by default as the reels are hard to see in the environment. Though there are a lot of guides on steam to help you out with it. There is a museum area where you can see the concept art for some enemies which were left out in the game and a bonus area mode in which you are given challenges to complete through a specific way the game tells you to do. They are all linked mainly to completing the in game achievments.
Also, many people are experiencing techincal issues in running the remastered version, I hope the devs fix this. For me, I faced occassional stutters in some areas of the game however the game never crashed for me.
As a fan of the System Shock series I truly loved this game and would definitely recommend it as it laid the foundation for some the games of the future..

I’ve never liked Civ Games in the past as I always had a hard time with kluging of the historical mechanics and seeing Napoleon strutting around with Stalin etc ….
I was / am very fond of SMAX  since it did not need the kluge and had very interesting factions / environment. I thought the Units were a little lack-luster however  – even with the Workshop
Civ BE on the other hand has been a true joy:
-	No History Kluge (Alien planet)
-	Interesting City / Empire development without it becoming too Math / Puzzle-like
-	Very enjoyable units with Purity so far  (have not played as the other 2 yet)
-	Atmosphere is awesome – love the music. It’s perfect for an alien planet (I really like EL, ES and AOW III – but  Jazz or World-music for 4x …. No way ….)
-	A well built up empire with Mag rails, trade routes, various improvements is a work of art … very pleasing to the eye – sometimes I just scroll around a bit and enjoy it like a well-built model or painting …
-	Alien life is exotic and adds to the immersion – but would like to see some eventual Cult of Planet / Mind Worm style connections etc  … and some Progenitors
-	Stable – not one crash – can Alt + Tab with no issues
On the slightly negative side , the Diplomacy is lacking – no Trading of Techs, No propositions to have joint attacks on enemy cities ….
Also – The Factions themselves don’t have a great deal of flavor so with the somewhat lacking diplomacy, I just keep them under control until I can enjoy annihilating them  ….
Overall – it is one of my favorite gaming experiences at the moment and I am looking forward to a nice expansion or 2 to get into the SMAX quality range ….

To anyone reading this review I'd like to share a warning, I am extremely biased when it comes to Bioshock. I think it's one of the greatest games ever to be forged and my review will most likely share this opinion. Now that that's out of the way, let me explain why I hold this fanatical love for Bioshock. P.S. I will mention some points about the Remaster, which this review is for.
There was a point in my gaming career that I strayed away from single-player games and this remained the case for a substantial period of time. They didn't interest me, I was now hooked on online co-op or multiplayer. Left 4 Dead, World of Warcraft, Team Fortress 2, Counter-Strike: Source, Payday: The Heist, the list can go on but these games all share one thing in common. They aren't meant to be played alone. And so the trend continued until one fateful Steam Halloween Sale (<3) where Bioshock was in the spotlight. I bought it, I mean why not (my reasoning for most of my Steam sale purchases). I didn't get to actually launching it till a month or so after, but thankfully I did. Bioshock managed to do something that seemed impossible, it made me enjoy single-player games again.
Now to talk about the game itself. Bioshock accomplished something, it made an impression. A powerful impression too that sticks with me to this day. The first thing that should be mentioned, that the game is notorious for, is the atmosphere . The world of Rapture is unlike anything else: art-deco monuments, eerily playing big band, flooded rooms, abandoned corpses, in all honesty I'm struggling to find a way to describe all of it. It's just an outstanding experience to travel the harrowing halls of the abandoned would-be utopia. If the visuals don't convince you then surely the audio-diaries of the cities inhabitants will. The voice acting and character packed into each of those little reels is fantastic, I can still quote some line for line. I won't bother mentioning the story, after ten years of raving praise it should be known that Mr. Levine wrote a masterpiece.
As far as gameplay I will say that it might be hit or miss. Some people won't mind, others might find it uncomfortable. Now when I say that I mean control-wise, I doubt anyone could complain about being a crossbow weilding badass that can summon a swarm of bees at command. The hacking mini-game has had a lot of critcism over the years, but I personally never really minded it (in fact I'd dare say I like the little pipe pass time). And when it comes to the camera, I like to look at it as a nice little addition, you can use it or not so it doesn't really hurt the game in any way. As far as AI I think you'd be surprised at how well enemies are made, for example: scorching a splicer will send him reeling for water where you can hand him a toaster for a nice shock. And yes, head shots do count for something.
Now I KNOW people who are reading this are asking themselves "why didn't he post this review in the original, he's not talking about the Remaster at all!". Well, I'm too lazy to make two reviews and I did state earlier I would talk about the Remaster. Foremost, it's been made aware that the Remaster has a slight tendency to crash and lose save data. This can be a deal-breaker for some, but strangely others have noted it never being an issue for them. I can say it's happened a grand total of twice for me, and not all save data was erased, just the most recent auto-save. With that out of the way I'd like to point out other parts of the Remaster that tend to be neglected in reviews. The bonus mini-games are honestly lovely, I really did enjoy them. Anything that brings me back to Rapture can't be bad in my book. And I liked the puzzle aspect, it's a cool change of pace. The directors commentary is also a nice addition, bringing you behind the scenes and sharing some facts that you might not have previously known. And the museum is a great way to show the process that inevitably led up to the creation of the game (yam-hand is hilarious). So all in all, the Remaster isn't terrible (or at least as bad as people claim it to be).
I really wish I could delve deeper (get it) into this review. Bioshock is one of my all time favorite games and I've always had a hard time convincing myself to write a review for it simply because I CAN talk about it forever. From the story to gameplay, I could just go on. I guess in the end all I can say is whether you go with the original or Remaster just give Bioshock a chance and hopefully it'll make an impression on you the same way it did me.

Hollywood Visionary is one of my favourite entries from the Choice of Games brand. For those unfamiliar with Choice of Games, they are a series of interactive stories inspired by the old 'choose your own adventure' books. The format has been improved upon, and the presentation is both slick and intuitive.
I went into this game a fan of the brand, but not expecting to be particularly enthralled with this story or setting. I was wrong. The premise is that you have a dream movie you wish to create, and the story that follows explores whether or not you can achieve this dream, and the ups and downs you experience on your journey to this end goal. These games tend to give a nice perspective of life, but I think this one was a standout.
If you are interested, I have a video discussing Choice of Games, and some of the entries within their series.

I feel like there's no better way to review these wonderful games than to give a summary of my experience.(Spoliers ahead for the path I've chosen)
I started out with a dream film: Faithful's Belligerents; A controvercial adventure flick set in the exotic streets of Morocco. A motley crew of troubled travelers had to deal with the cutthroat culture of a demanding, crime filled, and face paced city.
Complications arose, and I had to start my production on my own and with help from my contacts. I esembled Hyphen Productions and got to work. I treated my crew well, almost too well as they slacked here and there, but we got our work done with a few pep talks at the right times. I also took the time to bond with my niece who suddenly came into my life when my long lost sister introduced me.
My directing and producing style gained ire of some, and the admiration of others. One such admiration came from my stage grip, Trudy. We talked of our personal lives and things hinted at going futher between us as time went on, but I was far too focused on bonding with my niece and perfecting my picture to care for romantics with a troubled girl like her.
More and more issues came about throughout my story; fire at the production studio, political tension between the law and communist propaganda(which I was wrapped into due to my associates), and people leaving the crew entirely.
Heading towards the end, my film was complete, the product of everything we all worked for. I saw the screening with my niece, and enjoyed it wholeheartedly. Apparently so did the critics, as my picture gained rave reviews. In the end, I was even awarded an Oscar for my production.
So in the end, this was a wonderful CYOA experience. Highly customizable, highly replayable, and very well written, even to the standards of the Choice of Games. This and Choice of Robots stands near the top for their best CYOAS.

The Vagrant introduces Vivian’s journey in Mystery Island named Mythrilia. This 2016 kickstarter project is heavily inspired from Dragon's Crown, Oboro Muramasa, and Castlevania X in term of gameplay and art direction.
The world filled by hand-drawing characters and charming environment. The variation of music is noticeable from acoustic to heavy metal. It’s very subjective taste but I found it fits very well.
The Vagrant offers simple mechanics (2D combat, exploration, character progression). The world is divided into many sub sections filled by different threats and themes. In combat, the game offers basic two-button sword action which can be expended by movement input and player position. Player can also use special skills which consume amount of rage gauge to unleash powerful attack. Each skills and combo are well designed and worth by purpose. Combined with responsive control and feedback, it creates fluid and solid action. Moreover, the boss fight design can be inconsistent in difficulty, but they’re fair challenge and fun once you figure out their patterns.
The exploration in Mythrilia offers fair rewards such as key item to learn new moves and new rage skills. Blending objects into environment keep enticing player to discover and learn world design.  All enemies and breakable object can drop gold and mana. Mana is mainly used to unlock skills and enhance gears. There are also small feature like enchant rune system that allow you to customize extra attribute for items and campfire cooking that give permanent bonus depends on choose receipt which are nice touch.
However, the game still need some improvement and tweaks during early access state. These include translation and UI accessibility for player. There’s also huge gap between some items and abilities, require huge grind which I feel like it keeps slow down on progression. Infinite spawn in some area can sometimes get frustrating in exploration. Finally, the rift area (unlock after defeat boss in each area) doesn’t offer worth payoff compared on cost you pay for rift access.
The Vagrant is still under development promised by six chapters (currently on three) and although it has major changes of design based on original project. But it’s very solid 2D action title with some interesting features that have potential. I believe that amount of feedback and right direction from developers with help to polish this gem to its best.
The Vagrant นำเสนอเรื่องราวของการผจัญภัยของวิเวียนในดินแดนแห่ง Mythrilia ภายใต้โปรเจค Kickstater ปี 2016 ที่ได้รับแรงบันดาลใจจากเกม Dragon's Crown, Oboro Muramasa, และ Castlevania X ในมุมมองของระบบการเล่นและทิศทางงานศิลป์
ดินแดนและตัวละครใน Mythrilia ถูกรังสรรค์ด้วยงานวาดมืออันน่าหลงไหล มีเสน่ห์ พร้อมด้วยเพลงประกอบอันหลากหลายตั้งแต่เพลงสไตล์อะคูสติกไปจนถึงจังหวะเฮฟวีเมทัลชวนระทึก เป็นที่น่าจดจำสำหรับบางคน
The Vagrant ดำเนินเกมภายใต้สูตรอันเรียบง่าย (ระบบต่อสู้สองมิติ, การสำรวจ, และการพัฒนาตัวละคร) แต่ละแผนที่จะประกอบไปด้วยพื้นที่เล็กๆ เชื่อมต่อกัน แต่แยกด้วยธีมและภัยอันตรายต่างชนิด ระบบการต่อสู้อาวุธดาบที่ประกอบไปด้วยการกดปุ่มแอคชั่นสองแบบ แต่สามารถสร้างคอมโบด้วยการกดทิศทางและตำแหน่งของวิเวียน พร้อมด้วยสกิลทรงพลังที่ใช้เกจเฉพาะอย่าง Rage แต่ล่ะสกิลและความสามารถออกแบบมาอย่างดีและมีประโยชน์ในทุกๆ สถาณการณ์ ร่วมกับการควบคุมที่ตอบสนองฉับไว แม่นยำ มันสร้างระบบแอคชั่นที่ลื่นไหลและหยิบยื่นความสนุกให้กับผู้เล่นทุกแนวได้ไม่ยาก แม้ว่าการออกแบบบอสจะมีความยากขึ้นลงในรูปแบบการโจมตีและความเสียหาย แต่โดยรวมเป็นความท้าทายที่สมเหตุสมผลและเรียกร้องการเรียนรู้ในระดับหนึ่ง
การสำรวจในดินแดน Mythrilia ให้ผลตอบแทนด้านไอเท็มสำหรับปลดล็อคสกิลและความสามารถใหม่ การออกแบบของงานศิลป์ที่กลืนวัตถุเข้ากับสภาพแวดล้อม เรียกร้องให้ผู้เล่นเข้าไปมีส่วนรวมและค้นหาด้วยตัวเอง เหล่ามอนสเตอร์และวัตถุที่ให้ Gold และ Mana ปัจจัยหลักในการพัฒนาความสามารถและอัพเกรดอุปกรณ์ของวิเวียน นอกจากนั้นยังมีระบบย่อยเช่น การปรับแต่งอุปกรณ์ด้วย Enchant Rune และการปรุงอาหารที่แคมป์ไฟเพื่อเลือกรับโบนัสถาวรตามชนิดของอาหารนั้นๆ
อย่างไรก็ตาม เนื่องจากตัวเกมอยู่ในขั้น Early Access ตัวเกมยังคงต้องได้รับการขัดเกลาในหลายจุด การแปลภาษา บทสนทนา และเมนูผู้ใช้งานที่ยังขาดความสะดวกสะบายเท่าที่ควร ไอเท็มบางชนิดที่ตั้งราคาสูงลิ่วจนเหมือนถูกบังคับให้ฟาร์มเม็ดเงินซ้ำแล้วซ้ำเล่า ไอเท็มชนิดเดียวกันแต่ถูกจำหน่ายต่างราคาจาก NPC บางจุดของเกมที่เรียกศัตรูออกมาไม่มีวันหมดจนสร้างความหงุดหงิดในการสำรวจ และสุดท้ายเขต Rift (พื้นที่พิเศษที่ปลดล็อคหลังปราบบอสแต่ล่ะพื้นที่) กลับไม่ได้ให้ผลรางวัลตอบแทนคุ้มค่าเท่าที่ Gold ที่เสียไป
The Vagrant อยู่ในช่วงพัฒนาโดยมีแผนสิ้นสุดถึงบทที่ 6 (ตัวเกมล่าสุดดำเนินถึงบทที่ 3) จนถึงกุมพาพันธ์ 2018 และแม้ว่าจะมีการเปลี่ยนแปลงการออกแบบในหลายๆ จุดเมื่อเทียบกับทิศทางดั่งเดิมของโปรเจคที่โฆษณาไว้ แต่สถานะปัจจุบันกลับมอบประสบการณ์การเล่นที่กระชับ เข้มข้น และเพลิดเพลินภายใต้ระบบต่างๆ ที่ดูเรียบง่ายในภายนอก หากถูกขัดเกลาจากการตอบรับของผู้เล่นและคงทิศทางของการพัฒนาไว้ The Vagrant จะไม่ต่างอะไรผลงานเกมชิ้นเลิศที่มีคุณค่าและความสนุกในตัวมันเอง

Kickstarter backer here. Writing now that it's out of early access. Well, it feels like it's still in early access to me.
As a big fan of X-Com (old and new) as well as Fallout (likewise), I figured this'd be right up my ally. And maybe it will be, once it gets another coat of polish. There's so much potential here, I'm sure it'll be great.
Man, though. That dialog. I'm sure there are people who like it. Good for them, I'm legit happy. But wow, I am not among their ranks.
(Edit; clarifying as per requests in the comments)
Reasonable! Let me go into more detail.
The dialog feels like the kind of writing you get out of 14-year old writers going for "Edgy." I have no issue with profanity, I find it can be a delightful spice for dialog. This was like eating a spoonful of raw cinnamon. I can't tell if they were going for a wacky comedy game, or a serious gritty wasteland tale. My guess is blending the two, as has been done successfuly with Wasteland, Fallout, etc.
It, in my estimation, fails absolutely on every count. It's tone is more in keeping with a YouTube video comments section than professional fiction of any stripe.
The voice acting is extremely disjointed. Not 90's Capcom Bad, insofar as I'm pretty sure these weren't cold reads by janitors, but it feels wildly disconnected; highly disjointed. At no point did I feel like these people were talking to each other.
As far as the early access, I was experiencing mouse lag on even medium settings - my compy's in the 84th percentile in horsepower & graphics, and this is hardly a graphics-intensive game. And yet.
The interface wasn't super intuitive. And okay, fine, you don't want to do a tutorial mode. Cool, that's old-school. Jagged Alliance & X-Com at least had manuals.
Overall, it's not bad. But I was really excited for the release, and now I'm more excited about uninstalling it, and reinstalling Jagged Alliance 2.
Hopefully that clears up my concerns.

Surprisingly good; quick and energetic little rounds that are always action-packed. Only annoying part is the number of reflective shields in this game and some of the heroes are a little obnoxious to play against that cause the game to be unfun. The arena formats are either 2vs2 or 3vs3, so bring a couple friends, because 3vs3 is pretty awesome.
With this type of game, there's something special about being able to just jump in and not worry about farming or setting up stuff, you plunging right in and having a blast. It's really great and quite refreshing.
The next part is going to deal directly with the business aspect, as I feel that's important for F2P games especially.
The microtransaction model is fair and everything can
be obtained in-game except certain 'limited time' chests that require premium currency. Yet to be determined if that pisses me off enough to downgrade my opinion of the game yet. Overall, doesn't seem to be that greedy, but the stench of this type of business practice isn't uncommon these days and that also means the fatigue of dealing with said model. Naturally, for a game trying to be competitive, these items and loot
. This is very important for a game wanting to be enjoyable and non-P2W; the developers realize this!
One important thing to note, is that the DLC for 'Ultimate Fan Pack' is pretty lacklustre for its price.
You have to keep that in mind when you look at the 'content' you're actually getting. I can get a full game AND all of its content for that price. I think that price needs a reality check; from what I've read about the DLC's reviews, other users agreed with my point-of-view.
Also, the premium currency value to financial expenditure doesn't feel worth it. $110 dollars is a lot of money and that gets you 10,000 (+2,000 for buying in bulk) gems. Now, these 'limited time' chests cost 1,900 in total to complete the 2-piece set. That makes this simple costume
20 dollars. I don't know, man. Seems cruel.
All-in-all, balanced and smooth. The UI is great, the heroes are varied enough to be interesting, the loadouts are interesting (although a bit basic), and the game feels like a quality game that took a lot of time to make. You can feel the quality in the sound and design, the achievements with phat rewards, quests (both daily and weekly), and level up rewards for both your account and heroes, all makes you want to keep coming back for more Battlerite.
: 7.5/10

Forewarning: I have not yet beaten this game. If you think that discredits my opinion on this title, feel free to stop reading at any point.
Anyone still here: Hatred, as most Steam users probably know, is a highly controversial isometric twin-stick shooter with a unique Sin City-inspired visual design that has garnered far more attention for its tangles with the ESRB and Steam, as well as its content, than it has for its merits as a game. So, how is it as a game?
To be fair, this isn't my normal kind of game. I don't play many twin-stick shooters, so I'm fairly new at this type of thing. I am also primarily a console gamer--I play on both Playstation and Xbox, with my laptop mainly being used for listening to music and playing Rollercoaster Tycoon. So I'm approaching this green as can be--I'm a filthy console gamer new to PC, I'm not much into twin-stick shooters, and my Steam account is brand-spanking new. Take everything I say with a grain, nay, a ♥♥♥♥ing barrel of salt.
I like it.
With a concept like the one Hatred carries around, this was always going to attract criticism, something the developers obviously knew. You play as The Antagonist, a man who hates the world and all people in it, probably including himself, and the object of most levels is to flat-out murder as many innocent civilians as possible. The effect is initially somewhat shocking, even knowing what this game is ahead of time. Following the tutorial, when The Antagonist takes his first steps out into his neighborhood and starts firing rounds, it definitely got me a bit "oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥.."
That all said though, this game isn't nearly as nefarious as people have made it out to be. It's CLEARLY tongue in cheek, unless you're deliberately fighting that aspect. The game's tutorial made me laugh out loud, instructing you on how to move around, jump over obstacles, shoot at targets and throw grenades....and then, before you leave the tutorial basement, you're instructed, in a very videogame way, to "kill your drugged captive". I snorted, it was so genius. Also adding to the tongue in cheek feel, your protagonist looks and talks like Nathan Explosion went to emo school, constantly growling lines like "And who ♥♥♥♥ing cares?" and, even better, "Only my weapons understand me."
In terms of gameplay, things are fine, if a bit standard. Weapons feel good, aiming feels good, etc. One thing Destructive Creations should have improved is doorway entry; The Antagonist definitely likes to get hung up on doors. Also, and this is a frankly unacceptable oversight, this is a largely black and white game where your target reticle is white. So it's FAR too easy to lose sight of your reticle during, say, a hectic fight with the military. Why they didn't make it red, I'm not sure, but they didn't, and it's just a silly thing that causes way more frustration than necessary.
Though I imagine most probably don't care about the story in a game like this, I feel like I should say it's fairly toss. It's basically a thin string of events to tie the levels together. That's fine, to be honest. It means we never learn much about The Antagonist, and that's really for the better, since if this guy was anything more than a charicature, it would probably become too silly.
So basically: this is a short, fun game with a brilliant art style and some minor gameplay flaws. I got it on sale for $11, and I'm satisfied with it for that price. I may not have been at $20, but I suppose it depends on your genre preferences. People need to lighten up. The developers of this game clearly knew what they were doing, and the tongue-in-cheek nature demonstrates that every step of the way. Check it out if you're into this sort of thing, or even if you just want to see what all the fuss was about.
7/10
Two side notes: If you are a fan of death metal, it would appear the developers are as well--I'm not sure of the specifics, but apparently they set up some sort of show with the band Decapitated, and if you're a metal fan, it's always worth supporting the community, so thanks to the developers there.
Also, on a downer--the game appears to be fairly poorly optimized. Granted, my laptop isn't the greatest, but this is really kind of a crapshoot. Sometimes the game runs absolutely flawlessly, other times it's borderline unplayable. This seems to have nothing to do with specific levels or activities. Just a note.

The game didn't launch for me. So I uninstalled it. I later upgraded my OSX (yes, I am on Mac) for Smite and decided, why don't give it a second try? So I reinstalled it, and launched the game again. It froze on the Titlescreen. I had to restart my PC, then it finally worked and I dove right into it...
The first thing I noticed was the music. It fits the game/theme perfectly, some sort of "Space Rock". It's the kind of music you would expect Han Solo to listen to whilest flying. The rythem is good, quality is good and the feeling is even better. I think the best thing in this game is the music (@Devs why don't publish the Soundtrack?).
My first 30mins with the game where not enjoyable. My camera was moving around like a drunk guy on a unicycle. I couldn't get ride of the feeling that mouse accelerations was on. I looked under controles, and the only option I saw was to turn down mouse sensitivity. After that it worked a bit better, was still frustrating though. I enjoyed the dialogues a lot too, the characters where what you expected, a bit clichée but still really fitting into the game. Your choices concerning responses are not amazing, but they give you a bit of choices, which added a nice little touch, which isn't useful, but I still considere well placed in the game.
And finaly, I came to the combat. Hell did it look cool, and hell did it play♥♥♥♥♥♥ After I died the first time, not knowing how to use my weapons properly, I closed the game and played something else. I was so frustrated. I later tryed again, giving the game 3 trys to convince me that the combat was fun. For me it never felt fun.
The biggest problems I encountered where the camera. The placement is awkward at best, and it can ruin everything. I sometimes couldn't even see where I shot because the camera backed down behind the ship, whilst I was aiming. And moving it back up again, well, now it goes way overbord and I ca't see the enemy ship properly.
Another aspect is the free movement in combat. You and other heavy ships are limited to a 2D combat field, whilst small fighters can fly all around you. That wouldn't be a problem, if you didn't have to fly, fight and try not to ram something at the same time.
To break it down: You will ram into things if you focuse on the combat aspect, and you will not fight well if you focuse on the flying aspect. The auto aiming of your beta canons it terrible. It locks you onto someone and you shoot. But if you have locked onto someone, you won't be able to aim at someone else. I would have liked to get a fonction where I can aim freely, and then press a button and that locks my aim onto that target I'm aiming at currently. Another problem with that auto-lockon is that your camera moves with the target. I had small fighters circleing around me, spinning my camera like crazy, making it impossible to fly properly.
My last, but not unimportant problem with combat is, that enemies fly away. But you are in free space, so they can fly where they want. So you have to concentrate on fighting them, and following them around, which to me, somebody uncapable of multitasking is too much of a challenge.
To summe it up, I really liked the music, fantastic. The dialogue is not really useful, but a nice touch. However, the combat system ruined it for me, to such an extend that I don't feel the need to continue. I know I didn't even play 3hs, but the combat is so frustrating to me, that I will probably not continue, as I play for fun, not to be more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off after then before (and yes, I'm not one of those oldschool elitsts that have to play every game for the challenge, I play them for fun).
So do I recommend this game. No, not really. I do recomment the soundtrack. And if you can multitask, otherwise, stay away. But who am I kidding, I'm a stranger on the internet, that hasn't even finished the game.
If you can, and have a friend who has the game, try it, see if it's for you, and then buy. For me this game was really disappointing, not because it's beyond bad, just because I came in with expectations that where not reached.

You know if you push past all the controvery and mixed to negative press surrounding Hatred and actually give the game a try you'll find one thing.
The game is really boring. In the short (but felt longer than they actually were) 2 hours I've played this game, I promptly became bored out of my skull. To be honest Im genuinely surprised that this game retains a mostly positive reception on Steam and not maybe a more mixed reception, since the game lacks any real substance whatsoever.
The story is non-existent, there's no motivation for anything to be happening in this game. You take on the roll of a sociopath who hates everyone and wants to commit mass genocide because... reasons.
Your character, who its made explicitly clear has a name which is unimportant, and is simply given the stupid title of "The Antagonost" has no character. He just kinda seems like a stereotypocal sociopath most people think off when they hear the word: A man who acts out aggresively without motivation for anything he does.
And the gameplay itself is as bland as the previous two elements. Unlike most games which feature a nice mix or fusion of different elements to create one pleasent, concise and cohesive experience, this game features two elements cobbled together into one crappy experience.
The Shooting: Its repetitive and boring. You run around and gun people down endlessly. For pretty much the entire game. (I imagine. I don't actually know. I didn't finish it because I didn't care enough to do so.)
The driving: You'll probably just end up crashing alot because driving in this games seems near impossible.
The AI is also crap. Standard NPC's charge around aimlessly like idiots until they either get off screen or get shot dead by you. Police meanwhile just kinda charge onto the scene in their cars, get out and then start shooting at you until you're either dead, running away, or you gun them down. Take your pick.
One last issue that needs mentioning is also the absurdly long load times between levels. Why do they take so long? This game is incredibly basic, it not should take so long to load the levels.
The only real positive points I can commend this game on are:
-The decent enough graphics.
-The destructable enviroments.
-The funny reviews.
Other than that, I can't give this game much praise for anything. Its a bland experience with no story, characters to get invested in with an annoying art direction that makes discerning things near impossible in some areas and losing track of the Antagonist easy, all on top of a boring twin stick shooter that has nothing really going for it beyond controversy and a bad run in with the press.
I honestly think this games existence and the highly controverisla nature around it was not just a means of selling copies of this game in particular, but rather purely as a means of Destructive Creations as an indie studio, who Im pretty sure were a no name company before this, to get their name out there. They certainly seemed to play the journalist industry to market this game itself, so I wouldn't be surprised if this was also a move to actually get them as devs name out in the open. They certainly didn't seem concerned with actually creating a fun experience.
Don't buy this game folks. Even if it goes on sale its not really worth it.
You'll probably just be bored througout the entire experience.
TL;DR:
Its a bland twin stick shooter that only sold copies because the developers played the news industry for a mass amount of free press. It lacks any sort of character, focus or story that could give meaning to why you're doing anything, and Im certain it was just made for the sake of getting the devs themselves noticed, not because they actually gave a toss about making a decent game.

Rebel Galaxy has just enough of the flair of the Firefly universe to make you smell the dust and leather of a brown coat in the distance while still being a unique and enjoyable contribution. Here's some Pros and Cons if you need them:
PROS:
Flexibility of playstyle - You need not be the good guy; you won't miss out on story events. (Major events happen at neutral locations, very likely an intentional decision.)
Flexibility of play method - I think it'd be a bit dull to make a life of it, but if you wanted to, you could mine and haul your way to a mighty endgame vessel, rather than doing it on the backs and blood of your foes.
Graphics - This isn't CCP's space-baby, but it's not a 1980s video game, either.
Flavor - Unique world and reasonably unique aliens.
MEH:
Story Writing - It's not bad, don't get me wrong, but shocking and unusual it was not.
Balance - If you take the time to get the very last ship in the game and outfit it properly, the last encounter is a silly joke. We could've used a little dynamic scaling here; the final encounters required no assistance at all, but I still got it.
No Planned DLC/Expansions - I can't put this in "CONS" because it's a choice the devs made and that's their right; the title's short, though, and there's plenty of room for further improvement here. Really guys? You made a super popular, semi-short title with lots of room to grow, that people WANT to give you more money for, and you won't expand on it? Well. Okay, you're the designer. Meh.
CONS:
Game Length - If you beelined it through the game, I'd guess you could finish the main storyline in 10-12 hours. That's very short for a release, but on the other hand, it's not an expensive game.
Gimmicks - There are a few gimmick strategies you can employ (not spoiling them here) that are definitely not exploits or bugs, but allow you to punch WAY outside of your weight class. (When you're smashing dreadnoughts with a frigate, that's a bit much.)

This little gem has got to be one of the best games I've played in a long time, hands down. Considering its been made by just two people, this game is worth 20 dollars. Heck, it's worth 40. The game throws you in to the rear end of the galaxy. Lawless land, pirates all around. Your objective? Find your Aunt Juno. How do you do that? Entirely up to you. You can become a do-gooder and side with the militia, or find your inner Captain Jack Sparrow and join the pirates. Or you can do a little of both and become a mercenary, working for whoever is willing to foot your bill. You can even become a trader, or a miner. As long as you're making credits. Work your way up from a lowly Corvette all the way up to massive Dreadnaughts. Or don't. It's up to you. Maybe you prefer your ships quick and nimble.
What I liked:
-Solid story. While it's not Oscar worthy, the story is engaging, and you won't be wishing you could do anything else while doing it. The voice acting is good, the objectives are fun, and it has a pretty decent length. It took me about 20 hours to complete the story, and I probably rushed things a little too much. I've heard of some players not even leaving the starting system for over 10 hours.
-Plenty of distractions, done right. Unlike games like Fallout 4, this game does repeating side missions right. They're pretty much essential for you to be able to afford the gear you'll need for the story missions, but they never really feel old. You pick up missions at stations, fly to the area, and when you're done, you've made some cred, a few friends, and maybe a few enemies too. Each mission rewards not only cold hard cash, but reputation with the main factions. Getting in good with some factions is important, as you gain access to ships that otherwise would be locked if they don't have an opinion of you, or just plain don't like you. And with two joinable guilds, plus citizens, militia, and pirates to potentially help, you'll never be wanting for variety.
-Progression, on your terms. The game doesn't force you to move to a new sector, or buy a bigger ship. If you want to upgrade, it's up to you to decide when. I went through most of the game in the Tennhausen and Sturville frigates, only bumping up to a Vanguard heavy frigate, which is my current ship and easily my favorite, at the last mission because I needed the extra firepower and survivability. There's a certain sense of joy that comes from taking out a ship five times your weight class and twenty times your cost.
-There's 21 ships. That's a lot of ships. A lot of them are also very expensive, so the biggest, baddest ships likely won't be even remotely available to you until after you've beaten the main story, unless you enjoy grinding side missions just so you can roflstomp everything in a 17 million credit Blackstar Dreadnaught and the millions of credits it takes to equip one properly.
-A living world. The world isn't just static targets for you to shoot. You'll come across traders under attack by pirates, bands of pirates roaming the black. Trade prices change regularly, and you need to dock regularly to keep up with the latest news on the market. Prices also change by station, and can be effected by different statuses, some of which you can even influence, if you're particualrly dastardly. See a trade convoy coming in to a station carrying expensive stuff? Blow it up, take it, and cause a sudden rise in demand for what that convoy was carrying at their destination. But be careful. Folks don't take too kindly to piracy. And, if you overtrade one good, or set of goods, a trade route can very easily dry up.
-Random generation. Each system is different every time you start a new game. New planets, new stations, new fun.
However, for as great as the game is, it has a few minor downsides, though neither effected my enjoyment of the game very much.
-No co-op, or multiplayer. Now, while the dev team has perfectly good reasons for this, the lack of a co-op function in the game limits its replayability somewhat. This is the perfect game for fans of old games like Freelancer, and the ability to play with a pal would make it so much better.
-Difficulty. It's erratic. When you first enter a new system, you'll find yourself occasionally running into ships that will utterly annihilate you, no matter how big your hull is. But once you start upgrading and reach the maximum for the tech level being sold in the area, you'll find yourself melting the meanest ships in the sector to slag for little to no return damage. If you're smart enough, and well armed enough, you'll rarely be paying repair costs. Using my three main ships, I died three times and came close to death perhaps another three times. That said, the game still feels challenging and fun, and enemies by and large scale with you, so most of the time you won't be utterly steam rolling the opposition as if they didn't exist.
Overall verdict:
-Why are you still here? Buy the game already! If you're even remotely a fan of space games, you'll love this. While the combat system is a little different from the usual 3D environment space games give us to play in, there's nothing more satisfying than giving a pirate dreadnaught a nice neutron laser broadside, and the variety of ships, solid mechanics, good story, and living surroundings will give you plenty to do.

One of the most fun real-time strategy games I've ever played.  Fans of the genre are missing out if they've never played SoSE.  There are a lot of space-based strategy games out there, but this one is the cream of the crop.
Gameplay:  9/10  You begin most games with a single homeworld, with the bare minimum upgrades/structures and a handful of resources.  You must expand to other planets, asteroids, moons, etc. by building different types of ships that can travel between worlds.  Once you capture a planet, you can upgrade it and build structures in orbit that allow you to do things like build more ships, establish trade routes between your planets, spread culture to other empires, etc.  You can also build defensive structures to protect your planets in case your fleets of ships are occupied.  The maps can be small, with only two empires and a handful of planets, to absolutely massive with hundreds of planets orbiting different stars.  Throughout each game you research new technologies that help you achieve you goals.  There are three races to play as, each with a loyalist and rebel faction that have different ships, upgrades, technologies, etc.  The only thing I wish this game had was a campaign for each of the three different races you can play as.
Graphics:  7/10  You'd think that a space strategy game wouldn't have great graphics, but this game has a surprising amount of detail.  You can zoom in on any ship, structure, or planet to see it up close.  You can rotate the camera freely to capture some awesome screenshots.  The only drawback is that a lot of the planets look the same and don't have discernable cities, landmarks, etc.
Once you get the hang of this game, you will likely spend hundreds of hours playing it, similar to other strategy games like Civilization.  Each new game you start presents new challenges, unike most other strategy games that become monotonous over time.  Definetley worth a try for fans of the strategy genre.

First off, don't buy RCT3, buy this instead. It is far superior.
I've been playing this game since i was about 5, [no not on steam lol] and I finally decided to grab it this summer sale after losing my disc a while ago.
I can't reccomend this game enough. It brings a happiness that nothing else can ever compete with. The premise of RCT2 is you pretty much just build god damn awesome parks, occasionally adgering to the objective. RRCT2 can be played in two ways. Follow what you're supposed to do regading the objective. Pretty simple play, but still incredibly fun. Other is to build your own absolutely insane park with the scenario editor and treat it as a sandbox, doing whatever you please treating you 'peeps' as vessels of your torture. [I preffer the latter]
There really is very few things wrong with the game. I'll name a few.
- AI can be a bit troublesome, but when you've got a couple thousand of them, It's bound to happen. The mechanics/cleaners are really the only ones with issues tbh. Can be rectified without too much effort.
- Isometric can make the game a bit difficult to see a few things, but hey, just god damn rotate the camera.
- Terrain is a bit 'ech', but defiantly better than RCT3. An issue is that you can't use the 'mountain/hill' tool outside of the scenario editor. Kinda takes a long time to make a mountain
Those aren't major my any scale. This game is liteally god tier. Seriously buy it if you're in any way creative. I've fallen in love with it.
Keep in mind that if you're buying this to complete scenarios, imo RCT1 scenarios are much better. RCT2 Scenarios seem somewhat soul-less. Sandbox is way better in RCT2 tho.

Civ Beyond Earth or Civ VI as I guess you could call it... what can I say about this game that people haven't said or thought about already? Well... to be honest, I rather enjoy this game and maybe, just maybe. Not for the reasons you the reader think I enjoy this game for... or at least possibly some other reasons which you didn't expect or believe.
Let's get the biggest issue out the way first, the Faction Leaders, no matter which way you look at them or analyse them, they will never hold the weight of the previous games historical leader. That was part of the charm of Civ V, you could have Nobunaga Oda, the demon king of Japan go up against Alexander the Great in an epic war. Part of the charm of Civ V was that you could create this entire parallel world where these leaders are all alive round the same time and at each others throats, that was part of what made Civ V great.
The Leaders in Beyond Earth will never be able to compete with that, they won't. So don't expect them too, Beyond Earth in my opinion was an experiment, using a new idea and a new setting that is completely different from Civ V.
That being said, I do agree that the new Factions are a little bit in-balanced, especially when analysed together. I do like how the cultures and the peoples of Earth have banded together in the future to create these new... almost Mega-Cultures I guess you could say that which to gain control of this new planet... planets depending on which map you pick.
One thing I will say about the Factions and the Leaders, is while they will never live up to the weight of the historical leaders of the past, I do believe they hold potential. Here is how I look at Civ Beyond Earth compared to Civ V. I look at Beyond Earth as Civ V was before Gods & Kings and Brave New World. That is how I look at Beyond Earth, I see it as a diamond in the rough that has a massive amount of potential and I pray, I really do pray that Firaxis follow through with this potential and continue to polish Beyond Earth because, it truly does hold a massive amount of potential I would be devastated to see wasted.
As a lover of the Civ franchise I read, watched and basically hunted with purpose, everything I could about Beyond Earth before I purchased it only 2 days ago. I currently as of this review have 25 hours logged on Steam playing Beyond Earth compared to my 239 hours logged for Civ V.
So, you could claim that this review isn't valid if you don't believe I have spent enough time playing the game to give a fair opinion and review, fair enough but I am giving it anyway. Recently I saw one of my favourite YouTubers give a review on the game, AngryJoe. He said and I quote "Beyond Earth feels like an incredible opportunity wasted." I do not agree with that, I agree the game doesn't live up to the expectations that were presented for it then again, we are talking about a Civ game, possibly the best strategy game franchise ever, in my opinion. I don't know, maybe Total War is better I have yet to play a Total War game but I plan on getting Shogun 2 which seems to be the best choice.
Back to the point, I do not believe the game is an opportunity wasted, I believe it is a diamond in the rough that with the proper care and love and grow to become something close to Civ V, I doubt it will ever beat Civ V mostly due to the weight the historical leaders brought, but it has a fighting chance of being close. However, you must remember, Civ V has G&K and BNW whereas Beyond Earth has nothing so far, which, is why I look at the current state of Beyond Earth as of the post date of this review as Civ V was before G&K and BNW enhanced the experience and made it something truly amazing.
I feel I have ranted on a little more than I should of about the comparison between this game and it's older brother Civ V but it was a point I felt I had to explain my own opinion for.
Let's move on before this review goes on for longer than it should. I've heard Rythian of the Yogscast another of my favourite YouTubers talk about the graphics of the game, how they look dirty and muddy. Honestly, I cannot tell as I haven't played the game on High or higher graphics, I play on Medium level as I use my laptop and the game runs perfectly so I may try a higher setting so I can look at it in full detail and have a better opinion. However, I agree and disagree with the comments they made, about the graphics.
I agree they do look dirty and muddy, they definitely have a darker colour palate for some terrains and a brighter one for others. These are enhanced through Mods which are easily integrated with the game through the Steam Workshop and if you play with the Distinctive Terrains mods, you will see more detailed terrains so I do recommend playing with those Mods just for the visual effect.
As for the graphics for the units and the cities, I honestly am not too sure. I feel they suit the purpose enough, they suit their purpose enough. I don't know, maybe as polish is added to the game as I believe it will, this is Firaxis we are talking about, as more polish is added to the game they may upgrade the textures to make them more pleasing or eye catching but for the most part they are descent enough.
Hmm... what else is there for me to talk about... I seemed to have focused a lot on what other people were saying about the game and what I believed so I am a little stick... bear with me a moment here. Okay, the Aliens, something you will be seeing a lot in Beyond Earth.
Personally, I believe these Aliens are done well and they are impressive to look at, especially some of the unique Harmony units like the Rocktopus and the Xeno Titan. However, the only game in which I got the Rocktopus it seemed to be bugged and wasn't able to move to the orbital level, whether I was doing it wrong and it needs something to latch onto I don't know but while I wasn't able to make full use of the Rocktopus, it is impressive to look at, as with the Xeno Titan which... as it's name suggests is like a Titan.
Talking of bugs, I have encountered a few but like I said, I do consider Beyond Earth is the state it is currently as of the post date of this review, do be a diamond in the rough so I can excuse these bugs because they don't really take away from the overall enjoyment I get from the game, other people might disagree.
The unit models when getting to a level three upgrade for the Soldier, seem to stay around when upgrading a different unit, meaning you'll have two conflicting unit models when upgrading but it does seem to go away or you just stop noticing it.
Oh! One thing I will say annoys the hell out of me, is that bloody ADVISR, I'll admit, it is nice to actually have a voice giving you advice and offering you guidance but for the love of all that is sacred in creation, turn it off the moment you can because it will constantly tell you about trades and pointless advise that you've already been told. That is a problem I have with the game but you can turn it off fairly easily so at least it can resolved that way but, I do believe they should patch it so the ADVISR doesn't keep annoying gamers with constant reminders on Trade.
Also, the new Tech-Web instead of the traditional Tech-Tree as we are used to, I think is a nice addition and it does add to the atmosphere of the game, you get this sense of, what the hell am I to research which, you will. It is confusing as hell when you first see it but you get the hang of it quickly if you take your time to learn it.
Another thing I will say, the Tech-Web incorporates the affinity system into it well, you can research techs that will give you affinity in either Harmony, Purity or Supremacy which basically means Aliens, Humans and Robots.
The Tech-Web while designed like a confusing web, actually has some tree like traits, each main Tech on the web is known as a branch and within each branch there is usually one or more additional specialist techs known as leafs, and it is usually these leaf
Still a great tool to learn the basics of MTG. It updates with every set and gives you insight into the lore.

This War of Mine is a game in which your goal is to manage a group of civilians in their attempt to survive while trapped inside a city near a warzone.
The game is 3D but characters move around on a 2D axis.
This War of Mine is played primarily using the mouse.  You click to select which character you want to control and simply left click the location you want your character to move to.
Buttons appear on objects in the environment when you can interact with them.  Typical actions include things like searching, hiding, climbing, lockpicking or prying things open and so on.
Weapons can be selected using the mouse as well.  While a weapon is drawn, contextual buttons will appear in the environment allowing you to take cover behind walls and tables and other things.
You play one day at a time.
There's a day phase where your civilians are in their shelter and your task is to take care of their needs and build things.
At night you can choose to select one of your civilians to go scavenge.
Acquire materials / food / weapons through whatever means you can.  Barter, loot, scavenge, steal, take by force.  Aid other people, take from them or even murder them.  The game does little to restrict your actions, but be prepared to face big consequences depending on what you do.....
If you're bored, have plenty of time to spare and don't mind the slightly sluggish pacing,  I definitely recommend this game.
