At Bomb Squad Academy, learn how to defuse bombs as you go level by level. Your instructor being very positive and eager to teach you the works of all the different concepts separated by eight different chapters. You'll be graduating in no time.
With the goal for players to understand how to defuse bombs, at least in-game, is very important that you nail a tutorial or that it can be understood by most of the players. Sometimes this will come before and hope that it can be remembered throughout the game or be optional if the player does not want to play or read through it. Bomb Squad Academy takes a different approach. The first thing you do in a chapter is tutorial levels in a school like way. This works well with how it was tackled. You are immediately introduced to this happy teacher showing you the ropes. Each on a tutorial circuit board, you are able to click, turn, or cut with no way to fail as it is not attached to a bomb. It doesn't try Backing off at the right time so you can prove that you learned that certain concept. I never thought there was too much tutorial bombs in a row and understood everything after. There was one that I did have to go back and redo, but it was due to a simple misunderstanding of a component.
As you pass the tutorials, the real thing is presented to you. Each level starts with the cheery teacher encouraging you before the bomb is revealed. The music changes to a tense theme as you try to complete a bomb before the timer goes out. All you have to do is either take away the power, or deactivate it by lighting up the disarming areas. The ticking of the timer staying in the back of your mind as you constantly look over as you try to deactivate it. Having to look over where the power will go and directing it's path with switches and dials. This is of course complicated by other components to trick you up such as wires directing power to other areas or AND and OR gates standing in your way. As each bomb uses logic and each board is constructed carefully, it does not seem like it was unfair. Pushing and cutting at random is not the way to go, especially when dealing with the be complicated ones.
You are mostly left alone with these bombs with the occasional notes to offer subtle hints such as "Closed Loop" or to give some humor. Let the timer go out and you are dead. Redirect the power to the detonate area and you are dead. There is not any consequences as you do get to start over, but there is a loud bang and a white light to symbolize an explosion. Your instructor also steps in with a dark but witty sayings after, "Too bad, you killed yourself, and everyone", bring the teaching setting further. The upside is that you do get a chance to see how you messed it up. Letting you not make the mistake again and plan for what you will do next.
What is interesting is how there are multiple designs for bombs. Simple ones looks like it's on a wrapped and duct tapped item while others have more of a outwards appearance of cylinders being together. Whether it be two, a few stuck together, or what suspiciously looks like a dynamite bomb. As the game acts like it is a school, it is cool to see that it brings in different designs to prepare the student to see when they do a real bomb.
The game will generally take at least over an hour to complete as it is easy most of the time. But the developer has said there are more things to come. More components are being thought up to put into the game. A circuit board editor is going to be worked on. Letting the players make workshop bombs and letting the developer make more boards faster. A random generator is also being thought up and trying to see if the feeling of a carefully constructed game can stay true. This is very encouraging to see how the developer wants to try and tackle hard goals and gives a lot of potential to Bomb Squad Academy.
+ Great way to show players how each component works with separating tutorials
+ The school vibe is handled well and persists throughout
+ The logic behind each is understandable to the player no matter how hard
- Can be too short for some to consider
Bomb Squad Academy is about defusing bombs by going through a logic puzzle. The way it keeps this learning area is great and works well in teaching the player. Giving a sense of urgency as each bomb has a timer ticking down as you try to deactivate it. However as the content can be finished in one to two hours, this can turn people away despite how polished and great this game is. There is a lot of potential for more content to be added to an already great game. It may even teach you something about electronics no matter how simplified it presents this. You can download the

Betrayer is an odd game to say the least. You play a shipwrecked character who has to search a strange island for clues while also dealing with deadly soldiers who appear to under some magical influence to attack you. The black and white surroundings with the occasional red to signify enemies and importatn opbjects is both a helpful tool and a very unique art choice.
The game can be fun to play in short bursts, however it is not a game I feel is good for playing in long periods, as you will die repeatedly if you aren't careful.As there are many ways to face different challenges. You can attack your enemies head on with a small variety of weapons and hope for the best, or you can sneak around and take your foes by surprise. The choice is yours
Pros
+Color Palette is dull but sparks interest
+Easy to get into
+Interesting mystery
+Good controls
+Can run on less powerful computers
+Alternative ways to approach situations
+Situations can really startle you at times (Whether this is a pro or con depends on you the reader)
Cons
-Very few weapon options
-The color palette, while interesting, can sometimes make it difficult to to spot things which should grab your attention, like enemies or pick ups
-Can get frustrating or boring if you aren't used to drawn out games
-AI at times can be either very stupid, or extremely sharp as they can sometimes spot you from across the map
Overall for the price, this game can provide you with a lot of fun, and can even provide you with a few scares. However there are a few things which hold it back from being an amazing game. As it is somewhat difficult to remain invested with the story. If you're still a bit cautios, then I'd suggest waiting for a sale.

Live the life of a film producer!  Complete with the option of being completely incompetent at producing films, or to be incompetent at something else yet insistent on being involved anyways.  Scrimp, save, and release a terrible movie, or blow your budget and make a terrible movie anyways!  Mind you, I'm exaggerating the difficulty here.  There's some replay value to be had in seeing how perfect a movie one can make, but producing a really terrible movie seems to require actively sabotaging your own run.
Much of the value of Hollywood Visionary comes from the imagination of the player.  The player extensively customizes what kind of movie they're making, and the author relieves the burden of representing all the ramifications of this choice by writing around the events of the movie.  (There's a recurrent "how the movie is progressing based on all your stats" screen that is seen several times per playthrough.)  I think it works.  The Auteur achievement is a great example of the spurs that the game can give to the imagination in spite of its sparse representation of the process.  Gained for producing a film in which the player is also the Writer, Director, and Starring Actor, this very difficult platespinning act is easily imagined as a parody of Hollywood narcissism.  There is as well an inexhaustible reservoir of imagination to be tapped in the movie customization options.  If you've ever wanted to envision a particular kind of movie sweeping the box office, play Hollywood Visionary and try to realize that vision in perfection.
As for the story around the production, it weaves a very interesting tale of the main character's social life in a stressful time.  It seems impossible to balance it in a way that keeps everyone involved happy, but the achievements I haven't got yet hint that there are still secrets hiding from me in the twists and turns of the game's story.  For one thing, I've only been able to ignore the kid partway, which has kept me from seeing all the content in the other relationships.  I adored her from the word go, because I know what it's like to have terrible parents. but my attachment was really sealed when I saw "Myna" in the list of names suggested for her.  She's a bright-minded chatterbox.  It was perfect.
On a less impressive side, there's also the occasionally heavy-handed portrayal of the Red Scare era of Hollywood.  The author offers a few bones to a player who wants to avoid the hypocrisy of bourgouis communism that has so often held sway in Hollywood's culture, but even if the player takes up such a character the author never delves into the mindset that would motivate opposition to communism.  The sympathies of the writer seem quite averse to exploring that perspective; communist agitation is simply treated as automatically more principled than communist opposition.
Still, in today's present era of liberal intolerance, the story serves as a timely reminder that we must respect tolerance as a principle and an ideal if we are to protect liberty.  The prior era of conservative intolerance is no long-forgotten remnant, but a reality that people suffered under as recently as twenty years ago.  At its apex in decades still farther back conservative intolerance promoted speech codes that strangled the creativity of America's artists.  Threats against free speech are not solely the province of the right or the left, but rather they come from authoritarianism and hateful partisanship, failings which must be guarded against no matter which side is being tempted into it.  People like Creed who insist that all opposition to them arises from evil are a real world hazard that principled idealists of every creed must be alert to defend against.
For the quality of its writing and the inclusion of appealing simulation elements, I consider Hollywood Visionary one of the finest entries in the Choice of Games catalogue.  It deserves a place in the collection of every Choice of Games fan.

Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Fallen: A2P Protocol.
From the captivating design of the maps, to every small detail, Fallen: A2P Protocol has the looks of an amazing game.
Following a story mode, it’s up to the player to choose the right moves, as well as the right weapon for the job, which can be a katana, a stop sign, an SMG, or even a sniper rifle.
The game also allows the player to choose which mission should be next, using a map and a vehicle, a caravan, to be more accurate. Since resourcers are scarce, driving around indefinitely is not an option, as there’s a sort of fuel resource limit. It’s also on the caravan that the player gets to use the hard earned experience to improve the unit’s skills, and even to gear them up, among other options.
If you’re looking for a good turn-based game, with an apocalyptic setting to it, and a bright future ahead of it, look no further.

YES it is black and white game with hints of red to identify important items. If you don't like b&w YES you can change it to colour (if you really want to). Although I'm not intirely sure why the developers portrayed it as a black and white game. Personally, I found the black and white very straining on my eyes and had to switch to colour.
So you play a person who ends up in old North America and investigates suspicious things. Talk to ghosts. Find out their history. Stealthily kill demons/zombies/evil spirits. In the end, figure out why the lands are so corrupted. There are so many NPCs it was a bit difficult to keep track. Luckily (perhaps), the game does the thinking for you. So there is really no need to use your brain at all. The game does all the investigating for you. yay.
The weapons are all range weapons. short bow, long bow, crossbow, pistol, musket. Throwable: tomahawk and explosives.
The short and long bow were the quickest to use. Since this story takes place in old North America, you will find yourself cursing your crossbow, pistol and muskets reloading time. You can melee an enemy, but even up close the enemies are quite deadly. I personally relied on my long bow (for walking long distances and sniping enemies) and my crossbow, pistol and musket for everything else. You can only have 3 weapons equipped at a time. Throwables are always equipped.
So there actually IS a story. You just need to read your way through it. (No voice acting at all.)
Regarding the stealth... well, for the most part you can sneak around, but some of the creatures are super sensitive and they will catch you, resulting in a fight. Fortunately, you can recover almost all your arrows. (I found the arrow and bolt weapons invaluable for stealth.) By the time I was half way through the maps, I got the hang of stealth and snipering every bloody creature I could find. It was satisfying.
The environtment had an Elder Scrolls kind of feel to it. Which was nice.
The game is pretty much the same thing over and over in each map, so it is a tad redundant.
As for the end... it is open to interpretation.
Personally, I enjoyed the game. At times it was challenging. Other times, it was just a lot of running around the maps.
There were a couple jump scares. Don't expect huge battles. I do recommend it. Just don't expect mindblowing.

This little gem has got to be one of the best games I've played in a long time, hands down. Considering its been made by just two people, this game is worth 20 dollars. Heck, it's worth 40. The game throws you in to the rear end of the galaxy. Lawless land, pirates all around. Your objective? Find your Aunt Juno. How do you do that? Entirely up to you. You can become a do-gooder and side with the militia, or find your inner Captain Jack Sparrow and join the pirates. Or you can do a little of both and become a mercenary, working for whoever is willing to foot your bill. You can even become a trader, or a miner. As long as you're making credits. Work your way up from a lowly Corvette all the way up to massive Dreadnaughts. Or don't. It's up to you. Maybe you prefer your ships quick and nimble.
What I liked:
-Solid story. While it's not Oscar worthy, the story is engaging, and you won't be wishing you could do anything else while doing it. The voice acting is good, the objectives are fun, and it has a pretty decent length. It took me about 20 hours to complete the story, and I probably rushed things a little too much. I've heard of some players not even leaving the starting system for over 10 hours.
-Plenty of distractions, done right. Unlike games like Fallout 4, this game does repeating side missions right. They're pretty much essential for you to be able to afford the gear you'll need for the story missions, but they never really feel old. You pick up missions at stations, fly to the area, and when you're done, you've made some cred, a few friends, and maybe a few enemies too. Each mission rewards not only cold hard cash, but reputation with the main factions. Getting in good with some factions is important, as you gain access to ships that otherwise would be locked if they don't have an opinion of you, or just plain don't like you. And with two joinable guilds, plus citizens, militia, and pirates to potentially help, you'll never be wanting for variety.
-Progression, on your terms. The game doesn't force you to move to a new sector, or buy a bigger ship. If you want to upgrade, it's up to you to decide when. I went through most of the game in the Tennhausen and Sturville frigates, only bumping up to a Vanguard heavy frigate, which is my current ship and easily my favorite, at the last mission because I needed the extra firepower and survivability. There's a certain sense of joy that comes from taking out a ship five times your weight class and twenty times your cost.
-There's 21 ships. That's a lot of ships. A lot of them are also very expensive, so the biggest, baddest ships likely won't be even remotely available to you until after you've beaten the main story, unless you enjoy grinding side missions just so you can roflstomp everything in a 17 million credit Blackstar Dreadnaught and the millions of credits it takes to equip one properly.
-A living world. The world isn't just static targets for you to shoot. You'll come across traders under attack by pirates, bands of pirates roaming the black. Trade prices change regularly, and you need to dock regularly to keep up with the latest news on the market. Prices also change by station, and can be effected by different statuses, some of which you can even influence, if you're particualrly dastardly. See a trade convoy coming in to a station carrying expensive stuff? Blow it up, take it, and cause a sudden rise in demand for what that convoy was carrying at their destination. But be careful. Folks don't take too kindly to piracy. And, if you overtrade one good, or set of goods, a trade route can very easily dry up.
-Random generation. Each system is different every time you start a new game. New planets, new stations, new fun.
However, for as great as the game is, it has a few minor downsides, though neither effected my enjoyment of the game very much.
-No co-op, or multiplayer. Now, while the dev team has perfectly good reasons for this, the lack of a co-op function in the game limits its replayability somewhat. This is the perfect game for fans of old games like Freelancer, and the ability to play with a pal would make it so much better.
-Difficulty. It's erratic. When you first enter a new system, you'll find yourself occasionally running into ships that will utterly annihilate you, no matter how big your hull is. But once you start upgrading and reach the maximum for the tech level being sold in the area, you'll find yourself melting the meanest ships in the sector to slag for little to no return damage. If you're smart enough, and well armed enough, you'll rarely be paying repair costs. Using my three main ships, I died three times and came close to death perhaps another three times. That said, the game still feels challenging and fun, and enemies by and large scale with you, so most of the time you won't be utterly steam rolling the opposition as if they didn't exist.
Overall verdict:
-Why are you still here? Buy the game already! If you're even remotely a fan of space games, you'll love this. While the combat system is a little different from the usual 3D environment space games give us to play in, there's nothing more satisfying than giving a pirate dreadnaught a nice neutron laser broadside, and the variety of ships, solid mechanics, good story, and living surroundings will give you plenty to do.

The idea of larger ships not having access to any better shields than a small ship just feels wrong. Obviously the bigger ships have larger power cores capable of powering larger weapon batteries; it would stand to reason these ships would be able to field a shield drastically larger than a tiny ship.
One feature i particularly liked about this game was the ability to swap gear. There is no penalty for swapping turrets/guns/components or even ships. Want to play around with different turret types and see how they feel? Go for it, theres no crippling penalty if you HATE what you switched to. I favored beam weapons for the reliability of damage, but YMMV. There is an advantage to a larger chassis in that you get more broadside guns and turret mounts, but is it worth the maneuvarability penalty you pay? Broadside batteries are a 1shot purchase, you dont have to purchase more of them as your ships get bigger. Turrets however, must be purchased individually, so that larger ship wont be any better unless you can put some decent guns on it. A huge ship with tier1 turrets is a ♥♥♥♥ing joke. Will that bigger ship be any better if you have to downgrade your turrets significantly in order to fill its hardpoints? These are management questions that i love dealing with and the middle of this game was full of them. Endgame was less so, but thats kinda to be expected that once you can fill a dreadnought class ship with top tier guns you ought to be able to melt fleets of opponents.

This game likes to stretch itself out. Normally i don't mind a game that takes me a long time to complete. I like feeling as if i got my money's worth. Good games (like Witcher 3) do this by giving you hours upon hours of enjoyable content and interesting plot. Rebel Galaxy stretches itself out by creating a vast emptiness between everypoint and making your speed very very slow. I get it, it's space, there is supposed to be an emptiness, vast distances between places. So what's the point of giving me a warp drive (one that no matter how much you upgrade still seems slow as hell) if it's still going to take me two minutes to reach anywhere i want to go, and that's only if i'm lucky enough to not get stopped by a group of pirates or an asteroid field.
I've spent 17 hours playing this game, the majority of it was spent in transit. All the tension this game gave me was not from space battles or plot development, but instead the worry of wether or not i would reach the next objective anytime soon.
If you want to pretend to be a space trucker hauling cargo for days on end, just to afford better gear to slowly move the story forward. then this game is for you.
If you're looking for fun, and excitement, look elsewhere.

I think its value for money and has improved (on the whole) from the previous iteration. That said some of the previous game modes and ideas have been dropped, which is a shame.
A couple of ideas..
I wish cards were released quicker. I'd rather have regular bi monthly releases of say 20 new cards rather than have to wait 6 months. The problem is after such a long period with no new content the meta game becomes stale quickly due to the relatively small card pool. Smaller regular releases might improve that and help keep the game fresh and encourage more players to try it and more players not to leave.
Once you've played vs an opponent it would be great if your game client downloaded the oppositions deck so you could then play vs that deck in single player mode, this would really keep things fresh for those players who don't like pvp or don't have regular/good internet access.
The ability to set up tournaments would be fantastic and I think would help make the community size grow and make it sustainable.
I'd love to see a mode that allows you to play a career of magic. Like IRL. ie you start as a  beginner with a handful of cards. You start to enter local tournaments, you get more cards, fame increases. You get sponsored, you enter PTQs. You go to World Championship etc. You get to play vs current and old hall of famers.
Another feature would be if the game added cards from year to year, rather than developing a brand new game each year (which must cost a lot to develop. Why don't you simply improve year on year instead? Improve the UX, support, add game modes and features. And keep previous cards year on year to improve the card pool.
As it is I think its a great game, I think you've really improved on last years. The UX from a design POV is much improved from last years game.
Keep up the good work :)

In this text-based interactive novel, you get to be the founder of your own independent film studio and possibly write, edit, direct, produce, and even star in your own film! Navigate your way through 50s Hollywood and decide where you want to spend your film budget -- will you ask your buddies to star as actors in your film or seek out more expensive but famous options? Not to mention who might direct your film... you could always get Hitchcock if you try your best! But maybe he wouldn't be the best for a sci-fi flick with a romance subplot.
The possibilities are endless. You get to customize your film on ALL levels, and will even get the opportunity to improve it on certain (weak) points while time progresses. In the meantime, against the backdrop of the Cold War, there's a lot of discussion about in what ways independent film studios are influencing the American public through Red propaganda. Are you a Commie or not? And is your film all you think about or do you have some time left for romance? Time will tell!
+ Real immersion in the 50s world of Hollywood
+ Lots of customization options for your own film that affect all the different endings
+ The ability to also customize the people around you (friends, family, actors)
- No save points
- Pretty short, can be finished in ± 1.5 hours
- The courtcase surrounding the whole communism/blacklist angle felt forced
The most enjoyable part about
was, to me, the ability to customize my film to such a great degree. You can truly create something that feels like it could be yours, and even get to enjoy the reviews/response once your film is released. The whole 50s vibe was amazing, mainly thanks to all the famous Hollywood people popping up here and there in the story. Though the Cold War angle could have worked, being pursued by an angry law-enforcing stereotype who drags you to court felt very forced (and distracted a lot from my precious film!).
If you like this kind of 50s Hollywood stuff, then this Choose Your Own Adventure game could be the one for you. I had a lot of fun directing and writing my own romance adventure film that bombed at the box office -- no hard feelings, because I eventually left Tinseltown with a happy threesome consisting of me, a handsome actor, and a stagehand.

My interest in this game began when I realized it was a "spiritual successor" to Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.  (Their words, not mine) and I have to say that the result both impresses me and lets me down.
On the one hand, it is (mostly) what I would want from a sequel/remake/redux of Alpha Centauri.  Updated graphics, same concept, familiar storylines and turn-based, sci-fi-fun!  I love the addition of the Virtues and Culture along with a better laid out tech tree.
On the other hand, the personalities of the factions are stagnant and impossible to really be surprised or developed.  The diplomacy of the previous game is far more limited than before, the alien races are unplayable (and sterile) (however it was not until Alien Crossfire, the expansion that this became an option).  With these fixed parameters, it makes replay value depreciate as each game goes through almost the same motions time and time again.  Also, I miss the victories from the previous game (getting elected to world leader, corning the Energy market, etc).
That being said, I still really enjoy the game.  Maybe it is the nostalgia, maybe it is the storyline but I appreciate the challenges each world, starting location, etc can bring.  The bonus is the fact that this game came MOD ready and there already tons of great add-ons that players can add to spice up the game.  As of the time of this review, I have yet to sample any as I'm still enjoying the vanilla version of the game but will find myself adapting it to my preference as time goes on.
Final words?  The gameplay of Beyond Earth is on some levels far better and more interesting than Alpha Centauri ever was and at the same time, simplified and well, vanilla.   As of right now, I do recommend the game, I really do.  It is a lot of fun and there is a bit of a learning curve for players to understand things like Health, Culture, Science, and Energy balance.  My hopes is that there is a shake-up to the factions with more dynamic personalities and increased diplomacy options.  I would happily purchase DLC like that and if they take this down the route of Civilization, we can certainly expect tons of updates and DLC to emerge over time.   Too bad that never happened.

I'm going to confess straight up that while I'm definitely "a reader", it's slowly dawning on me that reading is not the main reason that I play video games.  This may have something to do with the fact that I'm currently a university student, so I have quite enough reading to do as is, thank ya very much!  As it stands, however, I finished this one in just a couple of sittings, thanks to how exceptionally well-written and cleverly designed it was, and it gave me a few solid chuckles along the way as well.

Now, if you're one of those people who finds themselves constantly complaining about the lack of actual CHOICES one gets to make in a lot of so-called "interactive novels", you're unlikely to complain about THIS one.  In the first ten minutes alone you're forced to choose the name and gender of not only your own but other characters, and almost everything that your character does or says from then on in requires a decision, sometimes from a pick of a good five to ten options!   You truly choose YOUR OWN adventure in this one.  (Just to give an example, by the end of my first scene I had decided that I was a film director named Cliff Flowers - I'm a Killers fan, what can I say - who had just pitched a studio exec a horror-comedy set during the Running of the Bulls in Spain!  That's exactly the kind of customisation you can expect if you give this baby a burl.)

Now whether or not the story in question is liable to set your world on fire is a slightly more subjective thing, and obviously all the non-readers out there should just LEAVE THE STORE PAGE NOW and go find themselves a Sam to get Serious with (it's literally JUST WORDS, not even any pictures or music)!  Personally, I found it all rather interesting and enjoyable,  but then again, I've been an amateur filmmaker myself and have always been fascinated by the dubious ins-and-outs of the movie business, and there's no denying that the McCarthy era makes an especially intriguing backdrop to a game.
I won't lie and say that I've played a whole lot of games in this style, but I'd be pretty darn surprised if this wasn't one of the better ones.  Oh, and for those of you concerned with cost, you can stop fretting: The sheer multitude of choices one can make guarantees EXCEPTIONAL replayability.  On my first two-hour playthrough, I've only netted 16% of available achievements, and I'm yet to even MEET Alfred Hitchcock, much less make a movie with him.  I CAN confidently say, however, that Orson Welles does have one little ♥♥♥♥er of a DOG...

Verdict: 8/10.

(PS You know you've got what it takes to be a real-life film writer/director/producer when you give yourself a CORONARY!  Even got the achievement to prove it!!)

Battlerite is a very slick PVP game, with fast paced and tactical combat. The immediate comparison is a MOBA teamfight (without all the farming etc.), as each hero has several abilities including an ultimate. While its tempting to see Battlerite purely as a condensed MOBA, I don't think it is. In fact seeing it in these terms put me off at first.
Once you play a few matches and get the rhythm of the combat I'd say it shares a lot with fighting games. Matches all come down to player ability as each hero is on a level playing field for each round of a match.
The Battlerite system itself is brilliant, and allows you to tweak your hero's abilities to suit your own play-style. Since leaving early access the community has swelled, and it is even easier to find matches against similarly skilled opponents.
tl;dr it's a brilliant fast paced combat game

Having been a fan of squad-based strategy games for many years, I just had to try Fallen: A2P Protocol. This game has promise as a great title, even though it is difficult to visualize the final product in its current state as Early Access. Set in a post-apocalyptic United States, you take command of a rag-tag group of scavengers that stumble upon a mystery of the wasteland. Each member of your squad can equip a variety of ranged and hand-to-hand weaponry, from makeshift swords to rocket launchers. Medikits, grenades, and armor are also available.
The developers helped to sell the post-apocalyptic setting by reducing the availability and limiting your access to weapons, equipment, and ammunition, both through NPC shops and on the battlefield. Granted you can buy and equip your squad with any items from the game at Level 1, assuming the NPC shop has it in its inventory and/or access to early dead body loot. However, ammunition is scarce, and you may only have one shot with that shiny new rocket launcher you have.
In battle, the game tallies and records all actions. Meaning, whenever a good guy or bad guy, shoots, throws an item, or uses a medikit, the game will make sure that item is expended, even after the end of the battle. Those item tallies will affect the items that can be looted from dead bodies. Example: If an enemy sniper has six bullets, and takes three shots by the time your men kill the sniper, looting his body will only get you the three remaining bullets, and his rifle of course.
The battlefield is also affect by weather conditions. Acid rain, extreme heat, and sandstorms are just a few examples. Each weather condition can appear and disappear without warning and will affect the battlefield for a random period of turns. Each weather condition will affect the battlefield in a different way, forcing you to change strategies in the middle of a fight.
There are a few drawbacks to this title that I do feel I need to mention. There a significant lack of roamability, random questing, and the ability to be a murderous vigilante to this post-apocalyptic world. The developers have emphasized (to my general disappointment) that Fallen: A2P Protocol is intended to be quite linear, and there will not be much deviation from the main story missions. Random encounters may be added to this title in the future, but that seems unconfirmed.
Another issue I see with Fallen: A2P Protocol is the lack of character individuality. (I am hoping in the long-term this evaluation is no longer applicable..) Every character you control in the game is a complete copy of the next, in terms of character stats, allowable equipment, and skill tree. (This is Early Access, so I will ignore the copy/paste character models and animations.) There is no variety for being a bunch of random misfits running around the ruins of the United States.
In conclusion, Fallen: A2P Protocol is a "Flubber" of a title. There is just enough content to feel interesting and worth peeking at. But it is not developed enough to know where it is going. It is too amorphous and not a lot of shape just yet. I do believe this game can be a great play option, like I said at the beginning of this review. However, I would only recommend this game to anyone who will actively participate in the Early Access improvement plan.

The Vagrant uses a two-button combo system--X and Y or J and K if you’re using a controller or keyboard respectively--and performing moves is based on the order in which you press them. A controller is recommended to play The Vagrant, but a keyboard controls adequately as well. Combos can be unlocked in the [abilities] tab by spending mana, which is dropped by defeated enemies.
Adding attacks to your roster makes combat more streamlined and as such, the game’s progression system is satisfying and effective.
Combat also utilizes special abilities that use Rage, which is accumulated when dealing and receiving damage. These are powerful attacks that can be unlocked in the abilities screen. One special attack can be equipped at a time, so choose the one that best suits your playstyle.
These include equipment and an ability tree that substitutes/combines stat management and skill-point distribution. Equipment can be looted, bought, and crafted by smiths if you have the required materials.
Slots include weapon, armor, and accessory + passive bonus. Armor and weapons can be enhanced using mana to increase their base stats, and the upgrade limit is represented by stars.
The skill web is standard RPG fare where you have to unlock nores in a sequence to acquire stronger skills and larger stat upgrades. This web also functions as the leveling up system and you are free to build Vivian as you wish, tailoring her attack and defense to suit your play style while also unlocking and strengthening combos.
Locations are divided into interconnected rooms, some of which require you to defeat a group of enemies before you can proceed.
You can move directly from where you are to the objective marked on the map or you can explore every room and hopefully get rewarded with loot for your trouble. Dead ends tens to hold treasure chests filled with gold, materials, and pieces of equipment.
Later in the game, you’ll be able to fast travel between campfires, which serve as places to save as well as to turn your raw produce into culinary delights.
Enemies are quick and aren’t above playing dirty. They’re particularly dangerous in groups as ranged enemies will dance behind stockier shield-bearing allies and shoot you without fear of retaliation.
They’re fast and you have to be faster, utilizing Vivian’s dodge and jump (a double jump can be unlocked in the ability web) to move out of harm’s way. Each enemy has its own way of approaching Vivian, and you’ll eventually figure out how best to deal with them.
Boss monsters in particular pose a challenge. These hulking monsters have multi-tiered health bars and pack a serious punch. Boss monsters have tells, so once you get their patterns down it gets a bit easier, but for every health bar you whittle down, they get even more ferocious!
The hand-drawn art is lovely, albeit a little gratuitous about its endowments, and the world is layered with characters who are interconnected in one way or another. Because there aren’t just your standard blank-faced NPC who only await your purchase, the world seems more believable and alive, which is a nice touch.
The music is also nice, though I haven’t come across anything that sent me scrambling to buy a soundtrack.
By the end of its Early Access stint, the game promises 6 chapters, polish (including a more functional translation and more supported languages), and more equipment and monsters. The developer is open to suggestions, so feel free to pitch in your feedback if you get the game early.
The price ($14.99) will not change between now and an estimated date of October 2017, so there’s no harm in waiting for the game to develop more before parting with your hard-earned buck
I've already posted these on the forums and the devs have acknowledged that there are improvements in the works--a definite thumbs-up in my book.
.Bottom Line.
The Vagrant is a side-scrolling action RPG detailing the story of Vivian, a Runewarden turned-sellsword. While its English translation may not wow anyone, it’s gorgeous hand-drawn art style will.
Combat, while flawed in some aspects is fast-paced and solid while exploring an area completely will yield treasure. In all,a very solid entry into the action adventure genre and one that will get better over the course of its Early Access period.
I recommend this game to those who seek a challenge, enjoy a detailed story, and aren’t put off by the hit miss translation. The game’s main focus is combat and, if the hiccups are fixed, it would do a “flawless” job as the Store page promises.

It was hard to stop playing to write this review. This is going to be a long one.
This is a 2.6 hour review with a level 13 character (Gauntlet Mage) on a PvE server.
Citadel: FwF is a decent game with a great premise.
~Character Customization
Not much to see here. Honestly a little lack luster. You are given a few basic head options and hair styles. You can then choose skin color(any color on the rainbow), hair color, nail color(not sure why?), and eye color. Personally, I had red skin and white hair with a long beard. Named myself Santa. You then choose where you spawn (out of three locations) and get going.
~Starting out
This game does not try to hold your hand. When my bud and I started out, the only tip we were given is the Inventory button. That leaves room for exploration (and confusion). You are then thrust onto the new world, ready to go.
~Progression
This game has a very good sense of progression. From choosing your first weapon and spells to learning how to make potions and structures. From level 1-10, I honestly felt like I was learning and improving. At times, the leveling can be slow. Just go find some orcs and get to slaying.
~Harvesting
Its fun. You either run around and gran it, use a spell that you learn at level 5, or kill things. That has been the extend of things for harvesting so far. Works as expected and you usually won't be doing it forever, so it doesn't take you out of the game.
~Crafting
Crafting happens slowly. One item (or multiple of that one item) at a time. No crafting queue. This carries over to the more advanced stations. You have to monitor if you want to craft more than one type of thing.
~Enemy AI
The AI in this game is... unintelligent to say the least. As a level 10, I was able to kill a level 26 Mountain Giant by running around a rock. Sometimes, enemys deaggro off you very quickly, breaking the intensity of combat. This, I hope, is being fixed.
~Combat
The combat in this game is great and bad. Great: You feel powerful when casting spells to decimate your enemys! Bad: The animations for enemy are janky and unpredictable. Sometimes attacks do not connect. No matter what you do. Orcs are Sonic in disguise with how fast they move. The only thing intense to fight are the bigger enemys. Easier to hit (even though they are blindlingly quick as well) because of the larger hitbox.
~Building
So much fun. The buildings come together nicely and it always feels nice. Pair it with the decent harvesting system and building can be pretty laid back. Only a few times has a roof not come together right. Easily fixed.
~Taming
Taming is temporary. You use a spell to tame a creature over time until it is pacified. Then, you may walk up to it and put a scroll in it for more time. The creatures we tested it was with a Dire Wolf, Bear, and RazorClaw Bear.
~Optimization
My biggest fear. To be honest, it was not bad for me. On high settings, I had a solid 50fps. It would occasionally stoop to 45fps but other than that, It was not bad. I run an overclocked gtx960 with 16gb of ram. My bud (not sure which card) was fairing better with a solid 60fps stooping to 55fps.
~Conclusion
Is this game amazing? No. Is it fun? Very. In my almost 3 hours of playing, I have not run in to any outright bugs. This does not mean there is not any. I just have not personally ran in to any. I do hope they fix AI and Combat in general. Not much to complain about in this game. Not a bad EARLY ACCESS starting point. They have a ways to go, and I cannot wait for the next update.
6/10... until the next update

I rate the game, Arcade Game Series: Galaga, 3/5. OK.
This is a fairly classic, fairly well-done and straight forward port of the original arcade game with very few bells and whistles. The game runs well but the control scheme keys cannot be remapped to other keys and there is no online multiplayer functionality.
+Classic arcade game graphics which include borders around the main screen which display the original arcade game cabinet art. The graphics seem very true to the original.
+The game runs fast with no freezes or hiccups that I noticed.
+/-Fairly intuitive and responsive default controls but they cannot be re-mapped to other keys and they do not conform to the control schemes of many other, newer schmups. Most notably, the fire button is mapped to the spacebar and cannot be changed to the Z key which is continuously irritating to me.
-Can only get steam achievements by using default difficulty and extra life settings which are fairly hard.
-Does not appear to be capable of any 2 player mode for online matches with other players.
-Very few bells and whistles or additional features or extras. It's pretty much just Galaga and a few basic menu options. It may be a bit overpriced when it's not on a special steam sale.
-Why does this game need 2 GB of RAM?
-Why does this game require a processor of 2.3 Ghz?
-Why aren't the installation options for this game far more flexible? This game should be advertised as being capable of being run on nearly any smartphone and the fact that this port does not actively support this as an option seems like a terrible oversight, particularly for such an old, relatively simple piece of software.

Many critics of Hitman: Absolution made the mistake to equate the whole series with Blood Money - maybe because this was the only game they have played.
People that know the whole series (including me) are aware of the fact that the very first game Codename 47 was also very mutch about action (think of the end) and even the second part had some hardcore areas that could only be solved by shooting your way through because of the aggressive AI. Contracts was a very dark game and rediscovered some aspects of the story...
Every Hitman game is unique in his own way, so where does this strange idea come from that every part has to be like Blood Money?? Yes, it was with no doubt a great game with a reliable disguise system and fantastic missions - but Absolution also has it's very own strengths: great sound and graphics, smooth and polished gameplay, cool cinematics and a lot of details in most levels. Some areas (like Hope and Chinatown) are bigger than others and this is completely fine. In my second playthrough, I discovered eastereggs, new rooms and new ways of eliminating the target. Yes, story and points system are strange and not every level offers a lot of stealth varieties but the game just didn't deserve all the extreme and frivolous reviews of some "fans".
Absolution is fine the way it is - because it's an individual part of the series that still upholds most of the traditions of Hitman. I rather like to play some new aspects than the same style and content again and again.
If all the haters wouldn't be so ignorant, we surely wouldn't have this reboot without name that is coming out today - and while it might be a great game again, it clearly shows the anxiety of the developers of a new ♥♥♥♥♥torm and the lower production value. It's maybe too much based on the general wish that every level has to be a large sandbox environment (that wasn't even the case in Blood Money!). And while I'm comletely fine with this new decision, I hope that
the current uncultivated zeitgeist doesn't rise again and destroys the creative work and motivation of the developers with flames, arrogance and disrespect.

Magic Duels is an ideal starting point for anyone new to the world of MTG.  A limited selection of cards (at the time of this writing, cards are used from the Magic: Origins and Zendikar blocks) can keep the novice from being overwhelmed by the sheer number of abilities, skills, and creatures available within the world of MTG with just enough going on to get a good sense of gameplay.  The antisocial can enjoy the Story Modes (which will also give you some background on the most popular Planeswalkers out there) or the Battle Mode against assorted system AI players.  Feeling pretty confident?  Build your deck using the Deck Wizard (either with or without any help from the system) and try your luck against other online opponents.  Spending gold can 'buy' you additional booster decks to round out our collection, but keep in mind there's no buying specific cards here... it's all in the draw of the pack!  As an aside, completing Quests can add to your gold stash without spending any of your real-world bucks.
If you're a hardcore real-world MTG player, you'll obviously find that this game is pretty limited and most likely you'll not be satisfied with it.  The gaming format is Standard, and I know too many players that have the "Only COMMANDER PLAY" mentality .  Personally, I do play IRL but I enjoy kicking this one around for a casual Magic fix - I don't always have the luxury of a few hours to kill and this game gives me enough of a fix.  For those who want a game that plays close to a real-life situation, you'll run into a few hiccups - sometimes it can be a bit dodgy with some of the card stack, and I have run into a few cards that didn't have the full range of abilities that are listed on the ones in my hard-copy collection.  Overall though, if you're not going in with a die-hard 'it must be exactly like the real thing' attitude, you'll find quite a bit of entertaining play here.  Again, I especially recommend it for any beginner who'd like to learn something of the real game dynamics BUT understand that this isn't a perfect replica of an actual real life card battle.

I've played This War of Mine for nearly twenty hours now and I am amazed by its qualities. The game is so deeply immersive that I didn't even notice the sun go down after beginning play at around 4pm. I found myself still sat playing at 2 in the morning and thinking how the f*ck did I get here ? So beware of this effect.
The game puts the player in a scenario that is rarely touched upon by developers and that is the survival of civillians in the midst of war. When hearing my friend talk about the game and watching the trailer I immediately thought of the scenes from the first Austin Powers film where noone cares about the family of the henchmen. It was at this point I realised that many games out there are so focussed around being a hero/heroine and fighting a war mostly by themselves which brings a sense of gratification for every minor objective. This game is the polar opposite. Survivng is not only difficult but frustrating and at points tedious and dull.
Now if anyone has bothererd to read this far (which I doubt anyone will read it full stop) you're probably wondering why I recommend this game if I describe parts of it as 'dull' and the simple answer is because of the effect this game has on each player. Every person I know who has played this game has each had a different output from the game and it truly makes you think about the world. As you take control of the several characters you can survive as you unravel more of their stories and their past making you connect with them. For me I became so grossly immersed in the character Arica and when she unfortunately died looting I honestly felt sad. This game, although being totally fictional in its storyline, has brought humanity to a war game so brilliantly. When you help a neighbour it truly feels like you're doing good for a community even though it doesn't exist ! I wont ramble on (great Led Zep song) because I'm only writing this out of sheer boredom however this game has inspired me to donate money to war child every month as it has truly opened my eyes to an experience that I hope to never go through myself but I am more aware of its impact thanks to this game.
The point I'm probably not getting across well is that this game can be played by most people (as it is not very demanding graphics wise) and should be because of its true potential to shed light on the horrible conditions some people live in even today if we look at Syria as an example. I rate this game 10/10 as it is truly fantastic in its setup. It's simple, clean and packs a fantastic message for any player with an open mind who's not stuffing their face with energy drinks and treating it like a challenge rather than an immersive experience. If that's the case I would suggest Counter Strike. If you have read this far I would suggest doing something better with your time as this is quite honestly just me typing random words that dont make sense now. Bannana, Dihydrocodeine, Golf, Aberdeen.

This war of Mine is a survival game set in a modern world at war where society collapses. You and other survivors find yourself scavenging for food and supplies to tough out a winter. You're forced into ethical dilemas where you have to decide whether to help your neighbors or steal their supplies and let them die. Your survivors suffer from morale, injuries, hunger, and sleep deprevation. You need to fortify your dilapidated shelter from other survivors and the weather, and build or scavenge everything you need to survive.
The game places you in situations where you see the effects of survival from a new angle not covered in games, one where you're not a superhero that doesn't have to deal with consequences. Death is a very prevalent reality in this game and combat, even among prior soldiers, is lethal and difficult. The game mechanics make it much easier to play this game creeping through shadows and avoiding others as you scavenge, rather than dealing with post-combat injuries and being a drag on the extremely limited resources while you heal. You need to decide whether it's better to give your injured/sick people more food, medicines, and bed space than your colonists that need to go out and look for supplies. You also need to decide whther you can handle bringing in new survivors or turning them out, or whther to help your neighbors with your limited supplies. The way the gasmer is paced and how everything is presented to you it becomes an emotional journey.
There is a fragile balance that needs to be maintained and there is never enough time or resources to keep on top of it, making it a balancing act of who can handle the imbalance while functioning well enough to help everyone else survive. Suriviors that don't get enough to eat, get enough sleep, or are too cold will get sick and eventually can die from their weakening states. People that are injured, sleep depreived, or sick will move more slowly and/or limp around. Basically everything affects morale, ability to move around, and ultimately how long you will live and how well you can help each other live. Survivors that are suffering from bad morale will stop, mope around, and question their life - even in critical situations, and can end up commiting suicide if it conitnues to spiral out of control. The game is played in real time with a limited time frame to get everything done for each day and night, and how you use that time will quickly allow you to see the consequences.
This War of Mine is both a powerful experience and a great game. I highly recommend you try it. It also has replay value, with each restart giving you different survivors/shelter.
Solid game but it gives you a lot to take care of. I'd like to see something along these lines but with writing a book instead of making a movie.

Vagrant is a 2D Action / RPG game, where you take a role of a travelling sellsword on her own mission. Combat lots of different creatures and explore the world on a journey through medieval fantasy world.
Overall, the gameplay itself is great. Attack Sequences: Animations are well done and you can chain the combos quite easily. The attack combos are introduced gradually (through your talent tree, where you can look up what they do and the keys to use them), which gives you enough time to practice them. The controls are responsive and make it easy to perform attacks.
And the whole game actually follows this practice: the difficulty gradually increases, throwing easy monsters at the start and then becoming more challenging towards the end. The seasoned players won’t be bored at the beginning either: at every world, there are optional rooms with higher rewards and more challenging monsters.
There’s also a vast ability tree, or rather a circle. You can level up everything, as long as you have mana and find relevant items. For people who like to grind – this can be a perfect opportunity to max out all possible stats.
And finally, the graphics are nice. The backgrounds seem to be hand-drawn and overall very clean. The game has a very distinct medieval-fantasy feel. I can’t say anything bad about the music, it’s there and it’s not annoying nor repetitive, so I can say that it’s a plus.
•	Can’t Skip the Cutscenes, there are not many of them, but sometimes when you die and have to redo it – it’s a pain.
•	Game Balance leaves some questions: potions are useless: they restore health, but have cooldown. Instead, you can open the equipment menu and use consumable food, that does the same and has no cooldown. There are even talents that reduce healing potion cooldowns. Why? You can essentially avoid that by just eating food (which is also encountered more often in game).
•	Translation shows errors now and then and then there are weird plot hole that I especially noticed: “everyone in the village got killed” – then you kill the boss – then everyone in the village (except for one house) is suddenly there again. The characters also seem to open up randomly: would you tell a random dude you’ve met a day ago that your father abandoned you? It’s up to you to judge.
•	Alright, I have to mention the breasts. Alright, I know there are fans of this style out there and I’m not here to complain about the size, but I can’t help but look at the heroine and ask “where’s the damn neck?” Breasts seems to be drawn too high, leaving no place for the clearly distinguishable upper chest and neck.
The game is not perfect. The plot might not be that great and the character introductions are somewhat rushed, but the combat system and the gradual change of sceneries make it well worth it. The ability to chain combos flawlessly, customize your abilities / equipment, as well as difficulty being just right – that makes the game good and because of this I can confidently recommend it.
I liked the game overall and I recommend it. Great atmosphere, beautiful story. 6 hours of fun.

This is a first impression of Fallen A2P Protocol.  The devs, Red Katana, wanted to share early access with me for creating this first impression.  The game is currently in Early Access Alpha so there are many game mechanics still being worked on.  We're discussing the game strictly as a work in progress.  This game is originally fan funded on Kickstarter.
So when you look at this game in action it immediately reminds you of Xcom. So fans of Xcom  and turn based strategy combat should be interested in this game.  It does derive a lot of gameplay elements from Xcom in the combat, but there are many differences as well.   It is not an Xcom clone, it has it's own style of gameplay.
It does take place in the post apocalypse and the game is built around this.  Everything is limited and you are literally scavenging to survive.  In combat you have a limited number of bullets and melee weapons are important.  You have to find or purchase ranged weapons, melee weapons are your backup.  So positioning for attack can vary based on whether you are using melee or ranged weapons.  The attack system is based on AP points and each move you do uses a different amount of AP.  So in order to attack you have to judge how much distance you can move and still fire your attack.  There are also different types of defenses.  There's “hunker down” which reduces the damage you take during the enemy turn.  Then there's “Overwatch” where your character will fire back when the enemy enters your line of sight.  Looting is also crucial.  After each enemy you kill, you'll have to use AP to move to the loot and pick it up.  This is the primary way you get ammo during combat.
When you finish combat, you'll find yourself in the overworld.  You can purchase new items, level up individual characters, and travel to different sites.  The different sites have shops and missions.  Leveling up characters can unlock new passive and active skills and this is done for each character.  So you definitely do not want to lose anyone in combat.  You can also move items around in your inventory.
I'll remind you the game is an Early Access Alpha, but I do see a lot of room for improvement.  The game needs to include basic hotkeys in combat and that to be integrated into the UI.  The overworld UI could use a lot more intuitive functions.  Currently, players have to figure it all out themselves.  The story cut scenes could definitely use more animation and preferably voice overs.
You may want to wait until the final or beta version, but this game is heading in the right direction.  Red Katana is trying to create a solid strategy game.  If you are a huge fan of strategy game and want to support the devs, buy the early access which retails at $15.

As of v0.5 (Alpha):
Fallen: A2P Protocol is a turn-based strategy game with RPG elements set in post-apocalyptic world.
If I would to compare it to existing games, I’d say it’s a combination of Fallout with new XCOM.
Even though at the moment the game is in early alpha (not all mechanics are there, the game’s very rough around the edges, some models are missing, textures are low-res, etc), you can pretty much already see what the game will be once it’s done.
If you’d enjoyed a tactical gameplay of XCOM, you’ll probably like the Fallen take on it.
It offers slightly different experience than XCOM because in addition to keeping your team alive, you also have to manage your limited resource - bullets and medkits do not magically refill on missions end here, you’ll actually have to scavenge or trade to get those.
The RPG element comes into play with team management - all of your caravan members have levels, stats (that are raised automatically) and skills (that you have to assign on your own).
Skills are basically the way to specialize your team members into being a melee attacker, ranged assault, medic or some weird mix of all.
Since stats are leveled up automatically (at least in current builds), some characters are going to be more fit for some roles.
The game currently features a couple of pre-made story and side-missions. They have a pretty amusing dialogues, but a lot of things are not quite clear because of the obvious gaps in the storytelling. But that’s something that’ll come later for sure.
Downsides right now:
Since this is alpha, there’s a lot of placeholders and things that are very rough around the edges
A lot of placeholders everywhere
UI is quite dodgy in places at the moment
Quite a lot of times UI does not properly communicates the stats (which is quite important for TBS in my opinion)
A lot of placeholders everywhere - most of the models are same (I wasn’t joking before)
Some of the textures are quite low-res and can be painful to look at in high res
But all of those downsides are very much things in progress and will surely be fixed. If you can put those aside, you’ll find a pretty fun (albeit raw) turn-based strategy experience.
If you think those are a bit too much for you, then wait a bit until beta.

UPDATE:  I am changing my review from "Thumbs down" to "Thumbs up."
The sound glitches appears to have been fixed in the latest update, which was my main objection.  There are still other issues, but the "ugliness" of the game interface also appears to be improved.
Still lacks key rebinding, but this is now a faithful Galaga emulation, and you can restart at the last level you completed.
Original "Thumbs Down" review below:
*****
Galaga is great!  But this is the worst of the 3-in-1 Namco pack games (Dig Dug, Pac Man, and Galaga), quality-wise. The other two are passable, but this, sold individually, is a pass....
Freeware emulators have been emulating "Galaga" better than this for over a decade. This is a bare-bones,  glitchy, and clunky port of a classic game.
Cons:
-  The sound is distractingly glitchy (on my  Windows 10 PC)
-  No key rebinding (if you want to play by keyboard).
-  Ugly, bare-bones interface.
Pros:
-  It's still Galaga, even with the glitchy sound and poor interface.
-  You can start a new game from the highest level you've reached.
-  The graphics are smooth and accurate.
-  Online leaderboards and high score tables.
So.... it's Galaga (thumbs up!). But the interface is poor, and it doesn't faithfully emulate the sounds on my bog-standard modern PC. If you're a Galaga  fan, this version will probably disappoint you. Namco could have done better.
I do like restarting at my previous highest level, though.

Naturally, for a game trying to be competitive, these items and loot
. This is very important for a game wanting to be enjoyable and non-P2W; the developers realize this!

People keep saying this little gem is 'the spiritual successor to "Freelancer"'...well, I feel it's more of 'the more faithful sequel to "Privateer" than "Freelancer" was'.
This is not to say that Digital Anvil's last(?) release was *bad*, but it's more like this later game manage to recapture the first game's core 'feel' than the sequel.  Make no mistake, it does fit in that same grove as both of Chris Roberts' titles, but it lacks the 'glitz' of a AAA-game like Freelancer; it's got more of a 'rough gem' feel like that Wing Commander spin-off was.
And tangible things bear me out: the 'meta-game' is very similar: you have stations/bases that allow you to buy and configure ships, commodity markets to buy and sell goods, a mission computer to take various jobs, a bar to meet storyline people, chat with the bartender for rumors and info and hire wingmen...and two 'guilds' - Merchant and Mercenary - who offer better jobs than the mish compy...with membership.
Rogue Galaxy adheres to this system, but adds a little to it; the guilds supply unique gear and ships, for example, and your standing can grow over requirement levels to make same available to you (there was little point in 'grinding favor' with factions in Privateer once you were 'friendly').
Now the core gameplay (combat and station-to-station travel) is different; you're captaining a large ship that operates like a blue-water vessel, rather than a glorified 'space plane', and combat is 'raking him with your broadsides' rather than 'curling in on his six and shooting him down', but even that difference doesn't weaken the bond.
Even the story premise - you speak with this person and that person, and are given an 'artifact' to hold on to momentarily for someone, and it proves to be very desirous for just about everyone else, painting a giant bullseye on the beam of your frigate.
But again, this seems to be loving and faithful emulation of a great older title, and it helps the new game.
If you liked Privateer (or even its 'big show' successor Freelancer) you WILL like Rebel Galaxy...even if you prefer dogfighting to battleship steerage.  It will 'scratch that itch' while you're waiting to see how Star Citizen will evolve into something that likely won't be able to.
...oh, and as I'm sure many others have said: the soundtrack is AMAZINGLY good; catchy tunes that you'll find yourself humming on the commute after a while playing. :)

Don't play the remaster. It may crash. It may not. It doesn't matter if you have the best rig in the world.
*edit*
If you do decide to play it, save every couple of minutes. Saves rarely crash. Maintain 3 saves. One autosave and 2 saves that you alternate between. You will at most lose 4 minutes of play. Just don't forget to save after every 1-2 rooms and definitely after every step of every objective. The more you save, the less you're going to have to redo when it crashes.
Also, very important. Play in 1080p. The crashes largely have to do with memory, UI problems, and save problems. Playing in 1080p will reduce most of the crashes. When I was in 4k, I was crashing every 5-10 minutes. 1080p is every 2 hours. Save before you handle any hints, maps, or buying from shops. Those can crash too!

I've always been a huge fan of the Bioshock series overrall. Since I decided to finally write up my review of it I'll give the Good and Bad parts of it.
The Good:
-The Storyline is very well made and put
-Side stories (the audios/collectibles you find) tell neat and hidden things you may have never known about
-The atmosphere that Rapture was built around is wonderful
-Voice Actors did their part good
The Bad:
-I've placed 500+ hrs into this game (remastered & originals together) across the 360, ps3, pc, ps4 and xb1, and there is no replay value at all (I've just dealt playing the same thing over and over at times just cause Im a fan)
-The Remastered on PC does crash quite a bit and I meet the recommended requirements to play it
-However the game may be big but I wish it was more of an open world based game
-It doesn't seem like 2K didn't think of a better loot system either, so there's not much to loot for
Overall:
It's not that bad of a series to play. This review I'm actually speaking my opinion of all 3 games together. Not just this one. I do recommend the series though if you're at least searching for a pretty good, well-told story. Especially if you're one who enjoys atmospheric, suspensful, fps games. It's a good experience and a good time. Well for me, It's a good old time.

So this was my original review after losing in combat for a second time (10h in):
"Stupid combat system. You die if someone else farted. I regret buying this game."
Some people didn't seem to like it :P
Here are the questions you should ask yourself :
Did you like playing The Sims but thought it was to upbeat for you?
Do you like getting in touch with your feelings?
Do you like resource management?
Do you like punishing game mechanics?
Do you like spending a lot of time (perhaps) doing nothing, just trying to get by?
Do you like to take things slow?
Do you like experiencing the struggle to survive?
Do you like to make tough choices, like who lives or who dies. Even between the ones close to you?
Do you like random♥♥♥♥♥♥happening to you? (The wrath of fate :)
Do you like hoarding, collecting, crafting, trading? (not in any particular order)
Do you don't mind simple game play?
Do you think the military is evil incorporated and deserves to be annihalated like some common thugs?
Do you like watching progress bars a lot?
If you answered yes to a fair amount of these questions then this game is for you.
After 40+h of game time :
I now had one successful playthrough and maybe it's time for more info. I don't regret buying the game any more but I'm not sure if I'll spend more time on it. Losing in combat can be infuriating because you didn't realise you were in combat, or the game simply did not respond to your command, ... . I'm just telling you upfront.
I still find it hard to recommend this game to others. Since I got passed the basics, my first playthrough was kind of boring and rather uneventfull. It was probably also the lowest difficulty level perhaps. I had one character die because of combat I wasn't aware of (again...) but after that it was really easy.
Think you can expect to spend like 20h before you get your first full playthrough if you go in blind and try to figure stuff out yourself. I just went through the experience twice because I put the game down for a long time.
The Good ( = loved it) :
- The atmosphere (some say it's depressing on it's own). I think it really draws you into the world. I think they did a really good job on that.
- The characters and the character bio picture at the bottom are nice. I thought it was kind of silly at first but it does help to give personality to the character. I feel it does help with the immersion
- Choices. Real tough choices. Sometimes easier ones. But always with consequences.
The Bad ( = room for improvement) :
- There is very little information given to you. This game does not hold hands! Now I don't mind that. Exploration and experimentation is all good to me. Don't get me wrong.
But I have put it under negative because I think they should have explained some things (or at least a little more), for example the combat system. But there also other aspects where I thought, why not just tell that instead of having to figure it out.
In my opinion there are 2 ways to get into this game. Either go in blind and expect a steep learning curve, with a big portion of frustration, just trying to understand/learn the basics. Or go and read/watch guides on the basics and getting beyond the basics and then jump in.
- music is not that amazing. You get a couple of songs on a loop and that's it basically. Not saying it's bad. I think it could have been better. I think they could have done more with the radio or more stuff like the guitar.
- game play itself is not that exciting. A lot of the game consists of just watching progress bars. I'm sorry but it's true.
- I found the ending very unsatisfying. (After spending that much time on it)
The Ugly ( = horrendous♥♥♥♥♥♥that should not be in the game) :
- The combat system. I know it's not supposed to be a combat-oriented game. But I feel the game does not explain the combat system and doesn't have enough visual clues in combat and I find that very hard to accept, for a mechanic that is so punishing. Some basic intro to combat, with the character (your character) saying stuff like "oh this is dangerous", "oh I better do this". There are certain parts in the game where they used that mechanic. Why not the same for the combat system.
On the other hand, killing from stealth seems a bit overpowered. But I feel it needs to be that way in order the compensate for open, full-on combat.
- Only auto-saving at the start of the day. No saving during scavenging ok, but I really miss the option to be able to just save during the day. why not give the user more game options : casual (save whenever), seasoned (only at start of day/week), iron-man, ... . It feels strange when a game is a about choices, you give the gamer none about how he/she wants to play the game. A bit strange ... just saying.
- Full screen mode / Windowed mode. The windowed mode doesn't work for me because when you move to another screen and back, the game behaves (almost) like you ALT+TAB to it. It minimizes the window (=the game) for some reason, thus negating the benefit of playing in windowed mode. You might as well ALT+TAB in full screen mode, because windowed mode doesn't give you any benefit. It was really annoying for me because I wanted to look stuff up or take notes and this made it impossible for me. It was just too annoying. I just ended up taking notes on a piece of paper. (Which did help me with immersion into the game though :P)
Anyway. I hope it's been helpfull. Thank you for reading if you got this far. xD

Cult of the Wind is a third person shooter developed by North of Earth and released 2014, the gimmick is all the characters are PRETENDING to be airplanes. They don't fly, just run around with their arms out making airplane noises.
Unfortunately the game is dead, I couldn't find anyone to play with anyway. There's only one dedicated server still active.
There really isn't any story that is given when you play. The game is presented as a casual third person shooter. But the steam store and the Cult of the Wind website describe the game as follows:
"In an unknown time and place, a cult that worships the wreckage of ancient airplanes gathers to mimic the dogfights of old. With the peak of humanity far behind, their world is a mausoleum to a lush and verdant Art Deco past."
That was descriptive. Basically everyone is doing what I did as a kid: Run around making airplane noises. Oh wait, no, I made star wars lightsaber fights and killed mercenaries, droids, and fought Darth Vader and Darth Maul.
You move with WASD, you apparently do more damage the faster you're moving
As I've already explained you don't actually fly in this game, you run in a direction, arms stretched out in a T-pose. There are a number of elements on the HUD worth explaining. In the bottom right of UI you see a water droplet which represents your fuel. If you run out of this you die. above the fuel
is your health, if you take fall damage, or collateral damage from your own weapons. In the bottom left corner of the screen is your various ammo. the lower one is your primary weapon, the one above it is your secondary. In the center bottom is a power-up item.
As I'm sure you've already deduced, there are items, powerups, and attack items in game. Specifically there are three colored Chinese-lantern-looking-things. Red kites provide: fuel, health, or primary ammunition. Purple kites provide a power up of some type
. Lastly Orange Kites provide a random weapon.
I'm going to tack this point onto the end of the review, since apparently the game feels the level editor is worth mentioning, I will too. It stinks.
I've gone to school to work in 3d graphic design, I worked with 3ds Max, mudbox, and maya while in college. And outside of college I've spent many hours in Blender. I've even used Steams Source SDK.
This Level Editor is cumbersome and painful to use, you're better off using Source SDK or Blender if you want to get into 3d modeling levels, and then at least you'd be able to make stuff for games which are played.
In conclusion... this game isn't worth it. I think even if there was a community for the game, there simply isn't enough content to justify spending $9.99. However, this game is very gimmicky and would be fun to play with other people. There's just not really much chance of actually getting that opportunity.
I don't really feel one way or another about this game. If there was a player base this game would probably be a pass and a nick gimmick for people who are looking to play an odd little shooter game. If you have a group of friends you could give this game a shot. As far as my own recommendation: contrary to my review (which forces me to thumbs up or down), I don't give it either, I could give it either.
And as always, thank you for reading my review.

Well, it is about time I wrote a review for this game. This game suprised me, too say the least. This is essesntially a  building and resource management game that is set in war zone.
