This is a neat game.  It's a puzzle game that teaches you rudimentary electronics under the guise of diffusing bombs.  It starts off simple, with basic concepts like switches and wire cutting, then gradually introduces more complex things, like capacitors, push buttons, a few logic gates, etc...
If I had to come up with a complaint, it's too short.  I finished it in a little over an hour, but that was in one sitting, and I was engaged the whole time, considering the possible ramifications of each little button press, each wire cut.
Now that the complaint is out of the way, here's what I liked:
1:  I greatly enjoyed the core concept, solving puzzles to diffuse bombs, but then again, I'm probably slightly biased toward puzzle games.
2:  I liked the implementation, specifically, how they ramped up the complexity rather than just dumping stuff on you all at once.  The way I see it, it makes the game approachable.
3:  I don't know why, but I really got a kick out of the tension created by the two constraints you have to operate under:  you have to get the circuit to behave the way you want to in a short time limit (anywhere from 1 minute to 1 minute 30 seconds, and sometimes even 2 minutes) AND you can't mess up.  That, I think, was the bigger part of that equation, predicting that this wire I'm about to cut will diffuse the bomb, being wrong, and being greeted by the White Screen of 'Asploding.
If this game gets updated, and/or gets Workshop implemented, I think it'll really shine.
TL;DR - Kinda short, but a fun puzzle game.

The away team is one of the coolest games I've been able to play. It is based on the idea that you are an Ai that is tasked with protecting a small number of humans after the destruction of earth. I had a very good time with the game, but recommend that if you're looking into it, buy it on sale.

- Interesting story with about four endings to be had.
- Entertaining and descriptive writing, that makes you feel invested in the characters and thier story
- Interesting character traits that factor into gameplay, often changing outcomes
- Entertaining puzzles and mind games
Cons:
- Very heavy reading (I would personally consider this a pro, but some don't)
- Some choices seemed forced or very meaningless

- The space travel with the ship seems kind of meaningless and doesn't serve too much of a purpose
- Crew can die a lot in the later difficulties
Ultimately whether you enjoy this game or not is entirely dependant on whether you like an interactive novel style game. Personally I'd recommend playing on easy or normal, so crew doesn't die as much. The crew really does open up a lot of scenarios that may not happen if they weren't there. Overall, great game in my opinion.

Great idea for a game, diffusing Bombs Old school with cliping wires and pressing switches. It's nicely polished as well, but it's lacking content. I think the average person will be done in less than an hour.
While playing the game you get the distinct feeling that the creators of the game didn't have a too firm grasp of the underlying concepts of logic gates or just plain electronics themselves. The OR Gate for example has a whole tutorial section, when it serves no function that a forked trace wouldn't have fullfiled in most cases. Also the last puzzle in the second to last section features a solution that is - in contrast to the rest of the game - physically impossible to create with real world electronics (a circuit that powers itself, though the mechanism is well described in the game so you are not likely to get stuck there).
I feel that the puzzle design in general is somewhat lackluster, some puzzles are solved by just clipping all wires or switching all switches and many don't even have a way for you to accidently trigger the explosion prematurely. In general they do not feel 'clever', the ones that are a bit more tricky are mostly so because of obfuscation and not because of clever circuit design (the final puzzle is a prime example of this).
The mechanical foundation on the other hand is very solid and if this ever gets workshop support i think the user generated content will make up for the easy and somewhat shallow puzzles included in the base game.
If one hour of casual - and maybe educational - distraction is worth the asking price for you then go ahead, otherwise i suggest waiting for future updates.

TLDR
If you liked the first Bioshock, gameplay in Bioshock 2 is a definite upgrade from its predecessor. Fun Game multiple endings, decent replay value.
In depth review (Spoiler Warning)
Well let me start off addressing why I've seen some negative reviews and opinions on why they "consider it bad".
From the Steam side here there seems to be a majority who suffer from game crashes. I for one have not experienced anything major enough to make playing the game in small enjoyable chunks painful. So on that, mileage may vary depending on you system and how far you push it.
On the wider side, many consider Bioshock 2, shallow from older opinions and reviews. Let me make this clear here, you "Return" to Rapture. Do you expect an entirely new redesigned city? Is it bad that it isn't? Honestly in my opinion, no not in the least. In the first Bioshock game you explore what seems to be a large area of Rapture so what else is there? The answer is plenty, there still is a lot to the massive under water city and its history to learn and explore.
Like the first game you get very little in terms of story to start out with. With Bioshock 2 the core story is this, you
are a Big Daddy, you lost you little sister, you want to find and reunite with her once more. That's basically it, shallow right and I half agree. It's like saying the first Bioshock is purely trying to escape Rapture as a story, its briefness doesn't do it any favours.
In Bioshock 2 you get to decide how, to a much much much greater degree, how the events will transpire. There are Multiple endings highly dependant on how you interact with certain NPCs. Do you seek revenge upon them or do you acknowledge their actions but give mercy and forgiveness? The little Sisters still play a major role in gameplay and ending so that's what I'll get to next.
In Bioshock 2 you get all new all old weapons back. Pistol? Rivet gun, check. Machine gun? .50cal Machine Gun, check. You do however get more in the way of creative applications. With all new trap abilities it makes you consider the environment more when you defend youself and/or your little sister.
Like Bioshock, the lore in Bioshock 2 is contained in audio logs scattered through Rapture as you progress through it. While most is completely optional, it explore in greater depths the history of Rapture, the individuals who designed it, built it and ran it. Also as a special mention there is a neat story of a father and his daughter who was captured and brought to rapture,
So enough of a rant here's how I score the game:
Gameplay - 7.5/10
While several great improvements over the first game were made, like the ability to use both hands at once (plasmid and weapons) as well as the ability to look down sights. The controls still felt clanky, mostly in aim and weight. Aiming from the hip just as in the first game felt more natural and you find yourself more often than not falling back onto only maybe 2-3 of you weapons as your defaults.
The ability to charge plasmids is a cool idea but more often than not I find that the basic plasmid can satisfy its purpose well enough to void the ability to charge or use it as a constant damage/effect which burns though Eve faster than I would like.
New content involving protecting little sisters is fun, especially with the traps you can set up. Early on, you'll probably burn most of your first aid when you fight your first Big Sister. Downside, it gets cramped and very fast. She likes to rush, so between blaring gunfire and plasmids to stun/damage her, attention for anything else is hard, to say anything if you can see anything else anyway, between lightning stuns and fire damage plasmids accompanied by shotgun blasts/machine gun fire.
Overall, an improvement over the first game, but not enough to fix some personal irks. Good not great
Story - 7.5/10
Core story is shallow but then again the expanded story of Rapture itself more expansive as you learn about individuals who made Rapture what it was. Unfortunately is not told to you directly, you have to piece it together youself from audio logs and environmental debris.
Audio & visuals - 8/10
Atmospheric and really suitable are the first things that can be said. Very similar to the first game but that's not a bad thing, although you would expect something different from a sequel.
Replay-ability - 7/10
Honestly I want to give it a higher score for this, I really do. However, gameplay can get repetitive with, go along this path to get here to do this to get here. Best played once, take a break and come back about ~1-2 weeks later fresh to enjoy the game again.
Overall Score - 7.5/10
Fun game, if you liked the first game it's a good sequel. Weaker narrative/story in general but with characters I find more interesting, especially your original little sister, Eleanor.
Best thing about the game: It definitely feels like an upgrade from the first game.
Worst thing: Feels a bit lazy, you get many of the same weapons/plasmids with few new additions. The new additions while fun and interesting don't change the fact that it still feels like the first game.
Recommended

Well. Homefront wasn't actually terrible. It wasn't very good either though.
Lets start with the flaws. For starters, the campaign is notably short and can be beaten in about 4 hours, which includes dying a number of times. The plot is basically Call of Duty: Red Dawn, but a lot less military based and a bit more guerilla warfare based. Basically, it's not very unique.
The context is that in 2013, after the Supreme Leader of North Korea dies, his son unites the North and South to form the Greater Korean Republic. This should be the biggest clue that Homefront is purely speculative fiction and not to be taken seriously as that will never happen. The South (South Korea) had seperated from North Korea just as the Korean war started because of the atrocities that were going on. Anyway, fast forward to 2025, the GKP is a world power and has already taken over four other countries and begins their invasion of the USA. Another two years later, it's 2027 and you are Robert Jacobs, a former Marine combat pilot who is awakes in his beat apartment in Montrose, Colorado. The Koreans have seized the town and are sending you to Alaska for "re-education". Well, as you can assume, you're rescued by the resistance and recruited to help fight the good fight. That's pretty much it. There's little development in character or tone, it's just very one sided. At least Call of Duty (everything since Modern Warfare)  gave the villains a sort of character to help build up their wrongdoings. You don't even get to know the Koreans, they're just targets for all of you.
SPOILERS: There is one level where there might be some shift in tone, but it ends up being a massive firefight anyway. American survivalists; those nut jobs who like to keep their guns close in case something like this would ever happen, which won't. It won't ever happen. But people like the people in this game do exist. In one of the missions, these survivalists have a helicopter you need and basically you end up killing them all.
Well, at least the audio design and graphics were nice. The campaign was still fun to play, but it's nothing special. More of thing where you play it just to pass the time and you only own it because it was in a THQ Humble Bundle or it was on sale for like 3 bucks.

I want to be clear here: My problem with Hatred isn't its violence. But once you get over the violent premise, there's really not much of a fun game left here. I would say at best it's very average, but Hatred does not live up anywhere close to its hype.
The best way to summarize Hatred is "kill x number of people to move on to the next level" about eight times, with the occasional side mission of "kill x people at this location on the other side of the map". After a while, it became a chore to get kills because of the dumb pedestrian AI, frequently running directly into fire and explosions I didn't even create.
The "armed" AI is a lot smarter, but quickly becomes frustrating as they have the ability to track and shoot you at a range much farther than what you see onscreen or your radar can see. I'm pretty sure 85% of the time I was getting shot at, it was by offscreen enemies. I played on the "Normal" difficulty, so this is probably even more frustrating on higher levels.
The black and white graphics also hinder the game a lot. While I got through most levels without too much trouble, the lack of coloring oftentimes making it tough to spot items or enemies that can be finished off. The only way to regain health is by these finishers, which repeat way too often. There's an option to disable the animations, which I imagine most people will end up doing just because there are only a handful of execution animations, so it gets old fast.
Finally, the weapons. Most of them work well enough, but the pistol does so little damage it makes me wonder why they even bothered to include it, usually taking a full clip to kill an unarmed enemy, even on the easiest difficulty. The shotgun does decent damage, but it has a stupid mechanic where it loads one shell at a time. You might be thinking "big deal, most shooters with shotguns do that", but Hatred makes you HOLD the Reload button to put every shell in, meaning that it's next to impossible to move while reloading with it. It's especially frustrating because no other gun in the game makes you hold the key, just tap R and you load a new clip in like every other shooter.
Honestly, I'd just stick with Postal 1 if you want a top-down shooter about a rampaging psychopath.

A hard one to judge only as a yes/no recommendation.
Theres little game here - not runing out of fuel, food and people - wich serves as needed pressure for making choices. Too little game for what itself proposes (i was expecting character changes in traits for example) for its normal price tag.
But for what little 'game' it contains it makes up for it with story and writting.
One of the most creative space opera journeys ive seen- one with more science in science fiction then pretty much any similar ive played and does Sci-fi right: what you meet on your journeys are the kind of interesting outcomes that are theorically viable considering how weird physics, evolution, space travel, time dillatation at relativistic speeds and others can shape the most outlandish outcomes.
My first run went down hill too quickly, so much i was ready to criticize on the forums... but i sticked with it.
It turned out to be a long journey downhill of 'bad choices' and ever smaller crew...
...and to my surprise...
...i reached my mission goal.
As an AI helping my crew find a new home for mankind. In the most unexpected way. One i would hardly agree with as a human, much less a 21st century one. But one i can't really argue against.
I will avoid spoilers. Suffice to say i went immediatly here to recomend the game.
-Don't come expecting challenging gameplay but challenging story choices.
-Around half of these (or more, depending on rng and crew) aren't even informed choices - wich ends up being very fitting for the whole theme and feeling as dealing with the unknow and surprises is a unavoidable part of such a journey.
-Have less variety and quantity in tone and encounters then similars ive played BUT
-Have more well tought, written and mindscrapping sci-fi then any of those; Also encounters aren't a single dialogue box with few choices if any of similars but small adventures; Chunks of a choose-your-adventure/game book.
-Could have been more, leaves me wanting- wich is as positive as negative: few games makes me want more of them.
Like story games and sci-fi? Then go for it.

I've been trying to think of a non-trope way to express my enjoyment of this game, and I just can't; there's no better way to describe it other than:
This game doesn't just mess with your expectations, it takes them and shapes them and rearranges them, then hands them back and encourages you to help it destroy them. I have completed most of the endings in less than 5 hours actual playtime, as well as being awarded most of the achievements. That doesn't matter though, I'm going to fire it up every few days just for another run through, because even though I've seen it all I haven't seen anything. There feels like a million different things that can happen, although there's only ("only"!) twenty different endings. It's the way you join up those endings that matters, and the multitudes of alternate dialogue lines that you can hear, and that one time you're not expecting it there will be something you've not heard before. Even though I don't think it makes any difference to the various stories, there's a choice I haven't yet been able to make in a different way because it's only appeared once.
Would I have paid full price? Probably not, but then I'm not sure how many people ever do nowadays; with a Steam sale every few weeks, there's little impetus to do so. Am I happy with the price I paid? Definitely.

The Away Team is a interactive sci-fi adventure novel in which you are the AI pilot of Earth's last interstellar ship, tasked with finding a home for your crew.
The gameplay is relatively simple in design, when beginning a new game you select a crew from a list of possible members each with their own set of careers, skills and personality which establishes your available team for the rest of the game.
The game then moves into the space exploration and resource management, in many cases there is only a single planet to select from which appears random on the small area of space that is traversable, it is here that fuel and food come into play as the ship moves to a world or to the edge of the map to light speed travel. Both tick down slowly fuel from movement and food in real time to add a sense of urgancy, as the game does not reveal this fact it comes across as more of an annoyance.
Once at a planet or station of interest the core mechanic of the game the away missions begin, from here you must select up to six people to send on a mission to investigate and search for resources, interacting with self contained stories on each world though in rare cases information gleamed on one world can aid choices on another.


Final verdict: I have had quite a bit of fun with the game but it does feel a tad overpriced and I predict replayability issues, however if the community gets behind this then the possibility for additional stories and developments through writting and modding can add a great deal of further life to this well written adventure
If you like adventure game books and the concept then grab it in a bundle or on sale when you can.

tl:dr: The store page is very honest about what this is. I strongly recommend reading all of it, because the excerpt in particular is very honest about what a lot of this game is. If you're intrigued by that, you'll probably love this. If you're unsure, you probably won't.
Your mileage with this one will depend entirely on whether text-only exploration in a choose your own adventure-style game is enough for you. The gameplay basically comes down to resource management and crew selection, but neither of these would be deep enough to sustain the game on their own. Look elsewhere if they're requirements for you.
Steam's suggestions for The Away Team are, for once, pretty accurate. Its world building and depth of scenarios is comparable to 80 Days. The investigation of failed societies and focus on generation ships is similar to Analogue: A Hate Story. The branching paths have a lot in common with Sorcery and assorted Choice Of games, although in this case the stats and traits are associated with your crew members rather than yourself.
I'm reluctant to say any more because the value of this game is really in the discovery. Suffice to say that you're looking at solid writing (albeit with noticeable typos), creative scenarios, and impressively detailed character personalities and interactions for what it is. You're not going to remember them in ten years, but they've got actual traits, motivations, and consistent behaviors, which is more than you can say for most redshirt analogues. Easy thumbs up.

I feel like I have to give this game a thumbs up because it's quite good and well-made in many ways. It's a logic puzzle game reminiscent of zachtronics games, based on circuitry and logic gates, where instead of being presented with a straight-up puzzle or being asked to produce a particular output, you have to disarm a bomb. It's quite good. It really eases you into it if you've never played such a game before, but it does throw in some clever tricks, and the sense of tension that goes along with a ticking bomb adds something to it. But it's too short.
I got through this entire game in 74 minutes, and I would say that despite having played similar games in the past I actually had a bit more trouble with it than I should have had. Even someone who's not a fan of logic games or puzzle games at all could get through the game at least as fast, probably faster.
The game desperately needs a level/bomb editor and workshop support. I really, really hope the dev uses some of the money they're getting from this to work on adding those things, along with some other additions: more mechanisms (particularly detonator types; I feel like there's some potential to get creative with bombs that need you to do things other than cut off the power or send power to the right places to defuse them) and possibly even stuff to build more than just bombs in an editor mode. With user content and Workshop support, this could be almost on par with some of the best games in the genre (i.e. zachtronics, pretty much) but more accessible to people who aren't puzzle/electrical engineering/programming nerds.
At CDN$ 6.62 (15% off), I was pretty disappointed. At the same time, let's be honest, some of my lunches cost more than $6.62, so I can't complain too much. It's not such an unfair price even if you can get more content for the same price in other games. But if the dev uses some of the money to add Workshop support and/or more content, I'll be more than satisfied.

Bioshock 2:
I played Bioshock 2 over a series of 3 months. It failed to maintain my immediate interest and remained in the shadows of more enthralling games, so my playthrough was erratic.
As a reader of this review, it would be a mistake to derive from this that Bioshock 2 is a bad title. It's a decent game, with its fair share of pros and cons. Ultimately though, there are better accomplished FPS games out there with more content, richer stories and more engaging combat.
+ The story is fine, once again it is heavily supported by the inclusion of audio logs that can be discovered in each level, which shed light on Rapture and the events transpiring. As a Big Daddy, you must rescue your daughter, Eleanor Lamb, from her Mother Sofia, who is intent on turning her into a "selfless person who works for the common good of humanity", but one that subsequently, has no free will.
~ The fighting is neither good nor bad, it's just so-so. There's no improvement to plasmids in comparison to the original Bioshock, bar some upgrades. They're the same plasmid abilities as before, nothing new or creative, copy and paste. There's several new weapons though - the multi barrel machinegun, the spear gun and of course the Big Daddy Drill, but this small variety is not enough to uplift the combat to high heights.
~ As with the first Bioshock, the graphics are not great and as a result they sabotage, to some extent, your feeling of immersion in the game.
~ Bioshock 2 has the same enemies as the first Bioshock, splicers return as the main enemy you'll encounter. Occasionally you'll come into contact with Big Sisters, a mini boss, sometimes super strong hulk-like creatures and Big Daddies protecting little sisters. But in the end, it doesn't feel very unique to the original.
- Linear game, much like the first. Go from point A to B. While this seems to be a common feature of FPS games, it doesn't mean it's fun or that it should be overlooked.
- 14 hours of gameplay time on medium difficulty, very short..
- Bioshock 2 is very generous in loot rewards (money, ammo, first aid kits, eve), meaning it is not challenging whatsoever. I started on hard and progressed with ease, until I died in a battle. My last save was a good 40-45 minutes ago and I couldn't be bothered slogging it out to get back there, so I turned it down to medium and left it there. Hard difficulty just means playing cautiously and more slowly. There's nothing inherently harder about it. Which brings me to my final point.
- Autosave is very unreliable, it amazes me this game lacks a proper autosave system.
Overall Score: 6.5/10
Bioshock 2 is a short-lived action game with a nice story, and ok combat, but too many recycled features from the original to stand on a pedestal and shine brightly. Worth purchasing on sale only.

That aside my review is based solely on the single player campaign and it is for those of you who are considering getting this game for the campaign.

I couldn't care less about any of the characters, in fact I wanted Connor to die. He annoyed the crap out of me.
The story/plot felt so mediocre that they even managed to fulfill the stereotypical Asian engineer/computer technical guy and the black guy that

Rebel Galaxy is a space trading and combat simulator that reminds me of Freelancer, but with bigger ships. In this game, you are a guy who gets a message from his Aunt Juno to take her old ship and fly to some station a long way from home to meet her. And guess what? She's not there. The story isn't as much the highest point of the game, but the gameplay and the galaxy you explore are phenominal.
Gameplay is based around trading or fighting to upgrade or replace your ship in order to meet the increasing difficulty that comes with each new sector. While you might think you're pretty strong in your big, bada$$ ship with lasers and cannons galore that rips apart other ships like they're made of thin paper, every new sector you go to will smack you down and force you to realize that there are people out there that will eat you for breakfast, spit you out, and do it again for lunch.
This spike in difficulty keeps the game fresh, as you don't get to feel like a demigod for very long, and if you want to stay feeling like a demigod, you have to actually work for it. The learning curve takes a while to get used to, but once you learn the basics, the game really opens up as you explore and fight your way through the galaxy fighting for pirates and outcasts for the good of the people, or robbing merchants and fighting the military because you can. Or, you can do what some AI who has downloaded inself into your ship's computer tells you to do and help it regain its memory.
Overall, I give this a 9/10 for a extreamly challenging and sometimes punishing experience, and for bringing a fresh perspective to the world of space combat and trading sims. Now I have to go back to wondering how I will blow up that Dreadnought looming in the distance... and now I'm dead because missiles and lazers.

I like this game.  A LOT!  I bought it because I was looking for something similar to EVE, but without the malicious player base that EVE is notorious for.  This game filled that nitch nicely.
PROS:
This is one of the few games I've played recently, where the keyboard/mouse control scheme is every bit as good as the Console Controller scheme.    Intuitive and effective keyboard control make this a joy to play without a controller.
The Graphics are Very nice, and Don't require a Monster video card to run.  (I'm running it on an old nvidia 9800 gt with 512mb of Vram and it runs just fine.  Framerate rarely drops below 60fps, unless I turn on depth of field and motion blur.  Then it still plays fine until I get into a nebula, where my framerate starts to crawl with certain effects, so I would recommend playing with those two settings turned off if you are using a lower end video card.
The story is interesting enough and the voice acting is well done.
The combat is where this Game really really shines.  It's very well executed, with controls that feel natural and fluid, and the explosions when enemy ships pop are extremely satisfying.
The 'Missions' section of the game  is well set up and fun to play.  Mining works fine, and trading is functional enough.
You can hire a mercenary (only one at a time) to fly with you and help you fight, and early in the game, they are quite strong.
This game has a really cool feature called 'warp pairing' where you escort a ship by moving up in a flanking position and select the 'enable warp pairing' feature, that basicly causes you to follow the lead ship through warp while staying in formation  (sort of like gang warping in EVE online)  It works well most of the time, however, asteroid fields and such can cause the ship you're escorting to get a little confused sometimes.  It's still fun to do though and is a nice change from the typical; "Go here and kill everything." type missions.
Cons:
One of the biggest Cons for me is the difficutly system.  It is based on a number of factors, (Star system, equipment grade, ship type, etc) and it works well early on.  However around the later part of the second system and beyond, the difficulty gets a bit unstable.  You will run into large difficulty spikes that seem to come out of nowhere.  It leaves the game feeling a little unpolished, and can be frustrating.  (in the second system, I was using all Mark III equipment and weapons, and I got a Mark IV mining laser from an enemy drop so I popped it on... and promptly got blown up over and over again until I took that little booger back off again.  Adding that one cheesy mining laser pushed me up into a higher difficulty bracket and made doing even simple missions very difficult or even impossible.  My advice?  Don't upgrade weapons one at a time.  Save your money and do them all at once so you actually have the firepower to take on that next difficulty bracket.)
Trading can be profitable, but is a bit clunky.  There is no realtime feed telling you what prices are in various stations/systems so the only way to see if you will make a profit is to physically go there and look for yourself.  A live feed (or at the very least a price list that updates once a day or so, would be a huge help, and would save the player from making tons of wasted trips to stations.)
One of the few things I dislike about the keyboard/mouse setup is what I call; "the-one-press-wonder-key".  The 'E' key does various things depending what is available at the moment.  The problem lies with the fact that if several options are open at the same time, the key starts popping from one option to another as you fly close to them.  I've been caught trying to 'tractor beam' some loot into my hold and had the prompt switch as I'm pressing the key so that instead of getting the loot, I warp away.  Same thing when trying to loot while close to a station.  You end up docking instead of looting.  This happens alot and is pretty frustrating sometimes.
Enemies tend to spam really annoying weapons at you when you move beyond the first area.  Leach missles and mines that screw up your engines and shields are used constantly in the later game and they are quite irritating.  There are ways to protect yourself to an extent, but they require precious component slots to equip, and most ships don't have enough space for all the systems you will need.
Verdict:
Even with the Cons mentioned above, I find this game very fun (I've spent over 300 hours on Rebel Galaxy at the time of this writing) and I would recommend it to anyone looking for a Space ship game based around Capital ship combat and broadside bombardments!  There's nothing as satisfying as scraping hulls with an enemy ship and unleashing your Broadsides into it!  Amazing!

Did you ever watch

If no, that means you're either in the wrong place or you haven't watched Firefly. Go do that now.

is a singleplayer open-world spaceship RPG set in distant future.
As the player, you receive a message from your old aunt Juno asking you to travel to the frontier. Riddled with piracy, military conflicts, intrigues and other mysteries your arrival marks the beginning of a long journey.
Aside from the story you can choose to undertake thousands (if not more) of different sidejobs, it can be anything from an escort mission to the elimination of a key pirate leader hiding in a asteroid field.
Freedom is key and the player has many choices available to them, each granting you different perks but also changing the way the rest of the galaxy sees you.
A player who help traders and merchants during distress calls or who actively pursue pirate fleets will be seen as friendly by the Confederate militia while a player who smuggles contraband, ambush militia patrols and disrupt authorities will be seen as a friend by the pirates.
In Rebel Galaxy the systems you fly in feel very much alive, stopping at a station just to view the newsboard inside the bar is a good idea as it will provide you with all kinds of information regarding politics, bounties or good trading opportunities.
Planets can go to war with eachother, raising the demand for military equipment which in turn allows you to profit from it. If you want the conflict to escalate you can destroy any treaty vessels which attempt to broke peace.
Or maybe you're more of a honest businessman? If so tech booms and market gluts will be your best friends, lowering the value of goods at certain stations so you can buy them en masse only to sell them off at a fringe world for a hefty sum of credits.
If that doesn't sound like your type of gig you can always become a freelancing bountyhunter or mercenary, tracking down pirate lords or escorting merchants through rough space.
The choice is yours.
Gameplay-wise Rebel Galaxy is pretty straightforward, with easy-to-understand mechanics, helpful tutorial prompts and simple controls.
In Rebel Galaxy the combat relies on three things: turrets, broadside ports and secondary ports.
When not controlled by the player, turrets will act independently and target any hostile craft within the range or specific craft (you can choose).
Broadsides are your main weapons and are used to obliterate enemy capital ships, broadsides can be anything from lasers to cannons.
Finally, secondary ports are used for equipping fixed weapons and launchers such as flak guns, dumbfire missile launchers or mine catapults.
Overall it's a very straightforward system even though it does get a bit repetitive after a certain point.
The controls for Rebel Galaxy are simple and easy to understand, the player has access to full control mapping.
As for the UI, it's very clean and elegant. It shows exactly what you need without cluttering up the screen.
All in all Rebel Galaxy is a fun game. While it might suffer from being repetitive at a certain point it's stilla solid game which I highly recommend.
Also, the soundtrack is amazing. Look it up.

The best way to describe this game, I think, is to imagine a simplified Freelancer that doesn't take itself nearly as seriously. It has this sort of disjointed western-slash-Caribbean pirate theme to it that works brilliantly in its favor, lending a much needed injection of comic-book stylization to the genre of space trade & combat sim.
The voice acting is good enough not to be grating or distracting, which is great.
What's a little less great (but maybe not by a lot) is the two-dimensional flight. Again, simplified. A 6DOF shooter, this is not. If you can do naval combat, you will probably do fine here. To me, this makes the game feel a little strange, not being able to fly up or down in space. But not a deal breaker.
The soundtrack is very fun and unique, but some of the tracks end up sounding a little same-y after a few hours.
Gameplay pacing moves about the same as Freelancer, so if you enjoyed that title, you will probably feel justified in spending full price on this one. If you're expecting a fast-paced space shooter, maybe wait until it goes on sale.

I like The Away Team in concept. Again, it's neat in theory, and the pixel crew and soundtrack are a nice touch, but unless you're really into text heavy space exploration, I can't see why you'd want to spend time or $10 on this.

This is NOT an FS2013 clone so if you want a farm tycoon, farm management sim DO NOT BUY. If you want auto everything DO NOT BUY.
This game is about BEING a farmer. It's hard graft and can get quite tedious. You do have AI of sorts but it's click-done AI, not a pixel farmer you can follow around.
My review gets a + only if you understand that it's about BEING a farmer. If that's what you like, get it. You'll enjoy it.
Now to flesh this out.
- The graphics are pretty good and on on i7/670gtx, it hums along maxed out at 60 (with vsync). Some of the detail is very well done, albeit with a very Euro flavour.
- The tute is on rails and must be followed but once you learn the locations and the techniques it's better to go freeplay.
- Tractor driving is very manual and takes some getting used to. NOTE: *Look* at the lower left for how to change the gearbox ratios.  (And reversing is REAL reversing, not just pressing a down key).
- Some machines are missing cruise control at time of writing. Missing as in, devs probably assumed it wasn't needed. They were wrong and as far as I know, will change it.
CROPS
- Limited but enough to keep interest. (and in reality, not all farms can grow all crops anyway)
- Seasonal variations (a big feature) in yield work fairly accurately and devs are working on making it better.
- Seed prices. Enough to make BEING a farmer worthwhile.
ANIMALS
- As good as non existent. Worth having for the extra income (3k or so per qtr) but there is no management or husbandry. (and it's incorrect for many to believe all farms have animals anyway - a common complaint. Most "real" farms are fairly dedicated enterprises. Such diversity is usually reserved for smaller hobby farms,  certainly in Australia anyway)
EQUIPMENT
- A bit short in this department (again devs are on it) but there is certainly enough to crop and harvest every field with ease.
- The equipment shop is badly designed and laid out (imho) but equipment purchases are close to a one-off in RL anyway.
FIELDS
- Some nice looking layering is used for the various states and the PDA provides field status etc. as you work.
- Crop yields etc. are RT as you harvest (F2 PDA)
MAP
- Big. Generous number of paddocks. No real monsters but you'll be working really hard if you own even a quarter of them.
- Shop to shop transactions. Poorly done. You gotta drive to the bank, the seed shop, the tractor shop manually - everytime. Will devs change this? Unknown but can be very, very tedious. (see gearbox ratios above - take stock of it).
OVERALL
- A good game for players who like the down and dirty of farming. I reiterate though, if you want an "auto" farm managment game, DO NOT BUY.
- Scenery is nice, gameplay is consistent. Some glaring anomalies but very easy to forgive.
- Sound is pretty ordinary and equipment sounds are pretty lame. No engine load being the biggest let down. It won't take long to despise the music but a few well placed Oggs can fix that.
There are some issues, some by poor design, some by poor release. Devs seem to be willing to listen and ready to take on constructive critique.
I'd say a price of $20 is reasonable but it's relative. If you're tight for cash but love to farm, wait for the specials.

This game is a marvelous piece of storytelling that kept me engaged to the very end.
It's the future.  The Earth is permanently screwed.  You are the AI on one of the last cryo ships to leave the planet in search of a new home for the humans in your care.  Your decisions are what will ultimately decide their fate.
The game plays like a Choose Your Own Adventure novel, and feels like you're directing your own episodes of Star Trek.  With each new planet you discover, you must weigh the risks of exploration.  Food and fuel are constantly being depleted, so will you push your away teams to dig deeper into alien territory and potentially stay ahead of the game, but risk losing some of them, or will you decide that the risk is too great, and potentially put them in danger of starving to death?  Will you judge situations with blind optimism, with fairness, with caution, or with an aggressive iron fist?
In any case, your decisions will most certainly have consequences, but you must weather them in order to achieve the ultimate goal; finding your human crew a place to hang their hats.
If heavy reading is not your thing, you probably won't enjoy this game very much.  However, if you like things that are intensely story-rich, then this should be right up your alley.  You'll be reading a lot of text, making choices, and deciding which crew to send where based on their strengths and weaknesses.  Some crewmembers are better in certain situations than others, so choose carefully.
The stories were varied, from humorous to ominous, and it was easy to imagine most of what was going on in my head.  At the very end of my first run, I found myself smiling.  It was not only entertaining, but highly satisfying.
A quality hidden gem, in my opinion, and most definitely deserving of a recommendation.

BioShock will have been out ten years ago tomorrow (August 21, 2007), so i figured it was long overdue to post a quick review of one of my favorite games of all time. With all the versions combined (the Xbox, original PC release, Remastered) i've easily spent over 500 hours playing and taking screenshots of the game, and to this day, it has never lost its special quality that hooked me from the very first time i booted up the demo. While this is mainly a review for the overall experience, which is pretty much identical between this version and the original, i'll add a few thoughts about remastered too.
~ Remastered version ~
I like about 85% of the texture changes. Most of them are equal, if not better, than the original, artistically speaking. A few though, are too detailed, too dark or too different for my tastes. The added plant and seal life are great, helping to make any scene out in the sea a treat to look at. This alone is the biggest selling point to me. The added 60fps physics are welcome too, making things look that much smoother (you can get a physics unlocker for the original PC version though). The included challenge maps and museum are really neat. I'm so glad they included them. And finally, plants and banners move now, which brings a little more life into the static environments.
I noticed a few changes i didn't like.
-The water cascading down stairs sometimes cuts off on the edge of each stair. As in, the water just disappears in thin slices. A small detail, but noticeable.
-The shiny/wet look has been toned down. This look really worked well for Rapture. Not sure why they changed it.
- Fire/flames aren't as smooth looking as before. It almost seems like its missing frames or something. Like the water cascading, its a small but noticeable detail, if you're looking for it.
- Similar to the fire, but much more noticeable, the weapon animations for zooming, reloading and swinging the wrench, stutter. Its not smooth and looks like its missing frames too.
- Certain bags/containers cant be opened anymore. I've only seen this a few times though.
- A couple of spots have changed/toned down lighting.
Overall, a very solid effort. If they had fixed a couple of these issues with some patches, i think this could have been the definitive version.
Big thanks to 2k for the review copy.
~ Original BioShock review ~
Rapture is a city like no other. Built on the seafloor of the North Atlantic ocean, it was a place to escape the growing threat of nuclear war, as well as government and religious interference, while at the same time championing things like personal freedom, science and industry. Construction began in 1945 and it was officially opened up to its carefully chosen guests on Nov 5, 1946. With its grand Art Deco architecture, glowing neon signs and glass tunnels connecting the towering buildings, it was a spectacle that could take your breath away, time and time again.
BioShock as a whole hits so many right notes and i feel it’s one of gaming’s crowning achievements, especially when it comes to its visuals. Something that’s quickly apparent is that you’ve never played a game that looks quite like this. Its well researched art direction is flawless and coupled with creepy atmosphere and the huge glass windows looking out into the depths, it has a way of mesmerizing you from the second you start playing.
Since this sunken metropolis is crumbling around you, letting the ocean leak in at any structural weak point, Irrational devoted an entire team to just the water effects. And it’s something you can see and feel at every turn, with each flooded room and cascading waterfall reminding you that the ocean is relentlessly beating down on Rapture. The fire and particle effects were cutting edge at the time back in 2007 and still look fantastic to this day. Tons of little touches help to immerse you in this dystopian world, like the eerie patches of thick fog and the always entertaining advertisements plastered around the city. The contrasted lighting fits the game perfectly, bringing tension and uncertainty to every room you explore. Level design is also top notch, with unique and well laid out areas full of visual storytelling. The amazing detail in every level truly helps to drive the narrative just as much as any character. From the the beautifully overgrown Arcadia to the glamorous and extravagant Fort Frolic, Rapture is an unforgettable place to visit.

There are already some great reviews here, so I'll keep mine brief and attempt to not repeat what has already been said.
I've only played about an hour and a half of this game and I'm already overwhelmingly impressed. I had this game on my wishlist for some time because I was unsure of how it would play. I managed to snag it on an 80% off sale, and I must say, had I known this game was so nice, I would have gladly paid full price for it.
So far, the only drawback of this game seems to be the lack of voice acting, but that's honestly nothing I've ever been upset about. I've even played my fair share of text based rpgs. I'm also not a graphics junkie so the assets don't bother me at all. Additionally, this game doesn't lead you by the hand, which really isn't a drawback in my opinion. If you read and observe your surroundings, you'll slowly peice together what it is you're meant to do... or at least, build a perception of what you believe you are supposed to do... who knows why you're truely here? I sure don't yet (and I'm excited to find out).
My review of this game?
The enemies are noticibly clever, and that always makes me happy. They pause to attack when you're reloading, aim where you will be as you straife instead of where you were, and search for you where they last saw you if they lose sight of you.
I enjoy piecing together plot through dialogue, and this game has that, by allowing you to find and converse with wraiths and shadows that either barely or don't at all remember who they once were. Being able to travel back and forth between the 'night' and the 'day' adds an extra dimension to the semi-open world.
I've always enjoyed horror, adventure, puzzle, games, much like Silent Hill, but I've never played one in a more wilderness style setting. It's quite refreshing to experience.
If these traits sound like something that will entertain you, and you don't mind the lack of spoken dialogue, prefab assets, and lots of reading and retracing your steps, this game is well worth $5, in my humble opinion. These are the sorts of games that should definitely be supported.

It's Magic: the Gathering that updates with each new set, letting you play with the flagship cards from each and play whenever you want. If you're a Magic player who has trouble finding people to play with or time to go to your local game shop, I can't recommend this enough.
Now understand, this isn't hardcore, competitive Magic. This isn't going to prepare you for the next PTQ, but that's not what it's meant to be. It's fun, casual Magic. You can just play around with silly, fun decks against the computer or try to be the best, playing against other humans. There's even 2-headed giant mode, though they're still fine-tuning the programming. The platform is very much still in development, and there's still a lot of work to be done, so keep that in mind.
It's free, updating Magic: the Gathering that you can play whenever you want. If that isn't going to make you play it, I can't imagine anything else that would.
It's a very funny game ifyou like solving puzzles! Try it out, you won't regret it! I'm 100% sure.

The developers kinda had their fun providing solutions for the very easy ones but nothing for the hardest, which is kinda a nonsense and the biggest flaw in my view. To make things worst, there's zero help on their website, other than cute coments, and found nothing relevant around the net.
So, I must make my recommendation both negative and positive:
- I recommend the game for the extensive content and the price. Is funny most of the time and the puzzles are different and mostly fair. Found no bug or crashes.
- I don't recommend the game if you want to finish it or if you are an achivement collector. These developers went from making something fun to make fun of the players not providing a "veteran" challenge at the last levels but rather an "Are you bored yet?" experience. Probably that's why most positive comments come from people that had little time playing this. Otherwise I think the reviews would be much negative. A casual game can be difficult, but not boring, purposely frustating difficult.
So, all things considered, I'll go for the negative.
The single player mode is sort of too short for the price $19.99, btw, everything is amazing, so consider before buying !

What's cool about the pvp is that you can type to people while you kill 'em, so there's a good, nice, hopeful community playing the game, we hope the community grows but it's definitely an older game. I think it's hard for me to express how much I'm in love with this game. The unique style of 'flat' space combat allows for combat to be focused on broadside cannons. The lack of a "Z" axis of movement allows focus for more tactical real time decision making in combat instead of focusing on keeping your nose pointed at a lead indicator like most space games.
The music and theme are amazing as well! This is the frontier of space, so naturally theres an old west theme throughout The music consists of driving rock & metal rooted in the old west. It evokes fond memories of the T.V. show Firefly during some chords.
It's worth mentioning that if you're looking for a space exploration game along the lines of the X series or Elite, that's not really what this is. This is a space adventure with exploration elements. On sale this game is an absolute must buy imo, but it's worth the current full price as well.

This game is almost good, but there are a few unpolished aspects of it that make the experience less enjoyable.
Mostly just minor shortcomings in rules and coherence, but also some major aspects of gameplay. Some examples:
-You cant view maps before playing them in singleplayer
-Your own ships wander stupidly into minefields even when you tell them to hold position
-There is only skirmish mode in singleplayer, despite the misleading cinematic trailer
-Pirates continue to launch raids after youve decimated their entire base
-Build times are painfully slow for everything, and there are constant deadlocks where your only option is just to wait and watch your resources tick upwards at an agonizing rate (this can probably be resolved on larger maps with more planets)
-Along a similar vein, upgrades are weak (5-10% bonuses, maybe 25% when maxed out) which is fine if you like the RPG style gameplay, but if you like shorter matches (smaller maps), you can only get fractional increases in power before you are at the endgame.
-Upgrades have very minor visual effects (if any) and battle amount to just watching ships stand in place repeatedly firing little uneventful beams at each other for minutes on end
etc..
I would hold off on this one unless you get it in a sale.

If you enjoy gunning down innocents and being an antagonist, then you'll enjoy this. I don't really have much else to add.
A couple tips to enjoying it, however:
First off, it's not optimized the best, so I recommend minimal settings, then adjusting up until you reach that middle.
Also, if you have minor problems, say, want to change all lamp posts into tall torches, and there is no mod for it, STAY AWAY FROM THE EDITOR. It is a convoluted mess.
(Okay, now I'm going to explain the editor, so if you aren't into modding, don't bother reading this.)
So there is a "The Room" mod for this game. It doesn't work due to the game's updates. So I decided to download the editor when it came out, and try getting it working, thinking the editor would be like Skyrim's Creation Kit or the Fallout GECK. You know, something easy to start up, use, and then be done with. I was dead wrong. First off, you have to download literally gigabytes, which I'm okay with, but if you are low on space, it might be a problem. Secondly, instead of ACTUALLY STARTING AN EDITOR, it shows a log in screen. For GitHub.
Now, that's not a problem. I can understand wanting to use an open-source coding website (if that's what it is. I still have no idea.) What is a problem is you have to jump through so many goddamn hoops. So if you love editing and all that, you won't really mind. Hell, it might even be BETTER than some modding tools I've seen. (I wouldn't know. I gave up after a few hours deciding cleaning and taxes is a better use of my time.)
BUT. AND I REPEAT. BUT, IF YOU WANT TO MAKE A SMALL TWEAK, THEN YOU'RE LIFE WILL BE HELL FOR A COUPLE HOURS.
And that's really where my resentment lies. That you have to go through so much, just to change ONE LITTLE THING. It's not friendly to those who out of the blue decide to do something with it, and make a small change. Because then they suffer hours of frustration and anger. (And then they probably give a reasonlessly spiteful review)
It's also not fun trying to figure it out, because you have to seriously SEARCH for instructions on how to get everything working.
Well, at least we have the Youtube video to show what it was like when "The Room" mod was playable. That's a small comfort.

The year is 2127. Earth has been destroyed, made uninhabitable by war, climate change and famine. You play as the AI on a ship containing the last known humans in the universe. Can you keep them alive as you search for a new home?
The Away Team is superbly written interactive fiction, a modern day ‘Choose Your Own Adventure’ set in space. There are survival elements too, in that you have to scavenge planets for food fuel; otherwise you’ll end up starving, or stranded in space forever.
The graphics are basic, but for what’s essentially a sci-fi novel, they fit well enough. The music is atmospheric and calming, the sort of thing you can have a good afternoon nap to (I’m so rock and roll, I know).
There’s a lot of reading in this game, as it features huge swathes of text. Not surprising, given the genre, but if reading’s not your thing, this game probably won’t be either. I thoroughly enjoyed it though, pootling around from planet to planet, frequently panicking, running out of food and fuel and sending my crew out on dangerous missions to replenish our stocks (where they died, more often than not).
One criticism I do have, however, is that when you make a choice that leads to the death of a crew member, the graphics show you instantly that they’re dead, despite the fact you won’t have reached that far in the text yet. It does spoil the surprise somewhat.
There was one particularly enjoyable segment featuring a mad robot who forces you to re-enact a blisteringly confusing Shakespearean play. The AI’s response? ‘Ah, I was wondering when we’d meet our first insane robot.’ Let’s face it, everyone loves a good space play.
There’s replayability here, not just because of the standard ‘search on the left’ or ‘search on the right’ mechanic, but also because you select your crew at the start of the game. Each crew member has their own back story and different traits, making some more suitable for roles or missions than others; and when you’re in a sticky situation, they can react differently based on their own strengths and weaknesses. It’s a neat addition.
Games like this succeed (or fail) on their story and writing, and The Away Team doesn’t disappoint in that regard. The writing is intelligent and witty, and the story is intriguing. It’s just a shame my entire crew were incinerated in an explosion.
If it sounds like it’s your sort of thing, then it probably is, and you should check this one out.

It is hard to name a genre most people would readily recognize for
.  A
book would be the most familiar analogue for gamers.  Like
, without the space combat and trade.  Right from the getgo I know we've lost some folk.  This is a niche, but one that is not flooded the way zombie survival shooters and block crafting games are.
In this you take on the role of the artificial intelligence tasked with saving a tiny crew of the last people to leave a dying Earth.  You select a crew that are for the most part interchangeable parts, then set out to find a new home.  In the course of your journey you use Food and Fuel while sending down crew members on Away Missions a la Star Trek.  Your three resources (Food, Fuel, Fools) will slowly trickle away as you pursue the new home your crew need.  Unfortunately for you and your crew you have become Lost In Space and though you set out in the most advanced ship available - you have fallen far behind those you were following.  You won't be finding much direct help from other survivors.
You are alone in a vacuum filled with things that intend to kill you.
There are branching stories you can work through, some beneficial and some outright dangerous. Missions vary, but you will find replays to be a little stale as you must go through the same prerequisite missions before you can make a different choice in a sequence.
I think the game would greatly benefit from the crew's traits and trust in the AI influencing events more, along with an increased number of starting level missions to encounter that let the AI and crew develop a relation (be it as an aloof AI, a kindly administrator, a mother figure, a mad scientist, an adventurer).  Maybe letting you influence the crew enough to alter traits.  I would have particularly liked to see some logic puzzles that the AI had to solve to gain the respect of the crew.  A reward of a new choice for starting crew member when successful would have been nice as well.
Enjoyable read, and a challenge.  I hope to see a followup where the game invokes elements of Escape Velocity and Faster Than Light.  Worth checking out.

This is one of those games that just kind of sneaks up on you. While at first it may not seem like much, the creators certainly spent a lot of time making the entire narrative very flexible yet engrossing. Every character is a unique individual, and each reacts in their own way to doing what has to be done. You can try to play the good guy and help those starving children, might even help keep moral up by doing so, but when you realize you gave away your last meal you'll end up robbing some old couple--which does wonders for that good samaritan feeling...
The combat system is actually fairly in-depth for a 2.5D game, even if having to use it means something probably just went very very wrong. The game constantly auto-saves and attempts to save-scum just end up with a corrupted game file that has to be manually removed in order to even start a new game. In other words, yeah, when you accidentally forgot to peek before you bust down a door and end up taking a shotgun to the face... maybe next time you'll walk. Or in my case: when it seems like a nice day out at 18 degrees C and you decide you don't need that extra log on the fire... only to come home and find Ronan froze to death because the temperature dropped sharply to -5 overnight... Short sweet intelligent adventure masterpiece.
The Away Team is as self described "interactive sci-fi adventure novel". If you're unsure what that means, it reminds me of a traditional/older visual novel I've played long time ago, Tsukihime which focused more on text driven narrative than visual and auditory aids. The American equivalent would be Goosebump novels I guess. I wouldn't really call it a text-based adventure
as in the same category of say.. Zork. During the course of the story telling, there are actions provided to you that may alter the story... and in some cases harm your crew.
Some love/some hate the soundtrack. Honestly, I didn't enjoy the music, not within the game at least, it started off with a good vibe, music well suited to the narrative, but proceeded to provide a jarring hindrance to my immersion. I quickly turned off the music within an hour. Don't get me wrong, I think the soundtrack is fantastic but several times the change in track playing would be suddenly upbeat and lively when the text describing the atmosphere suggests otherwise. Having sampled the music outside of the game, they are excellent tracks: "Astrum Cloud" had hints of FTL while "It's Out There" reminded me of the latest Deus Ex and Tron. "Somewhere Far" being my favorite of the list provided a subtle mysterious yet seductive vibe.
The mechanism for delivery is excellent. I enjoyed the graphics and the clean nature of the interface. Keeping things simple yet elegant. However, the clarity of the text quickly became apparent--the font had to go.  At its intended resolution was fine but
at my native resolution of 2560x1440 was somewhat difficult to read with soft edges, some pixel type-face don't scale well. Thankfully a wonderful thread in Discussions shows how to replace the font, with a pretty good alternative selection too!
Fantastic story-writing. At first, all I could think of was, "Oh great, prepare for wall of text" but it quickly evolved from plain mindless tales of planet hopping to, "Ooooh fu- damn you have my attention I wonder how this will play out". The story itself isn't long, it took me approximately four hours to get my first ending and of course it's based on the route(s) you take and how quickly you can read. There seems to be four endings according to the Steam Achievements. I've hit two so far but know that I could have gotten another earlier on if I chose different actions. Did I mention there are a slew of crew members each with different traits? These traits may alter how each event plays out on away missions. Time to start with different crew members!
However, the experience did not go without a few minor hiccups. In one instance selecting an dialogue option broke the game, no further dialogue nor could I progress further; needless to say I reloaded and chose another option. One time, I had a dead crew member still listed after an away mission.. tried using him on my next mission but proved to be dead weight (haha), pun intended, and was removed afterwards. Like I said, minor stuff.
I speak with a heavy heart, wishing The Away Team was a bit longer of an adventure; it felt like it had just started in a way that I became attached to my character. Sort of like watching a story arc from any of the Star Trek series and if it were to quickly conclude as it started. Ultimately, I still thoroughly enjoyed the story and it's delivery, I hope you give it a chance too!
Edit: v1.1 fixes the font so what I said about the font has been dealt with. Also wanted to add on the topic of replayability. The game isn't long as I've said before, I've replayed the game over half a dozen times in rapid succession to test various choices and various crew members; some have more dialogue. I ran into some bugs where one of the ending planets showed up as first or second planet when starting a new game. If you wanted all four endings it will take about 7 hours; shorter if you save scum. I explored all the game has to offer in 9 hours with
, I doubt many reviewers could say the same.

What a phenomenal game, from beginning to end.
First, the [intended] visual style of monochrome black/white with punctuated red icons and points of interest is brilliant.  I can’t believe that some people complained enough to get a standard color version added to the game [later].  It’s a shame that they can’t appreciate the artistic vision that the design team had.
The game relies on sound, as there are mechanics associated with exploring each area and also for stealth combat.  There is no music which makes the sounds of the wind, birds and enemies enjoyably pure.
The item system is simple, but ramps up appropriately until the end.  There was never a point where I felt particularly flooded or starved for ammo.
Combat is of a straight forward, first-person style with weapons and items appropriate for the time period.  Stealth is a reliably useful ability that punishes people who run headlong into battle.
Finally the story… despairing, brutally violent, suspenseful.
I strongly recommend this game.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

Great game, terrible port.
I love Galaga, but this port needed more work.
- Controllers\Joysticks not officially supported, and only kinda work
I tried using an Xbox 360 controller and it did work.  However there's no joystick deadzone, so if your joystick isn't PERFECTLY centered at rest then you'll be unable to control your ship properly.
Come on, who forgets to put decent joystick support in an arcade game?
- Can't rebind keyboard keys
- Poor fullscreen support
Full screen isn't an option in the display settings, but you can make the game fullscreen by pressing ALT+Enter.  If you do that however, you won't be able to quit the game without pressing ALT+F4 to close it or by taking it out of fullscreen with ALT+Enter to bring back the X in the upper right corner.
- Doesn't work well in Steam Big Picture mode
This is related to the above point and again, this is something that does work with fiddling.  It just doesn't work like it should.
If you put the game in fullscreen mode with ALT+Enter, then close the game it will open in fullscreen next time you open it.  If you do that before starting Big Picture mode then the game will start in full screen on your TV.  However since there's no quit button inside the game you'll have to use Big Picture's 'Close Game' option to make the game close.
I'm using a TV set up as a second monitor.  If you're using a Steam Link or Steam Box I don't know if this will work or not.

One of the most affecting games I have played in recent memory and one that often lingers and haunts me after a play session. There are slight echoes of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. (mood and pacing) alongside a subject matter that was reminiscent of the film The VVitch (yes, I know the game predated that film's release) with combat inspired by Skyrim and Far Cry.
I started the game about 8 months ago and then was pulled away from it after only playing the first few hours due to a busy life schedule. Since then I have started and played other games but Betrayer stood out in my mind and left a lasting mark. I kept thinking about my brief initial experience and finally decided to revisit the game in recent weeks. I am glad I did and played it through to the end.
Despite some moderate repetition and a playtime that lasted a little longer than the core concept could sustain comfortably I had a very positive experience with the title. I loved the colonial setting which is noticeably underexplored in gaming and the flintlock firearms and bows made for very tense and deliberate combat--just like in Far Cry 2 the experience is best when you crank the enemy difficulty up!
Overall the strongest element is the unsettling and foreboding mood laced with just enough unexpected disruptions and peripeteia to keep the tension high and the player questioning. This game is worth playing for the setting and the mood and will leave a lasting impression in an age of well-crafted but forgettable alternatives.

The game is well supported and while the cost to buy packs of cards is rather steep the game is very well tuned.
Primary concern stems from the fact that the rares are restricted to "2-of's" and the Mythic Rares are "1-of's" which makes building a powerful deck with lots of rares a rather awkward experience since your draws are so inconsistent.
Additionally, the latest expansion brought even more colour fixing to the game at the same time as it brought the mechanic Converge. The inclusion of Converge and the additional fixing now allows for more decks to play whatever they want. While this innitially is not of great concern, it should be noted that Magic 2015 had similar issues as 5 colour "good stuff" decks became more and more prevalent.
However, the overall experience has become more fine tuned and the inclusion of "free tapping" and other features in recent patches shows that the developers really care about the future of this game.
Moving forward, it is this reviewers hope that there is an expansion on the ranking system, the option to have a 15 card Sideboard, and that we get back the camera tools that we had in previous games.

Okay...so I played for about 3 hours, and might play a few more to be sure, but I do have something to say about this game and the only word that I can come up with is "unsure"
Let me start saying that the game is very good: the graphics are very nice and I like the style used for the heroes and their design is actually well done - it's not uncommon to see certain heroes in some mobas be hit or miss. The controls works fine and there's enough depth in each hero with the battlerites - essentially talent - and the lootboxes are actually very rewarding, as they constantly give cosmetics and NOTHING is pay to win.
I repeat, NOTHING is pay to win: lootboxes is just cosmetics like Overwatch, except that the doubles give more coins.
With that said, Battlerite is essentially a MOBA without the usual MOBA staples: there's no laning and there's no grinding, there's no creeps and there's no core to defeat. The only objective is to kill your enemies and after winning 3 matches, you win the game
So in a sense this game is legitimately a MOBA, since it's quite literally a Multiplayer Online Battle Arena, as in it's literally an arena based game.
You got 3 roles: melee, ranged and support, which is pretty straightforward, with some heroes being more tanky than others and more healing based than others. The fights are usually 2v2 or 3v3 so composition is key to win - and a good amount of luck too. Unlike usual MOBAS however you don't click to move but instead use a WASD controls to move around and the mouse to point at the enemies, like a top down shooter.
Overall, it works: I had fun using the free heroes and I even got one with the coins, since the game is VERY generous with them, and if you like the game there's even a pack to buy all the current heroes!
With that said...why did I put the word "unsure"? I honestly don't know and I can't point what's the problem! Is it the 2v2 or 3v3 action? is the fact that there's just not much else? I really can't understand why but, this game just doesn't click with me and the more I play, the more I can't understand "why" and the only reason I will keep on playing, is to make sure my point is the same.
Honestly, I think the issue is that fighting in a 2v2 and 3v3 isn't...as complex as a real moba with 5v5 and I think that's what makes the game - FOR ME - very redundant. As soon as you master your hero you're basically done and since the teams are small, you can technically kill the other team if you're skilled enough. On top of that I don't see particularly advanced tactics rather than "kill the support/squishy" and then the other
So my point is simply one: it's not very complex than a real moba and besides these arena fights that won't last more than 5 minutes, there isn't much else to do really and you might get tired really quickly.
With that said, I still recommend it because...heck why not? It's good, I liked it, but it clearly isn't for me but I'm 1000% sure others will LOVE this game and its pvp centric gameplay. Me, I like a bit more of teamplay with tanks, healers, dps and all that stuff so while I might jump into the game from time to time, I won't really make it my first priority.
Afterall, I still think Heroes of the storm did a better job at "trimming the fat" from the usual moba staples DESPITE having the usual moba staples, but I digress.

Hatred is a video game that is centred around being violent and offensive, which is why I don't understand why people expected an amazing story. I'm going to review this game in term of its GAMEPLAY, and not its story, and I'm going to keep this review short and sweet.
Hatred is not unique, but it's still a damn good game. When you look past the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ filters and edgy one-liners, you are left with a pretty solid isometric shooter. Hatred marketed itself wrong, it was supposedly a pretty free game in which you could kill people in fun ways, but it ended up being a linear slaughterfest. Is this a bad thing?
To answer this, I'd actually point you towards Postal 2. The maps aren't exactly huge, nor are they here, and they both have linear storylines with little customability. However, there are secondary tasks you can perform. Postal 2 does this right, making them enjoyable and funny as hell, but Hatred dishes out the same thing over and over.
This game is underrated, but it's still kind of a one trick pony, I'd be suprised if you get over 50 hours of this game, and if you do, please consult a psychologist.

I....am a sucker for spaceships. Large lumbering beasts floating weightlessly in space, sides bristling with state-of-the-art weaponry and defense systems. Whew. So naturally I was drawn to this game. Drawn to its galaxy spanning matches. Drawn to its badass space battles where titanic flagships lead countless lesser vessels in all-out battles. Drawn to its mid-complexity empire building mechanics where it's not too complex that no one can jump right in and not too simple where anyone will get bored of it. There's something utterly satisfactory about amassing a fleet and jumping straight into the enemy's main fleet and engaging them in a tense battle as they desperately try to stave off your advance and trickle more units into the fray, with you watching with glee as your fleet sends them packing and only one planet stands between you and their homeworld. But one other thing is the mods.
Holy shiz, the mods. I haven't tried anything much except one in particular. Sins of The Prophets. That one adds in UNSC and Covenant ships from the Halo franchise. Mix that with the amazing fleet battles and you're on your way to becoming the next Lord Hood.
So? If you like strategy games, and get hot over starships and phase jumps, then maybe this one is for you. Just be prepared for long battles. Sometimes these can drag on for hours as you bide your time and hassle enemy supply lines. But it'll be all worth it in the end.

For single-player only guys, this isn't an issue as you can use the content at your whim, but it's been the multiplayer that kept this game going for me

You can beat them in "lesser" cars, but only if you absolutely nail every single braking point and apex of every single metre of track. Cars which are already powerful get a great number of upgrade slots, while poor cars only have space for a handful, which don't even make a difference.
